docs.title: Pia: Proved In Advance
docs.text:
Pia is a programming language whose compiler proves your code correct before it runs.

Every integer overflow, every array index and every contract in a Pia program is a proof obligation. The compiler discharges them at compile time, with interval analysis and the Z3 SMT solver. When a proof fails, you get a compile error with a counterexample. When every proof succeeds, the checks are gone from the machine code, because they can never fail.

The quickest way to see it is the REPL, where every cell is proved before it runs, and the MCP server, which gives the same session to an agent such as Claude.

docs.title: Prove as you type: the REPL
docs.text:
pia repl is a verified REPL. Each definition joins a persistent environment only when everything in the environment still proves, and each expression is proved, then compiled and run. Here is a short session, one cell per line:

let bump (a : u8) : u8 = a + 1
let bump (a : u8) : u8 requires a < 255 = a + 1
bump 41
bump 255
let twice (a : u8) : u8 requires a < 100 = bump (bump a)
:redef let bump (a : u8) : u8 requires a < 10 = a + 1
twice 41

$ pia repl < home.pia
[1]:1:28: failed: '+' does not overflow u8
  counterexample: a = 255, result = 256
[1]: error: 1 obligation failed; nothing was committed
bump : (a : u8) -> u8  (* 1 proved *)
- : u8 = 42
[4]:1:1: failed: the precondition of 'bump' holds
[4]: error: 1 obligation failed; nothing was committed
twice : (a : u8) -> u8  (* 2 proved *)
[5]:1:50: failed: the precondition of 'bump' holds
  counterexample: a = 64
[5]:1:44: failed: the precondition of 'bump' holds
  counterexample: a = 9
[6]: error: 2 obligations failed; the redefinition is not committed
- : u8 = 43

The first bump can overflow, so it is refused with the input that breaks it, and nothing is committed. The second adds a precondition and proves. bump 255 breaks that precondition, so it is refused at compile time and never runs. twice is proved against bump, so the :redef that would tighten bump to a < 10 is refused, with errors pointing at the calls in twice that it would break. The environment is always a program that proves.

The REPL page has the rest: state with invariants and verified migration, :load for files, and live redefinition of code that background tasks are running.

docs.title: A REPL for agents: the MCP server
docs.text:
pia mcp serves a REPL session over the Model Context Protocol, so an agent can write Pia one proved cell at a time. It has two tools, execute and poll, and it teaches the language as it goes:

  • A primer when the agent connects, under 2 KB: the binding form, bounded integers, where contracts go, no shadowing, and a list of guide topics.
  • :help <topic> returns one section of the guide, such as syntax, facts, contracts, loops or pitfalls, cut from the same agent skills the documentation tests prove.
  • A hint on every failed cell, saying which kind of fix it needs and where to read about it.
  • What each proof cost: the time for the cell, how many goals it raised and how each was proved, and the slowest solver goals with their Z3 resource counts.

Here is what Claude sees when it sends the first bump above, verbatim:

>>> execute {"code": "let bump (a : u8) : u8 = a + 1"}
<<< (isError) [1]:1:28: failed: '+' does not overflow u8
  counterexample: a = 255, result = 256
[1]: error: 1 obligation failed; nothing was committed
hint: arithmetic is checked at the operands' width: bound the inputs with a range type (int{0..99}) or a requires, or widen with a typed let. (:help facts)
took 831 ms: verifying 205 ms (preparing 3.4 ms, solving 202 ms), parsing and compiling 626 ms
goals: 1 from this cell (0 by intervals, 1 by the solver) and 0 re-proved from the environment: 0 proved, 1 failed
slowest solver goals in this cell:
  202 ms  [1]:1:28 bump: '+' does not overflow u8 (failed, cost 357)

To use it from Claude Code, after building Pia:

claude mcp add pia -- "$PWD/bazel-bin/tools/pia/pia" mcp

Agent skills teach an agent the working loop, and Debugging C++ with the REPL follows Claude through a whole session, from a literal port of a C++ parser to a verdict and a fix.

docs.title: A first proof
docs.text:
let average (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  ensures 2 * result <= a + b && a + b <= 2 * result + 1
= (a + b) / 2

This is the classic way to average two bytes, and it is wrong for large inputs, because a + b overflows a byte. Pia refuses it, and says why:

$ piac --verify average.pia
average.pia:3:6: failed: '+' does not overflow u8
  counterexample: a = 255, b = 255, result = 510
average.pia:3:11: proved: the divisor is not zero [intervals]
average.pia:3:11: proved: '/' does not overflow u8 [intervals]
average.pia:2:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
3 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

Add in a wider type, and every goal is proved, including the postcondition:

let average (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  ensures 2 * result <= a + b && a + b <= 2 * result + 1
= let total : u16 = a + b in total / 2

$ piac --verify average_fixed.pia
average_fixed.pia:3:23: proved: '+' does not overflow u16 [intervals]
average_fixed.pia:3:36: proved: the divisor is not zero [intervals]
average_fixed.pia:3:36: proved: '/' does not overflow u16 [intervals]
average_fixed.pia:3:3: proved: the value fits in u8 [smt]
average_fixed.pia:2:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
5 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

docs.title: What is in Pia
docs.text:
• A verified REPL and an MCP server. pia repl proves every cell before it runs and checks every redefinition against the code that uses it; pia mcp gives that session to an agent, with a guide to the language, hints and proof costs.
  • Proved, not checked. Overflow, bounds, division by zero, preconditions, postconditions, assertions and quantified properties are all proved at compile time. The strongest guarantee is the default, and weaker behaviour, such as wrapping arithmetic, is explicit.
  • An ML-style language. One let for every definition, including types, which are values. Records as values, range types such as int{0..255}, and parameters that state their ownership and access.
  • Metaprogramming from day one. Operators are metaprograms in the prelude, and derives such as @derive(eq) generate code that is then proved like code you wrote.
  • Built on MLIR. piac proves goals in its own MLIR dialects, then compiles through LLVM to arm64 for Apple Silicon, with NEON vectorisation.
  • Proofs in your editor. A language server shows failed goals and their counterexamples as you work, in VS Code or any LSP editor.

docs.text:

  • Demo: edge detection: a real program built with Pia, and a bug the compiler catches
  • Demo: stream delineation: a literate Pia program that finds the streams and watersheds in a terrain, with every step proved
  • A tour of Pia: the language as it is today, every example tested

docs.title: Shared libraries and published proof certificates
docs.text:
Status: certificates accepted, 2026-11-21; object layout proposed. Decision records: ADR 0024 (certificates, accepted) and ADR 0030 (object layout). Builds on ADR 0010 (modules, interfaces and certificates) and on the trusted-contract rules proposed in docs/stdlib.md.

A Pia shared library carries, inside the binary, the interfaces it exports, their contracts and a proof certificate. Before a Pia program binds to that library, something checks that the library still provides exactly the interfaces the program was proved against. This page says what the certificate contains, what is hashed and what is re-checked, how a library can evolve without breaking its importers, how the check works on macOS/arm64 first, and what the certificate does and does not let you trust.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
ADR 0010 makes verification assume-guarantee: module B is proved while assuming the contracts of the interfaces it imports from A, and A is proved to guarantee them. The two halves only compose if the A that runs is an A that was proved against the same interface B assumed.

With static linking, the link checker sees both halves at once and refuses a mismatch. A shared library breaks that: libA.dylib can be rebuilt, upgraded or swapped after B was linked. If the new A weakened a postcondition, B is still running on a proof that no longer holds, and nothing tells anyone. Every C and C++ ABI has this problem with types (the symbol still resolves, the struct layout changed). Pia has it with contracts too, which is worse, because a contract change is invisible in the machine code.

The goal: a proof made against an interface is never used with a library that does not provide that interface, and the check costs about as much as symbol binding.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
System What travels with the binary What the consumer checks What Pia takes Proof-carrying code (Necula and Lee, 1996-97) Native code plus a proof, in LF, that it meets a safety policy Regenerates the verification condition from the code and checks the proof with a small LF checker. No trust in the producer The ideal end state: re-checkable evidence. Too costly for a loader, and needs a proof format Z3 does not stably produce Foundational PCC (Appel, 2001) Proof down to machine semantics Same, with a smaller trusted base Shows that "how much must the consumer trust" is a dial, not a yes/no Typed assembly language (Morrisett et al., 1998) Type annotations on assembly Linear-time type checking of the annotations Certificates that are cheap to check even if expensive to find. Pia's hash check is the degenerate case JVM bytecode verifier and StackMapTable Type state at branch targets Linear-time verification at class load Ship the hard part (the invariants), check the easy part at load WebAssembly Module with typed imports and exports Validation is a linear type check; instantiation checks each import against the provider's export type The import-matches-export check at bind time, on interface identity instead of structural types OCaml .cmi CRCs and Dynlink Each compilation unit records a digest of every interface it was compiled against The linker and Dynlink refuse "inconsistent assumptions over interface" Closest match. Pia does the same with contract-aware hashes, and also at dyld load Rust crate metadata (SVH) A hash of the crate's public surface in rlib metadata rustc refuses a dependency whose hash changed Hash the exported surface, not the whole crate, so private changes do not force rebuilds Swift library evolution, .swiftinterface, ABI checker A textual interface plus a baseline of the published ABI The ABI checker diffs the new interface against the baseline at library build time Compatible evolution through a checked-in baseline, proved instead of diffed ELF symbol versioning (VERDEF/VERNEED) Version names on exported symbols, required versions in importers ld.so refuses a missing version before any code runs Make the system loader enforce the check by turning interface hashes into symbols it must bind Mach-O code signing Hashes of every page, in LC_CODE_SIGNATURE, signed The kernel checks pages as they are paged in; library validation checks the signer Integrity of the certificate comes free if it lives in a signed segment glibc LD_AUDIT (la_objopen), dyld _dyld_register_func_for_add_image Nothing Callbacks when an image loads Hooks for richer policy checks. dyld has no pre-bind hook, so Pia cannot depend on one

Two lessons decide the design:

  1. Every system that works at load time checks identity, not proofs. OCaml, Rust, Wasm and ELF versioning all compare names or digests. Re-checking proofs is done once, offline, if at all. Pia does the same: the loader compares hashes, and re-verification is an audit tool.
  2. The cheapest reliable enforcement is the one the system loader already does. dyld refuses to start a program with a missing non-weak symbol. If a mismatched interface means a missing symbol, the check needs no hook, no runtime, and no cooperation from the program.

docs.title: Design overview
docs.text:
The check runs in three layers. Each catches everything the layer below it catches, and more.

Layer When Who What it checks Cost 1. Witness symbols Launch, dlopen dyld (or ld.so) Each imported interface's hash, and each imported type's shape or layout hash, is provided by the library actually loaded One symbol bind per imported interface and type 2. Certificate check Static link, launch, Pia.Dl.open piac link, the Pia runtime Layer 1, plus folded constants, ABI version, trusted-base policy, compiler identity Reads a small section per image 3. Audit Any time, offline pia-cert audit Layers 1 and 2, plus recomputes every hash from the embedded interfaces, re-proves interface refinements and optionally replays the proofs Seconds to minutes. Never on the load path

Layer 1 alone already gives the core guarantee for programs launched normally. Layers 2 and 3 add policy and assurance.

docs.title: The interface hash
docs.text:
Each exported interface gets an interface hash: SHA-256 over a canonical serialisation of the interface. "Canonical" means two interfaces that mean the same thing hash the same, whatever their source formatting, and two that differ in anything an importer could rely on hash differently.

The serialisation is built from the type-checked interface, after metaprogram expansion and monomorphisation, never from source text. It contains, in this order:

  1. Domain prefix: the string pia-iface, the Pia ABI version (below) and the target triple (arm64-apple-macos). A change to the calling convention changes every hash.
  2. Interface identity: the fully qualified module and interface name.
  3. Every exported symbol, sorted by name. For each:
  4. its kind: function, type, fixed value, state symbol;
  5. its type, with range types (int{0..255}) and parameter modifiers (ownership, access, modifiability). Memory layout is not part of the interface hash: it has its own shape and layout hashes, so a layout change forces a relink but never a re-proof (see Object layout);
  6. its contract: requires, ensures, refinements and state invariants, as pia_contract terms. Bound variables are numbered (de Bruijn style), names are module-qualified as in ADR 0022, and terms are simplified only by a fixed, versioned set of rewrites so the hash does not depend on optimiser changes;
  7. trust marks that are part of the interface: an @assume that design.md says "is a visible note in the interface", and whether the symbol is an extern with a trusted contract.
  8. Concept instances and adapters the interface exports, by concept and type.

What is not in the interface hash: function bodies, private symbols, proof details, which solver proved what, source locations and comments. A module can be rewritten, re-optimised or re-proved without changing its interface hash, so its importers neither rebuild nor relink.

docs.title: The inline surface hash
docs.text:
An interface may export fixed values and let inline or const symbols whose values importers fold into their own code (ADR 0010). Importers prove against the symbol's type and refinement, which is in the interface hash, but once they fold the value, they also depend on the value itself.

These values get a second hash per interface, the inline surface hash, over the canonical IR of every foldable value and inline body. It is separate so that a library can change an inline body and break only the importers that actually folded something, which the importer's certificate records.

docs.title: Proof and build identity
docs.text: Not hashed into anything an importer depends on, but recorded in the certificate for policy and audit: the compiler version and a hash of the piac binary, the Z3 version and options, and the hash of the module's optional proof bundle (below).

docs.title: The certificate format
docs.text:
Each Pia image (an executable, a .dylib, a .o) holds one image certificate. It is a small binary blob, little-endian, versioned, with no pointers, so it needs no relocations and can live in a read-only, signed section.

header       magic "PIAC", format version, Pia ABI version, target triple
image        flags (has_trusted, allowed_unproved), compiler identity, proof bundle hash
modules[]    one per Pia module linked into the image:
  name         fully qualified module name
  provides[]   interface name, interface hash, inline surface hash,
               and the hashes of every older interface version it also provides (see ABI evolution)
  requires[]   interface name, interface hash it was proved against,
               inline surface hash if any value was folded, else zero
  layouts[]    shape and layout hash of every type the module defines and exports
               (descriptors themselves are in __pia_layout)
  uses[]       type name, and the shape or layout hash this module's code was
               compiled against, with a flag if a proof depended on it
  trusted[]    this module's own trusted items: kind (extern contract, @assume,
               allowed-unproved goal, unsafe call site, lowering), symbol,
               source location, hash of the trusted contract, goal or MLIR
  lean[]       lemmas proved in Lean: lemma, statement hash, theorem,
               Lean toolchain, axioms of the proof (ADR 0061)
strings      string table for the names above

What is built so far is a text body (src/cert/Certificate.h): format 1 has the module and its provides and requires, format 2 its trusted lowerings, and format 3 (ADR 0073) the Pia ABI version and target triple (abi 1 arm64-apple-macos), piac's version (prover piac 0.0.0+512.9f3c2e1a7b04, dev in a build that is not stamped) and the solver's (solver z3 5.4.1). piac --version prints the same three. The link check refuses objects for different ABI versions or targets, and objects in formats 1 and 2, which record none. Format 3 also lists the proof engines that discharged a goal (engines intervals,z3). The check also refuses objects proved by a piac or solver version that an advisory says may prove false goals, unless they are accepted by name.

Decisions behind the format:

  • One certificate per image, with one entry per module. An image can contain several Pia modules. The static link step merges the modules' object-file certificates into one image certificate and checks the requires against the provides it can already see.
  • Trusted items are listed per module, not transitively. A module's certificate records only its own trusted items. The whole trusted base of a program is computed by walking the certificates of every image it loads: piac link --trust-report at link time, and pia-cert trust-report on a built program. If a dependency replaces a proved body with an @assume behind an unchanged interface, the importer's proof is still valid by assume-guarantee, so its certificate should not go stale, but the report must still show the new trusted item. This answers the open question in docs/stdlib.md: yes, certificates list trusted contracts, and the linker and the trust report read them.
  • Lemmas proved in Lean are a third status (ADR 0061): neither proved by Z3 nor trusted. Each is listed with the SHA-256 of its Lean statement and the definitions it uses, the theorem that proves it, the Lean toolchain and the axioms of its proof. Importing a module with Lean facts needs no trusting. A Lean proof by native_decide trusts Lean's compiler, so it is also a trusted item, native_decide, allowed only in a @trusted module.
  • Five kinds of trusted item. An extern declaration's contract and an @assume, both allowed only in @trusted modules; an obligation accepted with --allow-unproved; each unsafe f x call site, the required spelling for a call to a foreign function declared without a contract; and a lowering, a function whose @lower MLIR replaced its proved body, recorded with the function, the ops its MLIR uses and the SHA-256 of the spliced text (ADR 0065; a schedule joins it with @schedule). The certificate also flags a module as @trusted.
  • --allow-unproved goals are trusted items. An obligation accepted with --allow-unproved (verifier.md) is recorded the same way as an @assume, so "this library has unproved goals" is visible to anyone who loads it.
  • Fixed-size hashes in the certificate, short ones in symbols. The certificate holds full 32-byte SHA-256 hashes. Witness symbols use the first 128 bits, base32-encoded, which keeps symbol names short while leaving accidental collisions out of reach.

docs.title: Where it lives on macOS/arm64
docs.text:
Mach-O location Contents Loaded Signed __TEXT,__pia_cert The image certificate Yes, read-only Yes, by the code signature's page hashes __TEXT,__pia_layout Layout descriptors of every exported type (the .pial contents) Yes, read-only Yes __TEXT,__pia_iface The canonical serialised interfaces the image provides (the .piai contents) Yes, read-only Yes __PIA_PROOF,__bundle (optional) Proof bundle: the module's obligations as pia_contract MLIR bytecode, plus solver settings No (stripped by default, or a sidecar .piap file) If present

Putting the certificate in __TEXT means every arm64 macOS image already protects it: all code on Apple Silicon must be signed (ad-hoc at least), and the kernel checks each page against the code directory as it pages it in. Tampering with the certificate of a signed library makes the page fail validation. No Pia-specific signature is needed for integrity.

Embedding the interfaces in __pia_iface means piac can import directly from a .dylib, with no separate .piai file to ship or keep in sync. The interface hash is recomputed from these bytes by the audit tool, so the embedded interface and the certificate cannot silently disagree.

docs.title: Layer 1: witness symbols
docs.text:
For every interface I a library provides, it exports one data symbol, a witness:

_pia$w$<module>$<interface>$<hash128>          interface hash
_pia$i$<module>$<interface>$<hash128>          inline surface hash (only if the interface has one)

Every image that imports I emits a non-weak reference to the witness for the hash it was proved against, and to the inline surface witness if it folded anything. The witnesses are one byte each and nothing reads them. They exist only so that the system loader must bind them.

  • On macOS, binding is two-level: the reference names both the symbol and the library's install name. With chained fixups (macOS 12 and later), all non-lazy binds are resolved at launch, before any initializer runs. A library that does not provide the hash makes dyld stop the program with Symbol not found: _pia$w$.... No Pia code, in the program or the library, has run.
  • On dlopen, the same bind happens at open time, and dlopen fails.
  • A library that provides several versions of an interface (see below) exports one witness per version, so old importers keep binding.
  • Exported function symbols keep plain, stable names (module-qualified, without the hash). Debuggers, profilers, crash reports and C callers see readable names, and the hash lives only in the witnesses.

The cost of Layer 1 is one extra bind per imported interface, which is a rounding error next to the binds for the functions themselves. The error message is cryptic, so the Pia runtime and pia-cert turn _pia$w$... into a readable explanation: which interface, which hash the program wanted, which hashes the library provides.

The same scheme ports to ELF with one symbol per witness, or with the hash as a GNU symbol version (PIA_<hash128>) on the interface's symbols, so ld.so reports version 'PIA_...' not found.

docs.title: Layer 2: the certificate check
docs.text:
Witnesses prove that the right interfaces are present. The certificate check adds what a symbol bind cannot express:

  • the image's Pia ABI version and target match the program's;
  • the trust policy holds: for example "no library with allowed-unproved goals", or "the only trusted items allowed are extern contracts in @trusted modules of Pia.*";
  • the compiler identity is in an allowed set, when a deployment asks for that;
  • every requires entry in every loaded image is met by a provides entry in the image the loader actually bound to (a belt-and-braces repeat of Layer 1 that also produces good errors).

It runs at three points:

  1. Static link (piac link, and the pia_library/pia_binary Bazel rules from M8). Reads the certificates of the objects being linked and of every .dylib on the link line, and refuses mismatches. This is the check ADR 0010 already requires, extended to shared libraries.
  2. Launch. The Pia runtime library runs a check before main. It walks the loaded images with _dyld_image_count/_dyld_get_image_header, reads each __pia_cert with getsectiondata, and checks every Pia image. It registers _dyld_register_func_for_add_image so later loads are checked as well.
  3. Pia.Dl.open, the Pia library's dlopen wrapper, used for plugins. It opens with RTLD_NOW | RTLD_LOCAL, checks the new image's certificate against the interfaces the caller names, and only then hands back symbols. On a failed check it closes the image and returns an error, with the reason.

Pia images have no static initializers. piac never emits __mod_init_func entries for Pia code: module-level values are constants resolved at compile time, and anything else must be explicit in main. This is what makes checking after dlopen sound: opening a Pia library runs none of its code, so the check happens before anything the certificate guards can execute. The certificate check rejects a Pia image that contains initializers. Non-Pia libraries (libSystem, C dependencies) can still have initializers. They are outside the proof anyway, and enter the trusted base through extern contracts.

Module initialisation still exists, but not through dyld. @init functions and registries are run by the Pia runtime after this check, in a proved order, and dynamic loading with Pia.Dl.open is provided by the opt-in Pia.Dyn environment, which calls each image's generated registration function (init.md, ADR 0033).

dyld has no hook that runs before binding, and with the hardened runtime DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES is disabled, so Pia does not rely on either. Layer 1 covers the window before the runtime's check runs.

docs.title: Layer 3: audit and re-checking
docs.text:
The loader never runs a solver. Proof search can take minutes (verifier.md), and a loader that runs Z3 would make startup time depend on solver heuristics. But hashes alone only say "some compiler said so". pia-cert audit closes as much of that gap as is practical, offline:

  1. Recompute every interface hash and inline surface hash from __pia_iface and compare with __pia_cert. Catches a buggy or tampered certificate in an unsigned image.
  2. Re-prove refinements. For every older interface version a library claims to provide, check the refinement obligations (below) with Z3 from the embedded interfaces alone. This needs no source.
  3. Replay proofs when a proof bundle is present: reload the module's obligations from the bundle and run the verifier on them, then check that the bundle's hash matches the certificate. This re-checks that the obligations are valid. It does not check that the obligations were generated faithfully from the machine code. That would need translation validation or a proof-producing code generator, which is out of scope.
  4. Report the full trusted base, transitively.

A future step toward real proof-carrying code is to store checkable proof objects instead of obligations, for example Alethe proofs from cvc5 checked by an independent checker such as Carcara, so a consumer can re-check without trusting the solver. Z3's proof output is not stable enough to ship today. The format reserves a section kind for proof objects so this can be added without a format change.

docs.title: ABI evolution
docs.text:
Exact hash matching would mean every change to a library breaks every importer. Pia allows compatible changes, proved compatible at library build time.

A library keeps ABI baselines: the canonical interfaces of every version it has published, checked into the repository (for example abi/Pixels.PixelOps.v1.piai). The library declares which baselines it still provides. When it builds, piac proves the current interface refines each declared baseline:

Element Compatible change (refinement) Symbol set New symbols may be added. No baseline symbol may be removed Types Identical for every baseline symbol. Layout is versioned separately: an auto layout change relinks importers, and a frozen layout cannot change (see Object layout) requires May get weaker: prove requires_old ⇒ requires_new ensures May get stronger: prove requires_old ∧ ensures_new ⇒ ensures_old Refinement on a result or fixed value May get stronger, same rule as ensures State symbol invariants May get stronger: prove invariant_new ⇒ invariant_old Foldable values and inline bodies Must be identical. A changed value changes the inline surface hash, which breaks importers that folded it (by design, per ADR 0010)

These are behavioural subtyping rules: anything a caller proved against the old interface still holds against the new one. Each one is an ordinary verifier obligation, so they get counterexamples like any other goal. When every refinement is proved, the certificate's provides entry lists the baselines' hashes, and the library exports a witness for each. Old importers bind to their witness and keep working without recompiling. New importers prove against the current interface.

To make a breaking change, the library drops the baseline from its declared set and bumps its install name's major version (libpixels.2.dylib), the usual dylib practice. Dropping a baseline is visible in review because the baseline file is deleted.

The Pia ABI version is a single integer in the compiler covering the calling convention, the certificate format and the canonical hash serialisation. The layout algorithm has its own version inside each layout descriptor, so improving layouts changes layout hashes (relink) without changing interface hashes (no re-proof). Bumping the ABI version changes every hash, so it is bumped rarely and on purpose, and the release notes say so.

docs.title: Object layout
docs.text:
The compiler is free to choose how every Pia type is laid out in memory: field order, packing, alignment, where sum-type tags go, and tag bits stashed in the low bits of pointers. The module that defines a type picks its layout and publishes it. Every importer that compiled code against that layout records a layout hash, and a library whose layout no longer matches cannot be loaded: dyld fails, and the importer must be relinked. Static links and rebuilds therefore always agree on how data is laid out and packed.

This is a deliberate choice against the alternatives:

Approach Example Why not for Pia Fixed, C-like layout rules C, C++ (the fragile base class problem) Forbids reordering, packing and niches, which is most of the optimisation Layout resolved at load time Objective-C 2.0 non-fragile ivars (offsets are symbols that dyld binds), Swift resilience (size and offsets read from value witness tables at run time) Offsets become run-time values: no constant folding, worse vectorisation, and proofs about sizes lose their constants Unspecified layout, no dynamic ABI Rust repr(Rust) Gives the optimisation freedom, but no shared libraries across builds Published layout, fail and relink Pia Full optimisation freedom, constant offsets, and a mismatch is caught at load instead of corrupting memory

docs.title: Layout never changes a proof
docs.text:
Proofs are about types and contracts, not offsets. Verification runs on layout-independent IR, and layout is chosen afterwards, in codegen. That gives the property the rest of the design depends on:

  • A layout change changes layout hashes only, never interface hashes, so importers are relinked, not re-verified. "Relink" means re-running layout lowering, codegen and the link from the importer's cached verified IR, against the new layout descriptors. The importer's proof certificate is reused unchanged.
  • In Bazel, verification actions depend only on .piai interfaces, and codegen actions also depend on .pial layout descriptors. A layout change reruns codegen and link actions only.
  • size_of t and align_of t are treated like exported fixed values (ADR 0010). Proofs see them as symbols with refinements (size_of t : int{1 .. 2^32}, align_of t a power of two), and codegen folds them. A proof that needs the concrete number makes the module record a dependency on the layout hash in its requires, just as folding a constant records the inline surface hash. A layout change then makes that module re-verify, and no other.
  • Layout respects the interface, never the reverse. If an interface lets importers borrow a field of an exported type, that field stays byte-addressable, so layout can never change what type-checks.

docs.title: The layout descriptor
docs.text:
Each module emits a descriptor for every type that is visible outside it, in a .pial file and in __TEXT,__pia_layout in the image:

type          fully qualified name, monomorphised (Pixels.pixel, Pia.Mem.pool<Pixels.pixel>)
policy        auto | c | frozen | packed
shape         size, alignment, calling-convention class (integer registers, HFA, memory)
fields[]      name, bit offset, bit width, encoding (plain, biased range, niche-carrying),
              addressable flag
tags          for sum types and dyn: where the tag lives (own field, niche in a field,
              low bits of a pointer field), its bit positions and the variant-to-value map
pointer_tags  for each pointer field: which low bits carry tags, and the alignment proof
              they rely on
components    layout hashes of every field and type argument
algorithm     layout algorithm version, and the profile hash if layout used a profile

Two hashes are computed from it, both SHA-256 over a canonical encoding:

  • Shape hash: size, alignment and calling-convention class. This is all an importer needs to pass a value of an abstract type (one whose definition the interface hides) or to embed it in its own records.
  • Layout hash: the whole descriptor. Needed by an importer that reads or writes fields, matches on variants, or unpacks tagged pointers. Only possible for types whose definition the interface exposes.

Hashes compose through components. Pia.Mem.pool<Pixels.pixel> has a layout hash that includes Pixels.pixel's, so a pool passed across a library boundary forces both sides to agree on its slot size.

An importer records, per type, the weakest hash it actually used. A library can therefore reorder or repack the fields of an abstract type freely, as long as its size, alignment and class stay the same, and importers that only hold it abstractly keep loading.

docs.title: Layout policies
docs.text:
• @layout(auto) is the default. The compiler orders fields to remove padding, packs range-typed fields into the bits they need (int{0..9} in 4 bits, bool in 1), puts sum-type tags into niches (an option<int{0..254}> uses 255 for None), and stashes tags in pointer low bits where the alignment allows. It may use a profile to place hot fields together, and then the profile's hash is part of the layout. The algorithm is deterministic: the same type, algorithm version and profile always give the same layout, so reproducible builds stay reproducible.
  • @layout(c) follows the platform C ABI exactly, with no tags or packing. It is required for every type that crosses an extern boundary.
  • @layout(packed) asks for minimum size even at the cost of unaligned access.
  • @layout(frozen) pins the current layout with a checked-in baseline (abi/<Module>.<type>.pial), like Swift's @frozen. The compiler must reproduce the baseline exactly, and a library release cannot change it without dropping the baseline and bumping its major version. Use it for types in a library's stable ABI. Everything else stays auto, and changes whenever the compiler finds a better layout.

docs.title: Pointer tagging rules
docs.text:
A tagged pointer keeps extra information in pointer bits that are always zero for valid addresses. Pia allows it under these rules, each checked by the compiler:

  1. Low bits only. A pointer may carry k tag bits only in bits 0 .. k-1, and only if every pointer of that type is proved to be aligned to at least 2^k. The proof comes from the pointer's provenance. Pia.Mem.alloc guarantees alignment of at least max 16 (align_of t) in its ensures (ADR 0026, PR #65), so any pointer from Pia.Mem has at least 4 free low bits. Static data gets the alignment codegen gives it. A pointer from an extern call has only the alignment its contract states.
  2. Never the high bits. On Apple Silicon the top bits belong to pointer authentication (arm64e), memory tagging (MTE) and top-byte-ignore, and which of these apply varies by process and OS release. Pia does not tag there.
  3. More tag bits mean more alignment. A layout that wants k > 4 tag bits raises the pointee's alignment to 2^k. That alignment is part of the pointee's shape, so it changes the shape hash and is visible to every importer.
  4. The tag encoding belongs to the containing type. Which bits are used and what each value means is in the descriptor of the type that holds the pointer, so changing it changes that type's layout hash.
  5. Tags never cross extern. @layout(c) types cannot hold tagged pointers, and passing a pointer to a foreign function strips its tag. A pointer received from C is never assumed to have free bits beyond its stated alignment.
  6. Tagging and untagging are checked operations. They are pia dialect ops whose obligations (alignment, tag in range, address bits untouched) go to the verifier like any other goal, and they are lowered to and/orr/bic or folded into load offsets when the tag is known.

docs.title: Free-list reuse
docs.text:
Free lists are where a layout disagreement does the most damage, so they get explicit rules. Pia.Mem (ADR 0026) keeps its free lists as side metadata keyed by size class, so the allocator itself only ever sees sizes and alignments, never layouts.

  • Both sides of a free use the same size. Allocation sizes come from size_of t, folded at codegen. If libA allocates a t and B frees it, both must agree on size_of t, or the block goes back into the wrong size class and a later allocation overlaps a live object. Both bind the same shape or layout witness for t, so dyld refuses the program before that can happen.
  • Typed pools compose. pool<t> slabs are sized by t's layout, and pool<t>'s own layout hash includes t's. Code that shares a pool across a boundary binds one witness for both.
  • Reuse never exposes old contents or old tags. A reused block comes back as out memory, so it must be fully written before it is read, and nothing of the old object's fields or pointer tags can be observed. Ownership and the borrow rules in ADR 0026 rule out a stale owner, or a stale tagged pointer, that still refers to the old object.
  • Reuse across types is by size class only. A block freed as t may come back as u from the same size class. That is safe because the allocator guarantees size and alignment for u, and u's layout does not depend on t's.
  • Alignment survives reuse. Every block in a size class has the class's alignment, at least 16, so the low-bit tags of any type allocated from it stay valid after reuse.

docs.title: The relink failure path
docs.text:
For each exported type a library makes visible, it exports one witness per hash, next to the interface witnesses:

_pia$s$<module>$<type>$<hash128>               shape hash
_pia$l$<module>$<type>$<hash128>               layout hash (only for types whose definition is exported)

An importer references the witness for each type it depends on, at the weakest level it used.

  • Launch. If the library's layout changed, dyld stops the program with Symbol not found: _pia$l$Pixels$pixel$... before any code runs. No Pia code can intercept that, so pia-cert check <binary> explains it: which type changed, which importer depends on it, what changed (size, field offsets, tag encoding), and that the fix is to relink, with no re-verification needed.
  • dlopen. Pia.Dl.open turns the failure into Err (LayoutChanged { type, wanted, found }) instead of a raw dlerror string.
  • Static link. The link checker compares the layout hashes every object was compiled against with the defining module's descriptors, and reports relink required with the list of objects whose codegen is stale. The Bazel rules rerun exactly those codegen actions.
  • Frozen types keep the same witness across releases. Auto types get a new one whenever their layout changes.

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text:
What a valid certificate tells you depends on what you trust. The design is explicit about each part.

You trust You get Nothing The witness and certificate check still stop accidental mismatches: stale libraries, wrong versions, partial upgrades. This is the main failure the design targets The code signature (Apple's chain, a Team ID) The certificate and interfaces are exactly what that signer shipped. With the hardened runtime's library validation, only libraries signed by the same team (or Apple) can load at all The signer's compiler The library's exported contracts were proved, except for the trusted items it lists The signer's compiler, plus the trusted items in the report The program as a whole meets its top-level contracts, by assume-guarantee over every image Only pia-cert audit and your own Z3 Interface hashes, refinements and (with a bundle) the obligations re-checked independently. The compiler that generated obligations and machine code is still trusted

What the certificate does not protect against: a malicious producer who signs a library whose code does not match its certificate. Hashes cannot catch that, only a re-check of the machine code can. Pia's position is the same as OCaml's and Rust's: certificates make honest-but-buggy builds safe to combine, and code signing decides whose builds you accept. Reproducible builds let anyone rebuild a library from source and compare it with the shipped one, which is the practical way to stop trusting a specific signer.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
• macOS/arm64 first. Everything above. Tested on the iMac and on the macos-15 CI runners.
  • Linux/ELF next. Certificate in a .pia.cert section inside a PT_NOTE segment (or an SHT_NOTE note with owner Pia), witnesses as symbols or GNU symbol versions, the launch check through the runtime with dl_iterate_phdr, and an optional LD_AUDIT module that checks each object in la_objopen before its symbols are bound. ELF images are not signed by default, so Layer 3's recompute step matters more there.
  • Static archives and objects carry per-module certificates. Only images (executables and shared libraries) carry merged image certificates and witnesses.

docs.title: Relation to the minimal core and stdlib
docs.text: The standard library (docs/stdlib.md and ADR 0023) is the first big user. Pia.Core, Pia.Mem and Pia.Io can ship as one shared libpia.dylib, versioned by ABI baselines like any other library. Its extern POSIX contracts and @assumes appear as trusted items under @trusted modules, so pia-cert trust-report of any Pia program lists exactly which libSystem contracts it rests on.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text:
Each step is a GitHub issue, tracked from M8 (#9) and the follow-up milestones.

  1. Canonical interface serialisation and the interface and inline surface hashes (#40).
  2. The certificate format: a small C++ reader and writer, and pia-cert dump (#41). Format 1 is implemented in src/cert, with a text body that holds the module, provides and requires. Format 2 adds trusted lines, so far only for lowerings (trusted lowering matmul <hash> linalg.matmul,memref.expand_shape), and trusted native_decide <lemma> <hash> <axioms> for a Lean proof that trusts Lean's compiler. Format 3 adds the lemmas proved in Lean, proved lean sum_nonneg <hash> Proofs.sum_nonneg leanprover/lean4:v4.36.0 propext (ADR 0061). piac writes the oldest format that holds what an object lists, so most objects stay format 1; pia-cert dump prints every line. The other fields, and the other kinds of trusted item, come later.
  3. Emit __pia_cert and __pia_iface in objects and merge them into image certificates at link (#42).
  4. Witness symbols: export them from libraries and reference them from importers (#43). Implemented for objects: the hash is over the whole .piai text until the inline surface gets its own hash, and the module path is spelled with $, as in pia$w$Image$Pixels$Ops$<hash>.
  5. The link checker for objects and .dylib inputs, including --trust-report (#44). pia-cert check checks objects, and pia_library runs it as a validation action; .dylib inputs and the trust report come later.
  6. Pia images without static initializers, the runtime's launch check, and Pia.Dl.open (#46).
  7. ABI baselines and refinement proofs (#49).
  8. pia-cert audit: recompute, re-prove refinements, replay proof bundles (#51).
  9. The ELF port (#53).
  10. Layout descriptors, shape and layout hashes, __pia_layout (#89).
  11. Layout-independent verification and relink without re-proof (#90).
  12. The @layout(auto) optimiser and the c, packed and frozen policies (#91).
  13. Verified pointer tagging (#92).
  14. Layout witnesses and the relink failure path (#93).
  15. Free-list reuse across a library boundary (#94).

docs.title: Advisories
docs.text: A Pia object is proved before it is compiled, so its certificate stands for those proofs (abi.md). If a piac or a solver had a soundness bug, an object it proved may rest on a goal that is false. An advisory says which piac or solver versions had the bug, and pia-cert check then refuses every object they proved until it is rebuilt with a fixed piac, or accepted by name (ADR 0073).

docs.title: Published advisories
docs.text:
Advisory Severity Affected Fixed in What went wrong PIA-2026-0001 unsound piac before 0.0.0+720 #496 Termination was checked only for direct recursion, so two lemmas that call each other could prove ensures false

Every published piac before 0.0.0+720 predates certificate format 3, and so records no piac version. pia-cert check already refuses those objects for having no Pia ABI version, so PIA-2026-0001 is a record of the bug more than a new refusal.

docs.title: What an advisory says
docs.text:
An advisory is a short file in security/advisories/, reviewed like any other change:

id = "PIA-2026-0001"
summary = "Termination was checked only for direct recursion, so mutually recursive lemmas could prove false goals"
piac = { introduced = "0.0.0+0", fixed = "0.0.0+720" }
engines = ["intervals"]          # optional: only objects proved with one of these
solver = { z3 = { introduced = "4.15.0", fixed = "4.15.2" } }   # optional
severity = "unsound"             # "incomplete" is recorded but never revokes
fixed_by = "https://github.com/deanberris/pia-lang/pull/496"

A certificate matches when its prover falls in the piac range, from introduced up to but not including fixed, or one of its solver lines falls in that solver's range. An advisory that names engines matches only certificates whose engines line includes one of them. piac lists, in a fixed order, intervals (interval analysis), z3, int-blast (ADR 0066), proof-cache (a goal answered by --proof-cache), generic (an instance proved by its generic's proof over sorts, ADR 0043), lean, and theory:<name> for each library theory whose axioms a proof used. A certificate with no engines line, from a piac before this list, could have used any engine, so it matches too. piac versions are compared by their commit count on main (0.1.0+512.9f3c2e1a7b04 is commit 512), so every build on main has its place in a range. An unstamped piac records dev, which no range covers.

Publishing an advisory goes with the fix and a regression test in tests/verify/ that the faulty piac proved and the fixed one refuses.

docs.title: Checking a build
docs.text:
The advisories are compiled into pia-cert, so every pia_library build checks its objects against every advisory older than the tools:

  • pia-cert check a.o b.o refuses each object an advisory matches. The refusal names the module, the version that proved it, the advisory, and the piac to rebuild with.
  • pia-cert check --advisories=<dir> a.o b.o adds the advisories in a newer directory, so an old toolchain can be checked against today's list. A file there replaces a compiled-in advisory with the same id.
  • pia-cert check --accept-advisory=PIA-2026-0001:Image.Pixels ... lets that one module through. The acceptance is printed as a trusted item (trusted advisory PIA-2026-0001 Image.Pixels), so trusting a known-faulty proof is never silent. An acceptance that names an unknown advisory is an error, and one that matches nothing draws a warning.
  • pia-cert check --require-released ... also refuses objects from an unstamped (dev) piac, for a deployment that wants only published compilers.
  • pia-cert advisories lists the advisories the check applies, and --advisories=<dir> adds to the list.

docs.title: piac checks itself
docs.text:
piac knows the same advisories, and --advisories=<dir> adds a newer set to it too. piac --version ends with a revoked by <id>: <summary> line for each advisory that revokes this piac or its Z3, and every run that proves warns about them, since pia-cert will refuse what it proves. A proof cache entry is keyed by Z3's version, so if an advisory revokes Z3, every entry piac could read was made by that Z3: piac then warns, and neither reads nor writes the cache. An advisory against piac alone leaves the cache in use, because a piac bug makes a wrong query, and the cached fact that a query is unsatisfiable is still true.

Proofs are deterministic, so the fix for a refused object is to rebuild it with a fixed piac. In Bazel that happens anyway when piac changes.

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text:
These parts of ADR 0073 come in later steps:

  • piac link --trust-report should list accepted advisories (step 3 prints them from pia-cert check only).
  • The runtime check at launch and in Pia.Dl.open waits for the certificate check in abi.md, Layer 2.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
Pia ships a pack of Agent Skills for coding agents such as Claude Code. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: instructions the agent loads when its description matches the task. These teach an agent to use Pia's tools the way they are meant to be used: prove one piece at a time, read counterexamples for what they say, state assumptions as contracts, and keep proof time down.

They live in skills/ in the repository. Every Pia example and every piac and pia command in them is run by the documentation tests (//tests/docs:skills_test), so they cannot drift from what the tools do.

Skill When an agent uses it pia-language writing or reviewing Pia code: syntax at a glance, where each fact belongs (types before contracts), the usual shapes for loops, errors, generics, lambdas and modules, and the pitfalls pia-porting porting from C, C++, Rust, OCaml, Zig or Go: a feature map from each language to Pia, what is designed but not built yet, and the traps each language sets pia-idioms a lint fired, or code is being reviewed for idiom: the rewrite each lint wants, when to keep a form with @allow, and keeping proofs cheap pia-contracts writing or repairing contracts: which fix each kind of failed goal needs, loop invariants, decreases, spec functions piac-verify proving files: the goal report, counterexamples, --allow-unproved, solver limits piac-build compiling and linking: emit modes, targets, modules and interfaces, calling C, the Bazel rules, --trust-report and proof certificates with pia-cert pia-fast-proofs a proof is slow, or one function is changing in a big file: --verify-only, --proof-cache, --jobs, --verify-stats, slicing pia-mcp a pia mcp server is connected: how execute and poll behave, reading results, the working loop, long-running cells pia-repl no MCP connection: pia repl on a pipe or with JSON lines, :redef, state with invariants and old, tasks, saving a session as a test pia-proof-debugging "is this C, C++ or Rust correct?": port it into cells, classify each counterexample, check assumptions against callers, report a verdict pia-lean proving a lemma in Lean 4 when Z3 cannot: = by lean T, piac --emit=lean, the proof file, pia_lean_proof receipts, stale receipts

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
The repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. Its one plugin, pia, installs the skills, the pia-lsp language server for .pia files, so Claude sees proof failures and lints as diagnostics as it edits, and the pia mcp server, so it can prove and run code cell by cell:

claude plugin marketplace add deanberris/pia-lang
claude plugin install pia@pia-lang

or, inside Claude Code, /plugin marketplace add deanberris/pia-lang and then /plugin install pia@pia-lang. The plugin follows the repository's main branch, so claude plugin marketplace update pia-lang brings the skills up to date with the language. Plugin skills are namespaced, as in /pia:pia-porting, and Claude loads them by itself when a task matches.

The language server and the MCP server are the repository's own tools, so they must be on your PATH. There are no release binaries before 0.1; build them and link them (a link into bazel-bin stays current after each rebuild):

bazel build //tools/pia //tools/pia-lsp //tools/piac
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -sf "$PWD"/bazel-bin/tools/pia/pia "$PWD"/bazel-bin/tools/pia-lsp/pia-lsp \
       "$PWD"/bazel-bin/tools/piac/piac ~/.local/bin/

Without them the skills still load, and /mcp shows the pia server as failed to connect until pia is found. In a checkout of the repository, Claude Code also finds the skills by itself, through .claude/skills.

docs.title: Other agents
docs.text:
Any agent that reads Agent Skills takes the same folders: copy or link skills/pia* into the directory the agent reads skills from (for Claude Code without the plugin, ~/.claude/skills/):

ln -s "$PWD"/skills/pia* ~/.claude/skills/

An agent without skill support can be given a SKILL.md as plain instructions. Any MCP client can run the REPL server as pia mcp over stdio; its initialize instructions teach the basics of the language, and :help <topic> returns a section of these skills. Any LSP client can run pia-lsp --stdio; the VS Code extension does.

docs.title: Keeping them current
docs.text: The skills are tested like the documentation. //tests/docs:skills_test proves every Pia example in them and runs every piac and pia command they show against the current compiler, and tools/skills/check.py, which CI runs on every pull request, fails when a keyword the lexer knows or a flag piac accepts is in no skill, or when a skill is missing from the plugin, the tests or these tables. tools/docs/check.py does the same for these pages: a feature, flag or library module that no public page mentions fails it. A pull request that adds a feature updates the skill that teaches it, and the documentation (CONTRIBUTORS.md).

docs.title: What a session looks like
docs.text: The REPL page shows Claude driving a session over MCP, and Debugging C++ with the REPL follows the proof-debugging loop from a literal port of a parser to a verdict and a fix.

docs.title: Contributing with an agent
docs.text:
An agent working on the compiler itself should start from CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads by itself, and CODEMAP.md, a map of where everything lives and which file to open for each kind of change. python3 tools/codemap/outline.py <file> lists a large file's functions with their line numbers, so an agent can read only the part it needs.

Contributions written with an agent are welcome, and they need no Co-Authored-By trailer or other attribution. The person who opens the pull request owns it, and it must pass the proofs and tests like any other change. CONTRIBUTORS.md has the policy.

docs.title: Pia compiler architecture
docs.text: Status: accepted, 2026-11-20. This breaks the design in design.md into compiler components and MLIR dialects. The dialect layering is recorded in ADR 0018.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  src[".pia source"] --> lex["Lexer"]
  lex --> parse["Parser: CST and AST"]
  parse --> meta["Meta engine: quote, splice, compile-time interpreter"]
  meta -- "generated syntax" --> parse
  meta --> sema["Sema: names, types, modifiers, concepts, deduction"]
  iface["Interface loader: .piai artifacts"] --> sema
  sema --> mono["Monomorphiser"]
  mono --> irgen["IRGen: AST to pia, contract and par dialects"]
  irgen --> ver["Verifier"]
  ver --> opt["Optimiser: fold, erase tags and checks, vectorise"]
  opt --> cg["Codegen: arith, scf, memref, vector, arm_neon, llvm"]
  cg --> obj["arm64 object + proof certificate"]
  sema --> iemit["Interface emitter: .piai"]
  obj --> link["Link checker: certificate hashes"]
Component Responsibility Built on Lexer, parser Tokens, concrete syntax tree, AST with source locations Hand-written C++ (recursive descent with Pratt parsing for operators) Meta engine Quote and splice, compile-time evaluation of let meta, the expansion loop to a fixed point, --meta-cycles A tree-walking interpreter over the AST first; JIT later if needed Sema Name resolution, type checking, parameter modifiers and ownership, concept checks, type argument deduction C++ over the AST Monomorphiser Instantiates generics so every later stage sees concrete types C++ over the AST IRGen Lowers the typed AST to Pia's MLIR dialects MLIR builders Verifier Turns contracts and implicit obligations (bounds, overflow, out fully written, exhaustiveness) into proofs. See below MLIR dataflow framework, smt dialect, Z3 Optimiser Uses proved facts to drop checks, erase dyn tags, fold constants and vectorise MLIR canonicalisation and custom passes Codegen Lowers to standard dialects and then LLVM for arm64 Upstream MLIR conversions Interfaces and certificates Emits .piai interface artifacts, records interface hashes in each object, refuses mismatched links. Shared libraries embed interfaces, certificates and witness symbols checked at load (abi.md) Small C++ library, pia-cert tool, runtime check, Bazel rules Runtime Concurrency (spread loops, collectives, later task graphs and futures) C++ runtime library linked into Pia programs Standard library Prelude (operators, vec, core concepts), Image.Png, Image.Gif Written in Pia once the compiler can build it

docs.title: Dialects
docs.text:
Pia has three of its own dialects and reuses upstream dialects for everything else.

Dialect Holds Lifetime pia Pia's types and values: range-typed integers (!pia.int<lo, hi>), fixed arrays and slices with lengths, structs, dyn with its tag set, functions with parameter modifiers as attributes IRGen to codegen pia_contract requires, ensures, invariant, decreases, assert, assume, old, quantifiers (forall, exists), and an obligation op that ties each proof goal to a source location IRGen to the end of verification, then erased pia_par Tiled grids with halos, spread, collectives (halo_exchange, all_reduce, scatter, gather), placement attributes IRGen to runtime lowering smt (upstream) Solver terms: bit-vectors, booleans, arrays, quantifiers, solver and assert ops Built by the verifier, exported to SMT-LIB for Z3 arith, scf, memref, vector, linalg, arm_neon, llvm (upstream) Codegen targets After verification

MLIR dialect namespaces cannot contain a ., so the contract and parallel dialects are spelled pia_contract and pia_par in IR (pia_contract.ensures, !pia_par.tiled<...>).

Design points:

  • Contracts are ops in their own dialect, not attributes, so they can reference SSA values and be verified, transformed and erased by ordinary passes.
  • Proved facts survive verification as attributes on the ops they justify (for example pia.proved = ["inbounds", "nooverflow"]), so the optimiser can act on them after contracts are erased.
  • Implicit obligations (index in bounds, no overflow under @overflow(proof), exhaustive match) are materialised as pia_contract.obligation ops by a single pass, so the verifier has one kind of goal to handle.

docs.title: Verifier
docs.text:
1. Obligation materialisation. Insert an obligation op for every implicit and explicit proof goal.
  2. Interval analysis. Run MLIR's integer range analysis (extended with Pia's range types) and discharge every obligation it proves on its own. Most bounds and overflow goals should end here. Then the Presburger stage takes goals that are affine in integer variables, such as aliasing of slices, loop-carried dependence and affine subscripts, and decides them exactly with MLIR's Presburger library (FPL) before falling back to SMT (ADR 0020). spread legality and the vectoriser use the same dependence relations.
  3. Verification-condition generation. For each remaining obligation, build the formula that must hold: loop invariants cut loops, calls use the callee's (or the imported interface's) contract, and old refers to entry values.
  4. SMT encoding. Emit the formula in the smt dialect: machine integers as bit-vectors, floats in the FP theory, dyn tags as datatypes, arrays as SMT arrays.
  5. Solving. Export to SMT-LIB and run Z3 in-process. unsat of the negated goal means proved. sat yields a model.
  6. Counterexamples. Map the model back to source variables and report it at the obligation's source location.
  7. Model checking (later). A separate pass checks collective protocols for the concurrency rules in ADR 0014.

Verifier v0 (M5) implements steps 2 to 6 for code without loops; verifier.md has the details and the limits. Codegen v0 (M6) erases contracts and lowers to an object file; see codegen.md.

docs.title: Bootstrapping order
docs.text: Operators are defined by metaprograms (ADR 0008), but the metaprogramming engine needs a parser that already handles expressions. The parser therefore starts with a fixed operator table matching the planned prelude. Since M7 the table comes from the prelude's operator declarations (meta.md), and the hard-coded one is gone.

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text:
Each milestone is a GitHub issue, built one at a time and merged to main.

# Milestone Done when M0 Bazel skeleton bazel build //... builds a pia-opt tool linked against MLIR and Z3, with one passing test M1 Grammar docs/grammar.md has the full grammar, and every example in design.md parses in a grammar test M2 Lexer and parser piac --dump-ast parses all design examples, with golden tests M3 Dialects pia, pia_contract and pia_par defined in ODS, with round-trip tests through pia-opt M4 IRGen, scalar subset let, functions, integers, if, for, arrays lower to the pia dialect M5 Verifier v0 Saturating add and the bad overflow example: the first proves, the second fails with a counterexample M6 Codegen v0 Saturating add runs on an Apple Silicon Mac and matches a C reference M7 Meta engine v0 Quote and splice, the expansion loop, @derive(eq), prelude operators from metaprograms M8 Modules and certificates Interfaces, explicit imports, .piai files, link-time hash checks, parallel Bazel builds M9 Generics and concepts Type functions, concept checks, laws, adapters, deduction M10 Vectorisation Auto-vectorisation from proved facts, vec<T, k>, dot product and clamp-and-scale examples M11 Floats Strict IEEE, @fp(reassoc), fast t, tiled matmul M12 Concurrency v0 spread loops, halo exchange and all_reduce on CPU threads, protocol checker M13 Image I/O Image.Png decode and encode with derived deserialise M14 Stream delineation The full demo: PNG in, delineated and coloured PNG out

docs.title: Demo: sediment transport by basin, in parallel
docs.text:
Cells in different basins never exchange sediment: water runs downhill from a cell to the cell below it, and a cell and the cell it drains to have the same watershed (sediment.pia.md, section 7). So every basin can run its time steps on its own core. This page is that version of sediment transport, a spread over the basins (ADR 0060), with the conservation law proved for each basin and summed over all of them:

sum bed + sum load + sum inflow + sum gone_by = old (sum bed + sum load + sum inflow)

exactly, where gone_by.[b] is what left the map through basin b's outlet. The page is its own module, so it proves in parallel with the others; main.c calls it with the labels and the height order that drainage computes, and checks that it gives the same result as the sequential sediment, cell for cell.

module Basins : BasinTransport

interface BasinTransport @abi(c) = sig
  let sediment_basins : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32])
      -> (label : [usize]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (steps : u32)
      -> (bed : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) -> (load : out mutable [u32])
      -> (inflow : out mutable [u32]) -> (flux : out mutable [u32])
      -> (gone_by : out mutable [u32]) -> (border : out mutable [usize])
      -> (keys : out mutable [usize]) -> (place2 : out mutable [usize])
      -> (pos2 : out mutable [usize]) -> (cnt : out mutable [u32])
      -> (first : out mutable [usize]) -> (next : out mutable [usize])
      -> (last : out mutable [usize]) -> (gowner : out mutable [usize]) -> u64
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len label = len fill && len order = len fill
    requires len bed = len fill && len load = len fill && len inflow = len fill && len flux = len fill && len gone_by = len fill
    requires len border = len fill && len keys = len fill && len place2 = len fill && len pos2 = len fill
    requires len cnt = len fill && len first = len fill && len next = len fill && len last = len fill && len gowner = len fill
    requires len fill >= 1 && len fill < max u32
    requires forall (k in 0..len down).
               down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
    requires forall (k in 0..len label). label.[at down k] = label.[k] && at label k < len fill
    requires forall (q in 0..len order). order.[q] < len fill
end

docs.title: 1. Sums, cells and steps
docs.text:
The pieces of sediment.pia.md this page needs, copied because a module cannot yet export lemmas over buffers (#327): the sum and its point update, one cell's erosion or deposition, and the arithmetic that chains them.

let spec elt (xs : [u32]) (i : usize) : u32
  requires i < len xs
= xs.[i]

let spec sum (xs : [u32]) (n : usize) : u64
  requires n <= len xs && n <= max u32 + 1
  ensures result <= (max u32 + 1) * n
  decreases n
= if n = 0 then 0 else sum xs (n - 1) + elt xs (n - 1)

let lemma step (xs : [u32]) (ys : [u32]) (n : usize) : unit
  requires 0 < n && n <= len xs && n <= len ys && n <= max u32 + 1
  requires sum ys (n - 1) = sum xs (n - 1) && ys.[n - 1] = xs.[n - 1]
  ensures sum ys n = sum xs n
= ()

let lemma step_after (xs : [u32]) (ys : [u32]) (i : usize) (n : usize) : unit
  requires i < n - 1 && n <= len xs && n <= len ys && n <= max u32 + 1
  requires sum ys (n - 1) + xs.[i] = sum xs (n - 1) + ys.[i] && ys.[n - 1] = xs.[n - 1]
  ensures sum ys n + xs.[i] = sum xs n + ys.[i]
= ()

let lemma step_at (xs : [u32]) (ys : [u32]) (i : usize) : unit
  requires i < len xs && i < len ys && i < max u32 + 1
  requires sum ys i = sum xs i
  ensures sum ys (i + 1) + xs.[i] = sum xs (i + 1) + ys.[i]
= ()

let lemma frame (xs : [u32]) (ys : [u32]) (i : usize) (n : usize) : unit
  requires len xs = len ys && n <= i && i < len xs && len xs <= max u32 + 1
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len xs). k <> i ==> ys.[k] = xs.[k]
  ensures sum ys n = sum xs n
  decreases n
= if n > 0 then (frame xs ys i (n - 1); assert ys.[n - 1] = xs.[n - 1]; step xs ys n)

let lemma update (xs : [u32]) (ys : [u32]) (i : usize) (n : usize) : unit
  requires len xs = len ys && i < n && n <= len xs && len xs <= max u32 + 1
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len xs). k <> i ==> ys.[k] = xs.[k]
  ensures sum ys n + xs.[i] = sum xs n + ys.[i]
  decreases n
= if n > i + 1 then (update xs ys i (n - 1); assert ys.[n - 1] = xs.[n - 1]; step_after xs ys i n)
  else (frame xs ys i i; step_at xs ys i; assert n = i + 1)

let lemma at_le (xs : [u32]) (i : usize) : unit
  requires i < len xs && i < max u32 + 1
  ensures xs.[i] <= sum xs (i + 1)
= ()

let lemma mono (xs : [u32]) (m : usize) (n : usize) : unit
  requires m <= n && n <= len xs && n <= max u32 + 1
  ensures sum xs m <= sum xs n
  decreases n
= if n > m then mono xs m (n - 1)

let lemma elt_le (xs : [u32]) (i : usize) (n : usize) : unit
  requires i < n && n <= len xs && n <= max u32 + 1
  ensures xs.[i] <= sum xs n
= at_le xs i; mono xs (i + 1) n

let lemma zero (xs : [u32]) (n : usize) : unit
  requires n <= len xs && n <= max u32 + 1
  requires forall (k in 0 .. n). xs.[k] = 0
  ensures sum xs n = 0
  decreases n
= if n > 0 then (zero xs (n - 1); assert xs.[n - 1] = 0)

let set (xs : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) (i : usize) (v : u32) : unit
  requires i < len xs && len xs <= max u32 + 1
  ensures xs.[i] = v
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len xs). k <> i ==> xs.[k] = old (xs.[k])
  ensures sum xs (len xs) + old (xs.[i]) = sum (old xs) (len xs) + v
= let w = xs.[i] in
  xs.[i] <- v;
  update (old xs) xs i (len xs);
  assert w = old (xs.[i])

let spec at (xs : [usize]) (k : usize) : usize
  requires k < len xs
= xs.[k]

let cell = type { bed : u32; load : u32 }

let erode_or_deposit (inflow : u32) (capacity : u32) (bed : u32) : cell
  requires bed + inflow <= max u32
  ensures result.bed + result.load = bed + inflow
  ensures inflow < capacity ==> result.bed <= bed && inflow <= result.load && result.load <= capacity
  ensures capacity <= inflow ==> bed <= result.bed && result.load = capacity
= if inflow < capacity then
    (let room = capacity - inflow in
     let e = if room < bed then room else bed in
     { bed = bed - e; load = inflow + e })
  else { bed = bed + (inflow - capacity); load = capacity }

let lemma balance (a : u64) (b : u64) (c : u64) (a0 : u64) (b0 : u64) (c0 : u64) (d : u32) (i : u32) (rb : u32) (rl : u32) : unit
  requires a + d = a0 + rb && b = b0 + rl && c + i = c0 && rb + rl = d + i
  ensures a + b + c = a0 + b0 + c0
= ()

let lemma chain (b : u64) (l : u64) (i : u64) (g : u64) (b1 : u64) (l1 : u64) (i1 : u64) : unit
  requires b + l + i + g <= max u32 && b1 + l1 + i1 = b + l + i
  ensures b1 + l1 + i1 + g <= max u32
= ()

let capacity_of (a : u32) (drop : u16) : u32 =
  let d : u32 = drop in
  let c : u64 = (a >> 4) + (d << 2) in
  if c < max u16 then c else max u16

let total (xs : [u32]) : u64
  requires len xs <= max u32 + 1
  ensures result = sum xs (len xs)
=
  let t : mutable u64 = 0 in
  for i in 0 .. len xs
    invariant t = sum xs i
  do
    t <- t + xs.[i]
  done;
  t

let blank (order : out mutable [usize]) (v : usize) : unit
  ensures forall (q in 0 .. len order). order.[q] = v
= for q in 0 .. len order
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. q). order.[j] = v
  do order.[q] <- v done

docs.title: 2. The height order grouped by basin
docs.text:
To visit a basin's cells in height order without scanning the whole map, the height order is grouped by basin: the same counting sort as height_order's, with the basin labels as keys and one bucket per cell that can be an outlet, so that the places first.[b] up to last.[b] of border are the cells of basin b, highest first.

How many of keys.[k ..] are h.

let spec kcount (keys : [usize]) (h : usize) (k : usize) : usize
  requires k <= len keys
  ensures result <= len keys - k
  decreases len keys - k
= if k = len keys then 0 else (if keys.[k] = h then 1 else 0) + kcount keys h (k + 1)

cnt.[h] is the number of keys equal to h, and cnt sums to n.

let ghistogram (keys : [usize]) (nb : usize) (cnt : out mutable [u32]) : unit
  requires len cnt = nb && nb >= 1 && nb <= max u32 && len keys <= max u32
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len keys). at keys k < nb
  ensures forall (h in 0 .. nb). cnt.[h] = kcount keys h 0
  ensures sum cnt nb = len keys
= for h in 0 .. nb
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. h). cnt.[j] = 0
  do cnt.[h] <- 0 done;
  zero cnt nb;
  for k in 0 .. len keys
    invariant sum cnt nb = k
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. nb). cnt.[h] + kcount keys h k = kcount keys h 0
  do
    let h : usize = keys.[k] in
    let c = cnt.[h] in
    elt_le cnt h nb;
    set cnt h (c + 1)
  done

Each key's bucket of places, the highest key first, stated by its neighbour.

let goffsets (n : usize) (nb : usize) (cnt : [u32]) (first : out mutable [usize]) (next : out mutable [usize]) (last : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len cnt = nb && len first = nb && len next = nb && len last = nb
  requires nb >= 1 && nb <= max u32 && sum cnt nb = n
  ensures last.[0] = n && first.[nb - 1] = 0
  ensures forall (h in 0 .. nb). next.[h] = first.[h] && first.[h] + cnt.[h] = last.[h] && last.[h] <= n
  ensures forall (h in 0 .. nb - 1). first.[h] = last.[h + 1]
= let acc : mutable u64 = 0 in
  for t in 0 .. nb
    invariant acc = sum cnt t && acc <= n
    invariant t > 0 ==> last.[0] = n
    invariant t > 0 ==> first.[t - 1] + acc = n
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. t). next.[h] = first.[h] && first.[h] + cnt.[h] = last.[h] && last.[h] <= n
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. t). h + 1 < t ==> first.[h] = last.[h + 1]
  do
    mono cnt (t + 1) nb;
    let c = cnt.[t] in
    last.[t] <- n - acc;
    acc <- acc + c;
    first.[t] <- n - acc;
    next.[t] <- n - acc
  done

Writes t into owner.[lo .. hi] and nothing else.

let gmark (owner : borrowed inout mutable [usize]) (lo : usize) (hi : usize) (t : usize) : unit
  requires lo <= hi && hi <= len owner
  ensures forall (j in 0 .. len owner). (lo <= j && j < hi ==> owner.[j] = t) && (j < lo || hi <= j ==> owner.[j] = old (owner.[j]))
= for q in lo .. hi
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. len owner). (lo <= j && j < q ==> owner.[j] = t) && (j < lo || q <= j ==> owner.[j] = old (owner.[j]))
  do
    owner.[q] <- t
  done

owner.[q] is the key whose bucket holds place q.

let gowners (n : usize) (nb : usize) (cnt : [u32]) (first : [usize]) (last : [usize]) (owner : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len cnt = nb && len first = nb && len last = nb && len owner = n && nb >= 1
  requires last.[0] = n && first.[nb - 1] = 0
  requires forall (h in 0 .. nb). first.[h] + cnt.[h] = last.[h] && last.[h] <= n
  requires forall (h in 0 .. nb - 1). first.[h] = last.[h + 1]
  ensures forall (q in 0 .. n). at owner q < nb && first.[at owner q] <= q && q < last.[at owner q]
  ensures forall (h in 0 .. nb) (q in 0 .. n). first.[h] <= q && q < last.[h] ==> at owner q = h
  ensures forall (a in 0 .. n) (b in 0 .. n). a < b ==> at owner b <= at owner a
= let w : mutable usize = n in
  for t in 0 .. nb
    invariant w <= n
    invariant t < nb ==> w = last.[t]
    invariant t = nb ==> w = 0
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. t). w <= first.[h]
    invariant forall (q in w .. n). at owner q < t && first.[at owner q] <= q && q < last.[at owner q]
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. t) (q in w .. n). first.[h] <= q && q < last.[h] ==> owner.[q] = h
    invariant forall (a in w .. n) (b in w .. n). a < b ==> at owner b <= at owner a
  do
    let lo = first.[t] in
    assert lo + cnt.[t] = last.[t] && lo <= w;
        gmark owner lo w t;
    w <- lo;
    if t + 1 < nb then assert lo = last.[t + 1] else ()
  done

Each place gets the next key's index, in key order; a place q holds a key equal to owner.[q].

let gplace (keys : [usize]) (nb : usize) (first : [usize]) (last : [usize]) (owner : [usize]) (next : borrowed inout mutable [usize]) (order : out mutable [usize]) (pos : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len first = nb && len last = nb && len next = nb
  requires len owner = len keys && len order = len keys && len pos = len keys
  requires forall (h in 0 .. nb). next.[h] = first.[h] && first.[h] + kcount keys h 0 = last.[h] && last.[h] <= len keys
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len keys). at keys k < nb
  requires forall (q in 0 .. len keys). at owner q < nb && first.[at owner q] <= q && q < last.[at owner q]
  requires forall (h in 0 .. nb) (q in 0 .. len keys). first.[h] <= q && q < last.[h] ==> at owner q = h
  ensures forall (q in 0 .. len order). order.[q] < len pos && pos.[order.[q]] = q && keys.[order.[q]] = at owner q
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len pos). pos.[k] < len order && order.[pos.[k]] = k
= blank order (len keys);
  assert (forall (q in 0 .. len keys). next.[at owner q] = first.[at owner q]);
  assert (forall (q in 0 .. len keys). next.[at owner q] <= q);
  for k in 0 .. len keys
    invariant forall (h in 0 .. nb). first.[h] <= next.[h] && next.[h] + kcount keys h k = last.[h]
    invariant forall (q in 0 .. len keys).
      (q < next.[at owner q] ==> order.[q] < k && pos.[order.[q]] = q && keys.[order.[q]] = at owner q)
      && (next.[at owner q] <= q ==> order.[q] = len keys)
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. k). pos.[j] < len keys && order.[pos.[j]] = j
  do
    let h : usize = keys.[k] in
    let p = next.[h] in
    assert kcount keys h k = 1 + kcount keys h (k + 1);
    assert p < last.[h] && last.[h] <= len keys;
    assert at owner p = h;
    order.[p] <- k;
    pos.[k] <- p;
    next.[h] <- p + 1
  done;
  assert (forall (h in 0 .. nb). next.[h] = last.[h]);
  assert (forall (q in 0 .. len keys). q < next.[at owner q])

The keys of the grouping: each place of the height order, labelled by its cell's basin.

let basin_keys (label : [usize]) (order : [usize]) (keys : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len order = len label && len keys = len label
  requires forall (q in 0 .. len order). order.[q] < len label
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len label). at label k < len label
  ensures forall (q in 0 .. len keys). keys.[q] = label.[order.[q]] && at keys q < len label
= for q in 0 .. len order
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. q). keys.[j] = label.[order.[j]] && at keys j < len label
  do
    keys.[q] <- label.[order.[q]]
  done

The cells grouped by basin, each basin's cells in the height order: the places first.[b] up to last.[b] of border are basin b's cells.

let basin_order (label : [usize]) (order : [usize]) (border : out mutable [usize])
    (keys : out mutable [usize]) (place2 : out mutable [usize]) (pos2 : out mutable [usize])
    (cnt : out mutable [u32]) (first : out mutable [usize]) (next : out mutable [usize])
    (last : out mutable [usize]) (owner : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len order = len label && len border = len label && len keys = len label
  requires len place2 = len label && len pos2 = len label && len owner = len label
  requires len cnt = len label && len first = len label && len next = len label && len last = len label
  requires len label >= 1 && len label <= max u32
  requires forall (q in 0 .. len order). order.[q] < len label
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len label). at label k < len label
  ensures forall (b in 0 .. len label). first.[b] <= last.[b] && last.[b] <= len label
  ensures forall (q in 0 .. len border). border.[q] < len label && label.[border.[q]] = at owner q
  ensures forall (b in 0 .. len label) (q in 0 .. len border). first.[b] <= q && q < last.[b] ==> at owner q = b
= let n = len label in
  basin_keys label order keys;
  ghistogram keys n cnt;
  goffsets n n cnt first next last;
  gowners n n cnt first last owner;
  gplace keys n first last owner next place2 pos2;
  for q in 0 .. n
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. q). border.[j] < n && label.[border.[j]] = at owner j
  do
    border.[q] <- order.[place2.[q]]
  done

docs.title: 3. A basin's sum
docs.text:
bsum xs label b n is the sum of basin b's cells among the first n. It says what it reads, the cells labelled b (ADR 0060, section 3), so a write in another basin leaves it alone, which is what lets a spread over basins prove a law per basin.
