The table is a summary. Each tool has more options than one cell can hold, and the sections below say what matters.

Three more features set Pia apart in combination, though each has close relatives:

Teaching the prover a domain Types as values Generic constraints and their laws Pia Library theories: sorts, abstract functions and axioms with triggers, with a sealed model that proves the axioms; metaprograms can write them Yes, at compile time: let binds types, and a generic type is a function that returns one Concepts, which are metaprograms, with laws that Z3 proves for each instance; adapters; a generic body is proved once against its concepts Dafny Bodiless functions and {:axiom} lemmas; abstract modules that a refinement can prove No Type characteristics and traits; a trait's lemmas must be proved by each class F* assume val and lemmas with SMTPat triggers; tactics Yes, by dependent types Type classes whose instances can carry proofs Lean 4 simp sets and tactics written in Lean; definitions rather than axioms Yes, by dependent types Type classes with law fields (LawfulBEq, Mathlib's hierarchy), proved by each instance's author Idris 2 Definitions and proofs; no solver to extend Yes, by dependent types Interfaces; laws as separate interfaces proved by hand ATS Axioms as praxi, taken on trust No; static indices on types Templates SPARK (Ada) Lemma libraries and ghost models; axioms through Why3 No Ada generics, proved instance by instance Liquid Haskell Measures and assume refinements No Type classes; laws stated and proved by hand with refinement reflection Rust verifiers Verus: broadcast lemmas with triggers; Kani: none No Traits; in Verus, specs on trait methods that each impl must meet Why3 Theories of types, functions and axioms, cloned and realised in Coq or Isabelle; drivers map them to prover built-ins No Cloning a module turns its axioms into goals for the instance

docs.title: What sets Pia apart
docs.text:
These are the choices that, taken together, no other language on this page makes.

  • Proving is compiling. There is no separate verifier to run, and no mode where contracts are comments. piac proves every goal and refuses to compile while one fails or is unproved, unless --allow-unproved accepts it (ADR 0004). Dafny comes closest: it verifies before it compiles by default, and it can be told not to.
  • The strongest guarantee is the default, on machine integers. A u8 is a byte, and a + b on two of them raises a goal that it does not overflow. Wrapping, saturating and trapping arithmetic exist, and each is something you ask for (the tour). SPARK shares this; Dafny, Lean, Idris and F* default to unbounded mathematical integers, which is easier to prove and further from the machine.
  • Cheap reasoning first. Interval analysis settles the easy goals before Z3 sees them, and a goal Z3 refutes comes back as a counterexample: concrete inputs that break the code (how verification works).
  • Built on MLIR. Goals live in Pia's own MLIR dialects, next to the code they are about, and the code goes through LLVM to native instructions with every proved check erased. A proved index has no bounds check, and the facts the proofs establish are planned to drive vectorisation (ADR 0011, ADR 0013).
  • Metaprogramming is part of the language, and its output is proved. Operators are metaprograms in the prelude, @derive writes functions, and tactics are metaprograms that write proof steps. Whatever a metaprogram generates is verified like code you wrote (metaprograms). Lean's macros and elaborators are at least as strong; Dafny, SPARK and Why3 have none.
  • Libraries teach the solver new domains, and prove what they teach. A theory is an ordinary library module: sorts, functions with no body, and axioms with the triggers Z3 should use. A model gives each sort a type and each function a body, proves every axiom as a lemma, and is then sealed, so clients prove from the axioms alone and cannot be misled by a theory that contradicts itself. A theory with no model must be imported with trusting, and piac --trust-report lists every axiom a build relied on. Theories can be written by metaprograms, and Pia describes its own memory model, allocators and targets this way (theories, ADR 0036, ADR 0049). Theories compared says which other tools come close.
  • Types are values, and concepts carry laws that are proved. One let binds functions, values and types alike, and a generic type is a compile-time function that returns a type (ADR 0002). A constraint on a type parameter is a concept: a metaprogram that checks what a type provides, in the spirit of C++ concepts or type traits, and states laws, such as reflexive equality, that Z3 proves for every type that meets it. Generic bodies are proved once against their concepts (ADR 0009, ADR 0034, ADR 0043). Types and concepts compared says where each idea comes from.
  • Proofs travel with the binary. Each object carries a certificate of the interfaces it provides and requires, and a library whose interface changed cannot bind to a program that was proved against the old one, because the witness symbols the loader must bind are missing (shared libraries and certificates). Most verifiers stop at the source: once compiled, nothing records what was proved.
  • A verified REPL, and an MCP server for agents. pia repl proves every cell before it runs, refuses a redefinition that would break a caller, and swaps proved code into running tasks (the REPL). pia mcp serves that session to an agent, and teaches it the language: a primer when it connects, :help topics, hints on failed cells and what each proof cost. Lean and Idris have excellent interactive loops, but they check code and run it as separate steps; Pia's REPL never runs a cell it has not proved.
  • No garbage collector, ever. Allocators are explicit and every allocation can fail (ADR 0026), as in SPARK, ATS and Rust.

docs.title: Feature by feature
docs.text:
The rest of the language, one feature per row, with what exists today and where the idea comes from. "Built" means piac compiles and proves it now; "designed" means an accepted ADR that is not built yet.

Feature In Pia State Closest elsewhere Errors and cleanup Closed error sets, e? and scoped handle arms, each arm proved at each ? that reaches it; defer runs on every exit, and cleanup never replaces the error in flight (ADR 0028) Built Zig's error sets, try and errdefer are the nearest; Rust's ? and Drop; Swift's typed throws. None of them proves the handlers Ownership borrowed, moved, in/out/inout parameters, @linear types that must be consumed, drop, and borrows that end at their last use (ADR 0005, ADR 0042) Built in part: regions on types and escape analysis are designed Rust's ownership (affine, with Drop); linear types in ATS, Linear Haskell and Austral; Mojo's as-soon-as-possible drop Memory No GC and no new: explicit allocators, every allocation can fail, arenas on the stack, and allocator behaviour stated as the theory Alloc, which each allocator proves it refines (ADR 0026, ADR 0041) Built Zig's explicit, fallible allocators; Rust's try_reserve. Neither proves what an allocator promises Metaprogramming let meta functions with quotes and splices, expanded to a fixed point with a cycle limit; hygiene by forbidding shadowing outright; operators, derives and tactics are all metaprograms (ADR 0007, ADR 0022) Built Lisp and Racket macros, Lean's macros and elaborators, Zig's comptime. Zig also forbids shadowing Specification state Spec-only types (int, real) and spec locals and buffers, which proofs use and codegen erases; no ghost keyword (ADR 0058) Built: fixed-size spec buffers first Ghost code in Dafny, Verus, SPARK and Why3 Cost bounds costs c <= e in a contract bounds the work a function does on a named counter, proved by Z3; asymptotic and closed-form facts go to Lean (ADR 0062, ADR 0061) Designed Research tools: RAML's resource analysis, time credits in Iris and CFML. No mainstream verifier proves complexity Facts Z3 cannot prove A goal Z3 cannot decide, such as a nonlinear or inductive fact, can be proved in Lean and used by Pia (ADR 0061) Designed Why3 and SPARK send such goals to Coq or Isabelle; F* has tactics Certificates Each object carries the interfaces it provides and requires, as hashes and witness symbols, so a stale library fails to bind; pia-cert check runs in every pia_library build (ADR 0024) Built: audit and trusted-item reports are designed Proof-carrying code (research); OCaml's interface digests, which check identity without contracts Parallel loops spread runs iterations in parallel, and the compiler proves from ownership footprints that no two iterations touch the same data (ADR 0060) Built: v0, on the CPU Rust's Send/Sync and Rayon, checked by types; OpenMP, not checked. Verus and Iris prove concurrent code by hand Concurrency Stackless coroutines, race freedom and lock-order deadlock freedom by proof, channel protocols checked by Z3 (ADR 0027, ADR 0053); the RC11 memory model as a theory with a litmus battery (ADR 0052) Designed; the memory model is built Session types; TLA+ and model checkers for protocols; Iris for proofs about atomics Tests from contracts Metaprograms generate test cases from contracts, types and theories; each case goes to the verifier first, and only the cases it cannot decide are run (ADR 0056) Built in part: the metaprogram builtins; generators next QuickCheck and Hypothesis, which run every case; Dafny's test generation Floating point Strict IEEE by default, three explicit ways to allow reassociation, kernels proved against real theories, and no trusted libm: every maths function written in Pia with its error bound in its contract (ADR 0012, ADR 0038) f32 and f64 are built, strict IEEE and bit for bit with C; proofs see exact IEEE order and conversion goals, while real-valued error bounds are designed, not built SPARK and Frama-C prove float code through Why3; Gappa and Flocq prove error bounds in Coq Integer types Range types int{0..255}, min u8 and max u32 folded to literals, and digit separators such as 100'000 (ADR 0059) Built Ada's range types and 'First/'Last; C++14's ' separators Literate programs Comments are syntax that metaprograms can read, and a .pia.md file is Markdown whose pia blocks are the program; the demos on this site are proved that way (ADR 0029) Built Literate Haskell, Agda's literate Markdown, Lean's doc-gen Tooling A language server, the verified REPL, an MCP server that teaches the language and reports proof costs, and agent skills whose examples are proved (the REPL, agent skills) Built Lean's and Dafny's language servers are more mature; MCP servers for Lean exist as community projects, while Pia's is part of the toolchain

docs.title: Where the others are ahead
docs.text:
Pia's choices have costs, and the other languages have years of work Pia does not.

  • Maturity. Dafny, SPARK, F*, Lean and Liquid Haskell have been used for real systems for a decade or more. SPARK is used in avionics and security work, F* produced the HACL* cryptography in Firefox and the Linux kernel, and Lean has Mathlib. Pia compiles a subset today, for one target (arm64 macOS); float error bounds, compiling recursive types and much of the concurrency design are not built yet (status).
  • Expressiveness. Lean, F* and Idris have dependent types, so a type can say almost anything, and a proof can be as long as it needs to be. Pia's goals are first-order formulas that Z3 decides or gives up on. A property that needs induction needs a lemma, and some nonlinear or deeply quantified goals will not prove automatically at all. Handing those to Lean is designed (ADR 0061) but not built.
  • The trusted base. Lean checks every proof with a small kernel, so a bug in a tactic cannot prove something false. Pia trusts Z3, the way the verifier encodes goals for it, and the compiler. Its certificates record which interfaces were proved, not proofs that someone else can check, and the planned pia-cert audit re-checks obligations with your own Z3, not the machine code (trust model).
  • Prover choice. Why3 and SPARK send a goal to several provers and keep the one that succeeds. Pia uses Z3 alone, with solver strategies (@solver) as the escape hatch.
  • Bounded model checking. Kani checks Rust code bit-precisely, unsafe code included, up to a bound, with no invariants to write. Pia needs a loop invariant for each loop, and has nothing like Kani for code that is not Pia.
  • Ecosystems. Rust, Haskell and Ada have libraries for everything. Pia's standard library is being written in Pia, over a small POSIX core (standard library, the C++ standard library in Pia).

docs.title: Types and concepts compared
docs.text:
Neither idea is new on its own, and Pia's take on each is narrower than the strongest version elsewhere.

  • First-class types. Lean, Idris, F*, Agda and Coq have dependent types, in which types are values in the fullest sense: a type can depend on a run-time value, and a function can return a type that is used to check the rest of the program. Pia's types are values at compile time only, as in Zig, whose generics are also functions from types to types. Pia does not have dependent types; what a dependent type would say, Pia says with a range type, a where refinement or a contract, and Z3 proves it.
  • Concepts. C++20 concepts check that a type provides the operations a template uses, and Pia's concepts check the same kind of thing, with a metaprogram instead of a requires expression. C++ concepts cannot check meaning: a concept's semantic requirements, such as that == is an equivalence, are documentation, and the axioms proposed for C++0x concepts were dropped. Haskell's and Rust's type classes and traits are in the same position. A Pia concept states such requirements as laws, and each instance proves them, automatically, before it can be used; an instance cannot assume them.
  • Laws elsewhere. Lean, F* and Idris can put proofs in a type class, and Mathlib's algebraic hierarchy is built that way: a stronger version of the same idea, since a law can be any theorem, but each instance's author writes its proofs. Dafny traits can declare lemmas that each class proves, and Why3 turns a cloned module's axioms into goals. Pia's contribution is to make lawful concepts the ordinary way to write generics, with the laws proved by Z3 for each instance and adapters for types that meet a concept only in their own way, such as f32 equality, which fails reflexivity at NaN (language design).

docs.title: Theories compared
docs.text:
Every verifier on this page lets a library add knowledge that the prover does not have built in. What differs is whether that knowledge is checked, and who can add it.

  • Why3 is the closest. Its theories declare types, functions and axioms, are instantiated by cloning, and can be realised in Coq or Isabelle, which proves the axioms, much as a Pia model does. Its drivers map a theory onto a prover's built-in theories. Pia's theories descend from these. The differences are that a Pia model is written in Pia and proved by the same solver, that sealing is enforced, so a client cannot see past the axioms to the model, and that theories can be generated by metaprograms.
  • F* and Verus let a lemma carry a trigger (SMTPat in F*, broadcast lemmas in Verus), so the solver applies it on its own wherever a matching term appears. That is the same mechanism as an axiom's trigger in a Pia theory, except that the fact is proved, not assumed. F* also has assume val for facts taken on trust, with no model to check them.
  • Dafny has functions with no body and lemmas marked {:axiom}, and abstract modules whose refinements must prove the abstract lemmas. That is close to a Pia theory with a model, though nothing stops a client from depending on an axiom that no refinement proves, and there is no report of which axioms a program used.
  • Lean needs no axioms at all for most domains: a domain is a set of definitions, facts about it are theorems, and simp sets and custom tactics, written in Lean, are how a library teaches automation about it. That is more general than Pia's theories and checked by the kernel; the cost is that the automation is a tactic search, not an SMT query that a trigger steers.
  • SPARK has lemma libraries and ghost models for its functional containers, and can pass external axiomatisations through to Why3. Liquid Haskell has measures and assumed refinements. ATS has praxi, axioms taken on trust. Idris and Kani have no solver theory to extend.

What Pia adds is the combination: a theory is a library like any other, a model proves it consistent and is sealed, trust is explicit and reported, --check-vacuity catches a goal proved only because trusted axioms contradict each other, and metaprograms can build theories and the tactics that use them.

docs.title: Dafny
docs.text: The closest in how it feels: an imperative and functional language with requires, ensures, loop invariants and decreases, proved automatically by Z3, with lemmas for the hard parts. Dafny's int is unbounded and it compiles to languages with garbage collectors, so it is often used to write and prove an algorithm that is then shipped in C#, Java or Go. Pia proves the machine-level program itself: fixed-width integers, slices with lengths, no GC, and native code with the checks erased.

docs.title: F*
docs.text: F* combines dependent types, an effect system, Z3 and tactics, and its Low* subset compiles to C that ships in Firefox and the Linux kernel. It can state far more than Pia can, and its proofs can be as manual as needed. Pia gives up dependent types for a smaller, automatic logic and an ML syntax that looks like ordinary code, and adds the REPL, metaprograms that run on every program, and certificates in the binary.

docs.title: Lean 4
docs.text: Lean is a theorem prover that is also a fast programming language, with a small trusted kernel, the strongest metaprogramming of any language here and Mathlib behind it. Proofs in Lean are mostly written, with tactics and increasingly strong automation. Pia proves goals without being asked, which is less expressive and needs no proof writing for the overflow, bounds and contract goals that make up most of a program. Pia's @by tactics borrow the idea, as metaprograms that write proof steps.

docs.title: Idris 2
docs.text: Idris makes types first-class and proofs programs, with quantitative types to track how often a value is used, and an interactive editor that fills holes and splits cases. Pia also treats types as values, under one let (ADR 0002), but checks contracts with a solver instead of type-level proofs, and compiles to native code without a garbage collector.

docs.title: ATS
docs.text: ATS combines dependent and linear types and compiles to C with no garbage collector, so it can prove low-level code safe at no run-time cost. That goal is Pia's too. ATS asks for proofs as terms and has a famously steep learning curve; Pia tries to reach the same place with contracts, a solver and counterexamples.

docs.title: SPARK
docs.text: SPARK is Pia's nearest neighbour in spirit, and the one with the longest industrial record. It proves the absence of run-time errors (overflow, range, index and division checks) and functional contracts in a subset of Ada, compiles to native code with no garbage collector, and has an ownership model for pointers. Pia differs in syntax (ML instead of Ada), in proving as part of compiling instead of in a separate GNATprove run, in using one solver with interval analysis in front instead of several through Why3, and in metaprogramming, the REPL, the MCP server and certificates, none of which SPARK has. SPARK has tool qualification for certified software, which Pia is a long way from.

docs.title: Liquid Haskell
docs.text: Liquid Haskell adds refinement types such as {v:Int | v > 0} to Haskell and checks them with Z3, inferring many refinements by itself. Pia's range types, such as int{0..255}, and where refinements on record fields are the same idea. Liquid Haskell keeps Haskell's laziness, garbage collector and ecosystem; Pia is strict, has no GC, and makes machine overflow a goal.

docs.title: Rust with Kani, Prusti, Verus or Creusot
docs.text: Rust already proves memory safety with its borrow checker, and these tools prove more on top: Kani by bounded model checking, Prusti, Verus and Creusot by contracts and deductive proof. Verus is the most like Pia, with Z3, contracts and ghost code in a Rust subset. The difference is that in Rust the verifier is a separate tool over a language that was not designed for it, so arithmetic overflow is a debug-build panic or a release-build wrap unless a tool proves otherwise. Pia designs the language around the proofs: overflow is a compile error by default, and contracts are part of every interface a module exports.

docs.title: Why3
docs.text: Why3 is a platform more than a language: WhyML programs and goals go to whichever provers can discharge them, and proofs can be finished by hand in Coq or Isabelle. SPARK and Creusot are built on it. Pia is a language with one compiler and one solver, which keeps the loop from code to counterexample short, at the cost of Why3's breadth.

docs.title: Others
docs.text: Frama-C with ACSL proves annotated C, VeriFast proves C and Java with separation logic, and Coq (now Rocq) and Isabelle prove programs that are then extracted to code. Each takes an existing language or a proof assistant as its starting point. Pia starts from the other end: a language where every program is a set of goals, and the compiler's job is to prove them before it emits anything.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text:
• To prove mathematics, or properties that need dependent types, use Lean, F*, Idris or Coq.
  • To ship certified safety-critical software today, use SPARK.
  • To prove an algorithm and ship it on a managed runtime, use Dafny.
  • To add proofs to an existing Rust code base, use Kani or Verus.
  • To try a language where machine-level code is proved as it is compiled, interactively and with an agent in the loop, try Pia: start with Getting started and the REPL.

docs.title: Coroutines, tasks and race freedom
docs.text:
Status: accepted design, 2026-11-21 (ADR 0027). Nothing here is implemented yet. Code blocks show designed syntax.

ADR 0014 made Pia concurrent by default, with spread loops, collectives, task graphs and futures. It settled one question about safety: tiles are moved to workers, so they cannot race. This page designs the rest:

  1. Coroutines and lightweight tasks, so a program can have many thousands of concurrent activities, such as I/O, pipelines and the task graph for flow accumulation, without one OS thread each.
  2. Locking, synchronisation and communication primitives: mutexes, atomics, channels, barriers and friends.
  3. A prover that answers "could access to this resource race?" for every piece of shared state, and refuses to compile the program when it cannot prove "no".
  4. How the answers reach proof certificates (ADR 0024), so a library's concurrency guarantees cross module and binary boundaries.

The rule from ADR 0004 applies throughout. An unproved race is an unproved obligation, so it is a compile error unless --allow-unproved names it.

docs.title: Summary of the choices
docs.text:
Each choice has a recommendation. The alternatives are below in each section.

# Question Recommendation 1 Stackless coroutines or stackful green threads? Stackless: compiler-built state machines with frames of known size. "Green threads" are tasks on a scheduler written in Pia 2 Structured or detached tasks? Structured: a task handle is @linear and must be joined inside the scope that spawned it 3 How is suspension visible? @suspends effect, inferred inside a module and written in exported interfaces. Two keywords: wait and yield 4 How is race freedom proved? Permissions first: ownership and borrows in the type checker, disjointness by Presburger (FPL) and Z3, and the model checker only for what types cannot express (the primitives themselves, protocols, deadlock) 5 How do locks work? A lock owns its data (mutex<T>), with a lock invariant and a static level. Levels must increase, which rules out lock-order deadlocks at compile time 6 Which memory orders for atomics? seq_cst, acquire, release and acq_rel are checked from day one. relaxed was to be an unproved obligation until the model checker supported RC11. ADR 0052 models RC11 from the start, so relaxed is proved like the other orders 7 How are deadlocks in channel communication (CSP) found? A deadlock goal for every scope: a forest-shaped channel topology is proved by a lemma, protocols inferred per channel end are checked for compatibility and matched against proved patterns (pipeline, worker pool, request and reply), and the model checker searches the rest for any set of tasks blocked forever 8 What does an unproved race or deadlock do? Compile error, with the accesses or blocked tasks and a witness. --allow-unproved=race:... or deadlock:... accepts it, records it in the certificate as trusted, and recommends a TSan build

docs.title: 1. Coroutines: stackless
docs.text:
A coroutine is a function that can suspend and later resume. A task is a coroutine that a scheduler runs. Pia's "green threads" are tasks: many of them run on a few OS worker threads.

There are two ways to build them:

Stackless (C++20, Rust async, Kotlin, Swift) Stackful (Go, Erlang, Java virtual threads, Lua) What suspends one function frame, which the compiler turns into a state machine a whole call stack, switched by the runtime Memory per task the frame: a size known at compile time a stack: guessed, grown, or segmented Calling a suspending function only from another suspending one ("function colouring") from anywhere Foreign code on the stack never across a suspension possible, and unsafe if foreign code keeps pointers into the stack For the verifier every suspension point is a visible state; the frame is a value with a type suspension hides inside any call; stack size is a proof goal Pia cannot discharge in general

Recommendation: stackless. It suits a language whose compiler must prove things:

  • No stack-size guess. A stackful task needs a stack big enough for its deepest call chain. Proving that bound is hard once there are function values, recursion or foreign calls, and an overflowed green-thread stack is exactly the kind of run-time failure Pia exists to remove. A stackless frame's size is computed by the compiler. A suspending function cannot recurse through a suspension except by spawning, which allocates the child frame explicitly.
  • Suspension points are states. The model checker (section 4) explores tasks as state machines whose transitions are the code between two suspension points. Stackless lowering produces exactly that machine. Module-state contracts (ADR 0006) and the protocol checker (ADR 0014) read the same states.
  • Borrows across suspension are checkable. A frame that holds a borrow across wait is a value holding a borrow, and the ordinary borrow rules apply to it.
  • Foreign code stays outside. No foreign frame is ever suspended, so foreign code never sees a stack move or a thread change under it.
  • Lowering exists. LLVM's coroutine intrinsics (llvm.coro.*, switched-resume lowering) build the frame and elide its allocation when the coroutine does not outlive its caller. MLIR's async dialect lowers to them already.

The cost is colouring: a function that suspends can only be called by one that also suspends, or handed to a scheduler. Pia makes the colour cheap instead of hiding it (below). It also stays honest: the colour is a fact the verifier and importers need anyway.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Two keywords, both single imperative words: wait suspends until a task or operation completes, and yield suspends a generator with a value. Everything else is library code.

import Pia.Task { scope, spawn, join }
import Pia.Io   { conn, read }

(* A suspending function. @suspends is inferred inside the module, and must
   be written when the function is exported. *)
let read_exact (c : borrowed inout conn) (dst : borrowed out mutable [u8; n]) : result<unit, io_error> @suspends
= let mutable got = 0 in
  while got < n
    invariant 0 <= got && got <= n
    decreases n - got
  do
    match wait (read c dst.[got .. n]) with
    | Ok 0   -> return (Err Eof)
    | Ok k   -> got <- got + k
    | Err e  -> return (Err e)
  done;
  Ok ()

(* A generator: yields each row, suspends between them. *)
let rows (img : borrowed in [u8; w * h]) : gen<[u8; w]> =
  for y in 0..h do yield img.[y * w .. (y + 1) * w] done

docs.title: Tasks are structured
docs.text:
scope opens a region. spawn s f starts f as a task in scope s and returns a task<T>, which is @linear (stdlib.md). It must be consumed by join (or wait) before the scope ends, so no task outlives the scope that started it. This is structured concurrency, as in Trio's nurseries, Kotlin's coroutineScope, Swift's task groups and Rust's thread::scope.

let total (xs : borrowed in [i64; n]) : i64 @suspends
  requires n >= 2
= scope (let (s) =>
    let lo = spawn s (let () => sum xs.[0 .. n / 2]) in
    let hi = spawn s (let () => sum xs.[n / 2 .. n]) in
    join lo + join hi)

Structure buys two things for proofs:

  • Tasks may borrow from their parent. Both tasks above borrow xs, because the scope cannot end while they run. Without structure, everything a task touches would have to be moved or reference-counted.
  • Arenas and regions nest. An arena region (stdlib.md) that encloses a scope encloses all its tasks, so a coroutine may hold arena borrows across suspension points.

Detached ("fire and forget") tasks are not in the first version. A long-lived service is a scope at the top of main. If they are added later, a detached task must own everything it touches (moved, no borrows) and is a sendable value (section 3).

Cancellation is cooperative and explicit in the first version: a scope can be given a cancel token, and operations that take one return Err Cancelled. Implicit cancellation at every wait interacts with @linear resources (a cancelled task must still consume its file descriptors), so it waits for experience with the explicit form.

docs.title: Errors and cleanup in tasks
docs.text:
Error propagation and scope cleanup are designed separately (ADR 0028, in review). The design here relies on four of its rules:

  • ? never crosses a task boundary. Inside a spawned closure it ends that task, and the error comes back from join.
  • Inside a lock body, ? leaves the closure, the lock is released, and the error is the closure's result.
  • A scope that exits early first joins (or cancels, then joins) every child still running, and only then runs the parent's defers, because children may borrow from the parent.
  • Drops and defers never suspend and never acquire a lock, so they cannot break the lock-level order.

docs.title: Calling suspending code from ordinary code
docs.text:
Pia.Task.run (f : () -> T @suspends) : T starts a scheduler, runs f to completion, and returns. main may itself be @suspends, in which case the runtime calls run for it. A non-suspending function cannot wait.

Generic code that takes a function, such as map, should work for both colours. That needs effect polymorphism over @suspends in generics (ADR 0009), which is designed with M9. Until then, the library has map and map_wait.

docs.title: Blocking calls
docs.text: A foreign call that blocks, such as read on a pipe or a long fsync, would stall a worker thread and every task queued on it. Foreign declarations (stdlib.md) say so with @blocking. Calling a @blocking function from @suspends code is an error unless it goes through Pia.Task.offload, which runs it on a separate blocking pool and suspends until it returns. This is Tokio's spawn_blocking and Go's handoff of a blocked M, made a compile-time rule.

docs.title: The scheduler is Pia
docs.text:
The scheduler lives in Pia.Task, written in Pia over the core (ADR 0023):

  • Workers: one OS thread per performance core (sysctlbyname), from Pia.Sys.Thread.
  • Queues: a work-stealing deque per worker (Chase-Lev), written in Pia over atomic<T> and proved by the model checker (section 4).
  • I/O: Pia.Io wraps kqueue/kevent on macOS (epoll or io_uring on a later Linux port). A task that waits on a descriptor parks until kevent reports it ready.
  • Timers: a timer wheel driven by the same kevent call.
  • Frames: a task frame's size is known, and it comes from the allocator the scope was given. Allocators are explicit @linear values, so a scope takes one, as any allocating function does (stdlib.md).
  • Deterministic mode: Pia.Task.run_deterministic seed f runs every task on one thread in an order chosen by seed. It is for tests, for replaying a counterexample trace from the model checker, and for the doc examples.

spread and the collectives move onto the same scheduler. A spread loop is a scope that spawns one task per chunk, and a collective is a synchronisation operation among those tasks. There is one runtime, not a worker pool beside a task scheduler. Device placement (ADR 0015) adds device queues: a GPU kernel is a task whose completion is a Metal event, and the buffers it uses are moved to it. Apple Silicon's unified memory means no copy, but ownership still moves, so the CPU cannot touch a buffer the GPU is writing.

docs.title: 2. Synchronisation and communication primitives
docs.text:
Every primitive lives in the library, in Pia.Sync and Pia.Chan. Each has a contract the race prover relies on, and its implementation is proved against that contract (section 4).

Primitive Type What it guarantees Mutex mutex<T> owns a T; the only access is inside lock; the lock invariant holds whenever it is unlocked Reader-writer lock rwlock<T> many read borrows or one write borrow Atomic cell atomic<T> T is an integer, bool or addr; every operation takes a memory order (stdlib.md) Channel chan<T, cap> send takes moved T, recv returns it; bounded by cap One-shot once<T>, promise<T> written exactly once, then shareable read-only Barrier barrier n releases when exactly n tasks arrive; the protocol checker proves all n arrive Semaphore semaphore n at most n holders Notify event wakes waiters; the replacement for condition variables

There are no bare condition variables. A condition variable's meaning (which predicate a waiter is waiting for) lives in comments, and its spurious wake-ups make every waiter a loop. event plus a lock invariant, or a channel, says the same thing in a form the prover reads.

docs.title: A lock owns its data
docs.text:
A mutex<T> holds a T. The only way to reach the T is lock, which passes a scoped mutable borrow to a closure. The borrow cannot escape the closure, so the data cannot be touched without the lock. Rust's Mutex<T> works the same way.

let pool = type { free : usize; used : usize } where free + used = cap

let slots : mutex<pool> @level(2) = mutex { free = cap; used = 0 }

let take () : bool @suspends =
  lock slots (let (p : borrowed inout mutable pool) =>
    if p.free > 0 then (p.free <- p.free - 1; p.used <- p.used + 1; true)
    else false)
  • Lock invariant. pool's refinement free + used = cap holds whenever the mutex is unlocked. Inside the closure it is assumed on entry and proved on exit, just as a loop invariant is. This is the "monitor invariant" of Chalice and VeriFast, and it is free in Pia: the refinement type already says it.
  • The body may not suspend. A lock closure must not wait. Critical sections stay short, a worker never parks while holding a lock, and lock-order checking only has to look at straight-line code. Allocation inside a lock body is allowed. Waiting for a lock does suspend the task, not the worker.
  • Two flavours. mutex is task-aware: a task that finds it held suspends. spin_mutex busy-waits and is for very short sections inside the runtime itself, such as the scheduler's queues.

docs.title: Lock levels rule out lock-order deadlocks
docs.text:
Every lock has a static level, written @level(n). A task may only acquire a lock whose level is greater than every lock it already holds. The type checker tracks the set of held levels through lock bodies and across calls. A function's interface records the highest level it may acquire, as @acquires(n), inferred inside a module and written in exported interfaces. A call to a function that acquires level 2 while holding level 3 is a compile error.

Acquiring in a fixed order is the classic lock-ordering argument, and it makes lock-order cycles impossible. Linux's lockdep checks it at run time; Pia checks it at compile time. Levels are numbers, not a declared lattice, which keeps the check simple. Locks of equal level may not be nested. Two locks of the same level that must be held together, such as two accounts in a transfer, are taken with lock2, which orders them by address and is proved once in the library.

Deadlocks through channels, joins and barriers cannot be ruled out by levels. They have their own checks (section 5).

docs.title: Channels move ownership
docs.text:
send takes its value moved, so the sender cannot touch it afterwards, and the receiver owns it. Nothing sent through a channel can be raced on, whatever it contains. A channel's two ends are separate values, and both are @linear. receiver<T> has one consumer. sender<T> can be cloned for more producers, every copy must be consumed, and the channel closes when the last one is. A borrowed sender<T> is shareable. select waits on several channels and returns the first ready one.

let pipeline (src : moved receiver<tile>) (dst : moved sender<tile>) : unit @suspends =
  for t in src do                        (* each t is owned here *)
    smooth t;                            (* so it can be mutated without a lock *)
    wait (send dst t)                    (* and handed on: t is dead after this *)
  done

docs.title: What a race is
docs.text:
Two accesses to the same resource race if they come from different tasks, at least one of them writes, at least one of them is not atomic, and neither happens before the other. That is the C++ and LLVM definition of a data race, applied to memory, and Pia applies it to other resources too (below).

The prover must show that for every pair of accesses that could run concurrently, one of these holds:

  1. Ownership. Only one task can reach the resource: it was moved to that task, or sent through a channel.
  2. Shared reading. Both accesses are reads through fixed borrows. A fixed value has no interior mutability, so any number of tasks may read it.
  3. Disjointness. Both tasks reach the same buffer, but through slices or index sets that are proved not to overlap.
  4. Protection. The resource is inside a mutex, rwlock or other primitive, and the accesses are inside its lock.
  5. Atomicity. Both accesses are atomic operations on an atomic<T>. They do not race, though whether the program is right is a separate goal (section 4).
  6. Ordering. A happens-before edge separates them: a join, a channel send and its receive, a barrier, or an acquire that reads a release.

docs.title: Who proves what
docs.text:
Each rule is discharged by the cheapest stage that can, in the verifier's fixed order (ADR 0020). The stage is recorded with the goal, as for every other goal.

Stage Proves How Types rules 1, 2, 4, 6 for joins and channels ownership and borrow checking, extended with the sendable and shareable concepts and with task boundaries Presburger (FPL) rule 3 when the indices are affine the access relations of two tasks, intersected; an empty intersection is a proof Z3 rule 3 when they are not data-dependent indices, as for any non-affine goal; a model is a counterexample Model checker rules 5 and 6 for atomics, the primitives' own implementations, protocols, and deadlock explores the interleavings of tasks as state machines

Most programs never reach the model checker. They use ownership, spread over disjoint tiles, locks that own their data and channels that move values. The type checker settles those quickly and predictably. The model checker is for the library's primitives, which are proved once, and for programs that build their own synchronisation from atomics.

docs.title: Types: sendable and shareable
docs.text:
Two concepts (ADR 0009) say which values may cross a task boundary. They are Rust's Send and Sync, named as Pia names things.

  • sendable T: a T may be moved to another task. True unless T holds a borrow that the receiving task could outlive. Inside a scope, borrows of the parent's data are fine.
  • shareable T: a T may be borrowed by several tasks at once. True for any fixed data, since fixed has no interior mutability. Of the types with interior mutability, only the primitives are shareable: atomic<T>, mutex<T>, rwlock<T>, sender<T>, once<T> and so on.

Both are derived by a metaprogram over a type's fields, as @derive(eq) is, so user types get them without writing anything. A @linear allocator is sendable but not shareable. spawn requires its closure's captures to be sendable if moved and shareable if borrowed. That one rule is what turns the existing borrow checker into a race checker.

Module-level mutable state is shared by every task in the program, so it must be shareable. A module-level let mutable of a plain type is a compile error when the module is used from more than one task. The fix is to wrap it in a mutex or make it atomic, or to keep it inside a task.

docs.title: Disjointness: FPL first
docs.text:
spread, and tasks that are spawned in a loop, are the main source of shared buffers. For each pair of tasks the verifier builds the relation "task i writes element e" and "task j reads or writes element e", adds i != j, and asks FPL whether the relation is empty. This is the same dependence relation spread legality and the vectoriser already use (ADR 0020). The same check covers slices handed to separately spawned tasks, as in total above, where 0 .. n/2 and n/2 .. n are disjoint.

When an index depends on data, such as a histogram whose bin comes from a pixel, the goal goes to Z3. If Z3 finds a model, it is the counterexample:

$ piac --verify hist.pia
hist.pia:12:7: error: possible data race on `counts.[b]`
  spread iterations i = 3 and j = 4 both write counts.[7]
  witness (z3): px.[3] = 200, px.[4] = 201, b = px / 32 = 7 in both
  help: give each task its own `counts` and merge with `all_reduce add`,
        or make the bins `atomic<u32>` and use `atomic_add relaxed`

The second suggestion leads to the next rule.

docs.title: Atomics and memory orders
docs.text:
Atomic accesses never race in the data-race sense, but code built from atomics can still be wrong. The usual mistake is to publish data with a flag that is written relaxed, so the reader sees the flag but not the data. Pia's rule is that a happens-before edge from atomics only counts if the orders create one, as C++ defines it: a release store read by an acquire load.

The model checker supports sequential consistency and release/acquire from the start. relaxed is harder: reasoning about it needs a weak memory model such as RC11, with the out-of-thin-air problem that comes with it. So the plan is:

  • relaxed operations whose results never create an ordering, such as a statistics counter or the histogram bins above, are accepted by the type checker. The rule is that the value read is not used to decide whether to touch other shared data.
  • Any other use of relaxed is an unproved obligation, so it is an error by default, until the model checker gains an RC11 mode. GenMC and CDSChecker show it can be done.

ADR 0052 replaces this plan: the language memory model is RC11 from the start (Pia.Memory), checked by a battery of litmus tests, so every order, relaxed included, is reasoned about under the same axioms.

docs.title: Resources other than memory
docs.text:
"Resource" means more than memory. Foreign declarations may give a footprint, a named abstract resource with an optional range, and the race prover treats it like a buffer.

  • File descriptors. An fd is @linear, so one task owns it, and two tasks cannot write to it at once. A shared<fd> is shareable, but it only offers positioned operations: pread and pwrite, whose footprint is fd[offset .. offset + len]. Two tasks writing to one file are race-free when FPL proves their ranges disjoint. That is how the flagship demo can write tiles of one output image in parallel.
  • Process-wide resources. Standard output, the working directory, the environment and signal dispositions are module state of Pia.Sys, behind primitives. print from two tasks locks stdout, so lines never interleave mid-line.
  • Out of scope. Pia cannot see other processes, so races on the file system between processes (one program renames a file another opens) are not proved. Advisory locks (flock) can be wrapped, but what another process does is not a Pia proof.

docs.title: Foreign code
docs.text: A foreign function is opaque. Its declaration says whether it may be called concurrently: @threadsafe means calls from several tasks may overlap, @serial means the library wraps it in a lock, and a declaration with neither may only be called from one task, as if it were @linear module state. A wrong @threadsafe is a trust item, like any other foreign contract, and it is listed in the trust report. This is also where TSan earns its keep (the sanitizer design, ADR 0025, in review): it instruments both sides, so a race between Pia and C code shows up in a --config=tsan run.

docs.title: 4. The model checker
docs.text:
The model checker pass, already planned in ADR 0014, covers what the type system cannot. It runs on the pia_par dialect after coroutine lowering, so each task is a state machine and each transition is the code between two synchronisation points.

What it checks:

  1. The primitives. mutex, rwlock, chan, barrier, once and the work-stealing deque are written in Pia over atomic<T> and the scheduler. Each is proved against its contract: mutual exclusion, the lock invariant, no lost wake-ups, FIFO delivery, the barrier releasing exactly when n tasks arrive. These proofs run once, when the library builds, and every program then relies on the contracts.
  2. Protocols and deadlock. No set of tasks is ever blocked forever on each other's channels, joins or barriers (section 5). The topology check, the protocol metaprogram and the library's patterns settle the regular cases. The model checker takes the rest.
  3. User code built from atomics, under the memory orders it uses.

How it works:

  • Exhaustive, never bounded. It explores every interleaving, using dynamic partial-order reduction (DPOR, as in Nidhugg, GenMC and Rust's Loom) and symmetry between identical tasks. A search that hits its state limit is unproved, not proved. A bounded check is a test, and Pia does not count tests as proofs.
  • Small models, parametric results. Checking a mutex for 2 or 3 tasks proves it for any number of tasks only when a cutoff argument justifies it. For the library primitives that argument is written once as a lemma. For user code, a parametric claim the checker cannot justify is unproved.
  • Abstraction. The data inside tasks is abstracted to what the protocol reads, the rest being havoc, with contracts carried over as assumptions. Without that, the state space is the product of every task's variables.
  • Counterexamples are schedules. A failure is a sequence of task steps. piac prints it with source locations, the language server shows it in the editor, and Pia.Task.run_deterministic replays it.

Writing a model checker is real work, so it comes after the type-level checks. The first programs, spread over tiles with collectives, need only types and FPL. The library primitives can start as trusted wrappers around os_unfair_lock and pthreads (both already in stdlib.md), and are replaced by proved Pia implementations when the checker lands. The trust report shows the difference.

docs.title: 5. Deadlock freedom for channel communication
docs.text: Programs in the style of CSP (Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes, as in occam and Go) build concurrency out of tasks that share nothing and talk only through channels. They cannot race, because send moves ownership. They can still deadlock: a set of tasks each blocked on a send or recv that only another task in the same set could complete. Lock levels do not help here. So every scope that uses channels gets a deadlock goal: no reachable state leaves a set of tasks blocked forever. Like any other goal, it is a compile error when it is unproved.

docs.title: What counts as a deadlock
docs.text:
In any state, every blocked task is waiting for someone:

Blocked on Can be woken by recv on an empty channel any holder of a sender, or the last sender being consumed, which closes the channel send on a full channel, or any send on a rendezvous channel (cap = 0, CSP's synchronous send) the holder of the receiver, or the receiver being consumed, which makes send return Err Closed join the child task barrier, event, promise the tasks that have not arrived yet, or the holders of the notifier or the writer select anyone who can wake any of its arms

A state is deadlocked when there is a non-empty set D of blocked tasks such that every task that could wake a member of D is itself in D. This covers partial deadlocks too, such as two workers stuck waiting on each other while a server keeps running, not only "every task has stopped". The condition is about a single state, so checking it needs no fairness assumptions.

Three rules from earlier sections keep the waits-for relation small and computable:

  • Who can wake a task is known. A receiver<T> is @linear, and a sender<T> is @linear too: more producers come from clone, and every copy must be consumed on every path. The holders of each end are therefore values the compiler tracks. A channel closes exactly when its last sender is consumed, so "forgot to close the channel" is a type error rather than a hang.
  • Mutexes are not in the relation. A lock body cannot suspend, so a task holding a mutex always makes progress, and waiting for a mutex always ends. Lock levels already rule out cycles among locks.
  • Channels are bounded. chan<T, cap> always has a capacity. There are no unbounded channels, which would hide memory exhaustion and give the model checker infinite states.

docs.title: Three stages, cheapest first
docs.text:
Stage 1: topology. The compiler extracts each scope's channel topology from ownership. The nodes are the tasks spawned in the scope and the parent. There is an edge wherever a task holds one end of a channel and another task holds the other, and from each child to the parent that joins it. Structured scopes make this graph static for most programs. If the graph is a forest, so that no two tasks are linked by two different paths, and every task drains its inputs (it receives until they close, then consumes its senders), then the scope is deadlock-free. A lemma proved once in the library covers this. Pipelines, broadcast trees and fan-in through one shared channel are all forests, and they cover most stream programs, including the flagship demo's tile pipeline.

A graph that only avoids directed cycles (a DAG) is not enough with bounded channels. In the diamond below, every channel points downstream, yet the program can deadlock:

let diamond (items : moved receiver<job>) (out : moved sender<res>) : unit @suspends =
  let (l_in, l_inr)   = chan 1 in
  let (r_in, r_inr)   = chan 1 in
  let (l_out, l_outr) = chan 1 in
  let (r_out, r_outr) = chan 1 in
  scope (let (s) =>
    let split = spawn s (let () => alternate items l_in r_in) in   (* l, r, l, r, ... *)
    let left  = spawn s (let () => work l_inr l_out) in
    let right = spawn s (let () => work r_inr r_out) in
    let merge = spawn s (let () => drain l_outr out; drain r_outr out) in  (* all of left first *)
    join split; join left; join right; join merge)

$ piac --verify diamond.pia
diamond.pia:6:3: error: possible deadlock in this scope
  tasks split, left, right and merge can all block forever:
    split  sends to r_in      (full, capacity 1)    diamond.pia:7
    right  sends to r_out     (full, capacity 1)    diamond.pia:9
    left   receives from l_in (empty)               diamond.pia:8
    merge  receives from l_out (empty)              diamond.pia:10
  witness (model checker): a schedule of 11 steps, replay with --replay=diamond.trace
  help: merge with `select` over both inputs, or use `Pia.Chan.fan_in`

Stage 2: protocols. For each channel end a function uses, the compiler infers a usage protocol: a finite automaton over its sends, receives and closes, which is the function's control flow projected onto that end. work above follows (recv; send)* ; close on its two ends. Protocols are inferred inside a module and written as @protocol on exported parameters, so the check is modular. The protocol metaprogram from ADR 0014 checks that the protocols at the two ends of every channel are compatible, as it already does for collectives. This is not session typing, which ADR 0014 rejected: the type system is unchanged, and protocols are contracts the metaprogram checks.

The library also ships patterns with deadlock-freedom lemmas proved once, for any number of tasks:

  • pipeline and broadcast tree (stage 1 already covers these);
  • worker pool: a dispatcher, n identical workers and a collector, joined through one fan-in channel;
  • request and reply: the request carries a one-shot promise for its reply, so the reply cannot block the server;
  • scatter and gather, the channel form of the collectives.

When a scope's topology and protocols match a pattern, the goal is discharged by the pattern's lemma, with no state exploration. This is how a worker pool of n tasks is proved for every n.

Stage 3: the model checker. Anything else goes to the model checker (section 4). The protocol automata of every task in the scope, together with the channel capacities, form a finite system once data is abstracted away. The checker explores it with DPOR and tests the deadlock condition in every state. It finds request cycles (A waits for B's reply while B waits for A's), the diamond above, and mismatched rendezvous orders. Parametric claims need symmetry and a cutoff lemma, otherwise they are unproved. Channels sent over channels (mobile topologies, as in the pi-calculus) are explored while their number stays bounded. Topologies that grow with the data, such as a task spawned for each element of an input stream, are unproved unless they match a pattern.

Timeouts. A select with an after d arm is never blocked forever, so it is not a deadlock. It can still spin forever. Deadlock freedom is a safety property, and proving progress (liveness) is a later extension.

docs.title: 6. Unproved races
docs.text:
An unproved race goal is like any other unproved goal: piac refuses to compile (codegen.md). The error names both accesses, the tasks they come from, the stage that tried, and a witness: an FPL sample point, a Z3 model, or a model-checker schedule.

To compile anyway, --allow-unproved accepts race goals by kind:

Flag Accepts --allow-unproved=race:hist.pia:12 the race goals on line 12 --allow-unproved=deadlock:pipeline the deadlock goals of scopes in function pipeline --allow-unproved=relaxed:Stats relaxed uses in module Stats that need RC11

An accepted race is a trust item in the module's certificate (below), and piac says that a --config=tsan build would check it at run time.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces and proof certificates
docs.text:
Modules are verified separately (ADR 0010), so every fact a caller's race proof needs must be in the interface. These join the interface, and so the interface hash and the witness symbols (ADR 0024):

Fact Example Why callers need it Suspension @suspends the caller must be @suspends or use run Blocking @blocking the caller must offload it Lock levels @acquires(3) the caller's held levels must be below 3 Concurrency of calls @threadsafe, @serial whether two tasks may call it at once Concepts of exported types sendable, shareable whether a value may cross a task boundary Module-state footprint which shared primitives a function touches rules 4 and 6 across modules Channel protocols @protocol((recv; send)* ; close) on a channel-end parameter deadlock goals across modules

A change to any of these changes the interface hash, so a library whose function starts acquiring a higher-level lock, or stops being @threadsafe, no longer loads against a binary built for the old one. The ABI evolution rules apply as before. Interfaces refine safely when a function acquires lower levels (or none), suspends where it used to block, or becomes @threadsafe where it was @serial.

The certificate records each race and deadlock goal with its stage: types, presburger, smt, topology, protocol (with the pattern it matched) or mc. Model-checker results also record the state count and the reduction used, and are only recorded when the search was exhaustive. The trust section gains:

  • race, deadlock and relaxed goals accepted with --allow-unproved;
  • @threadsafe claims on foreign declarations;
  • primitives that are still trusted wrappers rather than proved Pia.

The loader checks nothing new at run time. The concurrency facts are part of the interfaces it already matches. pia-cert audit and piac --trust-report show them alongside the other trust items.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
System What Pia takes Rust (Send, Sync, Mutex<T>, thread::scope, async) ownership-based race freedom; locks that own data; scoped tasks; stackless coroutines C++20 coroutines, LLVM llvm.coro.* the stackless lowering and frame elision Trio, Kotlin, Swift structured concurrency tasks joined inside the scope that started them Go, Erlang, Java virtual threads the case for stackful green threads, and why Pia does not take it Pony (reference capabilities) race freedom from capabilities checked by the type system Chalice, VeriFast, Iris and RustBelt lock invariants; the theory for proving primitives built from atomics Linux lockdep, Fuchsia lock levels static lock ordering GenMC, CDSChecker, Nidhugg, Loom exhaustive checking with DPOR under C11-style memory models SPIN, TLA+ and TLC explicit-state model checking of protocols CSP and FDR, occam channel-only concurrency, and refinement checking of CSP processes for deadlock freedom Go (runtime detector; static checkers such as Gong and Godel) Go's runtime detects only global deadlock; the static checkers extract channel behaviour and model-check it, as Pia's stages 2 and 3 do Kobayashi's deadlock-free pi-calculus types the idea that a forest-shaped topology and usage protocols are enough for most programs Eraser, RacerD, TSan lockset and happens-before race detection, which is dynamic or unsound, so Pia uses TSan only for the trusted boundary

Two alternatives were considered and set aside. Lockset analysis (RacerD, Eraser) finds many races cheaply but is not sound, so it cannot discharge a proof goal. Full separation-logic annotations (Iris, VerCors, Viper) are sound and very expressive, but ask every user to write permissions by hand. Pia's types infer the common cases, and the heavier reasoning is kept for the library primitives, which are written once.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text:
The order follows what the flagship demo needs, then general programs:

  1. Race checks in the type checker: sendable and shareable, task boundaries, module-level state. spread over moved tiles needs only this.
  2. Disjointness goals for concurrent slices and footprints, through FPL then Z3, with counterexamples.
  3. Coroutine lowering: wait, yield, @suspends inference, frames of known size, lowering to llvm.coro.*.
  4. Pia.Task: scope, spawn, join, the work-stealing scheduler, the deterministic mode, and moving spread onto it.
  5. Pia.Io: kqueue, timers, offload and @blocking.
  6. Pia.Sync and Pia.Chan: primitives as trusted wrappers first, with lock invariants, lock levels and @acquires.
  7. The model checker: DPOR, SC and release/acquire, deadlock, schedule counterexamples. Then proved Pia implementations of the primitives replace the trusted wrappers.
  8. Certificates: the concurrency facts in interfaces and hashes, race goal kinds, trust items, --allow-unproved=race:....
  9. RC11 mode for relaxed atomics.
  10. Deadlock freedom for channel communication: channel topology and the forest lemma, then inferred protocols with compatibility checks and pattern lemmas, then the waits-for deadlock check in the model checker.

Each step is a GitHub issue under the tracking issue #74: #75 to #83 for steps 1 to 9, and #111, #112 and #113 for step 10.

docs.title: The C++23 standard library in Pia
docs.text:
Status: proposed design (ADR 0040). This page maps every C++23 standard header onto the Pia module that provides it, and is updated by each library pull request, so it is also the library's status page. The first pieces are in the core, and lib/ has its first modules, Pia.Core.Bit, Pia.Core.Int, Pia.Core.Order, Pia.Core.Option and Pia.Core.Result (lib/Pia/Core/, tested in tests/std/).

Pia gives what the C++ library lets a program do, in Pia's idioms: slices instead of iterator pairs, result and ? instead of exceptions, explicit allocators instead of std::allocator, concepts instead of comparator objects, and metaprograms instead of type traits. Every function has a contract that the compiler proves, so what is undefined behaviour in C++ is a proof goal at the call in Pia.

Kinds. Direct: the same capability under a Pia name. Idiom: replaced by a different Pia mechanism, named in the row. Core: already part of the language. Deferred: waits on the named language or library work. Out: not provided, for the reason given.

Status. planned (phase number from the ADR), done (with the pull request), or n/a.

docs.text: Header Pia Kind Status <iterator> slices, usize indices (with len xs for "not found"), and container cursors Idiom n/a <ranges> eager algorithms over slices; views such as filter, transform, zip Deferred: function values phase 6 <algorithm> non-modifying Pia.Core.Algo.Search: find, count, contains, mismatch, equal, starts_with, ends_with, search, adjacent_find, min_element, max_element, minmax_element (first smallest, last largest), is_sorted_until, is_sorted, exported as generic functions over Pia.Core.Order's Eq and Ord and proved once (ADR 0043); a position is a usize, len xs when there is none. Pia.Core.Order has min, max, clamp (C++'s ties: the first argument when equivalent), lexicographical_compare (generic over Ord, proved once, exported for every integer type) and lexicographical_compare_three_way (for u8). Overloads taking a predicate or comparator wait for function values (section 6) Direct Pia.Core.Algo.Search, Pia.Core.Order's done <algorithm> modifying Pia.Core.Algo.Modify: fill, copy and copy_backward into an out slice of the source's length, swap_ranges, reverse, replace (by value over Eq, or by a predicate as C++'s replace_if), shift_left, shift_right (the new end or start, as C++20), remove (in Pia.Core.Algo.Remove, so its proof runs in parallel: each kept element at its rank among them, a spec over old xs), each generic and proved once (ADR 0043) with every element of the result in its contract; Pia.Core.Algo.Heap's is_heap_until, is_heap, push_heap, pop_heap, make_heap, sort_heap and sort xs less (a heap sort), with the same comparator law, proved once (185 goals): the heap is stated parent to child, (k - 1) >> 1, sort ensures Pia.Fn.sorted less xs and permutation xs (old xs); sort xs by Ord's less waits for its proof from the comparator form; Pia.Core.Algo.BinarySearch's lower_bound, upper_bound, equal_range and binary_search, by a comparator and by Ord, proved once (99 goals), with C++'s precondition: the range partitioned with respect to the value (below, above), which a sorted range meets; equal_range returns a span and is proved at its instances; Pia.Core.Algo.Partition's is_partitioned, partition_point (by binary search) and partition (a permutation of the input), each with a predicate and proved once (57 goals); Pia.Core.Algo.PartialSort's partial_sort (the first m sorted, none after them less, a permutation) and nth_element (as partial_sort of the first n + 1, O(n log n), with the stronger contract), proved once (82 goals); Pia.Core.Algo.Merge's merge of two sorted ranges into an out slice (sorted, each value as often as in both, stable), proved once (57 goals); next_permutation and prev_permutation parked: their scans are cheap since #282 (a helper spec rise brought one from 232M to 3.5M), but reversing the suffix costs 482M on one invariant and the generic proof does not yet hold; stable forms phase 2 <algorithm> set operations Pia.Core.Algo.Set (includes, set_intersection, set_difference) Pia.Core.Algo.SetUnion (set_union) and Pia.Core.Algo.SetSymmetric (set_symmetric_difference), by a strict weak order, into the first result places of a destination at least as long as the output can be Direct done, proved once (75, 65 and 66 goals), on sets: ranges strictly increasing by less, where C++'s multiset semantics and membership (member, some element equivalent) agree; includes uses binary_search, O(m log n); each operation counts what it writes (members) and writes it strictly increasing; set_union (129M) and set_symmetric_difference (137M) cost most of the set operations to prove, so each is its own module and they prove in parallel; each operation's count is a spec of its own (members, nonmembers), which keeps the proofs cheap; multisets with duplicate elements wait <algorithm> permutations Pia.Core.Algo.Perm Direct phase 1 <algorithm> _if forms, all_of/any_of/none_of, transform, comparator and operation forms no _if names: overloads of find, count, remove, replace, copy, sort, accumulate and the rest that take a predicate, comparator or operation (find xs p, sort xs less); all, any, none Idiom: overloads (ADR 0040 section 6) Pia.Core.Algo.Search's find, count, all, any, none with a predicate (proved once, over a Function object) and mismatch, equal with a binary predicate (proved at each call) done; adjacent_find with a predicate and the comparator forms of min_element, max_element, minmax_element, is_sorted_until, is_sorted, which require Pia.Fn.strict_weak_order less and are proved once (is_sorted says Pia.Fn.sorted less xs), done; the rest phase 6 <numeric> Pia.Core.Int (gcd, midpoint), Pia.Core.Algo.Numeric (iota, accumulate, reduce, inner_product, transform_reduce, partial_sum, inclusive_scan, exclusive_scan, adjacent_difference) Direct gcd (of signed values, unsigned), midpoint done; gcd's contract states its exact value, the exported spec function euclid, and divides is exported with quot_rem; that gcd divides both, and lcm, wait for nonlinear facts the verifier cannot prove yet. Pia.Core.Algo.Numeric's algorithms done, each with its operation as a function value and proved once (165 goals): the contract states the result as a left fold (fold, fold2, scan1, iterate), so overflow is the operation's, one written @overflow(wrap), saturating, or with a requires; reduce and transform_reduce fold in order. iota counting by one also for each integer type but i64, requiring that the last value fits. Exact integer sums by + (an int spec against a fixed-width accumulator) and iota at i64 wait for cheaper proofs C++26 saturation (add_sat, sub_sat, mul_sat, div_sat, saturate_cast) add_sat, sub_sat are the core builtins (+|, -|); mul_sat, div_sat and saturate_cast_<t> (from i64 and u64, since the target cannot be a type argument yet) in Pia.Core.Int Direct done <execution> spread and Pia.Par Idiom (ADR 0014) deferred: M12 <generator> coroutines Deferred (ADR 0027) phase 5
