docs.title: Pia-only modules
docs.text:
These have no C++ standard header. They are listed here because they are library modules with the same three tests each in tests/std.

Module What Status Pia.Image.Bits LSB-first bit fields over a byte slice, as GIF's LZW and deflate read them: read_bits and write_bits for fields of up to 16 bits, proved against bits_at, the field as its bits, with the write's frame proved (ADR 0054) done (173 goals) Pia.Image.Raster image dimensions (dims), the index of a sample and the rows of a rectangle, each proved to lie below size w h c (ADR 0054) done (50 goals) Pia.Image.Gif.Spec, Pia.Image.Gif.Lzw GIF's LZW decoder, codes of 3 to 12 bits with the deferred clear, into a caller's buffer with a 12288-byte dictionary table the caller lends; total on every input, each code's string proved to be the spec's (sym), every index proved below 2^m, and checked against giflib on five streams (ADR 0054) done Pia.Image.Gif.Decode the GIF container: info (screen, frame count, NETSCAPE2.0 loop count) proved to return Ok exactly when Gif.Spec's block grammar accepts the input, and decode_frame, which composites frames 0 to k into a caller's RGBA buffer with local or global palettes padded to 256 colours, interlacing (its row order proved a permutation), transparency, disposal and clipping to the screen; checked against giflib on three files, every truncation and every one-byte corruption (ADR 0054) done Pia.Image.Gif.LzwEncode, Pia.Image.Gif.Encode animated GIF encoding: encode_animation writes a global palette, the NETSCAPE2.0 loop count, and per frame a Graphic Control Extension and only the rectangle that changed, LZW-coded over a hash in a caller's table with a clear when the dictionary fills; every code proved below 2^width at width at most 12, the output proved to fit in size_bound bytes, and Ok proved to be a GIF by Gif.Spec's grammar with the frames and screen asked for; checked with giflib and Gif.Decode on two animations (ADR 0054) done; the round trip waits on ADR 0058 Pia.Image.Gif.Quantise RGB to a palette of at most 256 colours and an index raster: the input's own colours when there are few enough (each pixel then proved to map to its exact colour), else median cut over caller-lent boxes and a histogram; every index proved below the palette size; and encode_rgb_animation, one shared palette for every frame; no claim about visual quality; checked with giflib on a 6-colour animation (exact) and a gradient (ADR 0054) done Pia.Compress.Huffman, Pia.Compress.Inflate.Spec, Pia.Compress.Inflate, Pia.Compress.Zlib deflate and zlib decoding into a caller's buffer: canonical Huffman tables whose completeness is the Kraft sum, stored, fixed and dynamic blocks with every distance proved at most the bytes written, lengths and distances proved to be RFC 1951's base plus extra bits, and Adler-32 proved equal to RFC 1950's definition; checked against zlib on 13 streams, every truncation and every one-byte corruption (ADR 0054) done; whole-stream conformance waits on ADR 0058

docs.title: Demo: edge detection
docs.text: This demo is a real program built with Pia: an image pipeline that finds the edges in a picture. It turns a colour image into brightness, blurs it to remove noise, and runs the Sobel operator to measure how sharply the brightness changes at each pixel. piac proves every array index, every sum and every narrowing in the pipeline before it generates any code, and the compiled loops have no bounds checks.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
On an Apple Silicon Mac, from a checkout of the repository:

bazel run //examples/edges

With no arguments the demo draws a test scene (a sky, a sun and a house, with some noise), runs the Pia pipeline over it, and writes two files in the directory you ran it from: edges-input.bmp and edges-output.bmp. It also prints both images as text, so you can see the result in the terminal: the outlines of the sun, the roof, the walls and the window, with the noise gone.

open edges-input.bmp edges-output.bmp

To run it on your own picture, convert it to BMP first. On macOS, sips does that:

sips -s format bmp photo.jpg --out "$PWD/photo.bmp"
bazel run //examples/edges -- photo.bmp photo-edges.bmp
open photo-edges.bmp

The image processing is all Pia, in examples/edges/edges.pia. Pia has no I/O yet, so a small C program, main.c, reads and writes the BMP files and calls the compiled Pia function edges through the C ABI. The tests compare each pass with a C reference over images of several sizes:

bazel test //examples/edges/...

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
(* Edge detection: the Pia demo (docs/demo.md).

   `edges` takes an image as packed RGB bytes, `w` pixels wide, and writes
   an edge map that is bright where the brightness changes sharply. It runs
   three passes, and the verifier proves every index, every sum and every
   narrowing in them before any code is generated:

   1. `gray`, from RGB to brightness,
   2. `blur`, a 3x3 box blur that smooths out noise,
   3. `sobel`, the Sobel operator, which measures how fast the brightness
      changes at each pixel.

   An image is stored row by row, so the pixel above `m` is `m - w` and the
   pixel below is `m + w`. The row loops keep a row on each side of the one
   they are working on, and the column loops keep a column on each side, so
   every neighbour is in bounds. Pia does not allocate memory yet, so the
   caller passes the buffers.

   The file is written to keep the solver's work small. It adds where it
   could multiply (`len dst + len dst + len dst`, `mr + mr`), because a
   module that multiplies is encoded with wider bit-vectors
   (docs/verifier.md). Each pixel is read by a function of its own, whose
   precondition says the whole 3x3 window is in bounds, and the column
   loops `assert` the step from the loop bounds to that precondition.
*)
module Edges : Pipeline
(* Brightness, as (r + 2g + b) / 4, a cheap stand-in for BT.601's
   0.299r + 0.587g + 0.114b. The weights add up to 4, so the result fits in
   a byte. *)
let luma (r : u8) (g : u8) (b : u8) : u8 =
  let y : u16 = r + g + g + b in
  y / 4

let gray (rgb : [u8]) (dst : out mutable [u8]) : unit
=
  for i in 0..len dst do
    let j = i + i + i in
    dst.[i] <- luma (rgb.[j]) (rgb.[j + 1]) (rgb.[j + 2])
  done

(* The mean of pixel `m` and its eight neighbours. *)
let mean_at (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (m : usize) : u8
  requires w < m && m + w + 1 < len src
=
  let a = m - w in
  let b = m + w in
  let s : u16 =
    src.[a - 1] + src.[a] + src.[a + 1]
    + src.[m - 1] + src.[m] + src.[m + 1]
    + src.[b - 1] + src.[b] + src.[b + 1]
  in
  s / 9

(* Blurs the row that starts at `r`, apart from its first and last
   pixels. *)
let blur_row (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (r : usize) (dst : inout mutable [u8])
  : unit
  requires len dst = len src && w >= 3 && w <= r && r + w + w <= len src
=
  for x in 1..w - 1 do
    assert x + 1 < w;
    assert r + x + 1 < r + w;
    dst.[r + x] <- mean_at src w (r + x)
  done

(* A 3x3 box blur, which smooths out noise. Border pixels are copied
   unchanged. *)
let blur (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (dst : out mutable [u8]) : unit
=
  for i in 0..len src do dst.[i] <- src.[i] done;
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while w <= len src - (r + w)
    invariant w <= r && r + w <= len src
    decreases len src - r
  do
    blur_row src w r dst;
    r <- r + w
  done

(* The Sobel gradient at a pixel, from its eight neighbours: how much
   brighter its right side is than its left side (gx), and its bottom than
   its top (gy). The edge strength |gx| + |gy| is clamped to 255. *)
let strength (tl : u8) (tc : u8) (tr : u8) (ml : u8) (mr : u8) (bl : u8)
    (bc : u8) (br : u8) : u8 =
  let right : u16 = tr + mr + mr + br in
  let left : u16 = tl + ml + ml + bl in
  let bottom : u16 = bl + bc + bc + br in
  let top : u16 = tl + tc + tc + tr in
  let gx : u16 = if right > left then right - left else left - right in
  let gy : u16 = if bottom > top then bottom - top else top - bottom in
  let g : u32 = gx + gy in
  if g > 255 then 255 else g

(* The edge strength of pixel `m`. *)
let strength_at (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (m : usize) : u8
  requires w < m && m + w + 1 < len src
=
  let a = m - w in
  let b = m + w in
  strength (src.[a - 1]) (src.[a]) (src.[a + 1])
    (src.[m - 1]) (src.[m + 1])
    (src.[b - 1]) (src.[b]) (src.[b + 1])

(* The edge strength of the row that starts at `r`, apart from its first
   and last pixels. *)
let sobel_row (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (r : usize) (dst : inout mutable [u8])
  : unit
  requires len dst = len src && w >= 3 && w <= r && r + w + w <= len src
=
  for x in 1..w - 1 do
    assert x + 1 < w;
    assert r + x + 1 < r + w;
    dst.[r + x] <- strength_at src w (r + x)
  done

(* The edge strength of every pixel. Border pixels are 0. *)
let sobel (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (dst : out mutable [u8]) : unit
=
  for i in 0..len src do dst.[i] <- 0 done;
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while w <= len src - (r + w)
    invariant w <= r && r + w <= len src
    decreases len src - r
  do
    sobel_row src w r dst;
    r <- r + w
  done

(* The whole pipeline. `luma_buf` and `smooth` hold the intermediate
   images. *)
let edges (rgb : [u8]) (w : usize) (luma_buf : out mutable [u8])
    (smooth : out mutable [u8]) (dst : out mutable [u8]) : unit
=
  gray rgb luma_buf;
  blur luma_buf w smooth;
  sobel smooth w dst

(* What main.c calls, by its C names (ADR 0039). The helpers above are
   private to the module. *)
interface Pipeline @abi(c) = sig
  let gray : (rgb : [u8]) -> (dst : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len rgb = len dst + len dst + len dst
  let blur : (src : [u8]) -> (w : usize) -> (dst : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len dst = len src && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len src
  let sobel : (src : [u8]) -> (w : usize) -> (dst : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len dst = len src && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len src
  let edges : (rgb : [u8]) -> (w : usize) -> (luma_buf : out mutable [u8])
      -> (smooth : out mutable [u8]) -> (dst : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len rgb = len dst + len dst + len dst && len luma_buf = len dst
    requires len smooth = len dst && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dst
end

Every goal in it is proved:

$ piac --verify edges.pia
...
115 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

The row loops are where the proofs matter. An image is stored row by row, so the pixel below m is m + w. In blur and sobel, the loop condition w <= len src - (r + w) says there is a whole row after row r, and the invariant r + w <= len src keeps that subtraction from going below zero. Together they prove the precondition of blur_row and sobel_row, r + w + w <= len src, and nothing in the loop can overflow: there is no r + 2 * w that could wrap around for a huge image. In the row functions, the column loop asserts x + 1 < w and then r + x + 1 < r + w. With r + w + w <= len src, that gives the precondition of mean_at and strength_at for pixel m = r + x: w < m && m + w + 1 < len src. That says the whole 3x3 window around m is in the image, from m - w - 1 up to b + 1 = m + w + 1, so each of the nine reads is proved from it directly.

Splitting the work up this way is for the solver's sake. Each query holds one function and the goals before it, so small functions with precise preconditions keep the queries small, and the two assertions give the solver the steps it would otherwise have to find itself. Written as one loop nest, the same program had goals that Z3 could not settle within its 10-second timeout.

The edges precondition is the contract the C caller has to keep: three bytes per pixel, buffers of the same size, and at least three rows of at least three pixels. Inside Pia, the calls to gray, blur and sobel are checked against their preconditions.

docs.title: A bug the compiler catches
docs.text:
Here is mean_at with a classic off-by-one. Its precondition leaves room for the pixel below m, but not for the one below and to the right:

(* A buggy `mean_at` for the demo (docs/demo.md): its precondition leaves
   room for the pixel below `m`, but not for the one below and to the
   right, so `b + 1` can be past the end of the image. `piac --verify`
   finds the input that breaks it, and `piac --emit=obj` refuses to
   compile it.
*)
let mean_at (src : [u8]) (w : usize) (m : usize) : u8
  requires w < m && m + w < len src
=
  let a = m - w in
  let b = m + w in
  let s : u16 =
    src.[a - 1] + src.[a] + src.[a + 1]
    + src.[m - 1] + src.[m] + src.[m + 1]
    + src.[b - 1] + src.[b] + src.[b + 1]
  in
  s / 9

piac finds an image where it reads past the end:

$ piac --verify edges_buggy.pia

docs.title: Pia language design
docs.text: Status: accepted baseline, 2026-11-20. Each decision here is recorded with its reasoning in docs/adr/. When an ADR and this document disagree, the ADR wins, and this document should be fixed.

docs.title: Purpose and principles
docs.text:
Pia is a formally verified language with an OCaml-like surface and Lisp-style metaprogramming. At compile time a solver (Z3) and cheaper formal methods (interval analysis, set reasoning) prove that each module is internally consistent and keeps the contracts it advertises.

The first milestone is a toy compiler written in C++ on MLIR. It proves and compiles simple SIMD data-processing pipelines for Apple Silicon. The flagship demo is stream delineation (see Stress test).

Principles:

  • Proved, not checked. Every bounds check, overflow rule and contract is a proof obligation at compile time. A runtime check survives only where the source asks for one. The strongest guarantee is always the default.
  • One binding form. let binds every value, including functions and types.
  • Explicit effects at the boundary. Ownership, access and mutability are written on parameters, so a module's interface says everything the prover needs.
  • Metaprogramming is part of the core. Derived code (serialisation, equality, operators) is generated before verification and proved like hand-written code.
  • Fold everything foldable. Facts the prover establishes feed constant folding and vectorisation.
  • Modules are the unit of proof, build and link. Imports name the interfaces they need, so modules build and verify in parallel.

docs.title: Bindings and functions
docs.text:
let is the only binding keyword. A function is a value whose type is an arrow, so naming a function and naming a number look the same.

let width : u32 = 1024
let square = let (x : i32) => x * x
let square (x : i32) : i32 = x * x        (* sugar for the line above *)
let compose f g = let (x) => f (g x)      (* functions take and return functions *)

let rec sum (xs : [i32]) (i : usize) : i64 =   (* recursion needs rec *)
  if i = len xs then 0 else widen xs.[i] + sum xs (i + 1)

let total =
  let a = 3 in
  let b = a * 2 in
  a + b                                    (* local scope with let ... in *)

A nameless let is a function literal: let (x) => x * x is a function object, so there is no fun or lambda keyword. Function literals are curried, so applying one to fewer arguments returns a function. Several parameters are written let (a) (b) => a + b, and each may carry types and modifiers like a named function's parameters.

  • Bindings are immutable. Mutation happens only through a mutable parameter or a mutable local.
  • let rec marks recursion, which the prover must see to demand a termination measure (decreases).
  • Closures capture by borrow unless the capture is written move, so the ownership checker sees every capture.
  • Top-level let in a module is private unless the module's interface exports it.

docs.title: Type system
docs.text:
Every expression has a static type, and there are no implicit conversions. Dynamic typing exists only as dyn, a tagged value whose tag is a closed sum the prover can enumerate.

let shape = type                     (* types are values, so let binds them too *)
  | Circle of f32
  | Rect of { w : f32; h : f32 }

let v : dyn = dyn 42u8              (* tag = u8, payload = 42 *)

let describe (v : dyn) : str =
  match v with
  | (x : u8)  -> "byte"
  | (x : f32) -> "float"
  | _         -> "other"           (* the prover checks this is exhaustive over the tags in scope *)

Types are compile-time values of type type, bound with let like anything else. There is no type declaration keyword: type is only the constructor expression on the right-hand side. A function from types to types is an ordinary function evaluated at compile time: let pair = let (a : type) (b : type) => type { fst : a; snd : b }.

  • A dyn is a pair of tag and payload in the proof model. Each tag maps to a Z3 datatype constructor, so a match over dyn is a case split the solver can check for exhaustiveness and reachability.
  • The set of tags a dyn may hold is part of its type when known (dyn[u8 | f32]), which narrows the case split.
  • Lowering erases a tag when the prover shows only one tag reaches that point, and erases the whole dyn when every use is resolved. The proof keeps the tags. The machine code does not.
  • Generics are monomorphised before verification, so every proof is about concrete types.

docs.title: Primitive types and overflow
docs.text:
Integers are bounded and every arithmetic op has a declared overflow behaviour. The default is @overflow(proof): the compiler must prove the result fits, or compilation fails.

Type Meaning u8 u16 u32 u64 i8 ... i64 machine integers, modelled as Z3 bit-vectors usize index type, bounded by the array it indexes f16 f32 f64 IEEE floats, modelled with Z3's floating-point theory bool true or false int{lo..hi} range type: an integer with static bounds, stored in the smallest fitting width Attribute On overflow Proof obligation @overflow(proof) (default) cannot happen result stays in range @overflow(wrap) modular wrap none @overflow(saturate) clamp to min or max none, maps to NEON saturating ops @overflow(trap) runtime trap none, but the trap is visible in the contract 
let add_px (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 @overflow(saturate) = a + b   (* lowers to uqadd *)
let idx (i : int{0..255}) : u8 = lut.[i]                      (* no bounds check: range proves it *)
let bad (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = a + b                         (* rejected: counterexample a=200, b=100 *)

The attribute can sit on a type (u8 @overflow(wrap)), a function, or a single expression (@wrap (a + b)). Floats get the same idea for NaN and infinity: @finite asks the prover to show no NaN or infinity is produced.

docs.title: Function parameters
docs.text:
Each parameter carries up to three modifiers, one per axis, and omitted ones take the default. The default is borrowed in fixed, a read-only borrow, so the common case needs no annotation.

Axis Options Default What the prover gets Ownership borrowed, moved borrowed a moved value is dead in the caller after the call, so no aliasing to track (checked by IRGen: irgen.md) Access in, out, inout in out must be fully written before return, in is never written Modifiability fixed, mutable fixed a fixed value's model is one constant for the whole call 
let scale
    (src : borrowed in [f32; n])
    (dst : borrowed out mutable [f32; n])
    (k   : f32)
  : unit
  requires n mod 4 = 0
  ensures forall i in 0..n. dst.[i] = src.[i] * k
= for i in 0..n do dst.[i] <- src.[i] * k done

let consume (buf : moved inout mutable [u8]) : [u8] = ...   (* takes ownership, may change and return it *)

Combination rules (proposed, not yet confirmed):

  • out and inout imply mutable, so writing out fixed is an error.
  • Two mutable borrows may not alias. The checker proves disjointness of array slices, which lets dst and src be parts of one buffer.
  • moved in fixed is allowed and means the callee owns a read-only value it may free or store.

docs.title: Structs, arrays and vectors
docs.text:
Structs and arrays are values: they can be bound, passed, returned and compared like integers. Array length is part of the type when known, which is what lets the prover discharge bounds checks.

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 }

let black : pixel = { r = 0; g = 0; b = 0; a = 255 }
let dim = { black with a = 128 }           (* functional update *)

let lut   : [u8; 256]  = ...                (* fixed length, known at compile time *)
let frame : [pixel; n] = ...                (* length is a type-level variable n *)
let row   : [pixel]    = frame.[0 .. w]     (* slice: length carried as a value the prover tracks *)

let v : vec<u8, 16> = splat 0u8             (* SIMD vector, maps to a 128-bit NEON register *)
  • [T; n] is a fixed array, [T] a slice with a proved length, and vec<T, k> a SIMD vector with k * sizeof T equal to 64 or 128 bits.
  • Indexing a.[i] creates the obligation 0 <= i < len a. A failed proof is a compile error with a counterexample.
  • Layout attributes (@packed, @align(16), @soa) control memory layout. @soa stores [pixel; n] as four [u8; n] arrays, which is often what SIMD wants.
  • Equality, ordering and serialisation of structs are not built in. They are derived by metaprograms.

docs.title: Generic types and concepts
docs.text:
Because types are values, a generic type is a compile-time function that returns a type, and users define their own with the same let. Constraints on type parameters are concepts. A concept is a metaprogram that inspects a type and either accepts it or returns a diagnostic.

(* a concept: a compile-time predicate over types, written as a metaprogram *)
let meta Numeric (t : type) : concept =
  has_fn t `( add  : $t -> $t -> $t ) &&
  has_fn t `( mul  : $t -> $t -> $t ) &&
  has_val t `( zero : $t )

let meta Eq (t : type) : concept =
  has_fn t `( eq : $t -> $t -> bool )
  && law `( forall (a : $t). eq a a )                (* a law: proved by Z3 for each instance *)

(* user-defined generic types *)
let pair = let (a : type) (b : type) => type { fst : a; snd : b }
let matrix = let (t : type where Numeric t) (rows : usize) (cols : usize) => type [t; rows * cols]

(* a generic function, checked against the concept once, then monomorphised *)
let sum (t : type where Numeric t) (xs : borrowed in [t]) : t = fold add zero xs

let p : pair u8 f32 = { fst = 1; snd = 2.0 }
let s = sum [1; 2; 3]                                (* t deduced as i32 from the call site *)
let w = sum<i64> [1; 2; 3]                           (* explicit: forces the i64 instance *)
  • Definition check. A generic body may use only what its concepts promise. sum can call add and zero but not <, so a body error is reported at the definition, not at a later instantiation.
  • Use check. At each instantiation the concept metaprogram runs on the concrete type. A failure reports the concept's own message, such as "f16 lacks zero".
  • Laws. A concept can state laws, such as reflexive equality or associative addition. Every instance must prove them, with no @assume escape. The optimiser may then rely on them, for example to reassociate a reduction for SIMD.
  • Adapters. A type that does not meet a concept gets an adapter: a value that supplies the functions the concept checks for, with its laws proved like any other instance. An adapter can be written in any module, not only the one that defines the concept or the type.
  • Derives fit in. @derive(eq) generates the functions that the Eq concept checks for, so derived types satisfy concepts with no extra code.
  • Deduction. Type arguments are deduced from the call site by default. Explicit arguments with angle brackets (sum<i64> xs) force a particular instance or resolve an overload.
  • vec<T, k> is an ordinary generic from the prelude, let vec = let (t : type where Lane t) (k : usize where k * size_of t in {64; 128}) => type ..., and the angle brackets are sugar for applying it.
(* f32's built-in = fails Eq's law: NaN = NaN is false. An adapter fixes that. *)
let eq_f32 : adapter Eq f32 = { eq = let (a) (b) => bits a = bits b }   (* bitwise, so eq a a holds *)

let unique = dedup<f32, eq_f32> samples      (* the adapter is named where it is used *)

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
A contract is any claim the prover must establish, and Pia has four forms. All four lower to the same thing: ops in Pia's contract dialect that become solver assertions.

Form Where Example Refinement type any type let byte_idx = int{0..255}, { x : f32 \| x >= 0.0 } Pre and postcondition function requires n > 0, ensures result <= max xs Invariant loop, struct, module invariant acc <= i * 255 State property module an exported state symbol, changed only as exported pre/postconditions allow 
let range = type { lo : i32; hi : i32 } where lo <= hi      (* struct invariant *)

let clamp (r : range) (x : i32) : { y : i32 | r.lo <= y && y <= r.hi } =
  if x < r.lo then r.lo else if x > r.hi then r.hi else x

interface Stream = sig
  let status = type | Closed | Open | Drained
  let state : status                      (* exported state is just another symbol *)
  let open_ : unit -> unit
    requires state = Closed   ensures state = Open
  let pull  : unit -> [u8]
    requires state = Open     ensures state = Open || state = Drained
  let close : unit -> unit
    requires state <> Closed  ensures state = Closed
end
  • Module state needs no special syntax. An interface is a set of exported symbols, each with its type and its pre- and postconditions, and exported state is one more symbol. An importer proves each call against those contracts, so calling pull on a closed stream fails to verify. The exporting module proves its bodies keep every postcondition.
  • Interval analysis runs first and discharges most bounds and overflow obligations cheaply. Only what remains goes to Z3.
  • An unproved obligation is an error by default. @assume accepts it with a visible note in the interface (never for concept laws), and @check turns it into a runtime check.

docs.title: Metaprogramming and operators
docs.text:
A metaprogram is an ordinary Pia function that runs at compile time and takes and returns syntax. Code is data in the Lisp sense: `( ... ) quotes a piece of code as a syntax value, and $x splices a value back in. Everything a metaprogram generates is type checked and verified like hand-written code.

(* a derive: generate structural equality for any struct *)
let meta derive_eq (t : type_decl) : item =
  let cmps = map (let (f) => `( a.$f = b.$f )) (fields t) in
  `( let eq (a : $t) (b : $t) : bool = $(fold_and cmps) )

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 } @derive(eq, serialise, deserialise)

Operators exist only through metaprograms. The core language has named functions (add, mul_sat), and an operator declaration maps a symbol, a precedence and the operand types to an expansion:

let meta operator ( + ) : prec 6 left = let (a) (b) => `( add $a $b )
let meta operator ( +| ) : prec 6 left = let (a) (b) => `( add_sat $a $b )   (* saturating add *)
let meta operator ( + ) for vec<T, k> = let (a) (b) => `( vec_add $a $b )

Design decisions:

  • Stages. Expansion runs to a fixed point. Code a metaprogram generates is parsed again, and any new metaprogram uses in it (a derive that emits a derive, an operator that expands to another operator) run in turn. Metaprograms see types only once they are fully resolved. A type may itself be generated by another metaprogram in a later pass, so a metaprogram that asks for an unresolved type is deferred to the next pass. The loop stops when a pass generates nothing new and nothing is waiting. A metaprogram still waiting at that point is an error that names the type it needed. This cost is deliberate: every generated item comes out of the loop as ordinary code that is then proved. Hygiene is on by default, and $!name breaks it on purpose.
  • Termination. A compiler flag such as --meta-cycles=N caps the number of expansion passes. Hitting the cap is a compile error that names the metaprograms still producing code. A fuel limit inside a single metaprogram is still useful, and proving termination of macros is a later option.
  • Serialisation targets. The first derives are eq, ord, hash, serialise and deserialise. A deserialise derive also emits the refinement checks, so a parsed value is proved to meet its type's invariants.
  • Prelude. + - * / < = ... are defined by operator metaprograms in a prelude module that every module imports by default.

docs.title: Modules, interfaces and imports
docs.text:
A module is the unit of proof, build and link. It exports named interfaces, and an importer must name each interface it uses, so a module depends on interface files only, never on another module's body.

(* pixels.pia *)
interface PixelOps = sig
  let pixel : type
  let blend : (a : pixel) -> (b : pixel) -> (t : int{0..255}) -> pixel
    ensures result.a = max a.a b.a
end

interface PixelCodec = sig
  let encode : borrowed in [pixel] -> [u8]
  let decode : borrowed in [u8] -> [pixel] | Error
end

module Pixels : PixelOps, PixelCodec = struct ... end

(* filter.pia *)
import Pixels.PixelOps                (* only PixelOps is visible, so filter.pia never rebuilds when PixelCodec changes *)
  • An interface is a set of exported symbols, each with its type, interface and pre- and postconditions. Each interface compiles on its own to a small artifact. Every module that imports it can then type check, verify and compile at once, in parallel.
  • Verification is assume-guarantee. A module proves its body meets its exported contracts while assuming the contracts of the interfaces it imports. No proof ever looks inside another module.
  • Each compiled module carries a proof certificate that records a hash of every interface it was proved against. The linker refuses to link when a hash does not match, so a stale proof cannot reach the binary. Shared libraries publish their interfaces and certificates in the binary, and dyld and the Pia runtime refuse a library that does not provide the hashes a program was proved against (abi.md, ADR 0024).
  • The detailed rules (privacy by default, matching, imports, state, the REPL and the language server) are in ADR 0039.
  • An interface may export a fixed value as a symbol. Importers see its name, type and refinement, and prove against those, so they still build in parallel. The value itself is resolved later, when cross-module constant folding runs. Changing an exported value invalidates the certificates that depend on it and forces dependents to recompile. Inlining works the same way through let inline and const symbols.

docs.title: Compilation pipeline
docs.text:
Verification sits in the middle of the pipeline: after metaprograms expand, so generated code is proved, and before optimisation, so proved facts drive folding and vectorisation.

flowchart TD
  parse["Parse: .pia source to syntax tree"] --> expand["Expand metaprograms: derives, operators"]
  expand -- "new metaprogram uses: parse again until fixed point or --meta-cycles" --> parse
  expand --> tc["Type check and monomorphise: types, tags, ownership, access, mutability"]
  ifaces["Imported interfaces: signatures, contracts, hashes"] --> tc
  tc --> lower["Lower to Pia MLIR dialects: contracts become ops"]
  lower --> verify["Verify: interval analysis, then Z3 on what remains"]
  ifaces --> verify
  verify -- fails --> err["Compile error with a counterexample"]
  verify --> opt["Optimise with proved facts: drop checks, erase tags, fold, vectorise"]
  opt --> cg["Lower to Apple Silicon: linalg/vector, arm_neon, LLVM, arm64"]

Imported interfaces feed type checking and verification as assumptions, which is why modules can build in parallel. An unproved obligation stops the build with a counterexample mapped back to the source line. The optimiser auto-vectorises every loop it can prove safe, using proved trip counts, alignment and non-aliasing. vec<T, k> is there when the author wants to fix the vector shape.

docs.title: Example pipelines
docs.text:
These become the first test suite.

  • Saturating add of two u8 images
  • Dot product of two f32 arrays
  • Clamp and scale an f32 buffer into u8
  • One serialise and deserialise round trip, to exercise derives
  • Tiled matrix multiply generated by a metaprogram from tile sizes

docs.title: Tiled matrix multiply as a metaprogram
docs.text:
Tile sizes are compile-time arguments to a metaprogram, so each instance is a separate, fully unrolled function with its own proof. The spec is the naive triple loop, and the generated body must be proved equal to it.

let meta tiled_matmul
    (name : ident) (t : type where Numeric t)
    (tm : usize) (tn : usize) (tk : usize)        (* register tile and k block *)
    (lanes : usize where lanes * size_of t = 16)  (* one 128-bit NEON register *)
  : item =
  let cols = tn / lanes in                         (* vectors per tile row *)
  `( let $name (m : usize) (n : usize) (k : usize)
         (a : borrowed in [$t; m * k])
         (b : borrowed in [$t; k * n])
         (c : borrowed out mutable [$t; m * n])
       : unit
       requires m mod $tm = 0 && n mod $tn = 0 && k mod $tk = 0
       ensures forall (i in 0..m) (j in 0..n).
         c.[i * n + j] = sum (0..k) (let (p) => a.[i * k + p] * b.[p * n + j])
     =
       for i0 in 0..m step $tm do
       for j0 in 0..n step $tn do
         let acc : mutable [vec<$t, $lanes>; $tm * $cols] = splat zero in
         for p0 in 0..k step $tk do
           $(unroll tk (let (pp) =>
             unroll tm (let (ii) =>
               `( let av = splat a.[(i0 + $ii) * k + p0 + $pp] in
                  $(unroll cols (let (jj) =>
                    `( let bv = load b ((p0 + $pp) * n + j0 + $jj * $lanes) in
                       acc.[$ii * $cols + $jj] <- fma acc.[$ii * $cols + $jj] av bv ))) ))))
         done;
         $(unroll tm (let (ii) => unroll cols (let (jj) =>
           `( store c ((i0 + $ii) * n + j0 + $jj * $lanes) acc.[$ii * $cols + $jj] ))))
       done done )

(* one instance for Apple Silicon: 4 x 16 f32 register tile, k blocked by 64 *)
tiled_matmul `sgemm_4x16 f32 4 16 64 4
  • Metaprogram helpers. unroll n f is itself a metaprogram that splices f 0 to f (n - 1). Its output contains further quotes, so expansion takes several passes to reach its fixed point.
  • Constraints on meta arguments. lanes * size_of t = 16 is checked when the metaprogram is called, so a tile that does not fit a NEON register fails before any code is generated.
  • Bounds proofs from preconditions. Every load, store and index is in range because of the requires clause and the loop steps. Interval analysis should discharge these without Z3.
  • Proving the tiled body against the spec. This holds exactly for integer t (with overflow proved). For f32, tiling reassociates the sum, so one of the approaches below is needed.

docs.title: Floating-point reassociation: three approaches
docs.text:
The default is strict IEEE semantics, so the tiled f32 matmul fails to verify until the author picks one of these. All three are part of Pia, and each trades a different guarantee.

1. Per-function attribute. The author licenses reassociation and fused multiply-add for one function. The prover checks ensures over real numbers, ignoring rounding, and codegen may reorder and fuse.

let sgemm (...) : unit @fp(reassoc, contract)
  ensures ... (* proved over reals *)
= ...

2. A type with a concept adapter. A wrapper type carries the licence, so it travels with the data instead of the function. Its Numeric adapter models addition as real addition in the proof, which lets the associativity law prove. Codegen still emits hardware floats.

let fast = let (t : type where Float t) => type t @fp(reassoc)
let numeric_fast_f32 : adapter Numeric (fast f32) = { add = fadd_reassoc; mul = fmul; zero = 0.0 }

tiled_matmul `sgemm_4x16 (fast f32) 4 16 64 4

3. A tolerance in the contract. Semantics stay strict IEEE, and ensures states an error bound instead of equality. This is the strongest guarantee and the hardest to prove. Bit-precise Z3 floats will not scale here, so it needs a rounding-error analysis pass in the style of interval analysis.

ensures forall (i in 0..m) (j in 0..n).
  abs (c.[i * n + j] - spec i j) <= k * eps f32 * sum (0..k) (let (p) => abs a.[i * k + p] * abs b.[p * n + j])
Approach Licence lives on What is proved Proof cost @fp(reassoc) one function result over reals low fast f32 adapter the type and its data result over reals, law per instance low Tolerance the contract IEEE result within a stated bound high

docs.title: Stress test: stream delineation
docs.text:
Stream delineation is the end-to-end program that exercises everything at once: image I/O, SIMD stencils, a graph algorithm, a conservation law and distributed execution. Input is a PNG or GIF heightmap. Output is a PNG or GIF with streams drawn and coloured by sediment load.

  1. Decode the heightmap with Image.Png or Image.Gif. Decoding is a derived deserialise, so a decoded [u16; w * h] is proved to have the declared size and range.
  2. Fill depressions (priority-flood) so every cell can drain. Proved invariant: after filling, every non-outlet cell has a neighbour that is lower, or equal and closer to an outlet.
  3. Flow direction (D8): each cell points to its steepest downhill neighbour. This is a 3 x 3 stencil and auto-vectorises. The invariant from step 2 proves the direction graph has no cycles.
  4. Flow accumulation: each cell's upstream area, computed in topological order over that acyclic graph. Proved: every cell is visited exactly once.
  5. Sediment transport: erosion from slope and accumulated flow, deposition where the slope flattens, iterated over time steps. Proved conservation law: total sediment eroded equals total deposited plus total leaving through outlets, within the chosen float tolerance.
  6. Render: cells above a flow threshold become streams, coloured by sediment load through a colour map, then Image.Png.encode or Image.Gif.encode.

docs.title: Concurrency by default
docs.text:
The runtime is concurrent by default, with MPI-like collectives as library metaprograms. The grid is split into tiles, each tile is moved to a worker, and neighbouring tiles exchange halo rows between steps.

import Pia.Par.Collectives          (* scatter, gather, halo_exchange, all_reduce *)
import Image.Png.Codec

let sediment_step (grid : borrowed in mutable tiled<cell, 256, 256, halo = 1>) : unit
  ensures total_mass grid = old (total_mass grid) - outflow grid
=
  halo_exchange grid;                               (* neighbours' edge rows, before any stencil read *)
  spread tile in grid @place(auto) do                (* the compiler picks CPU cores or GPU per tile *)
    erode_and_deposit tile
  done;
  let lost = all_reduce add (map outflow_of grid) in  (* collective: every worker joins *)
  record_outflow grid lost

What the prover must establish for this to count as correct by construction:

  • No data races. Each tile is owned by exactly one worker (moved), and halo rows are read-only borrowed copies.
  • Stencils stay in bounds. A 3 x 3 read touches at most 1 cell outside its tile, which is exactly what halo = 1 provides.
  • Collectives match. Every worker reaches every all_reduce and halo_exchange in the same order, so no worker waits forever. A protocol metaprogram checks at compile time that every worker issues the same sequence of collectives. A model checker pass then explores the interleavings that the protocol check cannot settle on its own.
  • Placement does not change results. Moving a tile from CPU to GPU must not change the proved result, which ties back to the float rules.

Coroutines, tasks, locks, atomics, channels and the race prover are designed in concurrency.md (ADR 0027).

Concurrency features are built in the order this demo needs them: collectives and spread loops first, then a task graph for flow accumulation (tiles wait on their upstream neighbours), then futures.

Placement has three forms. @place(auto) lets the compiler's cost model choose. @place(gpu) or @place(cpu) fixes the device. @place(auto, prefer = gpu) keeps the cost model but overrides its choice. CPU cores and the GPU (through Metal) are reachable from MLIR. The Neural Engine is only reachable through Core ML, so it fits fixed operations such as convolutions, and is a later, optional target.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
• Compiler in C++ on MLIR, with Z3 as the solver. See ADR 0011.
  • Build with Bazel (bzlmod), depending on LLVM/MLIR and Z3 as Bazel modules rather than vendored checkouts. See ADR 0017.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page builds piac, proves a first program, compiles it, and sets up VS Code.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Bazelisk. Pia builds with Bazel, at the version in .bazelversion. Bazelisk reads that file and fetches the right Bazel. On macOS, brew install bazelisk.
  • A C++17 compiler. On macOS, Xcode or its command line tools. On Linux, Clang or GCC.
  • Network access to the Bazel Central Registry and GitHub for the first build, which fetches LLVM, MLIR and Z3.

Pia is developed on Apple silicon Macs, and builds, proves, compiles and runs on Linux x86_64 too (ADR 0049).

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/deanberris/pia-lang.git
cd pia-lang
bazel build //tools/piac //tools/pia-lsp

The first build compiles the parts of LLVM and MLIR that Pia uses, which takes 15 minutes or more. Later builds reuse the disk cache in ~/.cache/pia-bazel-disk, including after bazel clean.

The compiler is now at bazel-bin/tools/piac/piac. The examples below call it piac, so put it on your PATH or make an alias:

alias piac="$PWD/bazel-bin/tools/piac/piac"

Run the tests with:

bazel test //...

docs.title: Prove a program
docs.text:
Save this as clamp.pia:

let clamp (lo : i32) (hi : i32) (x : i32) : i32
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
  ensures lo <= x && x <= hi ==> result = x
= if x < lo then lo else if x > hi then hi else x

requires is a precondition: callers must prove it, and the body may assume it. ensures is a postcondition, where result is the value returned. Ask piac to prove it:

$ piac --verify clamp.pia
clamp.pia:3:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
clamp.pia:4:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
2 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Each line is one goal, a fact the compiler had to establish, with its source location and how it was proved: intervals for the cheap range analysis, smt for Z3. The exit status is 0 when nothing failed.

Now break it. Change the postcondition to the wrong claim ensures lo < result, and piac shows inputs where it is false:

let clamp (lo : i32) (hi : i32) (x : i32) : i32
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo < result
= if x < lo then lo else if x > hi then hi else x

$ piac --verify clamp_bad.pia
clamp_bad.pia:3:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample: lo = 1028093, hi = 2147483647, x = 0
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The counterexample is an input that breaks the claim. Here x is below lo, so clamp returns lo, and lo < lo is false. Z3 picks whichever values it finds first, so they can look arbitrary, but they always break the goal.

docs.title: Compile a program
docs.text:
piac --emit=obj proves the program, then compiles it to an object file for the machine it runs on. Code is generated only when no goal fails.

A file is a module, and everything in it is private unless an interface the module claims lists it (ADR 0039). A file with no module header exports nothing. To call clamp from C, give the file a header and list clamp in an interface marked @abi(c), which keeps C names:

module Clamp : Clamping

interface Clamping @abi(c) = sig
  let clamp : (lo : i32) -> (hi : i32) -> (x : i32) -> i32
    requires lo <= hi
    ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
end

let clamp (lo : i32) (hi : i32) (x : i32) : i32
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
  ensures lo <= x && x <= hi ==> result = x
= if x < lo then lo else if x > hi then hi else x

The interface can promise less than the function proves: here it leaves out the last postcondition, and the compiler proves that what the function ensures implies what the interface says.

piac --emit=obj -o clamp.o clamp_c.pia

Each exported function becomes a C function. A C declaration for clamp is:

#include <stdint.h>
int32_t clamp(int32_t lo, int32_t hi, int32_t x);

cc main.c clamp.o -o main

The C ABI section of the codegen notes says how slices, arrays and records are passed. Other outputs stop earlier in the pipeline: --emit=mlir prints the Pia dialects, --emit=core the core MLIR dialects, --emit=llvm the LLVM IR and --emit=asm the assembly.

docs.title: Contracts written once
docs.text:
When a definition's contract is the same as its interface's, leave it off the definition. A function an interface lists, defined with no requires, ensures, costs or reads, takes the interface's contract, with the parameters renamed to the definition's (ADR 0077). The body is proved against it, and callers in the module use it, so here five proves from what count_to inherited, even though count_to's loop hides its result from the verifier:

module Counting : Counter

interface Counter = sig
  let count_to : (n : u32) -> u32
    requires n < 1000
    ensures result = n
end

let count_to (m : u32) : u32
=
  let i : mutable u32 = 0 in
  while i < m
    invariant i <= m
    decreases m - i
  do
    i <- i + 1
  done;
  i

let five (k : u32) : u32
  ensures result = 5
= count_to 5

It is all or nothing: a definition that states any of those clauses states its whole contract, which may be stronger than the interface's, as clamp's is above. A decreases measure alone does not count. A goal an inherited clause raises points at the interface's line, where the clause is written. The repeated_contract lint flags a definition that states exactly its interface's contract, with a fix that deletes it, and pia-lsp shows an inherited contract when you hover over the function.

docs.title: Use another module
docs.text:
Another file reaches clamp by importing the interface that lists it. The importer is built against the interface alone, as an interface artifact, which piac --emit=interface writes, one file per interface (here Clamp.Clamping.piai):

$ piac --emit=interface -o . clamp_c.pia

import Clamp.Clamping finds that file on the interface path, which --iface-path gives, and the module's items are then Clamp.clamp:

import Clamp.Clamping

let fit (lo : i32) (hi : i32) (x : i32) : i32
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result
= Clamp.clamp lo hi x

$ piac --verify --iface-path=. fit.pia
fit.pia:6:3: proved: the precondition of 'Clamp.clamp' holds [smt]
fit.pia:5:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
2 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

The call is checked against the interface's contract, never against the body of clamp: fit proves the precondition lo <= hi from its own, and its postcondition follows from what the interface ensures. The artifact holds only the interface, without comments, private items or bodies, so changing any of those leaves it byte-for-byte the same, and nothing that imports it is rebuilt. To link, compile both files to objects and pass both to the linker. In Bazel, the pia_library rule in //tools/piac:pia.bzl does all of this, and each module sees only the interfaces of the modules it lists in deps (ADR 0039).

docs.title: piac at a glance
docs.text:
Command What it does piac --verify f.pia prove every goal and print a report piac --emit=obj -o f.o f.pia prove, then compile to an object file piac --emit=asm f.pia prove, then print assembly (also llvm, core) piac --emit=obj --report=f.goals -o f.o f.pia the same, also writing the goal report --verify prints to f.goals; pia_library keeps it as <name>.goals, so a test can check what the build proved without proving it again piac --emit=interface -o dir f.pia write the module's interface artifacts to dir piac --verify --iface-path=dir f.pia prove a program that imports interfaces found in dir piac --emit=mlir f.pia print the program in Pia's MLIR dialects piac --verify --emit=mlir f.pia both, with each proved op marked pia.proved piac --dump-smt f.pia print each SMT query sent to Z3 piac --dump-tokens f.pia print the token stream piac --dump-ast f.pia print the syntax tree piac --dump-expanded f.pia print the syntax tree after metaprograms run piac --check f.pia parse only piac --check --fragment=contracts f.pia parse a file of contract clauses alone

--target=<triple> and --cpu=<name> choose the machine (arm64-apple-macosx14.0.0 with apple-m1, or x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu with x86-64-v3; the default is the host), and -O0 to -O3 the optimisation level (default -O2). --meta-cycles=N caps metaprogram expansion (default 32).

The exit status is 0 on success, 1 when the program has an error or a goal fails, and 2 for a usage error.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
The VS Code extension in editors/vscode runs pia-lsp, Pia's language server. It shows failed goals with their counterexamples as errors in the editor, the proofs of each expression on hover, syntax errors as you type, go to definition, an outline and completion.

bazel build //tools/pia-lsp
cd editors/vscode
npm install
npx vsce package
code --install-extension pia-0.1.0.vsix

Then point the extension at the server in VS Code's settings:

"pia.server.path": "/path/to/pia-lang/bazel-bin/tools/pia-lsp/pia-lsp"

By default it verifies when you save. Set "pia.verify.on": "change" to verify as you type. The extension's README lists the settings and how to use pia-lsp from Neovim, Helix, Emacs, Zed or Sublime Text.

docs.title: CPU and GPU, side by side
docs.text:
The terrain demo runs on the CPU and on an Apple GPU, from the same proved Pia. This page puts the two side by side on one real tile, stage by stage. It also says how to run the comparison yourself, and what is proved, what is tested and what is trusted on each side.

The stages are those of the stream delineation and sediment in pull form pages:

  • D8 directions. Each cell points at its lowest neighbour.
  • The picture. Each cell's height and flow become a pixel.
  • The sediment pull step. Each cell takes in what flows into it, then erodes or deposits, one wave of equal-height cells at a time.

On the GPU, the first two stages are each one placed spread (D8 directions and the picture on the GPU). The pull step is a placed for over the waves, which runs a whole step as one Metal command buffer (the sediment pull step on the GPU).

docs.title: The numbers
docs.text:
These are from tile N46E008 in the Swiss Alps: 3601 × 3601 cells, and 3,924 waves in each pull step. They were taken on an Apple M3 iMac on 2026-11-28, over three runs, with the GPU kernels pre-warmed at load (ADR 0068, step 4b). "Warm" is a later run, after the first.

Stage CPU GPU, warm GPU, first run GPU speed-up, warm D8 directions 42 to 43 ms 6 to 7 ms 13 to 19 ms about 6× The picture 30 to 38 ms 8 to 9 ms 24 to 40 ms about 4× Sediment pull, per step 509 to 524 ms 235 to 253 ms 246 to 274 ms about 2.1×

The GPU's results match the CPU's on every cell, in every run. That holds for the directions, the picture's pixels, and each cell's bed and load after four pull steps, and both send 2,861,964 units of sediment off the map.

A whole run of the comparison takes about 53 s.

How the GPU got here:

  • Copies. At first, each run copied every buffer into Metal and back, and the GPU was slower than the CPU. On Apple silicon the CPU and GPU share memory, so the shim now wraps each page-aligned buffer where it is.
  • One command buffer per step. With a command buffer per wave, a pull step took 33 to 57 s, because each of its 3,924 waves waited for the GPU. As one command buffer, the step waits once.
  • Pre-warming. A stage's first run used to open the device and build its pipeline, which put the first run of directions at 42 to 57 ms. Every placed kernel is now built in the background while the program starts.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
You need a Mac with Apple silicon and Xcode's Metal toolchain. Fetch a tile, then build and run the comparison:

examples/streams/fetch_srtm.sh /tmp/srtm
bazel run //examples/streams:srtm_gpu -- /tmp/srtm/N46E008.hgt

It prints one line for each stage, with the CPU time, the GPU's warm and first-run times, and how many cells differ. Then it prints how the buffers were bound, how many dispatches the sequences made, and how many kernels were pre-warmed. It exits non-zero if any cell differs. PIA_GPU_WARM=0 turns pre-warming off, so you can time a cold first run. bazel test //examples/streams:srtm_gpu_run_test runs the same comparison on a 256 × 256 fixture.

docs.title: What is proved, tested and trusted
docs.text:
CPU GPU The algorithm proved: each stage meets its specification, and the pull step conserves mass the same proof, since placement adds no goal Each thread writes only its own cells not needed: the loops are sequential proved, by the ownership check of ADR 0060 The waves of a step proved equal to the sequential step (same_step) proved, when the sequence returns Ok Errors none each GPU stage returns result unit gpu_error, and the caller decides The compiler below Pia's IR LLVM, trusted SPIR-V, SPIRV-Cross, Metal's compiler and the shim, trusted and tested by this comparison (ADR 0068, section 6)

The GPU is trusted no more than the CPU's compiler, and it is tested more: every cell of every stage is compared with the CPU on a real tile.

docs.title: Pia grammar
docs.text:
Status: accepted for milestone M1 (#2), 2026-11-20. The disambiguation rules are recorded in ADR 0019.

This document is the specification. Two files make it executable:

  • grammar/pia_lexer.py is the reference lexer, including the layout rule.
  • grammar/pia.lark is the reference phrase grammar, run by Lark's Earley parser.

tests/grammar/test_grammar.py parses every ocaml code block in design.md, the cases in tests/grammar/valid/, and checks that every case in tests/grammar/invalid/ is rejected. The C++ front end (M2) must accept and reject the same corpus.

Run the tests with pip install -r tests/grammar/requirements.txt and then python3 tests/grammar/test_grammar.py. Bazel will wrap this as a py_test in M0.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: The phrase grammar uses EBNF. x? is optional, x* is zero or more, x+ is one or more, ( ... ) groups, | separates alternatives, and quoted text is a literal token. Names in UPPER_CASE are tokens from the lexical grammar.

docs.title: Whitespace and comments
docs.text:
Spaces, tabs and newlines separate tokens. There are three kinds of comment (ADR 0029):

Comment Spelling Notes Block (* ... *) Nests, as in OCaml. Because (* always opens a comment, the multiplication operator value is written ( * ) with spaces Doc (** ... *) A block comment that documents the code after it. (**) and (*** are ordinary comments Line \ to the end of the line Backslash is used nowhere else outside strings. // and -- stay free for operators, and # for directives

Comments never change how a program parses, and they do not count for the layout rule. They are not thrown away either.

docs.title: Comments in the syntax tree
docs.text:
The parser keeps every comment as a Comment node attached to the node it describes, beside that node's children. Each has a style (line, block, doc or prose), a place and its text, which is the content without delimiters, trimmed, and with the indentation its later lines share removed. Line comments alone on consecutive lines are one comment.

  • A trailing comment has code before it on its line and none after it. It goes to the outermost node that ends at the token before it and starts on that line; if none starts on that line, as after done, to the innermost node that ends there. A ;, , or in before the comment is skipped, so let m = n + 1 in \ one more documents n + 1. After a token that leads into what follows (=, ->, =>, <-, then, else, with, | or an opening bracket), a comment leads instead.
  • Any other comment is leading on the outermost node that starts at the next token, looking past opening brackets. A blank line in between makes it detached, like a section heading. Sequences, parameter lists, contract lists and other groups never take a comment; their first member does.
  • A comment with no code after it is detached on the program.

piac --dump-ast --comments shows where each comment went.

docs.title: Literate files
docs.text:
A file whose name ends in .pia.md, or any file with piac --literate, is Markdown. Only fenced blocks whose info string is pia are code; other fences are prose. A code block must close every bracket it opens, and the last one needs its closing fence. Lines and columns are those of the Markdown file.

The prose between two code blocks is one prose comment, leading on the first item of the block after it. Prose after the last block is detached on the program.

docs.title: Identifiers and keywords
docs.text:
IDENT = ( letter | "_" ) { letter | digit | "_" | "'" } ;

A prime (') may follow the first character, as in x' and x''. Pia has no shadowing (ADR 0022), so primes are the usual way to name a value related to x. Nothing else in the language uses ': there are no character literals, and type variables are written <T>.

Reserved words:

let rec meta in type of where if then else match with for spread while do done
requires ensures invariant decreases assert assume forall exists
interface sig module struct end import operator true false
borrowed moved out inout fixed mutable mod handle defer as

step is a keyword only inside a for or spread header, between the keyword and do. Everywhere else it is an ordinary identifier, so a function can still be called step. Likewise reads is a keyword only first on a line and before a name, where a spec function's reads clause starts.

costs is a keyword only before a name and <=, where a cost clause starts, costs iterations <= len xs (verifier.md, ADR 0062), so a function can still be called costs. Its counters iterations and calls are names only after costs and after spent, as in spent iterations.

theory, sort and axiom are keywords only right after let, when a name follows, and model only in let model m : (verifier.md). spec and lemma are keywords only right after let or let rec, when a name follows: let spec sorted ... defines a spec function and let lemma split ... a lemma (verifier.md). let spec = 3 binds a value called spec. Inside a body, let spec ref : mutable [u8; 4096] = zeros in ... binds spec state, and (spec log : inout [u16; 64]) is a spec parameter, where spec is a keyword only when a name and a colon follow it, so (spec : u8) is still a parameter called spec; likewise spec seen : [u8; 256] in a record type is a spec field (verifier.md, ADR 0058).

A lemma's body may be by lean T, where T is a dotted Lean name: let lemma sum_nonneg (n : int) : unit requires n >= 0 ensures sum n >= 0 = by lean Proofs.sum_nonneg is proved by the Lean theorem Proofs.sum_nonneg (verifier.md, ADR 0061). by and lean mean this only right after a lemma's =; everywhere else they are ordinary identifiers. The reference grammar reads the form as an application.

Names such as result, old, dyn, concept, adapter, item, ident, prec, left and right are ordinary identifiers that the prelude or the contract checker gives meaning to.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
INT    = digits [ suffix ] | "0x" hexdigits [ suffix ] | "0b" bindigits [ suffix ] | "0o" octdigits [ suffix ] ;
FLOAT  = digits "." digits [ exponent ] [ suffix ] | digits exponent [ suffix ] ;
suffix = ( "u" | "i" | "f" ) digits | "usize" | "isize" ;     (* 42u8, 1i64, 0.5f32, 3usize *)
STRING = '"' { char | escape } '"' ;

Digits may be grouped with ' or _ (100'000, 0xFFFF'FFFF, 1_000_000), which mean nothing to the value. A ' must sit between two digits of the literal's base, as in C++14, so 100' and 1'_0 are errors. , cannot group digits, because it already separates tuple elements and arguments: f (1,000) would be ambiguous. A ' after a name is a prime, as in x', which is part of the name. A float needs a digit after the point, so 0..n lexes as 0, .., n.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
An operator is a maximal run of + - * / < > = | & ^ ~ ! % ?. A few spellings are reserved by the grammar:

Token Meaning = Binding, and the equality operator -> Function type, match arm => Function literal <- Assignment \| Variant, match arm, union type, refinement ? Passes an error on: e? (ADR 0028)

Every other operator gets its precedence from the operator table. The table comes from the let meta operator declarations in the prelude (meta.md) and in the program. Operators not in the table get a level from their first character, as in OCaml.

Level Operators Associativity 1 ==> <==> right 2 \|\| right 3 && right 4 = <> < > <= >= none 5 .. (range) none 5.5 << >> left 6 + - +\| -\| left 6.3 \| (bitwise or, inside brackets) left 6.4 ^ left 6.5 & left 7 * / % mod left prefix - ~ application left .f .[i] name<...> postfix

The levels match the design's let meta operator ( + ) : prec 6 left. A level may have one decimal place, as in prec 6.5. A user operator declared at a level above 7 binds tighter than * and looser than application.

Unlike C, the bit operators bind tighter than comparisons, so x & mask = 0 is (x & mask) = 0. Because | also separates variants and match arms, it is bitwise or only inside parentheses, brackets or braces, and not directly in a match arm's body there: | A -> (x | y) needs its parentheses. ~x is the builtin bnot x. The lexer reads a run of operator characters as one token, so a&~b is the operator &~; write a & ~b.

docs.title: Other punctuation
docs.text: Token Spelling Notes QUOTE_OPEN `( Quoted syntax, closed by ) QIDENT `name A quoted identifier, e.g. `sgemm_4x16 SPLICE_IDENT $name, $!name Splice a metaprogram value. $!name escapes hygiene (meta.md) SPLICE_OPEN $( Splice an expression, closed by ) ATTR, ATTR_OPEN @name, @name( Attributes; arguments follow ( with no space TARGS_OPEN < straight after an identifier Explicit type arguments, see below LBRACE_ADJ { straight after an identifier Range types such as int{0..255} DOT_LBRACKET .[ Indexing and slicing QDOT . followed by whitespace Ends quantifier binders DOT . followed by anything else Field access and paths DOTDOT .. Ranges HOLE ... A hole, see below SEMI, SEP ;, ;; Sequencing; explicit item separator

docs.title: Adjacency rules
docs.text:
Spacing decides three things.

  1. name< opens type arguments. sum<i64> xs and vec<u8, 16> instantiate. Less-than must be written with a space: a < b. Writing x<y is an error that names the rule. Inside the list, > closes it, and >> closes two lists.
  2. name{ opens a range type. int{0..255} is a range-refined integer. Bare int, with no brace straight after it, is the spec-only unbounded integer (verifier.md). A record literal passed to a function is written with a space, f { x = 1 }.
  3. A dot followed by whitespace ends quantifier binders. In forall i in 0..n. p i the dot is QDOT. Field access never has a space after the dot.

docs.title: Layout rule
docs.text:
Pia is not indentation-sensitive, except in one place. Top-level items start in column 1, and the lexer inserts an item separator (SEP) before a token in column 1 when three things hold:

  • it is outside every bracket, sig/struct ... end and do ... done
  • it can start an item: an identifier, literal, let, interface, module, import, (, [, a quote or a splice
  • it is not the first token in the file

So a continuation line is either indented or starts with a token that cannot start an item, such as =, |, && or end. This matches every example in the design: = for i in 0..n do ... done in column 1 continues the definition above it, and tiled_matmul ... in column 1 starts a new item. ;; is an explicit separator for anyone who wants to put two items on one line.

Without this rule, a bare top-level metaprogram call would be read as further arguments to the expression that ends the previous item.

docs.title: Programs and items
docs.text:
program   = [ ( module_header | item ) { SEP item } ] ;  (* ADR 0039 *)
item      = let_item | meta_operator | interface | module | import | theory | model | file_attr | expr_item ;
expr_item = application ;                         (* a compile-time call that yields items *)
import    = "import" path [ "as" IDENT ] [ "{" IDENT { "," IDENT } "}" ] [ "trusting" ] ;   (* as, { }: ADR 0039; trusting: ADR 0036 *)
path      = IDENT { "." IDENT } ;

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
let_item  = "let" [ "rec" ] [ "meta" ] binder { param } [ ret_annot ] { contract } [ "with" names ] "=" handled ;   (* with: reveal, ADR 0063 *)
let_in    = "let" [ "rec" ] [ "spec" ] binder { param } [ ret_annot ] { contract } "=" handled "in" seq ;
handled   = seq [ "handle" [ "|" ] arm { "|" arm } ] ;
binder    = IDENT | SPLICE_IDENT ;
param     = IDENT | SPLICE_IDENT
          | "(" [ "spec" ] ( IDENT | SPLICE_IDENT ) ":" annot { contract } ")"
          | "(" ")" | "(" "..." ")" ;
ret_annot = ":" annot { attribute } | attribute { attribute } ;
contract  = "requires" stmt | "ensures" stmt | "decreases" stmt
          | "reads" stmt     (* a spec function's footprint, ADR 0060 *)
          | "costs" IDENT "<=" stmt ;   (* a cost bound, ADR 0062 *)

lambda    = "let" [ captures ] lparam { lparam } [ ":" annot ] { contract } "=>" seq ;
captures  = "[" capture { "," capture } "]" ;
capture   = [ "borrowed" | "inout" | "moved" ] IDENT ;   (* copied, borrowed, referenced or moved *)
lparam    = "(" pattern [ ":" annot ] ")" | "(" ")" ;

meta_operator = "let" "meta" "operator" "(" operator ")"
                [ ":" "prec" ( INT | FLOAT ) ( "left" | "right" | "none" ) ]
                [ "for" type ] "=" seq ;

A parameter whose type is a function type may end with contracts, which belong to its innermost arrow and may name the arrow's parameters and result: (f : (x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 255 ensures result > x). Only a parameter's annotation takes them; after an item's result type, contracts are the item's own.

let followed by ( is a function literal, a lambda. Like a named function, it may give its result type and contracts before the =>, as in let (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 255 => x + 1 (ADR 0044). let followed by a name is a binding. Pia has no tuple destructuring in let today; if it is added, the => still tells the two apart.

docs.title: Annotations and types
docs.text:
annot      = modifiers union_type [ "where" stmt ]
           | arrow_type [ "where" stmt ] ;
modifiers  = [ "borrowed" [ lender ] | "moved" ] [ "in" | "out" | "inout" ] [ "fixed" | "mutable" ] ;
lender     = "(" IDENT ")" ;                      (* borrowed(m), with no space before "(" *)

type       = arrow_type | union_type ;
arrow_type = arrow_dom "->" type ;
arrow_dom  = modifiers union_type | "(" [ "spec" ] IDENT ":" annot ")" ;
union_type = app_type { "|" app_type } ;
app_type   = type_atom { type_arg } ;             (* pair u8 f32, adapter Eq f32 *)
type_arg   = type_atom | INT | "(" expr ")"
           | "(" "borrowed" lender [ "in" | "out" | "inout" ] [ "fixed" | "mutable" ] union_type ")" ;

type_atom  = IDENT
           | "type"                               (* the type of types *)
           | IDENT "." IDENT { "." IDENT }        (* a theory's sort: Lip.layer *)
           | IDENT "<" targ { "," targ } ">"      (* vec<u8, 16>, tiled<cell, 256, 256, halo = 1> *)
           | IDENT "{" expr ".." expr "}"         (* int{0..255} *)
           | "[" type "]"                         (* slice, length carried at run time *)
           | "[" type ";" expr "]"                (* array, length known to the prover *)
           | "{" field_decl { ";" field_decl } [ ";" ] "}"
           | "{" IDENT ":" type "|" stmt "}"      (* refinement *)
           | "(" type ")" | "(" ")"
           | SPLICE_IDENT | "$(" expr ")" ;
targ       = type | elem | IDENT "=" elem ;
field_decl = [ "spec" ] IDENT ":" annot { attribute } ;   (* attributes a derive reads; spec: ADR 0058 *)

Modifiers come in a fixed order: ownership, then access, then mutability. Each one is optional. Before a function type they belong to its first parameter: borrowed in [pixel] -> [u8] takes a borrowed input slice.

borrowed(m) in a function's result type names the parameter m that the result is borrowed from, as in let alloc (m : borrowed arena) (n : usize) : result (borrowed(m) out mutable [u8]) OutOfMemory (#70). It is written with no space before the parenthesis: borrowed (t) is borrowed before a parenthesised type. Inside a type argument, such as result's, the parenthesised argument carries the modifiers.

A type value is an expression. A let whose value names a type, such as let byte = u8, let percent = int{0..100} or let bytes = option byte, is another name for that type, and type makes a new one (ADR 0064). So let length = type u32 is a type distinct from u32, and length 5 and u32 l convert between them.

The type value:

type_value = "type" ( variants | type ) { attribute } [ "where" stmt ] { attribute } ;
variants   = "|" ctor { "|" ctor } ;
ctor       = IDENT { attribute } [ "of" app_type ] ;
attribute  = "@" IDENT [ "(" attr_arg { "," attr_arg } ")" ] ;
attr_arg   = stmt | IDENT "=" stmt ;

A constructor's payload is one type application. A union or function payload needs parentheses, since | A of t | B already means two constructors. A record type written in place, | Rect of { w : u16; h : u16 }, is a type of its own named <variant>_<Ctor>, here shape_Rect (irgen.md).

Attributes on a field, x : i32 @json(name = "x"), and on a constructor, between its name and of or the next |, as in | Rect @json(name = "r") of rect, are for a derive to read (meta.md). Attributes after the last constructor's name, when it has no payload, are the type's, so | A | B @derive(eq) derives eq for the type as it always did.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Constructs that extend as far right as possible sit at the sequence level. The rest are ordered by the operator table.

expr   = seq ;
seq    = stmt [ ";" [ seq ] ] | let_in | match | lambda | "with" names "in" seq ;   (* reveal in one expression, ADR 0063 *)
names  = IDENT { "." IDENT } { "," IDENT { "." IDENT } } ;
elem   = stmt | "let" lparam { lparam } "=>" elem ;     (* list, record and argument elements *)

stmt   = postfix "<-" stmt
       | "if" seq "then" stmt [ "else" stmt ]
       | "for" pattern "in" or_e [ "step" add_e ] { attribute } { loop_annot } "do" handled "done"   (* @place(gpu): a placed sequence, ADR 0068 *)
       | "spread" pattern "in" or_e { attribute } { loop_annot } "do" handled "done"
       | "while" seq { loop_annot } "do" handled "done"
       | quantifier
       | "assert" imp_e | "assume" imp_e
       | "defer" imp_e
       | type_value
       | sig_value
       | imp_e ;
loop_annot = "invariant" stmt | "decreases" stmt ;

quantifier = ( "forall" | "exists" ) qbinder { qbinder } QDOT stmt ;
qbinder    = IDENT [ ":" type ] | IDENT "in" range_e
           | "(" IDENT ":" type ")" | "(" IDENT "in" range_e ")" ;

imp_e   = or_e [ "==>" ( imp_e | quantifier ) ] ;
or_e    = and_e [ "||" ( or_e | quantifier ) ] ;
and_e   = cmp_e [ "&&" ( and_e | quantifier ) ] ;
cmp_e   = range_e [ cmp_op ( range_e | quantifier ) ] ;
range_e = add_e [ ".." add_e ] ;
add_e   = mul_e { add_op mul_e } ;
mul_e   = unary { mul_op unary } ;
unary   = "-" unary | "~" unary | mode unary | application ;
mode    = "@wrap" | "@trap" | "@saturate" | "@proof" ;   (* one expression's overflow mode *)
application = postfix { postfix } { "?" } ;   (* f x? is (f x)? *)

postfix = atom
        | postfix "." ( IDENT | SPLICE_IDENT )
        | postfix ".[" seq "]"                    (* xs.[i], frame.[0 .. w] *)
        | postfix "<" targ { "," targ } ">" ;     (* sum<i64> *)

atom = IDENT | INT | FLOAT | STRING | "true" | "false"
     | IDENT "{" add_e ".." add_e "}"                (* a range type as a value: let percent = int{0..100} *)
     | QIDENT | "..."
     | "(" handled ")" | "(" ")" | "(" operator ")"
     | "[" [ elem { ";" elem } [ ";" ] ] "]"
     | "{" field_init { ";" field_init } [ ";" ] "}"
     | "{" postfix "with" field_init { ";" field_init } [ ";" ] "}"
     | "`(" quoted ")"
     | SPLICE_IDENT | "$(" seq ")" ;
field_init = IDENT "=" elem ;

quoted = let_item { [ SEP ] let_item }            (* items *)
       | IDENT ":" type                            (* a declaration: `( add : $t -> $t -> $t ) *)
       | seq ;                                     (* an expression *)

match = "match" seq "with" [ "|" ] arm { "|" arm } ;
arm   = pattern { ( "requires" | "ensures" ) stmt } "->" seq ;

e? passes an error on (ADR 0028): it applies to the whole application before it, so read_all m f? is (read_all m f)?, and it binds tighter than every binary operator. handle ends the expression before it and attaches to what encloses it: a function body, a let value, a parenthesised expression (which is how a let ... in scope gets one) or a loop body. Its arms are parsed like a match's. defer e; rest registers e as cleanup for rest, the rest of the sequence it starts; defer with nothing after it is an error.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
pattern      = pattern_core [ "as" IDENT ] ;                          (* NoEntry as e *)
pattern_core = IDENT pattern_atom { pattern_atom } | pattern_atom ;   (* Num n *)
pattern_atom = IDENT | INT | STRING | "true" | "false" | SPLICE_IDENT
             | "(" pattern ":" type ")" | "(" pattern ")"
             | "{" pfield { ";" pfield } [ ";" ] "}"
             | "[" pattern "]" | "[" pattern ";" pattern "]" ;       (* types *)
pfield       = IDENT [ "=" pattern ] ;

_ is an ordinary identifier pattern that binds nothing. p as x matches p and also binds x to the whole value, as in a handler arm | NoEntry as e -> Err (Wrapped e).

docs.title: Modules and interfaces
docs.text:
interface = "interface" IDENT { attribute } "=" "sig" { sig_item } "end" ;   (* @abi(c), @within(...) *)
sig_item  = "let" binder ":" annot { attribute } { contract } [ "=" seq ]   (* exported symbol; "= v" shows a value *)
          | "let" "meta" binder ":" annot                         (* exported concept, "let meta Ord : concept" *)
          | "let" "spec" binder ":" annot { attribute } { contract }   (* exported spec function, with its definition *)
          | "let" binder "=" type_value                           (* exported type *)
          | "let" binder "=" type                                 (* exported alias, "let byte = u8" (ADR 0064) *)
          | "let" binder "=" "let" lparam { lparam } "=>" type_value   (* exported generic type *)
          | "..." ;
sig_value = "sig" { sig_item | concept_item } "end" ;          (* a concept's body *)
concept_item = "include" type                                  (* "include" is contextual *)
             | "let" "lemma" IDENT { param } { contract } ;   (* a law *)
adapter   = "let" "adapter" IDENT ":" type "=" "struct" { item } "end" ;  (* "adapter" is contextual *)
module    = "module" IDENT [ ":" path { "," path } ] "=" "struct" { item } "end" ;
module_header = "module" path { attribute } [ ":" path { "," path } ] ;  (* a file's first item only *)
theory    = "let" "theory" IDENT "=" ( "sig" { theory_member } "end"   (* ADR 0036 *)
                                      | application ) ;               (* a metaprogram builds it *)
theory_member = "let" "sort" IDENT [ "=" type ]
              | "let" "spec" binder ":" annot { attribute }           (* abstract: no body *)
              | "let" "axiom" IDENT { param } [ ret_annot ] contract { contract }
              | let_item ;
model     = "let" "model" IDENT ":" IDENT "=" "struct" { model_member } "end" ;
model_member = "let" "sort" IDENT "=" type | let_item ;
file_attr = ATTR ;                                             (* `@trusted`, on its own line *)

A file is one module. Its first item may be a module header, module Pixels : PixelOps, PixelCodec, which names the module and the interfaces it claims; the rest of the file is the module's body. A let is private unless one of those interfaces lists it, and each item an interface lists is checked against the module, with contracts proved (ADR 0039). A header anywhere but first is an error. module M : I = struct ... end is a module nested in a file.

docs.title: Disambiguation
docs.text:
The grammar is ambiguous in a few places. Each one is settled by a rule, and each rule has a test in Disambiguation in the test file.

  1. Contract predicate before the body. A definition with contracts reads let f ... ensures p = body, and p may itself contain =. The predicate takes the longest reading: if it can end after a top-level comparison, it does, and the next = starts the body. ensures total g = old (total g) - drained g = step g therefore ensures total g = old (total g) - drained g. If the last predicate has no comparison (requires sorted xs = body), there is only one reading. A body that is itself a comparison, after a predicate that is not, needs parentheses. A hand-written parser does this by parsing the predicate greedily and, if no body = follows, splitting the last top-level = of the final clause.
  2. Comparisons do not associate. a = b = c is an error. This is what makes rule 1 work.
  3. Layout. A column-1 token that can start an item starts one. See Layout rule.
  4. name< is instantiation. See Adjacency rules.
  5. Named type arguments. In tiled<cell, 256, halo = 1>, halo = 1 is a named argument, not a comparison.
  6. Type or value. Since types are values, sum<f32, eq_f32>, pair u8 f32 and adapter Numeric (fast f32) have arguments that could be types or expressions. The parser accepts both readings and Sema decides.
  7. Right-extending constructs. let ... in, match, function literals, if and quantifiers extend as far right as they can, as in OCaml. Inside a list, record or argument list, a function literal stops at the next ; or ,. A nested match needs parentheses.
  8. Modifiers before a function type belong to its first parameter.

docs.title: Holes
docs.text: ... is a hole. The parser accepts it as an expression, a parameter list, a contract predicate, an interface item or a module body, so sketches like the ones in the design parse. Sema reports every hole as an unfinished definition, so a program with holes never compiles.

docs.title: Not yet in the grammar
docs.text:
These are in the design's direction but have no syntax yet. Each will get an ADR when it is needed.

  • Tuple types, values and patterns (planned in ADR 0040 section 9; an ADR of their own)
  • Guards on match arms (when)
  • Placement and task-graph syntax beyond spread and @place (M12)
  • Doc comments

docs.title: Idiomatic Pia
docs.text: Pia can often say one fact in several ways. A bound on an argument can be a requires clause or the argument's type. A family of functions can be written out by hand, made generic, or generated by a metaprogram. A hard proof can be one big goal or several small ones. Each version is correct, but they differ in where the fact lives, who has to prove it again, and how much work the solver does. This page gives the house opinions on which to choose, and why. They are opinions, not rules: the compiler warns when code goes against one, and every warning can be turned off (ADR 0037).

docs.title: The hierarchy
docs.text:
Prefer the earliest rung that can say what you mean:

  1. Make illegal states unrepresentable. Put facts in types: range types such as int{0..99}, ranges on the elements of a slice, variants instead of integer tags, slices instead of a buffer and a separate length, and buffers of records instead of parallel arrays. A fact in a type travels with the value, through calls, fields and returns, and costs nothing where it is used: interval analysis decides it before the solver is asked.
