  2. Contracts for facts that relate several values. requires i < len xs, requires lo <= hi, ensures result >= a: no single type can say these. A contract is a cut point. The callee is proved once against it, and each caller proves it at the call.
  3. Spec functions and lemmas to name ideas and prove hard steps once. A let spec names a property that several contracts share. A let lemma proves a fact once, and each use only assumes it.
  4. Generics, concepts and metaprograms for families. When the same body appears at several types, write one generic function constrained by a concept. When it differs in constants or in structure, take the constants as parameters or generate the family with a metaprogram, such as @derive(eq).
  5. Assertions as stepping stones. assert inside a body splits one hard goal into smaller ones the solver can take in turn.
  6. Escape hatches, last. assume, @overflow(wrap) where you do not mean modular arithmetic, --allow-unproved and, when it lands, unsafe. Each one moves a fact out of the proof and onto the reader.

The order is also the order of proof cost. A type is checked where a value is made and then never again. A contract is proved once in the callee and again at every call. A lemma is proved once and assumed where it is used. An assertion is a goal of its own. An escape hatch costs nothing to prove, because nothing is proved.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Each pair below says the same thing two ways. The costs are Z3's resource counts from piac --verify --solver-cost on the iMac (they vary by about 1% from run to run), summed over the file:

Fact As a contract As a type a parameter below 100, with x + 1 in the body and a caller passing y / 3 2 goals to the solver 1 goal to the solver, x + 1 by intervals inc and twice above, with x < 255 and x < 200 5 goals, all to the solver, cost 1,261 4 goals, 3 to the solver, cost 711 every element of xs below 16, then t.[nibble_at xs i] into a 16-entry table cost 10,022, and the table index still fails: nibble_at's u8 result does not keep the bound cost 96, and the table index is proved by intervals w * h fits, for w and h up to 1000 requires w * h <= 1000000: cost 1,075,117, 87 ms int{0..1000} each: cost 0, proved by intervals

The third row is the point of this page in one line: a fact in a contract stops at the function, and a fact in a type does not.

docs.title: A constant bound on one value is a range type
docs.text:
A precondition that only bounds one parameter by constants says what a range type says:

let scale (p : u8) : u16
  requires p <= 100
= p * 3

The fact holds only inside scale. A caller proves it at every call, and the value it passed does not keep it. As a type it goes wherever the value goes:

let scale (p : int{0..100}) : u16 = p * 3

piac says so, and pia-lsp offers the same text as a quick fix:

$ piac --check percent.pia
percent.pia:2:3: warning: this precondition only bounds 'p' by constants; say it in the type instead, (p : int{0..100}), so the fact travels with the value and intervals can use it [range_requires]
    requires p <= 100
    ^
  fix: Move the bound into the type: (p : int{0..100})

What it costs: a caller that passes y / 3 for an x < 100 precondition proves it with one solver query, the precondition of 'f' holds [smt], and so does a caller whose argument is already int{0..50}, because a precondition is always sent to the solver. With the range type, a caller whose value already has a narrower range passes it with no goal at all: widening between range types is free. A caller with a wider value proves the value fits in int{0..99}, one goal, as before. Inside the function, arithmetic on the parameter is decided by intervals instead of the solver: x + 1 with x < 100 is [smt], and with x : int{0..99} it is [intervals].

Two things change with the type, and the warning says when either applies:

  • Storage. A range type is stored in the smallest machine integer that holds it, so (x : u32) bounded by x <= 1000 becomes a u16, which changes the C signature of an exported function.
  • Arithmetic with nothing wider expected. Arithmetic happens at the join of its operand types and the type its context expects. x - 1 returned as a u8 is computed in u8, but let d = x - 1 in with x : int{1..64} is computed in int{1..64}, and fails when x is 1. Give the let a type, let d : u8 = x - 1 in, or compare in a wider type.

A one-sided bound on a wide type, such as w >= 3 on a usize, stays a contract for now: as a type it would read int{3..18446744073709551615}. Ranges with an open side are a planned follow-up (#153).

docs.title: A constant bound on the result is a range return type
docs.text:
let low_nibble (x : u8) : int{0..15} = x & 15

let lookup (t : [u8; 16]) (x : u8) : u8 = t.[low_nibble x]

With ensures result < 16 instead, the index into t needs the solver. With the return type it is proved by intervals, since the index's type alone keeps it in the table. The lint is range_ensures.

docs.title: Ranges on the elements of a slice
docs.text:
A quantified precondition that bounds every element by constants is an element type:

let nibble_at (xs : [int{0..15}]) (i : usize) : int{0..15}
  requires i < len xs
= xs.[i]

instead of requires forall (k in 0..len xs). xs.[k] < 16. Quantifiers are the most expensive thing a query can hold: every goal in the function assumes the forall, and the solver has to find the right instance of it. The element type needs no quantifier at all. The lint is range_requires, on the quantified part.

docs.title: Bounds the type already says
docs.text: requires x >= 0 on a u8 restates the type. It costs a little in every query of the function, and it suggests to a reader that the type could be negative. The lint is redundant_bound, and its fix removes the clause.

docs.title: Other facts that belong in types
docs.text:
These have no lint yet, but the same opinion applies:

  • An integer that stands for a choice is a variant. requires mode < 3 on a u8 is a three-constructor variant, type | Read | Write | Append. match must cover every constructor, and the verifier knows which one built a value.
  • A buffer and a separate length is a slice. (buf : [u8]) (n : usize) requires n <= len buf is buf.[0 .. n]: a slice carries its length, and its bounds are one goal where it is made.
  • Parallel arrays of the same length are a buffer of records. requires len fill = len dem on every function that takes both is a slice of { fill : u16; dem : u16 }, stored as one buffer per field anyway, so the layout does not change and the lengths are equal by construction.
  • Facts about several fields will be record invariants. let range = type { lo : i32; hi : i32 } where lo <= hi states once what every function on ranges would otherwise require. Record where invariants and refinement types such as { y : i32 | lo <= y } are designed but not implemented yet (status).

docs.title: Facts between values: contracts
docs.text:
A contract is for what no single type can say:

let plus (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  requires a + b <= 255
  ensures result = a + b
= a + b

let plus3 (a : u8) (b : u8) (c : u8) : u8
  requires a + b + c <= 255
= plus (plus a b) c

plus3 is proved against plus's contract, not its body. Its two calls are two goals, and the outer one is proved from the inner call's postcondition. This is the right shape for a relation, and the cost is one goal per call.

Where a contract and a type can both say it, the type wins. Range types work with contracts too:

let inc (x : int{0..254}) : u8
  ensures result = x + 1
= x + 1

let twice (x : int{0..199}) : u8
  ensures result = x + 2
= inc (inc x)

The inner call passes an int{0..199} where an int{0..254} is expected, a widening with nothing to prove. Only the outer call has a goal, that inc's result fits, which the postcondition proves.

docs.title: Naming ideas and proving them once
docs.text: A spec function names a property that several contracts use, so it is written once and read once. A lemma proves a fact once, and a call to it adds the fact where it is needed, instead of each function proving it again (the verifier). Keep @fuel low: @fuel(n) unfolds a recursive spec function n times in every query that mentions it, and a lemma proved by induction does the same work once. The lint deep_fuel warns above @fuel(4).

docs.title: Families: generics, concepts and metaprograms
docs.text:
The same body at several types is one generic function:

let max_u8 (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = if a > b then a else b
let max_u16 (a : u16) (b : u16) : u16 = if a > b then a else b

$ piac --check maxes.pia
maxes.pia:2:5: warning: 'max_u16' has the same body as 'max_u8' (line 1) at other types; write it once as a generic function, '(t : type where C t)', where the concept C names what the body uses, and its laws are proved once per type instead of once per copy [generic_candidate]
  let max_u16 (a : u16) (b : u16) : u16 = if a > b then a else b
      ^

Written once, with a concept that names what the body needs, the body is checked once at its definition (the tour), and each type proves the concept's laws once, however many functions use them.

Bodies that differ only in their constants want the constants as parameters, range-typed so callers keep the facts, or a metaprogram that generates the family (metaprogram_candidate). A function that compares every field of a record is what @derive(eq) makes, with a postcondition that stays in step when a field is added (derivable_eq). An exact copy is a call (duplicate_function).

docs.title: Decomposed reasoning
docs.text:
Every goal is its own solver query (ADR 0032), with the function's preconditions and the code before it as assumptions. So the cost of a function grows with how much each query has to carry, and these keep queries small:

  • Functions are proof boundaries. A loop body moved into a function with its own contract is proved once, and the loop sees only the contract. A caller never sees a callee's body.
  • Keep preconditions linear. A precondition is assumed in every goal of the function. A product of two variables, or a division by one, in an inequality makes every query nonlinear, which the solver has no decision procedure for. Bound the factors with range types so intervals decide the product, compute it in a helper with @overflow(saturate) and a linear contract, or prove the fact once as a lemma. The lint is nonlinear_contract.
  • Split a hard goal. An assert before a hard postcondition is a stepping stone: it is proved on its own, then assumed by the goals after it.
  • Prove one goal at a time while you work. --verify-only=file:line proves just that goal, with everything before it still assumed, and --proof-cache skips goals proved before.
  • Watch the cost. After --verify, a goal that costs 10% or more of the solver's resource limit gets a costly_goal warning that names it and says how to split it. --costly-goal=<n> sets the threshold, and --verify-stats reports how many goals the types raised and how many the contracts stated, and what each group cost:
verify-stats: goals=4 unselected=0 intervals=1 ... type=2 type_smt=1 type_cost=529 contract=2 contract_smt=2 contract_cost=182

A program that moves facts into types shows more type goals proved by intervals and fewer contract goals sent to the solver.

docs.title: Escape hatches
docs.text: assume p tells the verifier that p holds without proving it, so it is allowed only in a file marked @trusted, and --trust-report lists each one. If callers can promise it, it is a requires; if it follows from what is known, it is an assert or a lemma. The lint is assume. @overflow(wrap) and @overflow(saturate) are for arithmetic that is meant to wrap or clamp, such as hashes and pixels, not a way to make overflow goals go away. --allow-unproved is for a goal the verifier cannot prove yet, named one at a time.

docs.title: The lints
docs.text:
Lint Warns about Better Fix range_requires a requires that bounds one parameter, or every element of a slice parameter, by constants a range type, or a slice of a range type yes range_ensures an ensures that bounds the result by constants a range return type yes redundant_bound a bound the type already says nothing yes generic_candidate a function with the same body as another at other types a generic function with a concept no metaprogram_candidate a function that differs from another only in constants parameters, or a metaprogram no duplicate_function a function with the same signature and body as another a call no derivable_eq a hand-written field-by-field equality @derive(eq) no nonlinear_contract a product of variables in a precondition's inequality, or a division by a variable in a contract range types, a saturating helper, or a lemma no deep_fuel @fuel(n) above 4 a lemma proved by induction no assume assume requires, assert or a lemma no costly_goal a goal that costs 10% or more of the solver's limit a smaller query: range types, a lemma, a helper function no needless_rec a let rec type that refers to no type of its cycle let without rec (ADR 0047) no repeated_contract a definition whose contract is exactly the one its interface states no contract on the definition, which then takes the interface's (ADR 0077) yes

Lints run on the program as written, before metaprograms expand it, in piac --check, --verify and every --emit mode. They are warnings and never stop a build. @allow(range_requires) on a function's return annotation turns one off for that function, piac --no-lint=<name> turns one off for a run, and piac --no-lint turns them all off. In VS Code they appear as warnings from pia-lint, with the fixes above as quick fixes.

let narrow (x : u32) : u8 @allow(range_requires)
  requires x < 256   \ kept as a contract: it mirrors the C API
= x

docs.title: Where Pia's own code does this
docs.text:
The lints were run over the documentation, the examples and the case studies when they were added. The tour now uses range types where it used constant preconditions. What remains is listed here, as material for later changes:

  • The stream delineation demo (streams.pia.md) passes fill and dem as parallel slices, and nearly every function requires len fill = len dem: a buffer of records would make that true by construction. Its walk requires bound < 4294967295, which range_requires suggests as int{0..4294967294}. Its relational forall (k in 0..len fill). fill.[k] >= dem.[k] wants a record invariant on that buffer's element, once record where invariants land.
  • The VecDeque case study (rust-vecdeque.pia.md) requires 0 < old_cap on a usize in four functions, a one-sided bound that an open range type would carry.
  • The tests keep constant preconditions on purpose, since they test contracts; they are not idioms to copy.

docs.title: Module initialisation and registries
docs.text:
Status: accepted, 2026-11-21. Decision record: ADR 0033. Builds on ADR 0024 (certificates and the loader), ADR 0006 (module state), ADR 0028 (errors and cleanup) and ADR 0026 (allocators), and follows the REPL's environment model (ADR 0031).

Programs need code that runs before main: tables to build, codecs to register, caches to allocate. C++ does this with static initializers, and almost everything about them is implementation-defined. The order across translation units is unspecified (the "static initialization order fiasco"), an initializer can read another one's object before it is constructed, it can throw, loop forever or start threads, and the platform runs it from inside the dynamic loader, before any program code can check anything.

Pia supports the same uses through one supported hook and one registration mechanism, both well-defined and proved in advance:

Need C++ Pia A table of things that other modules add to (codecs, commands, tests, plugins) A global object whose constructor registers itself A registry: declarative entries collected at link time. No code runs State that must be computed at run time (allocate a cache, read the environment) A static initializer One @init function per module, run by the Pia runtime in a proved order Teardown Static destructors, in reverse of an order nobody knows The module state's Drop, in exact reverse init order

Anything that can be computed at compile time still is: module-level let values are constants, folded by the compiler (ADR 0010), and need neither mechanism.

docs.title: Registries: registration without code
docs.text:
A module declares a registry, with the type and refinement every entry must meet. Any module that imports it can add entries, which must be compile-time constants (records, function values, strings):

\ image.pia
let codecs : registry codec
  where unique (.name)                  \ no two entries share a name

\ png.pia, which imports Image
@register(Image.codecs)
let png = { name = "png"; magic = "\x89PNG"; decode = Png.decode; encode = Png.encode }
  • No code runs. piac link collects every entry for a registry into a constant table in the image. Reading a registry is reading a constant slice.
  • Deterministic order. Entries are ordered by the registering module's fully qualified name, then by the entry's name. The order never depends on link order, file order or load order.
  • Proved entries. Each entry is proved against the registry's element type and refinement where it is defined, like any other value. A registry's contents are therefore known to meet the refinement, and proofs about a registry quantify over its entries (forall c in Image.codecs. ...).
  • Cross-entry properties are checked when the set is known. A property over the whole set, such as unique (.name), cannot be proved by any one module. The static linker checks it when it builds the table, and the loader checks it again whenever Pia.Dyn.open adds entries (below). A duplicate is a link error, or an Err (RegistryConflict ...) from Pia.Dyn.open, never a silent override.
  • Dynamic libraries add entries. Each image carries its entries in a __DATA_CONST,__pia_reg section (read-only after fixups, so code signing covers it). Pia.Rt.entries Image.codecs returns a borrowed snapshot of the entries from every loaded image. Pia.Dyn.close cannot run while a snapshot is borrowed, by the ordinary borrow rules, so no entry can disappear under a reader.

Registries cover most of what static initializers are used for, with nothing to order and nothing that can fail.

docs.title: @init: the run-time hook
docs.text:
When a module's state genuinely has to be built at run time, the module declares one initialiser:

\ glyphs.pia
let cache : state glyph_cache                       \ module state, ADR 0006

@init
let setup (env : borrowed Pia.Rt.init_env) : glyph_cache
  ensures valid result
  = Glyph_cache.create env.alloc 256

The rules, all checked by piac:

  1. One @init per module, and only in the module that owns the state. It returns the initial value of the module's state symbol, and its ensures must establish the state's invariant. Its signature and contract are part of the module's interface, so they are in the interface hash.
  2. Proved to terminate. Loops need decreases measures and recursion needs a variant, as for any total function. There is no "loops until something else is ready".
  3. Infallible by default. An @init has no error set unless it declares one, so the strongest guarantee is the default (ADR 0004). A fallible init declares its error set, : result glyph_cache (OutOfMemory), which becomes part of the interface, and the loader handles failure as described below. It can never fail in a way nobody handles.
  4. Explicit capabilities. An init gets only what init_env gives it: the root allocator, the program arguments and environment, and a clock. It can call extern functions only through @trusted modules, as everywhere else. It cannot spawn tasks that outlive it, await, or take locks, so inits run sequentially and never deadlock.
  5. It may read only what is already initialised. An init may read the state of a module only if that module is one of its imports. Every function that reads module M's state carries an implicit precondition initialised M, which the verifier discharges from the init order below. Calling such a function from an init that does not depend on M is a verification error with the call chain as the counterexample. This is what rules out the order fiasco: the problem becomes a proof goal.
  6. Teardown is the state's Drop. If the state type has a Drop instance, it runs at exit (or Pia.Dyn.close) in exact reverse init order. Cleanup cannot fail (ADR 0028), so teardown cannot fail either.

docs.title: The order
docs.text:
Imports are explicit and form a DAG (ADR 0010). The init order is a topological order of the init dependency graph: an edge from N to M whenever N's init (or anything it calls) reads M's state. Ties are broken by fully qualified module name, so the order is a pure function of the program's modules, the same on every run and every machine. A cycle in the init graph is a compile error (or a link error, when it spans modules compiled separately) that names the cycle.

The compiler computes each init's dependency set and records it in the certificate. The order for a whole program is then computed from certificates alone, at link time for static links and at load time for Pia.Dyn.open, without looking at code. pia-cert audit recomputes the dependency sets from the embedded proof bundle and checks that the certificate's claims are right.

docs.title: Dynamic registration: Pia.Dyn
docs.text:
Loading code at run time works like the REPL (ADR 0031, repl.md) without the JIT. The REPL keeps an environment of verified definitions, each with its interface hash. Pia.Dyn keeps the same kind of environment, filled by loading compiled, certified libraries instead of compiling cells. Like Pia.Live, it is opt-in: Pia.Rt does not contain it, and a program has none of its machinery unless it imports Pia.Dyn.

let env = Pia.Dyn.create root_alloc                  \ an empty environment, owned by the caller
let lib = Pia.Dyn.open env "libpng_codec.dylib" ?   \ check, register, run inits
let png = Pia.Dyn.bind env Codec.Interface lib ?    \ typed record of Codec's functions
let img = png.decode bytes ?
Pia.Dyn.close env lib

docs.title: The registration hook
docs.text:
A Pia library does not register itself when dyld loads it. Instead piac generates one registration function per image, _pia$register$<image>, which is the image's only entry point for the runtime. Pia.Dyn.open calls it after the certificate check, passing a runtime handle, and the function calls back into the runtime:

register_symbols  handle  [ (qualified name, interface hash, symbol pointer, eval adapter) ... ]
register_entries  handle  [ (registry, entry) ... ]
register_inits    handle  [ (module, init function, dependency set, drop function) ... ]

Every argument is a constant table that the compiler builds from the module's exports, @register entries and @init functions. The registration function itself contains no user code, so it trivially terminates and cannot fail. The runtime, not the library, decides what to do with what was registered: it checks that no qualified name is already in the environment, checks registry constraints, computes the init order, and runs the inits. The same tables are also emitted as data (__TEXT,__pia_init and __DATA_CONST,__pia_reg), so pia-cert and the static linker can read them without running anything, and the audit checks that the function and the tables agree.

A library loaded by a C host goes through the same path, with pia_rt_open as the C face of Pia.Dyn.open.

docs.title: Typed lookup
docs.text:
The main way to use a loaded library is to bind an interface:

Pia.Dyn.bind env Codec.Interface lib : result (Codec.Interface.record) (Missing | Mismatch)

The caller names, at compile time, an interface it imports, so it was proved against that interface's contracts. bind compares the interface hash in the caller's certificate with the hashes the library registered (including older versions it proves it refines, abi.md). On a match it returns a record of function values typed by that interface. Calls through it are ordinary calls whose contracts the caller already proved, so no run-time contract checking is needed. On a mismatch it returns Err, never a value with the wrong contract. A lookup can never return a function whose contract differs from what its certificate says, because the hash compared is the certificate's.

Pia.Dyn.find env "Png.decode" : option (symbol) looks up a single name and returns its qualified name, type and interface hash. Pia.Dyn.bind_symbol<t> turns it into a value of type t under the same hash check, for callers that need one function instead of a whole interface.

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
For code that does not know the type at compile time (a command console, a scripting bridge, the REPL calling into a loaded library), Pia.Dyn.eval env name args calls a registered function on dyn arguments (ADR 0003):

  • The arguments' tags are checked against the function's registered type, so a wrong type is Err (TypeMismatch ...), never undefined behaviour.
  • The function's requires cannot have been proved by the caller, so it is checked at run time. For every exported function that may be evaled, piac compiles its requires into a checker, the same code @check produces, and registers it as the eval adapter. A failed check is Err (PreconditionFailed ...) and the function does not run.
  • The result comes back as a dyn whose ensures holds, because the function was proved to meet it.
  • Whether a function can be evaled is its module's choice (@eval on the export, or on the module), so libraries that never want dynamic calls carry no adapters. Adapters are listed in the certificate, so the trust report shows which preconditions are checked at run time instead of proved.

This is the same split as the REPL: proved, typed calls are the default, and the dynamic path is safe because it checks exactly what a proof would otherwise have covered.

docs.title: Consistency with the REPL
docs.text:
REPL session (ADR 0031) Pia.Dyn environment Holds Verified definitions with interface hashes Loaded symbols with interface hashes from certificates Adds definitions by Compiling and verifying a cell, then JIT Loading a certified library, then its registration function Initialisation Cells run in order @inits run in the proved init order Name clash Error; :redef replaces with re-verification Error; close the old library first. Live replacement is Pia.Live's job Lookup By name inside the session bind by interface hash, find, eval Opt-in Pia.Live Pia.Dyn

The two share one environment representation, so the REPL can load a compiled library into a session through Pia.Dyn, and its cells can then call the library's functions with full proofs, or eval them.

docs.title: Loader integration
docs.text:
Pia images still run no code when dyld loads them. That keeps the soundness argument of docs/abi.md: the certificate check always runs before any code it guards. Inits are run by the Pia runtime, after the check, from a table instead of __mod_init_func:

__TEXT,__pia_init   per module: module name, init function, state symbol,
                    declared error set, init dependency set (module names
                    and interface hashes), drop function or none

The certificate records the same per-module facts (has init, error set, dependency set), and the init's contract is part of the interface hash, so an importer proved against "state initialised with this invariant" cannot bind to a library whose init no longer establishes it.

At launch, a Pia program's entry point (in Pia.Sys.Process, see stdlib.md) does, in order:

  1. the certificate check for every loaded Pia image (Layer 2 in abi.md);
  2. registry cross-entry checks;
  3. every @init in the global order;
  4. main;
  5. state drops in reverse order, then exit.

If a fallible init fails, the inits already run are dropped in reverse order, main never runs, and the program exits with a fixed status and a message naming the module and the error. There is no implicit initialisation path: a program that never imports Pia.Dyn initialises only the images it was linked against, at launch.

On Pia.Dyn.open, the runtime checks the new images' certificates, calls their registration functions, computes the init order of the modules that are not initialised yet (modules shared with images already loaded keep their state), checks the new registry entries against the existing ones, and runs the new inits. If any step fails, it drops the new modules' state in reverse order, closes the images, removes their registry entries and returns Err (InitFailed { module, error }) or Err (RegistryConflict ...). The program's state is exactly what it was before the call.

On Pia.Dyn.close, the closed images' state is dropped in reverse init order. A module that other loaded images still depend on stays loaded, as dyld already does for its dependencies.

docs.title: What this replaces in abi.md
docs.text: docs/abi.md said that Pia images have no static initializers. That is still true at the dyld level: no __mod_init_func, and the certificate check still rejects a Pia image that has one. What changes is that module initialisation now exists, as @init and registries run by Pia.Rt after the check.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• C++ static initialization and the order fiasco; [[gnu::init_priority]] and function-local statics as workarounds. Pia makes the order a property of the import graph, and reading uninitialised state a proof failure.
  • Ada elaboration: pragma Elaborate_All, Preelaborate, Pure, and GNAT's static elaboration model, which checks at compile time that no unit is used before it is elaborated. This is the closest relative. Pia's initialised M precondition is the same check, made a proof goal.
  • Go package init functions run in dependency order, but can fail only by panicking and can do arbitrary work.
  • Rust has no life-before-main by design. Lazy statics and ctor crates exist outside the language.
  • Linker sets (FreeBSD SET_DECLARE, ELF and Mach-O custom sections collected by the linker): Pia's registries are linker sets with types, refinements and a deterministic order.
  • Swift global variables are lazily initialised on first access with swift_once. Pia rejects lazy init because it hides the order and adds a check on every access.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text: Issues are listed in ADR 0033.

docs.title: IRGen: the scalar subset
docs.text:
Status: implemented in M4 (#5).

piac --emit=mlir file.pia lowers a program to the pia and pia_contract dialects (ADR 0018), with control flow in upstream scf and functions in func. This page describes the subset it accepts and how each construct lowers. Anything outside the subset is reported as "not supported yet" at its source location.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
1. Parse (src/syntax) to the uniform syntax tree.
  2. Expand metaprograms (src/meta, meta.md). Binary operators become calls of core builtins, @derive runs, and the let meta items are removed.
  3. Sema (src/sema) resolves written types and collects the signature of every top-level let, so a function can be called before its definition. It reports items outside the subset (types, modules, metaprograms) before any code is generated.
  4. IRGen (src/irgen) type checks expressions as it lowers them. A separate typed AST comes when the language outgrows the scalar subset.
  5. The module is run through the MLIR verifier.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Pia IR u8 u16 u32 u64, i8 ... i64 !pia.int<lo, hi> with the machine range usize, isize the 64-bit ranges, printed as the aliases !usize and !isize int{lo..hi} !pia.int<lo, hi> (bounds are integer literals for now) bool i1 [T; n] !pia.array<n x T> (n is a literal for now) [T] !pia.slice<T> atomic T !pia.atomic<T>, for an integer type or bool (ADR 0052) unit no value; a function returning unit has no results let pixel = type { r : u8; ... } !pia.record<"pixel", r : !pia.int<0, 255>, ...>, printed as !pixel

Types are structural: u64 and usize are the same type. int{0..255} is u8. Records are the exception: they are named, so two record types with the same fields are different types. let byte = u8 is another name for u8, and let percent = int{0..100} for that range: a let whose value is a type names it (ADR 0064). type makes a new type: let length = type u32 is a distinct type (ADR 0064, step 2). The expander (makeDistinct in src/meta/Expand.cpp) makes it a record of one field, raw#length, which no source can name, flagged distinct, and two conversions, length#of (x : u32) : length and u32#of (x : length) : u32. A type applied to one value, length 5 or u32 l, is a call of <type>#of, so the overloads are told apart by the argument's type. Since records are scalarized before the verifier and codegen, a length proves and runs as a u32. Not yet: importing a distinct type, a distinct type with a where, derives other than eq, and returning one as its scalar in the C ABI.

docs.title: Integers
docs.text:
• Literals take the type the context expects. With no context they are i32, or i64 or u64 if the value does not fit. A suffix (42u8) fixes the type. A literal that does not fit its type is an error.
  • Binary operators arrive from expansion as calls of core builtins (a + b is add a b, meta.md). IRGen lowers a builtin call as the operator it stands for. They compute at the join of the operand types, the smallest range holding both. When the context expects a wider integer, they compute at that type, so dst.[i] <- src.[i] * 3 with u8 source and u16 destination multiplies at u16. The other operand is widened with pia.convert. A literal takes the other operand's type, whichever side it is on.
  • Conversions: wherever a value meets a declared type (a parameter, a return type, an annotated let, an assignment, an element store), IRGen inserts pia.convert. Widening always holds. Narrowing is a proof obligation for the verifier (M5).
  • Overflow: + - * / % lower to pia.add, sub, mul, div, rem with the function's overflow mode. The default is proof. @overflow(wrap | saturate | trap) on the return annotation sets another mode, @wrap e (and @trap, @saturate, @proof) sets it for one expression, and +| -| always saturate. The parser writes @wrap e as the prelude builtin #overflow wrap e, as it writes ~x as bnot x. mod is %.
  • Type bounds min t and max t, for an integer type t, are folded to the bound as a literal before overload resolution (ADR 0059), so they take their context's type and read in contracts as the numbers did: ensures a * b > max u16 ==> result = max u16. A call of min or max whose one argument names an integer type is a bound; every other call, such as Pia.Core.Order's max a b, resolves as before. Where a local called max is in scope, max u8 is that local applied. max usize is the bound of the target's usize. A generic body's type parameter has no known bounds yet.
  • Negation -x is 0 - x at x's type, so it is an obligation for unsigned and minimum values. -5 is a literal.
  • Comparisons lower to pia.cmp at the joined type. = and <> on bools lower to arith.cmpi.

docs.title: Buffers
docs.text:
• Indexing xs.[i] is pia.load, and xs.[i] <- v on an out or inout parameter is pia.store.
  • Slicing xs.[a .. b] is pia.slice, a view of the same storage. An array passed where a slice is expected becomes a pia.slice of all of it.
  • Array literals [1; 2; 3] where an array type is expected, and top-level let t : [T; n] = [...], are pia.const_array. A top-level constant is not a function: each use is a pia.const_array with the constant's name as its label. Passing constant data, or a slice of it, to an out or inout parameter is an error.
  • Local arrays are values with storage of their own. A let of an array that is mutable, or whose literal computes its elements, as in let a : mutable [u8; 3] = [x; y; z], is a fresh pia.region on the stack: the literal's elements are stored into it one by one, and any other array is copied in with pia.copy, which the verifier reads as the array taking the other's elements. So let b : mutable [u8; 3] = a in b.[0] <- 0 leaves a as it was. A mutable one can be written, a.[i] <- v, and a whole array assigned to it, a <- b, is copied in. A literal of computed elements anywhere is one too. Arrays stay values wherever they go: a let of a name or field holding an array copies it, a record literal copies an array it reads from a mutable local, and assigning a record to a mutable local copies the arrays it holds into storage of that assignment's own, since an array a call returns in a loop lives in storage the next iteration's call reuses. A function may return a local array, or a record holding one: codegen passes it a buffer its caller makes (codegen.md), and the verifier sees the result as a value (tests/verify/local_arrays.pia, tests/verify/array_results.pia, tests/irgen/local_array_errors.pia, tests/codegen/local_arrays.pia).
  • abort () is pia.abort, with a result of the type the context expects.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
A variant let shape = type | Circle of u16 | Empty is a record named shape with a field tag, int{0..n-1}, and one field per constructor that has a payload, named after the constructor. A constructor's tag is its position. Circle r is a pia.record with tag 0, r in Circle, and a fixed value in every other payload field. Only constructors and match see these fields: .tag and record literals are errors on a variant. Records then scalarize as usual, so the verifier and codegen need nothing new, and a variant crosses the C boundary as its fields. A payload written as a record in place, | Rect of { w : u16; h : u16 }, is a record type of its own, shape_Rect, which expansion defines just before the variant; the payload names it, its fields keep their attributes for the variant's derives, and it derives what the variant derives (tests/verify/record_payloads.pia). A generic variant cannot have one yet. - Recursive types (ADR 0047, step 1). A type that refers to itself, directly or through others, is declared let rec, every type in the cycle so, or it is an error that suggests let rec; a let rec type in no cycle is the lint needless_rec. Every cycle must pass through an indirection, box, vec, ref or weak, so each type has a size: a type that holds itself, or two that hold each other, directly is an error that suggests box. A generic recursive type applies itself to its own parameters, in order (regular recursion), and every recursive type must have a value that can be built without one already, so let rec l = type | Cons of { h : u8; t : box l } is an error. A payload record of a recursive variant is in its cycle. The Indirect concept over type constructors waits for concepts on them, so the indirections are those four names for now (tests/irgen/rec_type_errors.pia, tests/lint/needless_rec.pia). - Recursive values (ADR 0047, step 2). Records are structural, so a recursive type cannot be one: it would contain itself. Each variant of a recursive group that passes is instead the leaf type !pia.rec<"tree">, and the module's pia.datatype @tree ctors ["Leaf", "Node"] payloads [none, !tree_Node] lists its constructors in tag order with their payload types. A generic recursive variant has a leaf per instance, !pia.rec<"list<u8>">. The group's records, such as lifted payloads, stay records, holding the leaf inside a box or vec, so none contains itself. A constructor is pia.rec_make "Node"(%payload), and match tests pia.rec_tag and takes pia.rec_payload %t, "Node"; ScalarizeRecords passes a record payload as its fields and takes it out as them, and leaves the leaf alone. A group of records with no variant is not built yet: a use of one says to make it a variant. Equality, error sets and @derive on recursive types come later (step 4). The verifier proves them as datatypes (verifier.md); codegen lays them out as structs of their tag and payload (codegen.md, step 3) (tests/irgen/rec_types.pia, tests/verify/rec_types.pia, tests/codegen/rec_types.pia, tests/codegen/rec_run.pia, tests/std/rec_mem.pia, tests/dialect/rec_types.mlir).

match checks its arms first: they must cover every constructor or end with a catch-all, and an arm after a catch-all, a constructor matched twice, or a catch-all after every constructor is an error. It then becomes a chain of ifs on the tag, the last arm untested, with each arm's payload bound by a let. So arms carry mutable locals and join their result types exactly as if does.

An arm may carry contracts between its pattern and -> (ADR 0035): | Some i requires i < len xs ensures result = xs.[i] -> xs.[i]. A requires is not a guard. It becomes an assertion at the start of the arm, so it is proved for every value that reaches the arm, from what is known at the match. An ensures becomes an assertion on the arm's value, result. Handler arms are arms of a match, so they take contracts too, proved at each ? that reaches them.

docs.title: Bindings and mutation
docs.text:
• let x = e in body binds an SSA value. An annotation converts e to the declared type.
  • There is no shadowing (ADR 0022). A let, parameter, loop variable or quantifier binder may not reuse the name of a local in scope, a function, a type or a core builtin. Assigning to a mutable local is not shadowing. The error suggests a primed name instead: x', or x'' if that is taken. A prime is an ordinary identifier character, so let x' = x + 1 in ... names a value related to x.
  • let x : mutable T = e in ... makes x assignable. There is no memory: each x <- v rebinds the SSA value, and structured control flow threads it through. A mutable local assigned inside if becomes an extra scf.if result, and one assigned inside a loop becomes a loop-carried value (iter_args for for, scf.while operands).
  • Parameters are mutable only with mutable. Their modifiers are kept as the pia.modifiers argument attribute.
  • inout and out scalars and records. A buffer is written in place, but a scalar or a record is an SSA value, so a function hands back the final value of each inout or out parameter that is not a buffer, as extra results after its own. The caller passes a mutable variable there, and the call rebinds it, so the caller sees the write and the callee's postcondition about it. A variable passed that way inside an if or loop is carried like one assigned there.
  • old e reads the parameters as they were on entry, including a mutable scalar or record parameter the body has assigned. old of a local declared in the body is its current value.
  • moved. A local or a moved parameter passed as a moved parameter is dead after the call: using it again is an error that says where it was moved. A local moved on only one branch of an if or match is maybe moved after it, which is an error too. A borrowed parameter (the default) cannot be moved, and a local bound outside a loop cannot be moved inside it. Values of scalar types (integers, bool, unit) are copied, so moving one leaves the caller's copy. Assigning a mutable local gives it a value again. Contracts may still name a moved value, since they describe values rather than use them. Moving a field or an element out of a value is not checked yet.
  • @linear (#56). A value of a type marked @linear (let file = type { fd : i32 } @linear), of an instance of a generic type marked so (let box = let (t : type) (r : region) => type { ... } @linear), or of a record, variant or instance holding one, must be consumed on every path out of its scope: passed as moved, or used as a value (returned, bound to another name, or put in a constructor or record). Reading a field, len, and passing it to a borrowed parameter only borrow it. A local that some path leaves unconsumed is an error at its let, and so is a moved parameter at the function's end. A borrowed linear parameter cannot be consumed. A defer that consumes the value counts on every exit. A match consumes its scrutinee, and match f with | { fd } -> e takes a record apart into its fields, which is how a linear value is finally released. A pattern that drops a linear payload or field with _, or leaves a linear field out, is an error. Taking a linear record apart is not yet limited to its own module.
  • Slices in records and variants. A record field or a constructor's payload may be a slice, as in result (borrowed(m) [u8]) OutOfMemory or { data : [u8]; used : usize }; the record is scalarized into its fields like any other, so the slice is a value of its own after that. The unused payload of a variant is pia.empty, a slice of length 0. A field may be an array, constant data or a local array: { c : [u8; 3]; alpha : u8 }, read as p.c.[i] and written in place through an inout record as p.c.[i] <- v. A buffer whose elements hold a slice is a buffer of slices, one per slice field (ADR 0048): reading xs.[i].slot and len xs.[i].slot works for any element type, and writing through such a slice is allowed only when the element owns it, being @linear or having a drop, as a box does; otherwise it is read-only. A slice taken out of an owned element is lent from the buffer while it is live. An element's slice may be reached through a record's field, as v.buf.[i].slot.[0] <- x writes through the ith box of a vector's buffer when v is inout. Codegen lowers each to a buffer of addresses and one of lengths (codegen.md; tests/verify/slice_buffers.pia, tests/verify/vec_boxes.pia, tests/irgen/slice_buffer_errors.pia, tests/codegen/vec_boxes_core.pia). An owning element read as a value moves out of its buffer: IRGen stores it back with every slice empty, a store marked pia.moved_out, which codegen keeps so that the element's length is 0 at run time too, and drops that store again when the read turns out to be a borrow, as in xs.[i].slot (ADR 0048, section 6). Moving one out of a buffer the function cannot write is an error (tests/irgen/move_out_errors.pia). A store of a whole owning element is marked pia.fills, and the verifier proves the element written over owns nothing; a function whose lent buffer is out is marked pia.out_result. A slice that an if or match chooses is read from the branch taken, but the verifier refuses a write through it, since it does not know which buffer the write reaches.
  • Writable loans. A local holding a borrowed buffer whose result type says out, inout or mutable, as alloc's borrowed(m) out mutable [u8] does, may be written, like an out parameter. A lender may be passed inout while it is lent, as alloc updates its allocator: the callee's contract is what keeps the earlier loans valid. Passing it out makes it anew, so that is an error while it is lent. The verifier sees a borrowed buffer result as fresh memory, which alloc's loans are; for a result that views its lender, as xs.[a .. b] returned through borrowed(xs), a write through it does not yet reach the lender's elements.
  • Fields as inout arguments. An out or inout argument may be a field of a mutable variable, at any depth, as take_slot g.small takes from one pool of a record of pools (tests/verify/size_classes.pia). After the call the variable holds a copy of itself with that field replaced, so the rest of the record is unchanged. The variable must not be lent at the call, as for g.f <- v.
  • Borrows into inout parameters. (v : borrowed(m) inout mutable vec) says that the new value of v may hold a loan from the parameter m, as push m v x may store a buffer from the allocator m in the vector v. After the call, the caller's variable borrows from the argument passed as m, so it cannot outlive it. A function that stores a value borrowed from another parameter in an inout or out parameter without saying so is an error.
  • Borrows (#70, ADR 0026). A function whose result type says borrowed(m) returns a value borrowed from its parameter m, as an allocator's alloc does. The argument passed as m must be a named value, or something already borrowed from one, and the call's result is then borrowed from it. A local holding such a value borrows from it too, and so does anything taken from that local: a field that is not copied, a slice, a match or ? payload, a record or constructor holding it, or either branch of an if. Only the parts of a value whose types some borrowed result borrows count, so an integer field of a borrow, a length, or the error of result (borrowed(m) [u8]) e borrows nothing. A borrow lasts until the last use of the local that holds it (ADR 0042), not to the end of its scope. Until then the lender cannot be moved or consumed, passed as out, inout or mutable, or assigned; each is an error that names the borrower and where it is used next. A use is a later mention of the local in its scope, in evaluation order, which follows the source; a mention in a cleanup, such as a defer or a drop, counts as later, since it runs at the exit; and inside a loop that began after the local was bound, the borrow lasts through the loop (tests/irgen/borrow_liveness.pia). A let's value cannot be borrowed from its own local, since it would outlive it, and a function's result can be borrowed only from the parameter its result type names. Borrows of slices of local arrays are not checked yet.
  • Region parameters (ADR 0042, step 2). A borrow can name a region instead of a value: (r : region) is a parameter of a generic type or a function, and borrowed(r) on a record field, a result or an inout parameter says the value borrows from r. So let vec = let (t : type) (r : region) => type { alloc : bump t r; buf : borrowed(r) mutable [t]; len : usize } holds both an allocator and the buffer it lent, and neither borrows from the other or from the vector (tests/verify/vec_region.pia). Regions are erased before anything else (irgen/Regions.cpp): vec u16 r and vec u16 are one type, and a type application may leave its regions out. Each region argument must name a region parameter in scope, and a function's borrowed(r) needs a parameter whose type mentions r. In a function, a parameter whose type mentions r holds loans from r, which is outside the function: they may go into another parameter whose type mentions r, or out through a result that mentions it, and nowhere else. A parameter of a type with region fields that names no region has a region of its own, so its loans stay in it. At a call, a result or inout parameter that mentions r borrows what the arguments for r's parameters borrow, not those arguments themselves: alloc v.alloc n does not lend v to the buffer push stores in it. A field read of a region field borrows what its record borrows, so the memory a region lends lasts as long as whatever lent it, such as a with_arena, and an allocator that frees blocks one by one must hand them out as owned or linear values instead (tests/irgen/region_errors.pia, region_sig_errors.pia). A concept may take regions too, let meta Allocator (a : type) (t : type) (r : region) : concept: a requirement's parameter whose type mentions one of the concept's type parameters is in its regions, and a requirement's result may say borrowed(r), so generic code over an allocator stores what it allocates (tests/verify/vec_allocator.pia). A type parameter such a constraint names, as a in (a : type where Allocator a t r), is in the constraint's regions, so a parameter (m : inout mutable a) holds loans from r and a result that mentions r may return what m allocates (lib/Pia/Mem/Box.pia's make, tests/irgen/region_concept_errors.pia). An interface (ADR 0039) may list a generic type with regions and a function with region parameters; they are erased there as in the module, and an importer checks its own uses against the regions the interface names (tests/modules/regions.pia, region_import_errors.pia). Regions of variants and regions of a lambda are not supported yet.
  • Scoped regions (#70, ADR 0026). with_arena 256 (let (a) => body) is a let of a : mutable arena, where arena is type { mem : [u8]; used : usize } (a program may define its own arena with these fields). a.mem views 256 fresh bytes (pia.region), every one zero, and used starts at 0, so a bump allocator over the arena is ordinary Pia, and a.mem.[i] <- x writes it (a field of a writable record can be written in place), as in tests/verify/arena.pia. The arena is borrowed from itself, so the with_arena's value can hold neither the arena, nor a view of its memory, nor anything allocated in it, and the arena cannot be moved; each is an error at the with_arena's body. The size is an integer literal of at most 1 MiB, since the region lives on the stack: codegen makes it once on entry to the function and zeroes it each time the with_arena is entered, so one in a loop does not grow the stack. Larger regions wait for pages over mmap.
  • xs.[i] lowers to pia.load and xs.[i] <- v to pia.store. Writing requires the parameter to be out or inout. Indices go through pia.to_index. len xs is pia.len followed by pia.from_index to usize.

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
• if c then a else b lowers to scf.if with the joined result type. An if without else must have type unit.
  • &&, || and ==> in code short-circuit, so they lower to scf.if. This keeps i < len xs && xs.[i] <> x from loading out of bounds.
  • for i in lo..hi step s do ... done lowers to scf.for over index. The bounds are joined to one type, and i is bound with pia.from_index at that type. The range is half-open. Two literal bounds are usize.
  • while c do ... done lowers to scf.while. The condition is computed in the before region.
  • a; b evaluates a for its effects. a may not be a result: a result is never dropped unexamined, and neither is a loop body's value.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
result t e (Ok of a t, or Err of an e) is in the prelude, unless the program defines its own result, Ok or Err. e? and handle follow ADR 0028:

  • A ? ends its scope early, so it must be in a tail of the scope: the scope itself, the body of a let ... in, the second part of a; b, a branch of an if or an arm of a match that is itself a tail, or anything those always evaluate first (a let value, an if condition, an operand). A ? inside a branch whose value the scope still needs, or in a loop body without a handle of its own, is an error.
  • There it becomes an if on the result's tag. Ok goes on with the rest of the scope, with the payload where the ? was. Err becomes the scope's value: Err e returned to the caller when no handle encloses it, which needs the function to return a result with the same error type, or the handler's arms for that error.
  • The arms are generated at each ? that reaches them, so each is checked and proved once per ?, knowing only what holds there: what was bound before it and what earlier calls promised. An arm that uses a name bound after some ? that reaches it is an error that names that ?.
  • At each ? the arms taken are those for the error type's constructors, in order, up to the first catch-all. A constructor no arm takes is an error at the ?, and an arm no ? reaches is an error at the arm, as is a handle with no ? in its scope.
  • | C p -> binds the payload, | e -> the whole error, and | C as e -> both tests C and binds the whole error.
  • An error set a | b is one variant holding the constructors of each member, ordered by the members' names, so b | a is the same type. A value of a member converts to the set: its tag moves to its block of the set's constructors. So a ? whose errors are a member of the function's error set passes them on, Err NoEntry builds the set directly, and a handler matches the set's constructors. Two members may not share a constructor name. A set does not yet convert to a larger set.
  • An expression is evaluated from its first ? on: in g a + f x?, f x runs before g a. A ? inside a handler arm is not supported yet.
  • defer d; rest registers d as cleanup for rest, the rest of its sequence (#85). Each normal exit from rest, a node whose value is rest's value (the body of a let, both branches of an if, each arm of a match), gets a copy of d after its value, and each ? that leaves the scope runs the scope's defers, innermost first, before its error goes to the handler or the caller. So cleanup runs in reverse order of registration on every exit, and the verifier proves it like any code at that exit. d must have type unit and contain no ?. The error in flight is the ?'s own payload, an immutable value read after the cleanup, so no cleanup can change or replace it. defer? is not supported yet.
  • drop (#85). A type has a drop when a drop (x : moved t) : unit is in scope, which is how it meets the Drop concept (ADR 0034). A generic one, drop (t : type) (r : region) (b : moved mutable box t r), gives a drop to each type its parameter deduces, as it would meet a requirement, and its instance drop<u16> is a drop too (ADR 0046, step 1; tests/irgen/drop_generic.pia). A record of another module is dropped by that module's drop, so an importer drops a Pia.Mem.Box.box u8 with Pia.Mem.Box.drop (tests/std/mem_edges.pia). A moved mutable parameter is the callee's alone, so its buffers may be written and an element read out of them moves it, as a box's drop takes its value out of its slot. A local or moved parameter of such a type is dropped at every exit from its scope that has not consumed it, as if by a defer registered where it is bound: after its scope's value on a normal exit, and before the error on a ?. Using it as a value or passing it as moved consumes it, so a returned value is not dropped. An exit where it is consumed on only some paths is an error, since there is no runtime flag to decide. drop itself does not drop its argument again; it takes it apart with a record match. @derive(drop) is not supported yet.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Pia IR requires p pia_contract.requires at function entry ensures p pia_contract.ensures before the return, with result bound to the return value decreases m on a function pia_contract.decreases at entry invariant p, decreases m on a loop at the head of each iteration: the start of the for body, or the before region of scf.while assert p, assume p pia_contract.assert, pia_contract.assume old e pia_contract.old forall (i in lo..hi). p pia_contract.forall whose block argument is i, yielding (lo <= i && i < hi) ==> p exists (i in lo..hi). p pia_contract.exists, yielding lo <= i && i < hi && p forall (k : u8). p quantifies over the whole type, with no guard

Several binders nest one quantifier op per name, so a later range can mention an earlier name. Inside contracts, which have no effects, &&, || and ==> are plain arith logic, and ==> is (a xor true) or b. Whether arithmetic in contracts is exact or follows the overflow mode is settled with the verifier in M5. Quantifiers are rejected outside contracts and assertions.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A let name = type { field : T; ... } item defines a record type. Records are values, like integers.

  • Literals. { r = v; g = 0; b = 0; a = 255 } lowers to pia.record, with the fields in declaration order, whatever order they are written in. Its type comes from the context. Failing that, it is the one record type whose fields are exactly these. Every field must be given, once.
  • Field reads. p.r lowers to pia.field %p, "r".
  • Field assignment. q.r <- v on a mutable local record rebuilds q with one field replaced. So, like any mutable local, q is an SSA value threaded through scf.if and loops.
  • Equality. p = q on records calls eq_<name>, which @derive(eq) makes (meta.md). <> negates it. The other operators on a record call lt_<name>, le_, gt_, ge_, add_, sub_, mul_, div_ and rem_ the same way, which the derives of a distinct type make (ADR 0064, section 4); a literal on the right takes the function's second parameter's type, so l * 3 multiplies by a u32. In a contract, a record or variant without an eq_ compares as a value: field by field, and a variant by its tag and then the payload it holds. Two arrays or slices compare by length and then element by element, as a forall. So a generic contract such as ensures result = v, which the definition check accepts for every type, means the same in every instance.
  • Buffers of records. [pixel; 8] and [pixel] hold records. xs.[i] reads one, xs.[i] <- p writes one, and xs.[i].a <- v reads element i, replaces its field and writes it back. Writing needs an out or inout parameter, as for any buffer.
  • Not yet supported: buffers inside records, and attributes on type items other than @derive.

The verifier and code generation do not see records. transforms::scalarizeRecords replaces each record value with its fields first, using MLIR's 1:N dialect conversion. A pixel parameter becomes four parameters named p.r, p.g, p.b and p.a, a pixel result becomes four results, and pia.record and pia.field disappear. old p becomes old of each field. A buffer of records becomes one buffer per field, struct of arrays: an xs : [pixel] parameter becomes xs.r, xs.g, xs.b and xs.a, and loads, stores, views and len apply to each. The field buffers of a slice share one length, so every one after the first carries {pia.length_of = k}, naming the argument whose length it has; the verifier gives them that length, and the C entry point takes it once. A store of a field read back from the same element is dropped, so xs.[i].a <- v writes only xs.a. The field copies of one load, store or view share its index and length, so every copy after the first carries the unit attribute pia.bounds_shared: the first carries the bounds goal, and the verifier only assumes it for the others, so each index is reported once. Copies of a load or view that nothing uses are erased, and the first copy still in use carries the goal, so a record read only by a contract raises no goal, as a scalar one would not.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Each top-level let f (x : T) ... : R = body becomes func.func @f. Parameters need annotations. A let with no parameters becomes a function with no arguments, and its uses call it. The return type may be left out, and then it comes from the body. Such a function cannot be called before its definition, or recursively. Calls must pass every argument, since partial application and functions as values come later.

A generic function, one with (t : type) parameters, is never generated itself. Each call works out the type arguments: first from f<u8> or f<t = u8>, then by matching the written types of the parameters that mention an unknown type parameter against the types of their arguments, which are generated first for this, then from the type the call is expected to have. The call goes to the instance, a private func.func @"f<u8>", which is made on first use and generated after the function that used it, with each type parameter naming its argument. Generic types work the same way: option u8 is a record type named option<u8>, made the first time it is used, and a generic constructor such as Some builds the instance it is expected to build, or else the one its payload's type gives.

A constraint on a type parameter, (t : type where Ord t), names a concept: a let meta C (t : type) : concept = sig ... end that the metaprogram pass keeps in the program. Each call checks that the deduced type arguments meet it (the use check of ADR 0034). A requirement let f : (a : t) -> bool is met by a function in scope with that name, those parameter types and modifiers, and that result, and include requires another concept. A generic function meets it too, at the type arguments its parameters and result deduce, when those meet its own constraints: alloc over bump t r meets Allocator's alloc for bump u16 at t = u16, and that instance is made and proved like any other (tests/verify/generic_meets_concept.pia, tests/modules/generic_meets.pia). A function that is not generic is tried first. A generic that would meet a concept only through its own constraint, such as let same (t : type where Same t) ... for Same, does not. Whether a concept is met is decided once per concept and type arguments. Each law, let lemma name params ensures p, becomes a lemma for those type arguments, @"Ord<u8>.irreflexive", generated and proved like any other function. A requirement's contract becomes one too, @"Ord<u8>.less.contract": under the requirement's requires it asserts the function's own requires, and it ensures the requirement's ensures of a call of the function. In an overload set, a generic whose type arguments do not meet its constraints is removed from the call, and the error for a call with no candidate left gives that reason.

A generic body is checked once, at its definition (the definition check). It is generated with each type parameter standing for an unknown type, a record named after the parameter with no fields, and then thrown away with every instance it made. A call with an argument of such a type resolves against the requirements of the concepts its constraints promise, including the ones they include, and a generic it calls must have constraints those concepts promise. Anything else, such as < on a t or a function the constraints do not require, is an error there, with a hint naming a concept that requires the function. A contract may still compare such values with =. Each instance then resolves its calls by its concrete types, which picks the function that met the concept at the use check, since two functions cannot share a name and parameter types.

An adapter, let adapter by_red : Same pixel = struct ... end, holds functions named after it, @"by_red.same", which no call reaches by name. The use check meets a concept directly when it can. Otherwise it uses the adapter the call names (alike<Same = by_red>), the one the function being generated already chose, or the only adapter in scope for that concept and those types. Two such adapters, with neither named, are an error. An instance made through adapters is named after them, @"alike<pixel, Same = by_red>", and while it is generated a call by a requirement's name goes to the adapter's function in place of any with the same parameter types. The concept's laws and requirement contracts are proved the same way, about the adapter's functions.

A type-level metaprogram, a let meta whose parameters are all types and that returns a type or a bool, also stays in the program (ADR 0035). A type such as widen u8 or widen t runs it on the types it is applied to, and gives the type it returns. A where may state a predicate over types beside its concepts: a comparison, ||, ==>, <==>, or a call of such a metaprogram that returns a bool, as in where Ord t && size_of t <= 8, or where t = u8 || t = i8. Each call evaluates it for the deduced type arguments; when it is false, the candidate is removed with the reason "the constraint 'small t' is false for t = u32". A concept can only be joined to the rest by &&. Types are the metaprogram's values: a type's name denotes it, = compares types, name t spells one, and size_of t gives the bytes it takes (an integer the smallest of 1, 2, 4 or 8 that holds its range, a bool 1, an array its elements', and a record the sum of its fields'; a slice has no fixed size). Such a metaprogram must terminate: recursion only on components of a type parameter, no mutual recursion, and nothing that reads or changes the program (meta.md); a use of one that may not is an error at the use. When a candidate's signature cannot be formed for the deduced types, because a metaprogram in one of its types or predicates fails, the candidate is removed with that reason, and the call falls back to the others (substitution failure, ADR 0035). Only the signature fails softly, never a body, and a metaprogram in a type outside a candidate's signature still fails with an error. piac --explain-overloads=file:line prints, as notes, each call on that line: its candidates, why each removed one was, and which one it chose. In the definition check, a type-level metaprogram applied to a type parameter stands for an unknown type too, and a signature with one has its body checked in each instance instead, since its types are only known there. A generic body may call a generic with a predicate only if its own constraints state the same predicate, and a generic whose constraints state every predicate of another's, and more, is the more specific. A type-level metaprogram applied in a parameter's type does not deduce its type arguments.

A name may have several generic overloads. The first keeps the name and the others are numbered, rank#2, and so are their instances, @"rank#2<u8>". When two generics both fit a call equally well by their arguments, the more specific one wins. A is more specific than B when A's parameter types, with stand-in types for its type parameters, are an instance of B's but not the reverse. When each is an instance of the other, A is more specific when its constraints entail B's and not the reverse. A concept is entailed when A's constraints promise it through include, or when the requirements they promise include every one of its requirements and it states no law or requirement contract. Laws and contracts would need a proof, which is not done yet. Two generics with the same patterns whose constraints entail each other are an error at the second definition. A call with no single most specific candidate is an ambiguity error that lists them. Overloads with the same parameter types are told apart by their preconditions. They must be ordered: each one's requires clauses, compared with the parameters renamed by position, include every clause of the next, which proves that each precondition implies the next. They must also return the same type. They are named copy(out [u8], [u8])#2 and on. A call that only they fit goes to the least specific, with all of them, most specific first, in pia.overload_candidates, and the verifier picks the most specific one whose precondition it proves at the call (the verifier). A call inside a contract uses the least specific, so a contract means the same in every build.

A higher-order function, one with a parameter of function type such as (p : u8 -> bool), is never generated itself either (ADR 0044, step 1). Sema records its function parameters. Each call that passes a lambda or the name of a top-level function for them goes to a specialisation, @"find[lambda@f.pia:12:9]", made on first use and cached by the function and its arguments: a copy of the function without those parameters, in which each one's name is the argument's symbol. The copy keeps the type parameters, so a generic one is then called through the generic path with the other arguments. A lambda becomes a private function @"lambda@f.pia:12:9" with its parameters, its result type if written (else the arrow's, else the body's), the arrow's requires renamed to its parameter names, its own requires asserted at the start of its body, and its own ensures and the arrow's. A named function is called directly when the arrow has no contract; otherwise through a wrapper, @"succ@f.pia:20:9", that has the arrow's contract. let sq = let (x : i32) : i32 => x * x in sq 3 binds sq to a lambda's function. A lambda anywhere else is an error naming ADR 0044.

Step 2 adds function objects and overloading (ADR 0044, section 4). A call g x where g is a local of a record or variant type is apply g x. A local passed for a function parameter must have such a type, with one apply whose first parameter is that type and which takes as many arguments after it as the arrow; the specialisation, @"find[below]", keeps the parameter, with the object's type, and calls apply (or, when the arrow has a contract, a wrapper @"apply@f.pia:30:11" with it) at each application. The prelude concept Function f a r, with the one requirement apply : (g : f) -> (x : a) -> r, is defined for a program that names it and defines no Function of its own, so a generic can take (f : type where Function f t bool) (p : f) and is proved once. Higher-order functions may share a name with each other and with ordinary overloads; they are named after their line, find#line12. At a call, a higher-order candidate is removed when an argument for a function parameter is not a lambda, a named function or a function object, or an argument for a value parameter is a lambda or a named function, and an ordinary one when any argument is a lambda or a named function, or the type of a named argument clashes with its parameter. One candidate must be left; --explain-overloads lists why each was removed.

Step 3 adds captures (ADR 0044, section 6). A lambda lists them after let: [lo, borrowed keys, inout n], a bare name copied, borrowed a shared loan and inout an exclusive one. Every local the body uses must be listed, once, and every listed name used; a copy must be of a copyable value, and an inout capture of a mutable variable; only an inout capture may be assigned; capturing a linear or drop value comes with step 7. A lambda that captures has its own record type, lambda@f.pia:12:9, with one field per capture, and its function is an apply, @"apply[lambda@f.pia:12:9]", whose first parameter is the record and whose body reads each capture as a field of it. As a value, anywhere, a lambda is that record, made by a record literal of its captures, so a let of it is a function object and where Function f t bool deduces f to it. Passed for a function parameter, it is a function object of that type, so the specialisation takes the captures in one argument. A borrowed or referenced capture is a loan the closure holds until its last use (ADR 0042): a borrowed variable cannot be assigned, nor a borrowed buffer's elements, and a referenced one cannot even be read. With an inout capture, apply takes the closure inout mutable, so each call threads it back; a let of such a closure is mutable, the variables it references are rebound to its fields after each call, and loops carry both. Passed for a function parameter written (f : inout t -> unit), it is made in a hidden mutable local and the specialisation takes it inout; an arrow without inout refuses it, and such an apply cannot be called in a contract. A lambda that captures nothing is still called directly.

Step 4 adds untyped and generic lambdas (ADR 0044, section 2). At a call of a generic higher-order function, its type parameters are first deduced from the arguments that fix them without being generated: named values, and the written types of typed lambdas, function objects and named functions. An untyped lambda parameter then gets the type of the arrow's domain under those bindings, written in the lifted function as a type alias, type#lambda@f.pia:12:9#x, and the deduced bindings join the specialisation's generic call. A lambda's result type, when it is not written and the arrow's cannot be resolved, is inferred by generating its body once in a function that is thrown away; its errors are dropped there, since they come again when it is generated for real. A let of a lambda that captures nothing and has untyped parameters is a generic function, lambda@f.pia:12:9, with an implicit type parameter x#type per untyped parameter; explicit (t : type where C t) parameters are kept, and when one has a constraint the lambda's definition is checked and proved once (ADR 0043), queued like an instance.

Step 6 proves each higher-order function once (ADR 0044, section 5; ADR 0043). Before any call, each pure function parameter p of f becomes a type parameter p#type constrained by a concept made for it, f#p, whose one requirement is apply with the arrow's types and its ensures; p gets that type, so p x is apply p x. The copy, f#proof, is checked like a written generic, and its generic proof is kept when it is parametric. Each specialisation of f is then marked as an instance of f#proof, and the verifier discharges it when its calls match the proof's, a call of apply matched by the argument's function, which must return: the argument's own check against the arrow's contract happens where it is passed (its lifted function's requires and ensures are the arrow's). A law applied to p in a contract, such as requires Pia.Fn.strict_weak_order p, is part of the copy, and so is an arrow's requires: in a definition check, each call of a requirement with a precondition asserts it with the call's arguments, and the requirement's axiom is guarded by it. An arrow with inout, a specialisation whose closure writes a capture, and a function whose copy is not parametric are proved at each specialisation, as before. Spec functions are left alone.

Step 7 adds partial application, functions as results and moved captures. A call of a lone top-level function with arguments left, below lim, is the lambda let [lim] (arg#1 : u8) : bool => below lim arg#1: a local argument is captured (copied, or borrowed when it cannot be), a literal is written in, and any other argument must be bound first. A function whose result is written as a function type, : u8 -> u8, has the type of the closure its body makes, found by generating the body once before its first call; callers apply it like any function object. A capture list may say [moved t]: the closure owns t, which the record literal that makes it consumes, and when a moved capture has a drop the closure gets one, @"drop[lambda@f.pia:12:9]", that takes it apart so each field is dropped once. A lambda in one place may be made with different captures in different copies of its body, such as a proof and a specialisation, and each copy gets its own closure type, lambda@f.pia:12:9#2.

docs.title: Atomics
docs.text:
An atomic cell, atomic t, is a place, not a value (ADR 0052). Its type is !pia.atomic<T> for an integer type or bool. A range type such as atomic int{0..64} is a refined cell: its range is an invariant of the cell across every task. The ops are core builtins with the order first:

Pia IR atomic_new v pia.atomic.new, the cell's type from the context or from v atomic_load o c pia.atomic.load o atomic_store o c v pia.atomic.store o atomic_swap, atomic_add, atomic_sub, atomic_and, atomic_or, atomic_xor, atomic_min, atomic_max pia.atomic.rmw <kind> o, with overflow(m) on an add or sub atomic_cas ok fail c expected desired pia.atomic.cas ok fail fence o pia.fence o
  • Orders are the names relaxed, acquire, release, acq_rel and seq_cst, read from the order position only. So an order is always a compile-time constant, and the names stay free for functions such as release. Each op takes the orders in ADR 0052's table, and a failure order of atomic_cas is relaxed, acquire or seq_cst and no stronger than the success order. Anything else is an error that lists the orders the op takes.
  • Values stored or combined are converted to the cell's type, so storing into a refined cell is a range goal. On a refined cell atomic_and, atomic_or and atomic_xor are errors, since their results cannot be proved to stay in range.
  • Overflow. atomic_add and atomic_sub take only a mode written on the expression itself, @wrap (atomic_add o c v), and are an error without one, even inside an @overflow(...) function. A plain cell takes wrap, trap or saturate. A refined cell takes only proof, and IRGen adds pia.add (or sub) of the old value and v in proof mode, whose goal is that the result stays in the range. Nothing reads its result, and codegen drops it.
  • Ownership. A cell is not copyable. Naming it in an op, or passing it to a borrowed parameter, borrows it; any other use as a value moves it, so it cannot be used afterwards. A cell local cannot be mutable. The ops are not allowed in contracts or ghost code.
  • Not yet: a cell in a record field, a buffer of cells, a function returning a cell, and a lambda capturing one. Each is an error that says so.

docs.title: Not yet
