docs.text: Local functions, captures, untyped lambdas and other function values, recursive types, dyn, spread and tiles (M8), type-level lengths ([T; n]), refinements (where on values), modules, decreases for metaprograms, generic adapters, entailment proved from laws and contracts, and precondition orders that need a proof rather than included clauses.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
Pia.Text.Json reads and writes JSON with every step proved against one grammar, RFC 8259's, stated as spec functions in Pia.Text.Json.Spec (ADR 0045). There are two ways in:

  • Straight into a type. @derive(json) writes a reader and a writer for a record or a variant, and Json.read<t> reads a whole text as a t, with an error type that has exactly the errors t can raise.
  • Through a document. Pia.Text.Json.Dom.parse reads any JSON text into a json value, a recursive type over the text, proved valid_dom. @derive(json, json_dom) then says when a document has a type's shape, and converts it, with no failure path left once it does.

Every example on this page is proved by piac.

docs.title: Building against the library
docs.text:
A program that uses the library imports its modules' interfaces, so it is proved against their contracts alone. piac --emit=interface writes each one as an artifact, here into the current directory:

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Spec.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Lex.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Read.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Write.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Derive.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Mem/Alloc.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Dom.pia

$ piac --emit=interface -o . lib/Pia/Text/Json/Shape.pia

and --iface-path=. finds them.

docs.title: @derive(json): a type's own codec
docs.text:
@derive(json) on a record of integers, range types and bools writes write_json_<t>, which writes a value into a buffer with the room its precondition states, and read_json_<t>, which reads one. A member's name is its field's, or @json(name = "..."). Json.read<t> reads a whole text, and its errors are Json.json_errors t: for point below, a syntax error, an unknown, duplicate or missing member, or a number out of its field's range, each at the position it was found.

import Pia.Text.Json.Spec.Grammar
import Pia.Text.Json.Lex.Lexer
import Pia.Text.Json.Read.Reader
import Pia.Text.Json.Write.Writer
import Pia.Text.Json.Derive.Derive as Json

let point = type { x : i32 @json(name = "xx"); y : u8; ok : bool } @derive(json)

(* The y of the point the text is, or 0. *)
let y_of (s : [u8]) : u8 =
  match Json.read<point> s with
  | Ok p -> p.y
  | Err _ -> 0

(* Why a text is not a point. *)
let why (e : Json.json_errors point) : u8 =
  match e with
  | Syntax_point _ -> 1 | Unknown_point _ -> 2 | Duplicate_point _ -> 3
  | Missing_point _ -> 4 | Range_point _ -> 5

The reader checks each integer's range as it reads its digits, so "y": 256 stops at the third digit, and it never reads outside the text. Every goal of the derived code is proved where it is derived:

$ piac --verify --iface-path=. point.pia
...
65 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

A field of another record with @derive(json) is a nested object, which that record's own reader and writer read and write. Its errors stay exact: the record's error set is the union of its own errors and the nested record's, (line_json_own_error | point_json_error), each once however many fields share the type, and each error says where in the text it is (error sets). Each derive also writes json_room_<t>, the room its writer needs, which counts a nested record's:

import Pia.Text.Json.Spec.Grammar
import Pia.Text.Json.Lex.Lexer
import Pia.Text.Json.Read.Reader
import Pia.Text.Json.Write.Writer
import Pia.Text.Json.Derive.Derive as Json

let point = type { x : i32; y : u8 } @derive(json)
let line = type { a : point; b : point } @derive(json)

(* Why a text is not a line: 1 when a point's number is out of range,
   2 when a point is not an object. *)
let why (e : Json.json_errors line) : u8 =
  match e with
  | Range_point _ -> 1
  | Syntax_point _ -> 2
  | _ -> 3

(* A line's text, in a buffer with its room. *)
let write (l : line) (dst : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len dst >= json_room_line
= write_json_line dst 0 l

$ piac --verify --iface-path=. line.pia
...
99 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

An option of a record works the same way: null or a missing member is None, and json_room_<t> counts the record's room for it. @derive(json_dom) takes one too. An array of records is not supported yet (#528).

docs.title: The document: Pia.Text.Json.Dom
docs.text:
json is a recursive type (recursive types) whose numbers and strings are spans of the text they were read from, so parsing copies nothing:

let rec json = let (r : region) => type
  | JNull
  | Bool of bool
  | Num of span
  | Str of span
  | Arr of vec (json r) r
  | Obj of vec (member r) r
let rec member = let (r : region) => type { key : span; value : json r }

Dom.parse s max_depth values members reads all of s as one document, nested at most max_depth deep, taking each array from values and each object from members: two bump allocators over memory the caller lends. Each container is counted before it is read, so it takes one allocation of exactly its length. Its errors are a lex error, a misplaced token, too deep, trailing input and no memory, each with its position; a document it returns is valid_dom s v, every number, string and key a token of its kind.

A walk over a document is structural recursion, which needs no measure:

import Pia.Text.Json.Spec.Grammar
import Pia.Text.Json.Lex.Lexer
import Pia.Mem.Alloc.Allocators
import Pia.Text.Json.Dom.Document

(* The values in v, itself included, capped at a million. *)
let rec nodes (r : region) (v : Pia.Text.Json.Dom.json r) : int{0..1000000} =
  match v with
  | Arr a ->
    let total : mutable int{0..1000000} = 1 in
    for i in 0 .. len a.items do
      (let n = nodes a.items.[i] in
       total <- if n <= 1000000 - total then total + n else 1000000)
    done;
    total
  | Obj o ->
    let total : mutable int{0..1000000} = 1 in
    for i in 0 .. len o.items do
      (let n = nodes o.items.[i].value in
       total <- if n <= 1000000 - total then total + n else 1000000)
    done;
    total
  | _ -> 1

(* The values in the text, or 0 if it is not one document. *)
let count (s : [u8]) (cells : borrowed mutable [Pia.Text.Json.Dom.json]) (mems : borrowed mutable [Pia.Text.Json.Dom.member]) : int{0..1000000} =
  let vs : mutable Pia.Mem.Alloc.bump Pia.Text.Json.Dom.json = { mem = cells; used = 0 } in
  let ms : mutable Pia.Mem.Alloc.bump Pia.Text.Json.Dom.member = { mem = mems; used = 0 } in
  match Pia.Text.Json.Dom.parse s 16 vs ms with
  | Ok v -> nodes v
  | Err _ -> 0

$ piac --verify --iface-path=. count.pia
...
8 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

docs.title: A document's shape: @derive(json, json_dom)
docs.text:
@derive(json_dom), from Pia.Text.Json.Shape, says when a document has a record's shape, and converts it. It sits beside @derive(json), whose member names it shares and whose writer to_dom uses, so that @derive(json) alone needs no document. For a record t of integers, range types and bools, options and fixed arrays of them, and other records with @derive(json, json_dom) and options of them, it writes:

Function What it does conforms_json_<t> s v a spec function: v is an object with exactly one member for each field, each called its name, each value a number in its field's range or a bool as its field is, and no other member. An option field's member may be missing or null, both None, an [e; n] field's is an array of exactly n values of e, and a record field's conforms to that record check_json_<t> s v decides it: ensures result = conforms_json_<t> s v from_dom_json_<t> s v requires conforms_json_<t> s v: the record, with no failure path, each field its member's value to_dom_json_<t> x text values members the document of x, written into text: Ok v is valid and conforms

A number conforms to an integer field when it has only digits after an optional minus, and its value is in the field's range: 1.5 and 1e2 are not integers, as for the streaming reader. So reading a point from a document is a check and a conversion, and the conversion cannot fail:

import Pia.Text.Json.Spec.Grammar
import Pia.Text.Json.Lex.Lexer
import Pia.Text.Json.Read.Reader
import Pia.Text.Json.Write.Writer
import Pia.Text.Json.Derive.Derive as Json
import Pia.Mem.Alloc.Allocators
import Pia.Text.Json.Dom.Document
import Pia.Text.Json.Shape.Shapes

let point = type { x : i32 @json(name = "xx"); y : u8; ok : bool } @derive(json, json_dom)

(* The point a document is, or that it is not one. *)
let get (s : [u8]) (v : Pia.Text.Json.Dom.json) : result point Pia.Text.Json.Shape.nonconforming =
  if check_json_point s v then Ok (from_dom_json_point s v) else Err Nonconforming

Every goal of the derived checks and conversions is proved where they are derived:

$ piac --verify --iface-path=. shape.pia
...
102 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

to_dom writes its value with @derive(json)'s writer, parses the text back and checks it, so the document it returns is proved valid and conforming. That the writer's text always parses and conforms, so that its Unparsed and Unconforming errors never happen, is not proved yet. Variants and recursive user types come next (ADR 0045, steps 5, 7 and 8).

docs.title: The standard library today
docs.text:
This page lists every module of Pia's standard library as it is built, in lib/Pia. Each module is written in Pia and proved: what its contracts promise holds for every input, so a caller proves its own code from those contracts alone. The standard library and its core is the design the library follows, and The C++23 standard library in Pia maps each C++ header to the module that covers it.

A program uses a module through an interface it names, import Pia.Core.Order.Compare (getting started, ADR 0039). In Bazel, each module is a pia_library target in lib/Pia/BUILD.bazel.

tools/docs/check.py fails a pull request that adds a module without a line here.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The vocabulary types, concepts and algorithms that everything else is built from (ADR 0040).

Module What it gives Pia.Core.Order The concepts Eq and Ord with their laws, and min, max, clamp, swap, exchange and lexicographical_compare over them: C++'s <compare> and <concepts> Pia.Core.Option option t, None or Some of a t, and the functions over it: C++'s <optional> Pia.Core.Result What C++23's std::expected has on top of the language's own result t e Pia.Core.Int gcd, midpoint, abs, div and saturating arithmetic for u8 to i64, with C++'s undefined cases ruled out by preconditions Pia.Core.Bit The rest of C++23's <bit>, beside the builtins clz, ctz, popcount, bswap, rotl and rotr Pia.Core.Hash The concept Hash, an Eq whose hash agrees with it, its instances, and @derive(hash) Pia.Core.Ratio C++'s <ratio>, as metaprograms over exact integers Pia.Core.Ascii C++'s <cctype> for ASCII bytes, each classifier exact Pia.Core.Utf8 UTF-8 decoding, encoding and validity, with both round trips proved Pia.Core.Charconv from_chars and to_chars for integers in bases 2 to 36, with the round trip proved Pia.Core.Digits The facts about digit strings that formatting and parsing proofs need, as lemmas Pia.Fn Laws of function arguments, such as strict_weak_order and sorted, that a higher-order function states as preconditions (ADR 0044) Pia.Time C++'s <chrono> durations, as types a metaprogram makes over a ratio Pia.Test.Gen Tests generated from a function's contract: boundary values, pairwise rows, and a specification check and an oracle per case (ADR 0056, meta)

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
C++'s <algorithm> and <numeric> on slices. Each takes its comparison or operation as a function value and is proved once, for every element type and every such function (ADR 0043).

Module What it gives Pia.Core.Algo.Search find, count, contains, equal, mismatch, search, min_element, is_sorted and the rest of the non-modifying algorithms Pia.Core.Algo.BinarySearch lower_bound, upper_bound, equal_range and binary_search Pia.Core.Algo.Modify fill, copy, copy_backward, swap_ranges, reverse, replace, shift_left and shift_right Pia.Core.Algo.Remove remove, whose contract says where each kept element goes Pia.Core.Algo.Numeric iota, accumulate, reduce, inner_product, the scans and adjacent_difference Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation The multiset spec functions that sorting states its results with Pia.Core.Algo.Sort insertion_sort: sorted, and a permutation of its input Pia.Core.Algo.Heap The heap operations, and sort as a heap sort Pia.Core.Algo.PartialSort partial_sort and nth_element Pia.Core.Algo.Partition is_partitioned, partition_point and partition Pia.Core.Algo.Merge merge of two sorted ranges Pia.Core.Algo.Set includes, set_intersection and set_difference on sorted ranges Pia.Core.Algo.SetUnion set_union Pia.Core.Algo.SetSymmetric set_symmetric_difference

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Allocators, boxes and vectors, with no garbage collector and every allocation fallible (ADR 0026, ADR 0041, ADR 0042).

Module What it gives Pia.Mem.Alloc oom, the one way an allocation fails; the concept Allocator a t r, an allocator of ts lent from the region r; and the bump allocator bump t r Pia.Mem.Box box t r, an owning box of one t, whose fullness is spec-only state, so a use after release is a failed goal; its type parameter is @unsized, so it may be a concept, and box Shape holds any type that meets Shape (ADR 0046) Pia.Mem.Vec vec t a r, a growable vector that holds its allocator, C++'s std::vector with every growth fallible

docs.title: Text and data formats
docs.text: Module What it gives Pia.Text.Json.Spec RFC 8259's token grammar, as spec functions over bytes, which the rest of the JSON modules are proved against (ADR 0045) Pia.Text.Json.Lex A JSON tokenizer over a byte slice that never reads outside its input and always ends Pia.Text.Json.Write A JSON writer into a caller's buffer, whose room is its precondition, so nothing fails at run time Pia.Text.Json.Read The token readers that derived decoders are built from Pia.Text.Json.Derive @derive(json): the metaprograms that write a JSON codec for a type Pia.Text.Json.Dom A JSON document as a recursive sum type over spans of its input, copying no text (ADR 0047) Pia.Text.Json.Shape Checks that a JSON DOM has the shape of a type, and builds that type from it, with @derive(json_dom) (JSON) Pia.Format.Safetensors The safetensors container that model weights come in, read from a file's bytes and proved total and safe on every input (ADR 0067) Pia.Llm.Tokenizer llama2.c's byte-pair tokenizer, read from its tokenizer.bin and proved (ADR 0067)

docs.title: Compression and images
docs.text:
The codecs are proved total and safe on every input, and allocate nothing: the caller lends every buffer (ADR 0054).

Module What it gives Pia.Image.Bits LSB-first bit readers and writers over a byte slice, as GIF and deflate read them Pia.Image.Raster An image's dimensions and the indices of its samples Pia.Image.Gif.Spec What a GIF means, as spec functions: the LZW dictionary of GIF89a Pia.Image.Gif.Lzw GIF's LZW decoder, proved against the spec's dictionary Pia.Image.Gif.Ref GIF89a's LZW reading of a whole code stream, as a trace spec (lzw_ok), which Lzw's decoder is proved against Pia.Image.Gif.LzwEncode GIF's LZW encoder Pia.Image.Gif.Decode The GIF container, proved to accept exactly what the spec's block grammar accepts Pia.Image.Gif.Encode Animated GIF encoding Pia.Image.Gif.Quantise An RGB raster to a palette of at most 256 colours and an index raster Pia.Compress.Huffman Canonical Huffman codes as deflate defines them, with the completeness check and decoding Pia.Compress.Inflate.Spec The parts of a deflate block, as spec functions Pia.Compress.Inflate.Ref What a deflate stream says, as a trace of its blocks (stream_ok), of a dynamic block's code lengths (cl_from) and of a Huffman block's symbols (blk_ok), which Inflate's inflate_ref and codes_ref are proved against Pia.Compress.Inflate Deflate decoding into a caller's buffer, after zlib's puff.c Pia.Compress.Zlib The zlib format, with adler32 proved equal to RFC 1950's definition

docs.title: The system and the GPU
docs.text:
Module What it gives Pia.Sys.Posix The contracts of the POSIX functions Pia calls, as one interface that every target meets (ADR 0057) Pia.Sys.Fs Files over Pia.Sys.Posix, written once for both targets: a @linear file that must be closed exactly once, open_read, create, read_some, write_all and close, each failing with a decoded errno Pia.Sys.Gen.arm64_macos The bindings for arm64 macOS, generated from the system headers by tools/bindings/gen.py, which CI checks are current Pia.Sys.Gen.x86_64_linux The same for x86_64 Linux Pia.Gpu Devices, buffers and kernels on the GPU through a Metal host shim, which --trust-report lists as trusted (ADR 0068)

A spread marked @place(gpu) runs on the GPU without calling Pia.Gpu itself: the GPU demo shows one.

docs.title: Metaprograms
docs.text:
Status: implemented in M7 (#8). Decisions: ADR 0007 and ADR 0008.

A metaprogram is a let meta function that runs at compile time. It takes and returns values, and syntax is one kind of value. src/meta holds the engine: a tree-walking interpreter (Interpreter.cpp) and the expansion loop (Expand.cpp). Expansion runs after parsing and before Sema, so everything a metaprogram produces is type checked and proved like hand-written code.

piac --dump-expanded file.pia prints the syntax tree after expansion. --dump-ast still prints it as parsed.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Pia has no built-in infix operators. Each one is a let meta operator declaration that gives a symbol its fixity and expands it to a call of a core builtin:

let meta operator ( + ) : prec 6 left = let (a) (b) => `( add $a $b )

The standard operators live in the prelude (src/syntax/Prelude.cpp), which every program imports:

Level Operators Associativity Builtins 1 ==> <==> right implies iff 2 \|\| right or 3 && right and 4 = <> < > <= >= none eq ne lt gt le ge 5.5 << >> left shl shr 6 + - +\| -\| left add sub add_sat sub_sat 6.3 \| left bor 6.4 ^ left bxor 6.5 & left band 7 * / % mod left mul div rem rem

Prefix ~x is built into the parser, like -x, and stands for bnot x. | is bitwise or only inside brackets (grammar.md).

The parser reads the fixities from these declarations. A program can declare its own operators, or redeclare a prelude one. When it does, parseProgram parses the program again with the new table. An operator nobody declares still parses, with a level from its first character (grammar.md), and expansion then reports it as undeclared.

let meta operator ( ** ) : prec 8 right = let (a) (b) => `( pow $a $b )
let pow (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = ...
let times : u16 = 2 * 3 ** 1        (* 2 * (3 ** 1) *)

Expansion replaces each binary node with the operator's result, innermost first. The new call takes the location of the operator token, so diagnostics and proof reports point where they did before. The builtins can also be called by name, as in add_sat x y. IRGen lowers a builtin call exactly like the operator it stands for (irgen.md).

-x is still built in. Operators declared for a type (let meta operator ( + ) for vec<T, k>) are not supported yet.

docs.title: The interpreter
docs.text:
Values are integers (128-bit, so every bound of every Pia integer type fits, u64's included; arithmetic that leaves that range is an error, not a wrap), bools, strings, syntax, lists, functions and unit. A metaprogram can use literals, names, application (curried, with partial application), let ... in (a local function may recurse), lambdas, if, ;, list literals, quotes, and + - * / % mod < > <= >= = <> && || on its own values. Inside a metaprogram these operators act on its values directly. They are not expanded.

Builtin Meaning map f xs apply f to each element fold f init xs f (... (f init x0) ...) xn length xs the number of elements fields t the field names of the record type item t, or of the record type it names, as strings name t the name of an item or a name, as a string concat a b two strings joined (an integer counts as its digits), or two lists param name type a parameter (name : type), for a quote's parameter list; type is a type's name or its syntax nth xs i the element at index i, counting from 0; outside the list is an error zip xs ys the pairs [x; y] of two lists of one length; different lengths are an error range n [0; 1; ...; n - 1] reverse xs the elements in the opposite order filter p xs the elements for which p returns true product xss every list that takes one element from each list of xss, the first varying slowest

Each expansion has a fuel budget of a million steps. Running out is an error.

docs.title: Type-level metaprograms
docs.text:
A let meta whose parameters are all types and that returns a type or a bool is type-level (ADR 0035). It stays in the program after expansion, because types and where predicates call it while the compiler checks types (irgen.md):

let meta widen (t : type) : type =
  if t = u8 then u16 else if t = u16 then u32 else if t = u32 then u64
  else fail (concat "no integer type is wider than " (name t))

let meta small (t : type) : bool = size_of t <= 2

let add_wide (t : type where small t) (a : t) (b : t) : widen t = a + b

There, types are values. A type's name, such as u8 or pixel, denotes the type, = and <> compare types, and name t spells one as Pia does (u8, option<u8>, [u8]).

Builtin Meaning size_of t the bytes a value of t takes: an integer the smallest of 1, 2, 4 or 8 that holds its range, a bool 1, an array its elements', a record the sum of its fields'; a slice has no fixed size, which is an error type_kind t "int", "bool", "unit", "array", "slice", "record" or "variant" element t an array's or a slice's element type field_types t a record's field types, or a variant's payload types, as a list type_args t a generic instance's type arguments, as a list (empty for any other type) type_named s the type named s, as Pia.Text.Json.Derive's json_errors names the error type a derive defined eq ne lt gt le ge add sub mul div rem and or implies iff the core builtins that a where predicate's operators expand to

match takes a type too, which reads better than a cascade of ifs:

let meta widen (t : type) : type =
  match t with
  | u8 ensures size_of result = 2 -> u16
  | u16 -> u32
  | u32 -> u64
  | _ -> fail (concat "no integer type is wider than " (name t))

let meta small (t : type) : bool =
  match t with
  | int -> size_of t <= 2
  | [e; n] requires n > 0 -> n <= 16 && small e
  | option e -> small e
  | _ -> false
  • A type's name matches that type, and int every integer type. [e] matches a slice and [e; n] an array, binding the element type and the length. A generic's name applied to patterns, as in option e, matches its instances, binding their type arguments. record fs and variant cs bind the list of field or payload types. Any other name binds the whole type, and p as x binds it as well as matching p.
  • Types are an open set, so a match on a type must end with a catch-all.
  • An arm's requires is not a guard: if a type reaches the arm and it does not hold, that is an error (or, during overload resolution, the candidate's reason). An arm's ensures is checked of the arm's value, result, when the arm is taken.
  • The same arm contracts work on a value match in ordinary code, where they are proof goals (irgen.md).

A metaprogram that runs during expansion has no type values: a type's name there is an unknown name, as before.

A type-level metaprogram that a type or a constraint uses must terminate, so that which overloads a call can choose never depends on the step budget. The compiler checks this where it is defined, and an error is reported only where one that may not terminate is used:

  • it may call the builtins, except listing and redefine, and other type-level metaprograms that terminate;
  • a recursive call must be on a component of a type parameter, in one parameter position that all its recursive calls share: element t, an element of field_types t or type_args t that map or fold hands to a lambda, a name that a match on t binds below its top (e in [e] or option e), or a component of one of those. Types are finite trees, so this always ends;
  • local functions may not recurse, it may refer to itself only by calling itself, and a cycle of metaprograms calling each other is rejected (it would need a measure they all decrease, which is not supported yet).
let meta plain (t : type) : bool =
  if type_kind t = "int" || type_kind t = "bool" then true
  else if type_kind t = "array" then plain (element t)
  else if type_kind t = "record" then
    fold (let (ok) (f) => ok && plain f) true (field_types t)
  else false

Running out of steps in such a metaprogram is an internal compiler error.

docs.title: Quotes and splices
docs.text:
`( ... ) builds syntax: an expression, one item, or several items. Inside a quote:

  • $x splices the value of x. Syntax is copied in. A string becomes a name, or a type name in a type position such as (a : $t). A type item in a type position becomes its name. An integer becomes a literal, and a bool becomes true or false.
  • $(e) splices the value of the expression e.
  • $x in a binder or field position (let $n, a.$f, a quantifier's exists ($n : t)) splices a string, or the name of an item, as that name.
  • $ps alone in a parameter list, as in let lemma $n $ps : unit = (), splices a list of parameters made by param, so a metaprogram can make a function with as many parameters as it needs. The prelude's litmus uses it for a test's registers.
  • [ $xs ] splices a list's elements into a list literal, { $fs } a list of [name; value] pairs into a record literal's fields, type { $fs } a list of [name; type] pairs into a record type's, | $c of t a string as a constructor's name, type | $cs a list of names and [name; type] pairs as a variant's constructors, and | $c x -> ... one as the constructor a pattern matches, so a derive can write bytes it computed, build a value of the type it was given, declare the records it needs, make an error set with one constructor per field it found, and name and match its own constructors (tests/meta/list_splices.pia). A nullary constructor in a quoted pattern is written $!None, since a bare name there is a variable that hygiene renames. with $f after a quoted function's contracts reveals the opaque spec function a metaprogram named, so a derive can keep the spec functions it writes opaque and reveal each only where it is proved (tests/meta/reveal_splice.pia).

The code a quote builds takes the location of the expansion site: the operator, the @derive attribute, or the top-level call. Spliced code keeps its own locations.

docs.title: Hygiene
docs.text:
The rules are ADR 0022. Pia has no shadowing: a binding written in the source may not reuse the name of a local in scope, a function, a type or a core builtin. So an unqualified name always means its one visible binding. On top of that, hygiene keeps a quote from capturing, or being captured by, names at the expansion site:

  • Names a quote binds are renamed. A let ... in, a parameter, a lambda or loop variable, or a quantifier binder inside a quote gets a fresh name such as t#1, so code spliced into its scope still sees the caller's t. The names of quoted top-level items are not renamed, since they are meant to be used.
  • Free names refer to the definition site. A free name in a quote is marked [prelude] when it is a core builtin, and [toplevel] otherwise. IRGen resolves a [prelude] name to the builtin and a [toplevel] name to a top-level function, never to a local. With modules (M8), these become module-qualified paths such as prelude.add.
  • Operators and derives for a type will use argument-dependent lookup. They are found in the module that defines the type and in adapter modules the program imports. Two candidates are an ambiguity error. This arrives with modules.
  • $!name opts out. It stands for the plain name name, bound or resolved where the code lands. derive_eq uses it for the parameters a and b, which two separate quotes share:
let meta derive_eq (t : type_decl) : item =
  let n = concat "eq_" (name t) in
  let c = fold_and (map (let (f) => `( $!a.$f = $!b.$f )) (fields t)) in
  `( let $n ($!a : $t) ($!b : $t) : bool ensures $!result <==> $c = $c )

docs.title: Theory-building metaprograms
docs.text:
let theory T = gen args runs the metaprogram gen (ADR 0036, step 5). It returns a list of items: exactly one let theory ... = sig ... end, under any name, and any number of models of it (let model m : ... = struct ... end) and other items. The theory is named T, and the models are models of T.

let conn_state = type | Closed | Open | Draining

let theory Conn = machine "conn" conn_state Closed
  [ edge Closed "connect" Open
  ; edge Open "send" Open
  ; edge Open "shutdown" Draining
  ; edge Draining "close" Closed ]
  • Total and pure. What the metaprogram returns becomes hypotheses of proofs, so it must terminate and read nothing of the program, by the rules for type-level metaprograms (ADR 0035, src/meta/Totality.cpp). It may not recurse except on a component of a parameter, may not call listing or redefine, and the same holds for the metaprograms it calls. A violation is an error at the let theory that says why.
  • Arguments. In a top-level call, the name of one of the program's items stands for that item, and a variant's constructor stands for its name. So conn_state above is the type item and Closed is the name Closed.
  • Quotes of theories. A quote can hold let theory, let model and theory members (let sort, an abstract let spec f : ..., let axiom). In a theory's or a model's body, $xs splices a list of members. let sort $s, let spec $f and let axiom $n splice names.
  • Hygiene. The members' names are kept, since they are meant to be used. Their parameters and binders are renamed as in any quote (Hygiene).
  • One theory per argument tuple. A second let theory U = gen args with the same call, written the same way, does not build again: U is another name for the first theory, so U.x is T.x.

The prelude's machine builds a state machine's theory and its model from a table of edges (theories.md). It is written in Pia with map and fold, so it is total.

The prelude's litmus is a top-level call that builds a lemma from a litmus test, a small concurrent program given as data: threads of write, read, store, load, swap, fetch_add and barrier events, and an outcome of is and final conditions (theories.md). It writes the test's RC11 consistency as boolean matrices over its events, so the lemma is a finite query.

docs.title: Lowerings
docs.text: @lower(gen args) on a function runs the metaprogram gen, which returns a string of MLIR, and the string becomes the function's lowering, as if @lower("...") were written (ADR 0065, codegen.md). Among the arguments, the function's parameters stand for themselves, as names, so concat "$" (name a) splices the parameter a. There are no type values during expansion, so a shape or an element type is passed as an integer or a string (tests/codegen/lower_meta.pia).

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
@by(t args) on a lemma runs the metaprogram t, a tactic, on the lemma's goal (ADR 0036, step 6). The tactic gets the goal first, then the arguments. Among the arguments, the lemma's parameters stand for themselves, as names. It returns a list of proof steps, which go before the lemma's body, and the verifier proves them like any others (verifier.md). So a tactic can make a proof possible, or faster, but not wrong.

let meta induction (g : syntax) (on : syntax) : list =
  let args = map (let (p) => if p = name on then `( $on - 1 ) else p) (params g) in
  [ `( if $on > 0 then $(make_call (name g) args) ) ]

let spec count (xs : [u8]) (n : usize) (v : u8) : usize
  requires n <= len xs
  ensures result <= n
  decreases n
= if n = 0 then 0 else count xs (n - 1) v + (if xs.[n - 1] = v then 1 else 0)

let lemma split_count (xs : [u8]) (n : usize) (v : u8) (w : u8) : unit @by(induction n)
  requires n <= len xs && v <> w
  ensures count xs n v + count xs n w <= n
  decreases n
= ()

The goal is the lemma, as written, before its operators expand:

Builtin Meaning hypotheses g the goal's requires clauses, as a list of syntax conclusion g its ensures clauses, joined by && (true when there are none) params g its parameters' names, as strings name g the lemma's name children x the parts of the syntax x, as a list: an operator's two operands, a call's function and arguments, an if's condition and branches op x an operator's spelling ("&&"), the name a call applies, a name's text, or "" make_call f args the call of f (a name, as a string or syntax) on the list args (syntax, or strings for names)

A step is an expression: a lemma call, an assert, an if for a case split, or a call or assert that instantiates a quantified fact at particular arguments. `( fuel 4 ) is a hint rather than code: it puts @fuel(4) on the lemma. A tactic that returns an item or a value that is not syntax is an error.

Total and pure. A tactic writes what a proof assumes, so, as for a theory-building metaprogram, the rules for type-level metaprograms apply (ADR 0035): it may not call listing or redefine, and it may recurse only on a component of a parameter. For syntax, the components are the elements of children p and hypotheses p that map or fold hands to a lambda, and conclusion p. This one recurses on the operands of && and asserts each conjunct of the goal as its own step:

let meta conjuncts (e : syntax) : list =
  if op e = "&&" then fold (let (acc) (c) => concat acc (conjuncts c)) [] (children e)
  else [e]

let meta split (g : syntax) : list =
  map (let (c) => `( assert $c )) (conjuncts (conclusion g))

let lemma each (x : u8) : unit @by(split)
  requires x < 10
  ensures x < 11 && x + 1 < 12
= ()

docs.title: Comments and literate programs
docs.text:
Comments are syntax (ADR 0029, grammar.md), and metaprograms can read them:

Builtin Meaning listing () the program's items in source order, as the current pass found them, then the comments at the end of the file comments x the comments attached to the syntax x, in source order doc x the text of the doc and prose comments leading x, joined by blank lines; "" when there are none text c a comment's text (also a string literal's value) style c "line", "block", "doc" or "prose" place c "leading", "trailing" or "detached" kind x the kind of a syntax value, such as "LetItem", "Apply" or "Comment", or "Unit" for unit, as variants gives for a constructor with no payload with_doc s x a copy of the syntax x (or the first of a list of items) with a leading doc comment s fail s stop with the error s, reported at the expansion site

In the REPL, metaprograms can also change definitions that already exist, through Pia.Live (ADR 0031). listing () there lists the whole environment.

Builtin Meaning redefine x the definitions in the syntax x, marked to replace the environment's definitions of the same names; the REPL proves the change like a :redef cell before it commits it (repl.md)

piac has no Pia.Live: a compiled program cannot redefine anything, so redefine fails there.

Comments survive everything expansion does:

  • Quotes keep the comments written inside them, at the expansion site like the rest of the quote.
  • Splices keep the comments on the spliced code. A comment on the splice itself, as in `( (** the sum *) $e ), moves to the code that replaces it.
  • Expansion moves the comments on a replaced node to its replacement: an operator's comments to the builtin call, and a top-level call's comments to the first item it makes.
  • Hygiene never looks inside a comment. Comments bind no names and refer to none.

A comment can be read but not spliced into code. To document generated code, use with_doc, as the prelude's derive_eq does, so eq_pixel reads "Field-by-field equality for pixel, made by @derive(eq)." on hover.

tests/meta/doc_lint.pia walks listing () and fails on an undocumented function, and tests/meta/literate.pia.md is a literate program that piac --verify proves. Rendering listings to LaTeX, HTML, SVG and DOT (#63) and a Jupyter kernel (#64) build on these.

docs.title: Derives
docs.text:
@derive(x) on a type item calls the metaprogram derive_x with the item and adds the items it returns after the type. The prelude defines derive_eq, and for a distinct type derive_ord, derive_add, derive_scale and derive_bounds (ADR 0064, section 4), which make lt_<t>, add_<t>, mul_<t> and the rest that <, + and * on the type call. For let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8 } @derive(eq) it makes:

let eq_pixel (a : pixel) (b : pixel) : bool
  ensures result <==> (true && a.r = b.r) && a.g = b.g
  = (true && a.r = b.r) && a.g = b.g

= on two values of a record type calls eq_<name>, and <> is its negation. Without the derive, comparing records in code is an error that suggests @derive(eq); in a contract they compare as values (irgen.md). Because eq_pixel has a postcondition, callers can prove facts about p = q, such as ensures result ==> p.r = q.r.

Pia.Text.Json.Derive exports derive_json (ADR 0045, steps 4 and 5): @derive(x) finds derive_x among the program's own metaprograms, or among those its imported interfaces export, and two imported ones of one name are an error that names both. For a record of integers, range types, bool, and options (Pia.Core.Option) or fixed arrays [t; n] of them, it makes:

  • write_json_<t> (dst) (pos) (v : t) : usize, which writes v as a JSON object with Pia.Text.Json.Write, one function per member, into room its precondition states as a constant;
  • read_json_<t> (s) (pos) : result <t>_json_read <t>_json_error, which reads one with Pia.Text.Json.Read. It finds a member by a decision tree built at compile time, on the name's length, then on the first byte where the names left differ, then one full compare. It keeps a flag per field, so a member given twice is Duplicate_<t> and one never given is Missing_<t>, and it checks each integer's range as its digits are read (Range_<t>). An unknown member is Unknown_<t>, and anything else Syntax_<t>, each with its position. The error type has exactly the constructors its type can raise: no Range_<t> without an integer field. The value is built only once every field has been read, so it is fully initialised.

A fixed-array field is a JSON array of exactly n values: too few or too many is Length_<t>, at the ] or at the value past the last, and the error type has that constructor only when there is an array field (tests/std/json_derive_array.pia, tests/std/Inputs/json_array_run.pia). An option field writes null for None, and reads null, or a missing member, as None (tests/std/json_derive_option.pia, tests/std/Inputs/json_option_run.pia). A member's name is its field's, or @json(name = "...") on the field, in printable ASCII with no quote or backslash. The generated code calls the JSON modules by their full paths, so a program that derives json imports the interfaces of Pia.Text.Json.Spec, Lex, Read, Write and Derive. Each derived type also gets read_json, the instance of the concept Json, so Json.read<point> text reads the whole text as a point, with only whitespace after it (anything else is Syntax_point where the value ends), and Json.json_errors point, a type-level metaprogram, is its error type, point_json_error; the error constructors still carry the type's name, since constructors are names of the module. tests/std/json_derive.pia proves the code it makes, and tests/std/Inputs/json_derive_run.pia runs it.

On a variant, derive_json follows ADR 0045, section 2. Untagged, the default, each constructor must be told apart from every other by its JSON: a record payload is an object, a number or bool payload is that, and a constructor with no payload is null; two objects are apart when one requires a member the other cannot have, and two numbers when their ranges do not meet. Any other pair is an error that names the two and suggests a tag. The reader scans an object's members into slots for every object constructor's members, by position, in a function of its own, then picks the one constructor they fit and reads each value with that payload's field readers, so a member whose type differs between constructors is read only once the constructor is known. @json(tag = "kind") on the type writes "kind": "<name>" first and accepts it anywhere among the members; each payload must then be a record, or none. A constructor's name is its own, or @json(name = "...") on it. A record payload, in place or named, derives json too, and the variant's codec calls it (tests/std/json_derive_variant.pia, tests/std/Inputs/json_variant_run.pia).

Other derives (ord, hash, serialise, deserialise) come later. A user can write their own derive_x.

A derive reads the type it is given with these builtins, besides fields, constructors and range_of (ADR 0045, step 3). t is a type item, or its name as a string:

Builtin Meaning field_type t f the type of the field f of the record t, as written, as syntax variants t the constructors of the variant t, each [name; payload], with its payload type as syntax, or unit when it has none attrs t the attributes on a type item, or on a function's return annotation, as written, @derive included field_attrs t f the attributes on the field f of the record t ctor_attrs t c the attributes on the constructor c of the variant t bytes s the UTF-8 bytes of the string s, as integers value x the value of a literal's syntax, such as an array type's length: an integer, a bool or a string

An attribute is [name; args], and each argument [key; value], with "" as the key of a positional one. A literal argument is its value and a name its spelling as a string, so @json(name = "x", ignore_unknown) is ["json"; [["name"; "x"]; [""; "ignore_unknown"]]]; any other argument is syntax.

A derive's own attributes are its options: @json(name = "x") on a field, | Rect @json(name = "r") of rect on a constructor (grammar.md), or @json(tag = "kind") on the type. Once every derive of the type has run, the attributes named after one leave the type, its fields and its constructors, so the rest of the compiler never sees them. An attribute on a field or a constructor that no derive of its type reads is an error that names the derive to add, rather than one that is ignored (tests/meta/derive_builtins.pia, tests/meta/derive_builtin_errors.pia).

docs.title: Generators
docs.text:
A generator is a metaprogram that reads a function's signature and contract and writes tests for it (ADR 0056). Besides params, hypotheses and conclusion (see Tactics), which work on any function item, it has:

Builtin Meaning param_types f the type of each parameter of the function f, as written, as a list of syntax return_type f f's return type, as written; a function without one is an error range_of t the bounds [lo; hi] of an integer type: u8, u64, i16, a range int{-2..2}, or a type value constructors t the constructor names of the variant type t (an item, or its name), as strings subst e n v the syntax e with every name n replaced by v: syntax, a string (a name), an integer or a bool. Pia has no shadowing, so this cannot capture

On an item from listing () or a top-level call's argument, the operators have already expanded, so hypotheses returns calls such as le lo hi, and conclusion joins the clauses with a call of and too. On a tactic's goal, which is the lemma as written, both keep the operators.

tests/meta/generators.pia has a generator that writes one case per combination of its parameters' bounds, and a runner that returns the number of the first case that fails:

let clamp (v : u8) (lo : u8) (hi : int{0..9}) : u8
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
= if v < lo then lo else if v > hi then hi else v

let meta conj (xs : list) : syntax = fold (let (a) (h) => `( $a && $h )) `( true ) xs

let meta check (f : syntax) (r : list) : syntax =
  let res = concat (name f) "_result" in
  let ret = return_type f in
  let call = make_call (name f) (params f) in
  let post = subst (conclusion f) "result" res in
  let body = `( if $(conj (hypotheses f)) then (let $res : $ret = $call in $post) else true ) in
  fold (let (acc) (pv) =>
         let p = nth (nth pv 0) 0 in
         let t = nth (nth pv 0) 1 in
         let v = nth pv 1 in
         `( let $p : $t = $v in $acc ))
       body (reverse (zip (zip (params f) (param_types f)) r))

let meta cases (f : syntax) : list =
  let rows = product (map range_of (param_types f)) in
  map (let (k) => let n = concat (concat (name f) "_case_") (k + 1) in
                  `( let $n () : bool = $(check f (nth rows k)) ))
      (range (length rows))

cases clamp

docs.title: Tests from contracts
docs.text:
Pia.Test.Gen (ADR 0056, step 2) packages a generator like the one above. G.cases f, after import Pia.Test.Gen.Gen as G, writes cases for f from its signature and contract, and the verifier decides each one where it lands:

  • Domains. edges f gives each parameter's boundary values: lo, lo + 1, 0, hi - 1 and hi of its integer type, c - 1, c and c + 1 for each constant c its requires compares it with, and false and true for a bool.
  • Rows. combine doms budget is their product, or, when the product has more than budget rows, a pairwise covering array: every pair of values of every two parameters appears in some row. cases uses a budget of 64. A row whose constants make f's requires false is dropped. One the constants do not decide keeps the requires as a hypothesis.
  • Two lemmas per row. f_spec_k, the specification check, says that some value of f's result type meets its ensures at the row's inputs. f_case_k, the oracle, is the ensures with the call in place of result. Each takes f's parameters with their own types, and its requires pins them to the row, so a failed case prints its inputs as the counterexample.

Both lemmas are contracts, so they are read over unbounded integers, as every contract is. result + 1 = d on a result of type int{-3..1} at d = 2 is 1 + 1 = 2, true, where the same expression run as code would overflow. What cases dec writes for that row is, by hand:

let dec (d : int{-2..2}) : int{-3..1}
  ensures result + 1 = d
= d - 1

let lemma dec_spec_5 (d : int{-2..2}) : unit @case(spec, dec, 5)
  requires d = 2
  ensures (exists (dec_result : int{-3..1}). dec_result + 1 = d)
= ()

let lemma dec_case_5 (d : int{-2..2}) : unit @case(oracle, dec, 5)
  requires d = 2
  ensures dec d + 1 = d
= ()

@case(spec, f, k) and @case(oracle, f, k) name what a lemma checks, so the report says case 5: some result can meet the ensures of 'dec' and case 5: 'dec' meets its ensures rather than "the postcondition holds".

A specification failure is a contract that no result can meet. ensures result = a + b on a u8 result cannot hold at a = b = 255, whatever the body does. For a function with a body, the body's own goals fail too, but for an extern nothing else would notice: every proof that assumes its ensures there follows from a contradiction, and so does its oracle. So the specification check comes first, and when it fails its goal carries the hint specification failure: no value of 'f''s result type satisfies its ensures at these inputs, with the inputs as the counterexample (tests/std/Inputs/test_gen_spec.pia). The fix is in the contract: correct the ensures, widen the result type, or add a requires. An extern gets only the specification check, since its oracle can be decided only by running it, which test mode adds (step 3). tests/std/test_gen.pia proves the cases of a function with a precondition, a range-typed result, a bool parameter, an extern and a pairwise array.

docs.title: Top-level calls
docs.text:
An item that is a call of a metaprogram, such as make_byte () in column 1, runs it. The items it returns replace the call. A metaprogram may return a list of items, which all replace the call. A metaprogram may also return a call of another metaprogram, which runs in the next pass.

A module exports a metaprogram by listing it in an interface with its result type, as let meta define : item (ADR 0039). The interface artifact carries its definition, and an importer runs it by its qualified name, as R.define "milli" (R.si "milli"). The names its quotes use are the defining module's: an importer's own ratio does not capture Pia.Core.Ratio.ratio. The module must define every metaprogram its interfaces list (tests/modules/metaprograms.pia). An exported metaprogram names another module's items in full, as Pia.Core.Ratio.num in Pia.Time: an alias is the defining module's own, and its importers need not share it. They do import that module's interface. Pia.Core.Ratio is built this way.

docs.title: The expansion loop
docs.text:
Expansion runs in passes, to a fixed point (design.md, "Stages"). Each pass looks only at the items that existed when it started:

  1. Each @derive runs.
  2. Each top-level metaprogram call runs.
  3. Each binary operator expands.

Code produced in one pass expands in the next. So @derive(eq) takes two passes: one makes eq_pixel, and the next expands the operators inside it.

A metaprogram sees a type only once it is defined. fields t on a record whose field types are not all defined yet defers the derive to the next pass. In this program the derive waits one pass for make_byte to define byte:

let wide = type { v : byte; w : u8 } @derive(eq)
let meta make_byte () : item = `( let byte = u8 )
make_byte ()

The loop stops when a pass changes nothing. A metaprogram still waiting then is an error that names the type it needed. --meta-cycles=N (default 32) caps the passes that may produce code. Reaching the cap is an error that names the metaprograms still producing code. Once expansion stops, the let meta items and operator declarations are removed, and Sema sees ordinary code. Sema defines types in dependency order, so a generated type may come after its uses.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
tests/meta/*.pia are lit tests:

Test Covers derive.pia @derive(eq) and record =/<>, proved; deferral until a later pass defines a type operators.pia a user operator's precedence, renaming and [toplevel] resolution errors.pia undeclared operators, unknown derives, failing metaprograms, operators for a type waiting.pia a derive waiting for a type that is never defined cycles.pia --meta-cycles and its default shadowing.pia, builtin_name.pia the no-shadowing rule, and that quote binders never trip it comments.pia where comments attach, and that quotes, splices, derives and operators keep them doc_lint.pia a metaprogram that walks listing () and insists on doc comments generators.pia, generator_errors.pia the list and signature builtins, a generator that writes one proved case per combination of bounds, and their errors; tests/std/test_gen.pia proves what Pia.Test.Gen writes tactic_errors.pia @by on something other than a lemma, tactics that are not total or pure, and tactics that return something other than proof steps; tests/verify/tactics.pia proves what tactics write literate.pia.md, literate_errors.pia.md, literate_unclosed.pia.md a literate program, proved, and its errors

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• operators for a type, and overloading
  • nested quotes
  • a metaprogram's errors are reported at the expansion site, not inside the metaprogram
  • concepts (let meta Numeric (t : type) : concept) and generic types
  • module-level prelude import control

docs.title: Demo: D8 directions and the picture on the GPU
docs.text:
Two stages of stream delineation do the same work on every cell and read only their inputs: the D8 direction of a cell, and its colour in the picture. Each is a spread (ADR 0060) in which iteration i writes only cell i, so here each is placed on the GPU with @place(gpu) (ADR 0068, step 3).

The proof does not change with the placement. Each spread is proved as on the CPU: its body, the ownership of its writes, and its ensures. piac then outlines the body as a kernel, one thread per cell, lowers it to SPIR-V, translates it to the Metal Shading Language with SPIRV-Cross, compiles it with fast math off, and embeds the .metallib in the object. At run time the Metal shim copies the buffers in, runs the kernel, waits, and copies back what it wrote.

A placed spread is fallible: it evaluates to result unit gpu_error, with gpu_error = Gpu_unavailable | Gpu_out_of_memory | Gpu_fault | Gpu_timeout in that order. Its ensures holds only when it returns Ok, since a failed run may leave a buffer part written, and an explicit placement never falls back to the CPU on its own (ADR 0068, section 5).

examples/streams/srtm_gpu.c runs both stages on the GPU and checks them against the CPU stages of streams.pia.md, cell for cell, on the SRTM fixture and on a whole tile:

$ bazel run //examples/streams:srtm_gpu -- /tmp/srtm/N46E008.hgt

On the iMac the CPU and GPU share memory, so the shim binds each buffer where it is, without a copy, when it starts on a page boundary (newBufferWithBytesNoCopy); only the few scalars, and any buffer that does not start on a page, are copied. On the whole tile, 3601 × 3601 cells, both stages match the CPU on every cell, and over three runs:

Stage CPU GPU, warm GPU, first run D8 directions 41 ms 6 to 16 ms 50 to 60 ms The picture 25 to 30 ms 9 to 12 ms 26 to 29 ms

The first run of directions also opened the device and loaded the kernel. The shim now pre-warms them instead: when the program loads, a background queue opens the device and builds every placed kernel's pipeline, so a first run finds them ready (ADR 0068, step 4b). On the tile that takes the first run of directions from 42 to 57 ms down to 13 to 19 ms, over three runs each way (2026-11-28). The first run of the picture, 18 to 40 ms, is the same with or without it, so its extra cost lies elsewhere, probably in the GPU's first touch of the newly wrapped buffers. PIA_GPU_WARM=0 turns pre-warming off. Before the buffers were wrapped, the copies in and back made both stages slower on the GPU than on the CPU (ADR 0068, step 3).

The device rules of ADR 0068, section 1 decide what a body may do. Its calls are inlined, since the GPU has no call stack, and after that it may use only integer arithmetic of 8 to 64 bits, loads and stores of integer buffers, and if, for and while. A record is not one of those yet, so the bodies below work in scalars: the best route as a target and a drop, and a colour as one packed u32.

The file is one module, Placed. Its interface is what the C program calls. Each function returns 0 when the stage ran, or 1 plus the gpu_error, in its order.

module Placed : PlacedStages

interface PlacedStages @abi(c) = sig
  let directions_gpu : (fill : [u16]) -> (w : usize)
      -> (down : out mutable [usize]) -> i32
    requires len down = len fill && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len fill
  let render_gpu : (dem : [u16]) -> (fill : [u16]) -> (acc : [u32])
      -> (basin : [usize]) -> (threshold : u32)
      -> (rgba : out mutable [u32]) -> i32
    requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
    requires len rgba = len dem
end

docs.title: D8 directions
docs.text:
As on the CPU, a drop to one of the four near neighbours is weighted by 10 and a drop to a diagonal by 7.

let tenfold (d : u16) : u32 =
  let d2 : u32 = d + d in
  let d4 : u32 = d2 + d2 in
  d4 + d4 + d2

Seven times a drop.

let sevenfold (d : u16) : u32 =
  let d2 : u32 = d + d in
  let d4 : u32 = d2 + d2 in
  d4 + d2 + d

The weighted drop from cell m to neighbour n, or 0 if n is not lower. A lower neighbour's drop is at least 7, so a gain above 0 means downhill.

let gain (fill : [u16]) (m : usize) (n : usize) (diagonal : bool) : u32
  requires m < len fill && n < len fill
  ensures result > 0 ==> fill.[n] < fill.[m]
=
  if fill.[n] < fill.[m] then
    (let d : u16 = fill.[m] - fill.[n] in
     if diagonal then sevenfold d else tenfold d)
  else 0

The target after considering a neighbour with gain g against the best drop so far: the neighbour wins only if it beats the best, so ties go to the first considered.

let better (g : u32) (best : u32) (n : usize) (t : usize) : usize =
  if g > best then n else t

The best drop after considering it.

let most (g : u32) (best : u32) : u32 = if g > best then g else best

The direction of a cell with all eight neighbours on the map, in the same order as steepest in streams.pia.md: row above, own row, row below. The CPU's consider takes a neighbour when it is lower and its weighted drop beats the best; here that is g > best, since g is 0 for one that is not lower. So both pick the same neighbour.

let steepest_at (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (m : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 1 && w < m && m + w + 1 < len fill
  ensures result = m || (result < len fill && fill.[result] < fill.[m])
=
  let a = m - w in
  let b = m + w in
  let g1 = gain fill m (a - 1) true in
  let t1 = better g1 0 (a - 1) m in
  let d1 = most g1 0 in
  let g2 = gain fill m a false in
  let t2 = better g2 d1 a t1 in
  let d2 = most g2 d1 in
  let g3 = gain fill m (a + 1) true in
  let t3 = better g3 d2 (a + 1) t2 in
  let d3 = most g3 d2 in
  let g4 = gain fill m (m - 1) false in
  let t4 = better g4 d3 (m - 1) t3 in
  let d4 = most g4 d3 in
  let g5 = gain fill m (m + 1) false in
  let t5 = better g5 d4 (m + 1) t4 in
  let d5 = most g5 d4 in
  let g6 = gain fill m (b - 1) true in
  let t6 = better g6 d5 (b - 1) t5 in
  let d6 = most g6 d5 in
  let g7 = gain fill m b false in
  let t7 = better g7 d6 b t6 in
  let d7 = most g7 d6 in
  let g8 = gain fill m (b + 1) true in
  better g8 d7 (b + 1) t7

The direction of cell m, given the start last of the last interior row. The CPU visits the interior a row at a time; a thread instead finds its own row and column. A cell is interior when its row starts at w to last and its column is 1 to w - 2; every other cell points at itself.

The first test, that all eight neighbours are on the map, holds for every interior cell, so it changes no direction. It keeps the mod away from the call's precondition, which the solver then proves quickly.

let direction_of (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (last : usize) (m : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w <= last && last + w + w <= len fill && m < len fill
  ensures result = m || (result < len fill && fill.[result] < fill.[m])
=
  if w < m && m < len fill - w - 1 then
    (let s = steepest_at fill w m in
     let col = m mod w in
     let row = m - col in
     if row >= w && row <= last && col >= 1 && col + 1 < w then s else m)
  else m

The start of the last interior row, as in streams.pia.md.

let last_row (n : usize) (w : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= n
  ensures w <= result && result + w + w <= n
=
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while w <= n - (r + w + w)
    invariant w <= r && r + w + w <= n
    decreases n - r
  do
    r <- r + w
  done;
  r

The stage: one thread per cell. When it returns Ok, every direction points strictly downhill or at the cell itself, the property flow accumulation needs.

let directions_on_gpu (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (down : out mutable [usize])
    : result unit gpu_error
  requires len down = len fill && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len fill
=
  let last = last_row (len fill) w in
  spread m in 0 .. len down @place(gpu)
    ensures down.[m] = m || (down.[m] < len fill && fill.[down.[m]] < fill.[m])
  do
    down.[m] <- direction_of fill w last m
  done

Its C entry point.

let directions_gpu (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (down : out mutable [usize]) : i32
=
  match directions_on_gpu fill w down with
  | Ok -> 0
  | Err e ->
    (match e with
     | Gpu_unavailable -> 1
     | Gpu_out_of_memory -> 2
     | Gpu_fault -> 3
     | Gpu_timeout -> 4)

docs.title: The picture
docs.text:
The colours of streams.pia.md, section 4, each cell's packed as red + 256 green + 65536 blue. Whether flow a is at least sixteen times threshold:

let major (a : u32) (threshold : u32) : bool =
  let t2 : u64 = threshold + threshold in
  let t4 : u64 = t2 + t2 in
  let t8 : u64 = t4 + t4 in
  a >= t8 + t8

A colour as one u32.

let pack (r : u32) (g : u32) (b : u32) : u32
  requires r < 256 && g < 256 && b < 256
= r + g * 256 + b * 65536

The red of watershed colour k, one of six.

let tint_red (k : usize) : u16 =
  if k = 0 then 214 else if k = 1 then 150 else if k = 2 then 200
  else if k = 3 then 120 else if k = 4 then 210 else 170

Its green.

let tint_green (k : usize) : u16 =
  if k = 0 then 168 else if k = 1 then 190 else if k = 2 then 140
  else if k = 3 then 170 else if k = 4 then 200 else 150

Its blue.

let tint_blue (k : usize) : u16 =
  if k = 0 then 110 else if k = 1 then 110 else if k = 2 then 160
  else if k = 3 then 160 else if k = 4 then 120 else 200

The colour of one cell, as paint gives it: streams in blue, lakes in pale blue, and the rest in its watershed's colour, darker where it is lower.

let paint_packed (h : u16) (f : u16) (a : u32) (outlet : usize) (threshold : u32) : u32 =
  if a >= threshold then
    (if major a threshold then pack 20 70 190 else pack 70 140 240)
  else if f > h then pack 150 205 235
  else
    (let k = outlet mod 6 in
     let shade : u16 = h / 256 in
     let r : u16 = tint_red k + shade in
     let g : u16 = tint_green k + shade in
     let b : u16 = tint_blue k + shade in
     pack (r / 2) (g / 2) (b / 2))

The stage: one thread per cell.

let render_on_gpu (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (acc : [u32]) (basin : [usize])
    (threshold : u32) (rgba : out mutable [u32]) : result unit gpu_error
  requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
  requires len rgba = len dem
=
  spread i in 0 .. len rgba @place(gpu) do
    rgba.[i] <- paint_packed (dem.[i]) (fill.[i]) (acc.[i]) (basin.[i]) threshold
  done

Its C entry point.

let render_gpu (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (acc : [u32]) (basin : [usize])
    (threshold : u32) (rgba : out mutable [u32]) : i32
=
  match render_on_gpu dem fill acc basin threshold rgba with
  | Ok -> 0
  | Err e ->
    (match e with
     | Gpu_unavailable -> 1
     | Gpu_out_of_memory -> 2
     | Gpu_fault -> 3
     | Gpu_timeout -> 4)

docs.title: Many spreads, one command buffer
docs.text:
Each placed spread on this page is a single GPU run: the shim wraps the buffers, commits one command buffer and waits for it. That is fine for a stage that runs once. A step made of thousands of small spreads in a row, such as the waves of the sediment pull step, would spend all its time waiting. For that, put @place(gpu) on the for that runs them instead (ADR 0068, section 9):

let run = for k in 0 .. waves @place(gpu)
    invariant ...
  do
    let lo = starts.[k] in
    let hi = starts.[k + 1] in
    wave ... lo hi;        (* a spread, through a call *)
    commit ... lo hi       (* another *)
  done
in
match run with
| Ok -> ...
| Err e -> ...

Every spread the body reaches, through calls too, becomes one dispatch of a single command buffer, in order, and the host commits and waits once. The loop is proved as an ordinary for, and evaluates to result unit gpu_error: its invariants hold after it only on Ok. Its spreads need no @place of their own, and may own cells through an owner array (@owns). The rest of the body runs on the host while the dispatches are encoded, before any of them runs, so piac checks that it only computes scalars, such as the bounds above, from buffers no spread in the loop writes, and that it assigns no variable from outside. The pull step on the GPU is built this way.

docs.title: What is proved, and what is checked
docs.text:
Claim Where A GPU direction points strictly downhill, or at the cell itself directions_on_gpu's spread, when it returns Ok Each thread writes only its own cell the ownership check of ADR 0060 Every index is in bounds and nothing overflows every function The GPU gives the CPU's directions and colours, cell for cell srtm_gpu, a differential test (ADR 0068, section 6)

The last line is a test, not a theorem. The bodies here are not proved equal to steepest and paint of streams.pia.md, which are written with records. The differential test checks that, and the toolchain from SPIR-V to Metal, on real terrain.

docs.title: Demo: sediment in pull form, proved equal to the sequential step
docs.text:
The sediment step of sediment.pia.md goes through the cells in height order, highest first. Each cell erodes or deposits, then pushes its load into the cell below it. That order is sequential: a cell needs every load pushed into it before it can move. ADR 0055, section 6, plans the GPU form, a pull step. Here every cell reads its eight neighbours and adds the loads of those that drain into it, so each cell writes only itself.

This page is that step. The cells are taken in waves, one for each height. A cell's upstream neighbours are strictly higher, so they belong to earlier waves. Within a wave the cells are independent. So a wave is a spread (ADR 0060) with the default identity ownership. Each iteration writes only its own slots of three scratch buffers, and a short pass then commits the wave in order.

The theorem is that it is the same step, exactly:

from the same bed, the pull step and the sequential step leave the same
bed and the same load leaving every cell, cell for cell, and send the
same mass off the map.

It is same_step, at the end of the page, and both_steps runs the two steps and states it as its postcondition. Exact conservation then carries over from the sequential step, as do the bounds that keep every sum in a u32.

docs.title: The proof, in outline
docs.text:
A step is pinned down by what each cell takes in. Call a step settled when every cell's bed and load are what erosion and deposition make of the inflow it took, seen.[c]. Call it linked when that inflow is the sum of the loads leaving those of its eight neighbours that drain into it. Two settled, linked steps from the same bed are the same step. Take the cells in height order: a cell's upstream neighbours come before it, so by its turn they agree, so its inflow does, so it does (agree).

So the work is to prove each step settled and linked. For the sequential step, transport_seen keeps three invariants as it goes:

  • every processed cell has settled (done_upto);
  • every processed cell is linked (linked_upto);
  • every cell not yet processed holds, as its inflow, the loads of exactly its processed upstream neighbours (pending).

For the pull step, the kernel computes each cell's inflow and result. The commit pass keeps the same linked_upto, and the pull step's own promise (holds_if), as it writes them back. The sums that both steps send off the map are the outlets' loads, added in height order (osum).

The predicates are opaque spec functions (ADR 0063), revealed only in small step lemmas. Without that, a hypothesis that reads flux at a cell's neighbours and one about every cell instantiate each other across the whole grid, a matching loop. Inflows are trees of two-term sums for the same reason: under a quantifier, Z3 proves two-term sums equal at once, and eight-term sums not at all.

The page is its own module. examples/streams/srtm.c runs it on a real tile and checks it against the sequential sediment cell for cell.

module Pull : PullTransport, PullWaves

interface PullTransport @abi(c) = sig
  let pull_step : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (order : [usize])
      -> (pos : [usize]) -> (w : usize) -> (bed0 : [u32])
      -> (bed : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) -> (flux : borrowed inout mutable [u32])
      -> (seen : borrowed inout mutable [u64]) -> (gathered : borrowed inout mutable [u64])
      -> (newbed : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) -> (newout : borrowed inout mutable [u32])
      -> (gone : u64) -> u64
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len order = len fill && len pos = len fill && len bed0 = len fill
    requires len bed = len fill && len flux = len fill && len seen = len fill
    requires len gathered = len fill && len newbed = len fill && len newout = len fill
    requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && len fill < max u32 && gone <= max u32
    requires forall (r in 0 .. len order). order.[r] < len pos && pos.[order.[r]] = r
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len pos). pos.[k] < len order && order.[pos.[k]] = k
    requires forall (a in 0 .. len order) (b in 0 .. len order). a < b ==> fill.[order.[b]] <= fill.[order.[a]]
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len down). down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len down). down.[k] < len fill
end

The page also provides a second interface, PullWaves, for the GPU form of the step in pull_gpu.pia.md. It is what a step needs to run its own waves and still be proved: the specification functions its promise is written in, the commit pass and the lemmas around it. A spec function is exported with its definition, so every one that a definition uses is listed too.

interface PullWaves = sig
  let spec nbr : (n : usize) -> (w : usize) -> (c : usize) -> (d : int{0..7}) -> usize
  let spec from : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (w : usize) -> (c : usize) -> (d : int{0..7}) -> u64
  let spec pair : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (w : usize) -> (c : usize) -> (h : int{0..3}) -> u64
  let spec half : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (w : usize) -> (c : usize) -> (g : int{0..1}) -> u64
  let spec inflow_of : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (w : usize) -> (c : usize) -> u64
  let spec el : (i : u64) -> (cap : u32) -> (bed : u32) -> u64
  let spec eb : (i : u64) -> (cap : u32) -> (bed : u32) -> u64
  let spec cap_rule : (a : u32) -> (drop : u16) -> u32
  let spec cap_of : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (c : usize) -> u32
  let spec at : (xs : [usize]) -> (k : usize) -> usize
  let spec holds_if : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (bed : [u32])
      -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (c : usize) -> bool
  let spec done_if_upto : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (bed : [u32])
      -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (pos : [usize]) -> (p : usize) -> bool
  let spec linked_upto : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (pos : [usize]) -> (p : usize)
      -> (w : usize) -> bool
  let spec ready_in : (down : [usize]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (w : usize) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (gathered : [u64])
      -> (q : usize) -> (hi : usize) -> bool
  let spec ready_vals : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (bed0 : [u32])
      -> (gathered : [u64]) -> (newbed : [u32]) -> (newout : [u32]) -> (q : usize) -> (hi : usize) -> bool
  let spec settled_if : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (bed : [u32])
      -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> bool
  let spec linked : (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (w : usize) -> bool
  let spec oterm : (order : [usize]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (q : usize) -> u32
  let spec osum : (order : [usize]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (p : usize) -> u64
  let lemma osum_next : (order : [usize]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (p : usize) -> unit
    requires p < max u32 + 1
    ensures osum order down flux (p + 1) = osum order down flux p + oterm order down flux p
  let lemma ready_init : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (w : usize)
      -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (gathered : [u64]) -> (newbed : [u32]) -> (newout : [u32])
      -> (lo : usize) -> (hi : usize) -> unit
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len order = len fill && len bed0 = len fill && len flux = len fill
    requires len gathered = len fill && len newbed = len fill && len newout = len fill && hi <= len fill
    requires forall (r in 0 .. len order). order.[r] < len fill
    requires w >= 3 && w < max usize
    requires forall (q in lo .. hi). gathered.[q] = inflow_of down flux w (order.[q])
    requires forall (q in lo .. hi). gathered.[q] + bed0.[order.[q]] <= max u32 ==>
      newbed.[q] = eb (gathered.[q]) (cap_of fill down acc (order.[q])) (bed0.[order.[q]])
      && newout.[q] = el (gathered.[q]) (cap_of fill down acc (order.[q])) (bed0.[order.[q]])
    ensures ready_in down order w flux gathered lo hi
    ensures ready_vals fill down acc order bed0 gathered newbed newout lo hi
  let lemma start_pull : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (bed : [u32])
      -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (pos : [usize]) -> (w : usize) -> unit
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len bed0 = len fill && len bed = len fill && len flux = len fill
    requires len seen = len fill && len pos = len fill && w >= 3 && w < max usize
    ensures done_if_upto fill down acc bed0 bed flux seen pos 0
    ensures linked_upto down flux seen pos 0 w
  let lemma finish_pull : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (bed : [u32])
      -> (flux : [u32]) -> (seen : [u64]) -> (pos : [usize]) -> (w : usize) -> unit
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len bed0 = len fill && len bed = len fill && len flux = len fill
    requires len seen = len fill && len pos = len fill && w >= 3 && w < max usize
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len pos). pos.[k] < len fill
    requires done_if_upto fill down acc bed0 bed flux seen pos (len fill)
    requires linked_upto down flux seen pos (len fill) w
    ensures settled_if fill down acc bed0 bed flux seen
    ensures linked down flux seen w
  let copy_back : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize]) -> (acc : [u32]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (pos : [usize])
      -> (w : usize) -> (bed0 : [u32]) -> (gathered : [u64]) -> (newbed : [u32]) -> (newout : [u32])
      -> (bed : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) -> (flux : borrowed inout mutable [u32])
      -> (seen : borrowed inout mutable [u64]) -> (lo : usize) -> (hi : usize) -> (v : u16) -> (g : u64)
      -> (g0 : u64) -> u64
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len order = len fill && len pos = len fill && len bed0 = len fill
    requires len gathered = len fill && len newbed = len fill && len newout = len fill
    requires len bed = len fill && len flux = len fill && len seen = len fill
    requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && lo <= hi && hi <= len fill
    requires forall (r in 0 .. len order). order.[r] < len pos && pos.[order.[r]] = r
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len pos). pos.[k] < len order && order.[pos.[k]] = k
    requires forall (a in 0 .. len order) (b in 0 .. len order). a < b ==> fill.[order.[b]] <= fill.[order.[a]]
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len down). down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
    requires forall (k in 0 .. len down). down.[k] < len fill
    requires forall (r in lo .. hi). fill.[at order r] = v
    requires done_if_upto fill down acc bed0 bed flux seen pos lo
    requires linked_upto down flux seen pos lo w
    requires ready_in down order w flux gathered lo hi
    requires ready_vals fill down acc order bed0 gathered newbed newout lo hi
    requires len fill < max u32 && g0 <= max u32 && g = g0 + osum order down flux lo
    ensures result = g0 + osum order down flux hi
    ensures done_if_upto fill down acc bed0 bed flux seen pos hi
    ensures linked_upto down flux seen pos hi w
  let wave_end : (fill : [u16]) -> (order : [usize]) -> (lo : usize) -> usize
    requires len order = len fill && lo < len fill
    requires forall (r in 0 .. len order). order.[r] < len fill
    ensures lo < result && result <= len fill
    ensures forall (r in lo .. result). fill.[at order r] = fill.[order.[lo]]
end

docs.title: 1. Neighbours and inflow
docs.text:
A neighbour is one of eight offsets away: a comes before b, one cell or about one row apart. The check is in usize, with no overflow.

let spec step_of (w : usize) (a : usize) (b : usize) : bool
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
= if a < b then (b - a = 1 || b - a = w - 1 || b - a = w || b - a = w + 1) else false

k and p are neighbours.

let spec adjacent (w : usize) (k : usize) (p : usize) : bool
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
= step_of w p k || step_of w k p

The neighbour of c in direction d (row order), or n if it is off the slice. It is total, with its guards inside, so that it can sit under a quantifier without a precondition to prove.

let spec nbr (n : usize) (w : usize) (c : usize) (d : int{0..7}) : usize
= if w < 3 || w = max usize || c >= n then n
  else if d = 0 then (if c >= w + 1 then c - (w + 1) else n)
  else if d = 1 then (if c >= w then c - w else n)
  else if d = 2 then (if c >= w - 1 then c - (w - 1) else n)
  else if d = 3 then (if c >= 1 then c - 1 else n)
  else if d = 4 then (if 1 < n - c then c + 1 else n)
  else if d = 5 then (if w - 1 < n - c then c + (w - 1) else n)
  else if d = 6 then (if w < n - c then c + w else n)
  else (if w + 1 < n - c then c + (w + 1) else n)

What neighbour d of c sends into c: its load, if it drains into c. Opaque: only the per-direction lemmas see its body.

let spec from (down : [usize]) (flux : [u32]) (w : usize) (c : usize) (d : int{0..7}) : u64 @opaque
  ensures result <= max u32
= let nb = nbr (len down) w c d in
  if nb < len down && nb < len flux then (if nb <> c && down.[nb] = c then flux.[nb] else 0) else 0

Two directions' terms.

let spec pair (down : [usize]) (flux : [u32]) (w : usize) (c : usize) (h : int{0..3}) : u64
  ensures result <= 8'589'934'590
= if h = 0 then from down flux w c 0 + from down flux w c 1
  else if h = 1 then from down flux w c 2 + from down flux w c 3
  else if h = 2 then from down flux w c 4 + from down flux w c 5
  else from down flux w c 6 + from down flux w c 7

Four directions' terms.

let spec half (down : [usize]) (flux : [u32]) (w : usize) (c : usize) (g : int{0..1}) : u64
  ensures result <= 17'179'869'180
= if g = 0 then pair down flux w c 0 + pair down flux w c 1 else pair down flux w c 2 + pair down flux w c 3

Everything c's upstream neighbours send it. It is a tree of two-term sums: under a quantifier, Z3 proves an equality of two-term sums quickly and an equality of eight-term sums not at all. Opaque, so that the frame lemmas can instantiate it as one term.

let spec inflow_of (down : [usize]) (flux : [u32]) (w : usize) (c : usize) : u64 @opaque
  ensures result <= 34'359'738'360
= half down flux w c 0 + half down flux w c 1

The load leaving a cell with inflow i, capacity cap and bed bed: what erode_or_deposit computes, as a spec function, total in i.

let spec el (i : u64) (cap : u32) (bed : u32) : u64
= if i > 34'359'738'360 then 0 else if i < cap then (if cap - i < bed then cap else i + bed) else cap

The bed it leaves.

let spec eb (i : u64) (cap : u32) (bed : u32) : u64
= if i > 34'359'738'360 then 0 else if i < cap then (if cap - i < bed then bed - (cap - i) else 0) else bed + (i - cap)

capacity_of, as a spec function.

let spec cap_rule (a : u32) (drop : u16) : u32
= let d : u64 = drop in
  let c : u64 = (a >> 4) + (d << 2) in
  if c < max u16 then c else max u16

Cell c's capacity, from its flow and its drop, total like nbr.

let spec cap_of (fill : [u16]) (down : [usize]) (acc : [u32]) (c : usize) : u32
= if c < len fill && c < len down && c < len acc then
    (let d = down.[c] in
     if d < len fill then cap_rule (acc.[c]) (if d <> c && fill.[d] < fill.[c] then fill.[c] - fill.[d] else 0)
     else 0)
  else 0
