  1. Pia cannot express it. It needs a machine instruction, an OS call, or memory that Pia has no way to describe. Examples: shifts, calling read, viewing a page that mmap returned.
  2. The verifier must know what it means. The solver needs its semantics as axioms, not as a body to walk. Examples: len, old, wrapping arithmetic, the meaning of a buffer that has been freed.
  3. It shapes the language. Other code cannot be written without it. Examples: modules, generics, sum types.

Everything else goes in the library, written in Pia, with contracts, and proved when the library builds. This is the same split as Rust's core, alloc and std. It is also how Zig and OCaml work: the library is ordinary code, and the compiler provides a short list of builtins (@ builtins in Zig, external primitives in OCaml). What Pia adds is that every library function carries a contract the compiler has proved. That also asks things of the core that an unverified language does not need: specification functions and lemmas (see Verification primitives).

The prelude already works this way for operators (ADR 0008). + is a metaprogram that expands to the core builtin add, and the builtin is what the verifier and codegen understand. The proposal extends that pattern to the rest of the library.

The rule from ADR 0004 applies throughout: the strongest guarantee is the default. The only things taken on trust are the compiler's builtins and the contracts of a short, audited list of POSIX functions. Each of those trusts is named in a proof certificate, so piac can print the trusted base of any program.

docs.title: What the core has today
docs.text:
Area Core today Arithmetic builtins add sub mul div rem add_sat sub_sat, with @overflow(proof\|wrap\|saturate\|trap) Comparison and logic eq ne lt gt le ge, and or implies iff Buffers len, indexing xs.[i], fixed arrays [T; n], slices [T] Contracts requires ensures assert assume old forall exists invariant decreases Types bounded integers, range types int{lo..hi}, bool, records, type aliases Meta builtins map fold length fields name concat, quotes and splices Prelude operator declarations, fold_and, derive_eq, held as a C++ string in src/syntax/Prelude.cpp

That is enough for the edge detection demo (examples/edges), but not for a library. The demo shows the gaps directly: main.c reads and writes the BMP files and allocates the buffers, because Pia has no I/O and no allocation, and grayscale is (r + 2g + b) / 4 rather than BT.601, because one * makes its loop goals time out. The gaps that block a library, roughly in order of how much they block:

  • No modules or imports. A library cannot be imported, so every program would have to paste it in. This is milestone M8 (ADR 0010).
  • No generics. Every function is for one concrete type. This is M9 (ADR 0009).
  • No sum types or match. So there is no option or result, and no way to return an error.
  • No bitwise operators or shifts. Hashing, checksums, bitsets, UTF-8 and the PNG codec in M13 all need them.
  • No memory allocation, and no calls to the outside world. All memory comes from a C caller, and there is no I/O.
  • Multiplication defeats the solver once loops are involved.
  • No calls inside contracts. A call in a contract is an unknown value (verifier.md). So a library cannot state ensures sorted xs, or ensures result = sum xs. Spec functions and lemmas (#52) now lift this (verifier.md).
  • No slicing xs.[a .. b], no buffers of records, no constant arrays, no function values.

docs.title: The proposed minimal core
docs.text: The core is grouped by what each group unlocks in the library. ★ marks what the first useful library (Pia.Core, below) cannot do without.

docs.title: 1. Modules and the prelude as a module ★
docs.text:
• module, interface, import as already designed in M8. The library is a set of modules: Pia.Core, Pia.Mem, Pia.Sys and so on.
  • The prelude becomes a real Pia module, Pia.Prelude, which every module imports implicitly. Today it is a C++ string. Moving it makes the operators ordinary library code, and lets the library be versioned with the compiler.
  • Proof certificates (ADR 0010) apply to the library like any other module. A program proved against Pia.Core's interface keeps its proof until that interface changes. Certificates also list the trusted contracts a module depends on (group 8).

docs.title: 2. Integer primitives ★
docs.text:
New builtins, each one or two MLIR ops, with exact SMT semantics (bvand, bvshl and so on):

Builtin Meaning Goal raised band bor bxor bnot bitwise logic, exact on the two's-complement form of the integers (bnot on an unsigned type flips the bits of its storage width) the result fits, in proof mode shl shr shifts: a * 2^b and floor(a / 2^b) 0 <= b < bits t (the shift goal), in every mode. shl in proof mode also proves no bits are lost rotl rotr, clz ctz popcount bswap bit counting, rotation and byte swap on the storage bits of an unsigned operand, through LLVM intrinsics; the counts are int{0..w}, and zero counts w. Implemented (ADR 0040) rotl and rotr: the shift goal, 0 <= b < w widen e to a wider type of the same signedness none narrow e narrowing conversion, the explicit form of what assignment does now the value fits wrap_to t e, sat_to t e conversion with a stated overflow mode none mul_wide a b the full product in a type twice as wide, u32 -> u32 -> u64 none to_bits from_bits reinterpret a float's IEEE encoding (built, M11) none

Their operators use C's symbols (Dean, 2026-11-21) and go in the prelude as metaprograms, like + today:

Operator Builtin Precedence ~x bnot prefix, binds like -x << >> shl shr 5.5, left (between .. and +) & band 6.5, left (between + and *) ^ bxor 6.4, left \| bor 6.3, left

Unlike C, bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so x & mask = 0 means (x & mask) = 0. Precedence levels may have one decimal place for this. ~x is built into the parser like -x, and stands for bnot x. Implemented in #48.

| is already a grammar token: it separates variants and match arms, and starts a refinement's predicate (grammar.md). So | means bitwise or only inside parentheses or brackets opened within the expression. At the top level of a match arm's body or a refinement it keeps its grammar meaning, and | A -> (x | y) needs the parentheses. || and && stay logical, and ^, &, << and >> are free today.

Everything else about integers is library code: min, max, clamp, abs, gcd, isqrt, ilog2, checked or wrapping helpers, is_power_of_two, align_up, and byte-order reads such as u32_be (PNG is big-endian, BMP little-endian), each with a postcondition the verifier checks against the arithmetic definition.

docs.title: 3. Sum types and match ★
docs.text: These are already designed (let shape = type | Circle of f32 | ...). Implementing variants and an exhaustive match, encoded as Z3 datatypes as design.md describes, unlocks option, result, ordering, and every API that can fail. Without them, the library can only report errors through out-parameters and flags. Implemented for non-generic variants with scalar or record payloads (#54), encoded as a tagged record rather than Z3 datatypes, since MLIR's smt dialect has none. Generic option<T> and result t e wait for generics, and buffer payloads for buffers in records.

docs.title: Errors and scope cleanup ★
docs.text:
Every API that can fail returns a result, so the library needs a way to pass errors on without writing a match at every call, and a way to clean up on every exit from a scope (ADR 0028).

Error sets. result t e holds Ok of a t, or Err of an e, where e is a closed variant type or a union of them: result [u8] (OutOfMemory | IoError). Error sets are part of a function's interface, as in Zig and Swift's typed throws, so a caller always knows the complete list. A result must be used: dropping one unexamined is a type error.

? passes an error to the scope's handler. e? is the Ok payload of e, or, for Err x, a jump to the nearest enclosing handler with x. A scope declares its handler with handle:

let load (m : borrowed general) (path : str) : result image LoadError =
  let f = open_read path? in            (* NoEntry | Denied | ... *)
  defer close f;
  let bytes = read_all m f? in          (* OutOfMemory | IoError *)
  decode_png m bytes?                   (* PngError *)
handle
| NoEntry | Denied -> Err (Missing path)
| OutOfMemory -> Err TooBig
| IoError -> Err Unreadable
| PngError p -> Err (BadImage p)
  • The handler covers a closed set. The compiler computes the set of every error a ? in the scope can produce, and the handler's arms must cover exactly that set: a missing case is an error, and so is a case that cannot happen. The verifier knows the Ok payload on the normal path and the Err value in the handler.
  • Without a handler, ? returns the error from the function, and the function's declared error set must include it. Calling a function adds its error set to the scope's, and nothing is inferred across an interface.
  • handle attaches to a function body, a let ... in scope, or a loop body. It is one keyword, in Dean's style.
  • An arm knows only what holds where its errors are raised (Dean, 2026-11-22). Each arm is checked and proved once per ? that can reach it, so the arm for decode_png's errors may use bytes, while the arm for open_read's errors may not. | PngError p -> binds the payload, and | e -> or | NoEntry as e -> binds the whole error.
  • A set has a name and converts to a larger one. let front_error = (lex_error | parse_error) names a union, a union may hold another ((name_error | front_error) has all three variants), and ? passes a smaller set's errors on to a function whose set holds every one of its variants, each error keeping its constructor and payload (tests/verify/error_set_unions.pia). This is how a reader derived for a record raises the errors of the records it nests (json.md).
  • Implemented (#84), with error sets: see irgen.md. Or-patterns in arms come next.
  • An open case in a closed set. A constructor may carry a box over a concept, let io_error = type | Closed | Cxx of box Exception, so the set's list of cases stays closed while that one case holds an error of any type that meets Exception. Err (Cxx (widen b)) boxes it, ? passes it on like any error, and a handler's | Cxx e -> code e calls Exception's requirements through the box, proved from the concept's contracts, which widen's use check proved for each type boxed (ADR 0046; tests/verify/box_error_payload.pia). This is how a C++ exception of any dynamic type will become one case of a Pia error set. Built within a module; a box made in one module and handled in another waits for boxes through tables (ADR 0071, section 6).

Cleanup at scope end. Two forms, both run in reverse order of registration on every exit from the scope: falling off the end, ?, a handler's result, and a loop's next iteration.

  • defer e registers e to run at scope end, as in Zig, Go and Swift. It is for one-off cleanup, such as defer close f above. Its scope is the rest of the sequence it starts. Implemented (#85): see irgen.md. defer? and Drop come next.
  • RAII through Drop. A type with a Drop instance (a concept, ADR 0009) is dropped at the end of the scope that owns it, unless it was moved or freed first. Buffers, arenas, read-only file descriptors and mappings have one, so anything not freed explicitly is freed by its scope. @derive(drop) drops each field. Implemented, except @derive(drop) (#85): see irgen.md.
  • Cleanup cannot fail, suspend or lock. defer bodies and drop have no error set, may not await, and may take no lock other than a top-level leaf lock, since cleanup also runs on exits from lock bodies (ADR 0027). Freeing into general qualifies: its central lists are behind exactly such a lock. A resource whose cleanup can fail is @linear instead and must be consumed explicitly, so its error goes through ? like any other.
  • Cleanup never shadows the error in flight (Dean, 2026-11-21). The verifier raises a cleanup goal at each exit: the error that reaches the handler is the one the ? raised. A release that can fail is written defer? e, with e : result unit c. Every cleanup still runs, and the scope's errors become cleanup_error<e, c> = | Failed of e | Cleanup of list c | Both of { error : e; cleanup : list c }, so a failed close on an error path is reported beside the original error, not instead of it. A @linear value whose consumption can fail may be live across a ? only when a defer? consumes it.
  • Cleanup is proved. Each exit's cleanup is walked by the verifier like ordinary code at that exit, so a drop's preconditions are goals there.
  • A trap does not run cleanup. It goes to Pia.Rt, which stops the process.
  • With concurrency (ADR 0027): ? never crosses a task or a lock closure. In a spawned task it ends the task, and the error comes back from join. In a lock body it leaves the body, releases the lock, and becomes the body's result. A structured scope that exits early first joins, or cancels and then joins, every child still running, and only then runs its own cleanup, because children may borrow from it. Cancellation is an explicit token: operations that take it return Err Cancelled, so a cancelled task leaves through ? and its cleanup runs in its own frame.

docs.title: 4. Generics and concepts ★
docs.text:
M9 as designed: type parameters, concepts with laws, monomorphisation before verification. Eq, Ord, Hash and Numeric are then library code, and so are @derive(ord, hash), written as metaprograms next to derive_eq.

There is a stopgap until M9 lands: metaprograms that stamp out one instance per type, for example instantiate_sort u8. The meta engine can already generate functions, so this works today. It gives a monomorphic library that can later be rewritten over generics without changing what callers write.

docs.title: 5. Verification primitives ★
docs.text:
This group has no counterpart in an unverified language's core. Without it, the library can be safe (in bounds, no overflow), but it cannot be specified. A sort could not promise that its result is sorted.

  • Specification functions. let spec sorted (xs : [i32]) : bool = forall (i in 1..len xs). xs.[i - 1] <= xs.[i]. A spec function is pure, total and side-effect free. It may be used in contracts, and the verifier gives its definition to Z3: as a macro when it is not recursive, or as define-fun-rec with its decreases measure when it is. This removes the "calls inside contracts are unknown values" limit. Dafny, F* and SPARK (whose expression functions play this role) are built on the same idea.
  • Lemmas. let lemma sum_split (xs : [u8]) (k : usize) : unit requires k <= len xs ensures sum xs = sum_to xs k + sum_from xs k = .... A lemma is proved once, erased from code, and a call to it adds its postcondition at the call site, through the existing rule that a call is taken on its callee's contract. It is what makes proofs about loops, recursion and multiplication scale.
  • Ghost values, possibly later. Locals and parameters that exist only in the proof, such as a model seq<T> of a vector's contents, erased by codegen like contracts are today. SPARK's formal containers use exactly this pattern: each container has a mathematical model, and its contracts are written against the model.
  • Permutation and multiset reasoning, possibly later. ensures permutation xs (old xs) is the other half of a sort's specification. It can be a spec function over counts first, with a dedicated encoding only if Z3 struggles.

docs.title: 6. Buffers ★
docs.text:
• Slicing xs.[a .. b], as a view with proved bounds. The library cannot split work, recurse on halves, or return part of a buffer without it. Implemented with abort (#50): pia.slice lowers to a strided memref view.
  • Constant data: array literals and module-level constant arrays (let crc_table : [u32; 256] = ...), placed in read-only data. Many library algorithms are table driven. Implemented for integer literals (#50): pia.const_array lowers to a constant memref.global.
  • Buffers of records in codegen, which the scalariser does not lower yet.

docs.title: 7. Linear resources and memory
docs.text:
Pia does not allocate. Two things fix that: one type rule, and allocation written in Pia over mmap.

@linear types. Pia already has moved parameters, which make a value dead in the caller after the call. A type marked @linear adds one rule to the type checker: a value of it must be consumed, by being passed as moved or returned, on every path out of its scope. A @linear type is for a resource whose cleanup can fail, such as a file opened for writing, whose close can report a lost write: it must be consumed explicitly, so the error is handled. A resource whose cleanup cannot fail, such as a read-only fd, a mapping or an arena, has a Drop instance instead, and is cleaned up at scope end if it is not freed first (ADR 0028). Either way, using a value after it is closed is the existing moved rule. Implemented: see irgen.md. This is the idea behind ATS's and Austral's resource types, kept to one attribute and no typestate (ADR 0006).

The memory manager. Pia.Mem is a memory manager written in Pia over mmap, with no garbage collector, now or later (ADR 0026). There is no new keyword: allocation is a call of a function in Pia.Mem, and every allocation can fail and must be handled where it is called. Every free is explicit, or happens at scope end through a cleanup handler (ADR 0028), or comes from freeing the arena the memory lives in. A single global malloc/free is not enough. Different lifetimes want different allocators, and the verifier can prove more about a specialised allocator than about a general heap.

Allocators are explicit values. Library code never allocates from a hidden global. A function that allocates takes an allocator parameter, as in Zig:

let Allocator (a : type) : concept = sig
  let alloc  : (m : borrowed a) -> (t : type) -> (n : usize) -> result (borrowed(m) out mutable [t]) OutOfMemory
    ensures match result with
            | Ok buf -> len buf = n && fresh m buf          (* enough memory, disjoint from every live block *)
                        && aligned buf (max 16 (align_of t))  (* low 4 bits of every block address are free *)
            | Err OutOfMemory -> unchanged m               (* or a clean failure *)
  let free   : (m : borrowed a) -> (buf : moved [t]) -> unit
    requires owns m buf
end

let read_all (m : borrowed a) (f : fd) : result [u8] (OutOfMemory | IoError) where Allocator a =
  let buf = m.alloc u8 (size f)? in      (* `?` hands OutOfMemory to the caller *)
  ...
  • An allocator is reached through a plain borrowed handle, so many containers can share one. Its state is module state that only Pia.Mem changes, and since an allocator that is not shareable stays in one task, sharing the handle is race-free.
  • The result is out, so reading memory before writing it is a proof goal.
  • Every allocation can fail, and the failure must be handled at the call site. alloc returns a result, a result cannot be ignored, and the caller either matches on it or passes the error on with ? to the scope's handler (ADR 0028). There is no trapping variant. A program that wants to stop on out of memory says so in its handler.
  • Enough memory, or fail. The postcondition above is proved for every allocator: Ok means n elements, disjoint from every live block, and Err OutOfMemory means the allocator's state is unchanged. fresh and unchanged are spec functions over the allocator's ghost model of its live blocks.
  • free takes the buffer moved, so use after free and double free are type errors, not proof goals. owns m buf is a ghost fact recorded when m handed out buf, so freeing into the wrong allocator is a proof goal.
  • main gets the program's root allocator as an argument. Nothing else is global.

The allocators. Each is a @linear value built on a page source, and each states its invariants as module state, proved once in Pia.Mem:

Allocator Frees Fits Invariant proved pages munmap of whole mappings the source for every other allocator; guard pages and huge-page hints mappings are disjoint and page aligned fixed_buffer all at once allocation over a caller's buffer, with no OS at all; usable from Pia.Core the bump pointer stays inside the buffer arena all at once (reset, or consuming the arena) pipelines and per-request or per-frame work, like the demos handed-out slices are disjoint and inside the arena's chunks scratch last in, first out, back to a mark temporaries inside a function or a loop iteration frees happen in reverse order of allocation pool<T> one object at a time, O(1) many objects of one type: graph nodes, tasks, coroutine frames the free list and the live set partition the slab general one buffer at a time lifetimes that don't nest: TCMalloc-style size classes (below) every block is in exactly one size class, and free or live

The general allocator is TCMalloc-style. Requests are rounded up to one of a fixed table of size classes (about 8 bytes to 256 KiB, spaced so the rounding waste stays under 12.5%), and larger ones go straight to the page heap. Three tiers keep the common path short:

  1. A per-task cache of free lists, one list per size class. It is a @linear handle moved into a task, worker or coroutine scope, so the fast path takes no lock and no atomic.
  2. Central free lists, one per size class, which refill and drain the caches in batches. They are behind the allocator's one lock, a top-level leaf lock that never suspends.
  3. A page heap of spans (runs of pages from pages), each span carved into blocks of one size class.

All free lists live inside Pia.Mem, and the proof covers them. Every block on a free list is free, lies inside a span of its class, and overlaps no live block. A cache, central list and page heap together hold each block exactly once. And alloc is total: it returns a block of the right class from the cache, or refills from the central list, or carves a span from the page heap, or returns Err OutOfMemory when mmap fails, and in that last case nothing has changed.

Arenas for tasks, fibers and coroutines. Every task, spread worker and coroutine scope gets an arena of its own by default, alongside its general cache. Its frame data and temporaries come from it, and the arena is freed when the task ends. A task that needs memory to outlive it allocates from an allocator its caller passed in.

Containers (vec, string, hash_map, the binary heap that priority-flood needs) take an allocator as a parameter, as C++'s pmr containers do, so the same vec can live in an arena or in a pool. They are the first place where specification functions and ghost models (group 5) pay off: push ensures model result = append (model old) x.

Lifetimes are proved, not collected. Two rules in Sema, with no lifetime syntax in ordinary code:

  1. A borrow cannot outlive its lender. borrowed(m) [t] says the slice is borrowed from m. While it is live, m cannot be moved, so it cannot be reset, freed or sent to another task. Borrows are lexical: they end at the end of the scope that holds them. Implemented: see irgen.md.
  2. Regions can be scoped. with_arena n (let (a) => body) makes an arena, runs body, and frees the arena. The arena's type is fresh to body, and body's result type cannot mention it, so nothing allocated in the arena can escape. This is Haskell's runST trick, and the region idea from Cyclone and the ML Kit, without region inference. Today the arena is a { mem : [u8]; used : usize } of a literal size, on the stack, and the escape check is the borrow check: the arena is borrowed from itself (docs/irgen.md, "Scoped regions").

Leaks are ruled out by cleanup at scope end. Allocators and the buffers they hand out have a Drop instance (ADR 0028): a buffer from general or a pool that is not freed explicitly is freed when its scope ends, on every exit including ?, and so is an arena. A buffer from an arena needs nothing, because freeing the arena frees it. So proved code cannot leak, double free, or use after free, and none of that costs anything at run time beyond the frees themselves.

Threads and coroutines. An allocator is a value, not a global, so concurrency needs no allocator locks by default. This follows the coroutine design in ADR 0027, which makes coroutines stackless:

  • A task, worker or coroutine scope gets its own allocator, moved to it. spread gives each tile's worker its own arena by default, and frees it when the worker joins. A @linear allocator is sendable (it can move to another thread) but not shareable.
  • Coroutine frames have a size known at compile time, and come from the allocator that the enclosing task scope was given, usually a pool of frames. Stackless coroutines need no green-thread stacks. The pool of fixed-size, guard-paged stacks is only for OS worker threads, so that a stack overflow faults into Pia.Rt instead of corrupting memory.
  • A coroutine may hold borrows from an arena across a suspension point, as long as the arena's region encloses the coroutine. Rule 1 enforces that the arena outlives every suspended borrow.
  • general is shareable by construction: its per-task caches are moved, and only its central lists are shared. shared<a> wraps any other allocator for use from several threads, in the same way. Both are shareable, it is the only allocator with synchronisation, and choosing it is explicit. The lock that refills its caches is a leaf lock at the top lock level, since it can be taken while user locks are held, and it never suspends. So allocating inside a lock body is allowed.

With sanitizers, every allocator poisons the memory it hasn't handed out and the blocks it has freed, so foreign code that strays into them is reported (sanitizers).

Prior art: Zig's explicit allocators, Odin's and Jai's allocator contexts, C++'s std::pmr, Rust's bumpalo and allocator API, mimalloc's sharded free lists, the Linux slab allocator, and Cyclone and the ML Kit for regions.

docs.title: The litmus test: a proved growable array
docs.text:
A first form is proved: tests/verify/vec_bump.pia is a growable vector of bytes over a bump allocator. push proves that the new element is stored and the earlier ones are kept, grow copies into a larger loan, and every allocation's failure is handled. The allocator is passed to each call that may grow the vector, Zig-style, since records hold values rather than references; (v : borrowed(m) inout mutable vec) keeps the vector from outliving it. The generic, allocator-holding form below comes next.

The memory design is accepted when this works end to end: a dynamically growing array over explicit heap allocation, with its bounds, capacity, initialisation and freedom from leaks all proved. It is a sketch in designed syntax. Pia.Mem.Vec is the first target of the implementation.

(* Pia.Mem.Vec *)
let vec = let (t : type) (a : type) => type {
  heap : borrowed a;            (* where buf came from: the vec cannot outlive its allocator *)
  buf  : moved mutable [t];     (* owned; len buf is the capacity *)
  len  : usize;
} where Allocator a
    && len <= len buf
    && owns heap buf            (* buf was handed out by heap, and not freed *)
    && written buf 0 len        (* the first len elements are initialised *)

(* What the vec means: its elements, as a sequence. *)
let spec model (v : vec t a) : seq t = take v.len v.buf

let empty (heap : borrowed a) : vec t a
  ensures model result = []
= { heap = heap; buf = Pia.Mem.empty_slice t; len = 0 }

let get (v : vec t a) (i : usize) : t
  requires i < v.len
  ensures result = nth (model v) i
= v.buf.[i]                                    (* in bounds: i < len <= len buf *)

(* Doubles the capacity, or fails and leaves the vec exactly as it was. *)
let grow (v : inout mutable vec t a) : result unit OutOfMemory
  ensures match result with
          | Ok () -> len v.buf > v.len && model v = old (model v)
          | Err OutOfMemory -> v = old v
=
  let cap = len v.buf in
  if cap >= max_elems t then Err OutOfMemory   (* doubling would overflow the address space *)
  else
    let cap' = if cap = 0 then 4 else min (cap + cap) (max_elems t) in
    let buf' = Pia.Mem.alloc v.heap t cap'? in  (* on failure, nothing has changed yet *)
    copy v.buf.[0 .. v.len] buf'.[0 .. v.len];
    let old_buf = replace v.buf buf' in
    Pia.Mem.free v.heap old_buf;               (* explicit free of the old buffer *)
    Ok ()

let push (v : inout mutable vec t a) (x : moved t) : result unit OutOfMemory
  ensures match result with
          | Ok () -> model v = append (old (model v)) x
          | Err OutOfMemory -> model v = old (model v)
=
  if v.len = len v.buf then grow v?;
  v.buf.[v.len] <- x;                          (* in bounds: grow made room *)
  v.len <- v.len + 1;
  Ok ()

let pop (v : inout mutable vec t a) : option t
  ensures match result with
          | Some x -> old (model v) = append (model v) x
          | None -> old v.len = 0
= ...

(* RAII: a vec that is not freed explicitly is dropped at scope end. *)
let drop (v : moved vec t a) : unit = drop_each v.buf.[0 .. v.len]; Pia.Mem.free v.heap v.buf
let drop_vec : adapter Drop (vec t a) = { drop = drop }

And a caller, where every allocation is handled and nothing can leak:

let squares (heap : borrowed general) (n : u32) : result (vec u64 general) OutOfMemory
  ensures match result with Ok v -> len (model v) = n | Err _ -> true
=
  let v = Vec.empty heap in
  for i in 0..n invariant len (model v) = i do
    Vec.push v (mul_wide i i)?                (* on failure: v is dropped, and the error returned *)
  done;
  Ok v                                         (* moved out, so not dropped here *)

What has to be proved, and which part of the design proves it:

Property Proved by Every index in bounds the type's where: len <= len buf, and grow's postcondition No read of uninitialised memory alloc's out result, and written buf 0 len in the invariant Capacity arithmetic cannot overflow max_elems t, and the ladder for cap + cap (multiplication) Growth gives enough memory or fails cleanly alloc's postcondition, and grow touching nothing before its ? Elements survive growth copy's postcondition, so model v = old (model v) No double free, no use after free free and replace take buf moved No leak Drop on vec at scope end, on every exit including ? Freed into the right allocator the ghost owns heap buf in the invariant The vec cannot outlive its allocator heap : borrowed a, by the borrow rule

The sketch needs, from the core: generics, record invariants (where on a record type), spec functions with seq, slicing, ?, Drop, moved fields with replace, and the Pia.Mem allocators. That makes it a good test of all of them together.

docs.title: The second test: free-list reuse
docs.text:
A memory manager is only useful if freed memory comes back. So the second acceptance test is reuse: a block that was freed is handed out again, and the proof shows the new owner cannot alias any live object, cannot be reached through a stale reference, and cannot read the old owner's data.

let reuse (heap : borrowed general) : result unit OutOfMemory =
  let nodes = Pool.create heap node 1024? in   (* a pool<node>, dropped at scope end *)
  let a = Pool.take nodes? in                  (* a box<node>: one slot, owned *)
  a.value <- 1;
  let r = a.value in                           (* a copy, not a reference *)
  Pool.give nodes a;                           (* a is moved: dead from here *)
  let b = Pool.take nodes? in                  (* may be a's old slot *)
  b.value <- 2;                                (* b is out: written before it is read *)
  assert r = 1;                                (* the copy is unaffected *)
  Pool.give nodes b;
  Ok ()
Property Proved by A reused block aliases no live object the allocator's invariant that free and live blocks are disjoint: give moves the block from live to free, take moves it back, and fresh in alloc's postcondition No stale owner give and free take the block moved, so the old name is dead (a above is a type error after give) No stale borrow the borrow rule: a block cannot be moved while something borrowed from it is live, so every borrow of a ends before give No stale raw address addr exists only in @trusted modules. In foreign code, ASan's quarantine delays reuse so a dangling C pointer is reported (sanitizers) The new owner cannot read the old data the reused block comes back out, so its contents are unknown to the verifier and must be written before they are read. alloc_zeroed is there for code that wants zeroes Each block is in exactly one place the free list, the live set, a per-task cache and the central list partition every span, and each move between them keeps the partition Reuse cannot cross allocators the ghost owns fact, so a block freed into one pool or size class is only handed out by it

Free lists are side metadata, not pointers in freed blocks. TCMalloc threads its free lists through the freed blocks themselves. Doing that in Pia would mean writing through addr, and Pia.Mem would become trusted. Instead, each span keeps its free list as a stack of slot indices ([u16], two bytes per slot) beside the blocks. Pushing and popping it are ordinary bounds-checked array operations, so the reuse invariants above are proved, and Pia.Mem stays out of the trusted base. Moving batches between a per-task cache and the central list happens under the central lists' leaf lock, so there is no lock-free ABA problem to prove.

docs.title: 8. POSIX: trusted declarations and typed wrappers
docs.text:
The core calls POSIX directly. On macOS that means libSystem, not raw system call numbers: Apple changes the syscall ABI between releases and supports only calls through libSystem, which is why Go moved to libSystem on macOS in Go 1.12. So a Pia program links against libSystem like any C program, and nothing between the two is written in C.

FFI: foreign functions with explicit contracts. extern "symbol" as a function body declares a function with the C calling convention, implemented outside Pia. It is an ordinary identifier that the core gives meaning to, like old and result, so let stays the only binding form (ADR 0002). The declaration's parameter types, modifiers, result type and contract are Pia's:

let crc32_z (crc : u32) (buf : [u8]) (n : usize) : u32
  requires n <= len buf
  = extern "crc32_z"                              (* zlib; reads n bytes, writes nothing *)

Any module may declare foreign functions, for its own C libraries as well as POSIX. The rules:

  • An explicit contract is required to call it normally. A contract is explicit when the declaration has at least one requires or ensures clause. ensures true counts: it says on purpose that nothing more is promised. Parameter modifiers carry much of an FFI contract, and their defaults are promises too: a plain [u8] parameter is borrowed in fixed, so the function only reads the buffer and keeps no pointer to it.
  • The contract is trusted, not proved. At each call, its requires is a proof goal like any other, and its ensures is assumed. Each contracted foreign function is a trusted item in its module's certificate.
  • A foreign function without an explicit contract can only be called as unsafe f x. Writing unsafe is the caller's statement that it has checked the call by hand. The verifier assumes nothing about the result beyond its type's range, and every buffer passed to it is treated as written with unknown contents. Each unsafe call site, by symbol and source location, is a trusted item in the certificate. Calling such a function without unsafe is a compile error that suggests writing the contract.
  • Foreign memory is seen through unsafe view addr n. It is the slice of the n elements at the address addr, such as the pages a foreign mmap returned; its element type comes from the context, as in let mem : [u8] = unsafe view addr n. The caller vouches that the memory is there and overlaps no other buffer. The verifier sees a new buffer of n elements with unknown contents, so a read proves nothing until the code writes it, and the trust report lists each view (tests/codegen/pages.pia).
  • unsafe is not a way around proof goals. An unsafe call still has its arguments checked against their types, and every goal around it is proved as usual. It only marks that the callee's behaviour is taken on trust.

Implemented (#55) for parameters of integer, bool and integer-buffer types and integer, bool or unit results: see codegen.md. addr, view and addr_of come next.

unsafe is a core form, like extern, not a block: it marks one call, so the trusted surface stays as small as the call. Rust's unsafe blocks and Verus's assume_specification are the prior art. Pia's version is narrower than Rust's, since a contracted foreign call needs no unsafe at all.

Raw addresses. addr is a raw machine address. It has no arithmetic and cannot be dereferenced. view (a : addr) (n : usize) : [T] turns an address into a slice, and addr_of (xs : [T]) : addr goes the other way. Both are trusted, so they and assume may only be used in a module marked @trusted. Pia.Sys.Posix and Pia.Rt are the only trusted modules in the library.

Pia.Sys.Posix declares, the rest of Pia.Sys proves. The trusted contracts are deliberately weak. They say only what POSIX guarantees, and each cites its manual page:

(* Pia.Sys.Posix, @trusted *)
let read (fd : i32) (buf : out mutable [u8]) (n : usize) : isize
  requires n <= len buf
  ensures result >= -1 && result <= n
  ensures result >= 0 ==> written buf 0 result      (* read(2): no more bytes than it returns *)
  = extern "read"

read returns at most n, or -1, and writes no more than it returns. It never says what a file contains. Every stronger claim is something the untrusted layer above has to prove. That layer turns integers and errno into types:

(* Pia.Sys.Fs, fully proved (lib/Pia/Sys/Fs.pia): 27 goals, no trusted rows of its own *)
let errno = type
  | Again | BadFd | Interrupted | Invalid | IoError | NoSpace | NoEntry
  | Denied | Exists | IsDir | NotDir | TooMany | Broken | Other of i32
let file = type { raw : i32 } @linear                        (* only built from a successful open *)

let open_read : (path : [u8]) -> result file errno            (* path ends in a NUL *)
let create : (path : [u8]) -> (mode : int{0..4095}) -> result file errno
let read_some : (f : file) -> (buf : out mutable [u8]) -> result usize errno
  ensures (match result with | Ok n -> n <= len buf | Err _ -> true)
let write_all : (f : file) -> (buf : [u8]) -> result unit errno  (* retries short and interrupted writes *)
let close : (f : moved file) -> result unit errno

Err carries a decoded errno, never a sentinel, and match must handle it. The errno values and open flags are Pia.Sys.Posix's opaque constants, so the same module builds for macOS and Linux. Forgetting close is a type error, and closing twice is a use after a move. errno itself is *__error() on macOS and *__errno_location() on Linux, which Pia.Sys.Posix declares with @deref (ADR 0057), so it is one row rather than a C helper. Not built yet: hiding raw from importers, fstat, seeking and directories.

The first set of declarations, enough for files, memory, time, threads and the demos:

Group libSystem functions Wrapped in Files open close read write pread pwrite lseek fstat ftruncate fsync unlink Pia.Sys.Fs, then Pia.Io readers and writers Memory mmap munmap madvise Pia.Sys.Mapping (a @linear region of pages), then Pia.Mem Process exit getpid getenv, and argc/argv Pia.Sys.Process Time clock_gettime nanosleep Pia.Sys.Clock: a monotonic instant and ordered duration Threads pthread_create pthread_join, pthread_mutex_*, pthread_cond_*, sysctlbyname for the core count Pia.Sys.Thread: spawn takes a moved closure and returns a @linear handle that join consumes Errors __error Pia.Sys.Errno

main and abort. let main (args : [str]) : u8 is a symbol Pia can export. A small entry function in Pia.Sys.Process builds args from argv, calls main, and passes the result to exit. So the edge demo's main.c becomes Pia. abort has the precondition requires false in proof mode, so every call to it is a proof that it cannot happen, or a visible --allow-unproved.

Keeping the trusted base honest. Each trusted declaration has a test that calls it on macOS and checks its contract's claims at run time, so a wrong trust shows up as a failing test rather than an unsound proof. Each module's proof certificate lists its own trusted items: contracted foreign functions, unsafe call sites, assumes and goals accepted with --allow-unproved, each with a hash of what is trusted. It does not copy its dependencies' items. The transitive trusted base of a program is computed by walking the certificates at link time, and piac --trust-report prints it. That way a dependency that swaps a proved body for an assume, without changing its interface, leaves importers' proofs valid (assume-guarantee) but still shows up in the report. The certificate format is ADR 0024's (abi.md).

docs.title: 9. Runtime errors
docs.text:
Most failures are ruled out at compile time, but a few happen at run time by design: @overflow(trap), abort reached through --allow-unproved, and faults inside foreign code (SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE). All of them go to one runtime error handler in Pia.Rt, written in Pia.

  • One entry point. Codegen lowers every trap to a call of pia_trap (kind, site), where site indexes a table of source locations the compiler emits into the binary. So a trap reports its Pia file, line and column, and what failed ("overflow in a + b, @overflow(trap)"), even in a binary without debug info.
  • Signals. At start-up, Pia.Rt installs handlers with sigaction on an alternate signal stack (sigaltstack), so a stack overflow or a fault in foreign code also reaches the handler.
  • Stack traces. The handler walks the frame-pointer chain, which arm64 macOS always keeps, and symbolises each return address with dladdr. When debug info is available (piac -g emits DWARF, and a .dSYM sits beside the binary), it adds file and line for each frame. Without it, it prints symbol names and offsets.
  • Debug info. It also prints the trap kind, the faulting address for a signal, the thread, and for unsafe sites, the foreign symbol that was being called.
  • Safe in a signal handler. The handler allocates nothing and writes with write(2) to standard error only, so it is async-signal-safe. It then exits with status 134, as abort would.
  • Replaceable. A program can install its own handler with Pia.Rt.on_trap, for example to flush a log first. The default stays the strong one: print everything, then stop.

Pia.Rt is trusted, since it reads frames and signal contexts through addr, so its items appear in every program's trust report. The prior art is Rust's panic handler and RUST_BACKTRACE, and Go's runtime traceback on a fatal signal.

docs.title: Sanitizers (compiler-rt)
docs.text:
Proved Pia code cannot overflow, index out of bounds, use freed memory or race, so sanitizers are not how Pia finds its own bugs. They earn their place at the edges of the proof, where the verifier takes something on trust (ADR 0025):

  • Foreign code behind extern and unsafe, which can corrupt Pia memory, free it, or race with Pia threads.
  • Trusted contracts. A wrong extern contract or assume makes a proof unsound without any failing goal. Run-time checks are the only way to catch it.
  • The trusted Pia modules, Pia.Sys.Posix and Pia.Rt, which use addr.
  • The verifier itself. A build that instruments everything and still finds nothing is evidence that the verifier, IRGen and codegen agree. A sanitizer report in proved code is a compiler bug.

What piac emits. piac --sanitize=<list> adds instrumentation through LLVM's own passes, so Pia and C code in one binary share one sanitizer runtime and one report format:

Sanitizer How piac emits it Pia-specific part address (ASan) sanitize_address on functions, then LLVM's AddressSanitizerPass Pia.Mem poisons arena memory that has not been handed out, and freed buffers, with __asan_poison_memory_region, since ASan does not know about memory from mmap thread (TSan) sanitize_thread, then ThreadSanitizerPass; atomics are instrumented by the pass the worker pool behind spread uses libSystem pthreads, which TSan intercepts, so it needs no annotations undefined (UBSan) LLVM has no UBSan pass; in clang it is front-end checks. Pia's equivalent is its goals every goal that is not proved (skipped, or accepted with --allow-unproved) becomes a run-time check contracts (Pia only) checks after each call the ensures of every foreign function and every assume is checked at run time, so a wrong trust fails loudly

Other sanitizers wait for a need: MemorySanitizer and HWASan do not support macOS on arm64, LeakSanitizer comes with ASan where the platform supports it, and libFuzzer (--sanitize=fuzzer) is the natural next step for fuzzing the trusted boundary and the image decoders. ASan and TSan cannot be combined, and piac says so.

Proved accesses are not instrumented by default. A load whose bounds goal was proved gets LLVM's nosanitize metadata, so ASan's cost falls on the trust boundary: buffers passed to foreign functions, slices made by view, and arena bookkeeping. --sanitize-proved instruments every access too, which is the build that checks the verifier. TSan always instruments everything, because a race needs both sides instrumented and the other side may be C.

With Pia.Rt. A sanitizer runtime installs its own fatal-signal handlers and prints its own report. In a sanitized build, Pia.Rt does not install signal handlers, and so does not fight the runtime for SIGSEGV. It registers __sanitizer_set_death_callback, so that after the sanitizer's report it adds the Pia view: the trap site's Pia location and, for an unsafe or foreign call, the symbol being called. A Pia trap (pia_trap) in a sanitized build prints its stack with __sanitizer_print_stack_trace, so every report in one run looks the same. Both symbolise through DWARF, so sanitized builds also pass -g.

The runtime libraries. compiler-rt's sanitizer runtimes are versioned with the instrumentation (__asan_version_mismatch_check_vN), so they must come from the same LLVM that piac links. They are built from the pinned llvm-project with rules_foreign_cc and CMake, as Z3 is, and cached. Xcode's runtimes (libclang_rt.asan_osx_dynamic.dylib) are a fallback only when their version matches.

Bazel. Sanitizers follow the C++ toolchain's features, so one flag sanitizes the C and the Pia in a target together:

# .bazelrc
build:asan --features=asan --copt=-fno-omit-frame-pointer --strip=never
build:tsan --features=tsan
build:ubsan --features=ubsan
build:contracts --//tools/piac:sanitize=contracts

pia_object reads ctx.features and passes the matching --sanitize to piac. contracts has no C++ feature, so it is a Pia build setting that adds to whatever the features say. bazel test --config=asan //... runs the suite sanitized. In CI, asan and tsan run on the macOS runner beside the plain build, at first on main only, since each one builds LLVM's runtimes and doubles the test time.

docs.title: 10. SIMD, floats and atomics
docs.text:
These come with milestones M10 to M12, but they are core builtins, so they are listed here.

  • Floats (M11): fadd fsub fmul fdiv fneg fsqrt fma fabs fmin fmax, comparisons, ftoi (with a range goal), itof, is_nan, is_inf, and the three reassociation choices from ADR 0012. Elementary functions (exp, log, sin, pow) are Pia in Pia.Math, never libm: range reduction and polynomials, with error bounds (in ulps or absolute) proved in their contracts. Only the sediment colour map needs them at first.
  • vec<T, k> (M10): splat, lane and with_lane (lane index proved), vload xs i and vstore xs i v (with i + k <= len xs proved), every integer and float builtin applied lane-wise with the same overflow modes, comparisons and vselect, constant shuffle, vwiden_lo/vwiden_hi/vnarrow, and horizontal vreduce_add/vreduce_max. They lower to MLIR's vector dialect, and to arm_neon where a pattern needs it. The verifier models a vector as k values.
  • Atomics (ADR 0052, built): atomic_new, atomic_load, atomic_store, atomic_swap, atomic_cas, atomic_add, atomic_sub, atomic_and, atomic_or, atomic_xor, atomic_min, atomic_max and fence on an atomic t cell of an integer type or bool, each with a memory order first (relaxed acquire release acq_rel seq_cst), checked against the orders the operation takes. atomic_add and atomic_sub state their overflow mode on the expression, as in @wrap (atomic_add relaxed c 1). They lower to LLVM atomics, and so to ldapr, stlr, ldadd, swp and cas on arm64 and to mov, xchg, lock xadd and lock cmpxchg on x86_64. Pia.Sync.atomic_update, the compare-and-swap loop for refined cells, is written in tests/verify/atomics.pia until Pia.Sync exists.

Concurrency is then library code. The worker pool behind spread is Pia in Pia.Par, over Pia.Sys.Thread and the atomics: a fixed set of threads, a work queue and a barrier. The collectives scatter, gather, halo_exchange and all_reduce are library metaprograms, as ADR 0014 already says. Race freedom stays in ownership, since tiles are moved to workers. The pool's own invariants (each task runs once, the barrier releases only when every worker arrives) are module-state contracts for the model checker pass. GPU placement (ADR 0015) lowers through MLIR's gpu dialect to Metal. Metal's host API is Objective-C, not POSIX, so it is a separate trusted module later, outside this minimal core.

docs.title: 11. Metaprogram builtins
docs.text:
The interpreter has map fold length fields name concat (meta.md), and ADR 0029 adds kind, fail (stop expansion with an error) and the comment builtins. Derives in the library need a few more, all read-only questions about types:

Builtin Answer field_type t f the type of field f of record t variants t the constructors of a variant type, with their payload types type_kind t "record", "variant", "int", "float", "array", "slice" or "vec" (kind, from ADR 0029, is the kind of a syntax value) size_of t, align_of t layout, as codegen will lay it out int_bounds t the bounds of an integer or range type attrs x the attributes on an item or field, with their arguments nth zip range list helpers the library would otherwise write recursively

Status (ADR 0045, step 3): field_type, variants, attrs (with field_attrs and ctor_attrs, and attributes on fields and constructors to read), bytes for the bytes of a string, and nth, zip and range are done, in expanding metaprograms (meta.md). int_bounds is range_of, which now covers u64 and usize, since metaprogram integers are 128 bits. type_kind and size_of work in type-level metaprograms; align_of waits on codegen's layout.

With these, @derive(ord), @derive(hash), @derive(serialise) and @derive(deserialise) are library metaprograms. A PNG chunk header can be declared as a record and read by a derived, bounds-proved reader.

docs.title: 12. Later
docs.text: • Function values and closures: map, fold and comparator-based sort over function values. Until then, generics plus concept instances (Ord t) cover most needs, which is also what lets them monomorphise and vectorise.

docs.title: Multiplication in the verifier
docs.text:
Today every integer in a module is a 68-bit bit-vector, or 132-bit if the module multiplies anywhere (verifier.md). So one * makes every goal in the module wider, and loop-nest bounds goals then time out. This is a verifier change rather than a builtin, but the library cannot be written until it is done, so it is part of the core. The design is a ladder, cheapest first. Each step is tried with a short timeout before the next.

  1. Width per goal, not per module. Each goal's width is computed from the ops it contains and the intervals of their operands. A goal with no multiplication stays at 68 bits however many * the module has elsewhere. This alone should fix the edge demo's timeouts.
  2. Multiplication by a constant is linear. 3 * i is encoded as shifts and adds, and an affine goal goes to the Presburger stage (ADR 0020).
  3. Intervals first. If interval analysis bounds both operands, it bounds the product, and the goal is settled without Z3, as for addition today.
  4. Opaque products and lemmas. A product of two variables is encoded as an uninterpreted function with its basic facts: zero, one, commutativity, sign, and monotonicity in each argument within the operands' ranges. Goals that need more call a lemma from Pia.Core.Arith (mul_le_mul, div_mul_le, mul_div_cancel, index_2d_lt), which are ordinary lemmas proved once. Most bounds goals in image code, such as y * w + x < w * h given y < h and x < w, are settled here.
  5. Exact nonlinear arithmetic, in a query of its own. Only when the steps above fail does the goal get the exact product, at the width it needs, in a separate query. Bit-vectors and Z3's nonlinear integer solver run as a portfolio, and the first answer wins.

Verus does the same: nonlinear facts are kept out of ordinary queries, proved in small by (nonlinear_arith) queries, and packaged as vstd::arithmetic lemmas. Dafny's standard library does it with nonlinear lemmas and an option that turns nonlinear reasoning off in ordinary queries. A goal that still times out is reported with the step it reached and a suggestion: a lemma that would close it, or an assert that splits it. Proof decomposition stays explicit and visible in the source. The same ladder applies to / and %, which today get special-case facts for non-negative operands.

docs.title: The library, layer by layer
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  b["Core builtins (in piac)"] --> pre["Pia.Prelude"]
  pre --> core["Pia.Core: no allocation, no OS"]
  core --> posix["Pia.Sys.Posix: extern declarations, @trusted"]
  posix --> sys["Pia.Sys: Fs, Mapping, Process, Clock, Thread"]
  posix --> rt["Pia.Rt: runtime error handler, @trusted"]
  sys --> mem["Pia.Mem: allocators, vec, heap"]
  mem --> io["Pia.Io: readers, writers, formatting"]
  io --> par["Pia.Par: worker pool, collectives"]
  io --> img["Image: Bmp, Png, Gif"]
Layer Needs from the core Contents (all Pia) Pia.Prelude modules operators, derive_eq, derive_ord, derive_add, derive_scale, derive_bounds; derive_hash is Pia.Core.Hash's Pia.Core groups 1 to 6 option result ordering; Eq Ord Hash Numeric; integer utilities and Arith lemmas; slice algorithms (fill copy equal find reverse rotate binary_search sort partition); fixed-capacity containers (array_vec, bitset, ring); crc32 adler32 fnv; UTF-8 validation; formatting integers into a buffer and parsing them Pia.Sys.Posix group 8 the trusted libSystem declarations, and nothing else Pia.Rt groups 8 and 9 the trap entry point, signal handlers, stack traces Pia.Sys groups 7 and 8 fd, mapping, errno, args, exit, clocks, threads: POSIX in strong types, fully proved Pia.Mem group 7 the Allocator concept; pages fixed_buffer arena scratch pool general shared; vec, string, hash_map, heap Pia.Io Pia.Sys, Pia.Mem reader and writer concepts with bounds-proved reads, buffered file I/O, str as [u8] refined to valid UTF-8, printing Pia.Math floats elementary functions with error bounds Pia.Par atomics, threads the spread worker pool, collectives Image.Bmp, Image.Png, Image.Gif all of the above BMP first, to replace the demo's main.c; then zlib inflate and deflate, PNG unfiltering, GIF LZW (M13)

Pia.Core needs no allocator and no OS, like Rust's core, so it can run anywhere the compiler targets, including a GPU kernel later on.

Every function in every layer has a contract that is proved when the library builds. Proved means at least the strongest-guarantee defaults (no overflow, in bounds, terminates). Where specification functions allow, it also means functional correctness: sort returns a sorted permutation of its input, binary_search finds the element if it is there, and write_all writes every byte or returns Err. The codecs are good stress tests: inflate's back-references need distance <= bytes written so far, Huffman decoding needs bounded table indices, LZW needs the code table to stay within 4096 entries, and the decoded image's length is proved against the header's width * height * channels, which is why multiplication comes first.

docs.title: What the codecs prove
docs.text:
The GIF and inflate codecs (ADR 0054) are built. Each one is total and safe on every input, allocates nothing, and writes into a buffer the caller lends it. Beyond safety, they prove the following:

  • Pia.Image.Gif.Lzw: each code writes exactly the string that the dictionary in Pia.Image.Gif.Spec gives it. decode_ref also proves the whole-stream theorem. Pia.Image.Gif.Ref writes GIF89a's LZW reading of a code stream as a spec, and whenever x is what that reading gives for a stream and x fits in the output, decoding returns Ok (len x) with x in the output. The trace and x are spec parameters (ADR 0058), so codegen erases them. decode is the same code with the check turned off.
  • Pia.Image.Gif.Decode: info accepts exactly the files that the block grammar accepts.
  • Pia.Image.Gif.Encode: the stream encode_animation writes parses with info and fits its proved size bound.
  • Pia.Compress.Huffman: build makes the canonical code's table, and on such a table decode returns the symbol whose canonical code is the bits it read, and fails only when no symbol's code is there. prefix_free proves that the canonical code is prefix-free, so the symbol decode returns is the only one it could be. kraft_room shows that an over-subscribed set of code lengths can't build.
  • Pia.Compress.Inflate: every back-reference stays within the bytes already written. codes_ref proves a Huffman block's theorem. Pia.Compress.Inflate.Ref writes RFC 1951's reading of a block as a trace of its symbols: each literal, or each length and distance with its copy, one byte at a time. Whenever the tables are the canonical codes of the block's code lengths and x is what that trace writes, decoding the block returns Ok at its end code with x in the output. Because the code is prefix-free, the symbol decoded is the trace's. inflate_ref proves the theorem for a whole stream of stored, fixed and dynamic blocks. Ref traces the stream block by block (stream_ok), and a dynamic block's code lengths by the symbols of its code length code (cl_from). Whenever x is what that trace writes and fits in the output, inflate returns Ok (len x) with x in the output.

These large specs are @opaque (ADR 0063), and only small step lemmas reveal them. That keeps the loops' goals small enough to prove.

docs.title: Suggested order
docs.text:
Each step unlocks a usable slice of the library, and the order follows the roadmap:

  1. Per-goal widths and the multiplication ladder. No language change, and it unblocks the edge demo's BT.601 grayscale today.
  2. Integer primitives, slicing, constant arrays, abort. Small compiler changes, and enough to write checksums, bit utilities and slice algorithms as a single-file library.
  3. Spec functions and lemmas, with Pia.Core.Arith. So the library can be specified as it is written, and not retrofitted later.
  4. Sum types and match, then ?, handle, defer and Drop. option, result, and fallible APIs.
  5. extern, unsafe, addr, @trusted, @linear, main, --trust-report, and the runtime error handler. Pia.Sys.Posix, Pia.Sys.Fs and Pia.Rt. A Pia program can read and write files without C. Until modules land, piac takes several source files compiled as one program, so this does not wait for M8.
  6. Modules (M8), with the prelude moved into Pia. The library becomes importable, and the trusted-module boundary becomes a module boundary.
  7. Pia.Mem and Image.Bmp. The edge demo drops main.c.
  8. Generics (M9). Rewrite Pia.Core generically. The metaprogram-instantiated versions show what the generic versions must match.
  9. Floats (M11), vec (M10), atomics and Pia.Par (M12), then the PNG and GIF codecs (M13) for the flagship demo.

Steps 1 to 5 need neither M8 nor M9, so they can start now, alongside M8.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
System What Pia takes from it Rust core / alloc / std, and the libc crate the split between what needs no OS, what needs an allocator, and what needs the OS Zig explicit allocators; on macOS, linking libSystem rather than raw syscalls (as Go 1.12 also chose) OCaml external a short list of primitives under an ordinary library ATS POSIX wrapped in linear types and proofs: closest in spirit to Pia.Sys Austral linear types for resources, kept simple SPARK Ada proved library code over a few bodies whose contracts are trusted; expression functions; formal containers with models Verus (vstd, assume_specification) trusted specifications for external functions; nonlinear arithmetic isolated in its own queries; arithmetic lemma libraries Dafny ({:extern}, standard libraries) externs with contracts; nonlinear lemmas; fuel for recursive definitions F* Low* and HACL* verified code over a small trusted C layer; memory regions Lean 4 (@[extern]) a self-hosted standard library over a few compiler builtins

The common lesson is that the trusted part should be small, listed, and tested against reality, and that nonlinear arithmetic needs help from the library rather than a bigger solver budget.

docs.title: Decided in this proposal
docs.text:
These were open questions in the first draft. ADR 0023 records the answers. No open questions remain.

  • Trusted items are listed in certificates. Each certificate lists its own module's trusted items (foreign contracts, unsafe calls, assumes, accepted unproved goals), and piac --trust-report walks them for the whole program. addr and assume are only allowed in @trusted modules.
  • Every allocation can fail and must be handled at the call site. There is no new keyword and no trapping variant.
  • Errors propagate with ? to a scope's handle block, which must cover the closed set of errors in that scope. Cleanup runs at scope end through defer and Drop (ADR 0028).
  • No garbage collection, ever. Memory is managed by explicit allocator values (arenas, scratch, pools, a general size-class allocator), with lifetimes proved by two Sema rules (ADR 0026).
  • extern is a function body, = extern "symbol", not a new declaration form, so let stays the only binding form.
  • FFI needs explicit contracts. A foreign function without one can only be called as unsafe f x, and each such call is a trusted item.
  • Sanitizers are for the edges of the proof: foreign code, trusted contracts and the verifier itself (ADR 0025).
  • Runtime errors go to one handler, Pia.Rt, which prints the Pia source location, a stack trace, and debug info when it is available.
  • Spec function unfolding: one level of unfolding by default (Dafny's fuel of 1), with lemmas for anything deeper and a per-function @fuel(n) to raise it.
  • libm is never trusted. Every maths function is written and proved in Pia (Dean, 2026-11-21), with its error bound in its contract.
  • Bit operators use C's symbols: & | ^ ~ << >>, with | as bitwise or only inside parentheses.
  • seq<T> is a library type whose model is an SMT array plus a length, introduced with ghost values. A core type can come later if the encoding needs it.

docs.title: Demo: stream delineation
docs.text:
Rain that falls on a landscape runs downhill, gathers in valleys and becomes streams. Stream delineation recovers those streams from a terrain model: given the height of every point on a grid, it works out where the water on each cell goes, how much water passes through each cell, which cells carry enough to be a stream, and which outlet each cell drains to (its watershed). It is Pia's flagship demo (ADR 0016), and its second half moves sediment down those streams, with the total mass proved to stay the same exactly (sediment.pia.md).

This page is the program. It is a literate Pia file, docs/streams.pia.md: the prose is Markdown, the fenced pia blocks are the code, and piac reads the whole file, attaching each paragraph to the function after it (ADR 0029). The build proves every goal in it before it generates any code, so what you read here is what was proved and what runs.

To run it on a Mac with Apple Silicon:

$ bazel run //examples/streams
$ bazel run //examples/streams -- ~/Pictures/terrain.png ~/Desktop/streams.png

The first command draws a synthetic terrain, saves it as streams-input.png in the current directory, and writes the result to streams-output.png. It prints a text preview of the map and how long each stage took; on an M-series iMac the whole 384x256 map takes about 30 ms. The second reads your own heightmap, in any format macOS can open (PNG, GIF, JPEG, TIFF, BMP), where brighter means higher, and writes the map as PNG, or GIF if the name ends in .gif. Use a 16-bit heightmap where you can: an 8-bit one has only 256 levels, so its terraces become flats, and filling slopes each flat gently towards its outlet, which the map shows as lake.

Or run it on real terrain, an SRTM tile (see Reading an SRTM tile):

$ examples/streams/fetch_srtm.sh /tmp/srtm
$ bazel run //examples/streams:srtm -- /tmp/srtm/N46E008.hgt ~/Desktop/alps.png
$ bazel run //examples/streams -- ~/Desktop/alps-quarter.png ~/Desktop/alps-map.png

The first command downloads the 1″ tile N46E008, in the Swiss Alps, and checks it. The second runs the pipeline on all 13 million cells, timing each stage. It writes the map, and a quarter-size view of the heights, which the third command turns into the animation of the evolving landscape.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  dem["heights<br/>(dem)"] --> fill["1. fill sinks"]
  fill --> dirs["2. D8 directions"]
  dirs --> acc["3. accumulate,<br/>label watersheds"]
  acc --> render["4. streams and<br/>colours"]
  render --> png["PNG / GIF"]
  acc --> sed["5. sediment<br/>transport"]
  sed --> png2["PNG by load"]
  1. Fill sinks. Real elevation data has pits, cells lower than all their neighbours, where water would get stuck. Filling raises each pit to the level where it spills, so every cell has a way down to the edge.
  2. D8 flow directions. Each cell sends its water to the one neighbour, of its eight, down the steepest slope.
  3. Flow accumulation. Following the directions from every cell counts how many cells drain through each cell, and the cell where each path ends labels its watershed.
  4. Streams. A cell is part of a stream when at least threshold cells drain through it. The last stage colours the map: streams in blue, filled pits as lakes, and every other cell by its watershed, shaded by height.
  5. Sediment. Water carries sediment down the same paths, eroding where it can carry more and depositing where it carries too much, and the stream cells are coloured by the load they carry.

What the verifier proves, function by function, is summed up at the end. The headline results are three theorems about the whole grid, each a postcondition with a forall:

  • filling never lowers the ground, fill.[k] >= dem.[k] for every cell, and every cell that is not an outlet has a neighbour that is lower, or as high and closer to an outlet;
  • every flow direction points strictly downhill, or nowhere;
  • no cell's accumulation exceeds the number of cells, and every watershed label is an outlet;
  • sediment transport conserves the total mass exactly: sum bed + sum load + sum inflow + gone never changes.

The second one is what makes the third possible: because water only ever runs strictly downhill, the path from a cell must end, and it cannot visit a cell twice.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
The heights arrive as a slice of u16, one per cell, stored row by row, w cells to a row. So the cell above cell m is m - w, and the one below is m + w. The first and last rows and columns are the border: water that reaches a border cell leaves the map. Every loop over the grid visits the interior the same way the edge detector does: a row at a time, starting at row offset r = w, and keeping one row on each side, so all eight neighbours of an interior cell are in bounds.

The program never multiplies. A module that multiplies is encoded with much wider bit-vectors, and loop proofs then time out (issue #45), so it adds instead: row offsets grow by w, and 3 * i is i + i + i.

The file is one module, Streams (ADR 0039). Its interface lists the nine functions the C program calls, with the preconditions a caller must keep; everything else on this page is private to the module:

module Streams : Delineation

interface Delineation @abi(c) = sig
  let load_hgt : (raw : [u8]) -> (dem : out mutable [u16]) -> usize
    requires len dem + len dem = len raw
  let fill_sinks : (dem : [u16]) -> (w : usize) -> (fill : out mutable [u16])
      -> (parent : out mutable [usize]) -> (rank : out mutable [usize])
      -> (next : out mutable [usize]) -> (head : out mutable [usize]) -> usize
    requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
    requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
    requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dem && len dem < max u32
  let directions : (fill : [u16]) -> (w : usize)
      -> (down : out mutable [usize]) -> unit
    requires len down = len fill && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len fill
  let accumulate : (fill : [u16]) -> (down : [usize])
      -> (acc : out mutable [u32]) -> (basin : out mutable [usize]) -> unit
    requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len basin = len fill
    requires len fill < max u32
    requires forall (k in 0..len down).
               down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
  let render : (dem : [u16]) -> (fill : [u16]) -> (acc : [u32])
      -> (basin : [usize]) -> (threshold : u32) -> (rgb : out mutable [u8])
      -> usize
    requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
    requires len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
  let delineate : (dem : [u16]) -> (w : usize) -> (threshold : u32)
      -> (fill : out mutable [u16]) -> (parent : out mutable [usize])
      -> (rank : out mutable [usize]) -> (next : out mutable [usize])
      -> (head : out mutable [usize])
      -> (down : out mutable [usize]) -> (acc : out mutable [u32])
      -> (basin : out mutable [usize]) -> (rgb : out mutable [u8]) -> usize
    requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dem && len dem < max u32
    requires len fill = len dem && len down = len dem && len acc = len dem
    requires len basin = len dem && len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
    requires len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem && len next = len dem
    requires len head = 65536
  let palette : (pal : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len pal = 768
  let render_load_index : (dem : [u16]) -> (fill : [u16]) -> (acc : [u32])
      -> (basin : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (threshold : u32)
      -> (idx : out mutable [u8]) -> unit
    requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
    requires len flux = len dem && len idx = len dem
  let render_load : (dem : [u16]) -> (fill : [u16]) -> (acc : [u32])
      -> (basin : [usize]) -> (flux : [u32]) -> (threshold : u32)
      -> (rgb : out mutable [u8]) -> usize
    requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
    requires len flux = len dem && len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
end

Heights are compared through a small helper whose postcondition says exactly what it returns, so callers can reason about the result:

let higher (a : u16) (b : u16) : u16
  ensures result >= a && result >= b && (result = a || result = b)
= if a > b then a else b

The offset of the last interior row: the last row that has a row after it. The loop walks down the rows; its measure is the distance to the end of the slice, which shrinks by w each time.

let last_row (n : usize) (w : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= n
  ensures w <= result && result + w + w <= n
=
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while w <= n - (r + w + w)
    invariant w <= r && r + w + w <= n
    decreases n - r
  do
    r <- r + w
  done;
  r

docs.title: Reading an SRTM tile
docs.text:
The heights can come from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission. An SRTM tile, a .hgt file, covers one degree of latitude and longitude. It holds nothing but its heights, in metres, as big-endian i16, row by row from the north-west corner. A 1″ tile is 3601 × 3601 cells, a 3″ tile 1201 × 1201, and the size follows from the length of the file. Cells the radar did not see hold -32768, a void.

Two bytes make one height. The high byte comes first, and a value of 32768 or more is negative.

let sample (hi : u8) (lo : u8) : i32
  ensures result >= min i16 && result <= max i16
= let h : i32 = hi in
  let l : i32 = lo in
  let u : i32 = ((h << 8) | l) in
  if u >= 32768 then u - 65536 else u

The width of a tile from its length in bytes: 3601 or 1201, or 256 for the 256 × 256 crops the tests use. Anything else is not a tile, and the result is 0.

let hgt_side (bytes : usize) : usize
  ensures result = 0 || result = 256 || result = 1201 || result = 3601
=
  if bytes = 25'934'402 then 3601
  else if bytes = 2'884'802 then 1201
  else if bytes = 131'072 then 256
  else 0

load_hgt turns a tile into the u16 heights the rest of the page uses, and returns its width, or 0 if the bytes are not a tile. It shifts every height up by the lowest one in the tile, so the lowest becomes 0. A tile spans at most 65535 metres, so every height fits. A void becomes 0 as well, a pit as deep as the lowest ground, and filling raises it to the level where it spills. So a void ends up filled from its neighbours, by the stage that fills every other pit, and the loader needs no rule of its own.

The postcondition is what the next stage requires, whenever the result is not 0: at least three rows of at least three cells. The if d < 0 cannot happen once base is the lowest height. The loop does not prove that, so the clamp keeps the narrowing to u16 safe without it.

let load_hgt (raw : [u8]) (dem : out mutable [u16]) : usize
  requires len dem + len dem = len raw
  ensures result = 0 || (result >= 3 && result + result + result <= len dem)
=
  let w = hgt_side (len raw) in
  let lowest : mutable i32 = max i16 in
  let b : mutable usize = 0 in
  for i in 0 .. len dem
    invariant b = i + i
    invariant lowest >= min i16 && lowest <= max i16
  do
    let v = sample (raw.[b]) (raw.[b + 1]) in
    if v <> min i16 && v < lowest then lowest <- v else ();
    b <- b + 2
  done;
  let base = lowest in
  b <- 0;
  for i in 0 .. len dem
    invariant b = i + i
  do
    let v = sample (raw.[b]) (raw.[b + 1]) in
    let d : i32 = if v = min i16 then 0 else v - base in
    dem.[i] <- if d < 0 then 0 else d;
    b <- b + 2
  done;
  w

docs.title: 1. Filling sinks
docs.text:
The method is priority-flood (Barnes, Lehman and Mulla, 2014). Water enters the map at the border, which is the edge of the world: every border cell is an outlet, at its own height. The flood then grows inwards, always from the lowest cell it has reached so far. Each cell it reaches for the first time takes the height

higher (dem.[nb]) (fill.[c] +| 1)

where c is the cell it came from. That is the ground if the ground already sits above c. Otherwise it is one unit above c, so a pit fills up to the point where it spills, plus one unit per cell back from that point. Even a filled lake slopes gently towards its outlet, and the next stage always finds a way down. The + 1 saturates at max u16, so heights near the top of the range cannot overflow. A cell there may find no lower neighbour, which the later stages handle.

Because the flood always grows from its lowest cell, the heights it gives are the lowest that drain: the same surface as Planchon and Darboux's iteration (2001), which this page used before. That method sweeps the map until nothing changes, which takes a few sweeps on a small map and hundreds on a real one. Priority-flood visits each cell once. The C tests check the two against each other.

The theorem is about the cell each cell was reached from, its parent, and the order cells were reached in, their rank. Rank 0 means not reached yet. A cell that is its own parent is an outlet. For every other cell that has been reached:

  • its parent is one of its eight neighbours;
  • its parent was reached earlier, so it has a lower rank;
  • its parent's height is at most its own.

Every cell also sits at or above the ground. So every cell that is not an outlet has a neighbour that is lower, or as high and closer to an outlet. Following parents from any cell, the rank falls at every step, so the path ends, and it ends at an outlet. That is the invariant the design asks of this stage. With the + 1, the parent is in fact strictly lower, until heights reach max u16.

A neighbour is one of eight offsets away. The check is in usize, with no overflow: a comes before b in the grid, one cell or about one row apart.

let spec step_of (w : usize) (a : usize) (b : usize) : bool
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
= if a < b then (b - a = 1 || b - a = w - 1 || b - a = w || b - a = w + 1) else false

let spec adjacent (w : usize) (k : usize) (p : usize) : bool
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
= step_of w p k || step_of w k p

drained is the theorem, as four foralls. Each one is kept separate, because Z3 instantiates small quantifiers more readily than one large one.

let spec drained (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (parent : [usize]) (rank : [usize]) (w : usize) : bool
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
= (forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0 ==> fill.[k] >= dem.[k] && parent.[k] < len dem)
  && (forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0 && parent.[k] <> k ==> adjacent w k (parent.[k]))
  && (forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0 && parent.[k] <> k ==> rank.[parent.[k]] > 0 && rank.[parent.[k]] < rank.[k])
  && (forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0 && parent.[k] <> k ==> fill.[parent.[k]] <= fill.[k])

The flood's queue is a bucket queue: one list of cells for each of the 65536 heights, so taking the lowest cell is a walk up the buckets, and the flood is linear in the number of cells. head.[h] is the first cell of height h's list and next.[k] the cell after k, with len dem meaning the end of a list. queued says every link is a cell or the end, which is all the indexing needs.

let spec queued (next : [usize]) (head : [usize]) : bool
  requires len head = 65536
= (forall (k in 0 .. len next). next.[k] <= len next)
  && (forall (j in 0 .. 65536). head.[j] <= len next)

Reaches nb from c: its height, its parent and its rank. The ensures keeps the theorem. Every other cell keeps its rank, which the callers need to know that c is still reached afterwards.

let settle_cell (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (c : usize) (nb : usize) (r : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) : u16
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
  requires c < len dem && nb < len dem && rank.[c] > 0 && rank.[nb] = 0
  requires adjacent w nb c && rank.[c] < r
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). k = nb || rank.[k] = old (rank.[k])
  ensures rank.[nb] = r && result = fill.[nb]
=
  let v = higher (dem.[nb]) (fill.[c] +| 1) in
  fill.[nb] <- v;
  parent.[nb] <- c;
  rank.[nb] <- r;
  v

Puts nb at the front of the list for height v.

let push (nb : usize) (v : u16) (next : inout mutable [usize]) (head : inout mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires nb < len next && len head = 65536
  requires queued next head
  ensures queued next head
=
  next.[nb] <- head.[v];
  head.[v] <- nb
