Looks at nb from c. A cell not reached yet is reached and queued. Every rank is below count, which grows by one each time, so a new cell's rank is above its parent's. If count ever reached max usize, which would take more cells than any machine has memory for, the cell would be left for the last pass to make an outlet.

let visit (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (c : usize) (nb : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : inout mutable usize) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 1 && w < max usize
  requires c < len dem && nb < len dem && rank.[c] > 0 && adjacent w nb c
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] < count
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures rank.[c] > 0 && count >= old count
=
  if rank.[nb] = 0 && count < max usize then (
    let v = settle_cell dem w c nb count fill parent rank in
    push nb v next head;
    count <- count + 1
  ) else ()

The neighbour d cells before or after c, or n if that is off the slice. The asserts name the step for the solver, which then proves the postcondition at once.

let before (n : usize) (w : usize) (c : usize) (d : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && c < n && (d = 1 || d = w - 1 || d = w || d = w + 1)
  ensures result = n || (result < n && adjacent w result c)
= if c >= d then (
    let nb = c - d in
    assert c - nb = d;
    assert step_of w nb c;
    nb
  ) else n

let after (n : usize) (w : usize) (c : usize) (d : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && c < n && (d = 1 || d = w - 1 || d = w || d = w + 1)
  ensures result = n || (result < n && adjacent w result c)
= if d < n - c then (
    let nb = c + d in
    assert nb - c = d;
    assert step_of w c nb;
    nb
  ) else n

The eight neighbours, numbered in row order. A border cell's offsets can wrap around to the other side of the map. Those cells are on the border too, and every border cell is an outlet before the flood starts, so the flood never reaches one through a wrap.

let neighbour (n : usize) (w : usize) (c : usize) (d : int{0..7}) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && c < n
  ensures result = n || (result < n && adjacent w result c)
=
  if d = 0 then before n w c (w + 1)
  else if d = 1 then before n w c w
  else if d = 2 then before n w c (w - 1)
  else if d = 3 then before n w c 1
  else if d = 4 then after n w c 1
  else if d = 5 then after n w c (w - 1)
  else if d = 6 then after n w c w
  else after n w c (w + 1)

Looks at all eight neighbours of c.

let expand (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (c : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : inout mutable usize) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize
  requires c < len dem && rank.[c] > 0
  requires forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] < count
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures count >= old count
=
  for d in 0 .. 8
    invariant forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
    invariant rank.[c] > 0 && count >= old count
  do
    let nb = neighbour (len dem) w c d in
    if nb < len dem then visit dem w c nb fill parent rank next head count else ()
  done

Makes k an outlet at its own height, rank 1, and queues it, unless it has been reached already. The result says whether it was new.

let seed (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (k : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : usize) : bool
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && k < len dem && count >= 2
  requires forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures rank.[k] > 0
  ensures forall (j in 0 .. len dem). j = k || rank.[j] = old (rank.[j])
=
  if rank.[k] = 0 then (
    fill.[k] <- dem.[k];
    parent.[k] <- k;
    rank.[k] <- 1;
    push k (dem.[k]) next head;
    true
  ) else false

Takes the first cell off the list for level, or returns len next if the list is empty.

let pop (level : u16) (next : [usize]) (head : inout mutable [usize]) : usize
  requires len head = 65536 && queued next head
  ensures queued next head && result <= len next
=
  let c = head.[level] in
  if c < len next then (head.[level] <- next.[c]; c) else len next

The start: every cell unreached, every list empty. With no cell reached, drained holds trivially.

let clear_flood (dem : [u16]) (w : usize)
    (fill : out mutable [u16]) (parent : out mutable [usize])
    (rank : out mutable [usize]) (next : out mutable [usize])
    (head : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] = 0
  ensures queued next head
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w
=
  let n = len dem in
  for k in 0 .. n
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. k). rank.[j] = 0 && next.[j] <= n
  do
    fill.[k] <- dem.[k];
    parent.[k] <- k;
    rank.[k] <- 0;
    next.[k] <- n
  done;
  for j in 0 .. 65536
    invariant forall (i in 0 .. j). head.[i] <= n
  do
    head.[j] <- n
  done

The border's outlets: the first and last rows, then both ends of every row between.

let seed_border (dem : [u16]) (w : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : usize) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dem && count >= 2
  requires forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
=
  let n = len dem in
  for k in 0 .. w
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. n). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  do
    let s0 = seed dem w k fill parent rank next head count in ()
  done;
  for k in n - w .. n
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. n). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  do
    let s1 = seed dem w k fill parent rank next head count in ()
  done;
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while r < n - w
    invariant w <= r
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. n). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
    decreases n - r
  do
    let s2 = seed dem w r fill parent rank next head count in
    let s3 = seed dem w (r + w - 1) fill parent rank next head count in
    r <- r + w
  done

Empties the bucket for one height. A cell reached from this level lands in a higher bucket, or in this one at max u16. The measure counts the cells taken, at most len dem per level. A list could only be longer if it had a cycle, which it cannot, but the loop does not need to know that.

let drain_level (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (level : u16)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : inout mutable usize) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize
  requires forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures count >= old count
=
  let n = len dem in
  let pops : mutable usize = 0 in
  let more : mutable bool = true in
  while more && pops < n
    invariant pops <= n && count >= old count
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. n). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
    decreases n - pops
  do
    let c = pop level next head in
    pops <- pops + 1;
    if c = n then more <- false
    else if rank.[c] > 0 then expand dem w c fill parent rank next head count
    else ()
  done

After the flood, any cell still unreached becomes an outlet of its own. On a grid every cell is reached from the border, so this finds none. The result counts them, and the tests check that it is 0. This last pass is what lets the postcondition say that every cell has been reached, with no proof that the flood itself gets everywhere.

let finish (dem : [u16]) (w : usize)
    (fill : inout mutable [u16]) (parent : inout mutable [usize])
    (rank : inout mutable [usize]) (next : inout mutable [usize])
    (head : inout mutable [usize]) (count : usize) : usize
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w < max usize && count >= 2
  requires forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
  requires drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0
  ensures result <= len dem
=
  let extra : mutable usize = 0 in
  for k in 0 .. len dem
    invariant extra <= k
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. k). rank.[j] > 0
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  do
    if seed dem w k fill parent rank next head count then extra <- extra + 1 else ()
  done;
  extra

The whole stage. The caller passes the scratch buffers, since Pia cannot allocate yet. The ensures is the theorem for every cell of the map.

let fill_sinks (dem : [u16]) (w : usize)
    (fill : out mutable [u16]) (parent : out mutable [usize])
    (rank : out mutable [usize]) (next : out mutable [usize])
    (head : out mutable [usize]) : usize
  requires len fill = len dem && len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem
  requires len next = len dem && len head = 65536
  requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dem && len dem < max u32
  ensures drained dem fill parent rank w
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. len dem). rank.[k] > 0
  ensures result <= len dem
=
  clear_flood dem w fill parent rank next head;
  let count : mutable usize = 2 in
  seed_border dem w fill parent rank next head count;
  for level in 0 .. 65536
    invariant count >= 2
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. len dem). rank.[j] < count
    invariant drained dem fill parent rank w && queued next head
  do
    drain_level dem w level fill parent rank next head count
  done;
  finish dem w fill parent rank next head count

docs.title: 2. D8 flow directions
docs.text:
D8 sends all the water on a cell to one of its eight neighbours, the one down the steepest slope. A diagonal neighbour is √2 times as far away as one beside or above, so its drop counts for less: drops are weighted by 10 for the four near neighbours and by 7 for the diagonals, since 10/√2 is 7.07. A cell with no lower neighbour, such as an outlet on the border, points at itself.

The direction of a cell is stored as the index of the cell it drains to, in a slice down. The property that matters downstream is that every direction points strictly downhill:

down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])

The verifier proves this for every cell, starting with one candidate at a time. A route is the best neighbour found so far, with its weighted drop.

let route = type { target : usize; drop : u32 }

Ten times a drop, by addition.

let tenfold (d : u16) : u32 =
  let d2 : u32 = d + d in
  let d4 : u32 = d2 + d2 in
  d4 + d4 + d2

Seven times a drop.

let sevenfold (d : u16) : u32 =
  let d2 : u32 = d + d in
  let d4 : u32 = d2 + d2 in
  d4 + d2 + d

Considers neighbour n of cell m against the best route so far. A neighbour wins only if it is lower than m and its weighted drop beats the best, so ties go to the first neighbour considered. Whatever happens, the route still points at m itself or strictly downhill: the precondition says so of best, and the postcondition of the result.

let consider (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (m : usize) (n : usize) (diagonal : bool)
    (best : route) : route
  requires m < len fill && n < len fill && w >= 3 && w < max usize && adjacent w m n
  requires best.target = m
           || (best.target < len fill && fill.[best.target] < fill.[m] && adjacent w m best.target)
  ensures result.target = m
          || (result.target < len fill && fill.[result.target] < fill.[m] && adjacent w m result.target)
=
  if fill.[n] < fill.[m] then
    (let d : u16 = fill.[m] - fill.[n] in
     let slope : u32 = if diagonal then sevenfold d else tenfold d in
     if slope > best.drop then { target = n; drop = slope } else best)
  else best

The D8 direction of interior cell m: the eight neighbours, row by row.

let steepest (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (r : usize) (m : usize) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w <= r && r + w + w <= len fill && r < m && m + 1 < r + w
  ensures result = m || (result < len fill && fill.[result] < fill.[m] && adjacent w m result)
=
  assert w < m && m + w + 1 < len fill;
  let a = m - w in
  let b = m + w in
  let none : route = { target = m; drop = 0 } in
  let r1 = consider fill w m (a - 1) true none in
  let r2 = consider fill w m a false r1 in
  let r3 = consider fill w m (a + 1) true r2 in
  let r4 = consider fill w m (m - 1) false r3 in
  let r5 = consider fill w m (m + 1) false r4 in
  let r6 = consider fill w m (b - 1) true r5 in
  let r7 = consider fill w m b false r6 in
  let r8 = consider fill w m (b + 1) true r7 in
  r8.target

The directions of the interior of the row that starts at r. The loop invariant is the downhill property for the whole slice: writing one cell's direction keeps it, because steepest guarantees it for that cell.

let directions_row (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (r : usize)
    (down : inout mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len down = len fill && w >= 3 && w <= r && r + w + w <= len fill
  requires forall (k in 0..len down).
             down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k] && adjacent w k (down.[k]))
  ensures forall (k in 0..len down).
            down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k] && adjacent w k (down.[k]))
=
  for m in r + 1..r + w - 1
    invariant forall (k in 0..len down).
                down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k] && adjacent w k (down.[k]))
  do
    down.[m] <- steepest fill w r m
  done

The whole stage. Every cell starts pointing at itself, which is trivially "downhill or nowhere", so border cells are outlets; then each interior row gets its directions. The row loop counts up to the last interior row rather than testing for room below, as the others do: with the downhill forall in its invariant, the solver could not see the subtraction in that test was safe within its timeout (issue #96), and comparisons with last need no subtraction. The postcondition is the second theorem. Unlike filling, each cell's direction depends only on fill, so the rows are independent; once spread is compiled (M12) they can run in parallel.

let directions (fill : [u16]) (w : usize) (down : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len down = len fill && w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len fill
  ensures forall (k in 0..len down).
            down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k] && adjacent w k (down.[k]))
=
  for i in 0..len down
    invariant forall (k in 0..i). down.[k] = k
  do
    down.[i] <- i
  done;
  let last = last_row (len fill) w in
  let r : mutable usize = w in
  while r <= last
    invariant w <= r && r <= last + w && last + w + w <= len fill
    invariant forall (k in 0..len down).
                down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k] && adjacent w k (down.[k]))
    decreases last + w - r
  do
    directions_row fill w r down;
    r <- r + w
  done

docs.title: 3. Flow accumulation and watersheds
docs.text:
The flow accumulation of a cell is the number of cells whose water passes through it, itself included. One way to count it is to start a drop of water on every cell in turn, follow the directions until it reaches an outlet, and add one to every cell on the way. The outlet where the drop ends is the cell's watershed label.

walk follows one drop from start. Two things about it are proved here that a C programmer would only argue in a comment.

It ends. The loop's measure is the height of the current cell, fill.[cur]. The downhill theorem says each step goes to a strictly lower cell, so the measure falls every iteration, and a u16 cannot fall forever.

It counts every cell at most once. Before the walk, no count exceeds bound. The invariant splits the grid by height: cells strictly below the drop have not been visited yet, so their counts are still at most bound, and every count is at most bound + 1. Stepping down to the next cell, it is below the drop, so its count goes from at most bound to at most bound + 1, and the cells below it are still below the drop. That is why the + 1 cannot overflow, with no saturation and no run-time check.

let walk (fill : [u16]) (down : [usize]) (start : usize) (bound : u32)
    (acc : inout mutable [u32]) : usize
  requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && start < len fill
  requires bound < max u32
  requires forall (k in 0..len down).
             down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
  requires forall (k in 0..len acc). acc.[k] <= bound
  ensures result < len fill && down.[result] = result
  ensures forall (k in 0..len acc). acc.[k] <= bound + 1
=
  acc.[start] <- acc.[start] + 1;
  let cur : mutable usize = start in
  while down.[cur] <> cur
    invariant cur < len fill
    invariant forall (k in 0..len acc).
                (fill.[k] < fill.[cur] ==> acc.[k] <= bound) && acc.[k] <= bound + 1
    decreases fill.[cur]
  do
    cur <- down.[cur];
    acc.[cur] <- acc.[cur] + 1
  done;
  cur

The whole stage: a walk from every cell. After s walks no count exceeds s, so at the end none exceeds the number of cells; and every label written so far is an outlet, a cell that points at itself. These are the third theorem. The precondition on len fill keeps the counts within u32. Its downhill precondition is exactly the postcondition of directions, which is how the stages compose: each is proved against the contract of the one before, not its code.

The cost is the total length of all the paths, which is fine for maps of a few million cells. A faster method visits each cell once in topological order, but needs a queue the size of the map, and Pia cannot allocate one yet (issue #86).

let accumulate (fill : [u16]) (down : [usize]) (acc : out mutable [u32])
    (basin : out mutable [usize]) : unit
  requires len down = len fill && len acc = len fill && len basin = len fill
  requires len fill < max u32
  requires forall (k in 0..len down).
             down.[k] = k || (down.[k] < len fill && fill.[down.[k]] < fill.[k])
  ensures forall (k in 0..len acc). acc.[k] <= len fill
  ensures forall (k in 0..len basin).
            basin.[k] < len fill && down.[basin.[k]] = basin.[k]
=
  for i in 0..len acc
    invariant forall (k in 0..i). acc.[k] = 0
  do
    acc.[i] <- 0
  done;
  for s in 0..len fill
    invariant forall (k in 0..len acc). acc.[k] <= s
    invariant forall (k in 0..s).
                basin.[k] < len fill && down.[basin.[k]] = basin.[k]
  do
    basin.[s] <- walk fill down s s acc
  done

docs.title: 4. Streams and the picture
docs.text:
A cell is on a stream when at least threshold cells drain through it. The picture shows streams in blue, darker where the flow is at least 16 times the threshold; cells that filling raised, the lakes, in pale blue; and everything else in its watershed's colour, darker where it is lower. Neighbouring watersheds can share one of the six colours, since the palette cycles by outlet index.

let colour = type { red : u8; green : u8; blue : u8 }

The colour of watershed outlet.

let tint (outlet : usize) : colour =
  let k = outlet mod 6 in
  if k = 0 then { red = 214; green = 168; blue = 110 }
  else if k = 1 then { red = 150; green = 190; blue = 110 }
  else if k = 2 then { red = 200; green = 140; blue = 160 }
  else if k = 3 then { red = 120; green = 170; blue = 160 }
  else if k = 4 then { red = 210; green = 200; blue = 120 }
  else { red = 170; green = 150; blue = 200 }

Whether flow a is at least sixteen times threshold, in u64 so the product cannot overflow.

let major (a : u32) (threshold : u32) : bool =
  let t2 : u64 = threshold + threshold in
  let t4 : u64 = t2 + t2 in
  let t8 : u64 = t4 + t4 in
  a >= t8 + t8

The colour of one cell: its height h before and f after filling, its flow a, and its watershed. A height is 0 to max u16, so h / 256 is a byte, and the average of a byte and a byte is a byte: the verifier proves both narrowings.

let paint (h : u16) (f : u16) (a : u32) (outlet : usize) (threshold : u32)
    : colour =
  if a >= threshold then
    (if major a threshold then { red = 20; green = 70; blue = 190 }
     else { red = 70; green = 140; blue = 240 })
  else if f > h then { red = 150; green = 205; blue = 235 }
  else
    (let t = tint outlet in
     let shade : u16 = h / 256 in
     let r : u16 = t.red + shade in
     let g : u16 = t.green + shade in
     let b : u16 = t.blue + shade in
     { red = r / 2; green = g / 2; blue = b / 2 })

The picture, as packed RGB bytes, and the number of stream cells, which the invariant bounds by the number of cells painted.

let render (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (acc : [u32]) (basin : [usize])
    (threshold : u32) (rgb : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
  requires len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
  ensures result <= len dem
=
  let streams : mutable usize = 0 in
  for i in 0..len dem
    invariant streams <= i
  do
    let c = paint (dem.[i]) (fill.[i]) (acc.[i]) (basin.[i]) threshold in
    let j = i + i + i in
    rgb.[j] <- c.red;
    rgb.[j + 1] <- c.green;
    rgb.[j + 2] <- c.blue;
    streams <- streams + (if acc.[i] >= threshold then 1 else 0)
  done;
  streams

docs.title: The whole pipeline
docs.text:
delineate runs the four stages and returns the number of stream cells. Each call's precondition is proved from the caller's own and from the postconditions of the calls before it; in particular accumulate needs the downhill theorem, which only directions provides. Swap the two calls and the program no longer compiles.

let delineate (dem : [u16]) (w : usize) (threshold : u32)
    (fill : out mutable [u16]) (parent : out mutable [usize])
    (rank : out mutable [usize]) (next : out mutable [usize])
    (head : out mutable [usize]) (down : out mutable [usize])
    (acc : out mutable [u32]) (basin : out mutable [usize])
    (rgb : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires w >= 3 && w + w + w <= len dem && len dem < max u32
  requires len fill = len dem && len down = len dem && len acc = len dem
  requires len basin = len dem && len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
  requires len parent = len dem && len rank = len dem && len next = len dem
  requires len head = 65536
  ensures result <= len dem
=
  let outlets = fill_sinks dem w fill parent rank next head in
  directions fill w down;
  accumulate fill down acc basin;
  render dem fill acc basin threshold rgb

docs.title: 5. Sediment transport
docs.text:
The second half of the demo moves sediment down the streams, and is its own page and module, sediment.pia.md, so the two prove in parallel. Its entry point takes the filled heights, the directions and the accumulation from this page, and returns flux, the load leaving each cell. This page draws it.

The colour of a stream cell by the load leaving it: a ramp over the binary logarithm of the load, from blue for 63 units or fewer to orange for 8192 or more, in eight steps. clz counts the leading zeros, so 32 - clz f is the number of bits in f, with no logarithm and no multiplication.

let load_colour (f : u32) : colour =
  let lz : u32 = clz f in
  let l : u32 = 32 - lz in
  let m : u32 = if l < 6 then 0 else if l > 13 then 7 else l - 6 in
  { red = 31 + (m << 5); green = 60 + (m << 4); blue = 230 - (m << 5) }

The picture after transport: stream cells coloured by their load, every other cell as in render.

let render_load (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (acc : [u32]) (basin : [usize])
    (flux : [u32]) (threshold : u32) (rgb : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
  requires len flux = len dem && len rgb = len dem + len dem + len dem
  ensures result <= len dem
=
  let streams : mutable usize = 0 in
  for i in 0..len dem
    invariant streams <= i
  do
    let c = (if acc.[i] >= threshold then load_colour (flux.[i])
             else paint (dem.[i]) (fill.[i]) (acc.[i]) (basin.[i]) threshold) in
    let j = i + i + i in
    rgb.[j] <- c.red;
    rgb.[j + 1] <- c.green;
    rgb.[j + 2] <- c.blue;
    streams <- streams + (if acc.[i] >= threshold then 1 else 0)
  done;
  streams

docs.title: 6. The animation's palette
docs.text:
An animated GIF has one palette for all its frames, so for the evolution's animation each cell becomes an index into one fixed palette rather than a colour. load_step is the step of the load ramp, as in load_colour.

let load_step (f : u32) : int{0..7} =
  let lz : u32 = clz f in
  let l : u32 = 32 - lz in
  if l < 6 then 0 else if l > 13 then 7 else l - 6

The palette index of one cell: the eight steps of the load ramp for streams, then the lake colour, then the six watershed tints in 32 shades of height each, 201 colours in all. outlet mod 6 and h >> 11 are both small, so the index is proved to be below 201 by its type.

let index_of (h : u16) (f : u16) (a : u32) (outlet : usize) (flux : u32)
    (threshold : u32) : int{0..200} =
  if a >= threshold then load_step flux
  else if f > h then 8
  else
    (let k : int{0..5} = outlet mod 6 in
     let s : int{0..31} = h >> 11 in
     9 + (k << 5) + s)

The colour of each index: the ramp and the lake as above, and a watershed shade as paint mixes it, with the height taken at the middle of its shade. Indices from 201 up are unused and black.

let index_colour (i : u8) : colour =
  if i < 8 then
    (let m : u8 = i in
     { red = 31 + (m << 5); green = 60 + (m << 4); blue = 230 - (m << 5) })
  else if i = 8 then { red = 150; green = 205; blue = 235 }
  else if i < 201 then
    (let j : u8 = i - 9 in
     let t = tint (j >> 5) in
     let shade : u16 = ((j & 31) << 3) + 4 in
     let r : u16 = t.red + shade in
     let g : u16 = t.green + shade in
     let b : u16 = t.blue + shade in
     { red = r / 2; green = g / 2; blue = b / 2 })
  else { red = 0; green = 0; blue = 0 }

The shared palette: 256 colours, three bytes each.

let palette (pal : out mutable [u8]) : unit
= for i in 0..256 do
    let c = index_colour i in
    let j = i + i + i in
    pal.[j] <- c.red;
    pal.[j + 1] <- c.green;
    pal.[j + 2] <- c.blue
  done

One frame of the animation: every cell's palette index, each proved to name one of the 201 colours palette fills.

let render_load_index (dem : [u16]) (fill : [u16]) (acc : [u32]) (basin : [usize])
    (flux : [u32]) (threshold : u32) (idx : out mutable [u8]) : unit
  requires len fill = len dem && len acc = len dem && len basin = len dem
  requires len flux = len dem && len idx = len dem
  ensures forall (k in 0..len idx). idx.[k] < 201
=
  for i in 0..len dem
    invariant forall (k in 0..i). idx.[k] < 201
  do
    idx.[i] <- index_of (dem.[i]) (fill.[i]) (acc.[i]) (basin.[i]) (flux.[i]) threshold
  done

docs.title: Why the order matters
docs.text:
Here is the walk without the downhill precondition. Nothing then stops down from containing a cycle, so the loop might never end, and the verifier says so: the measure is not proved to decrease, and piac refuses to compile it.

let walk (fill : [u16]) (down : [usize]) (start : usize) : usize
  requires len down = len fill && start < len fill
  requires forall (k in 0..len down). down.[k] < len fill
=
  let cur : mutable usize = start in
  while down.[cur] <> cur
    invariant cur < len fill
    decreases fill.[cur]
  do
    cur <- down.[cur]
  done;
  cur

$ piac --verify walk_unproved.pia
...
walk_unproved.pia:8:5: failed: the measure decreases
...

docs.title: What is proved
docs.text:
Every goal in this file is proved, by interval analysis or by Z3, before piac generates code:

Goal Where Every slice index is in bounds every function No arithmetic overflows, and every narrowing fits every function; walk's + 1 by its invariant Every loop ends for loops always; while loops by decreases; walk by the height of the drop An SRTM tile's heights fit in u16, and a tile is at least 3 × 3 sample, load_hgt Filling never lowers the ground settle_cell up to fill_sinks Every cell drains: its parent is a neighbour, reached earlier, and no higher settle_cell up to fill_sinks (drained) Every direction points strictly downhill or nowhere consider up to directions Accumulation never exceeds the number of cells walk, accumulate Every watershed label is an outlet walk, accumulate The number of stream cells is at most the number of cells render, render_load Every animation frame's index names one of the palette's 201 colours index_of, render_load_index

What is not proved yet: that the flood reaches every cell from the border, so that fill_sinks returns 0 (the tests check that it does), that its surface is the lowest that drains, and that the D8 choice is the steepest, rather than just downhill. None of these affect safety or termination.

docs.title: What is missing
docs.text:
The demo works around parts of Pia that are not built yet:

  • Image I/O. Pia has no I/O, so main.c reads and writes images with macOS's ImageIO and hands Pia the heights. PNG and GIF codecs written in Pia are M13, on top of the minimal core (ADR 0023).
  • Allocation. The caller passes every buffer. With the memory module (issue #86), delineate could allocate its own and use a queue for a linear-time accumulation.
  • Multiplication in loops makes proofs time out (issue #45), so the code adds instead, and the slope weights are tenfold and sevenfold.
  • Floats (M11) would give true slopes in place of the 10:7 weights.
  • Vectorisation and parallelism. Today LLVM vectorises only the simple loops: the copies in clear_flood and down.[i] <- i in directions become NEON loads, stores and adds. The stencil kernels (settle, steepest) and the walks are scalar. steepest and paint are branch-free enough to vectorise once proved facts drive it (M10), and directions and render are independent per row and per cell, so spread (M12) can run them across cores. Priority-flood fills in height order, so it stays sequential.
  • Solver robustness. Goals beside a forall are slow for the solver, and some slices' element ranges are lost inside quantifiers (issue #96); the code is shaped around both, as noted where it matters.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text:
This page says how code in the Pia repository is written: the C++ compiler and tools, the Python test and build scripts, the Bazel files, and the documentation. Pia code itself has its own page, Idiomatic Pia, and the lints that go with it (ADR 0037). This page does not repeat them.

The rules are here so that a reader, whether a person or an agent, can find their way around any file in the same way. Two of them apply to every language in the repository and matter more than the rest.

docs.title: Return early
docs.text:
Handle the special cases first and return, so the main path of a function reads straight down at one level of indentation. Do not nest the main path inside a chain of if statements.

Instead of this:

std::optional<Interval> rangeOf(const Node &type) {
  if (type.kind == NodeKind::RangeType) {
    if (type.kids.size() == 2) {
      auto lo = constant(*type.kids[0]);
      auto hi = constant(*type.kids[1]);
      if (lo && hi) {
        return Interval{*lo, *hi};
      }
    }
  }
  return std::nullopt;
}

write this:

std::optional<Interval> rangeOf(const Node &type) {
  if (type.kind != NodeKind::RangeType || type.kids.size() != 2)
    return std::nullopt;
  auto lo = constant(*type.kids[0]);
  auto hi = constant(*type.kids[1]);
  if (!lo || !hi)
    return std::nullopt;
  return Interval{*lo, *hi};
}

The same goes for loops: use continue to skip the elements a loop does not care about, rather than wrapping its body in an if. Do not write else after a return, break or continue. When a function needs more than two or three levels of nesting, split part of it into a helper with a name that says what it does.

This is the LLVM rule too, and clang-tidy checks the else part of it (readability-else-after-return).

docs.title: Comments say why
docs.text:
The code already says what it does. A comment is for what the code cannot say: why it is written this way, what would go wrong if it were written the obvious way, which invariant it relies on, which ADR or issue decided it, and what a measurement showed.

Do not write comments like these, which repeat the code:

// Increment the counter.
++count;

// Loop over the goals.
for (const Goal &g : goals) {

Write comments like these, which tell the reader something the code cannot:

// Interval analysis runs first because it settles most bounds goals without
// calling the solver; only what it cannot decide goes to Z3 (ADR 0020).
if (auto r = intervals.decide(goal))
  return *r;

// Lints read the syntax tree before metaprograms expand, so a warning points
// at text the user wrote rather than at generated code.

Some more guidance:

  • A header starts with a comment that says what it is for, and where its design is written down. See src/syntax/Lint.h for an example. A .cpp file that implements one header needs no comment of its own; one that stands alone, such as a tool's main, gets one.
  • A declaration in a header gets a comment saying what it promises its callers: what it returns, what it requires, and what it does when something goes wrong. That is the contract, and it is not obvious from the signature.
  • Link to the decision. When code is the way it is because of an ADR, an issue or a measured result, name it: (ADR 0026), (#152). The reasoning lives there, and the comment stays short.
  • Keep comments true. A comment that no longer matches the code is worse than none. When you change code, read the comments around it.
  • Do not leave code commented out. Git remembers it.
  • TODOs name an issue: // TODO(#153): open-sided ranges. A TODO without an issue tends to stay forever.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
The compiler, the language server and the tools follow the LLVM Coding Standards. Read them once; most of what follows is a reminder of the parts that come up most, and of the few places where Pia adds to them.

The language is C++17 (.bazelrc).

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Formatting is whatever clang-format produces with the repository's .clang-format, which is LLVM style: two-space indentation, 80 columns, and & and * next to the name (const Node &n).

$ pip install clang-format==18.1.8
$ git clang-format origin/main

The first line installs the same clang-format that CI uses, since versions differ in small ways. The second formats only the lines your branch changed since main. Format what you touch, and do not reformat whole files in a change that is about something else: it buries the real change in the diff and conflicts with other work in flight. A pull request that only reformats is welcome when nobody else is working in that file.

A table laid out by hand, such as the X-macro list of token kinds in src/syntax/Token.h, goes between // clang-format off and // clang-format on, with a comment saying why. clang-format would otherwise reflow it, and not always the same way twice.

CI checks the lines a pull request changes with git clang-format --diff (.github/workflows/style.yml). Lines you did not touch are not checked.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Pia's C++ uses the names MLIR uses, which is the LLVM standard with lower-case variables:

What Style Example types, classes, structs, enums UpperCamelCase TextEdit, NodeKind functions and methods lowerCamelCase, a verb lint, printLint, rangeOf variables, parameters, fields lowerCamelCase, a noun fixTitle, source enumerators UpperCamelCase NodeKind::RangeType namespaces lower case pia::syntax private data members of a class lowerCamelCase_, with a trailing underscore diags_, pos_ macros UPPER_CASE PIA_SYNTAX_LINT_H

The code is built on MLIR and calls its APIs everywhere, so following MLIR keeps one style across the boundary. The trailing underscore is Pia's own addition, used throughout src/: it tells a member from a local at a glance in long methods. Public fields of a plain struct have no underscore. Short names (n, os, loc) are fine for a value whose scope is a few lines. Longer scopes get longer names.

docs.title: Files and headers
docs.text:
• Source files are .cpp and headers are .h, named after the main thing they define (Lint.h, Verifier.cpp).
  • Header guards are PIA_<DIRECTORY>_<FILE>_H, such as PIA_SYNTAX_LINT_H.
  • Include what you use, and nothing more. Includes are ordered as LLVM orders them: the file's own header first, then Pia's headers, then LLVM and MLIR, then the C++ standard library, each group sorted. clang-format sorts within a group.
  • Do not put using namespace in a header.
  • Give helpers that are private to a .cpp file internal linkage: static for functions, an anonymous namespace for types.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• Early returns and continue, as above.
  • auto where the type is obvious from the right-hand side or does not help the reader (iterators, dyn_cast results). Spell the type out otherwise.
  • Errors in the compiler are diagnostics, reported against a source location, with a message that says what went wrong in the user's terms. Do not abort or assert on bad user input; assert is for things that cannot happen if the compiler is correct, and its message says what was expected.
  • Prefer LLVM's and MLIR's containers and utilities where the surrounding code uses them (SmallVector, StringRef, llvm::any_of), and the standard library where it does not. Code in src/syntax does not link LLVM, so that pia-lsp can share it, and uses the standard library only.
  • No RTTI, as in LLVM: use isa, cast and dyn_cast rather than dynamic_cast.
  • Errors are values: std::optional, llvm::Expected, mlir::LogicalResult or FailureOr. Do not add new exceptions. The parser and the metaprogram interpreter throw internally to unwind to a recovery point, and catch before anything crosses their public API; keep it that way.
  • Keep functions short. A function that does not fit on a screen usually hides two or three smaller ones with names worth reading.

docs.title: clang-tidy
docs.text: The repository's .clang-tidy turns on a small set of checks that match the rules on this page, including readability-else-after-return, readability-identifier-naming and LLVM's own checks. Editors that use clangd pick it up. It is advice for now: CI does not run it, because it needs the whole build's compile commands.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: Python in tests/ and tools/ follows PEP 8 with four-space indentation. Scripts use only the standard library unless a requirements.txt next to them says otherwise, and start with a docstring that says what the script is for and how to run it. Return early and comment why here too.

docs.title: Bazel
docs.text: BUILD.bazel and .bzl files are formatted by buildifier. Targets in a file are listed in the order a reader needs them, usually the library first and its tests after.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Write in plain, full sentences, in British spelling, as the existing pages do.
  • Every example is a test. Each ocaml block in the user documentation goes through piac --verify, and each console block that starts with $ piac must match the real output (bazel test //tests/docs:doc_examples_test). Paste output from a real run. Do not edit it by hand.
  • A change to how the language works starts as a design note or an ADR, so the reasoning is written before the code.
  • The site must build with mkdocs build --strict.

docs.title: A catalogue of theories
docs.text:
A theory teaches the verifier about a domain. It declares new sorts, functions on them that have no body, and axioms about them, and it lives in a library, not in the compiler (ADR 0036). This page is a catalogue of worked theories. Each one shows the theory, a model that proves its axioms, a proof that uses the theory, and a mistake that the theory catches.

Status

Theories, models and sealing are implemented (ADR 0036, steps 1 to 5), and the documentation test proves every example below with piac --verify, and checks that each mistake fails. Consistency checks of trusted theories, --trust-report --why and import ... trusting (step 4) are implemented too. Theory-building metaprograms (step 5) are implemented too, so every example on this page is proved, and so are solver strategies and tactics (step 6). piac --verify --check-vacuity (step 7) checks that no goal proved with a trusted axiom was proved from a contradiction (verifier.md).

docs.title: How to read an entry
docs.text:
Every theory has the same four parts.

  1. The theory. A sig of sorts (let sort), abstract spec functions (let spec with no body) and axioms (let axiom). Everything in it is spec-only: it can appear in contracts, spec functions and lemmas, and codegen erases it.
  2. The model. A struct that gives each sort a concrete type and each function a definition, so that every axiom becomes a lemma the solver proves. A theory with a proved model cannot contradict itself, so its axioms cannot make the verifier accept a false goal. Then the model is sealed: code that imports the theory sees the axioms, never the model.
  3. A proof that uses it. A lemma or a function contract that the axioms prove.
  4. A mistake it catches. A version that is wrong and fails with a counterexample.

A module cannot import another's theory yet, since interfaces do not carry theories, so each entry is one program, with the theory, its model and its clients together. A client still sees only the theory's axioms, because the model is sealed. The report under each program shows the lines that matter: the client's goals, and the model meeting each axiom. When a theory has a model, a counterexample is found in the model, where everything is concrete, and the report says so: a goal that is false in a model that meets the axioms is not a consequence of them.

An entry also says whether anything in it is trusted. A trusted theory has no model that the program can find, so it is declared in a @trusted module and imported with trusting. Trust covers the whole theory, and the compiler lists every axiom it brings in piac --trust-report.

Theory What it proves Trusted Tested from Lock levels a lock discipline rules out lock-order deadlock nothing step 3 Happens-before release/acquire publishes data, relaxed does not nothing step 3 The memory model RC11's executions, and litmus tests of what they allow nothing built in Probability union bounds on failure; independence as an explicit trust independent only steps 3 and 4 Fail-safe control a controller falls back to a safe command on a sensor fault nothing step 3 State machines a protocol is followed, from a table of transitions nothing step 5 Clocks elapsed time over many ticks, by induction that a tactic writes nothing step 6 Units of measure quantities are combined with the right dimensions nothing step 3 Network shapes and bounds layer shapes match and Lipschitz bounds compose nothing step 3 Allocators a block from take aliases no live block, and a given-back block is dead nothing step 3

The steps are the implementation order of ADR 0036: (1) spec-only real and int, (2) theories in @trusted modules, (3) models and sealing, (4) certificates and trusting, (5) theory-building metaprograms, (6) solver strategies and tactics, (7) --check-vacuity.

docs.title: Lock levels
docs.text:
ADR 0027 rules out lock-order deadlock with static lock levels: a task may only take a lock above every level it holds. The compiler checks Pia's own mutex that way. A library with its own lock discipline, such as a database lock manager or a kernel's spinlock hierarchy, can state the same rule as a theory, and the verifier then checks it in that library's users.

held is the set of levels a task holds, and below h n says every held level is less than n:

let level = int{0..63}

let theory Levels = sig
  let sort held
  let spec none : held
  let spec take : (h : held) -> (n : level) -> held
  let spec drop : (h : held) -> (n : level) -> held
  let spec holds : (h : held) -> (n : level) -> bool
  let spec below : (h : held) -> (n : level) -> bool

  let axiom none_below (n : level) ensures below none n
  let axiom take_holds (h : held) (n : level) (m : level)
    ensures holds (take h n) m = (m = n || holds h m)
  let axiom drop_holds (h : held) (n : level) (m : level)
    ensures holds (drop h n) m = (m <> n && holds h m)
  let axiom take_below (h : held) (n : level) (m : level)
    requires below h n && n < m
    ensures below (take h n) m
  let axiom drop_below (h : held) (n : level) (m : level)
    requires below h m
    ensures below (drop h n) m
  let axiom below_held (h : held) (n : level) (m : level) @trigger(below h n, holds h m)
    requires below h n && holds h m
    ensures m < n
end

\ Levels are bits of a u64: bit n is set when level n is held.
let model bits : Levels = struct
  let sort held = u64
  let spec none : u64 = 0
  let spec take (h : u64) (n : level) : u64 = (h | (1 << n))
  let spec drop (h : u64) (n : level) : u64 = h & ~(1 << n)
  let spec holds (h : u64) (n : level) : bool = ((h >> n) & 1) = 1
  let spec below (h : u64) (n : level) : bool = (h >> n) = 0
end

\ accounts are level 2 and the ledger is level 3
let lemma transfer_order (h : Levels.held) : unit
  requires Levels.below h 2
  ensures Levels.below (Levels.take h 2) 3
= ()

let lemma ledger_then_account (h : Levels.held) : unit
  requires Levels.below h 3
  ensures Levels.below (Levels.take h 3) 2
= ()

$ piac --verify levels.pia
...
levels.pia:40:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
levels.pia:45:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample in the model 'bits': h = 0
...
levels.pia:24:5: proved: the model 'bits' meets the axiom 'Levels.below_held' [smt]
19 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The model's obligations are bit-vector facts, such as (h >> n) = 0 && n < m ==> ((h | (1 << n)) >> m) = 0, which Z3 decides. piac proves each axiom as a lemma over the model, and reports it as the model 'bits' meets the axiom ....

A lock manager's acquire takes the task's held set as a ghost argument and requires the new level to be above it, and its users prove their own lock orders from the axioms: transfer_order proves. Taking the ledger first and then an account, ledger_then_account, is the deadlock the rule exists to prevent, and it fails.

The counterexample is in the model: from h = 0, taking level 3 sets bit 3, and 3 >> 2 is not 0, so the held set is not below 2. Over the axioms, take_holds says the task now holds level 3, and below_held says a held level must be below 2. below_held needs a written trigger with two terms, since neither below h n nor holds h m mentions all three of its parameters.

docs.title: Happens-before and memory orders
docs.text:
ADR 0027 counts a happens-before edge from atomics only when the memory orders create one: a release store read by an acquire load. The usual bug is publishing data with a flag written relaxed. As a theory, the rule is four axioms over events:

let theory Order = sig
  let sort event
  let spec po : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> bool        \ program order, one thread
  let spec rf : (w : event) -> (r : event) -> bool        \ r reads the value w stored
  let spec releases : (w : event) -> bool                 \ a store at release or stronger
  let spec acquires : (r : event) -> bool                 \ a load at acquire or stronger
  let spec hb : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> bool        \ happens before

  let axiom po_hb (a : event) (b : event) requires po a b ensures hb a b
  let axiom sync_hb (w : event) (r : event)
    requires rf w r && releases w && acquires r
    ensures hb w r
  let axiom hb_trans (a : event) (b : event) (c : event) @trigger(hb a b, hb b c)
    requires hb a b && hb b c
    ensures hb a c
  let axiom hb_irrefl (a : event) ensures hb a a = false
end

\ Every event gets a global time: a sequentially consistent execution.
let stamp = type { thread : u32; time : int; rel : bool; acq : bool; read_from : int }

let model timeline : Order = struct
  let sort event = stamp
  let spec po (a : stamp) (b : stamp) : bool = a.thread = b.thread && a.time < b.time
  let spec rf (w : stamp) (r : stamp) : bool = r.read_from = w.time && w.time < r.time
  let spec releases (w : stamp) : bool = w.rel
  let spec acquires (r : stamp) : bool = r.acq
  let spec hb (a : stamp) (b : stamp) : bool = a.time < b.time
end

let lemma publish (data_w : Order.event) (flag_w : Order.event)
                  (flag_r : Order.event) (data_r : Order.event) : unit
  requires Order.po data_w flag_w && Order.releases flag_w
  requires Order.rf flag_w flag_r && Order.acquires flag_r
  requires Order.po flag_r data_r
  ensures Order.hb data_w data_r
= ()

let lemma publish_relaxed (data_w : Order.event) (flag_w : Order.event)
                          (flag_r : Order.event) (data_r : Order.event) : unit
  requires Order.po data_w flag_w
  requires Order.rf flag_w flag_r && Order.acquires flag_r
  requires Order.po flag_r data_r
  ensures Order.hb data_w data_r
= ()

$ piac --verify order.pia
...
order.pia:36:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
order.pia:44:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample: data_w = Order.event!val!0, flag_w = Order.event!val!1, flag_r = Order.event!val!2, data_r = Order.event!val!3
...
order.pia:16:35: proved: the model 'timeline' meets the axiom 'Order.hb_irrefl' [smt]
5 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The message-passing idiom, publish, proves: the data store is before the flag's release store in its thread, the flag's acquire load reads it, and the data load comes after in the reader's thread, so the data store happens before the data load. With the flag stored relaxed, there is no releases flag_w, and the same goal, publish_relaxed, fails. hb_trans has two terms in its trigger, since no single term mentions all three events.

Here the counterexample comes from the axioms, not the model, and this entry shows why a model is sealed. In the timeline model, every execution is sequentially consistent, so hb is just "earlier in time" and publish_relaxed would be true. A client sees only the axioms, and they do not prove it, because on real hardware it is false. The model shows the axioms are consistent. It is not what clients reason with. A weaker memory model, such as RC11 for relaxed, is a larger theory of the same shape.

docs.title: Probability
docs.text:
Failure budgets, retries and randomised algorithms are arguments about probabilities. Here events are abstract and pr gives each one a probability:

let theory Prob = sig
  let sort event
  let spec pr : (e : event) -> real
  let spec either : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> event
  let spec both : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> event
  let spec opposite : (a : event) -> event

  let axiom pr_range (e : event) ensures 0.0 <= pr e && pr e <= 1.0
  let axiom union_bound (a : event) (b : event)
    ensures pr (either a b) <= pr a + pr b
  let axiom both_le (a : event) (b : event)
    ensures pr (both a b) <= pr a && pr (both a b) <= pr b
  let axiom complement (a : event) ensures pr (opposite a) = 1.0 - pr a
end

\ An event is only its probability. `either` and `both` take the
\ worst case the axioms allow (the Fréchet bounds).
let chance = type { p : real where 0.0 <= p && p <= 1.0 }

let model bounds : Prob = struct
  let sort event = chance
  let spec pr (e : chance) : real = e.p
  let spec either (a : chance) (b : chance) : chance =
    { p = if a.p + b.p <= 1.0 then a.p + b.p else 1.0 }
  let spec both (a : chance) (b : chance) : chance =
    { p = if a.p + b.p >= 1.0 then a.p + b.p - 1.0 else 0.0 }
  let spec opposite (a : chance) : chance = { p = 1.0 - a.p }
end

let lemma request_budget (a : Prob.event) (b : Prob.event) (c : Prob.event) : unit
  requires Prob.pr a <= 0.001 && Prob.pr b <= 0.001 && Prob.pr c <= 0.001
  ensures Prob.pr (Prob.opposite (Prob.either (Prob.either a b) c)) >= 0.997
= ()

A request fails if any of three stages fails. Each stage's failure rate is at most one in a thousand, so request_budget proves that the request succeeds at least 99.7% of the time. The refinement on chance is what makes the model meet pr_range: every chance has 0.0 <= p && p <= 1.0, and each of the model's functions proves it of the chance it returns.

Independence is a trusted axiom. A tighter bound, such as "two replicas both lose a write with probability at most p²", needs independence, and no deterministic random number generator is truly independent. That is the idealisation every analysis of a randomised algorithm makes, so Pia makes it visible: the axiom lives in a theory with no model, which only a @trusted module may declare, and its users import it with trusting. Trust covers the whole theory, so Ideal holds only the axiom that needs it.

A module cannot import another's theory yet, so this program repeats Prob and its model, and declares Ideal in the same @trusted file. In a library, Ideal would be its own module, Pia.Rand.Ideal, and the client would write import Pia.Rand.Ideal trusting.

@trusted

let theory Prob = sig
  let sort event
  let spec pr : (e : event) -> real
  let spec either : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> event
  let spec both : (a : event) -> (b : event) -> event
  let spec opposite : (a : event) -> event

  let axiom pr_range (e : event) ensures 0.0 <= pr e && pr e <= 1.0
  let axiom union_bound (a : event) (b : event)
    ensures pr (either a b) <= pr a + pr b
  let axiom both_le (a : event) (b : event)
    ensures pr (both a b) <= pr a && pr (both a b) <= pr b
  let axiom complement (a : event) ensures pr (opposite a) = 1.0 - pr a
end

\ An event is only its probability. `either` and `both` take the
\ worst case the axioms allow (the Fréchet bounds).
let chance = type { p : real where 0.0 <= p && p <= 1.0 }

let model bounds : Prob = struct
  let sort event = chance
  let spec pr (e : chance) : real = e.p
  let spec either (a : chance) (b : chance) : chance =
    { p = if a.p + b.p <= 1.0 then a.p + b.p else 1.0 }
  let spec both (a : chance) (b : chance) : chance =
    { p = if a.p + b.p >= 1.0 then a.p + b.p - 1.0 else 0.0 }
  let spec opposite (a : chance) : chance = { p = 1.0 - a.p }
end

\ Independence is an idealisation: no model of Prob here has it (in
\ `bounds`, two events of probability 0.01 have a joint probability of
\ 0), so it is a theory of its own, trusted, and this file says so.
let theory Ideal = sig
  let spec lost : (replica : u32) -> Prob.event
  let axiom independent (i : u32) (j : u32)
    requires i <> j
    ensures Prob.pr (Prob.both (lost i) (lost j)) = Prob.pr (lost i) * Prob.pr (lost j)
end

import Ideal trusting

let lemma two_replicas : unit
  requires Prob.pr (Ideal.lost 0) <= 0.01 && Prob.pr (Ideal.lost 1) <= 0.01
  ensures Prob.pr (Prob.both (Ideal.lost 0) (Ideal.lost 1)) <= 0.0001
= ()

$ piac --verify --trust-report --why ideal.pia
ideal.pia:37:3: the theory 'Ideal' is consistent: the solver found a witness, a model of its axioms
ideal.pia:42:1: trusting the theory 'Ideal'
ideal.pia:37:3: trusted: the axiom 'Ideal.independent', since the theory 'Ideal' has no model
  used by: ideal.pia:46:3
1 trusted item
1 of 26 proved goals rest on a trusted axiom; the other 25 are fully proved
...
26 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Ideal is consistent with Prob's axioms, but not with its bounds model, in which two events of probability 0.01 have a joint probability of 0. That is fine, because clients reason with Prob's axioms and never with the model, and it is a reminder that bounds is a worst-case summary, not a probability space. When Ideal is compiled, piac asks Z3 whether its axioms and the Prob axioms they use are consistent, and finds a witness. The trust report lists Ideal.independent, and with --why the goal two_replicas that used it. The other goals, including Prob's model check, rest on nothing trusted.

docs.title: Fail-safe control
docs.text:
A controller must do something safe when its inputs cannot be trusted. Which command is safe depends on the plant: a gas valve fails closed, a fire door fails open. The theory names the safe command and says it keeps a safe plant safe:

let command = type | Fill | Hold

let theory Tank = sig
  let sort plant
  let spec safe : (p : plant) -> bool
  let spec allows : (p : plant) -> (c : command) -> bool
  let spec step : (p : plant) -> (c : command) -> plant

  let axiom hold_allowed (p : plant) requires safe p ensures allows p Hold
  let axiom allowed_safe (p : plant) (c : command)
    requires safe p && allows p c
    ensures safe (step p c)
end

\ A tank that one step of filling raises by up to 10 units.
let tank = type { level : int where 0 <= level && level <= 200 }

let model levels : Tank = struct
  let sort plant = tank
  let spec safe (p : tank) : bool = p.level <= 150
  let spec allows (p : tank) (c : command) : bool =
    match c with
    | Fill -> p.level + 10 <= 150
    | Hold -> true
  let spec step (p : tank) (c : command) : tank =
    match c with
    | Fill -> { level = if p.level + 10 <= 200 then p.level + 10 else 200 }
    | Hold -> p
end

let spec decide (want : command) (sensor_ok : bool) : command =
  if sensor_ok then want else Hold

let lemma fail_closed (p : Tank.plant) (want : command) (sensor_ok : bool) : unit
  requires Tank.safe p
  requires sensor_ok ==> Tank.allows p want
  ensures Tank.safe (Tank.step p (decide want sensor_ok))
= ()

let spec decide_open (want : command) (sensor_ok : bool) : command = want

let lemma fail_open (p : Tank.plant) (want : command) (sensor_ok : bool) : unit
  requires Tank.safe p
  requires sensor_ok ==> Tank.allows p want
  ensures Tank.safe (Tank.step p (decide_open want sensor_ok))
= ()

$ piac --verify tank.pia
...
tank.pia:37:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
tank.pia:45:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample in the model 'levels': p.level = 150, want.tag = 0, sensor_ok = false
...
tank.pia:12:5: proved: the model 'levels' meets the axiom 'Tank.allowed_safe' [smt]
10 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The controller, decide, passes the operator's command through when the sensor is healthy and the command is allowed, and holds otherwise, so fail_closed proves. A controller that keeps doing what it was told when the sensor fails, decide_open, which is failing open for a tank, does not.

The counterexample, found in the model, has sensor_ok = false and want = Fill (tag 0) at a level of 150, where filling would pass the safe limit and nothing says the plant allows it. The real controller in code reads integers from a sensor. It connects to the theory through an abstraction function from its readings to Tank.plant, defined in the model's module (ADR 0036), so its command function is proved with the same lemma.

docs.title: The memory model: RC11
docs.text:
Memory is the language's memory model, RC11 (Lahav, Vafeiadis, Kang, Hur and Dreyer, 2017), the repaired C11 model (ADR 0052, section 4). It is built into piac, as Target is: a program that names Memory gets the theory, written in src/irgen/Memory.pia. It is the larger theory of the same shape that the happens-before entry above calls for. An execution is a sort of events with program order po, reads-from rf, the modification order mo and the read-modify-write pairs rmw. From-reads fr, the extended coherence order eco, release sequences rs, synchronises-with sw, happens-before hb and the SC order psc are given by lower bounds: each axiom says what makes them hold. RC11's own axioms only forbid: hb is irreflexive and hb ; eco is too (coherence), nothing comes between a read-modify-write's read and write in mo (atomicity), and psc and po ∪ rf are acyclic, which is said with a rank of each event (the SC order, and no values out of thin air). So whatever follows from the lower bounds holds of every consistent execution, and message passing proves from the axioms:

let lemma publish (dw : Memory.event) (fw : Memory.event) (fr : Memory.event)
                  (dr : Memory.event) : unit
  requires Memory.po dw fw && Memory.is_write fw && Memory.releases fw
  requires Memory.is_atomic fw && Memory.rf fw fr && Memory.is_read fr
  requires Memory.is_atomic fr && Memory.acquires fr && Memory.po fr dr
  ensures Memory.hb dw dr
= ()

The model timeline gives every event a time and makes every relation follow it, which is a sequentially consistent execution, so the axioms are consistent. tests/memory/theory.pia proves it once, when the compiler is tested.

Litmus tests. A litmus test is a small concurrent program, a few threads over a few locations, with an outcome that RC11 allows or forbids. The prelude's litmus turns one into a lemma. Threads are lists of events: write loc v and read loc r are plain accesses, store o loc v, load o loc r, swap o loc v r and fetch_add o loc v r are atomic, and barrier o is a fence, each with its order as a string. The outcome is a list of is r v (register r read v) and final loc v (the last write to loc in mo stored v):

litmus "mp_rel_acq"
  [ thread [ write "data" 1; store "release" "flag" 1 ]
  ; thread [ load "acquire" "flag" "r1"; read "data" "r2" ] ]
  "forbidden" [ is "r1" 1; is "r2" 0 ]

litmus "mp_rlx"
  [ thread [ store "relaxed" "data" 1; store "relaxed" "flag" 1 ]
  ; thread [ load "relaxed" "flag" "r1"; load "relaxed" "data" "r2" ] ]
  "allowed" [ is "r1" 1; is "r2" 0 ]

$ piac --verify litmus.pia
litmus.pia:1:1: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
litmus.pia:6:1: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample: r1 = 1, r2 = 0
1 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

Both lemmas claim that no consistent execution ends with the outcome. A forbidden outcome is proved. An allowed one fails, and its counterexample is a witness: an execution that RC11 allows and that ends that way, with each register's value and each <loc>_final. A third verdict, "race", claims that no execution has a data race: two accesses to one location, one of them a write and one of them plain, with neither happening before the other. It fails with a racy execution when there is one.

A test has a handful of events, so the lemma is finite. litmus numbers the events, starting with an initial write of 0 to each location, and each relation becomes an array of booleans indexed by pairs of events: rf with each read reading exactly one write to its location, a rank per write for mo, and lower bounds for the derived relations, exactly as in the theory. Each acyclicity is a rank per event. The query is a few thousand clauses over booleans and integers, which Z3 decides in well under a second. Expanding the test takes longer than solving it: the expansion is the interpreter building those clauses.

tests/memory/ is the battery, one file per family: message passing with every pairing of orders and fences, store buffering, load buffering, the four coherence shapes, read-modify-write atomicity and release sequences, WRC, ISA2, IRIW, S, R and 2+2W, and races. Each expected result is RC11's. When tasks land, each test also becomes a program of spawned tasks with the same outcomes, for the model checker, and the hardware models of each target are checked against the same battery (ADR 0052, section 5).

docs.title: State machines
docs.text:
A protocol is a table of states and transitions, and a metaprogram can turn the table into a theory and its model, so a library describes the protocol once as data and nothing about it is trusted. The prelude's machine does this (step 5). Its first argument names the theory's sort, then come the type of states, the initial state and the table, one edge per transition. A full session proves, and sending after shutdown does not:

let conn_state = type | Closed | Open | Draining

let theory Conn = machine "conn" conn_state Closed
  [ edge Closed "connect" Open
  ; edge Open "send" Open
  ; edge Open "shutdown" Draining
  ; edge Draining "close" Closed ]

let lemma session (c : Conn.conn) : unit
  requires Conn.at c = Closed
  ensures Conn.at (Conn.close (Conn.shutdown (Conn.send (Conn.connect c)))) = Closed
= ()

let lemma send_after_shutdown (c : Conn.conn) : unit
  requires Conn.at c = Closed
  ensures Conn.allowed_send (Conn.shutdown (Conn.connect c))
= ()

$ piac --verify conn.pia
...
conn.pia:11:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
conn.pia:16:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample in the model 'conn_states': c.tag = 0
...
conn.pia:3:1: proved: the model 'conn_states' meets the axiom 'Conn.close_from_Draining' [smt]
10 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

machine is an ordinary metaprogram, written in Pia with map and fold, so it is total, as a metaprogram that builds a theory must be (ADR 0035): what it returns becomes hypotheses of proofs. It builds an abstract sort conn, the state at c of each c, and a start in the initial state. For each event it builds an abstract function, a predicate saying where the event is allowed, and one axiom per edge saying where it leads. It also builds a model, conn_states, in which a conn is just its state, and the model proves every axiom, so nothing is trusted. The counterexample comes from that model: from Closed (tag 0), connect then shutdown leads to Draining, where send is not allowed. For shutdown, what it builds amounts to this:

let conn_state = type | Closed | Open | Draining

let theory Conn = sig
  let sort conn
  let spec at : (c : conn) -> conn_state
  let spec shutdown : (c : conn) -> conn
  let spec allowed_shutdown : (c : conn) -> bool
  let axiom shutdown_allowed (c : conn) ensures allowed_shutdown c = (at c = Open)
  let axiom shutdown_from_Open (c : conn) requires at c = Open ensures at (shutdown c) = Draining
end

let model conn_states : Conn = struct
  let sort conn = conn_state
  let spec at (c : conn_state) : conn_state = c
  let spec shutdown (c : conn_state) : conn_state = if c = Open then Draining else c
  let spec allowed_shutdown (c : conn_state) : bool = c = Open
end

The generated binders are named c#machine, a name no source can write, and the member names (shutdown, allowed_shutdown, shutdown_from_Open) are kept, so clients can name them (ADR 0022). One table builds one theory: a second let theory with the same call names the same theory, rather than building a second one. The library's socket API requires the event to be allowed, as in let send (s : socket) ... requires Conn.allowed_send (abs s), so a program that sends after shutting down fails at the call.

A variant type and spec functions could say the same thing without a theory. The theory adds three things: the sort conn is abstract, so users cannot depend on how a connection is represented; the axioms are small facts rather than definitions to unfold; and one table generates the theory, its model and its proofs, for every protocol a library has. This is how ADR 0006's module state-machine properties can be written by libraries.

docs.title: Clocks: a proof written by a tactic
docs.text:
Some facts about a theory need induction: one axiom says what a single step does, and a lemma says what many steps do. The proof is the same every time, the lemma calling itself one step smaller, so a tactic can write it (ADR 0036, step 6). A tactic is a metaprogram that @by(...) on a lemma runs on the lemma's goal. It returns proof steps, and the verifier proves them like steps written by hand. So a tactic can make a proof possible, but it cannot make a wrong one (meta.md).

Here the theory is a clock, with one axiom: a tick adds one to the time. ticks c n is n ticks from c. induction writes the step if n > 0 then elapsed c (n - 1), and with it the lemma is proved. Without the step, the same goal fails, and the report says why it may: ticks was unfolded only once.

let theory Clock = sig
  let sort clock
  let spec time : (c : clock) -> int
  let spec tick : (c : clock) -> clock
  let axiom tick_time (c : clock) ensures time (tick c) = time c + 1
end

let model counter : Clock = struct
  let sort clock = int
  let spec time (c : int) : int = c
  let spec tick (c : int) : int = c + 1
end

let rec spec ticks (c : Clock.clock) (n : int) : Clock.clock
  requires n >= 0
  decreases n
= if n = 0 then c else Clock.tick (ticks c (n - 1))

let meta induction (g : syntax) (on : syntax) : list =
  let args = map (let (p) => if p = name on then `( $on - 1 ) else p) (params g) in
  [ `( if $on > 0 then $(make_call (name g) args) ) ]

let lemma elapsed (c : Clock.clock) (n : int) : unit @by(induction n)
  requires n >= 0
  ensures Clock.time (ticks c n) = Clock.time c + n
  decreases n
= ()

let lemma unaided (c : Clock.clock) (n : int) : unit
  requires n >= 0
  ensures Clock.time (ticks c n) = Clock.time c + n
= ()

$ piac --verify clock.pia
...
clock.pia:25:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
clock.pia:31:23: proved: the precondition of 'ticks' holds [smt]
clock.pia:31:3: failed: the postcondition holds [the solver gave up: smt tactic failed to show goal to be sat/unsat (incomplete quantifiers)]
  hint: a recursive spec function was unfolded only as far as its @fuel allows, so this goal may hold; raise @fuel on the function or the lemma, or prove the fact by induction in a lemma
clock.pia:5:35: proved: the model 'counter' meets the axiom 'Clock.tick_time' [smt]
8 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

induction reads the goal's parameters with params g, replaces n with n - 1, and builds the call with make_call. It recurses on nothing, so it is total, as a tactic must be: like a theory-building metaprogram, it may not read the program, and it must terminate (ADR 0035). The lemma still needs its decreases n, and the recursive call is checked against it, so a tactic that wrote a call that is not smaller would fail to prove it rather than prove the lemma wrongly. Nothing here is trusted: the model counter, where a clock is an integer, proves the axiom.

A theory can also choose how Z3 solves its members' goals, as in let theory Geometry @solver(nlsat) = sig ... end for nonlinear real arithmetic. Each member without its own @solver uses it. A strategy affects only how fast a goal is proved, never whether it is (verifier.md).

docs.title: Units of measure
docs.text:
Adding metres to seconds is a type error in physics. Dimensions form a group, and the obvious theory, with axioms for associativity and commutativity, makes Z3 instantiate those axioms over and over. A better theory reduces a dimension to its exponents, which is linear arithmetic, and has no axiom that can loop:

let theory Dim = sig
  let sort dim
  let spec metres : (d : dim) -> int       \ the exponent of each base unit
  let spec seconds : (d : dim) -> int
  let spec kilograms : (d : dim) -> int
  let spec length : dim
  let spec time : dim
  let spec mass : dim
  let spec times : (a : dim) -> (b : dim) -> dim
  let spec per : (a : dim) -> (b : dim) -> dim

  let axiom length_exp ensures metres length = 1 && seconds length = 0 && kilograms length = 0
  let axiom time_exp ensures metres time = 0 && seconds time = 1 && kilograms time = 0
  let axiom mass_exp ensures metres mass = 0 && seconds mass = 0 && kilograms mass = 1
  let axiom times_exp (a : dim) (b : dim)
    ensures metres (times a b) = metres a + metres b
         && seconds (times a b) = seconds a + seconds b
         && kilograms (times a b) = kilograms a + kilograms b
  let axiom per_exp (a : dim) (b : dim)
    ensures metres (per a b) = metres a - metres b
         && seconds (per a b) = seconds a - seconds b
         && kilograms (per a b) = kilograms a - kilograms b
  let axiom same (a : dim) (b : dim) @trigger(metres a, metres b)
    requires metres a = metres b && seconds a = seconds b && kilograms a = kilograms b
    ensures a = b
end

let exps = type { m : int; s : int; kg : int }

let model exponents : Dim = struct
  let sort dim = exps
  let spec metres (d : exps) : int = d.m
  let spec seconds (d : exps) : int = d.s
  let spec kilograms (d : exps) : int = d.kg
  let spec length : exps = { m = 1; s = 0; kg = 0 }
  let spec time : exps = { m = 0; s = 1; kg = 0 }
  let spec mass : exps = { m = 0; s = 0; kg = 1 }
  let spec times (a : exps) (b : exps) : exps = { m = a.m + b.m; s = a.s + b.s; kg = a.kg + b.kg }
  let spec per (a : exps) (b : exps) : exps = { m = a.m - b.m; s = a.s - b.s; kg = a.kg - b.kg }
end

let lemma distance : unit
  ensures Dim.times (Dim.per Dim.length Dim.time) Dim.time = Dim.length
= ()

let lemma newton : unit
  ensures Dim.metres (Dim.per (Dim.times Dim.mass Dim.length) (Dim.times Dim.time Dim.time)) = 1
= ()

let lemma speed_is_length : unit
  ensures Dim.per Dim.length Dim.time = Dim.length
= ()

$ piac --verify dim.pia
...
dim.pia:43:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
dim.pia:47:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
dim.pia:51:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  false in the model 'exponents'
...
dim.pia:25:5: proved: the model 'exponents' meets the axiom 'Dim.same' [smt]
8 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

A quantity library tags each value with a ghost dim, and add requires equal dimensions. Speed times time is a length (distance), and a force is a mass times a length per time squared (newton). Treating a speed as a length, speed_is_length, fails.

The lemma has no parameters, so there are no values to show: it is false in the model, where per length time has seconds -1 and length has 0. The @trigger on same is the one written by hand: it fires only when two dimensions' exponents are both in the query, which is when equality could matter.

docs.title: Network shapes and bounds
docs.text: The worked example of ADR 0036 is a theory Lip of neural network layers, with a shapes model in which a layer is its input width, output width and a Lipschitz bound. A residual block proves both its shape and lip <= 3.0 from five axioms, and a residual around a layer whose widths differ fails at compile time. That entry also shows where trust enters: claiming that lip bounds the true Lipschitz constant of a kernel is a trusted axiom, and it is listed.

docs.title: Allocators
docs.text:
An allocator promises a few things about the blocks it hands out: a block it hands out was not live, its memory is apart from every other block's, and a block given back is dead until it is handed out again. Each allocator keeps those promises with its own data structure, such as the free stack of tests/verify/pool.pia, and proving them there takes quantifiers over the pool's arrays. A theory states them once, as facts about an abstract heap, so the users of any allocator reason with small axioms instead (ADR 0041):

let blk = int{0..63}

let theory Alloc = sig
  let sort heap
  let spec none : heap
  let spec live : (h : heap) -> (b : blk) -> bool
  let spec take : (h : heap) -> (b : blk) -> heap
  let spec give : (h : heap) -> (b : blk) -> heap
  let spec base : (b : blk) -> int              \ where the block's 16 bytes start

  let axiom none_live (b : blk) ensures live none b = false
  let axiom take_live (h : heap) (b : blk) (c : blk)
    ensures live (take h b) c = (c = b || live h c)
  let axiom give_live (h : heap) (b : blk) (c : blk)
    ensures live (give h b) c = (c <> b && live h c)
  let axiom apart (b : blk) (c : blk) @trigger(base b, base c)
    requires b <> c
    ensures base b + 16 <= base c || base c + 16 <= base b
end

\ The live blocks are bits of a u64, and block b is bytes 16b to 16b + 15.
let model bits : Alloc = struct
  let sort heap = u64
  let spec none : u64 = 0
  let spec live (h : u64) (b : blk) : bool = ((h >> b) & 1) = 1
  let spec take (h : u64) (b : blk) : u64 = (h | (1 << b))
  let spec give (h : u64) (b : blk) : u64 = h & ~(1 << b)
  let spec base (b : blk) : int = b * 16
end

\ A block that was not live, once taken, is apart from every live block.
let lemma fresh_apart (h : Alloc.heap) (a : blk) (b : blk) : unit
  requires Alloc.live h a && Alloc.live h b = false
  ensures Alloc.live (Alloc.take h b) a
  ensures Alloc.base a + 16 <= Alloc.base b || Alloc.base b + 16 <= Alloc.base a
= ()

\ docs/stdlib.md's reuse: take a, give it back, take b, which may be a's
\ old block. b is live, and a is dead between the give and the take.
let lemma reuse (h : Alloc.heap) (a : blk) (b : blk) : unit
  requires Alloc.live h a = false
  requires Alloc.live (Alloc.give (Alloc.take h a) a) b = false
  ensures Alloc.live (Alloc.give (Alloc.take h a) a) a = false
  ensures Alloc.live (Alloc.take (Alloc.give (Alloc.take h a) a) b) b
= ()

\ Wrong: a block given back is not live.
let lemma use_after_give (h : Alloc.heap) (a : blk) : unit
  ensures Alloc.live (Alloc.give h a) a
= ()

$ piac --verify alloc.pia
alloc.pia:34:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
...
alloc.pia:49:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample in the model 'bits': h = 12297829382473034410, a = 2
...
alloc.pia:18:5: proved: the model 'bits' meets the axiom 'Alloc.apart' [smt]
18 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

fresh_apart and reuse prove from the axioms alone, with no quantifier in sight, and use_after_give fails: using a block after giving it back is the use-after-free the theory exists to rule out. In the counterexample, h is 0xAAAA...AAAA, whose bit 2 is clear, so block 2 is dead after the give. The bits model proves every axiom, so nothing is trusted.

A running allocator follows the theory through spec-only state (ADR 0041): a field of a spec-only type, such as heap : Alloc.heap, which the verifier sees and codegen erases, with no new keyword. tests/verify/pool_alloc.pia is the pool with such a field. Its take_slot sets p.heap <- Alloc.take p.heap s and ensures p.heap = Alloc.take (old p.heap) b.i and Alloc.live (old p.heap) b.i = false; its give_slot requires Alloc.live p.heap b.i. The pool proves once, in the spec ok, that its arrays match the heap: a slot is live in the heap exactly when it sits at or above the free stack's top. Its users prove from Alloc's axioms alone, as reuse there does. Each pool also has a spec-only id, and each block a spec-only owner: give_slot requires b.owner = p.id, so a block goes back only to the pool that handed it out, at no run-time cost (tests/verify/pool_owner_errors.pia shows the failure).
