Size classes compose pools: in tests/verify/size_classes.pia, general holds a 16-byte and a 64-byte pool, alloc n takes from the smallest class that holds n bytes, and free gives the block back to the pool of its class. Generic code reaches an allocator through the Allocator concept, whose requirements are stated with the theory: in tests/verify/vec_allocator.pia, Allocator a t r requires held : a -> Alloc.heap and an alloc that leaves the heap unchanged when it fails, and a vector that stores an allocator of any such type proves that a failed push leaves the allocator's heap alone.

docs.title: The target
docs.text:
Target is a theory built into the compiler (ADR 0049). It names the facts about the machine a proof may use: pointer width, byte order, the alignment allocations get, page size, cache line and the widest native vector. Each target Pia compiles for is a model of it. A program that names Target gets the theory, and the model of the target it is compiled for, with no import:

let lemma big_pages : unit ensures Target.page_size >= 4096 = ()

let fits_in_page (n : usize) : usize
  requires n <= 4096
  ensures result <= Target.page_size
= n

The program sees only the axioms, which hold on every target, so it proves the same way for Apple silicon and for x86_64 Linux. Target.page_size = 4096 does not prove, because the page is 16384 bytes on Apple silicon: the model is sealed, like any other. Each axiom must hold on every build of the architectures Pia targets, not just on today's two triples, which is why the pointer width is a value of each model rather than an axiom. The theory and its models, as compiled into piac:

(* Pia.Target (ADR 0049, section 3): the facts about the machine that a
   proof may use, as a theory with one model per target. piac adds the
   theory, and the model of the target it compiles for, to every program
   that names `Target`, so no import is needed. A program sees only the
   axioms: what holds on every target. A function marked `@target(m)`
   also sees its own model's values, and is compiled only for that target.

   Each axiom must hold on every build of the architectures Pia targets,
   not only on today's triples, so a later triple can never break a
   target-generic proof. That is why pointer width is a model value and
   not an axiom: x86_64 runs 32-bit pointers in compatibility mode and
   under the x32 ABI.

   The models are proved to meet the axioms when the compiler is tested
   (tests/verify/target_theory.pia), not in each program that uses them. *)

let theory Target = sig
  let spec ptr_bits : usize
  let spec little_endian : bool
  let spec max_align : usize    \ the alignment Pia.Mem.alloc guarantees
  let spec page_size : usize
  let spec cache_line : usize   \ the destructive interference size
  let spec vector_bits : usize  \ the widest vector the CPU runs natively
  let spec rmw_flags : bool     \ an atomic add sets overflow and carry flags

  let spec is_pow2 (n : usize) : bool = popcount n = 1

  let axiom ptr_pow2 ensures is_pow2 ptr_bits && ptr_bits >= 32
  let axiom little ensures little_endian
  let axiom align_16 ensures max_align = 16
  let axiom page_pow2 ensures is_pow2 page_size && page_size >= 4096
  let axiom line_pow2 ensures is_pow2 cache_line && cache_line >= 64
  let axiom vector_min ensures vector_bits >= 128
  (* rmw_flags has no axiom: the targets differ, and no proof may depend
     on it. Codegen reads it to lower an atomic add's overflow check
     (ADR 0052, section 2). *)
end

(* Apple silicon: 16 KiB pages, 128-byte cache lines, 128-bit NEON, and
   LSE atomics, whose `ldadd` sets no flags. *)
let model arm64_macos : Target = struct
  let spec ptr_bits : usize = 64
  let spec little_endian : bool = true
  let spec max_align : usize = 16
  let spec page_size : usize = 16384
  let spec cache_line : usize = 128
  let spec vector_bits : usize = 128
  let spec rmw_flags : bool = false
end

(* x86_64 Linux at x86-64-v3: 4 KiB pages, 64-byte lines, 256-bit AVX2,
   and a `lock`-prefixed add that sets the overflow and carry flags. *)
let model x86_64_linux : Target = struct
  let spec ptr_bits : usize = 64
  let spec little_endian : bool = true
  let spec max_align : usize = 16
  let spec page_size : usize = 4096
  let spec cache_line : usize = 64
  let spec vector_bits : usize = 256
  let spec rmw_flags : bool = true
end

Each model is proved to meet the axioms when the compiler is tested (tests/verify/target_theory.pia), not again in every program that uses it. Code that needs one target's own values says so with @target(m), after the return type like @overflow:

let take_page (n : usize) : usize
  requires n <= Target.page_size
  ensures result = n
= n

let huge_page_count (bytes : usize) : usize @target(x86_64_linux)
  requires bytes <= 1000000
  ensures result * Target.page_size >= bytes
= (bytes + 4095) / 4096

let whole_page (x : u8) : usize @target(x86_64_linux)
  ensures result = 4096
= take_page 4096

A function marked @target(m) is compiled, and proved, only for the target whose model is m, and its proofs see m's values as well as the axioms. So huge_page_count can use the page size of 4096, and whole_page meets take_page's target-generic precondition with it. Only a function for the same target may use one, on every target: a target-generic function that called whole_page would be an error even on x86_64, so a program that compiles for one target compiles for the others. tests/verify/target_items.pia proves functions for both targets.

Code can also use the constants as values. Target.cache_line in a function body compiles to 128 on Apple silicon and 64 on x86_64, while its proof still sees only the axioms. if Target.is m then a else b is folded when the program is compiled, so a is compiled only for m's target and b only for the others, and a may call @target(m) functions:

let wide (x : u8) : usize @target(x86_64_linux) = Target.vector_bits

let vector_width (x : u8) : usize
  ensures result >= 128
= if Target.is x86_64_linux then wide x else Target.vector_bits

tests/codegen/target_values.pia checks the values each target compiles to.

docs.title: Writing a theory
docs.text:
• Write the model first. If no model is easy to write, the axioms may say more than you mean. A theory without a model needs @trusted, and every user must import it with trusting. Keep trusted axioms in a theory of their own, as Pia.Rand.Ideal does, since trust covers a whole theory. A model can also live in another module, found by the ADL rule, which suits a theory with several implementations.
  • Prefer functions into decided theories. The units theory maps dimensions to integers instead of stating group laws. Axioms that only relate a function's value to its arguments' values give Z3 nothing to loop on.
  • Check the triggers. piac --verify-stats shows the trigger chosen for every axiom. An axiom should fire only on the terms it is about.
  • Seal on purpose. Clients prove from the axioms only. A fact that is true in the model but not stated as an axiom is a fact clients cannot use, as the happens-before entry shows, and that is usually what you want.
  • Measure. A theory in the standard library joins the proof benchmark (tools/bench/corpus.txt), so a slow axiom shows up as a resource-count regression.

docs.title: A tour of Pia
docs.text:
This tour covers the language as piac implements it today. Every example on this page is a complete program, and the test suite proves each one with piac --verify. The last section shows the parts of the language that are designed but not built yet, and those examples are marked as such.

Pia's syntax is close to OCaml. Comments are (* ... *), which nest, and \ comments to the end of a line. (** ... *) is a doc comment. The compiler keeps every comment, so metaprograms and your editor can read them (Comments and literate programs).

docs.title: Bindings and functions
docs.text:
let is the only way to define anything. A top-level let with parameters is a function. Each parameter has a type, and so does the result:

let width : u32 = 1024

let area (w : u32) (h : u16) : u64 = w * h

let pixels : u64 = area width 768

Function application is by juxtaposition, as in OCaml: area width 768. Functions are curried in the design, and every call passes all of its arguments for now.

Inside a function, let ... in binds a local value, and ; sequences expressions:

let sum_of_squares (x : u16) (y : u16) : u64 =
  let xx : u32 = x * x in
  let yy : u32 = y * y in
  xx + yy

let rec marks a recursive function. The prover sees the recursion, and a decreases clause gives the measure that will prove it terminates:

let rec gcd (a : u32) (b : u32) : u32
  decreases b
= if b = 0 then a else gcd b (a mod b)

docs.title: No shadowing
docs.text:
A binding may not reuse a name that is already in scope: a local, a parameter, a function, a type or a core builtin. So every name in a function means exactly one thing, for you and for the prover. Primes are ordinary identifier characters, and the compiler suggests them when you need a new name for a related value:

let next (x : u8) : u16
  ensures result = x + 1
= let x' : u16 = x in x' + 1

docs.title: Mutation
docs.text:
Bindings are immutable unless they say mutable. A mutable local is assigned with <-:

let count_up (n : u8) : u8 =
  let i : mutable u8 = 0 in
  if n > 10 then i <- 10 else i <- n;
  i

docs.title: Integers
docs.text:
Integers are bounded, and there are no implicit narrowing conversions. The types are u8 u16 u32 u64 i8 i16 i32 i64, usize and isize, bool, and range types such as int{0..255}. A range type is an integer whose bounds are part of its type, and it is stored in the smallest machine integer that holds the range.

A literal takes the type its context expects, and a suffix such as 42u8 fixes it. Digits group with ' or _, as in 100'000 or 0xFFFF'FFFF. min t and max t are the bounds of an integer type, as literals, so max u16 is 65'535 and a contract never needs to spell it out. Widening is implicit and always safe. Narrowing is a goal: it must be proved to fit.

let widen (x : u8) : u32 = x

let clamp_byte (x : u32) : u8 = if x < 256 then x else 255

The narrowing in clamp_byte is proved by the branch it is on.

Ranges carry facts the prover uses for free. Here the index can never be out of bounds, and the divisor can never be zero, because the parameter types say so. A bound on one value belongs in its type rather than in a requires clause, so that it travels with the value (Idiomatic Pia):

let lookup (lut : [u8; 256]) (i : int{0..255}) : u8 = lut.[i]

let per_tile (n : u32) (tile : int{1..64}) : u32 = n / tile

docs.title: Overflow is explicit
docs.text:
By default an arithmetic result must be proved to fit its type: this is @overflow(proof). The other modes give overflow a defined meaning, and then there is nothing to prove:

Mode On overflow @overflow(proof) (default) cannot happen: the compiler proves it @overflow(wrap) wraps around, modulo the size of the type @overflow(saturate) clamps to the type's minimum or maximum @overflow(trap) stops the program

The mode goes after the result type and applies to the function's arithmetic. The operators +| and -| saturate whatever the mode is.

let add_px (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 @overflow(saturate)
  ensures result >= a && result >= b
= a + b

let tick (x : u8) : u8 @overflow(wrap)
  ensures x = 255 ==> result = 0
= x + 1

let brighten (p : u8) : u8 = p +| 40

Wrapping and saturating arithmetic are modelled exactly, so the postconditions above are proved too. In loops, LLVM vectorises saturating arithmetic into NEON's saturating instructions, such as uqadd.

docs.title: Floats
docs.text:
f32 and f64 are IEEE 754 floats, and strict: each operation is rounded once, to nearest, a * b + c is two roundings rather than a fused multiply-add, and subnormals are kept, so a result is the same bit for bit as C's built with -ffp-contract=off. A float literal has a decimal point or an exponent, and takes the float type its context expects, or a suffix such as 0.5f32. An integer literal is never a float: write 2.0, not 2.

Floats never mix with integers implicitly. A type applied to a value converts it: f32 n rounds an integer to the nearest float, f64 x widens an f32, and i32 x truncates a float toward zero. Truncating is a goal, since C leaves it undefined for a NaN or a value out of range, so the range is stated where the float comes from. to_bits x and from_bits u are the IEEE encoding as a u32 or u64.

let mean (xs : [f32]) : f32
  requires len xs > 0
=
  let s : mutable f32 = 0.0 in
  for i in 0..len xs do s <- s + xs.[i] done;
  s / f32 (len xs)

let to_byte (x : f64) : u8
  requires -1.0 < x && x < 256.0
= u8 x

let abs32 (x : f32) : f32 = from_bits (to_bits x & 2147483647)

The prover sees a float as its bits. Comparisons are exactly IEEE's, so it knows a NaN is unordered and -0.0 = 0.0, which is what proves u8 x fits in to_byte. What + and * compute is not modelled yet, so a goal that depends on a sum's value fails rather than being proved wrongly; proving float kernels against real-valued specifications, with their rounding error, is ADR 0038, still to come.

docs.title: Arrays and slices
docs.text:
[T; n] is an array of a fixed length n, and [T] is a slice whose length is known at run time as len xs. Both are indexed with xs.[i], and every index is a goal: 0 <= i < len xs.

let first (xs : [i32; 4]) : i32 = xs.[0]

let last (xs : [u8]) : u8
  requires len xs > 0
= xs.[len xs - 1]

xs.[a .. b] is a slice of elements a up to but not including b. It is a view, not a copy: it shares the buffer's storage, so a function that writes a slice writes that part of the buffer, and the verifier knows the rest is unchanged. Its bounds are a goal, 0 <= a <= b <= len xs. An array also passes where a slice is expected, as a slice of all of it.

let fill (dst : out mutable [u8]) (v : u8) : unit =
  for i in 0..len dst do dst.[i] <- v done

let clear_tail (xs : out mutable [u8]) (n : usize) : unit
  requires n <= len xs
= fill (xs.[n .. len xs]) 0

An array literal [a; b; c] gives an array its values. At the top level it is a constant table in read-only data, and the verifier knows every value in it:

let squares : [u16; 4] = [0; 1; 4; 9]

let square (i : int{0..3}) : u16
  ensures result = i * i
= squares.[i]

Constant data cannot be passed to an out or inout parameter. For now the elements must be integer literals.

Arrays are values, so a function can return one. The caller makes room for it, and the result is a copy, never storage the callee owned:

let reversed (xs : [u8; 4]) : [u8; 4]
  ensures forall (i in 0 .. 4). result.[i] = xs.[3 - i]
= let r : mutable [u8; 4] = [0; 0; 0; 0] in
  for i in 0 .. 4
    invariant forall (j in 0 .. i). r.[j] = xs.[3 - j]
  do r.[i] <- xs.[3 - i] done;
  r

let first_of_reversed (xs : [u8; 4]) : u8
  ensures result = xs.[3]
= let r = reversed xs in r.[0]

The caller sees only reversed's contract, and that is enough for first_of_reversed.

abort () stops the program. Its precondition is false, so every abort is a goal that it is never reached: it marks a case the contracts rule out.

docs.title: Parameter modifiers
docs.text:
Parameters say how a function uses what it is given, on three axes, so a function's signature tells callers and the prover everything about its effects:

Axis Options Default Ownership borrowed, moved borrowed Access in, out, inout in Modifiability fixed, mutable fixed

The default is a read-only borrow. Writing to a buffer requires out or inout, and mutable:

let swap (xs : borrowed inout mutable [u8; 2]) : unit
  ensures xs.[0] = old (xs.[1]) && xs.[1] = old (xs.[0])
= let t = xs.[0] in xs.[0] <- xs.[1]; xs.[1] <- t

old e in a postcondition is the value of e when the function was called.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Types are values in Pia, so a record type is bound with let like anything else. Records are values too: they can be built, passed, returned and copied.

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 }

let opaque (p : pixel) : pixel
  ensures result.a = 255 && result.r = p.r
= { r = p.r; g = p.g; b = p.b; a = 255 }

let luma (p : pixel) : u16 = p.r + p.g + p.b

let byte = u8 gives another name to a type: a type is a value, so a let can name it. type always makes a new type, so let length = type u32 is a type of its own, which never mixes with a u32 or with another type over one. Every conversion is written, by applying a type to a value: length 5 makes a length, and u32 l takes one apart. The bounds of the type underneath carry over, and a length proves as the number it holds, at no cost:

let length = type u32

let area (w : length) (h : length) : u64
  requires u32 w * u32 h <= max u32
= u32 w * u32 h

let longer (a : length) (b : length) : length
  ensures u32 result >= u32 a
= if u32 a >= u32 b then a else b

A length has no operators of its own, so w * h is an error rather than a length. Each family of operators is opted into with a derive (ADR 0064): ord compares, add gives + and - between two lengths, scale gives *, / and % by a u32 on the right, and bounds gives the constants min_length and max_length. Each is stated in terms of the numbers underneath, and requires that its result fits, so overflow stays the caller's goal:

let span = type u32 @derive(eq, ord, add, scale, bounds)

let total (a : span) (b : span) : span
  requires u32 a <= 1000 && u32 b <= 1000
  ensures u32 result = u32 a + u32 b
= a + b

let wider (a : span) (b : span) : span
  ensures u32 result >= u32 a
= if a < b then b else a

a * a is still an error, since a length times a length is an area: a program writes that function itself.

Two derives come from library modules, for programs that import them: @derive(hash) from Pia.Core.Hash, so hash_all<span> works and a span hashes as the u32 it holds, and @derive(json) from Pia.Text.Json.Derive, which writes and reads a span as the bare JSON number, 5, not an object.

A field of a mutable record can be assigned:

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 }

let without_red (p : pixel) : pixel
  ensures result.r = 0 && result.g = p.g
= let q : mutable pixel = p in
  q.r <- 0;
  q

Records have no built-in equality. @derive(eq) generates it, as a function with a postcondition that says what it means, so callers can prove things about p = q:

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8 } @derive(eq)

let same (p : pixel) (q : pixel) : bool
  ensures result ==> p.r = q.r
= p = q

A record can carry an invariant over its fields, written where after its closing brace. Every value of the type keeps it: a function may assume it of each parameter, and must prove it of its result and of each out or inout parameter it hands back, so no function restates it and none can break it. Here width cannot underflow, and widen keeps lo <= hi:

let span = type { lo : u32; hi : u32 } where lo <= hi

let width (s : span) : u32 = s.hi - s.lo

let widen (s : inout mutable span) : unit
  requires s.hi < max u32
= s.hi <- s.hi + 1

A field can also carry a refinement of its own, v : u8 where v <= 100, which the record's invariant may rely on. The verifier has the details.

Arrays and slices can hold records. The compiler stores them as one buffer per field, so a loop over one field reads contiguous memory and vectorises:

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 }

let set_alpha (xs : inout mutable [pixel]) (i : usize) (v : u8) : unit
  requires i < len xs
  ensures xs.[i].a = v && xs.[i].r = old xs.[i].r
= xs.[i].a <- v

docs.title: Variants and match
docs.text:
A variant type lists its constructors, each with at most one payload. match takes a value apart. Its arms must cover every constructor, or end with _, and an arm that can never be reached is an error. The verifier knows which constructor built a value, so a match on a known constructor picks its arm:

let opt = type | None | Some of u32

let get_or (o : opt) (d : u32) : u32 =
  match o with
  | Some x -> x
  | None -> d

let roundtrip (x : u32) : u32
  ensures result = x
= match Some x with
  | Some y -> y
  | None -> 0

A payload's type can be an integer, bool, a record, another variant or unit. Arrays and slices inside a variant are not supported yet. Patterns are a constructor with a name or _ for its payload, () for a unit payload, a name that matches anything, or _.

docs.title: Recursive types
docs.text:
A type that refers to itself is declared let rec, and every type in a cycle of types that refer to each other must be. Each recursive occurrence sits inside an indirection, a box or a vec, so every type has a size, and at least one constructor must build a value without already having one (ADR 0047). Here a box is a record holding a slot, a slice of one element, as Pia.Mem.Box's does:

let box = let (t : type) => type { slot : [t] }

let rec tree = type
  | Leaf
  | Node of { left : box tree; key : u32; right : box tree }

(* The keys in a tree, capped at a million. *)
let rec total (t : tree) : int{0..1000000} =
  match t with
  | Leaf -> 0
  | Node n ->
    let l = if len n.left.slot = 1 then total n.left.slot.[0] else 0 in
    let r = if len n.right.slot = 1 then total n.right.slot.[0] else 0 in
    let lr : int{0..2000000} = l + r in
    if n.key <= 1000000 && lr <= 1000000 - n.key then lr + n.key else 1000000

total has no decreases: each call is on a value its argument holds, so the recursion is structural, and the verifier proves it ends:

$ piac --verify tree.pia
tree.pia:12:47: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
tree.pia:12:41: proved: the recursion terminates: 't' is smaller in each recursive call [smt]
tree.pia:13:48: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
tree.pia:13:42: proved: the recursion terminates: 't' is smaller in each recursive call [smt]
tree.pia:14:34: proved: '+' does not overflow int{0..2000000} [intervals]
tree.pia:15:42: proved: '-' does not overflow u32 [smt]
tree.pia:15:58: proved: '+' does not overflow u32 [smt]
tree.pia:9:3: proved: the value fits in int{0..1000000} [smt]
8 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Other recursion takes a measure, which may be depth t or size t, spec-only ints that are smaller for a value's parts than for the value. The verifier treats a recursive value as an SMT datatype, so a goal knows which constructor built a value and what it holds. Forgetting rec is an error that says so:

let box = let (t : type) => type { slot : [t] }
let chain = type | End | Link of box chain

$ piac --verify chain.pia
chain.pia:2:1: error: 'chain' refers to itself; declare it 'let rec chain = ...' (ADR 0047)
  let chain = type | End | Link of box chain
  ^

A recursive value compiles to a struct of its tag and its constructors' payloads, with a box's slot as a pointer and a length into the memory its allocator lent. Building a node allocates its boxes explicitly, through its allocator, so every allocation is visible and can fail where it is made. Equality on recursive values, @derive(eq) for them, and dropping one that an allocator frees block by block come later.

docs.title: Generics
docs.text:
A generic type is a function from types to a type, and a generic function takes type parameters, written (t : type), before its other parameters. Each use names concrete types: option u8 is an instance of option, and a call of unwrap_or with an option u16 calls its instance unwrap_or<u16>. Every instance is generated and proved on its own, so each goal is about concrete types. As with any call, a caller knows only what the instance's contract says, so same proves from id's ensures:

let option = let (t : type) => type | None | Some of t
let result = let (t : type) (e : type) => type | Ok of t | Err of e
let oom = type | OutOfMemory

let unwrap_or (t : type) (o : option t) (d : t) : t =
  match o with
  | Some v -> v
  | None -> d

let first (v : u16) : u16 = unwrap_or (Some v) 0

let id (t : type) (x : t) : t
  ensures result = x
= x

let same (v : u8) : u8
  ensures result = v
= id v

let reserve (n : usize) : result unit oom =
  if n > 4096 then Err OutOfMemory else Ok ()

The type arguments are deduced. A constructor takes its instance from the type it is expected to have, as Err OutOfMemory does from reserve's result, or else from its payload, as Some v does. A call takes them from its arguments, then from the type it is expected to have. To force a choice, give them: unwrap_or<u16> (Some v) 0, or by name, unwrap_or<t = u16>. A generic function needs its return type written, and recursive generic types, such as a list, are not supported yet.

A generic type can also take values, written (n : usize) beside its type parameters, so a length is part of the type. block u8 4 and block u8 5 are different types. Inside the type, the parameter can be an array's length, an argument to another type, or a name in an invariant, so row 8 r below promises a slice of exactly eight bytes to every function that takes one (ADR 0074). An argument is an integer literal for now. A function can be generic over one: a name in a value parameter's place that no parameter declares, n in (b : block t n), is deduced from the argument like a type parameter, and in the body and contracts it is the argument's value. Each instance is proved on its own.

A value parameter can also be a shape, (s : shape): a list of extents such as [4; 4], whose length is its rank, so one type covers vectors, matrices and every other rank. In the body, and in a function generic over it, s is a constant [usize; r], so len s is the rank and s.[i] an extent. A function names the extents it needs, [m; k], or the whole shape, s:

let grid = let (s : shape) (r : region) => type {
  data : borrowed(r) [u8]
} where len s = 2 && len data = s.[0] * s.[1]

let corner (r : region) (g : grid [4; 4] r) : u8 = g.data.[15]

let first (r : region) (g : grid [m; k] r) : u8
  requires 0 < m && 0 < k
= g.data.[0]

let cells (r : region) (g : grid s r) : usize
  ensures result = s.[0] * s.[1]
= len g.data

A record can also say what it is in MLIR. @lower("memref<$s x i8>", data) after grid's invariant makes each value of it a memref view of its bytes, 4 x 4 for grid [4; 4] r, where $s is the shape and i8 is how MLIR spells a byte. A function's own @lower that splices a grid then works on that view, as in linalg.matmul ins($a, $b : $a.type, $b.type) outs($c : $c.type). The Pia definition is still what the verifier reasons about. This is how a library type such as a tensor reaches MLIR without a new primitive (codegen.md, ADR 0074).

let block = let (t : type) (n : usize) => type { cells : [t; n] }

let top (b : block u8 4) : u8 = b.cells.[3]

let row = let (n : usize) (r : region) => type {
  data : borrowed(r) [u8]
} where len data = n

let last (r : region) (v : row 8 r) : u8 = v.data.[7]

let size (t : type) (b : block t n) : usize
  ensures result = n
= len b.cells

let four (b : block u8 4) : usize
  ensures result = 4
= size b

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
A concept says what a type must provide. It is a metaprogram that returns a signature: each requirement is a function a type must have, a law is a lemma every type must prove, and include brings in another concept. A constraint on a type parameter, (t : type where Ord t), names one:

let meta Same (t : type) : concept = sig
  let same : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
  let lemma reflexive (a : t) ensures same a a
end

let meta Ord (t : type) : concept = sig
  include Same t
  let less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
  let lemma irreflexive (a : t) ensures less a a = false
end

let same (a : u8) (b : u8) : bool
  ensures result <==> a = b
= (a = b)

let less (a : u8) (b : u8) : bool
  ensures result <==> a < b
= (a < b)

let max (t : type where Ord t) (a : t) (b : t) : t =
  if less a b then b else a

let biggest (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = max a b

A type meets a concept when a function with each requirement's name and exact type is in scope, so u8 meets Ord through the two functions above. Each law is then proved for u8, from those functions' contracts. A call with a type that does not meet a constraint is an error that says what is missing: bool does not meet Ord: no function 'same : bool -> bool -> bool' (from 'include Same'). A generic body may use only what its constraints promise, and that is checked where the generic is written: with (t : type where Same t), a call less a b is an error that suggests constraining t by Ord t, even if no caller has used the generic yet.

An adapter supplies a concept's requirements for a type that does not meet it, or meets it in a way a caller does not want. Its functions are reached only through it, never by their own names:

let meta Same (t : type) : concept = sig
  let same : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
  let lemma reflexive (a : t) ensures same a a
end

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8 }

let adapter by_red : Same pixel = struct
  let same (p : pixel) (q : pixel) : bool
    ensures result <==> p.r = q.r
  = (p.r = q.r)
end

let alike (t : type where Same t) (a : t) (b : t) : bool = same a b

let red_alike (p : pixel) (q : pixel) : bool = alike p q

A type that meets a concept directly uses its own functions. An adapter is used when the call names it, as in alike<Same = by_red> p q, or when it is the only way the type meets the concept, as here. Its laws are proved about its own functions. Two adapters for the same concept and type, with neither named, are an error that names both.

Functions may share a name when their parameter types differ. They form an overload set, and each call picks the one that fits its arguments best: an exact type beats a conversion, and a function that is not generic beats a generic one. A generic overload whose type arguments do not meet its constraints drops out of the call, so it is only chosen for the types it can serve. Overloads with the same parameter types are told apart by their preconditions, and each call gets the most specific one whose precondition is proved where it is made. The choice is made at compile time, from proofs, and never adds a test at run time:

let pick (x : u8) : u8
  ensures result = 0
= 0

let pick (x : u8) : u8
  requires x < 10
  ensures result = 1
= 1

let by_branch (x : u8) : u8
  ensures (x < 10 ==> result = 1) && (x >= 10 ==> result = 0)
= if x < 10 then pick x else pick x

Their requires clauses must be ordered, each overload's including every clause of a less specific one, so the most specific is always well defined. Between two generics that both fit, the one whose parameter types are an instance of the other's wins (pair t t over pair a b), and then the one whose constraints entail the other's: a rank for Ord t beats a rank for Same t when the type meets both, because Ord includes Same. Two concepts that require the same functions and state no laws entail each other, whatever their names, so two overloads that differ only by them are an error at the second.

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
if ... then ... else is an expression. &&, || and ==> short-circuit, so a guard protects what follows it:

let starts_with_zero (xs : [u8]) : bool = len xs > 0 && xs.[0] = 0

for i in lo..hi do ... done loops over a half-open range, optionally with step. while c do ... done loops while c holds, and can carry an invariant and a decreases measure:

let add_rows (a : [u8]) (b : [u8]) (dst : out mutable [u8]) : unit
  requires len a = len dst && len b = len dst
= for i in 0..len dst do dst.[i] <- a.[i] +| b.[i] done

let find (xs : [i32]) (x : i32) : usize =
  let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && xs.[i] <> x
    invariant i <= len xs
    decreases len xs - i
  do
    i <- i + 1
  done;
  i

The verifier proves each invariant on entry and after an arbitrary iteration, proves the goals in the body for every iteration where the invariant holds, and knows only the invariant after the loop. A while loop needs a decreases measure that is never negative and goes down, or its termination is not proved. Both loops above are proved, and add_rows becomes a NEON loop that adds 16 bytes at a time. The verifier has the details.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
A contract is a claim the compiler must prove. Pia has these today:

Clause Meaning requires p precondition: proved at every call, assumed in the body ensures p postcondition: proved at every return, assumed by callers; result is the returned value assert p proved at that point assume p assumed at that point, without proof; only in a file marked @trusted invariant p, decreases m on a loop: holds at every iteration, and the measure decreases old e in a postcondition, e as it was on entry forall (i in lo..hi). p, exists (i in lo..hi). p quantifiers, in contracts and assertions

Calls are checked against contracts, not bodies. A caller proves the callee's precondition and then knows its postcondition, so proofs stay local to each function:

let plus (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  requires a + b <= 255
  ensures result = a + b
= a + b

let plus3 (a : u8) (b : u8) (c : u8) : u8
  requires a + b + c <= 255
  ensures result = a + b + c
= plus (plus a b) c

Arithmetic inside a contract is exact mathematics, so a contract can say a + b without worrying that it overflows:

let avg (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  ensures 2 * result <= a + b
= (a +| b) / 2

let below (xs : [u8]) (lim : u8) : bool
  requires forall (i in 0..len xs). xs.[i] < lim
  ensures len xs > 0 ==> xs.[0] < lim
= true

docs.title: Cost bounds
docs.text:
costs bounds what a function spends, and the bound is proved like any other contract (ADR 0062). Each bound names its counter: iterations counts the iterations of the function's loops, and calls its calls, each of which also adds the callee's own bound at its arguments. In an invariant, spent c is what the function has spent on c so far:

let find (xs : [u32]) (v : u32) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  costs iterations <= len xs
  costs calls <= 0
=
  let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && xs.[i] <> v
    invariant i <= len xs && spent iterations <= i && spent calls = 0
    decreases len xs - i
  do
    i <- i + 1
  done;
  i

let has (xs : [u32]) (v : u32) : bool
  costs iterations <= len xs
  costs calls <= 1
= find xs v < len xs

has proves its bounds from find's, without looking at its loop. A function that calls one with a loop and no bound cannot bound its own cost, and that is an error that names the callee.

docs.title: Function values
docs.text:
A nameless let is a function literal, a lambda: there is no fun keyword. A parameter with a function type, (p : u8 -> bool), takes a lambda or the name of a top-level function. Each call compiles to its own copy of the function with the argument called directly, so a lambda costs what writing its body in the loop would (ADR 0044).

A lambda's body is its definition: where it is passed, the verifier knows what it computes. So find's contract, which mentions p, means x > 3 at this call, and the lambda needs no contract of its own:

let find (xs : [u8]) (p : u8 -> bool) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  ensures result < len xs ==> p xs.[result]
= let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && p xs.[i] = false
    invariant i <= len xs
    decreases len xs - i
  do i <- i + 1 done;
  i

let first_big (xs : [u8]) : usize
  ensures result < len xs ==> xs.[result] > 3
= find xs (let (x : u8) => x > 3)

A function type can carry a contract that names its parameters and result. The function that takes it may call it wherever its requires holds and relies on its ensures, and every argument is proved to meet both. A lambda may also give a result type and contracts before its =>:

let apply_twice (x : u8) (f : (y : u8) -> u8 requires y < 200 ensures result > y) : u8
  requires x < 100
  ensures result > x
= let a = f x in
  if a < 200 then f a else a

let plus2 (x : u8) : u8
  requires x < 100
  ensures result > x
= apply_twice x (let (y : u8) : u8 requires y < 250 => y + 1)

A function object is any record or variant whose module defines apply for it. Applying it, g x, calls apply g x, and it can be passed wherever a function is expected, carrying state in its fields. Function, a standard concept, is what all of these meet, and a generic can say so itself, (f : type where Function f t bool). A name may have one overload that takes a value and one that takes a function: a lambda, a named function or a function object only fits the second, and anything else only the first.

let meta Eq (t : type) : concept = sig
  let same : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
end

let same (a : u8) (b : u8) : bool = (a = b)

let find (t : type where Eq t) (xs : [t]) (v : t) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
= let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && same xs.[i] v = false
    invariant i <= len xs
    decreases len xs - i
  do i <- i + 1 done;
  i

let find (t : type) (xs : [t]) (p : t -> bool) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  ensures result < len xs ==> p xs.[result]
= let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && p xs.[i] = false
    invariant i <= len xs
    decreases len xs - i
  do i <- i + 1 done;
  i

let below = type { lim : u8 }
let apply (g : below) (x : u8) : bool = (x < g.lim)

let where3 (xs : [u8]) : usize = find xs 3

let first_below (xs : [u8]) (lim : u8) : usize
  ensures result < len xs ==> xs.[result] < lim
= let b : below = { lim = lim } in
  find xs b

A lambda lists what it captures, in brackets after let, and says how: a bare name is copied when the lambda is made, borrowed x is a shared read-only loan, and inout x is an exclusive loan the lambda may write. A local the body uses but does not list is an error that suggests the three forms. While the lambda is live, a borrowed variable cannot be written, and a referenced one cannot be touched at all; its writes are seen after the lambda's last use. A lambda with an inout capture has an effect, so it is never called in a contract, and it can be passed only for a parameter whose function type is written (f : inout t -> unit). Each lambda has its own type, a record of its captures that meets Function, so passing one costs what passing its captures does, and its body is still known at the call:

let find (xs : [u8]) (p : u8 -> bool) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  ensures result < len xs ==> p xs.[result]
= let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && p xs.[i] = false
    invariant i <= len xs
    decreases len xs - i
  do i <- i + 1 done;
  i

let first_between (xs : [u8]) (lo : u8) (hi : u8) : usize
  ensures result < len xs ==> lo <= xs.[result] && xs.[result] <= hi
= find xs (let [lo, hi] (x : u8) => lo <= x && x <= hi)

let for_each (xs : [u8]) (f : inout u8 -> unit) : unit =
  for i in 0 .. len xs do f xs.[i] done

let count_small (xs : [u8]) : usize =
  let n : mutable usize = 0 in
  for_each xs (let [inout n] (x : u8) : unit =>
    if x < 10 && n < 65535 then n <- n + 1 else ());
  n

A lambda's parameter types may be left out where it is passed: they come from the parameter's function type, once the other arguments have fixed its type parameters, so find xs (let (x) => x > 3) with xs : [u8] makes x a u8. A typed lambda fixes them itself. A let of a lambda with untyped parameters and no captures is generic, like a C++ auto lambda: each use is an instance, proved on its own. A lambda can also take type parameters with constraints, which is proved once over them. A lambda's result type, when not written, comes from its body:

let meta Ord (t : type) : concept = sig
  let less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
end

let less (a : u8) (b : u8) : bool = (a < b)

let both_small (a : u8) (b : u16) : bool =
  let small = let (v) => v < 100 in
  small a && small b

let smaller (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 =
  let min = let (t : type where Ord t) (x : t) (y : t) : t =>
    if less y x then y else x in
  min a b

A higher-order function can require a law of its function argument, such as requires Pia.Fn.strict_weak_order less on a sort. Pia.Fn defines the laws as spec functions; the function assumes the law, and each caller proves it for its argument, which for a lambda over a small type is a bit-vector fact.

A function with parameters left is a value: below lim passes a lambda of the rest, capturing lim. A function whose result is written as a function type returns the closure its body makes, and a lambda can own what it captures with [moved t], after which the closure is dropped like a record holding it:

let below (lim : u8) (x : u8) : bool = (x < lim)

let adder (n : u8) : u8 -> u8 = let [n] (x : u8) : u8 => x +| n

let compose (f : u8 -> u8) (g : u8 -> u8) : u8 -> u8 =
  let [f, g] (x : u8) : u8 => f (g x)

let five (x : u8) : u8
  requires x < 100
  ensures result = x + 5
= let add5 = adder 5 in add5 x

let small (x : u8) : bool = let is_small = below 9 in is_small x

A top-level function is a value too, and a let of a function type holds a reference to it (ADR 0071). There is no address operator: the name is the value, and a reference can be copied but never makes a copy of the function. When the arrow has a contract, the function is proved against it once, where the reference is made, and every call through the reference sees only the arrow's contract, so grow below knows result > x but not that h y is y + 1:

let succ (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 255 ensures result = x + 1 = (x + 1)

let half (x : u8) : u8 = x / 2

let grow (y : u8) : u8 requires y < 10 ensures result > y =
  let h : (x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 100 ensures result > x = succ in
  h y

let quarter (x : u8) : u8 =
  let g : u8 -> u8 = half in
  g (g x)

A reference is fixed, like every binding, unless it is mutable. A mutable reference is rebound with <-, each function bound to it is proved against the arrow where it is bound, and a call through it is an indirect call that sees only the arrow's contract, whichever function it holds:

let succ (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 255 ensures result = x + 1 = (x + 1)

let twice (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 128 ensures result = x + x = (x + x)

let pick (op : u8) (y : u8) : u8 requires y < 100 ensures result >= y =
  let h : mutable ((x : u8) -> u8) requires x < 100 ensures result >= x = succ in
  if op = 2 then h <- twice else ();
  h y

The parentheses make mutable the reference's, not its parameter's. A stored reference takes and returns integers, bools and floats for now; copies of a mutable reference, references in records and buffers, and references passed to C come later.

docs.title: Parallel loops
docs.text:
spread is a for loop whose iterations run at the same time, on every core (ADR 0060). It is proved one iteration at a time, with one more goal at every access to a buffer the body writes: the iteration owns that cell. By default iteration i owns cell i; @owns(buf, owner) says iteration b owns the cells c with owner.[c] = b instead. No two iterations own a cell, so a proved spread has no data race:

let brighten (px : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) : unit =
  spread i in 0 .. len px do
    if px.[i] < 200 then px.[i] <- px.[i] + 50 else px.[i] <- 255
  done

let clear_basins (label : [usize]) (v : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) (nb : usize) : unit
  requires len label = len v
= spread b in 0 .. nb @owns(v, label) do
    for c in 0 .. len v do
      if label.[c] = b then v.[c] <- 0 else ()
    done
  done

A body that reads a cell another iteration writes is a race, and a failed goal:

let blur (v : borrowed inout mutable [u32]) : unit
  requires len v >= 2
= spread i in 1 .. len v do v.[i] <- v.[i - 1] done

$ piac --verify blur.pia
blur.pia:3:29: proved: the iteration owns the cell it writes in 'v' (c = i) [smt]
blur.pia:3:43: proved: '-' does not overflow usize [smt]
blur.pia:3:38: failed: the iteration owns the cell it reads in 'v' (c = i)
...
4 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

A spread whose iteration i writes only cell i can run on the GPU instead: @place(gpu) after its range moves the body into a GPU kernel, and the proof stays the same. A placed spread can fail at run time, if there is no GPU or it runs out of memory, so it is a result the caller handles (D8 directions and the picture on the GPU, ADR 0068).

docs.title: Metaprograms
docs.text:
A metaprogram is a function marked let meta that runs at compile time. It takes and returns values, and code is one kind of value: `( ... ) quotes code, and $x splices a value into it. Whatever a metaprogram produces is type checked and proved like code you wrote.

Pia has no built-in operators. Each one is a metaprogram that gives a symbol a precedence and expands it to a function call. The prelude defines the usual ones, such as let meta operator ( + ) : prec 6 left = let (a) (b) =>( add $a $b )`, and a program can add its own:

let meta operator ( ** ) : prec 8 right = let (a) (b) => `( pow $a $b )

let pow (a : u8) (b : int{0..1}) : u8 = if b = 0 then 1 else a

let times : u16 = 2 * 3 ** 1

A top-level call of a metaprogram is replaced by the items it returns, and @derive(x) on a type calls the metaprogram derive_x. Expansion runs to a fixed point, so a metaprogram can generate code that uses other metaprograms:

let meta make_byte () : item = `( let byte = u8 )

make_byte ()

let wide = type { v : byte; w : u8 } @derive(eq)

Quotes are hygienic: names a quote binds are renamed so they cannot capture yours, and free names in a quote refer to where the metaprogram is defined. Metaprograms describes the interpreter, its builtins and the expansion loop.

Metaprograms also write tests. G.cases f, from Pia.Test.Gen, reads f's parameter types and contract and writes, for each combination of boundary values its requires allows, a lemma that some result can meet f's ensures there and a lemma that f does. A contract that no result can meet, such as ensures result = a + b on a u8 result, fails as a specification failure at the inputs that break it (tests from contracts).

docs.title: Comments and literate programs
docs.text:
Comments are part of the program. The compiler attaches each one to the code it describes, and a doc comment, (** ... *), is the documentation that hovering over a name shows in your editor:

(** The number of elements in one SIMD tile. *)
let tile : u32 = 16  \ a NEON register holds 16 bytes

\ Two `\` lines in a row are one comment.
\ Neither is a doc comment.
let tiles (n : int{0..4096}) : u32 = (n + 15) / 16

A metaprogram sees the comments too. listing () gives it the program's items, and doc x an item's documentation, so a project can insist on documenting everything:

(** Fails unless every top-level function has a doc comment. *)
let meta require_docs () : item =
  let check (item : expr) : unit =
    if kind item = "LetItem" && doc item = "" then
      fail (concat (name item) " has no doc comment")
    else () in
  fold (let (acc) (i) => check i) () (listing ())

(** Adds one, saturating at 255. *)
let bump (x : u8) : u8 = x +| 1

require_docs ()

A file named *.pia.md is a literate program: Markdown whose fenced pia blocks are the code. The prose before a block is the documentation of its first item, so the page you read and the program you prove are the same file. Metaprograms lists the builtins, and ADR 0029 the rules.

docs.title: Designed but not built yet
docs.text:
These parts of Pia are designed, and the parser reads most of them, but piac does not compile them yet. Language design has the full picture, Status the order they arrive in, and the feature index what is built.

dyn, a tagged value whose tags the prover can enumerate:

let shape = type
  | Circle of f32
  | Rect of { w : f32; h : f32 }

let describe (v : dyn) : str =
  match v with
  | (x : u8)  -> "byte"
  | (x : f32) -> "float"
  | _         -> "other"

Collectives and tiles. spread and @place(gpu) are built; collectives such as halo_exchange and all_reduce, which the compiler will prove every worker reaches in the same order, tiled grids, and @place(auto), which lets the compiler choose the device, are not:

let sediment_step (grid : borrowed in mutable tiled<cell, 256, 256, halo = 1>) : unit
  ensures total_mass grid = old (total_mass grid) - outflow grid
=
  halo_exchange grid;
  spread tile in grid @place(auto) do
    erode_and_deposit tile
  done;
  record_outflow grid (all_reduce add (map outflow_of grid))

More floats and SIMD vectors. f16, @finite to prove no NaN or infinity appears, three explicit ways to allow reassociation, and float kernels proved against real arithmetic (ADR 0038). vec<T, k> fixes a SIMD shape where auto-vectorisation is not enough. Refinement types such as { y : i32 | lo <= y && y <= hi } and where invariants on values.

docs.title: How verification works
docs.text: piac does not compile a program until it has proved it. This page explains what it proves, how, and how to read its reports. The verifier notes have the details of the encoding.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
A goal is a fact the compiler must establish. Some come from your contracts, and the rest come from the code itself:

Goal Raised by no overflow + - * /, the bit operators and shifts in the default @overflow(proof) mode, and every narrowing conversion nonzero divisor every /, % and mod shift amount every << and >>: the amount is at least 0 and less than the width of the shifted value in bounds every xs.[i], read or written, and every slice xs.[a .. b] precondition every call, for each of the callee's requires postcondition every return, for each ensures assertion every assert loop invariant and measure each loop's invariant and decreases

piac --verify prints one line per goal, in program order, then a summary. This function raises three goals, one for each operation:

let scale (xs : [u16]) (i : usize) (k : u16) : u32
  requires i < len xs
= xs.[i] * k / 2

$ piac --verify scale.pia
scale.pia:3:3: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
scale.pia:3:10: proved: '*' does not overflow u32 [intervals]
scale.pia:3:14: proved: the divisor is not zero [intervals]
scale.pia:3:14: proved: '/' does not overflow u32 [intervals]
4 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Every line has the source location, the claim, and the method that settled it. A goal is proved, failed (with a counterexample when the solver has one), or skipped when this version of the verifier cannot decide it yet.

docs.title: Intervals first, then Z3
docs.text:
Most goals are easy, and the verifier settles those without a solver. Each value has a range: its type, narrowed by constants, widening conversions and arithmetic. If a : u8 and b : u8, then a + b lies in [0, 510], so it fits in a u16. A goal proved this way is marked [intervals]:

let mac (a : u8) (b : u8) (c : u16) : u32 = a * b + c

$ piac --verify mac.pia
mac.pia:1:47: proved: '*' does not overflow u32 [intervals]
mac.pia:1:51: proved: '+' does not overflow u32 [intervals]
2 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Everything else goes to Z3. Each remaining goal becomes one query: the function's parameters with their types' ranges, its preconditions, the operations up to the goal, the goals before it (each is proved in its own query, so this is sound), and the negation of the goal. If Z3 finds that query unsatisfiable, no input can break the goal, and it is proved. If Z3 finds a model, the model is an input that breaks it: the counterexample.

The query is built in MLIR's smt dialect, exported to SMT-LIB and solved by Z3 inside the compiler. piac --dump-smt prints each one.

docs.title: Reading a counterexample
docs.text:
A counterexample names the function's parameters, using p.r for a field of a record and len xs for the length of a slice. For an overflow it adds the exact result that did not fit, and for an index the index and length.

let second (xs : [u8]) : u8 = xs.[1]

$ piac --verify bounds.pia
bounds.pia:1:31: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len xs = 0, index = 1, length = 0
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

An empty slice breaks the index, and so would any slice shorter than two elements. The fix is to say what the function needs, which moves the obligation to every caller:

let second (xs : [u8]) : u8
  requires len xs >= 2
= xs.[1]

docs.title: Contracts are the interface
docs.text:
When one function calls another, the verifier does not look inside the callee. It proves the callee's preconditions with the arguments substituted, then assumes its postconditions about the result. So each function is proved once, on its own, and a call is only as strong as the contract it calls.

let plus (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  requires a + b <= 255
  ensures result = a + b
= a + b

let plus3 (a : u8) (b : u8) (c : u8) : u8 = plus (plus a b) c

$ piac --verify calls.pia
calls.pia:4:5: proved: '+' does not overflow u8 [smt]
calls.pia:3:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
calls.pia:6:51: failed: the precondition of 'plus' holds
  counterexample: a = 255, b = 255, c = 0
calls.pia:6:45: failed: the precondition of 'plus' holds
  counterexample: a = 3, b = 252, c = 255
2 proved, 2 failed, 0 skipped

Both calls fail: the inner one when a + b is too big, and the outer one when the inner sum plus c is. Adding requires a + b + c <= 255 to plus3 proves both, the inner call from it directly and the outer one from it and plus's postcondition. This is the same assume-guarantee rule that modules will use across files, where a module is proved against the interfaces it imports and never against another module's code.

docs.title: Spec functions say what code means
docs.text:
A contract often needs to name an idea, such as "the larger of two values" or "how many elements equal v". A spec function does that. It is pure and total, it can be used in contracts, and the verifier knows its definition, so a caller can prove things about it. Codegen erases it.

let spec max (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = if a < b then b else a

let larger (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8
  ensures result = max a b
= if a > b then a else b

A recursive spec function needs a decreases measure, and each call is unfolded once. Facts that need induction, such as one about every prefix of an array, are lemmas: functions that return unit, proved once and erased from code, whose postcondition holds after each call. A recursive lemma is a proof by induction (verifier.md).

Specifications can also use two types that code cannot: int, an integer with no bounds, and real, an exact real number. Nothing in them overflows, so a contract can state what a machine type cannot hold, and the verifier hands them to Z3 as its Int and Real (verifier.md):

let lemma wide (a : u64) (b : u64) : unit
  ensures int a * int b <= 340282366920938463426481119284349108225
= ()

let halve (x : u8) : u8
  ensures real result <= real x / 2.0 && real x / 2.0 < real result + 1.0
= x / 2

docs.title: What it means for code generation
docs.text:
Codegen runs only when no goal has failed. It erases every contract and everything only contracts used, such as quantifiers and old. A proved index needs no bounds check and a proved addition needs no overflow check, so the machine code has none. Proved facts are also what lets LLVM vectorise loops safely.

A skipped goal is not proved either, so piac refuses it too, and piac --verify fails, unless --allow-unproved accepts that case. Today that means a while loop or a recursive call with no decreases measure; see Status.

docs.title: Where it goes next
docs.text:
• Presburger arithmetic for affine goals. Subscripts such as xs.[2*i + 1], aliasing between buffers and loop-carried dependence are linear integer problems. MLIR's Presburger library will decide them between intervals and Z3 (ADR 0020).
  • Modules and proof certificates. Each compiled module carries a certificate naming the hashes of the interfaces it was proved against, the Pia ABI version and the piac and Z3 versions that proved it, and pia-cert check refuses a stale or mismatched one (ADR 0010, ADR 0073). Advisories that revoke proofs made by a faulty piac come next.

docs.title: Verifier v0
docs.text:
Status: implemented in M5 (#6).

piac --verify file.pia lowers a program (irgen.md) and tries to prove every goal in it. It prints one line per goal and a summary, and exits with status 1 if any goal fails, or is skipped without --allow-unproved accepting it (the same flag as codegen, codegen.md):

overflow.pia:18:36: failed: '+' does not overflow u8
  counterexample: a = 248, b = 248, result = 496
overflow.pia:23:38: proved: '+' does not overflow u16 [intervals]
3 proved, 2 failed, 0 skipped

piac --verify --emit=mlir prints the IR as well, with the report on stderr. Every op whose goals all hold carries pia.proved = "intervals" or pia.proved = "smt". piac --dump-smt prints each solver query.

This follows the pipeline in architecture.md. The limits of v0 are listed at the end.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
The verifier walks each function in order and collects these goals:

Goal Raised by nooverflow pia.add, sub, mul, div, band, bor, bxor, shl, shr and narrowing pia.convert in overflow(proof) mode, which is the default. Also pia.to_index on a signed type (the index is not negative) and pia.from_index to a type narrower than usize. nonzero the divisor of pia.div and pia.rem, in every mode shift the amount of pia.shl and pia.shr lies in [0, w), w the storage width of the shifted value's type, in every mode inbounds pia.load and pia.store: 0 <= i < len. pia.slice: 0 <= lo <= hi <= len assert assert p, and pia.abort, whose claim is false: the path to it is impossible ensures each postcondition, at the return requires each of the callee's preconditions, at a call invariant each loop invariant, on entry and after each iteration (Loops) decreases each loop measure, and the function's measure at each recursive call (Termination) nonzero the step of a for loop, when it is not a constant emptyslot a pia.store marked pia.fills, which stores a box or other owning element: the element written over owns nothing (ADR 0048, section 6)

wrap, saturate and trap arithmetic raises no overflow goal. Wrapping and saturating results are modelled exactly. A trapping result is the exact value, since the program stops if it does not fit.

Specifications are exact. Ops that only feed contracts, such as the arithmetic in ensures 2 * result <= a + b, compute mathematical values and raise no goals. A contract can mention a + b without it overflowing, and len xs > 0 ==> xs.[0] < 10 can read xs.[0] under its guard.

Goals are kept in the verifier's own list, in walk order. The architecture describes materialising them as pia_contract.obligation ops, and that waits for the modular and incremental work, where obligations must outlive one run. The verifier already accepts obligation ops, and nonzero was added to the obligation kinds.

docs.title: Intervals first
docs.text:
Before calling the solver, the verifier tries the operand ranges. A value's range is its type, narrowed through widening conversions, constants and other proof-mode arithmetic: a * b + c on u8, u8 and u16 lies within [0, 130560], so it fits in u32. These goals are proved by intervals:

  • arithmetic whose exact range fits the result type
  • a divisor whose range excludes zero
  • a quotient of non-negative operands, which lies in [0, a]
  • an index into a fixed array whose range lies within the array, such as lut.[i] with i : int{0..255} and a 256-element lut (design.md)

Everything else goes to Z3.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
Each remaining goal becomes one query in the upstream smt dialect. The query is exported to SMT-LIB and decided by Z3 in-process (ADR 0011). It holds:

  • every parameter as a constant, with its type's range assumed
  • the function's ops up to the goal, as terms
  • every earlier goal as an assumption, which is sound because each is checked in its own query
  • the goal's negation under the path condition

unsat means the goal holds. With sat, the model is the counterexample.

Integers are bit-vectors. Every Pia integer is a signed bit-vector of one width per function: 68 bits, wide enough for the exact sum or difference of any values in [-2^63, 2^64 - 1]. A multiplication widens a function to 132 bits only when its exact product can need more than 66 bits, which the operands' types decide: u8 * u8 or 77 * r stays at 68, u64 * u64 or a product of usize values does not. The function's callees count too, since their contracts are encoded at each call. So one wide product slows only the functions that compute it, and the encoding never wraps by accident. Ranges are constraints on these bit-vectors. wrap reduces into the type with bvsmod, and saturate clamps with ite. index uses the same sort.

Booleans are SMT booleans. In contracts &&, || and ==> are already plain logic. In code they arrive as scf.if, which becomes ite.

Arrays and slices are SMT arrays from index to element. A fixed array's length is its type's. A slice's length is a constant in [0, 2^64 - 1]. pia.store produces a new array term. After an if, the two branches' arrays merge with ite. A constant array (pia.const_array) is a broadcast array with each value stored into it, so every element is known. A with_arena's region (pia.region) is a new broadcast array of zeros each time it is reached. A slice pia.slice has no array of its own: the verifier tracks its length and its offset in the root buffer, and reads and writes it there. A callee sees a slice argument as a fresh array, linked to the root by forall i. 0 <= i < len ==> v[i] = root[off + i]. A callee that writes it leaves a fresh root that equals the old one outside [off, off + len). Every loaded element is assumed to lie in its element type's range.

Control flow. The two branches of scf.if are walked under the condition and its negation, and the results merge with ite.

Atomics (ADR 0052, section 3). Another task may write a cell between any two accesses, so the verifier models nothing of the cell itself. Each atomic_load, and the old value each read-modify-write or atomic_cas returns, is a fresh value of the cell's type with its range assumed, so two loads of one cell may differ. atomic_cas succeeded exactly when its old value equals expected, which needs no extra fact, since that is the comparison the program makes. Stores and desired meet the cell's type through IRGen's conversion, which is a goal on a refined cell, so a refined cell's range holds across every task, one store at a time. An @proof add on a refined cell is the goal that the old value plus the operand stays in the range, for an old value about which only the range is known. A function with an atomic op never defines a value, so its callers use its contract, never its body.

Records are replaced with their fields before encoding (irgen.md). So a pixel parameter is four constants, and its counterexample values are named p.r, p.g, p.b and p.a.

Buffers of slices (ADR 0048) are an array of arrays with an array of their lengths. xs.[i] is element i's array and length; a write through it goes back into xs, and every other slice read from xs is read again from it, so two reads of one element agree. Distinct elements are distinct arrays, which is sound because only elements that own their slices can be written through. A callee that may write such a buffer leaves its contents and lengths unknown. A callee's contract and a spec function see the elements' lengths too: a spec function over a buffer of slices takes them as one more argument, so calls with different lengths are different applications, and old reads them as they were on entry. An if that replaces an element in one branch merges the lengths as it merges the contents (tests/verify/vec_boxes.pia). An element moved out (pia.moved_out) gets length zero and keeps its contents, which the moved value reads, so the element left behind owns nothing and every access through it is out of bounds. A store marked pia.fills is a goal, "the element written over owns nothing": the old element's length is zero. An out buffer of slices, whether a parameter or what a function marked pia.out_result lends, starts with every length zero.

Calls use the callee's contract, not its body. Its preconditions become goals, with the arguments substituted. The result is a fresh value of the result type. The callee's postconditions are assumed about it, with old reading the arguments as they were before the call. A call under old, as in ensures held m = old (held m), is the call the walk made with the parameters' entry values, so it means what the callee's contract says; this holds for a parameter holding a buffer too, when the callee's postconditions read no buffer's elements (tests/verify/old_calls.pia). A function with a spec-only result whose body only computes on its parameters, such as held (m : bump) : Alloc.heap = m.h, is unfolded at its callers like a pure function of scalars. A callee that returns one of its parameters unchanged gives a result equal to that argument. Repeated calls of a pure function — one in the module that writes no parameters and performs no atomic, foreign or unsafe operations — are bound to one uninterpreted function per result field, so mentioning a call several times in a contract (or across code and a contract) refers to the same value (tests/verify/pure_contract_calls.pia). Buffers the callee may write (out or inout) are fresh arrays afterwards. Recursion needs nothing special.

What the rule guarantees is proved in Lean, in tests/lean/CallRule.lean (checked by //tests/lean:call_rule_test). For code that runs, the rule is sound with no termination argument: every run that returns meets its contract. For a call that never runs, a lemma call or a call in a contract, it is sound only because each callee terminates, which is why a call within a cycle of the call graph is a termination goal (Termination). A caller's proof holds for every implementation of its callees that is verified against their contracts, and a weaker precondition with a stronger postcondition keeps it, which is what separate builds and the certificate check rely on. What the rule gives up is precision: a contract weaker than its body proves less than the body would. Within a module, a pure function of scalars is unfolded at its callers ("Pure functions of scalars" below), but an importer sees only its contract, so the same call can prove in its own module and fail in another. ADR 0076 (Proposed) exports such bodies so that a module boundary never changes what proves.

old e reads the function's arrays as they were on entry.

Quantifiers. forall (i in lo..hi). p becomes an SMT forall over the bound variable, (type range && lo <= i && i < hi) ==> p. exists conjoins the guard instead.

Division. Z3 bit-blasts division, and cannot show a mod b < b on 68-bit values, or (a / b) * b + a mod b = a on 32-bit ones, within its timeout. So beside each division the encoding states, when b is not zero, the facts of truncating division: (a / b) * b + a mod b = a; the remainder has the dividend's sign and -|b| < a mod b < |b|; the quotient lies between zero and a (or -a), is a or -a when b is 1 or -1, and is strictly inside when |b| >= 2; and for non-negative operands 0 <= a / b <= a and 0 <= a mod b < b. Inside a quantifier, where the operands may be bound variables, it does not. A goal whose query divides by a value that is not a constant is first tried with bvsdiv, bvsrem and bvmul as uninterpreted functions, in a Z3 context of its own and with a small budget (500,000 rlimit units): any function models an uninterpreted one, so unsat there is a proof, and goals that follow from the facts alone, such as a quotient fitting its type, are proved without bit-blasting a divider. Otherwise the exact query decides, and gives the counterexample. Bit-blasted dividers are also what makes a goal's cost vary between runs on different numbers of threads, so this keeps proof cost reproducible (ADR 0032).

Products. Bit-blasting is exact, but a 68- or 132-bit multiplier is a large circuit, and goals such as a <= b ==> a * c <= b * c, or a pixel index (y * w + x) * c + k < w * h * c, time out on it. So a quantifier-free nonlinear goal, one whose query multiplies two non-constant terms or divides by one, is next tried with Z3's int-blasting solver (ADR 0066). That solver is (then ackermannize_bv smt) with smt.bv.solver = 2, which reduces ground uninterpreted function applications and decides the bit-vector query as integer arithmetic. It runs in a context of its own, with a budget of 5,000,000 rlimit units. The translation is exact, so unsat is a proof, and on anything else the bit-blaster decides and gives the counterexample. Goals with a @solver strategy, theory axioms, assumes or quantifiers keep the bit-blaster. --verify-stats counts the goals proved this way as intblast=, and --no-int-blast turns the attempt off.

Timeouts. Each obligation is one Z3 query with two limits. The one that decides is --solver-rlimit=<n>, Z3's deterministic resource count, which does not depend on load or on the machine's speed; piac defaults to 1,200,000,000. --solver-timeout=<ms> is a wall-clock safety net, 600 seconds by default. A wall-clock limit alone would depend on load: a goal that proves in 5 seconds alone can time out while other goals and builds share the cores, and that is the normal case now that goals are solved in parallel. (pia repl and pia-lsp still use a wall-clock limit, --timeout-ms, since they answer interactively.) --solver-cost verifies like --verify and prints each proved SMT goal's resource count, as (cost N), so a limit can be chosen from measurements. --goal-times prints how long each proved goal took to solve, as (N ms). A slow proof can be cheap: its time may go into encoding the queries, not solving them, which the sum of these times shows. A goal the solver gives up on is reported as failed, with the reason, such as [the solver gave up: timeout] or [the solver gave up: max. resource limit exceeded]. The pia_object Bazel rule passes --solver-rlimit=1200000000, about 20 times the costliest goal in the repository (settle in docs/streams.pia.md, 56,923,063), and a 600-second timeout that serves only as a safety net, so whether a build proves its goals does not depend on load.

Counterexamples name the parameters, using the names IRGen records in the block arguments' locations, and slice lengths as len xs. They add the values that explain the goal: result for an overflow, index and length for bounds. Array contents are not shown yet.

docs.title: Parallel, sliced and cached proving
docs.text:
Build time is a benchmark (ADR 0032). Goals are listed and encoded in walk order on one thread, then the SMT queries are decided on a pool of threads, one per core unless --jobs=N says otherwise, each in its own Z3 context. The report keeps the walk order, and under an rlimit every goal has the same result on any number of threads.

Slicing cuts a query to the goal's cone of influence: the negated goal, and every assertion that shares a symbol with one already kept, transitively. A precondition about b stays out of a goal about x. An unsat slice proves the goal, since only hypotheses were dropped. Otherwise the whole query is solved again, so slicing never stops a goal from proving, and a counterexample always comes from the full query. By default it is automatic, and only in a function with a buffer of records, which ScalarizeRecords marks {pia.record_buffers}. There, a goal is sliced when the slice drops a whole declaration, a symbol the goal cannot reach: one buffer per field means a goal about xs.[3].a is asked alongside quantified facts about xs.g and xs.b that it never needs. Those facts make Z3's search grow quickly with the number of fields. Copying four-field records through a view costs 777 million resource units in full and 1.6 million sliced. --slice slices every goal whose slice is smaller, and --no-slice always solves the full query. Elsewhere slicing costs more than it saves: applied to every query that drops a declaration, it raises the streams demo from 269 million resource units to 395 million, and forcing it with --slice gives 392 million and 47 seconds on one thread, against 269 million and 33 seconds without. Smaller queries are not always easier for Z3, and a goal whose slice is satisfiable is solved twice. With the rule limited to buffers of records, every file in the benchmark (tools/bench) costs what it did before. The benchmark keeps measuring it.

Selecting goals. --verify-only=<spec> proves only the goals the spec selects, and can be repeated; a goal is proved if any spec selects it. piac takes one input file, and a second is an error, so a selection that a shell passed with a space before it, as zsh passes an unquoted variable, is reported rather than verifying the whole module (#376):

piac --verify-only=settle streams.pia.md          # one function
piac --verify-only=streams.pia.md streams.pia.md  # one module
piac --verify-only=edges.pia:41 edges.pia         # the goals on one line

Earlier goals are still assumed, as in a full run. Unselected goals are left out of the report, and a selective run never generates code.

Proof cache. --proof-cache=<dir> keeps a file per proved goal, named by the SHA-256 of the Z3 version, the rlimit and the query. A goal whose query is unchanged is not solved again, and calls are encoded from contracts, so editing a callee's body does not invalidate its callers. Failures are never cached. If an advisory revokes piac's Z3, every entry piac could read was made by that Z3, so it warns and neither reads nor writes the cache.

Statistics. --verify-stats prints one line to stderr, here for docs/streams.pia.md on one thread:

verify-stats: goals=243 unselected=0 intervals=21 skipped=0 solved=222 cached=0 sliced=0 unsliced=0 threads=1 cost=269094119 encode_ms=947 solve_ms=30213 ...

solved counts the queries sent to Z3, cached the goals the cache answered, sliced the queries slicing made smaller, unsliced the slices solved again in full, intblast the nonlinear goals Z3's int-blasting solver proved (--no-int-blast turns it off), and cost Z3's resource count over every query. The rest of the line splits the goals by where they came from (ADR 0037): type, type_smt and type_cost for goals the types of values raise (overflow and narrowing, bounds, divisors, shifts, exhaustiveness, out parameters), and contract, contract_smt and contract_cost for written ones (preconditions at calls, postconditions, invariants, measures, assertions, laws), with how many of each needed the solver and what they cost. After the report, a goal that cost a tenth of the rlimit or more gets a costly_goal warning (Idiomatic Pia). tools/bench/proof_bench.py runs these over the benchmark corpus on one thread and on every core, and CI fails when the cost of any corpus file grows by more than 10%. On pull requests CI proves each file once, on every core, in three shards on Linux (--passes=parallel, --shard=K/3); the nightly run proves on one thread too. Z3's resource count varies by about 1% from run to run, since some of Z3's hash tables depend on memory addresses, so the benchmark compares reports exactly and costs within 5% over tools/bench/baseline.json.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
A loop is cut at its invariants, so the verifier never unrolls it.

let sum_to (n : u16) : u32 =
  let s : mutable u32 = 0 in
  for i in 0..n invariant s <= i * 65535 do s <- s + i done;
  s
  1. On entry, each invariant is a goal, with the loop variable at its first value and the loop-carried values (s here) as they are before the loop.
  2. One arbitrary iteration is then walked. The loop variable and the loop-carried values are fresh, and so is every buffer the loop writes. A for loop's variable satisfies lo <= i < hi and is a whole number of steps from lo. The invariant is assumed where it is written, so the goals in the body, such as s + i not overflowing, are proved for every iteration where it holds. At the end of the body, each invariant is a goal again, for the next value of the loop variable and the values the body leaves.
  3. After the loop, what it computes and writes is fresh again, and only the invariant is assumed. A for loop's variable has then passed hi by less than one step, or equals lo if the loop never ran. A while loop's condition is also false.

The iteration's assumptions hold under a fresh guard in the path condition, so they say nothing about the code after the loop. A loop without an invariant still works, but nothing is known about its loop-carried values in the body or afterwards: without its invariant, s + i above could overflow.

A while loop's invariant is written before do and holds each time the condition is evaluated. The condition's own goals, such as the bounds of xs.[i] in while i < len xs && xs.[i] <> x, are proved in the iteration, under the invariant.

docs.title: Termination
docs.text:
A for loop always ends. A while loop ends when it has a measure, decreases m, that is never negative and goes down on each iteration. That is a decreases goal at the end of the body, m >= 0 && m' < m, where m' is the measure after the iteration. A function's decreases is checked the same way at each call of the function by itself: gcd b (a mod b) with decreases b needs b >= 0 and a mod b < b, under the path condition b <> 0.

A recursive call on a value of a recursive type needs no measure when it is structural: its first argument of a recursive type is a component of the parameter, as a name a match binds below the top is, or an element of a box or vec such a name holds (recursive types). Its goal, "the recursion terminates: 't' is smaller in each recursive call", is that the argument's depth is smaller than the parameter's.

Mutual recursion. Functions that call each other, directly or through others, form a cycle, and each call within the cycle is a termination goal too. A call is taken on its callee's contract, so without one, two lemmas that each call the other would "prove" ensures false, and since codegen erases lemmas and calls in contracts, nothing would ever run them to find out. When every function in the cycle has a measure, the goal at a call from f to g is "the measure of 'g' at the call is below the measure of 'f'": g's measure at the arguments is smaller than f's on entry, and f's is not negative. is_even and is_odd, each with decreases n and calling the other at n - 1, are proved. A cycle with a function that has no measure gets a skipped goal at each call within it, "'f' and 'g' call each other, and 'f' has no 'decreases' measure" (tests/verify/mutual_recursion.pia). A cycle never crosses modules, since an imported function is only its contract and imports form no cycles.

Any other while loop or recursive call with no measure gets a skipped goal ("the loop terminates", "the recursion terminates"). So piac --verify fails, and piac generates no code, unless --allow-unproved accepts it (codegen.md).

docs.title: Recursive types
docs.text:
A value of a let rec variant (ADR 0047) is a value of an SMT-LIB datatype: mutually recursive types and the types they hold are declared as one declare-datatypes, a generic one once per instance, and each constructor holds its payload's fields. A constructor, a match and its payload names are the datatype's constructor, tester and selectors, so the proof sees what a value was built from, as it does for a variant.

  • A buffer in a payload, such as a box's slot or a vec's items, holds what it held when the value was built: since box and vec own their contents uniquely, the proof sees a recursive value as a value, not as a heap. That holds while only the value owns the buffer, so a function that writes a buffer after building a value with it, or writes a buffer taken out of a value, is not verified: each of its goals is unproved, with that reason. Z3 does not decide datatypes whose constructors hold arrays well, so the field is a handle, an element of an uninterpreted sort, and the array is a function of the handle.
  • depth t and size t are spec-only ints, for decreases and other contracts.
