The verifier knows only that a depth is at least 0 and a size at least 1, and that a component's, including each element of a box or vec in the payload, is smaller than its holder's. That is what a measure needs; their exact values are not known.
  • Structural recursion is a decreases depth t on the function's first parameter of a recursive type (termination).

A counterexample shows a recursive value as its constructor and its payload's fields in order, Node {_, 7, 4294967295, _, 0}, where _ is a buffer (tests/verify/rec_types.pia, tests/verify/rec_aliasing.pia). Equality of recursive values, @derive(eq) and structural lemmas come with metaprograms over recursive types (step 4).

docs.title: Cost bounds
docs.text:
A function may bound what it spends on a counter with costs c <= e, after its other contracts (ADR 0062). Every clause names its counter: iterations counts each iteration of a loop in the function, and calls each call of a function that is not a spec function or a lemma. A function has at most one clause per counter, and each is proved on its own. A function without a clause is generated and proved exactly as before.

let find (xs : [u32]) (v : u32) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  costs iterations <= len xs
  costs calls <= 0
=
  let i : mutable usize = 0 in
  while i < len xs && xs.[i] <> v
    invariant i <= len xs
    invariant spent iterations <= i && spent calls = 0
    decreases len xs - i
  do
    i <- i + 1
  done;
  i

spent c is what the function has spent on c so far: 0 on entry, one more at the start of each iteration's body, and at each call one more on calls plus the callee's own bound on each counter, with its parameters bound to the call's arguments. IRGen keeps it as a mutable local, so it is threaded through ifs, && and ||, loops and ? like any other, and a loop havocs it: an invariant has to bound it, as spent iterations <= i does above. spent c may appear in loop invariants, asserts and lemma calls, and only for a counter the function bounds. At the end of the body, which every ? reaches as a branch, spent c <= e is a goal, "the cost on iterations is within its bound", reported with the contract goals at the clause. e is read at the parameters' entry values, so it takes no old.

A callee's bound. A callee with a clause for the counter contributes its bound at the call's arguments. A callee without one has a bound only if it has no loop and no recursion: the compiler adds up the calls its body makes, through any callees of its own, taking the larger branch of each if, and a C function (= extern) has 0. That bound is a constant, filled in once every function is made. Any other callee is an error at the call:

report.pia:15:3: error: 'wrapped' has no bound on iterations, so the cost of 'report' on iterations cannot be proved; add 'costs iterations <= ...' to 'wrapped', which calls 'total', which has a loop

A function with a clause that calls itself needs a decreases measure, since its own bound is then assumed at the call, as its ensures is.

Encoding. A count is a usize, a bit-vector like every machine integer, and adding to it saturates at 2^64 - 1, which no run reaches, so a bound below that is exact and the additions raise no goal. It is not the int that ADR 0062 first described: Z3 relates an int to a loop's machine integers through bv2int, and the invariant c = int i of a loop that adds one to an int c timed out at 20 seconds, where spent iterations <= i proves in under 100 ms. e is an integer at its own types, converted to usize, so n * m on u8 values keeps the function at 68 bits; an int bound is compared through int spent, which a caller cannot yet add to its own count. Codegen leaves the counter's arithmetic in place, with nothing reading it, and LLVM removes it, so find compiles to the same code with or without its clauses.

Loops in a costed function. Bounds multiply loop variables, as in spent iterations <= i + i * m for nested loops, and after the loop Z3 would bit-blast exit * m and n * m as two products it cannot tell are equal. So in a function with a cost clause, a for loop with a step of one also states exit = hi outright, unconditionally when the bounds' ranges say lo <= hi, as for 0..n. A product of two usize values still widens the function to 132 bits and is slow to prove: nested loops over two slices need a lemma that does the multiplication, which is step 2's business with Pia.Math.Log.

Not yet (ADR 0062's later steps): function counters such as less, cost clauses in interfaces, amortised bounds with old, and a spread in a function with a cost clause, which is an error. tests/verify/costs.pia has proved bounds and a failing one, and tests/irgen/cost_errors.pia and cost_bound_errors.pia the errors.

docs.title: Spec functions and lemmas
docs.text:
let spec f ... defines a spec function: pure and total, used to say what code means. Contracts, other spec functions and lemmas can call it. Code cannot, and codegen erases it. It cannot loop, write a buffer, abort, or call anything but spec functions and pure functions of scalars. A recursive one needs decreases, and spec functions cannot be mutually recursive yet. Its body is checked like any function's: its own goals, its ensures, and its measure at each recursive call. A spec function imported from another module's interface comes with its definition, which importers unfold, but its goals are proved once, in its own module, not again in each importer (ADR 0039).

To the solver, f is an uninterpreted function F with one argument per scalar parameter and two, the array and its length, per buffer. A call f a, wherever it is, is F a, with these facts:

  • F a is in the result type's range.
  • pre(a) ==> post(a, F a): f's postconditions, where its preconditions hold.
  • pre(a) ==> F a = body(a): the definition, unfolded once. A recursive call in the body is F again, with the two facts above but no definition. @fuel(n) on the return annotation unfolds n levels.

The definition is guarded by the precondition because termination is proved only where the precondition holds, so outside it the body could define F in terms of itself. Inside a quantifier, the facts for calls that mention the bound variables become hypotheses of the quantifier. A call that passes a view inside a quantifier is left uninterpreted, and so is a definition with a value the encoding cannot model.

A call in code to a spec function is a goal for its precondition, as for any call. In a contract, the call is checked the same way where it is walked, and is a plain term inside quantifiers and old.

let lemma f ... defines a lemma, which returns unit. It is proved once, like any function, and a call to it is a statement whose precondition is a goal and whose postcondition is assumed afterwards, by the usual rule for calls. Codegen erases lemmas and calls to them. An interface can list a lemma as let lemma f : (a : int) -> unit requires ... ensures ... (#305). The lemma is proved once, in its module. An importer calls it as M.f a, and that call works like a call to a local lemma: its precondition is a goal at the call, and its postcondition is assumed after it. The interface's contract must follow from the definition's, as for any function: the check calls the lemma, so it assumes what the lemma proved, by induction or otherwise. The interface and the definition must agree on which items are lemmas (tests/modules/lemma.pia). A recursive lemma with decreases is a proof by induction:

let spec count (xs : [u8]) (n : usize) (v : u8) : usize
  requires n <= len xs
  ensures result <= n
  decreases n
= if n = 0 then 0 else count xs (n - 1) v + (if xs.[n - 1] = v then 1 else 0)

let lemma split (xs : [u8]) (n : usize) (v : u8) (w : u8) : unit
  requires n <= len xs && v <> w
  ensures count xs n v + count xs n w <= n
  decreases n
= if n > 0 then split xs (n - 1) v w

One unfolding proves each step: the lemma's call for n - 1, plus count's definition at n. Without the lemma, a goal about every n needs more unfoldings than any fixed fuel gives.

Opaque spec functions (ADR 0063). A spec function marked @opaque keeps its definition out of every goal: a call f a still gets its result type's range and pre(a) ==> post(a, F a) from f's ensures, but not F a = body(a). f's own goals are unchanged. This is for a spec over a whole stream or table, whose unfolded body would otherwise sit in every goal of a loop that mentions it, including goals that never needed it. with f, g after a function's or lemma's contracts reveals f and g in its whole body, and the expression with f in e reveals f only in e. A revealed definition is a fact for every call met in the scope, and for the calls already met before it, such as one in the precondition; after the scope, a call with new arguments is opaque again. The intended pattern is to reveal in small step lemmas, never in the loop itself. An imported opaque function stays opaque, since the interface carries @opaque with its definition. A goal that fails while an opaque function was left unrevealed has the hint "'f' is opaque here; 'with f' may prove it". Codegen erases with (tests/verify/opaque.pia, tests/modules/opaque.pia).

let spec small (x : u8) : bool @opaque = x < 10

let shown (x : u8) : u8
  requires small x
  ensures result < 20
  with small
= x + x

Parameters of spec functions and lemmas cannot be out, inout or mutable. spec and lemma are keywords only between let (or let rec) and the name (grammar.md).

Pure functions of scalars. An ordinary function with scalar parameters and one scalar result, whose body has no loop, buffer access, abort or recursion, and calls only other such functions, always returns exactly what its body computes. A call to one, in a contract, a spec function or code, is its body's value where its precondition holds: with no precondition the call is the body's term itself, and with one it is if pre then body else F a. Since that needs no definition as a fact, it keeps its meaning inside an assumed forall, as in a callee's ensures forall (k in 0..result). p xs.[k] = false. A call in a contract to one without a precondition, whose arguments are loads, constants or other such calls, is specification like the arithmetic around it, so it may be guarded: result < len xs ==> p xs.[result] reads xs.[result] only where it is in bounds. This is what makes a lambda's body known where it is passed (ADR 0044): the lambda is a private function lambda@file.pia:line:col, and the specialisation of the higher-order function calls it. A function object's apply is one too once its record is split into fields, and so is a capturing lambda's, which unfolds at the call with the captured values (unless it reads a captured buffer), and so is a call of a generic proof's abstract function, a concept requirement such as same xs.[result] v in an ensures. So a generic's contract that names a concept function, such as ensures result = (if less b a then b else a) in min, means b < a at the u8 instance, where less is a < b, and a spec function over Ord t can call less (lex_from in lib/Pia/Core/Order.pia). A call to any other function in a contract is still an unknown value, constrained only by the callee's own ensures (tests/verify/pure_calls.pia). A call in a contract to a function with a precondition, such as a spec function, is needed only where its value can matter, so its precondition is a goal, and its postconditions are facts, under the short-circuit guard it sits behind: the right operand of a ==> b and of a && b where a holds, and of a || b where a does not. r < len xs ==> ok xs r checks ok's requires k < len xs only where r < len xs, as xs.[r] would be read there; ok xs r || r < len xs, with the call on the left, checks it everywhere (#282, tests/verify/contract_guards.pia). The guard is followed along single uses up to the contract; a call whose value is used twice, or which code reads, is checked unguarded.

Lemmas proved in Lean (ADR 0061). A lemma whose body is by lean T is proved by the Lean 4 theorem T instead of the solver. It states only requires and ensures, and callers use it like any lemma. piac --emit=lean translates its statement, ∀ params, requires → ensures, into a Lean Prop, together with the spec functions and record types it uses, over int and bool: a spec function is a def, an opaque constant outside its precondition, where Pia says nothing either, and ending by its decreases measure, and a record is a structure. The pia_lean_proof rule (tools/lean/lean.bzl) runs the pinned Lean release on the statements and the proofs, checks that T has the statement's type, and writes a receipt with the statement hash, the SHA-256 of the Lean text of the statement and of every definition it uses, and the axioms T depends on. piac --verify --lean-receipt=<file> reads receipts: the lemma's one goal, "the Lean theorem 'T' proves 'l'", is proved [lean] when a receipt has its current hash and only Lean's own axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), or, in a file marked @trusted, those of native_decide, which trusts Lean's compiler, and fails otherwise: [no receipt], [stale receipt] when the lemma or anything it uses has changed since, [axiom X], sorryAx included, or [native_decide] outside a @trusted file. Lean never runs in piac, the REPL or the language server. A proved Lean lemma is not trusted, but --trust-report lists it in a section of its own, with its theorem, toolchain, axioms and statement hash, since it rests on Lean's kernel and on piac's translation of the statement; --why names the goals that use it, and a native_decide proof is also a trusted item. The object's certificate records it as a proved lean line (abi.md). The translation types every literal as Int, so a term of literals is never a Nat, where 0 - 1 = 0. It translates only int, bool and records of them, with + - *, comparisons, the logical operators, if, let, record literals, fields and updates, calls, and quantifiers in a lemma's contracts; anything else is an --emit=lean error (tests/lean, tests/verify/by_lean.pia).

docs.title: Spec-only int and real
docs.text:
Two types exist only for specifications (ADR 0036, step 1):

  • int, an unbounded mathematical integer. Bare int is unbounded, and int{lo..hi} is still a range type: a range is written with its braces right after int, so the two spellings cannot be confused (grammar.md). The verifier encodes int as the SMT Int sort. An element of a slice read in a spec function's body keeps its type's range, as it does where code loads one: an element of a [u32] is between 0 and 2^32 - 1 there, so a sum of them as an int does not decrease.
  • real, a mathematical real number, encoded as the SMT Real sort. It is not a floating-point type.

They have +, -, *, unary - and the comparisons, and real also has /. All of it is exact, so nothing overflows and no nooverflow goal is raised. A real division raises a nonzero goal for its divisor where it is walked as code, such as in a spec function's body. An integer literal takes either type from the context, and an int literal may be larger than any machine type. A literal with a decimal point or an exponent, such as 0.5 or 1.0e3, is a real, read as an exact rational (1/2, 1000), unless a float is expected there: a suffix such as 0.5f32 makes it a float, which is not a real ("Floats" below).

Conversions are exact, so none raises a goal. int x turns any integer into an int, and an integer also widens to int wherever an int is expected, as a range type widens to a larger one. real x turns an integer or an int into a real. There is no conversion back: a value of a machine type cannot come from a specification.

let spec half (x : real) : real = x / 2.0

let lemma product (x : real) (y : real) : unit
  requires 0.0 <= x && x <= 1.5 && 0.0 <= y && y <= 2.0
  ensures x * y <= 3.0
= ()

let lemma wide (a : u64) (b : u64) : unit
  ensures int a * int b <= 340282366920938463426481119284349108225
= ()

let halve (x : u8) : u8
  ensures real result <= half (real x) && half (real x) < real result + 1.0
= x / 2

product is nonlinear, and Z3 decides it with its nonlinear real arithmetic; with x * y < 3.0 it fails with the counterexample x = 3/2, y = 2. A counterexample shows a real as a fraction, and an irrational value from a nonlinear model as a decimal approximation marked ~.

Spec-only. int and real may appear in spec functions, lemmas, contracts and quantifiers (forall (y : real). y * y >= 0.0), and in the arguments of a lemma call. Code may not compute with them. It may only store one in a spec-only place: a parameter, local or record field of a spec-only type, as in let steps : int = 10 or t.heap <- Alloc.take t.heap b (ADR 0041). The expression stored is checked as spec code, so it may call spec functions. A field of a buffer's records may be spec-only, as state is in a buffer of { slot : [u16]; state : int }: it is a buffer of its own, which the verifier sees and codegen erases, so C passes only the other fields (tests/verify/spec_buffers.pia, tests/codegen/spec_state.pia). A buffer whose elements are wholly spec-only, such as [int], is an error, since its length is in code; a spec local of fixed length, let spec sums : mutable [int; 9] = zeros, is not (Spec state). Any other expression of such a type in code is an error. let positive (x : u8) : bool = real x > 0.5 gives:

positive.pia:1:32: error: this expression has the spec-only type real; int and real can be used only in spec functions, lemmas, contracts and quantifiers, not in code (ADR 0036); code can only store it in a spec-only place, such as a field, local or parameter of that type (ADR 0041)

So nothing the program computes depends on a spec-only value. The verifier sees spec-only state like any other, and codegen erases it, along with spec functions, lemmas and contracts (see codegen.md, "Spec-only state").

Encoding. int uses the upstream smt dialect's Int sort and its operations. The dialect has no Real sort at our LLVM pin, so the verifier extends it in the smallest way that keeps it the one encoding: real is written as a sort named Real, and the operations the dialect lacks (Real + - * / and comparisons, to_real, and bv2int for converting a bit-vector) are declared as functions under their SMT-LIB names and applied with smt.apply_func. When the query is exported to SMT-LIB, those declarations and the sort's declare-sort are dropped, so Z3 reads each use as SMT-LIB's own interpreted symbol. A machine integer becomes an Int as bv2int of its bit-vector, less 2^w when it is negative, since bv2int reads a bit-vector as unsigned. A real literal n/d is (/ (to_real n) (to_real d)).

docs.title: Floats
docs.text:
f32 and f64 are IEEE 754 binary32 and binary64. No float operation raises a goal, since IEEE 754 defines every result: an overflow is an infinity and 0.0 / 0.0 is a NaN. Until the real-valued encoding of ADR 0038 lands, a float is its bit pattern, a bit-vector of its width, and the solver knows this much of it:

  • A literal is its exact bits, and negation flips the sign bit, so both are exact. So are to_bits x, the bits as a u32 or u64, and from_bits u, the float a u32 or u64 encodes.
  • =, < and <= are IEEE's, computed from the bits: a NaN (exponent all ones, fraction not zero) is unordered, so every comparison with it is false, and the other floats are ordered as their magnitudes with their signs are, so -0.0 = 0.0 and the infinities lie past every finite float. <> is not =, and > and >= are < and <= with the operands swapped.
  • +, -, * and /, f32 n of an integer, and f64 x and f32 x between the widths are uninterpreted functions of the bits (f32.add and so on): the same operands give the same result, and nothing else is known.
  • i32 x, or any integer type applied to a float, truncates toward zero and raises a nooverflow goal, "the float is a number that fits in i32 when truncated": x is not NaN and lies strictly between lo - 1 and hi + 1 for the type's range [lo, hi], so the C conversion it compiles to is defined. Each bound is compared as the float nearest it inside that interval when it is not a float itself, so -1.0 < x && x < 256.0 is exactly the goal for a u8. The result is uninterpreted, within the type's range.

So a goal that follows from those facts is proved, such as (x < y) = (-y < -x), and a goal that needs what a float operation computes, even one IEEE 754 guarantees such as x + y = y + x, fails rather than being proved wrongly. A float in a counterexample is shown as a float, read from its bits, such as x = nan. Indices, lengths and integer goals in float code are proved as anywhere else. tests/verify/floats.pia has examples of both.

docs.title: Spec state
docs.text:
spec marks a local or a parameter as spec-only whatever its type (ADR 0058). It is how a proof keeps state that evolves with the code, such as a reference implementation run beside a fast one, or the trace of what a loop has written. For now a spec local is a fixed array [t; n], whose length is a constant, and its elements may be machine integers, bool, int or real. zeros makes an array of zero elements of the type it is bound at, in code too.

let record (spec log : inout [u16; 64]) (i : int{0..63}) (v : u16) : unit
  ensures log.[i] = v
  ensures forall (k in 0 .. 64). k <> i ==> log.[k] = old (log.[k])
= log.[i] <- v

let twice (a : u16) (b : u16) : u16
  ensures result = a
= let spec log : mutable [u16; 64] = zeros in
  record log 0 a;
  record log 1 b;
  assert (log.[0] = a && log.[1] = b);
  a

The rule is the one for int: a spec value flows only into spec places and into contracts.

  • Code may write spec state. log.[i] <- v is a spec write. Its index and value are specification, so they may read spec state too, as in sums.[i + 1] <- sums.[i] + xs.[i], and its index is still a goal. A spec local's initial value may be any value of its type, so let spec snap : [u8; 4] = a keeps a snapshot of a code array.
  • Only specification may read it: contracts, loop invariants, asserts, lemma calls, and the argument for a spec parameter. Anything else is an error, such as s.[0] as a function's result, sum4 s, or if s.[0] = 0 then ....
  • A spec parameter the callee writes (out or inout) takes a spec local or spec parameter by name, since codegen erases the write: a code buffer passed there would not change at run time, though the proof would say it does. An in spec parameter takes any value.

The verifier sees spec state as it sees any buffer: an SMT array, fresh at its let (an array of zeros for zeros), updated by each store, and fresh after a loop or a call that may write it. A spec write is no effect for a spread's ownership goals: spec state is per-thread. An interface lists a spec parameter as (spec log : inout [u16; 64]) -> ..., and it must agree with the definition. Codegen erases a spec local's storage, every write to it, each spec parameter and the arguments calls pass for it, so record above is void record(uint8_t i, uint16_t v) to C (codegen.md; tests/verify/spec_locals.pia, tests/irgen/spec_local_errors.pia, tests/codegen/spec_state.pia).

Spec fields. A record field marked spec, as in type { n : u8; spec seen : [u8; 256]; spec total : int }, is spec state of any type, under the same rule: code may write it (c.seen.[c.n] <- v, c.total <- c.total + v, or a record literal's seen = zeros), and only specification may read it, so c.owner as a function's result is an error. This generalises ADR 0048's spec-only fields, whose types had to be spec-only: in a buffer of records such as [{ spec owner : u8; v : u8 }], owner is a buffer of its own that the verifier sees and codegen erases, so C passes only the vs and their length, even with owner first. Codegen erases a spec field from records, buffers of records, parameters and results, and from the values loops and branches carry, so count_from (z : int{0..15}) : counted, with counted = type { n : u8; spec seen : [u8; 16] }, is uint8_t count_from(uint8_t z) to C. As for any record holding an array, the verifier cannot yet encode a loop that carries one (tests/verify/spec_fields.pia, tests/irgen/spec_field_errors.pia).

docs.title: Theories
docs.text:
A theory teaches the verifier a domain: new sorts, functions on them with no body, and axioms about them (ADR 0036, and the worked examples in theories.md). Steps 2 and 3 of the ADR are implemented: theories, and models that prove them consistent.

@trusted

let theory Lip = sig
  let sort layer
  let spec in_w : (f : layer) -> usize
  let spec out_w : (f : layer) -> usize
  let spec lip : (f : layer) -> real
  let spec seq : (f : layer) -> (g : layer) -> layer
  let spec residual : (f : layer) -> layer

  let axiom lip_nonneg (f : layer) ensures lip f >= 0.0
  let axiom seq_shape (f : layer) (g : layer)
    requires out_w f = in_w g
    ensures in_w (seq f g) = in_w f && out_w (seq f g) = out_w g
  let axiom seq_lip (f : layer) (g : layer)
    requires out_w f = in_w g
    ensures lip (seq f g) <= lip f * lip g
  let axiom residual_shape (f : layer)
    requires in_w f = out_w f
    ensures in_w (residual f) = in_w f && out_w (residual f) = out_w f
  let axiom residual_lip (f : layer) @trigger(residual f)
    requires in_w f = out_w f
    ensures lip (residual f) <= 1.0 + lip f
end

let lemma block_bound (a : Lip.layer) (b : Lip.layer) : unit
  requires Lip.in_w a = 512 && Lip.out_w a = 512 && Lip.lip a <= 0.5
  requires Lip.in_w b = 512 && Lip.out_w b = 10 && Lip.lip b <= 2.0
  ensures Lip.lip (Lip.seq (Lip.residual a) b) <= 3.0
= ()

What a theory holds.

  • let sort s declares a new uninterpreted sort, and let sort s = t is another name for the type t.
  • let spec f : (a : t) -> r is an abstract function, with no body. Its parameters are named.
  • A let spec with a body defines a spec function as usual.
  • let axiom name params requires ... ensures ... states a fact for all values of its parameters. It has no body.
  • A let lemma is proved from the axioms, as any lemma is.

theory, sort and axiom are keywords only between let and a name, like spec and lemma.

Names. Inside its theory, a member is used unqualified (lip f, layer). Everywhere else it is T.x: Lip.lip, Lip.layer. An interface lists functions and types, not theories, so a module cannot import another's theory yet (ADR 0039): a theory is used in the file that declares it, and import T of such a theory does nothing. A module header's @trusted (module M @trusted) marks the file like a @trusted line. A name the theory does not declare is an error (the theory 'Lip' has no 'nope'). A member cannot shadow a name that is visible inside the theory, such as another item, a core builtin like len, or a builtin type. A parameter of a member cannot take a member's name either (ADR 0022).

Spec-only. A theory's sorts and functions are spec-only, like int and real. Code cannot compute with them, but it can hold a sort's value in a spec-only parameter, local or field, which is how an allocator tracks Alloc.heap (ADR 0041). Codegen erases the theory along with every contract and spec-only value that uses it. A sort has only = and <>.

Models. A model gives each sort of a theory a type and each abstract function a definition:

let summary = type { in_w : usize; out_w : usize; lip : real where lip >= 0.0 }

let model shapes : Lip = struct
  let sort layer = summary
  let spec in_w (f : summary) : usize = f.in_w
  let spec out_w (f : summary) : usize = f.out_w
  let spec lip (f : summary) : real = f.lip
  let spec seq (f : summary) (g : summary) : summary =
    { in_w = f.in_w; out_w = g.out_w; lip = f.lip * g.lip }
  let spec residual (f : summary) : summary =
    { in_w = f.in_w; out_w = f.out_w; lip = 1.0 + f.lip }
end

A model must define every sort and every abstract function of its theory, and nothing else, and each function must have the theory's type with the theory's sorts replaced by the model's. model is a keyword only in let model m : T. Inside the model its members are used unqualified, and they are m.x elsewhere.

The model check. Each axiom of the theory, with the model's types and functions in place of the theory's, becomes a lemma m.a, which is proved like any lemma and reported as the model 'shapes' meets the axiom 'Lip.seq_lip'. If every one is proved, the theory is consistent: whatever its axioms prove is true in the model. A model that breaks an axiom fails verification, with a counterexample in the model's values.

Field refinements. A record field may carry a refinement, lip : real where lip >= 0.0, in which the field's name stands for the field. It is an implicit requires on every parameter of that record type, and of records that contain it, and an implicit ensures on every result. So a function that builds the record proves the refinement, and one that takes it may assume it. Models need this: lip_nonneg holds in shapes because every summary has lip >= 0.0.

Record invariants. A record may carry an invariant over all of its fields, type { lo : u32; hi : u32 } where lo <= hi, in which each field's name stands for that field (ADR 0074, step 1). It works like a field refinement, and comes after the fields' own refinements, so it can rely on them: a grid whose rows and cols are each bounded can state where len cells = rows * cols without an overflow goal. It is assumed of every parameter of the type and proved of every result and of every out or inout parameter the function hands back, so a function that writes a field must keep it. Field refinements are proved of handed-back parameters in the same way. See tests/verify/record_invariants.pia.

Sealing. A client of the theory, such as the lemma block_bound, uses Lip.lip and the other abstract functions, never the model's. Its queries get the axioms and do not even declare the model's functions. So a fact true in the model but not stated as an axiom cannot be used, and changing a model's definitions does not change a client's proofs. A theory lemma is proved from the axioms in the same way.

Counterexamples in the model. A goal over a modelled theory is first tried in a copy of its function, called its witness, in which the model's types and functions stand for the theory's. There everything is concrete, so the solver decides it quickly. If it is false there, the model is a counterexample to the axioms as well, since the model meets them, and the report says so:

levels.pia:45:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample in the model 'bits': h = 0

A goal with no parameters reports false in the model 'm'. A model's counterexample is reported only when the witness query is complete: if it stopped unfolding a recursive spec function at its fuel, the function is uninterpreted past that point, so the model may give it a value its definition does not, and the goal is decided over the axioms instead (#188). Any failed goal whose query stopped at the fuel says so, with hint: a recursive spec function was unfolded only as far as its @fuel allows ..., since raising @fuel or proving the fact by induction may prove it. If the goal holds in the witness, it is decided over the axioms as above, with the fallback, so a goal that is true in the model but not proved by the axioms still fails. A witness is made for lemmas and spec functions that use a modelled theory, except those that use a theory member a model does not define, such as a theory lemma. This matters for speed: the queries over the axioms have quantifiers, and with them Z3 can search a long time for a counterexample that a concrete model gives at once.

Trust. Without a model, nothing proves that a theory's axioms are consistent. So a theory with axioms and no model in the program needs its file marked @trusted, on a line of its own, and every axiom is a trusted item. A theory with a model needs neither, and none of its axioms is trusted. piac --verify --trust-report lists the trusted axioms:

lip.pia:16:3: the theory 'Lip' is consistent: the solver found a witness, a model of its axioms
lip.pia:16:3: trusted: the axiom 'Lip.lip_nonneg', since the theory 'Lip' has no model
...
5 trusted items

assume needs @trusted too. Nothing checks an assume p, so it is allowed only in a file marked @trusted (ADR 0023); anywhere else it is an error that suggests assert, a lemma or a requires instead. (addr, the other construct ADR 0023 restricts, does not exist yet.) Each assume is a trusted item. Its assertion is tracked in the unsat core like an axiom's, so --why lists the goals whose proofs used it, and the callers of a function whose proof did:

next.pia:11:3: trusted: the 'assume' in 'next'
  used by: next.pia:12:5, next.pia:21:3
...
2 of 5 proved goals rest on a trusted axiom or 'assume'; the other 3 are fully proved

A goal whose query asserts an assume is solved a second time, tracked, to find its core, as for axioms. Files without assume are solved exactly as before.

Consistency of a trusted theory. A trusted theory is checked once, when its file is verified: are its axioms, with the axioms of other theories they use (by the relevance closure), satisfiable, under the usual rlimit? The answer is in the trust report. sat means Z3 found a witness, a model of the axioms, so they cannot contradict each other. unknown leaves the theory unchecked, and the report says so with the solver's reason. unsat is an error that names the axioms that contradict each other, from the unsat core:

bad.pia:6:3: failed: the axioms of the theory 'Bad' are consistent [they contradict each other: Bad.one, Bad.zero]

A theory with a model needs no check: the model is the witness, and its check proves it.

Which axioms a goal used. With --verify-stats, --trust-report, --check-vacuity or --proof-cache, a goal proved with theory axioms (or an assume) is solved a second time with each axiom tracked, and the unsat core of that run names the axioms the proof used. The first run is untracked, because tracking slows the search for a counterexample. Only queries with axioms are solved twice, so every other query is solved exactly as before. Without those flags nothing reads the core, so the second solve is skipped: it can cost far more than the proof (minutes against 2.7 seconds for tests/verify/size_classes.pia on Z3 5.4.1), and the goal records every axiom it was given instead. The tracked solve also gives up after 10 seconds, or --solver-timeout if that is less, and the goal then records every axiom it was given; only a tracked solve that finishes adds to cost, so cost stays independent of the machine. The proof cache keeps each core, so a run with --proof-cache still tracks. The core is kept in the goal's proof cache entry, as a line axioms <name>,... after proved <cost>. --verify-stats adds used=... to each such goal's line. piac --verify --trust-report --why lists, under each trusted axiom, the goals that used it. A call to a lemma assumes what the lemma proved, so a goal also rests on the axioms of every lemma its function calls, transitively. The report ends with how many proved goals rest on a trusted axiom. The others are fully proved, even in a file that trusts a theory:

trust_checks.pia:16:3: trusted: the axiom 'Good.f_small', since the theory 'Good' has no model
  used by: trust_checks.pia:32:38, trust_checks.pia:38:39
trust_checks.pia:17:3: trusted: the axiom 'Good.g_small', since the theory 'Good' has no model
  used by no proved goal
...
2 of 3 proved goals rest on a trusted axiom; the other 1 are fully proved

Vacuity, opt-in. A consistent theory can still contradict a goal's own hypotheses: with the axiom f x < 10, a lemma that requires f x > 20 proves anything. So can an assume that cannot hold. piac --verify --check-vacuity (ADR 0036, step 7) finds such proofs. Each goal proved with a trusted axiom or an assume is solved again from its hypotheses alone, the same query without its negated goal. If they are unsatisfiable, the goal was proved from a contradiction, and that is an error naming the trusted items in the unsat core:

vacuity.pia:25:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
vacuity.pia:25:3: failed: the proof is not vacuous [its hypotheses contradict each other, so 'the postcondition holds' was proved from a contradiction: Good.f_small]
vacuity.pia:30:3: failed: the proof is not vacuous [its hypotheses contradict each other, so 'the postcondition holds' was proved from a contradiction: the 'assume' at vacuity.pia:31:3]

A goal whose proof used nothing trusted is not checked: if its own preconditions contradict each other, that is the contract's business, and a goal in unreachable code is proved for the same reason. A vacuous goal is not proved, so its op is not marked proved and codegen refuses it like any failed goal. Finding a contradiction is usually quick, but showing that hypotheses with quantified axioms are satisfiable can mean a long search for a model. So each check has a budget of its own, ten times the resource count of the goal's proof and at least a million, within --solver-rlimit. A check the budget cannot decide leaves the goal proved, and piac prints a note with how many there were. The check costs one more query per goal it checks, which --verify-stats reports as verify-stats-vacuity: checks=N vacuous=V unknown=U cost=C. It is meant for CI and audits, not for every edit.

import M trusting. An importer accepts a trusted theory as a whole with import M trusting. There is no list of axioms to grant, and it is written only in the source, so it works the same in a file and in the REPL. trusting is a keyword only at the end of an import. Interfaces do not carry theories yet, so today the only theory a module can name in an import is its own, where import T trusting changes nothing: T is trusted there already. The grant is recorded, and the trust report lists it (trusting the theory 'Ideal'). The check that an import of another module's trusted theory needs trusting comes when interfaces can export theories.

Encoding. A sort is an uninterpreted SMT sort named after it ((declare-sort Lip.layer 0)), and an abstract function is a declare-fun under its qualified name (Lip.lip). The function's result is assumed to lie in its type's range. An axiom is an smt.forall over its parameters, requires ==> ensures, with each trigger as a pattern. The export cannot name an assertion, so the verifier adds the name afterwards as (assert (! ... :named |Lip.seq_lip|)). An axiom with several triggers is asserted once per trigger, under |Lip.residual_lip#2| and so on, since the export writes the terms of one quantifier as a single pattern.

Triggers. The solver instantiates an axiom where a term matches one of its triggers. @trigger(seq f g) sets one, and @trigger(t1, t2) sets a pattern of several terms that together mention every parameter. Otherwise piac infers them as Z3 would: every smallest call of a theory function that mentions all the parameters. It leaves out a term that would loop, one where the axiom holds a larger instance of it. An example is in_w f in residual_shape, which also holds in_w (residual f): each instance would make the next, so the trigger chosen is residual f. An axiom with no such term is an error at its definition. --verify-stats prints each axiom's triggers:

verify-stats-axiom: Lip.seq_lip triggers=(Lip.seq f g)
verify-stats-axiom: Lip.residual_lip triggers=(Lip.residual f)

Only the axioms a goal needs. A query starts with the theory functions its goal's walk applies. An axiom is added when every function in one of its triggers is in the query. The functions it brings can add more, until nothing changes. A query that applies no theory function gets nothing, so it is the same, byte for byte, as without theories. Leaving out an axiom only removes a hypothesis, so a proof found this way is a proof. If the goal is not proved, it is solved again with every axiom of every theory whose functions it mentions, and the counterexample comes from that run, so it is never spurious because an axiom was missing. The proof cache keys that run by its own query. --verify-stats prints the axioms each goal was given, and marks the goals that needed the fallback:

verify-stats-goal: lip.pia:31:3 axioms=Lip.lip_nonneg,Lip.seq_shape,Lip.seq_lip,Lip.residual_shape,Lip.residual_lip
verify-stats-goal: closure.pia:33:45 axioms=Counter.value_small,Counter.label_one fallback=all

These lines have their own prefixes, so tools/bench still reads the single verify-stats: line.

Not yet. These come in the ADR's later steps:

  • models in another module, found by the ADL rule, and the trusting check on imports between modules, once modules can import one another;
  • trust recorded in proof certificates (ADR 0024), which are not built yet;
  • --check-vacuity (step 7).

A counterexample over the axioms shows a value of a sort as Z3 names it (b = Lip.layer!val!0). It does not yet show the theory functions' values at it.

docs.title: spread
docs.text:
A spread i in lo .. hi do ... done runs its iterations at the same time (ADR 0060). The verifier walks one arbitrary iteration, as for a for loop, and adds a goal at every access to a buffer the body writes: the iteration owns the cell. By default iteration i owns cell i; @owns(buf, owner) on the spread gives the cells of buf with owner.[c] = i instead. These goals imply that no two iterations touch the same cell, since an owner is a function, so no goal compares two iterations. The body may not assign a variable declared outside it, and may only index a buffer it writes.

A spread's ensures p is proved at the end of one iteration, after every cell that another iteration owns has been given an unknown value, so it holds whatever the other iterations write; after the loop, forall (i in lo .. hi). p is a fact. A function with @owns(buf, owner, b) after its return type touches only the cells of buf with owner.[c] = b: every access to buf in it is that goal. A spread may pass a buffer it writes to such a function, if its own @owns names the same owner, and the call's goal is that its b is the iteration (tests/verify/spread.pia, tests/verify/spread_ensures.pia, tests/irgen/spread_errors.pia).

After a spread over lo .. hi, the cells that no iteration of the range owns keep their values (ADR 0068, section 9): with the identity owner those are the cells outside lo .. hi, and with @owns(buf, owner) the cells whose owner is outside it. An iteration writes only the cells it owns, so this holds on the CPU and on the GPU. It lets a spread over one range, such as one wave of the sediment pull step, promise that the cells of every other range are unchanged (tests/verify/spread_frame.pia).

A spec function over a buffer may say which cells it reads, reads xs.[lo .. hi] (ADR 0060, section 3). piac then writes its frame lemma f'frame, for two buffers that agree on the footprint f gives the same result, and proves it by induction on f's own decreases, asserting that every element f reads is in the footprint. Where a buffer changes outside a framed call's footprint, by a store or by a spread's forgetting of the cells other iterations own, the verifier states that the call on the new contents equals the call on the old, so a sum over a range survives writes elsewhere with no lemma by hand (tests/verify/frames.pia).

docs.title: Solver strategies and tactics
docs.text:
Two ways to help a proof the solver cannot find, or finds slowly (ADR 0036, step 6). Neither can make a wrong proof.

@solver(...) on a lemma, a function or a theory chooses the Z3 strategy for its goals. @solver(nlsat) uses Z3's strategy for nonlinear real arithmetic (qfnra-nlsat), and any other name is one of Z3's tactics, such as @solver(smt). @solver(tactic = "...") takes a combination in SMT-LIB's syntax for check-sat-using: (then t1 t2 ...), (or-else ...), (par-or ...), (par-then ...), (repeat t n), (try-for t ms) and (using-params t :key value ...). An unknown tactic is a compile error. On a theory, let theory T @solver(nlsat) = sig ... end, it applies to each member without its own @solver, and to the checks of its model and of its consistency. --dump-smt shows the strategy as (check-sat-using ...).

let lemma product (x : real) (y : real) : unit @solver(nlsat)
  requires x > 1.0 && y > 1.0
  ensures x * y > 1.0
= ()

A strategy changes only how a query is solved. Any tactic Z3 runs is sound, so unsat is still a proof, and a strategy that gives up leaves the goal failed, never proved. The strategy is part of the proof cache's key, so a goal proved one way is not taken as proved another way. The unsat core that says which axioms or assumes a goal used (Trust) is still found with Z3's default solver.

Tactics. @by(t args) on a lemma runs the metaprogram t on the lemma's goal and returns proof steps, which go before the lemma's body and are proved like steps written by hand (meta.md):

  • a lemma call, l x, whose precondition is a goal and whose postcondition is known afterwards;
  • an assert p, a goal that is known afterwards;
  • a case split, if c then assert p else assert p;
  • an instance of a quantified fact, as a lemma call or an assert at particular arguments;
  • fuel n, a hint rather than code: it puts @fuel(n) on the lemma, which unfolds every spec function at least n levels in the lemma's goals. @fuel(n) can also be written on a lemma by hand.

A tactic must terminate and be pure, by the rules for type-level metaprograms (ADR 0035), so what a proof means never depends on a step budget or on the rest of the program. This is the LCF approach: the tactic is outside the trusted base, since everything it writes is checked. theories.md shows a tactic that writes a proof by induction.

Proof by reflection is not implemented yet. It needs a datatype of formulas, and recursive types are not supported yet (status.md). The plan is in ADR 0036: a total spec function decide : formula -> bool with a soundness lemma decide f ==> eval f proved once, and a tactic that reifies the goal into a formula and proves it from decide f = true.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
A generic function is proved once at its definition, over its type parameters, and its instances are then proved by that proof (ADR 0043, steps 1 and 2).

  • Encoding. The definition check (ADR 0034) generates the body with each type parameter as a stand-in, a record with no fields. When the body is parametric, that function is kept as the generic's proof, marked pia.generic_proof, with the instances it makes at the stand-ins (lex_from<t>). ScalarizeRecords sets these functions aside, and the verifier encodes each stand-in as an uninterpreted sort, generic.t, and a buffer of one as an array of that sort. Codegen erases them.
  • Concepts. Each requirement of the constraints is an uninterpreted function of a theory named after the concept at the stand-ins, Ord<t>.less (in full, Pia.Core.Order.Ord<t> for an imported concept), so a call in code and one in a contract are the same term. Each requirement's contract, Ord<t>.less.contract, and each of the concept's laws, Ord<t>.less_transitive.law, is an axiom of that theory (step 3), with the relevance closure of any theory (Theories); a law whose hypotheses chain calls, like transitivity's, is triggered by all of them together, and one the solver could not instantiate is left out. None is trusted: the use check proves each at every type that meets the concept. A proof gets only the axioms of the concepts its own constraints promise.
  • Imported generics. An importer does not prove an imported generic again: its module proved it, and a build of the module requires that (ADR 0039). The importer keeps the proof only to match its own instances against it, so they are discharged too. A generic over another module's concept calls the concept's functions by their own names, same, and an importer's instance finds them in the concept's module, Pia.Core.Order.same.
  • old in a lemma's arguments. A lemma's arguments are spec, so they may name the state on entry: exchange asserts swapped_count (old xs) xs i j (len xs), a spec function whose contract relates how often each value occurs before and after, and so ensures it keeps every count.
  • old xs as a spec argument. A whole slice in its state on entry, old xs, may be passed to a spec function, as in ensures result = kept (old xs) v (len xs): it is the slice's memory on entry with its length, which a slice keeps, so len (old xs) is len xs.
  • Spec facts at computed arguments. A spec function's definition and its ensures are claimed of a call only where its proof covers them: its precondition holds and each integer argument the spec body computed, such as k - 1, is in its parameter's type. Spec arithmetic is exact, so unfolding cnt xs (k - 1) at k = 0 makes a call at -1, where requires k <= len xs holds; without the range, ensures result <= k there contradicted the result's type, and every goal in its scope was proved (tests/verify/spec_arg_range.pia). Parameters, loads and constants are in their types already.
  • Facts under an assumed quantifier. The definitions and contracts of the functions a quantifier's body calls, instantiated at its bound variables, are hypotheses of the quantifier, and are also asserted on their own as a forall: they hold for every value, so this is sound whatever the quantifier's polarity, and an assumed forall k. if same old.[k] v then ... from a callee's contract then tells the caller about each element. Without it, the solver would have to prove same's contract at each element before it could use the quantifier, which it cannot.
  • Closures with no captures. A lambda that captures nothing, passed as a function object, is a record with no fields, which has one value: the verifier gives such a record an uninterpreted sort and one constant, so a spec function such as Search's count_where can take the closure, and the closure's apply unfolds to the lambda's body in a contract.
  • Imported functions in specs. An imported function of scalars is, to the verifier, an uninterpreted function that meets its interface contract, since its body here is only that contract. So an imported spec function that calls one unfolds at the importer: Pia.Core.Order.lex_from<u8> calls Order's less on u8, whose contract says it is <, and an importer proves that the empty slice is before every other.
  • Equality. = and <> on values of a type parameter, which contracts may write, are equality in its sort (a call of pia.eq<t> that the verifier encodes as SMT equality). Any model reads that as equality of the instance's values, so a proof that uses it holds at every instance.
  • Instances. Generic proofs are solved first. When every goal of a generic's proof holds, each instance whose body is the generic's is not proved again: the report gives it one line, proved: 'lex_compare<u8>' is an instance of the generic proof of 'lex_compare' [generic]. An instance is the generic's body when its calls are the proof's, one for one: each call of a concept's function goes to a function that returns (no while without a measure, no recursion without one, and the same of what it calls), each call of another generic at the type parameters goes to that generic's instance, and every other call to the same function. A call that resolves to a more specific overload at the instance's types makes the instance a body of its own, proved at its types. So is an instance of a generic whose proof failed, was not selected by --verify-only, or fell back. Calls into an instance still prove its precondition at the call, as for any function. The types meet the concepts' laws and requirement contracts because the use check proves those at each type, and a failure there still fails the program.
  • Reports. The proof's goals are reported at the generic's lines with [generic]. A generic with a false contract fails at its definition even if nothing instantiates it, with a counterexample over its sort (a = generic.t!val!0). --verify-stats adds generic=, the proof goals, and instances=, the instances its proofs discharged.
  • Fallback. A generic the verifier cannot prove over sorts is proved only at its instances, and the report says why, as not proved generically: 'f' is proved at each instance, since .... In step 1 that is a generic whose signature applies a type-level metaprogram to a type parameter, one with a where predicate that is not a concept, one whose concepts have a requirement with a precondition or a record result, and one that takes, makes or returns a value of another type built from a type parameter, such as option t or pair a b. So is any body that applies an operation other than a call, a return, an if, a loop, a load, a store, a slice or a length to a value of a type parameter. The classifier errs towards falling back, which is today's behaviour.

docs.title: Higher-order functions proved once
docs.text: A higher-order function is proved once, like a generic (ADR 0044, step 6): its function parameters are values of types that meet a concept whose apply is uninterpreted and has the arrow's ensures as an axiom. Each specialisation at a lambda, a named function or a function object is reported as an instance of that proof, 'find[lambda@f.pia:12:9]' is an instance of the generic proof of 'find#proof'. A law of a function parameter in a contract, requires Pia.Fn.strict_weak_order less, is part of the copy: it is applied to the abstract apply, and the law's spec function at the proof's stand-in and at an instance's argument count as the same call when the instance is discharged, so an insertion sort over any strict weak order is proved once and its instances at a > b or at Pia.Core.Order's less are discharged. A copy whose check or proof fails is reported as not proved generically, with the goal or error that stopped it, and its specialisations are proved each; a module with no specialisation of its own does not pass silently. A function the copy calls that is itself proved once is not proved again inside it: the call is discharged by that function's own proof, so a chain of such calls (sort, make_heap, sift_down) is proved once along the chain, and an importer's specialisations along it are each an instance of its proof. An arrow's requires is part of the copy too: a concept requirement's precondition is a goal at each call in a generic body, and its axiom holds where the precondition does, so apply_twice (f : (y : u8) -> u8 requires y < 200 ensures result > y) is proved once. Arrows with inout, and functions whose copy is not parametric, are still proved per specialisation.

docs.title: Choosing overloads by precondition
docs.text: Overloads with the same parameter types are told apart by their preconditions (ADR 0034). IRGen leaves a call between them open: a func.call of the least specific one, with every candidate, most specific first, in pia.overload_candidates. Before verification and code generation, resolveOverloads decides each open call. For each candidate but the last, it encodes the calling function with the call retargeted to that candidate and asks whether each of its preconditions holds at the call, from everything known there: the caller's requires, the branches the call is under, loop invariants and earlier calls' ensures. The first candidate whose preconditions are all proved is called. If none is, the call keeps the least specific candidate, whose precondition is then an ordinary goal. This runs in every build, with or without --verify, and --verify-only does not limit it. Each query uses the proof cache like any goal.

docs.title: Limits of v0
docs.text:
• Loops whose bounds or loop-carried values cannot be encoded have every goal inside reported as skipped, and what they compute or write is unknown afterwards.
  • Calls through a function reference (ADR 0071) are outside the call graph that finds cycles, so recursion through one needs its own termination rule.
  • Affine goals in loops, such as subscripts like xs.[2*i + 1], aliasing and loop-carried dependence, still go to Z3. A Presburger stage will decide them first (ADR 0020).
  • A call to an ordinary function inside a contract stands for a value that meets the callee's postconditions, and inside a quantifier for an unknown value. To say what a function means in a contract, use a spec function.
  • Ops the verifier does not model produce unknown values of their types, which is sound but may cause failures.
  • Interval analysis is local to each goal. Extending MLIR's integer range analysis, so that ranges flow through control flow, comes later.

docs.title: 1. Record architecture decisions
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Pia is a solo project with many interlocking language and compiler decisions. Later work (and later Claude sessions) needs to know what was decided and why, without re-deriving it from chat history.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Record each significant decision as a short ADR in docs/adr/, numbered in order, with Status, Context, Decision and Consequences. docs/design.md is the readable overview; ADRs are the source of truth when they disagree. A changed decision gets a new ADR that supersedes the old one, rather than an edit that erases history.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every design change touches an ADR first.
  • ADRs stay short; detail and examples live in docs/design.md.

docs.title: 2. let is the only binding form
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Pia aims for a minimal core with OCaml-like syntax. Separate keywords for values, functions, lambdas and type declarations multiply the grammar and the cases the verifier must model.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: let binds every value, including functions and types. A nameless let is a function literal: let (x) => x * x. There is no fun, lambda or type declaration keyword. Function literals are curried (let (a) (b) => a + b), not tupled. let rec marks recursion so the prover can demand a termination measure. Bindings are immutable; mutation goes only through mutable parameters or locals.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The grammar has one binding production plus the type constructor expression.
  • Types being values means type-level functions are ordinary compile-time functions (see ADR 0009).
  • Partial application is always available, so the optimiser must handle closure creation well.

docs.title: 3. Strong static typing; dynamic typing only through tagged values
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The prover needs every value's type to be known to reason completely, but some programs (decoders, heterogeneous data) want dynamic typing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Every expression has a static type and there are no implicit conversions. Dynamic typing exists only as dyn, a tagged value whose tags form a closed sum the prover can enumerate (optionally narrowed, as in dyn[u8 | f32]). Each tag maps to a Z3 datatype constructor, so matches over dyn are checked for exhaustiveness. Lowering erases tags the prover shows are unique; the proof model always keeps them. Generics are monomorphised before verification.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Proofs are about concrete types only.
  • dyn costs nothing at runtime when the prover can resolve it.

docs.title: 4. The strongest guarantee is always the default
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Many features have a strict mode and weaker, cheaper modes (overflow handling, float semantics, unproved obligations). Defaults decide what most code actually gets.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The strongest guarantee is the default everywhere, and weaker modes must be asked for explicitly. In particular: integer arithmetic defaults to @overflow(proof) (the compiler must prove no overflow; wrap, saturate and trap are opt-in), floats default to strict IEEE semantics, and an unproved obligation is a compile error unless the source writes @assume or @check.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Some correct programs will initially fail to compile until annotated; this is intended.
  • Every weakening is visible in the source and, where it affects callers, in the interface.

docs.title: 5. Parameters carry ownership, access and modifiability modifiers
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The prover needs aliasing, write and lifetime facts at every call boundary, and interfaces must carry them so modules can be verified separately.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Each parameter has three independent modifiers: ownership (borrowed | moved), access (in | out | inout) and modifiability (fixed | mutable). The default is borrowed in fixed. out must be fully written before return. Closures capture by borrow unless written move.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Interfaces state everything the prover needs about effects at the boundary.
  • Combination rules (for example out implies mutable; mutable borrows may not alias, with slice disjointness proved) are proposed in docs/design.md and still need confirming.

docs.title: 6. Contracts, refinement types, and module state as exported symbols
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Pia must prove modules keep the contracts they advertise, including stateful protocols such as open/pull/close on a stream.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: There are four contract forms: refinement types (int{0..255}, { x : f32 | x >= 0.0 }), pre and postconditions (requires, ensures), invariants (loop, struct, module), and state properties. Module state has no special syntax: an interface is a set of exported symbols, each with its type and pre/postconditions, and exported state is one more symbol constrained by those conditions. All forms lower to contract ops in Pia's MLIR dialects and become solver assertions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Importers prove each call against exported contracts; exporters prove their bodies keep every postcondition.
  • No typestate machinery is needed in the type system.

docs.title: 7. Metaprogramming from day one, expanded to a fixed point
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Serialisation, equality adapters, operators and code generators (such as tiled kernels) are core use cases, and generated code must be proved like hand-written code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A metaprogram is an ordinary Pia function (let meta) that runs at compile time over quoted syntax (`( ... ) and $x splices), with hygiene on by default. Expansion loops back to parsing until a fixed point: generated code may contain further metaprogram uses. Metaprograms see types only once fully resolved; one that needs a type still being generated is deferred to a later pass, and is an error only if the loop settles with it still waiting. A compiler flag (sketched as --meta-cycles=N) caps the number of passes. The first derives are eq, ord, hash, serialise and deserialise; deserialise emits refinement checks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Compile time is spent deliberately on expansion so that results are provable by construction.
  • Type checking and expansion interleave, which shapes the compiler driver.

docs.title: 8. Operators are defined only through metaprograms
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Built-in operators would hard-code arithmetic semantics and overflow modes into the core language.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The core language has named functions only (add, add_sat, vec_add). Every operator, including + - * / < =, is declared by an operator metaprogram that maps a symbol, precedence, associativity and operand types to an expansion. The standard operators live in a prelude imported by default.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The parser must support user-declared infix operators with precedence.
  • Overload resolution for operators uses the same rules as for generics (ADR 0009).

docs.title: 9. User-defined generics, checked concepts with laws, and adapters
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Users need their own generic types and constrained generic functions, and the optimiser wants algebraic laws (for example associativity) it can rely on.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A generic type is a compile-time function returning a type. Constraints are concepts, written as metaprograms that accept a type or return a diagnostic. Concepts are checked both at the generic definition (the body may use only what its concepts promise) and at each use. Concepts may state laws; every instance must prove them, with no @assume escape. A type that does not meet a concept needs an adapter, a value supplying the required functions with its laws proved, which may live in any module. Type arguments are deduced from the call site by default; explicit arguments (sum<i64> xs) force an instance or resolve an overload.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Laws give the optimiser proven rewrites.
  • Adapters avoid orphan-rule restrictions while keeping every instance proved.

docs.title: 10. Modules export interfaces; imports name them; proofs carry certificates
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The language must support massively parallel build and link while proving properties across module boundaries and still allowing aggressive constant folding.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A module exports named interfaces: sets of symbols with types and pre/postconditions. Imports must name the interfaces they use, so a module depends on interface artifacts only. Verification is assume-guarantee. Each compiled module carries a proof certificate with a hash of every interface it was proved against, and the linker refuses mismatches. Interfaces may export fixed values as symbols: importers prove against the symbol's type and refinement, and the value is resolved later during cross-module constant folding. A changed value invalidates dependent certificates and forces dependents to recompile.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Modules type check, verify and compile in parallel.
  • Cross-module folding happens late, behind certificate checks.

docs.title: 11. Compiler in C++ on MLIR, verifying with interval analysis then Z3
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The prototype must reach Apple Silicon codegen and solver-backed verification quickly, reusing existing infrastructure.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The compiler is C++ on MLIR. Pia lowers to its own dialects that carry contracts, then verification runs interval analysis first to discharge cheap obligations, and sends the rest to Z3. For the solver encoding, Pia targets MLIR's upstream smt dialect (from CIRCT, upstream since LLVM 21.1), exported to SMT-LIB and handed to Z3 in-process; a direct Z3 C++ API bridge is the fallback if the exporter is too limiting. Machine integers are bit-vectors, floats use the FP theory, and dyn tags are datatypes. Codegen goes through linalg/vector to arm_neon and LLVM for arm64.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Requires an LLVM new enough to have the smt dialect (see ADR 0017).
  • Pipeline order: parse, expand (fixed point), type check, lower, verify, optimise with proved facts, codegen.

docs.title: 12. Three ways to license float reassociation and FMA
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Strict IEEE semantics block reassociation, so tiled and vectorised float reductions cannot be proved equal to their naive specification.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Strict IEEE is the default (ADR 0004). Pia supports three opt-in approaches: a per-function @fp(reassoc, contract) attribute (contracts proved over reals); a wrapper type such as fast f32 with a Numeric adapter whose proof model uses real addition; and an error tolerance stated in ensures with strict IEEE semantics, proved by a rounding-error analysis pass.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Authors choose where the licence lives: function, type, or contract.
  • The tolerance approach needs a dedicated error-analysis pass; bit-precise Z3 floats won't scale.

docs.title: 13. Auto-vectorise as much as possible; keep vec<T, k> for explicit control
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SIMD performance on Apple Silicon is the first milestone, and proved facts (trip counts, alignment, non-aliasing) are exactly what vectorisers need.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The optimiser auto-vectorises every loop it can prove safe. vec<T, k> remains an ordinary prelude generic for authors who want to fix the vector shape themselves.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • Vectorisation quality depends on the verifier exporting facts to the optimiser.

docs.title: 14. Concurrent by default: collectives, task graphs, futures; collectives proved to match
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The flagship demo needs distributed, data-parallel execution, and deadlock freedom must be provable at compile time.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The runtime is concurrent by default. Pia will have MPI-like collectives, task graphs and futures, built in the order the stream delineation demo needs them: collectives and parallel spread loops first, then task graphs (for flow accumulation), then futures. Matching of collectives is proved by a protocol metaprogram that checks every worker issues the same sequence, backed by a model checker pass for interleavings it cannot settle. Session types are rejected as too runtime-dependent. Tiles are moved to workers, so data races are ruled out by ownership.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Needs a model checker pass in the verifier.
  • Collectives are library metaprograms, not built-ins.

docs.title: 15. Device placement: compiler cost model, explicit, or overridable
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Work may run on CPU cores, the GPU, or eventually the Neural Engine, and authors sometimes know better than a cost model.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Three forms are supported: @place(auto) uses the compiler's cost model; @place(gpu) or @place(cpu) fixes the device; @place(auto, prefer = gpu) keeps the cost model but overrides it. Placement must never change the proved result. CPU and GPU (Metal) are first targets; the Neural Engine is reachable only through Core ML, so it is a later, optional target for fixed operations.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • Placement interacts with float rules (ADR 0012).

docs.title: 16. Stream delineation on Apple Silicon is the flagship demo
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The language needs one end-to-end program that exercises every feature and is provably correct by construction.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The flagship demo is GIS stream delineation: decode a PNG/GIF heightmap, fill depressions, compute D8 flow direction, accumulate flow, simulate sediment transport with a proved conservation law, and render a PNG/GIF coloured by sediment load. It runs concurrently on Apple Silicon. Image I/O libraries (Image.Png, Image.Gif) are part of the work. Smaller pipelines (saturating add, dot product, clamp and scale, serialise round trip, tiled matmul) come first as the test suite.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • Features are prioritised by what this demo needs next.

docs.title: 17. Build with Bazel; depend on LLVM/MLIR and Z3 as Bazel modules
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project needs reproducible builds of a C++ compiler against LLVM/MLIR and Z3, without vendoring a checkout of llvm-project. The Bazel Central Registry's llvm-project module stops at 17.0.4, which predates MLIR's smt dialect (LLVM 21.1).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use Bazel with bzlmod. Depend on llvm-project through its own bzlmod overlay module (utils/bazel/MODULE.bazel on llvm-project main) with a git_override pinned to a specific main commit, and on Z3 from the Bazel Central Registry. Do not vendor or check out llvm-project into the repository.

docs.title: Amendment, 2026-11-20: how the overlay is consumed
docs.text:
llvm-project's utils/bazel/MODULE.bazel (module llvm-project-overlay) only defines its source repository @llvm-raw when it is the root module, and the @llvm-project repository it configures is private to that module. A bazel_dep on it with a git_override therefore cannot give Pia's targets @llvm-project//mlir:.... Instead, MODULE.bazel does what the overlay's README recommends for downstream projects:

  • fetch llvm-project as the module @llvm-raw with bazel_dep plus git_override, pinned to one main commit (LLVM_COMMIT). patch_cmds add a minimal root MODULE.bazel and the empty root files LLVM's configure.bzl expects. It has to be a module, because MODULE.bazel can only load .bzl files from modules, not from a repository made with use_repo_rule.
  • run LLVM's own llvm_configure rule from it, for the AArch64 and X86 targets
  • bazel_dep on the same modules as the overlay's MODULE.bazel, with the same repo names

Z3 builds through rules_foreign_cc's CMake rule. A one-line patch (third_party/rules_foreign_cc/absolute_linker_path.patch, applied with single_version_override) makes the linker path absolute so CMake can find Apple's wrapped clang.

This is still LLVM's own Bazel build at a pinned main commit, fetched by Bazel and never checked into the repository.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Bumping LLVM means changing LLVM_COMMIT, re-syncing the mirrored bazel_dep list with the overlay's MODULE.bazel at that commit, and fixing any API breakage.
  • First builds of LLVM/MLIR are long; remote or disk caching will matter.

docs.title: 18. Three Pia dialects over upstream MLIR, with smt for solving
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The compiler needs IR for Pia's own types and values, for contracts that must be proved and then erased, and for concurrency. Upstream MLIR already provides codegen dialects and, since LLVM 21.1, an smt dialect with SMT-LIB export.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Define three Pia dialects: pia (types, values, functions with parameter modifiers), pia_contract (contracts and proof obligations as ops), and pia_par (tiles, spread loops, collectives, placement). The verifier encodes obligations in the upstream smt dialect and hands SMT-LIB to Z3 in-process. After verification, contracts are erased, proved facts remain as attributes, and code lowers through upstream arith, scf, memref, vector, linalg, arm_neon and llvm. Interval analysis builds on MLIR's integer range analysis.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One verifier pipeline handles both explicit contracts and implicit obligations.
  • Pia avoids maintaining its own solver IR.
  • GPU placement needs a path to Metal that upstream MLIR does not provide directly; this is deferred until the concurrency milestone.

docs.title: 19. Grammar disambiguation rules
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-20

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The design's syntax is OCaml-like: application by juxtaposition, = for both binding and equality, items without terminators, and types that are values. Writing the grammar down (grammar.md) and parsing every design example with a reference parser exposed these ambiguities:

  • A contract predicate and the body share =: ensures total g = old (total g) - drained g followed by = step g has two readings.
  • A bare top-level metaprogram call (tiled_matmulsgemm_4x16 f32 4 16 64 4`) after a definition reads as more arguments to that definition's last expression.
  • sum<i64> xs and a < b both use <.
  • forall i in 0..n. p uses ., which is also field access.
  • borrowed in [u8] -> [pixel] could put the modifiers on the whole function or on its parameter.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Comparisons do not associate, and a contract predicate takes the longest reading that still leaves a body. Then the = after a complete comparison starts the body. An = that starts a line always starts the body (#259): without it, a predicate that ends in an application, ensures result <==> sorted less xs, read a body that is itself an equation, = is_sorted_until xs less = len xs, as sorted less xs = is_sorted_until xs less and left the body len xs. An interface prints each exported definition on one line but keeps that line break, and --emit=interface parses its text back and checks each definition is the one written.
  2. Top-level items start in column 1. The lexer inserts an item separator before a column-1 token that can start an item, outside brackets, sig/struct ... end and do ... done. ;; is an explicit separator.
  3. < straight after an identifier opens explicit type arguments. Less-than needs a space before it.
  4. { straight after an identifier opens a range type (int{0..255}).
  5. A dot followed by whitespace ends quantifier binders.
  6. Modifiers before a function type belong to its first parameter. They come in a fixed order: ownership, then access, then mutability.
  7. ==> (implication) is added to the bootstrap operator table at level 1, below ||, because contracts need it.
  8. The parallel loop keyword is spread (spread tile in grid @place(auto) do ... done), chosen as a single imperative word. scatter and gather were ruled out because they name collectives. step is a keyword only inside a for or spread header. The parameter modifiers, spread and mod are reserved words.
  9. ... is a hole token. It parses wherever the design's sketches use it, and Sema rejects it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every example in design.md parses unchanged, and the tests pin each rule.
  • Spacing is significant in three places (name<, name{, .). A formatter that always spaces binary operators makes these rules invisible in practice.
  • The layout rule is the only indentation sensitivity. A top-level body written flush left in column 1 starting with an identifier would split, so bodies are indented, as in all the examples.
  • The C++ parser (M2) can implement rule 1 deterministically. It parses the predicate greedily, and if no body = follows, it splits at the last top-level = of the final clause.
  • Reserving in, out and fixed takes them away as names.

docs.title: 20. Decide affine aliasing and dependence goals with MLIR's Presburger library
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Several proof goals are about integer sets defined by linear constraints. Examples:

  • Two mutable borrows must not alias (design.md). When both are slices of one buffer, this means their index ranges are disjoint.
  • A spread loop (ADR 0014) is legal only if no iteration writes an element that another iteration reads or writes.
  • Auto-vectorisation (ADR 0013) needs the loop-carried dependence distances.
  • Loop goals in the verifier often include bounds on affine subscripts such as xs.[2*i + 1].

Each of these asks whether a system of linear equalities and inequalities over integers has a solution. The variables are loop indices, sizes, offsets and lengths, and the system often comes with existential quantifiers. Z3 can decide such systems, but its bit-vector encoding is heavy for this kind of goal. Pairs of loop iterations double the number of variables, and quantifier alternation makes the solver slow or unpredictable.

MLIR ships the Fast Presburger Library (FPL), in mlir/Analysis/Presburger. It decides the emptiness of integer sets and relations exactly, using simplex with generalised basis reduction, and computes with arbitrary-precision integers.
