It can also produce an integer sample point, eliminate variables, and compute unions, intersections and complements. It is part of @llvm-project//mlir:Analysis, which the build already depends on.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The verifier gets a Presburger stage between interval analysis and SMT. A goal goes to FPL when every term in it is affine in integer variables. Affine means:

  • sums of variables
  • multiplication by constants
  • floor division and modulo by constants
  • comparisons

The goal must also have no other side conditions. Examples are aliasing, dependence and affine bounds goals. The stage builds an IntegerRelation whose constraints are the following:

  • the path condition
  • each variable's type range
  • the goal's negation

An empty relation means the goal is proved, and the goal is marked pia.proved = "presburger". A non-empty relation gives a sample point, which becomes the counterexample just as a Z3 model would.

Goals outside the affine fragment still go to Z3, as do goals where FPL hits a resource limit. Examples are products of two variables, data-dependent indices, wrap arithmetic and anything involving array contents. The stages are tried in a fixed order: intervals, then Presburger, then SMT. The stage that proves a goal is recorded, so certificates and reports say how each goal was proved.

Dependence analysis for spread and the vectoriser uses the same relations. The access relations of two iterations are intersected under i != j. An empty intersection proves independence. Otherwise the vectoriser reads the distance set from the relation.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Aliasing and dependence proofs become exact and predictable, with no solver timeouts on the common affine cases.
  • The verifier has two decision procedures, so it needs one shared lowering of affine terms. Both stages must also agree on goal semantics. Tests run selected affine goals through both stages and check that they agree.
  • FPL works over unbounded integers. Type ranges must therefore always be added as constraints, and wrap or saturate arithmetic is never sent to FPL.
  • No new external dependency is needed. FPL's API is less stable than SMT-LIB, so upgrading the pinned LLVM may require changes in the Presburger stage.

docs.title: 21. A language server, pia-lsp, with a VS Code client first
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia's promise is that programs are proved before they run. Today the proof results only appear when piac --verify runs in a terminal. The place a programmer wants to see "this + can overflow when a = 248, b = 248" is the editor, on the +, while they type.

The Language Server Protocol (LSP) lets one server work with many editors: VS Code, Visual Studio, Neovim, Emacs, Helix, Zed and others. Writing editor support once, as a server, is much cheaper than writing a plug-in per editor, and it keeps the language knowledge in the compiler's own C++ code instead of a reimplementation in TypeScript.

The compiler is split so that the front end (src/syntax) has no LLVM dependency and builds in seconds, while IRGen and the verifier need MLIR and Z3. Verification can take seconds per goal (the per-goal timeout is 10 s), so it cannot run on the editor's critical path.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A server binary, //tools/pia-lsp, speaks LSP 3.17 over stdio. It is built from the compiler's own libraries, so the editor sees exactly what piac sees. The protocol code lives in //src/lsp with a small JSON reader and writer of its own, so the front-end part of the server builds and tests without LLVM, like piac -DPIA_NO_MLIR.

Two kinds of analysis, on two schedules.

  • Front end, on every change. The server keeps each open document's text (full sync), reparses it on each change and publishes syntax errors at once. The same parse feeds document symbols, hover, go-to-definition and completion. Names are resolved over the syntax tree with the language's scoping: top-level lets are visible everywhere (IRGen allows calls before the definition), parameters in the contracts and body, let ... in in its body (and its value when rec), loop, lambda, quantifier and match binders in their bodies.
  • Proofs, in the background. IRGen and the verifier run on a worker thread, by default when a document is opened or saved (pia.verify.on: save, change or off, and the pia.verify command on demand). Type errors from IRGen and every failed goal become diagnostics with source pia-verify; the counterexample is part of the message, and the goal kind (nooverflow, inbounds, ensures, ...) is the diagnostic code. Skipped goals are information diagnostics, since v0 cannot prove them yet. Proved goals are hints only if pia.verify.showProved is set. Results for a document version that has since changed are dropped, and an edit clears the old proof diagnostics, whose positions would be stale. Newer requests for a document replace older queued ones.

Hover shows proofs. Hovering a name shows its definition: a function's signature and contracts as written, or a parameter's annotation. Hovering an operator, call or index shows every goal the verifier raised there, with its status and the method that proved it (intervals, presburger, smt) or the counterexample. This is where "proved in advance" becomes visible.

Positions. The compiler counts byte offsets and 1-based byte columns. The server converts to LSP's UTF-16 positions per line, which every client supports.

VS Code first, in editors/vscode. A small extension in plain JavaScript (no TypeScript build step) uses vscode-languageclient to start pia-lsp, and adds a TextMate grammar and language configuration for highlighting, brackets and (* *) comments. Settings: pia.server.path, pia.verify.on, pia.verify.showProved, pia.trace.server. It is packaged as a .vsix with vsce.

Visual Studio later, through the same server. Visual Studio 2022 hosts LSP servers through its ILanguageClient extension API, so supporting it needs only a small VSIX that starts pia-lsp, with no change to the server.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Diagnostics in the editor are the compiler's, from the same code, so they cannot drift from piac.
  • The front-end features work in a build without MLIR, and their tests run in seconds. The proof features need the full build.
  • A program with a syntax error gets no proof results until it parses. The parser's recovery (ADR 0019) still reports every broken item.
  • Verification of one file is not incremental yet: each run re-verifies the whole file. Per-function caching keyed by the function's text and its callees' contracts comes with proof certificates (ADR 0010).
  • Hover and definition work within one file. Cross-module navigation waits for modules and imports in the compiler.
  • Semantic highlighting, rename, code actions (such as "add @overflow(saturate)" on an overflow goal) and inlay hints for inferred ranges are natural follow-ups on the same server.

docs.title: 22. Hygiene and name lookup: no shadowing, renamed quote binders, qualified names, ADL
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0007 makes metaprograms hygienic by default, with $!name breaking hygiene on purpose. It does not say what hygiene means for Pia, or how names are found once modules arrive. When a quote is spliced into user code, two kinds of capture can happen.

A name the quote binds captures a name in spliced code.

let meta operator ( +^ ) : prec 6 left = let (a) (b) => `( let t = $a in t + $b )
let f (t : u8) (x : u8) : u16 = x +^ t

Spliced naively, this is let t = x in t + t: it type checks and silently computes 2x. Lexical scoping cannot catch this, because after splicing the wrong t really is the closest binding.

A free name in the quote is captured at the expansion site. The prelude's + expands to the builtin add. In let scale (add : u8) (x : u8) : u8 = x + add, resolving add at the expansion site finds the parameter.

Shadowing in user code causes the same confusion without any metaprogram. Once there are modules, a helper that a quote in module M calls would also resolve against the program that uses the quote, not against M.

Full syntax-object hygiene, as in Racket, tracks scope sets on every identifier. That is more machinery than v0 needs, and it would also reject the design's own derive_eq: its a and b are bound in one quote and used in another.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. No shadowing. A binding written in the source may not reuse a name that is visible where it is written. That covers a local in scope, a top-level function, a type, and a core builtin (add, eq, and, ..., len, old). Parameters, let ... in, loop variables and quantifier binders are all checked. Breaking the rule is an error, and the error suggests a primed name instead (x', or x'' if that is taken). Primes were always identifier characters (grammar.md), so let (x') => x' + 1 and let x' = x + 1 in ... introduce related names without shadowing. Assigning to a mutable local is not shadowing.
  2. Names a quote binds are renamed. A let ... in, parameter, lambda or loop variable, or quantifier binder inside a quote gets a fresh name (t#1), so it can never capture or shadow a name in spliced code. The names of quoted top-level items are kept, since they are the metaprogram's output. A name that the generated code clashes with, such as a hand-written eq_pixel, is reported as already defined.
  3. Free names in a quote are qualified. A free name refers to its definition at the metaprogram's site. Before modules exist, a core builtin is marked [prelude] and anything else [toplevel]. IRGen resolves [prelude] to the builtin and [toplevel] among top-level functions, never among locals. With modules, quotes produce module-qualified paths instead (prelude.add, M.pow), and the marks go away.
  4. $!name opts out. It stands for the plain name, bound or resolved where the code lands. Quotes that work together, like the two in derive_eq, share names this way. Rule 1 still applies to the code it produces.
  5. Argument-dependent lookup for operators and derives on types. An operator declared for a type (let meta operator ( + ) for vec<T, k>), and a derive_x for a type, are found in two places. One is the module that defines the argument's type. The other is the adapter modules the program imports explicitly. Finding more than one candidate is an ambiguity error, never first-match. Built-in integer types use the prelude's operators. Both arrive with modules (M8) and operators for a type.
  6. Locations. Code a quote builds takes the expansion site's location. Spliced code keeps its own.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An operator always means its declaration, whatever the program names its locals, and an unqualified name always means the one visible binding. Readers never have to work out which of two same-named bindings is meant.
  • Some OCaml habits are errors in Pia, such as let x = x + 1 in ... and an inner loop reusing i. A mutable local, or a new name, replaces them.
  • Renamed binders appear in diagnostics and counterexamples as t#1. A later change keeps the original name with a hidden scope id, prints it as t (from +^), and lets the language server jump from it to the binder in the quote.
  • Scope ids should come from the expansion site, not a global counter, before generated names can reach module interfaces. Otherwise an unrelated edit would change them and force recompiles (ADR 0010).
  • Scope-set hygiene stays possible later. The names marked by rule 3 would become identifiers with a definition-site scope.

docs.title: 23. A minimal core, with the standard library written and proved in Pia
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Pia needs a standard library, and Dean wants it written in Pia so that it is verified like any other Pia code. Today Pia has no I/O, no allocation, no sum types and no bitwise operators, so the edge demo needs a C main for BMP files and buffers. The flagship demo needs PNG and GIF codecs in Pia. And any * in a module widens the whole SMT encoding to 132 bits, so loop goals time out. Dean's requirements: the core calls POSIX directly and wraps it in strongly typed, contract-constrained functions; FFI carries explicit contracts, with calls marked unsafe where it does not; and a runtime error handler prints stack traces and debug info when available. The detail is in docs/stdlib.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A feature is in the core only if Pia cannot express it, the verifier must know its meaning, or it shapes the language. Everything else is library code in Pia, proved when the library builds.
  • The core adds: integer bit builtins (with C-style prelude operators & | ^ ~ << >>, where | is bitwise or only inside parentheses), widen/narrow/mul_wide, sum types and match, spec functions and lemmas, slicing and constant arrays, @linear types, extern, unsafe, addr, @trusted, metaprogram type queries, and later float, vector and atomic builtins. Modules (M8) and generics (M9) are core as already decided.
  • FFI is = extern "symbol" as a function body. A foreign function with a requires or ensures clause is called normally: its preconditions are goals and its postconditions are trusted. One without a contract can only be called as unsafe f x, which assumes nothing about the result.
  • POSIX is reached through libSystem, declared with weak, cited contracts in one trusted module, Pia.Sys.Posix. The rest of Pia.Sys wraps it in strong types and is fully proved: errors are a result of a decoded errno, and handles such as fd are @linear, so they are closed exactly once.
  • addr and assume are only allowed in modules marked @trusted. Each module's certificate lists its own trusted items (foreign contracts, unsafe call sites, assumes, accepted unproved goals), and piac --trust-report computes a program's transitive trusted base from the certificates. The format is ADR 0024's.
  • Allocation is Pia over mmap, through explicit allocators (ADR 0026). Allocation failure is a result by default.
  • Every run-time trap and fatal signal goes to one handler in Pia.Rt, written in Pia: it prints the Pia source location, a frame-pointer stack trace symbolised with dladdr, DWARF file and line when available, and exits with status 134. Programs may replace it.
  • Multiplication is handled by a ladder in the verifier: per-goal bit widths, linear encoding of constant products, intervals, an opaque product with library lemmas, and exact nonlinear arithmetic only in a query of its own.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The trusted base is the compiler, Pia.Sys.Posix, Pia.Rt, and whatever a program marks @trusted or unsafe, and it can always be listed.
  • The edge demo can drop main.c once files, main and arenas exist, and use BT.601 once per-goal widths land.
  • unsafe becomes a word the core gives meaning to, as extern does. Neither is a reserved keyword.
  • Much of the work (the multiplication ladder, bit builtins, spec functions, variants, FFI) does not need modules, so it can proceed alongside M8.
  • libm is never trusted: every maths function is written and proved in Pia, with its error bound in its contract.

docs.title: 24. Shared libraries publish interfaces and proof certificates; loaders check them
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0010 makes verification assume-guarantee across modules and has the static linker refuse a module whose certificate names an interface hash that does not match. Shared libraries can be rebuilt, upgraded or replaced after an importer was linked, so a static check is not enough: a program could run against a library that no longer guarantees what the program assumed, and since contracts leave no trace in machine code, nothing would notice.

Prior art splits in two. Proof-carrying code (Necula) and foundational PCC ship proofs that the consumer re-checks, which removes trust in the producer but is too slow for a loader and needs a stable proof format. Practical systems (OCaml interface CRCs and Dynlink, Rust's crate hash, WebAssembly import checks, ELF symbol versions) compare identities at link or load time and leave re-checking to offline tools. dyld has no pre-bind hook, but it does refuse to launch a program with a missing non-weak symbol, and all macOS arm64 code is signed page by page.

The full design, prior art and trade-offs are in docs/abi.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Interface hash. Each exported interface is hashed (SHA-256) over a canonical serialisation of its type-checked form: a domain prefix with the Pia ABI version and target, then every exported symbol with its type, parameter modifiers, contract (normalised pia_contract terms with numbered binders), and trust marks. Bodies, private symbols and proof details are not hashed. Memory layout is not in the interface hash either: it is published and checked separately (ADR 0030), so a layout change forces a relink but not a re-proof. Foldable values and inline bodies get a separate inline surface hash.
  • Certificate in the image. Each image carries one certificate in __TEXT,__pia_cert (macOS) listing, per module, the interfaces it provides (with every older version it is proved to refine), the interfaces it requires with the hashes it was proved against, and its own trusted items: extern contracts, @assume, --allow-unproved goals and unsafe call sites. The canonical interfaces are embedded in __TEXT,__pia_iface, so piac can import from a .dylib. Code signing protects both.
  • Three layers of checking.
  • Witness symbols: a library exports _pia$w$<module>$<interface>$<hash> per provided interface version, and importers reference the one they were proved against, so dyld itself refuses a mismatch before any code runs.
  • Certificate check at static link (piac link, Bazel rules), at launch (Pia runtime, before main) and in Pia.Dl.open: ABI version, inline surfaces, trust policy, compiler identity. Pia images never contain static initializers, so checking after dlopen is sound.
  • Offline audit (pia-cert audit): recompute hashes, re-prove refinements and optionally replay a proof bundle. The loader never runs a solver.
  • ABI evolution by proved refinement. A library keeps baselines of the interfaces it has published. At build time piac proves the current interface refines each baseline: same types and layout, no removed symbols, weaker requires, stronger ensures and invariants, identical foldable values. Proved baselines are listed in the certificate and get witnesses, so old importers keep working. Breaking changes drop a baseline and bump the dylib major version.
  • Trust model. Certificates make honest-but-buggy builds safe to combine. Integrity and provenance come from code signing. Correctness of the library rests on the producer's compiler plus the trusted items its certificate lists. The transitive trusted base is computed by walking certificates (--trust-report), not copied into each one.
  • macOS/arm64 first, then ELF (.pia.cert note, witnesses or GNU symbol versions, optional LD_AUDIT module).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A stale or swapped library fails at launch or dlopen with no runtime cost beyond one bind per imported interface.
  • Library authors can ship compatible updates without recompiling importers, and every compatible change is a proof, not a diff.
  • Any Pia binary can report the exact set of trusted contracts it depends on, including libSystem externs from the standard library.
  • Pia code cannot rely on static initializers. Module-level state must be constant or set up from main.
  • The canonical serialisation and the Pia ABI version become compatibility promises: changing either changes every hash.
  • A malicious, signed producer can still ship code that does not match its certificate. Closing that needs re-checkable proof objects (for example cvc5 Alethe proofs) and translation validation, left for later; the format reserves room for them.

docs.title: 25. Sanitizers check the edges of the proof
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Dean wants the runtime core to support compiler-rt's sanitizers (ASan, TSan, UBSan and others). Proved Pia code cannot have the bugs they find, but Pia programs call foreign code, trust extern contracts and assumes, and depend on the verifier, IRGen and codegen being right (ADR 0023). The detail is in docs/stdlib.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• piac --sanitize=address|thread|undefined|contracts (a list). address and thread use LLVM's ASan and TSan passes, so Pia and C in one binary share one runtime. undefined turns every unproved goal into a run-time check. contracts checks every foreign ensures and every assume at run time.
  • ASan does not instrument accesses whose bounds were proved, unless --sanitize-proved asks it to. That build is the check on the verifier. TSan instruments everything.
  • Pia.Mem poisons arena memory for ASan. In a sanitized build, Pia.Rt leaves fatal signals to the sanitizer runtime and adds the Pia trap site through __sanitizer_set_death_callback. Sanitized builds carry DWARF.
  • The runtimes are built from the pinned llvm-project with rules_foreign_cc, so they match the instrumentation.
  • Bazel configs asan, tsan and ubsan set the C++ toolchain features, which pia_object maps to --sanitize. contracts is a Pia build setting.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A sanitizer report in proved code is a compiler bug, which makes sanitized test runs a soundness test.
  • Each sanitized configuration builds compiler-rt and doubles test time, so CI runs them on main first.
  • MemorySanitizer and HWASan are out on macOS arm64. libFuzzer is the next candidate, for the trusted boundary and the image decoders.

docs.title: 26. A memory manager of explicit allocators, with no garbage collection
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Dean: the runtime needs a real memory manager. Naive malloc and free aren't enough; Pia needs arena allocators and explicit memory management, and no garbage collection. There is no new keyword: allocation is an explicit function of the memory module, which keeps TCMalloc-style size classes and arenas for tasks, fibers and coroutines. Its free lists must be proved to supply enough memory or fail, and every allocation must be handled at its call site. ADR 0023 sketched Pia.Mem as an arena plus alloc/free over mmap. The detail is in docs/stdlib.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Pia has no garbage collector, now or later, and no new keyword. All memory is managed by allocators written in Pia over mmap, through ordinary function calls.
  • Allocators are explicit values, reached through borrowed handles that many containers can share, that meet an Allocator concept (alloc, free, resize), passed as parameters. Library code never allocates from a hidden global, and main receives the root allocator.
  • Pia.Mem provides pages, fixed_buffer, arena, scratch (LIFO with marks), pool<T> (fixed-size slab), general (TCMalloc-style: size classes, per-task caches, central free lists and a page heap of spans) and shared<a> (thread-safe wrapper with per-thread caches). Each proves its invariants as module state.
  • Lifetimes are checked by two Sema rules, with no lifetime syntax in ordinary code: a borrowed(m) result cannot outlive m, and m cannot be moved while it is lent; and with_arena scopes a region so that nothing allocated in it escapes. Freeing into the wrong allocator is a proof goal, through a ghost owns fact.
  • Every alloc returns a result that must be handled where it is called (with match or ?, ADR 0028); there is no trapping variant. Its proved postcondition is enough memory, disjoint from every live block, or Err OutOfMemory with the allocator unchanged. All free lists live in Pia.Mem, and the proof covers them.
  • Each task, worker and coroutine scope gets its own arena and general cache by default.
  • Allocators and their buffers have Drop instances, so memory not freed explicitly is freed at scope end (ADR 0028).
  • Concurrency: each task, worker or coroutine scope gets its own allocator by move. Stackless coroutine frames come from the task's allocator (ADR 0027). shared<a> is the only synchronised allocator, and its refill lock is a top-level leaf lock that never suspends.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
The design is accepted when Pia.Mem.Vec, a growable array over explicit heap allocation, is implemented and proved end to end: indices in bounds, no uninitialised reads, no overflow in capacity arithmetic, growth that gives enough memory or fails leaving the vec unchanged, no double free or use after free, no leak (RAII on every exit), frees into the right allocator, and no vec outliving its allocator. The sketch is in docs/stdlib.md.

The second acceptance test is free-list reuse (sketch): a freed block handed out again provably aliases no live object, is reachable by no stale owner or borrow, and comes back out, so the old contents cannot be read. Free lists are side metadata (slot-index stacks per span), not pointers threaded through freed blocks, so Pia.Mem needs no addr and stays out of the trusted base.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Proved code cannot leak, double free or use after free, with no run-time cost and no pauses.
  • Every allocating API takes an allocator parameter, which is more to write than with a global heap, but shows where memory comes from.
  • Sema needs a lexical borrow check for borrowed(m) results. It is smaller than Rust's, because borrows are lexical and regions are scoped.

docs.title: 27. Stackless coroutines, structured tasks, and race freedom proved from permissions
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted (2026-11-21, with deadlock freedom for channel communication added at Dean's request)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Dean wants coroutines or green threads in Pia, locking and synchronisation and communication primitives, and a prover that says whether access to a resource could race. ADR 0014 made Pia concurrent by default and ruled out races on tiles by moving them to workers, but did not cover tasks, locks, atomics, channels or shared resources in general. ADR 0004 requires an unproved race to be a compile error. The detail is in docs/concurrency.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Stackless coroutines. A function that suspends is compiled to a state machine whose frame has a size known at compile time, lowered through LLVM's llvm.coro.* intrinsics. Stackful green threads are rejected, because their stack size is a goal Pia cannot prove in general. "Green threads" are tasks on a scheduler written in Pia (Pia.Task: work-stealing workers over Pia.Sys.Thread, kqueue for I/O, a deterministic mode for tests and counterexample replay). spread and the collectives run on the same scheduler.
  • Keywords wait and yield, and an @suspends effect that is inferred inside a module and written in exported interfaces. Blocking foreign calls are marked @blocking and must go through Pia.Task.offload from suspending code.
  • Structured tasks. spawn returns a @linear task<T> that must be joined inside the scope that started it, so tasks may borrow from their parent. No detached tasks in the first version. Cancellation is an explicit token.
  • Primitives in the library (Pia.Sync, Pia.Chan): mutex<T> and rwlock<T> own their data and are reached only through scoped lock closures that may not suspend, with the data type's refinement as the lock invariant. atomic<T>, channels whose send takes moved, once, barrier, semaphore and event. No bare condition variables.
  • Static lock levels. Each lock has @level(n). A task may only acquire a lock above every level it holds, and interfaces record @acquires(n). Lock-order deadlock is then a type error.
  • Race freedom from permissions. Every pair of possibly concurrent accesses must be justified by ownership, shared fixed reading, proved disjointness, a lock, atomicity, or a happens-before edge. The type checker settles most of these, using the sendable and shareable concepts (derived over fields) and task boundaries. Disjointness goes to FPL (ADR 0020), then Z3. The model checker settles the rest: the primitives' own implementations, protocols and deadlock, and user code built from atomics. Non-memory resources (positioned file I/O, stdout) carry footprints that are checked the same way.
  • Deadlock freedom for channel communication (CSP). Every scope that uses channels has a deadlock goal: no reachable state has a set of tasks that are all blocked forever, each waiting on a send, recv, join, barrier or select that only another task in the set could complete. This includes partial deadlocks. Both channel ends are @linear (more senders come from clone), so the tasks able to wake each waiter are known, and channels are always bounded. The goal is proved in three stages. First, the channel topology is extracted from ownership: a forest whose tasks drain their inputs is deadlock-free by a lemma. Second, per-end usage protocols are inferred (and written as @protocol on exported parameters), checked for compatibility by the protocol metaprogram, and matched against library patterns with proved lemmas for any number of tasks: pipeline, worker pool, request and reply, scatter and gather. Third, the model checker searches the remaining scopes' protocol automata for a deadlocked state.
  • Memory orders. Sequential consistency and release/acquire are checked from the start. relaxed is accepted where its value orders nothing, and otherwise is an unproved obligation until the model checker has an RC11 mode.
  • The model checker is exhaustive. It uses DPOR and symmetry reduction. A search that hits a limit is unproved, never proved.
  • Unproved races, deadlocks and relaxed uses are compile errors, with a witness (FPL sample, Z3 model or schedule). --allow-unproved=race:..., deadlock:... and relaxed:... accept them as trust items.
  • Certificates. @suspends, @blocking, @acquires, @threadsafe/@serial, sendable/shareable of exported types, and module-state footprints are part of the interface and its hash (ADR 0024). The certificate records each race goal's stage and, for the model checker, the exhaustive search size. Accepted races, @threadsafe foreign claims and still-trusted primitives are trust items.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The borrow checker becomes the race checker. Most programs never reach the model checker.
  • Function colouring is visible, and generic code over both colours needs effect polymorphism in generics (M9).
  • The model checker is substantial work. Until it lands, the primitives are trusted wrappers over os_unfair_lock and pthreads, and the trust report says so.
  • Races between processes, for example on the file system, are out of scope.
  • Channel protocols join the interface, so changing how an exported function uses a channel changes its interface hash.
  • Implementation is tracked in #74.

docs.title: 28. Errors propagate with ? to a scope's handler; cleanup runs at scope end
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-21), on the condition recorded under "Cleanup never shadows the error in flight"

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every allocation and every system call can fail, and Dean wants each failure handled where it happens (ADR 0026). He likes ?-style propagation where a scope defines one handler for the closed set of errors that can occur in it. He also wants RAII for anything not freed explicitly, so the language needs cleanup handlers that run at scope end. The detail is in docs/stdlib.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• result t e carries a closed error set e, a variant type or a union of them, and error sets are part of function interfaces. A result must be used.
  • e? yields the Ok payload or jumps with the error to the nearest enclosing handle block. With no handler, the error is returned, and the function's declared error set must include it.
  • A handle block on a function body, let ... in scope or loop body must cover exactly the closed set of errors its scope's ?s can produce. The compiler computes that set.
  • defer e registers cleanup for scope end. Types with a Drop instance are dropped at the end of their owning scope unless moved or freed. Both run in reverse order on every exit, including ?.
  • Cleanup has no error set, cannot suspend, and takes no lock other than a top-level leaf lock. A resource whose cleanup can fail is @linear and must be consumed explicitly. A trap runs no cleanup.
  • Cleanup never shadows the error in flight (Dean's condition on accepting this ADR). Two rules make it hold:
  • It is a proof obligation, not only a type rule. Every defer body and drop must have an empty error set, and the verifier raises a cleanup goal at each exit: the error that reaches the handler is the one the ? raised, unchanged by the cleanup run on the way.
  • A release that can fail, such as closing a file opened for writing, is written defer? e, with e : result unit c. Every cleanup still runs, and the scope's errors become the aggregate cleanup_error<e, c> = | Failed of e | Cleanup of list c | Both of { error : e; cleanup : list c }. Exiting normally with failed cleanups gives Cleanup cs, in the order they ran. Exiting with e gives Failed e, or Both when cleanups also failed. The original error is never lost, and the scope's handler covers the aggregate like any other closed set. A @linear value whose consumption can fail may be live across a ? only when a defer? consumes it.
  • With ADR 0027: ? does not cross a task or lock closure (a task's error returns from join; a lock body's error is its result, after release). A scope exiting early joins or cancels-then-joins its children before running its own cleanup. Cancellation is an explicit token that yields Err Cancelled.
  • A handler arm knows only what holds where its errors can be raised (Dean, 2026-11-22). Each ? that can raise an arm's error reaches that arm from its own point in the scope, so the arm is checked, and proved, once for each such ?: it may use a binding, and rely on a callee's postcondition, only if that holds at every ? that reaches it. In let a = f x? in let b = g a? in ..., an arm for an error only g raises may use a and what f ensures about it, and an arm for an error only f raises may not mention b. An arm reached by both may use neither. A catch-all arm is reached by every ? whose errors no earlier arm takes.
  • handle and defer become reserved words, and defer? is defer followed by ?.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Failure paths are visible and exhaustively handled, and cleanup is guaranteed on all of them, which is what lets every allocation be fallible without clutter.
  • The verifier walks each exit's cleanup as code at that exit, so drops are proved like everything else.
  • IRGen needs scope-exit lowering (a cleanup chain per scope), which is also what coroutine cancellation uses (ADR 0027).

docs.title: 29. Comments are syntax: \ line comments, doc comments, and literate .pia.md files
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia has one kind of comment, OCaml's nesting (* ... *) (grammar.md), and the lexer throws it away. Two things are missing.

A line comment. Short notes at the end of a line are awkward as block comments. The obvious spellings are taken or reserved: // and -- are kept as future operators, # is kept for directives, ;; is the item separator and ; is sequencing. Every run of operator characters (+ - * / < > = | & ^ ~ ! % ?) is a possible operator, so any spelling built from them, such as %%, would take a symbol away from the operator space for good.

Comments a program can see. Dean wants literate programming: a metaprogram should be able to walk a listing and see the prose as well as the code. Uses include checking that every exported function is documented, copying documentation into generated code, the language server showing a definition's documentation on hover, and later a library that renders listings as LaTeX, HTML, SVG or DOT (#63) and a Jupyter kernel (#64). None of this works if the lexer discards comments.

Compilers that keep comments do it in one of two ways. Roslyn and Swift keep trivia on every token, which round-trips source exactly but makes every consumer step over it. Go's ast.CommentMap and rustc's doc attributes attach comments to the nearest syntax node, which is what a reader means by "the comment on this function". Pia's metaprograms work on nodes, so the second fits.

docs.title: Lexical
docs.text:
1. \ starts a line comment that runs to the end of the line. Backslash is not used anywhere else outside string literals, so this takes nothing away from operators, directives or separators. It is Forth's line comment.
let tile : u32 = 16  \ elements per SIMD tile
  1. (* ... *) is unchanged. It still nests, and (* still always opens a comment, so multiplication as a value is still ( * ).
  2. (** ... *) is a doc comment, as in OCaml. (**) is an empty ordinary comment, and (*** starts an ordinary comment, so banner lines of stars stay ordinary.
  3. Comments are still invisible to the layout rule and to the phrase grammar. A comment can go anywhere whitespace can, and no program changes meaning.

docs.title: Comments in the syntax tree
docs.text:
1. Every comment is kept as a Comment node with a style (line, block, doc or prose), a place (leading, trailing or detached) and its text. The text is the comment's content without its delimiters, trimmed of surrounding whitespace. Line comments on consecutive lines, each alone on its line, merge into one comment, so a paragraph written with \ is one node.
  2. Comments are attached to the node they describe, not stored as items. A node keeps its comments beside its children, so no existing pass, child index or golden test changes. The parser attaches each comment once:
  3. A trailing comment has code before it on its line, and nothing after it. It goes to the outermost node that ends at the token before it and starts on that line, or, if no node starts on that line (as with done), to the innermost node that ends there. A ;, , or in before it is skipped. After a token that leads into what follows, such as =, then or an opening bracket, the comment leads instead.
  4. Any other comment goes to the outermost node that starts at the next token. It is leading if no blank line separates them, and detached otherwise, like a section heading or a licence header.
  5. A comment with no token after it goes to the program, as detached.
  6. Hygiene does not apply to comments. Comments bind no names and refer to none, so renaming never looks inside them and a name in a comment never resolves. Hygiene (ADR 0022) is about code; the text of a comment is the author's.

docs.title: Metaprograms
docs.text:
1. Builtins:
Builtin Meaning listing () the program's items in source order, followed by the comments at the end of the file comments x the comments attached to x, in source order doc x the text of the doc and prose comments leading x, joined by blank lines; "" when there are none text c, style c, place c a comment's text, style and place, as strings kind x the kind of a syntax value, such as "LetItem" or "Comment" with_doc s x a copy of the syntax x with a leading doc comment s fail s stop with the error s, reported at the expansion site

A comment value can be inspected but not spliced into code: there is no code it could become. with_doc is the way to put documentation on generated code. 9. Quotes keep their comments. A comment written inside `( ... ) is attached to the quoted code, and the code the quote builds carries it, at the expansion site's location like the rest of the quote. 10. Splices keep comments. Spliced syntax keeps the comments attached to it. A comment attached to the splice itself, as in `( (** the sum *) $e ), moves to the code that replaces it. 11. Expansion keeps comments. When expansion replaces a node, such as an operator becoming a builtin call or a top-level metaprogram call becoming the items it returns, the comments move to the replacement (the first item, for a list).

docs.title: Literate files
docs.text:
1. A file ending in .pia.md is literate. It is Markdown: prose by default, and code only inside fenced blocks whose info string is pia. Other fences, such as ocaml or console, are prose. Line and column numbers are those of the Markdown file, so diagnostics point into it.
  2. Prose becomes prose comments. The prose before a code block, up to the previous block, is one comment that leads the block's first item, so it is that item's documentation even with the blank line Markdown puts before a fence. Prose after the last block is detached on the program. Code blocks are joined in order into one program, and each block must close every bracket it opens.
  3. piac --literate reads any file as literate, and piac --dump-ast --comments and --dump-expanded --comments show the comment nodes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Programs can see their own documentation without a separate tool, and the language server can show it on hover. A metaprogram can enforce a documentation policy, or carry docs from a type to the code derived from it.
  • Rendering to LaTeX and other formats (#63) still needs a metaprogram output channel that is not code, and the source spelling of a node (source x), which needs end positions in the syntax tree. The attachment pass already computes node extents, so this is a small step.
  • A Jupyter kernel (#64) maps onto literate files directly: Markdown cells are prose, code cells are fenced pia blocks.
  • Comments are not round-tripped byte for byte: whitespace inside them is trimmed, and a comment's exact column is not kept. A formatter would need more.
  • Attachment is a heuristic. A comment between two arguments attaches to the second; a comment after a then on its own line leads the then branch. The rules are simple to state, and --dump-ast --comments shows the result.
  • \ reads as an escape to C programmers. It cannot be confused with one in Pia, since escapes only exist inside strings.

docs.title: 30. Optimised object layouts are published, and a changed layout fails to load until relinked
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-27)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean wants the compiler free to optimise data layout: reorder fields, pack them, choose alignment, and stash information in the low bits of pointers. Modules should advertise the layout they chose, so rebuilds and static links agree on how data is laid out. When a library's layout changes, dynamic loading must fail and the importer must be relinked. Free-list reuse is a case that must stay safe.

ADR 0024 publishes interfaces and proof certificates in shared libraries and makes dyld refuse a library with the wrong interface hash. Folding layout into that hash would force a re-proof on every layout change, though proofs never depend on offsets. The alternatives elsewhere are fixed C-like layout (no optimisation), layout resolved at load time (Objective-C non-fragile ivars, Swift resilience: offsets become run-time values, which blocks folding and vectorisation), or no dynamic ABI at all (Rust).

The full design is in docs/abi.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The defining module chooses and publishes each type's layout. It emits a layout descriptor (shape, fields with bit offsets and encodings, sum-type tag placement, pointer tag bits, component hashes, layout algorithm version, profile hash) in a .pial file and in __TEXT,__pia_layout.
  • Two hashes per type, separate from the interface hash. The shape hash covers size, alignment and calling-convention class, which is what abstract uses need. The layout hash covers the whole descriptor, for importers that touch fields, variants or tags. Hashes compose through component types. Each importer records the weakest hash it used.
  • Layout never changes a proof. Verification runs before layout is chosen. size_of and align_of are symbols with refinements in proofs, folded at codegen. A proof that needs a concrete size records a dependency on the layout hash. A layout change therefore means a relink: re-run codegen and link from cached verified IR, reusing the certificate.
  • Fail at load, relink to fix. Libraries export _pia$s$ and _pia$l$ witness symbols per type and hash. Importers reference the ones they used. A changed layout makes dyld refuse to launch, or Pia.Dl.open return LayoutChanged. The static link checker reports which objects need their codegen rerun.
  • Policies. @layout(auto) (default, optimised, deterministic), @layout(c) (required across extern), @layout(packed), and @layout(frozen) (pinned by a checked-in baseline, for stable library ABIs).
  • Pointer tagging. Low bits only, k bits only when the pointee's alignment of at least 2^k is proved from provenance (Pia.Mem.alloc guarantees 16-byte alignment, so 4 bits). Never the high bits, which arm64e pointer authentication, MTE and top-byte-ignore claim. More tag bits raise the pointee's alignment, which is part of its shape. Tags are part of the containing type's layout, never cross extern, and tagging and untagging are verified ops.
  • Free-list reuse. Allocator free lists see only sizes and alignments (ADR 0026). Allocating and freeing sides bind the same shape witness, so they agree on the size class. Pools compose their element's hash. Reused blocks come back as out memory, so old fields and tags are unobservable, and size-class alignment keeps low-bit tags valid.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The compiler can reorder, pack, niche-fill and tag without any ABI promise to break, and offsets stay compile-time constants for folding, vectorisation and proofs.
  • A layout change costs importers a relink, never a re-verification, and in Bazel only codegen and link actions rerun.
  • Shipping a library with a stable binary layout takes an explicit @layout(frozen) and a checked-in baseline.
  • One extra witness bind per imported type, at load.
  • dyld's own error for a missing witness is cryptic, so pia-cert check is needed to explain it.

docs.title: 31. A verified REPL over a reusable session, with proved live redefinition
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-27)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean wants Pia usable interactively, building up an environment the way a Lisp REPL does: each definition joins a persistent environment, and later input can use and redefine it. Claude should be able to drive it too, so it needs a scriptable mode with machine-readable output, then an MCP server with just two tools, execute and poll, in the style of Code Mode. The planned Jupyter kernel (#64) needs the same core.

Dean also wants code sent to the REPL to change the environment the way Lisp code can, including metaprograms that modify live, running code. Two constraints come with that. Every live transformation must be proved safe with all of the language's verification facilities: there are no unchecked hot-swaps. And the live facilities belong to the REPL, which is a self-contained programming environment. Pia.Rt must not carry them, so a normal compiled program has none of that machinery unless it explicitly imports it.

Three existing rules shape the design:

  • Unproved obligations are compile errors unless a flag accepts specific ones (ADR 0004, --allow-unproved).
  • There is no shadowing, even in nested scopes (ADR 0022). A Lisp REPL rebinds a name freely; Pia cannot.
  • Interfaces evolve by proved refinement: a new version is compatible with an old one when it has the same types and layout, a weaker requires and a stronger ensures (ADR 0024). Layout has its own hashes, and a layout change costs a relink, never a re-proof (ADR 0030, proposed).

Prior art: OCaml's toplevel and utop keep a typed environment and allow shadowing. Common Lisp and Clojure redefine through a global indirection (the symbol's function cell, or a var) so running code picks up new definitions at the next call. Erlang hot code loading keeps two versions of a module, and processes move to the new one at their next external call. Julia's world age makes new definitions visible only at the top level, so a running function keeps seeing the methods it started with. Dafny and F* have IDE modes that re-verify on each edit but no live environment.

docs.title: The session is the core
docs.text:
• pia::repl::Session holds the environment and runs cells. A cell is Pia code or a :command. The environment is the list of top-level items that earlier cells committed, kept as source. Each cell is parsed together with the environment (so operators and metaprograms declared earlier apply), expanded to a fixed point, lowered and verified as one program.
  • Cells are transactions. A cell is committed only if the whole environment plus the cell verifies: every obligation is proved, or accepted by :allow (the REPL's --allow-unproved). Otherwise nothing changes and the cell's failures, counterexamples and unproved goals come back as events. So the environment is always a program that verifies.
  • Expressions are evaluated only after they are proved. An expression in a cell becomes a hidden constant, is verified like any definition (a call outside a precondition fails before anything runs), then compiled through the normal codegen pipeline and run with the ORC JIT through MLIR's ExecutionEngine. Its value and type are shown. Constants that a cell defines are evaluated the same way. Evaluation always terminates, because termination is one of the obligations (decreases); only :allow can admit code that might not.
  • Front ends only render events. Session::execute returns a list of typed events (defined, redefined, removed, value, type, proof, error, info). pia repl renders them as text; pia repl --json speaks one JSON object per line in each direction; the MCP server and the Jupyter kernel serialise the same events.
  • pia::repl::Kernel makes it asynchronous. It runs a session on a worker thread, takes cells as numbered jobs and lets callers poll them with a timeout. That is exactly the shape of the MCP tools: execute submits a cell and waits briefly, returning the result or a job handle, and poll waits for a handle. Jupyter's execute_request maps onto the same calls.

docs.title: Redefinition under the no-shadowing rule
docs.text:
• Defining a name that exists is an error, with the ADR 0022 message: rename it x', or replace it.
  • :redef replaces a definition explicitly. The old item is removed and the new one is checked in its place, together with everything else, so every dependent is re-verified against the new definition. If any dependent's proof breaks, the redefinition is refused and the error lists the dependents that use it. :forget removes a definition the same way, and is refused while anything uses it.
  • A name generated by a metaprogram call belongs to that call: redefining it means redefining the call.

docs.title: Live redefinition
docs.text:
The first version re-verifies and recompiles the whole environment for each cell, and each evaluation runs to completion before the next cell, so nothing runs while the environment changes. Live redefinition, where a cell or a metaprogram replaces a function while tasks are still running it, keeps the same soundness argument by classifying each change:

  1. A refinement swaps in place. If the new definition has the same type and layout, its requires is implied by the old one's, and its ensures implies the old one's under the old requires, it refines the old interface (the ADR 0024 check, run by the verifier). Every dependent's proof assumed only the old contract, so all of them still hold without re-verification. The new code is installed behind the function's indirection slot with one atomic store; calls that start after the store run the new code, and frames already running finish on the old code, which stays mapped until no frame uses it (an epoch counter per code version, reclaimed when its count drops to zero).
  2. Any other contract change re-verifies its dependents, transactionally. The new definition and every transitive dependent are verified together against the new contract. If all of them hold, the whole set is swapped at once, at a point where none of them has a frame on any task's stack (the runtime waits for, or asks for, that quiescent point). If any fails, nothing changes.
  3. A change of type or layout is a relink. The layout and shape hashes of ADR 0030 change, so every dependent is recompiled from its verified IR, and its proofs are reused when the interface hash did not change. A live value of the old layout can only cross over through a migration function from the old type to the new one, which is itself verified (total, and preserving any invariant the new type states). Without one, the change is refused while values of the old type are alive.
  4. Module state invariants must hold across the swap. When a function belongs to a module with state invariants (ADR 0006), the swap happens only between calls into the module, where the invariant is known to hold, and the new definitions must preserve the same invariant.

In each case the REPL session holds a certificate for its environment, as a library does under ADR 0024: one interface hash per definition, recorded with the hashes its proofs assumed. A swap updates the certificate in the same transaction, so :proof always shows what the running code is proved against.

docs.title: What is built
docs.text:
The first live phase is built (docs/repl.md, "Live redefinition"):

  • Tasks. :spawn e runs an evaluation on its own thread; :tasks lists them and :wait n waits for one. A task's reach is every definition its expression can call, through the environment's references.
  • Slots. In the REPL, every call from one definition to another loads the callee's address from a slot with an acquire load and calls it indirectly. Each cell's code is compiled into its own engine, and its addresses are stored into the slots with release stores. An engine stays alive while any task that might run its code is alive, which is a coarser form of the per-version epoch above.
  • The refinement rule, as built. When :redef (or a metaprogram) replaces a definition in a running task's reach, the new definition must have the same shape (parameter count, kinds and types, and result type), and its body must be proved against the old contract: a hidden function with the new body and the old requires and ensures (renamed to the new parameter names) goes through the verifier with everything else. This is case 1, checked directly instead of by comparing contracts, so a new body that meets the old contract is accepted even when its own contract changed. If it holds, the new code is swapped in; otherwise nothing is committed and the error names the task and the failing claim.
  • Cases 2 and 3, for code. A change that does not refine, or that changes a function's type (including through a record type it uses, since shapes compare types in full), is verified with everything else as usual. Then the changed definitions and every definition that calls one of them, in its old or new version, are swapped together at a quiescent point. Code a task may run counts its calls in progress in a per-definition gate: before it loads the callee's slot, a call adds one to the callee's counter with a sequentially consistent atomic add and checks the gate's flag, and it subtracts one when it returns. To swap, the session sets the flag on every gate in the set, waits until all of their counters are zero, stores the new code into the slots, and clears the flags. While a flag is set, a call into the set from a definition outside it backs out and waits, while a call from inside the set goes ahead so that the set drains. If the set does not drain within quiesceMs (two seconds), nothing is committed, and the error names the definitions the task never left. Callers outside the set relied only on contracts that did not change, so their running frames stay valid. This is sound because every frame of the set either finished before the swap or starts after it: no frame runs old code proved against a contract that no longer holds.
  • State, migration and invariants (cases 3 and 4). The REPL has state: a top-level let count : mutable u8 invariant count <= 100 = 0 keeps its value between cells (docs/repl.md, "State"). It stands in for module state until M8, with the same proof obligations:
  • Every definition that uses a state, directly or through a call, takes it as a borrowed inout mutable one-element buffer, requires its invariant and ensures it, has it as an invariant of each of its loops, and ensures the state unchanged if it never writes it. The rewrite needs no new verifier support, and the no-shadowing rule makes it exact: a state's name means the state wherever it appears.
  • Live values migrate through a verified function. A redefinition whose initial value names old count becomes a hidden function of the old value that requires the old invariant and ensures the new one. Proving it shows that every value the old invariant allows maps to one the new type and invariant allow. The session runs it on the stored value, and commits only if it was proved. Without old, a redefinition starts again from its initial value.
  • Invariants hold across swaps. A state belongs to the running task that uses it until the task finishes: the session cannot read, write, redefine, migrate or forget it in the meantime, so a migration never races with code running on the old value. The functions that use the state can be swapped while the task runs. Their contracts include the invariant, so a refinement keeps it, and a contract change waits for a quiescent point as above. Either way, a swap happens between calls, where the invariant is known to hold, and the new code is proved to preserve it.
  • Not yet. A state of a record or array type, and module state in compiled programs (M8). :forget or :reset of anything a task can reach waits for the task.
  • Pia.Live. The metaprogram builtin redefine marks the items it returns as redefinitions, so a metaprogram can replace live code through the same checked path as :redef. Only the REPL enables it; piac reports it as an error.

docs.title: The environment as data
docs.text: Metaprograms in the REPL can read and change the environment, as Lisp code can: list its definitions as syntax, fetch one, and define, redefine or forget items. These builtins belong to a REPL-only module, Pia.Live. A metaprogram's changes go through exactly the same path as a typed cell: the result is a transaction that is verified before it is committed, under the rules above. Nothing a metaprogram does can install unverified code.

docs.title: Kept out of ordinary programs
docs.text: The session, the JIT, the indirection slots and Pia.Live are part of the REPL tool, not of the language runtime. Pia.Rt does not contain them, ordinary compiled programs call functions directly with no indirection, and code that wants live redefinition must import Pia.Live explicitly, which only the REPL (or a program that deliberately embeds it) provides.

docs.title: Teaching the language (amendment, 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
Dean asked that the MCP server also teach Pia's syntax and semantics, so that an agent connected to it, with or without the skills loaded, wastes fewer cells and less context. The server still has exactly two tools; the teaching goes through the surfaces MCP already has and through execute:

  • instructions are a primer of under 2 KB (skills/pia-mcp/instructions.md), with the list of guide topics. Clients put them in the agent's context at connection, so they cost every session, and they hold only what prevents the most failed cells.
  • :help <topic> is a REPL command, so it works in every client and in pia repl. Each topic is one section of the pia-language, pia-contracts or pia-mcp skill. The same text is served as MCP resources, pia://guide/<topic>, for clients that attach resources. A new tool for it was rejected: it would add a schema to every session for something one command already does.
  • Hints. A failed cell's result ends with one line per kind of failure, recognised by the diagnostic's wording, saying the fix and the topic. They are added by the MCP server only, so pia repl's text, which the docs' console blocks check, is unchanged.

The guide is not a second copy. src/repl/embed_guide.py cuts it from the skills when the server is built, and fails the build when a skill gains a section that is neither a topic nor deliberately skipped. The skills' examples are already proved by //tests/docs:skills_test, so what the server teaches is checked against the compiler.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every value the REPL prints comes from code that was proved first, so the REPL teaches the language's main rule rather than bending it.
  • Each cell re-verifies the whole environment. That is simple and obviously sound, and fast enough for interactive sizes; caching proofs per definition by interface hash is the planned optimisation.
  • The MCP server and the Jupyter kernel are thin layers over Kernel, with no second implementation of the language.
  • Live redefinition reuses the refinement check that shared libraries need anyway, so the REPL and ADR 0024 share one notion of compatible change.
  • Running code that is swapped out keeps running on its old version until it returns, so a long-running task sees a consistent set of definitions, much like Julia's world age.
  • Mutable top-level state, I/O and the concurrency runtime do not exist yet; when they arrive, quiescent points and migration functions become runtime work, not just compile-time checks.

docs.title: 32. Proofs run in parallel, one goal per solver, sliced, cached and selectable
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Build time is a benchmark Pia always watches. Every build proves every goal, so proving is on the critical path of every edit, and it grows with the program: the stream delineation demo (docs/streams.pia.md) has a goal that costs Z3 about 57 million resource units.

The verifier (src/verify/Verifier.cpp, docs/verifier.md) already decides each goal in its own query, with its own z3::context, and calls use the callee's contract rather than its body. But it solved the queries one after another on one thread. Each query held everything before its goal (every parameter's range, every op, every earlier goal as an assumption) whether the goal needed it or not. There was no way to prove one function or one goal on its own, and an unchanged goal was proved again on every run. The Presburger stage of ADR 0020 is not implemented yet.

PR #108 made pia_object decide goals by Z3's deterministic resource limit (--solver-rlimit) instead of the wall clock, so a goal's result no longer depends on load. That is what makes parallel proving safe: running many queries at once can no longer turn a proof into a timeout.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• One goal, one solver, many threads. Goals are still listed and encoded in walk order on one thread, because encoding builds smt dialect IR in the module's MLIRContext. The encoded SMT-LIB queries are then decided on a pool of threads, one per core by default (--jobs=N), each in a fresh z3::context. Larger queries start first. Each job writes only its own outcome, so the report keeps the walk order, and with an rlimit the result of every goal is the same on one thread or many. The REPL, pia-lsp and pia_object all get this through verifyModule.
  • Goal slicing, measured and off by default. With --slice, a query is cut to its cone of influence: the goal's own assertion (the encoder asserts the negated goal last) plus, transitively, every assertion that shares an uninterpreted symbol with one already kept. Dropping assertions only weakens the hypotheses, so an unsat slice proves the goal. A slice that is sat or unknown may have lost an assumption that mattered, such as a contradictory path condition, so the whole query is solved again and its model is the counterexample. Slicing therefore changes how fast a goal is proved, never whether it is. On the benchmark it lost: the streams demo took 392 million resource units and 47 seconds on one thread sliced, against 269 million and 33 seconds unsliced, because smaller queries are not always easier for Z3 and a goal whose slice is satisfiable is solved twice. So it stays off until a better slicing rule (for example, slicing only queries above a size, or giving the sliced attempt a fraction of the rlimit) wins on the benchmark.
  • Modular reasoning stays at contracts. A call contributes its callee's requires as a goal and its ensures as assumptions, never the callee's body, so a callee is proved once, in its own function, and a caller's query does not grow with the callee's implementation. Today a query still holds every earlier goal of its function as an assumption; slicing is the tool for trimming that once it pays.
  • Selecting a subset. --verify-only=<spec> (repeatable) proves only the goals a spec selects: a function name, a module (its file name, edges.pia or streams.pia.md), or a location file:line[:col], the same forms as --allow-unproved. Earlier goals are still assumed, exactly as in a full run, since a full build proves them in their own queries. A selective run never generates code: --verify-only implies --verify.
  • Proof cache. --proof-cache=<dir> records each proved goal under the SHA-256 of a domain prefix, the Z3 version, the rlimit and the whole query (<dir>/<2 hex>/<hash>, written to a temporary file and renamed, so concurrent builds can share a directory). A goal whose hash is present is not solved again. Only proofs are cached, so a failing goal always reports a fresh counterexample. The rlimit is in the key so that a warm cache cannot prove a goal that a cold build would give up on. Because a call is encoded from its callee's contract, a callee's body change leaves its callers' hashes alone, and a contract change changes them: the same rule as the interface hashes of ADR 0024, at the granularity of one goal. When those interface hashes exist, a module's cached goals can be keyed by its imports' interface hashes as well. In Bazel, pia_object actions are already cached per file; the proof cache serves piac, the REPL and the language server between edits.
  • Build time is a tracked benchmark. tools/bench/proof_bench.py verifies the files in tools/bench/corpus.txt (the edges and streams demos and the verifier tests; the standard library joins as its modules land) on one thread and on every core. It records, per file, the goals, the solver queries, the total Z3 resource count and the wall times, and compares them with tools/bench/baseline.json. The resource count is deterministic, so CI fails when it grows by more than 10%. Wall times are gated (--wall-threshold) only against a baseline from the same host, and CI reports them in the job summary and keeps the JSON as an artifact. The benchmark also fails if the report differs between one thread and many, or the cost by more than 5%: Z3's resource count varies by about 1% between runs, because some of its hash tables depend on memory addresses. --verify-stats prints the same counters for any piac run.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Proving scales with cores. A file with many SMT goals finishes in about the time of its costliest goal rather than the sum of all of them.
  • Measured on Dean's 8-core iMac (tools/bench/baseline.json): the corpus verifies in 61 seconds on one thread and 32 on eight. The streams demo goes from 33 seconds to 11, and edges from 13 to 6. With a warm proof cache, streams verifies in 2.6 seconds, of which 1.5 is startup and 1 is encoding. Once there are cores to spare, the costliest single goal sets the time, so splitting such goals (by cases, or through intermediate lemmas) is the next lever.
  • Every piac run used to spend about 1.5 seconds in dyld before main, binding about 365,000 weak symbols (LLVM, MLIR and Z3 templates) against its own 420,000-entry export trie. The tools now export only their Mach-O header and are dead-stripped (tools/link.bzl, issue #120), which brings startup to 8 ms. Since then the corpus verifies in 43 seconds on one thread and 14.5 on eight, and about 97% of that time is spent in Z3. Z3 is built optimised even in fastbuild, so -c opt and --config=lto change the size of piac but not its proof time.
  • One function or one goal can be proved on its own, for editors and for iterating on a hard goal, without loading every proof.
  • The resource count per goal changes with slicing, so the pia_object rlimit is re-measured against the benchmark rather than the old per-goal numbers.
  • Encoding is still sequential and costs time proportional to goals times function size. Making it parallel needs a thread-safe way to build queries outside the module's context (separate contexts per function, or encoding straight to SMT-LIB), and is left for when the benchmark shows it matters.
  • pia_object actions run in parallel in Bazel and each also uses every core, so a large build can oversubscribe the machine. That costs throughput, not correctness, because the rlimit decides results. A solver_jobs attribute can cap it if the benchmark shows a loss.
  • The Presburger stage (ADR 0020) slots in as another kind of job in the same pool.

docs.title: Amendment, 2026-11-24: CI runs the benchmark only when it can move
docs.text:
Dean asked for the benchmark to run only when something that matters to it changes. It proves the corpus twice and took 69 minutes on Linux and 56 on macOS in the run that added this (PR #407), against 8 to 11 minutes for the build and tests, so it was most of a cached CI run, and BuildBuddy's remote execution cannot help, because the benchmark times proofs on the runner itself.

  • A what changed job in .github/workflows/ci.yml passes the changed paths to tools/bench/needs_bench.py, and both jobs run the benchmark step only when it says yes. The jobs themselves, and their required checks, run as before; only the step is skipped.
  • What can move a gated cost: the files in tools/bench/baseline.json and the library modules they import, transitively; src/ except the language server, the REPL, code generation and certificates, none of which runs under piac --verify; tools/piac/piac.cpp; tools/bench/; third_party/, the module files, .bazelrc and .bazelversion; and the CI workflow. A file that is not in the baseline is reported as new and never gated, so new library modules, demos and tests do not need a run until they join the baseline.
  • When the job cannot tell what changed, the benchmark runs. Pull requests compare with the base they merge into, pushes to main with the commit before, and queue groups with their base.
  • A nightly run on main (16:00 UTC) builds, tests and benchmarks everything, so a change the path list misses is still caught within a day. A night with no new commits skips it. Running the workflow by hand also runs the benchmark.
  • Over the last 60 commits on main, 28 would have skipped it: ADRs, docs, case studies, skills, CI tweaks, and test-size changes.

docs.title: 33. Module initialisation: registries, proved @init hooks, and opt-in dynamic registration
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-21

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0024 keeps Pia images free of dyld-run static initializers, so the certificate check always runs before any guarded code. Dean accepted it on condition that Pia gets a supported hook and a standardised registration mechanism for initialisation. In C++ that is implementation-defined; in Pia it must be well-defined and proved in advance. He added that at dynamic load time a library should call a runtime-provided function that registers its initialisers, much like the REPL (ADR 0031) but without a JIT: newly loaded symbols and functions are registered with the runtime and can be looked up, including through an eval-like mechanism.

C++ static initialization has an unspecified cross-unit order, lets one initializer read another's unconstructed object, lets initializers throw, loop or start threads, and runs them inside the loader. Ada's elaboration checks, Go's dependency-ordered init, Rust's refusal of life-before-main, and linker sets are the main alternatives. The full design is in docs/init.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Registries for registration without code. let r : registry t where P declares one; @register(M.r) let e = ... adds a compile-time constant entry, proved against t where it is defined. The linker collects entries into a constant table ordered by module name then entry name. Whole-set properties such as unique (.name) are checked by the static linker and again by the loader when libraries add entries.
  • One @init per module, for state that must be built at run time. It returns the module state's initial value and establishes its invariant; its signature and contract are in the interface hash. It must be proved to terminate, is infallible unless it declares an error set (which is then in the interface), gets only the capabilities in init_env (root allocator, arguments, environment, clock), and cannot spawn, await or lock. Teardown is the state's Drop, which cannot fail.
  • A proved order. Every function that reads module M's state has an implicit precondition initialised M. Inits run in a topological order of the init dependency graph (an edge where an init reads another module's state, which must be an import), with ties broken by module name. Reading state that is not yet initialised is a verification error, and a cycle is a compile or link error. Dependency sets go in the certificate, so the order is computed from certificates alone.
  • The runtime runs inits, never dyld. Images carry __TEXT,__pia_init and __DATA_CONST,__pia_reg tables and no __mod_init_func. At launch, the Pia entry point runs the certificate check, the registry checks, the inits in order, main, then the drops in reverse. A failed init drops what already ran, and main never runs.
  • Opt-in dynamic registration, Pia.Dyn, on the REPL's environment model without a JIT. Each image has one compiler-generated registration function, _pia$register$<image>, which Pia.Dyn.open calls after the certificate check. It hands the runtime constant tables of symbols (name, interface hash, pointer, eval adapter), registry entries and inits. The runtime rejects name clashes, checks registries, runs the new inits in order, and undoes everything on failure. Pia.Rt does not contain Pia.Dyn, just as it does not contain Pia.Live.
  • Typed lookups. Pia.Dyn.bind env I lib returns a record typed by interface I only if the library registered I's hash, or a version proved to refine it. find and bind_symbol<t> do the same for one symbol. So a lookup never returns a value whose contract differs from its certificate.
  • eval on dyn values. Pia.Dyn.eval env name args checks argument tags against the registered type, and checks the function's requires at run time with a compiled checker (the eval adapter), because no proof covered the call. Results satisfy the ensures. Only exports marked @eval get adapters, and the certificate lists them.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Issues: registries and @register (#100); @init, initialised M and the init order (#101); __pia_init/__pia_reg and the launch sequence in Pia.Rt (#102); Pia.Dyn with registration functions, open and close (#103); typed bind, find and eval with eval adapters (#104).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Initialisation order is a pure function of the program's modules, and the order fiasco becomes a proof goal with a counterexample.
  • Most static-initializer uses need no run-time code at all: registries are constant data.
  • Pia images still run nothing at dyld load, so ADR 0024's soundness argument holds.
  • Programs that never load code dynamically carry none of Pia.Dyn.
  • The REPL and dynamic loading share one environment representation and one notion of compatible change.
  • eval trades proofs for run-time precondition checks, visibly, and only where a module opts in.

docs.title: 34. Concepts as checked signatures, and concept-based overload resolution
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0009 decided that constraints on type parameters are concepts: checked metaprograms that can state laws, which every instance proves, with adapters for types that do not meet them. Generic types and generic functions landed in PR #137, but without constraints. A generic body can use any operation, and an instance only fails when it is generated. The standard library needs concepts before it can be written generically: Eq, Ord and Hash for containers, Numeric for reductions, and Allocator for Pia.Mem (ADR 0026).

Dean asked for concept-based overload resolution as the step after concepts, because it is what lets a library offer one name with several implementations, and lets the most specific one win. He also asked that constraints, specifications and contracts disambiguate by what they say, not only by named subsumption. Examples: a sort for any Ord t and a faster one for Radix t, or a copy that becomes a memcpy when its buffers are proved disjoint.

The existing sketches disagree on syntax. design.md writes a concept as a metaprogram over has_fn and law predicates, and stdlib.md writes Allocator as a sig ... end. Pia also has no overloading of any kind yet: a name means exactly one top-level function.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
A concept is a metaprogram that takes types and returns a signature, the same sig ... end that interfaces use. Each requirement is a function with a type and, optionally, a contract. A law is a lemma, as in the spec functions of PR #133, and include brings in another concept's requirements:

let meta Eq (t : type) : concept = sig
  let eq : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
  let lemma reflexive (a : t) ensures eq a a
  let lemma symmetric (a : t) (b : t) ensures eq a b ==> eq b a
end

let meta Ord (t : type) : concept = sig
  include Eq t
  let lt : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool
  let lemma irreflexive (a : t) ensures lt a a = false
  let lemma transitive (a : t) (b : t) (c : t)
    ensures lt a b && lt b c ==> lt a c
end

Because a concept is a metaprogram, its body can compute the signature, for example adding a requirement only when size_of t is small, or stopping with its own diagnostic (fail "f16 has no total order"). The first implementation accepts a literal sig with the parameters spliced in. The has_fn and law sketch in design.md is replaced by this form, which is one syntax shared with interfaces (ADR 0024) and lets a requirement carry a contract.

A constraint goes on the type parameter, as design.md already shows: (t : type where Ord t), with && for several (where Eq t && Hash t).

docs.title: Meeting a concept
docs.text:
A type meets a concept when every requirement, with the type arguments substituted, is met:

  • A function requirement is met by a function in scope with that name and exactly that signature: the same parameter types, modifiers and result type. Scope is the type's own module plus imported modules, the ADL rule of ADR 0022. If the requirement has a contract, the candidate must honour it, and that is proved: the requirement's requires implies the candidate's, and the candidate's ensures implies the requirement's.
