A candidate with no contract of its own meets only requirements with no requires, and only ensures it can be proved to satisfy from its body.
  • A law is proved once per instance, as a lemma whose body is checked against the instance's functions. There is no @assume escape (ADR 0009).
  • An included concept must be met as well, and its requirements are part of this one.

The check runs when a generic is instantiated (the use check). A failure names the concept, the requirement and the type, as in "u8 does not meet Ord: no function 'lt : u8 -> u8 -> bool'", or gives the law's counterexample.

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text:
An adapter supplies a concept's requirements for a type that does not meet it, or meets it in the wrong way, such as f32, whose = fails reflexive on NaN:

let adapter bitwise_eq : Eq f32 = struct
  let eq (a : f32) (b : f32) : bool = bits a = bits b
end

An adapter's functions and laws are proved like any other instance. It can live in any module. A type that meets a concept directly uses its own functions, and an adapter is used only when it is named (dedup<t = f32, Eq = bitwise_eq> xs) or when it is the only way the type meets the concept. Two adapters for the same concept and type in scope, with neither named, are an ambiguity error that names both.

docs.title: Definition check
docs.text:
A generic body may use only what its constraints promise. A call whose arguments have a constrained type parameter's type resolves against the requirements of that parameter's concepts (including the included ones), and against other generic functions whose constraints those concepts imply. Anything else is an error at the definition: in let max (t : type where Eq t) (a : t) (b : t) : t = if lt a b then b else a, the error is that lt is not promised by Eq t, with a hint to constrain t by Ord t.

The binding is made at the definition. The instance max<u8> calls the function that met Ord u8 at the use check, whatever else is in scope when it is generated, so an instance can never pick up a different lt than the one the concept checked.

Each instance is still proved on its own, so goals stay about concrete types. Proving a generic body once against the concepts' contracts would save build time (ADR 0032). It is sound once requirement contracts are proved at the use check, and it is left as a measured follow-up. ADR 0043 proposes it.

docs.title: Overloading
docs.text:
Several top-level functions may share a name. They form an overload set, and they may differ in their parameter types, in their constraints, or only in their contracts. This is not shadowing in the sense of ADR 0022: no name hides another, every overload is visible, and a call chooses among them. Two overloads with the same parameter types whose preconditions are equivalent (each proved to imply the other), or two generics with the same parameter patterns and equivalent constraints, are an error at the second definition, because no call could ever choose between them.

Types, concept constraints and contracts all take part in choosing. A call resolves in three steps.

  1. Viable candidates. For each overload with the right number of arguments, deduce its type arguments as today (explicit arguments, then the arguments' types, then the expected type). A candidate is viable if deduction succeeds, every argument converts to its parameter type, every constraint is met by the deduced types, and its precondition is proved at the call, from everything the verifier knows there: the caller's own requires, the path conditions of the branches the call is under, loop invariants, and the ensures of earlier calls.
  2. Ranking. Candidate A is better than B if it is at least as good for every argument and better for one, or else equal on arguments and more specific. The tests apply in order, and the first that tells A and B apart decides:
  3. per argument, an exact type match is better than a conversion (such as a literal's or a widening);
  4. a non-generic function is more specific than a generic one;
  5. between generics, A is more specific if A's parameter types are an instance of B's but not the reverse: f (xs : [u8]) over f (t : type) (xs : [t]), and f (p : pair t t) over f (p : pair a b);
  6. A is more specific if its constraints entail B's and not the reverse (see below): sort (t : type where Radix t) over sort (t : type where Ord t);
  7. A is more specific if its precondition implies B's and not the reverse. With copy (dst : out [u8]) (src : [u8]) requires disjoint dst src and a copy with no precondition, a call where the buffers are proved disjoint gets the first (a memcpy), and any other call gets the second (a memmove).
  8. Choice. The unique best viable candidate wins. No viable candidate is an error that lists each overload and why it failed: wrong arity, deduction, conversion, an unmet requirement, or an unproved precondition with its counterexample. Two or more best candidates are an ambiguity error that lists them, and suggests explicit type arguments or a fact that would separate them.

Entailment between constraints is decided from what concepts say, not only from their names. A's constraints entail B's when every concept in B's is entailed by one in A's. Concept C entails concept D:

  • at once, if include reaches D from C. This is the cheap, common case;
  • otherwise, if every requirement of D has a match in C with the same name and signature and a contract at least as strong (D's requires implies C's, and C's ensures implies D's), and every law of D follows from C's laws and contracts. Both are proved by the solver, over the concepts' type parameter left abstract, once for each pair of concepts. The result is part of the module's proof certificate and is cached like any goal.

So two concepts that say the same thing under different names entail each other, and an overload set that differs only by such concepts is rejected at its definition as never able to choose. Laws take part through entailment: Ord with a transitive law entails a Preorder whose only law is transitive.

Precondition order between overloads, A's requires implying B's, is proved once per pair when the overload set is defined, with the parameters universally quantified, so calls do not repeat it.

Choosing by contract is static. It happens at compile time, from proofs, and never adds a run-time test. A program that wants to test at run time writes the if itself, and each branch then calls the overload its path condition proves. A candidate's ensures never makes it viable: what a call means cannot depend on what the caller goes on to prove with its result.

Where it runs. IRGen ranks by types and by constraints, which need no proof of the call site. Only when candidates are still tied, and their preconditions differ, does IRGen leave the call open: a func.call of the least specific candidate that names them all, most specific first, in a pia.overload_candidates attribute. The verifier chooses at that point of the function, where it has the path facts, and retargets the call before verification and code generation. (This was first sketched as a pia.overload_call op; an attribute on the call keeps the IR valid, and the least specific candidate correct, before the choice is made.) These choices are part of compiling, not of optional verification: piac --emit=obj without --verify still decides them, --verify-only still decides every choice in the selected functions, and an --allow-unproved flag never makes a candidate viable. Each choice costs one query per tied candidate, run in parallel on ADR 0032's pool and cached by its proof cache, and calls whose types already decide cost nothing.

In a generic body, a choice by contract can use only facts that hold in every instance: the body's own contracts and path conditions, and the requirement contracts of its constraints. Every instance therefore makes the same choice, the one the definition check made.

Explicit arguments narrow the candidates before ranking, so sort<t = u32, Ord = by_value> can force the general overload for a type that also meets Radix.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text: An instance of a generic is named after its type arguments, max<u8>, as today. When a name is overloaded, every overload's symbol also carries its parameter types, eq(u8, u8) and eq(pixel, pixel), and so does its C entry point, as eq__u8_u8. Overloads with the same parameter types, told apart by contracts, add their position in the set: copy(out [u8], [u8])#2. A name that is not overloaded keeps its plain symbol and entry point, so existing C callers do not change. The published interface of ADR 0024 lists overloads separately, and adding an overload to a module changes its interface hash.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Library code can be generic and checked at its definition, and a missing operation is reported where the generic is written, not deep inside an instance.
  • Overloading lands with concepts, not after them, because structural matching needs it: eq for u8 and eq for pixel are both requirements' candidates, so they must coexist under one name. @derive(eq) then generates an eq overload instead of eq_<name>, and the record = expands to eq.
  • Ranking is a partial order, so some overload sets have no best candidate for some calls. Those are reported as ambiguity at the call, with the candidates listed, rather than resolved by declaration order.
  • Every requirement contract and every law adds proof goals per instance. They are proved once per (concept, type) pair, not once per use, and they are cached by ADR 0032's proof cache like any other goal.
  • Name lookup in a generic body is fixed at the definition, so adding a function to a module can never change what an existing instance calls. It can only make a future call ambiguous, which is reported.
  • Overload resolution can need the solver, so the solver is on the path of every build, not only of --verify. Types decide most calls with no query, and the queries that remain are small (one precondition at one call), parallel and cached.
  • Implementation order: (1) overloading of concrete functions by parameter type, with symbols and C entry points; (2) sig concepts, where constraints, the use check, include, requirement contracts and laws; (3) the definition check; (4) adapters; (5) ranking by constraints, with entailment by include and then by proof; (6) choosing by precondition in the verifier, with pia.overload_candidates. Each is a PR with its own tests.

docs.title: 35. Substitution failure removes a candidate, and constraints are proved to terminate
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), on the condition recorded under "Matching on types"

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0034 chooses among overloads by types, constraint entailment and proved preconditions. Each candidate's type arguments are deduced and then substituted into its signature. Some signatures cannot be formed for some types. A result type may be computed by a type-level metaprogram that is defined only for some types, a where predicate may be false, or a concept's metaprogram may stop with its own diagnostic. Dean asked for Pia's version of C++'s "substitution failure is not an error" (SFINAE): such a candidate drops out instead of failing the build, on the condition that the constraints can be proved to terminate.

C++ shows what to avoid. Whether an error is a soft failure or a hard one depends on an "immediate context" that is hard to see. An error in a function body is always hard, so a candidate that passes its signature can still break the build inside its instance. And template recursion is cut off by an implementation's depth limit, so which overload is chosen can depend on the compiler. Pia's metaprograms (ADR 0007, docs/meta.md) are cut off the same way, by a budget of a million interpreter steps.

docs.title: What may fail softly
docs.text:
Substituting a candidate's deduced type arguments into its signature is the candidate's substitution. It covers:

  • resolving each parameter type and the result type, including generic types and type-level metaprograms such as widen t below;
  • evaluating its where constraints: concepts (ADR 0034), and compile-time predicates over types such as size_of t <= 8;
  • proving the requirement contracts and laws that a concept constraint brings (ADR 0034, "Meeting a concept").

Any failure there, whether an unmet requirement, a fail from a metaprogram, a false predicate or a type that cannot be formed, removes the candidate from the call. It is not an error unless no candidate is left. The failure is kept as the candidate's reason, and the "no viable overload" error lists every candidate with its reason. piac --explain-overloads=<file:line> prints the reasons even when a candidate wins.

let meta widen (t : type) : type =
  if t = u8 then u16 else if t = u16 then u32 else if t = u32 then u64
  else fail (concat "no integer type is wider than " (name t))

let sum (t : type) (xs : [t]) : widen t = ...    (* never overflows *)
let sum (t : type where Numeric t) (xs : [t]) : t
  requires ...                                      (* the caller proves the bound *)
  = ...

sum xs with xs : [u16] gets the first overload, which returns a u32. With xs : [u64], widen u64 fails, so the first overload drops out and the second is the only candidate.

Nothing else fails softly. A body is never part of the substitution, and it does not have to be: the definition check of ADR 0034 proves that a generic body uses only what its constraints promise, so a body cannot fail for a type that met them. Errors in the body of a generic are reported once, at its definition, for every type. That closes the C++ gap where a candidate passes its signature and then breaks the build in its instance.

docs.title: Constraints are total
docs.text:
Which candidates survive must be a function of the types alone: the same in every build, on every machine, with any --jobs, and never decided by a step budget. So every metaprogram that runs during substitution must be proved to terminate. This covers concepts, type-level metaprograms used in a type, and where predicates. Such a metaprogram is total when:

  • it calls only total metaprograms and the interpreter's builtins (fields, name, map, fold, length, concat and the rest are total: each walks a finite value once);
  • it is not recursive, or each recursive call is on a strictly smaller argument, or it has a decreases measure.
  • Structural recursion is recognised without a proof: a call on a component of a type parameter (a field's type, a payload's type, an element type, a type argument of an instance) or on the tail of a list parameter. Types are finite trees, so this always ends.
  • Anything else needs decreases m, where m is an integer that is at least 0 and smaller at each recursive call. These goals are proved by the verifier exactly like the measures of spec functions (PR #133), with the metaprogram's integer and boolean code encoded the same way.
  • Mutual recursion needs one measure that every function of the cycle decreases, and until that is implemented it is rejected, as it is for spec functions.

Totality is checked once, where the metaprogram is defined. A metaprogram that is not total is still a metaprogram, and expansion can still run it under the step budget, but using it in a constraint or a type is an error at that use: "'widen' is used in a constraint, so it must terminate: the recursive call at 4:12 has no decreasing argument; add 'decreases ...'".

Constraint metaprograms are also pure: they inspect types and return a signature, a type, a boolean or a diagnostic, and they cannot add items to the program. So substitution cannot feed the expansion loop of ADR 0007, and --meta-cycles never affects which overload is chosen.

The step budget stays as a guard against interpreter bugs. Running out of it during substitution is an internal compiler error, never a substitution failure.

docs.title: Recursion through types
docs.text: A constraint may require constraints on other types: Eq (pair a b) requires Eq a and Eq b. These obligations are also constraints, so they too must end. Each one must be on a strictly smaller type than the one that required it, which holds for components of the type by the same structural rule. A cycle that grows types, such as C t requiring C (wrap t), is rejected at the concept's definition, because it has no decreasing measure.

docs.title: Matching on types
docs.text:
Accepted on a condition (Dean, 2026-11-22): metaprograms need a way to pattern-match on a type instead of cascading if t = u8 then ... else if .... match already takes values, and types are values, so it takes a type too, with type patterns:

let meta widen (t : type) : type =
  match t with
  | u8 -> u16
  | u16 -> u32
  | u32 -> u64
  | [e] -> [widen e]                 (* a slice, binding its element type *)
  | option e -> option (widen e)     (* an instance, binding its arguments *)
  | _ -> fail (concat "no integer type is wider than " (name t))
  • A type name (u8, pixel) matches exactly that type. [e] and [e; n] match a slice or an array and bind its element type (and length). A generic's name applied to patterns, as in option e or result t e, matches its instances and binds or matches their type arguments.
  • A lower-case name that is not a type binds the whole type, and _ matches anything. Kind patterns match by shape: record fs and variant cs bind the list of field or payload types, int matches every integer type. A name that is both a type and a binder is an error, as shadowing always is (ADR 0022).
  • Types are an open set, so a type match must end with a catch-all. An arm after one that already covers it is an error, as for value match.
  • The names a type pattern binds are components of the matched type, so a recursive call on them is structural recursion under "Constraints are total", with no decreases needed.
  • It is core match, not a library metaprogram. Dean weighed a switch metaprogram and chose core match (2026-11-22); a library form would also have needed declared expression forms and type constructors as metaprogram values. It is ordinary metaprogram code, so it needs no new keyword, and the interpreter evaluates it arm by arm. A predicate can use it as well: let meta small (t : type) : bool = match t with | u8 -> true | [e; n] -> n <= 16 && small e | _ -> false.

Arms carry contracts. This is why the match is core and not a library form (Dean, 2026-11-22): a pattern can have a precondition and a postcondition, written between the pattern and ->, with result naming the arm's value:

let meta widen (t : type) : type
  ensures size_of result > size_of t
=
  match t with
  | u8  ensures size_of result = 2 -> u16
  | u16 ensures size_of result = 4 -> u32
  | u32 ensures size_of result = 8 -> u64
  | [e; n] requires n <= 4096 -> [widen e; n]
  | _ -> fail (concat "no integer type is wider than " (name t))
  • requires c on an arm is not a guard: it does not decide which arm runs. It is an obligation on every value that reaches the arm, proved where the match is. For a type match it is checked when the arm is taken, and a false one is the candidate's reason under soft failure, so a constraint can say why a type does not fit.
  • ensures d on an arm is proved for that arm's value, and after the match it is known under the arm's pattern: t = u8 ==> size_of result = 2. For a type-level metaprogram this is what the definition check of ADR 0034 is missing: it relates widen t to t, so a generic body that uses widen t can be checked once, from the arm postconditions and the metaprogram's own ensures, instead of in every instance.
  • The same syntax applies to a value match in ordinary code, where both are verifier goals: | Some x requires x < len xs -> xs.[x] proves the bound at the match for every value that can be Some x, and | Err e ensures result = 0 -> 0 adds a fact to the Err path. A handler's arms are a value match, so they take contracts too, proved once per ? that reaches them (ADR 0028).

It was built right after ? and the error handlers (#84).

docs.title: Results are cached
docs.text: A candidate's substitution result, viable with its instance's signature or failed with its reason, depends only on the candidate and the type arguments. It is computed once per pair in a build, and its proof goals (requirement contracts and laws) go through the proof cache of ADR 0032 like any other goal.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A library can offer an overload that only exists for some types, and fall back to another, without users writing explicit dispatch, and the choice is the same everywhere.
  • Error messages for "no viable overload" can always say why each candidate failed, since every failure is a recorded reason rather than an aborted instantiation.
  • Some useful metaprograms need a decreases measure before they can be used as constraints. Structural recursion over types and lists, the common case, needs nothing.
  • Because bodies never fail softly, a generic's body errors are always reported at its definition, never at a use. That depends on the definition check of ADR 0034 landing first.
  • Implementation order, after ADR 0034's steps: (1) type-level metaprograms in signatures, and where predicates; (2) the totality check (purity, builtins, structural recursion, then decreases with verifier goals); (3) soft failure in overload resolution, with recorded reasons and --explain-overloads. Step (3) needs (2), so that soft failure is never decided by a step budget.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• Step 1 (type-level metaprograms in types, and where predicates): a where predicate is any conjunct that is a comparison, a connective other than &&, or a call of a type-level metaprogram returning bool; a false one removes the candidate with its reason. Until steps 2 and 3, a metaprogram's failure in a type or a predicate is a hard error. In the definition check, a type-level metaprogram applied to a type parameter gives a stand-in type, and a signature that has one is checked in each instance rather than once, since nothing yet relates widen t to t; concept requirements that mention type-level metaprograms would close that gap. A generic whose constraints state every predicate of another's is the more specific, and a generic body may only call a generic whose predicates its own constraints state.
  • Step 2 (the totality check): structural recursion is recognised on element p and on the elements of field_types p and type_args p that map or fold hand to a lambda, transitively. Since a type-level metaprogram's parameters are all types, an integer decreases measure has nothing to measure yet; it waits for metaprograms with value parameters in constraints. Local functions may not recurse, listing and redefine are impure, and a cycle between metaprograms is rejected.
  • Matching on types (the acceptance condition): the interpreter evaluates match with type patterns (type names, int, [e], [e; n], instances such as option e, record fs, variant cs, as) and requires a catch-all on a type. An arm's requires that fails for a type that reaches it, and an ensures that its value breaks, are metaprogram failures, so they are candidates' reasons during overload resolution. On a value match, both become assertions in the arm. The totality check counts names a type pattern binds below its top as components. Arm postconditions do not yet feed the definition check, so widen t is still checked per instance.
  • Step 3 (soft failure): a metaprogram's fail while a candidate's signature is substituted, or while its predicates are evaluated, removes the candidate with the reason. Running out of steps there, and a use of a metaprogram that may not terminate, stay errors. Results are not cached per candidate and type arguments yet; concept checks already are. --explain-overloads=<file:line> prints the candidates, their reasons and the choice, as notes.

docs.title: 36. Libraries extend the solver with theories: sorts, functions and axioms, proved consistent by a model or listed as trusted
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (2026-11-22, with Dean's answers to its open questions below, and a catalogue of example theories added at Dean's request: docs/theories.md)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked whether metaprograms could add facts and domains that reach the solver, so that a library can extend what the verifier reasons about without changes to the core compiler. His motivating case is machine learning: layers, weights, activations and residual connections, with higher-level properties such as "this network keeps its shapes consistent" or "this residual block is at most 1.5-Lipschitz" proved at the level of the network rather than of its kernels.

Pia already has most of the pieces, but not this one:

  • Spec functions and lemmas (PR #133, docs/verifier.md) add defined functions to the solver. Each is an uninterpreted function F plus its definition, guarded by its precondition, and a lemma is proved once and then assumed at its call. Everything they add is definitional, so they can never make the solver accept something false.
  • Concepts (ADR 0034) are signatures with laws, and every instance proves the laws. An adapter supplies an instance.
  • Trusted items (ADR 0023): assume and addr only in @trusted modules, unsafe calls, foreign contracts. Each is listed in its module's certificate (ADR 0024), and piac --trust-report lists them for a whole program.
  • Slicing and the proof cache (ADR 0032) keep each goal's query small and avoid re-proving.

What is missing is a way to declare a domain: a new sort (an abstract layer), functions on it that have no body (lip, residual), and facts about them (axioms). That is what SMT solvers call a theory, and Z3 takes one as declarations and quantified assertions.

The danger is plain. An axiom is a hypothesis of every query it is sent to. One wrong axiom, such as forall x, f x = 0 && f x = 1, makes every such query unsatisfiable, and the verifier reports every goal as proved. That breaks Pia's promise (ADR 0004) more quietly than any other feature could, so soundness decides the design.

Prior art: Why3 and Boogie let theories declare types, functions and axioms freely, and leave consistency to the author. Dafny and F* allow assume-style axioms but warn, and F* checks that an interface is realised by an implementation. Lean, Coq and Isabelle extend the logic by definitions, which are conservative, and they list the axioms a theorem depends on (#print axioms). ML module systems seal a structure with a signature, so clients see only the signature while the structure proves it can be met. Coq's ring and lia are decision procedures written in the prover and proved correct once (proof by reflection). Z3 itself offers a user propagator API, which runs arbitrary code inside the solver.

docs.title: A theory is a signature over new sorts
docs.text:
A theory is a module-level item, written like a concept's signature:

let theory Lip = sig
  let sort layer
  let spec in_w : (f : layer) -> usize
  let spec out_w : (f : layer) -> usize
  let spec lip : (f : layer) -> real
  let spec seq : (f : layer) -> (g : layer) -> layer
  let spec residual : (f : layer) -> layer

  let axiom lip_nonneg (f : layer) ensures lip f >= 0.0
  let axiom seq_shape (f : layer) (g : layer)
    requires out_w f = in_w g
    ensures in_w (seq f g) = in_w f && out_w (seq f g) = out_w g
  let axiom seq_lip (f : layer) (g : layer)
    requires out_w f = in_w g
    ensures lip (seq f g) <= lip f * lip g
  let axiom residual_shape (f : layer)
    requires in_w f = out_w f
    ensures in_w (residual f) = in_w f && out_w (residual f) = out_w f
  let axiom residual_lip (f : layer)
    requires in_w f = out_w f
    ensures lip (residual f) <= 1.0 + lip f
  let lemma residual_twice (f : layer)
    requires in_w f = out_w f
    ensures lip (residual (residual f)) <= 2.0 + lip f
= ()
end

A theory can contain:

  • let sort s, a new uninterpreted sort. let sort s = t is only an abbreviation for an existing type.
  • Abstract spec functions, let spec f : type with no body. To the solver, each is an uninterpreted function. A spec function with a body may appear too, and it means what it means today: a definition, with decreases if it recurses.
  • let axiom name params requires ... ensures ...: a fact, universally quantified over its parameters. To the solver it is forall params, requires ==> ensures.
  • let lemma, proved from the theory's axioms and definitions, once, like any lemma.

Theory sorts and functions are spec-only. They can appear in contracts, spec functions, lemmas and other theories, never in code, and codegen erases them, as it erases spec functions. The spec-only types real and int (unbounded, SMT Real and Int) are available in theories for the same reason: a Lipschitz constant is a real number, not an f32. They already appear in the semantics of @fp(reassoc) (ADR 0012), which proves ensures over reals. Relating float code to a real-valued theory needs an error bound in the contract, as ADR 0012's tolerance form does. That relation is out of scope here.

theory, sort and axiom are keywords only between let and the name, like spec and lemma (grammar.md).

docs.title: Metaprograms can build theories
docs.text:
A metaprogram can return a theory, as a concept metaprogram returns a signature:

let meta shape_theory (ops : [op_spec]) : theory = ...

So a library can describe its domain as data (a table of layer kinds, each with a shape rule) and generate the sorts, functions and axioms, and also the model below that proves them. This is how a domain reaches the solver without touching the compiler. A theory-building metaprogram must be total and pure, by the rules of ADR 0035, because what it returns becomes hypotheses of proofs, and the hypotheses must be the same in every build. Its result is computed once per argument tuple, named after its arguments as a generic instance is (shape_theory<...>), and shared by every module that uses that instance. (As implemented in step 5, let theory T = shape_theory ops names the result T, and a second let theory with the same call in the same module is another name for it; sharing an instance across modules waits for interfaces that carry theories. The prelude's machine, a state machine's theory and model from a table of transitions, is the first such metaprogram: docs/theories.md.)

docs.title: Soundness: every theory is either modelled or trusted
docs.text:
A theory with axioms has one of two statuses, recorded in its module's certificate.

Modelled (the default, and nothing is trusted). A model is given, in the theory's module or in another module found by the ADL rule (see the answers below): a structure that picks a concrete Pia type for each sort and a spec function for each abstract function, and proves every axiom as a lemma about them.

let summary = type { in_w : usize; out_w : usize; lip : real where lip >= 0.0 }

let model shapes : Lip = struct
  let sort layer = summary
  let spec in_w (f : summary) : usize = f.in_w
  let spec out_w (f : summary) : usize = f.out_w
  let spec lip (f : summary) : real = f.lip
  let spec seq (f : summary) (g : summary) : summary =
    { in_w = f.in_w; out_w = g.out_w; lip = f.lip * g.lip }
  let spec residual (f : summary) : summary =
    { in_w = f.in_w; out_w = f.out_w; lip = 1.0 + f.lip }
end

The model is checked like an adapter meeting a concept (ADR 0034, "Meeting a concept"). Each sort and function has the stated type, and each axiom, with the model's definitions substituted, is proved for all values of the model's types. Here seq_lip becomes f.lip * g.lip <= f.lip * g.lip, and lip_nonneg follows from the refinement on summary.lip. A theory with a proved model is consistent: anything provable from its axioms is true in the model, so false cannot be. That is consistency by interpretation, the standard argument, and the solver checks it. (As implemented in step 3, each axiom becomes a lemma shapes.seq_lip with the model's sorts and functions in place of the theory's, proved like any lemma and reported as "the model 'shapes' meets the axiom 'Lip.seq_lip'"; the adapter check itself is not reused. A model's record types may refine their fields with where, which the model's functions must keep.)

Then the model is sealed, as an ML structure is sealed by its signature. Outside the model's own body, layer is abstract, and a query that uses the theory gets only the sorts, the abstract functions and the axioms, never the model's definitions. That keeps clients' queries small, and it keeps them independent of the model, so the model can change without re-proving clients as long as the theory does not change.

A model proves that the axioms are consistent. It does not prove that they mean what their names suggest. shapes is a summary, not a semantics of neural networks: in it, a layer is its shape and its bound. That is the same position as any specification. A wrong axiom with a model can make a proof say less than the author meant, but it can never make the verifier accept a false goal about the program, because the program's own goals are about the program's code. How a theory's meaning connects to code is under "Connecting a theory to code" below.

Trusted. A theory without a model, or with a model that does not prove every axiom, is allowed only in a @trusted module, the same rule as assume (ADR 0023). Every axiom that the model does not prove is a trusted item, so it is listed in the certificate and in --trust-report. Trust is for facts that are true but beyond what the solver can check from a model in Pia: statements about function spaces, real analysis, or a library's external behaviour. Spectral norms are an example. The spectral norm of a matrix is at most its Frobenius norm, which is a theorem, but not one Z3 will prove over a faithful model of matrices.

Three checks make trusted axioms safer, and none of them makes them proved:

  1. Consistency check at the definition. piac asks the solver whether the trusted axioms, with the base theories, are satisfiable, under the usual rlimit. unsat is an error that prints the unsat core: the axioms that contradict each other. sat with a model from Z3's model-based quantifier instantiation is recorded as a witness in the certificate. unknown leaves the theory trusted and unchecked, and says so. This is cheap, once per theory, and catches the usual mistakes, such as an inverted inequality or a missing precondition.
  2. Axiom use per goal. Every axiom sent to the solver is a named assertion. When a goal is proved, the unsat core says which axioms it used, and that list is stored with the goal in the proof cache. So piac --trust-report --why can say "these 12 goals depend on the trusted axiom Nn.dense_lip", and a goal that used no trusted axiom is reported as fully proved even when its module imports a trusted theory. Unsat cores are computed only for queries that contain theory axioms.
  3. Vacuity check, opt-in. --check-vacuity re-solves each proved goal that used a trusted axiom without its negated goal. If its hypotheses alone are unsat, the goal was proved from a contradiction, which is reported as an error. It costs one more query per such goal, so it runs in CI and in pia-cert audit, not in every edit.

Importing trust is explicit. A module that imports a theory whose certificate lists trusted axioms must say so: import Pia.Nn.Spectral trusting. Without trusting, the import is an error that lists the trusted axioms. So a library cannot grow its users' trusted base by a version bump, which fits the rule that the strongest guarantee is the default (ADR 0004). A modelled theory needs no trusting.

docs.title: Connecting a theory to code
docs.text:
Code reaches a theory through contracts, and the link is proved in the module that owns the model. A kernel module defines an abstraction function from its run-time representation to the theory's sort, inside the model's scope, and states its kernels' contracts in theory terms:

let spec abs (w : dense_weights) : Lip.layer
  = { in_w = w.cols; out_w = w.rows; lip = frobenius w }

Inside that module, abs unfolds into the model, so the kernels are proved against concrete definitions. Its interface publishes abs sealed: importers know in_w (abs w) = w.cols from the published contract, but not how lip is defined. This is data refinement, as in Dafny's and B's abstraction functions, and it is where a model's meaning matters. If the model is only a summary, as shapes is, then the guarantee clients get is about that summary (lip here is the Frobenius norm of the weights), and documentation says so. If the library wants lip to mean the network's true Lipschitz constant, the link between the summary and the real function is exactly the kind of fact that is a trusted axiom, and it is listed.

docs.title: Tactics and decision procedures
docs.text:
There are three levels, and only the first two are part of this decision.

  1. Solver strategy. A theory, lemma or function can choose how Z3 solves its goals, with @solver(nlsat) or @solver(tactic = "..."), which becomes (check-sat-using ...). This affects only speed, never soundness. The strategy is part of the proof cache key.
  2. Tactics as proof-writing metaprograms. A tactic is a metaprogram that takes a goal (its hypotheses and conclusion as quoted terms, through a goal value) and returns proof steps: lemma calls, asserts, case splits, explicit quantifier instances and @fuel hints. The steps are then verified like hand-written ones, so a tactic can make a proof faster or possible but cannot make it wrong. This is the LCF approach. Proof by reflection fits in the same form. A library writes a decision procedure as a total spec function, such as decide : shape_formula -> bool, and proves once a lemma decide φ ==> eval φ. The tactic reifies the goal into a shape_formula, and the verifier proves decide φ = true by unfolding. That is a decision procedure written and proved in Pia, with nothing trusted beyond the evaluator that is already trusted.
  3. Native decision procedures through Z3's user propagator run arbitrary code inside the solver. They are deferred. If they come, they will be @trusted, and the format reserves a trusted-item kind for them, unless they emit a certificate that a small checker validates.

docs.title: Hygiene and names
docs.text:
The names a theory declares are top-level items of its module. They are kept, not renamed, and are qualified like any other item, Lip.lip (ADR 0022, rules 2 and 3). An axiom's parameters are binders, so a theory built by a quote renames them. The no-shadowing rule applies: a theory cannot declare add, len or a name already visible. Two libraries that both declare a sort layer declare two different sorts. A module that wants them to be the same must write a model of one in terms of the other.

In SMT-LIB, symbols are named after the module path and, for a generated theory, the instance (|Pia.Nn.Lip.lip|, |shape_theory<...>.rows|), so that queries combining two theories can never confuse their symbols.

docs.title: Concepts, laws and overloading
docs.text:
A theory and a concept are both signatures with facts. They differ in who proves the facts. A concept's laws are proved by every instance, and its users may assume them. A theory's axioms are proved once, by its model, or trusted. The model check reuses the adapter check unchanged.

Concepts can mention theory functions, and laws can rest on axioms: let meta Layer (t : type) : concept = sig let abs : (x : t) -> Lip.layer ... end. When an overload is chosen by constraint entailment or by a proved precondition (ADR 0034), and that proof uses a trusted axiom, the overload choice depends on that trust. That is recorded like any other goal's axiom use, so --trust-report --why shows it.

docs.title: Lowering to the smt dialect
docs.text:
A theory lowers once per module, in the verifier (ADR 0018), to a named fragment of smt operations:

  • a sort to an uninterpreted sort (!smt.sort<"Pia.Nn.Lip.layer">);
  • an abstract function to smt.declare_fun with an !smt.func type, and each use to smt.apply_func;
  • an axiom to an smt.forall over its parameters, with its trigger patterns, asserted under a name;
  • real and int to the SMT Real and Int sorts.

The upstream dialect has uninterpreted sorts, functions, quantifiers with patterns and Int. If it still lacks Real at our LLVM pin, the first implementation adds it in a small Pia extension that the SMT-LIB export prints, and offers it upstream. Step 1 found it lacking: real is written as a sort named Real, the Real operations as functions declared under their SMT-LIB names, and the export drops those declarations so Z3 reads them as its own (verifier.md).

Every quantified axiom needs a trigger, because an axiom without one is either ignored by E-matching or instantiated without limit. piac infers triggers as Z3 would (the smallest terms that mention every bound variable) and shows them in --verify-stats, and @trigger(seq f g) sets them explicitly. An axiom with no term that covers all its variables is an error at the definition.

docs.title: Build time: only the facts a goal needs
docs.text:
A large theory must cost nothing for goals that do not use it. That is a requirement, not an option, so it does not wait for --slice.

  • Relevance closure. A query starts with its goal's own terms. An axiom is added when every function symbol in one of its triggers appears in the query, and then the closure is repeated with the symbols the new axioms bring, to a fixed point. Importing a theory costs nothing for a goal that never mentions its symbols. Leaving out an axiom only removes a hypothesis, so a proof found with the closure is a proof.
  • Fallback on failure. If a goal is not proved with the closure, it is solved again with every axiom of every theory whose symbols it mentions, the same fallback as slicing. The counterexample comes from the larger query, so it is not spurious because of a missing axiom.
  • Sealing keeps queries small. Clients get the axioms, never the model. A client's query does not grow with the model, and a model's proof is in its own module, proved once and cached.
  • Lemmas over re-derivation. A theory lemma is proved once and is one fact in its users' queries, which is how a library hides an expensive chain of axiom instantiations.
  • Caching follows the facts used. The cache key is the query, which holds only the axioms the closure added, so changing an axiom a goal never used does not invalidate the goal.
  • Parallel and measured. Model obligations, consistency checks and vacuity checks are ordinary goals in ADR 0032's pool. Theories in the standard library join tools/bench/corpus.txt, so a theory whose axioms loop under E-matching shows up as a resource count regression in CI.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text: A theory is part of its module's interface (ADR 0024). Its sorts, function signatures, axioms and triggers are hashed with the interface, in the canonical form with numbered binders, so a changed axiom changes the hash and forces importers to re-prove. The certificate records each theory's status: modelled, with the hash of the model's proved obligations, or trusted, with each trusted axiom, its consistency result (sat with a witness, or unknown, since unsat is already an error) and whether it is a native decision procedure. Importers record the theory hashes they were proved against, and the loader checks them like any other interface. The model's body is not in the interface hash, since clients never see it.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The theory Lip and model shapes above are in the library Pia.Nn. A network builder metaprogram turns a description of a network into a term over Lip, and the properties of the whole network are lemmas about that term:

import Pia.Nn.Lip

let lemma block_bound (a : Lip.layer) (b : Lip.layer) : unit
  requires Lip.in_w a = 512 && Lip.out_w a = 512 && Lip.lip a <= 0.5
  requires Lip.in_w b = 512 && Lip.out_w b = 10 && Lip.lip b <= 2.0
  ensures Lip.in_w (Lip.seq (Lip.residual a) b) = 512
  ensures Lip.out_w (Lip.seq (Lip.residual a) b) = 10
  ensures Lip.lip (Lip.seq (Lip.residual a) b) <= 3.0
= ()

The goal mentions seq, residual, in_w, out_w and lip, so the closure brings in residual_shape and residual_lip (triggered by residual a), then seq_shape and seq_lip (by seq (residual a) b), and lip_nonneg. Z3 instantiates them: residual a is 512 to 512 with lip <= 1.5, so seq applies, and lip <= 1.5 * lip b <= 1.5 * 2.0 = 3.0, using lip b >= 0 for the product. The model never enters the query, and nothing is trusted.

The shape rule catches a mistake before any kernel exists. Applying the residual to the wrong layer:

let lemma wrong (b : Lip.layer) : unit
  requires Lip.in_w b = 512 && Lip.out_w b = 10
  ensures Lip.lip (Lip.residual b) <= 1.0 + Lip.lip b
= ()

fails: the precondition of residual_lip, in_w b = out_w b, does not hold, so the axiom gives nothing, and the counterexample is a layer with in_w = 512 and out_w = 10, whose residual has some unconstrained lip. In shapes the goal happens to be true, so the counterexample comes from the axioms, and today it shows only that b is some layer (b = Lip.layer!val!0), not the functions' values at it or the axiom whose precondition did not hold; both are later work. A goal that is false in the model gets its counterexample from the model instead, with concrete values.

The weights enter through the kernel library's abstraction function (abs above): a dense kernel's contract says Lip.lip (abs w) = frobenius w, proved in the model's module. For activations, relu is a layer whose lip is 1. In the summary model that is a definition, so it costs nothing to trust. Claiming that lip bounds the true Lipschitz constant of the code's function is a trusted axiom in Pia.Nn.Spectral, and a network proof that uses it says so in --trust-report --why.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A library can teach the verifier a domain (shapes, units, protocols, probability, network properties) as sorts, functions and axioms, without changing the compiler, and generate it from data with a metaprogram.
  • By default nothing is trusted: a theory must come with a model whose obligations the solver proves, so a library's axioms cannot make the verifier accept a false goal. Trusted axioms exist, but only in @trusted modules, only imported with trusting, checked for consistency where possible, and listed per goal.
  • A model shows consistency, not meaning. Documentation has to say what a theory's functions mean, as it does for any specification, and the worked example's lip means "the summary's bound", not "the true Lipschitz constant".
  • Clients reason over the abstract theory, so their queries stay small and do not change when a model does. The relevance closure keeps a large theory free for goals that do not use it, and its fallback keeps counterexamples honest.
  • Quantified axioms bring E-matching, and with it the risk of matching loops and slow goals. Required triggers, the corpus benchmark and the rlimit contain that risk, but theory authors will need guidance on triggers in docs/verifier.md.
  • Unsat cores are needed for per-goal trust, which costs some solver time on queries with theory axioms. If the benchmark shows it matters, cores can be computed only when a trusted axiom is in the query.
  • New spec-only types real and int, and the keywords theory, sort, axiom, model and trusting in their positions.
  • Implementation order, each step a PR with tests: (1) spec-only real and int, with their smt lowering; (2) let theory with sorts, abstract functions and axioms, in @trusted modules only, with SMT-LIB names, triggers and the relevance closure; (3) let model, the model check (reusing the adapter check) and sealing, which lifts the @trusted requirement; (4) certificate status, models found by ADL, trusting imports, consistency checks and per-goal axiom use in --trust-report --why; (5) theory-building metaprograms; (6) @solver strategies and tactics as proof-writing metaprograms, then proof by reflection; (7) --check-vacuity. Native decision procedures stay deferred.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
Dean answered the three questions this ADR ended with when he accepted it (2026-11-22):

  • Trust is declared only in the source, and it covers a whole theory. import M trusting is the only way to trust a theory, so it works the same in a file, in the REPL and in an MCP session (ADR 0031), and there is no command-line flag for it. It trusts every trusted axiom of every theory M exports. A theory is trusted as a whole or not at all, so there is no list of individual axioms to grant. The compiler generates the list of trusted axioms from the trusting imports: it is part of the importer's certificate, and --trust-report prints it, with --why naming the goals that used each axiom.
  • A model is found by the ADL rule. A model need not be in its theory's module. As for adapters and operators (ADR 0022, rule 5), a model of theory T counts where it is found in T's own module or in a module the program imports explicitly. A theory with no model found that way is trusted, so importing it needs trusting. Importing a module that holds a proved model makes the theory modelled for that importer, with no trusting. Unlike adapters, two models found at once are not an ambiguity: a model is evidence that the axioms are consistent and never chooses what code means, so any one of them is enough. A module that declares a theory without a model must still be @trusted, and a model's certificate records the theory hash it models, so the loader can check it like any other interface hash.
  • Floats against real-valued theories get their own ADR: ADR 0038, for Dean's review. The catalogue's examples use integers, booleans and reals, so nothing in them waits on it.

docs.title: 37. Idiomatic Pia: facts in types first, written as opinions and checked by lints
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked what the difference is between a function with requires x <= 100 on an integer parameter and one whose parameter is a range type, whether the compiler should say which one is checked by types and which by the prover, and whether it should push code towards types. He then asked for more of the same: anti-patterns that people can write, the better form of each, a philosophical hierarchy of how to say things in Pia, given as opinions rather than rules, and lints that point out where a metaprogram, a concept or a decomposed proof would be better, so that idiomatic Pia is defined early and the checkers do not take forever.

For one value checked against constants, a precondition and a range type say the same thing. What differs is where the fact lives, and what it costs. Measured on the iMac with piac --verify --solver-cost:

  • A precondition never uses intervals. f (y / 3) for requires x < 100 sends the precondition of 'f' holds to Z3, and so does a call whose argument is already int{0..50}. With (x : int{0..99}), an int{0..50} argument widens with no goal, and a wider one raises one narrowing goal, as before.
  • Inside the function, a range type turns solver goals into interval goals. x + 1 under requires x < 100 is [smt]; with x : int{0..99} it is [intervals].
  • A fact in a contract stops at the function. With requires forall (k in 0..len xs). xs.[k] < 16, a caller's t.[get xs i] into a 16-entry table fails, because get's u8 result does not keep the bound; the file costs 10,022 resource units. With xs : [int{0..15}] and an int{0..15} result, the same index is proved by intervals and the file costs 96.
  • Nonlinear preconditions are expensive. requires w * h <= 1000000 on u32 costs 1,075,117 units for one overflow goal (87 ms); with int{0..1000} parameters it is proved by intervals at cost 0.
  • inc/twice with constant preconditions is 5 solver goals at cost 1,261; with range types, 4 goals, one by intervals, at cost 711.

Two measurements show where range types are not yet free:

  • Arithmetic with nothing wider expected happens at the range. With x : int{1..64}, let d = x - 1 in d fails at x = 1 ('-' does not overflow int{1..64}), while x - 1 as a u8 result is proved by intervals. IRGen computes arithmetic at the join of the operand types and the expected type, and an unannotated let expects nothing.
  • A literal takes the range's type. x + 200 with x : int{0..99} is rejected, 200 does not fit in int{0..99}, even in an @overflow(wrap) function returning u8.

docs.title: An "Idiomatic Pia" page of opinions
docs.text:
docs/idioms.md gives the house opinions, as a hierarchy to prefer from the top:

  1. Make illegal states unrepresentable with types: range types, element ranges on slices, variants instead of integer tags, slices instead of a buffer and a length, buffers of records instead of parallel arrays, and later record where invariants and refinement types.
  2. Contracts for facts that relate several values.
  3. Spec functions and lemmas, to name an idea once and prove a hard step once.
  4. Generics with concepts for the same body at several types; parameters or metaprograms for bodies that differ in constants or structure.
  5. Assertions as stepping stones that split a hard goal.
  6. Escape hatches last: assume, wrapping arithmetic that is not meant to wrap, --allow-unproved, unsafe.

The order is the order of proof cost: a type is checked where a value is made and then never again, a contract once in the callee and again at every call, a lemma once, an assertion as one more goal, and an escape hatch not at all. The page states each opinion with its measured cost, and keeps a catalogue of where the repository's own code still goes against one.

These are opinions. Nothing in this ADR makes a program that was accepted before an error.

docs.title: Lints
docs.text:
A lint is a warning with a name, a message that says what is better and why, and, where the change is mechanical, a fix. They live in src/syntax/Lint, on the syntax tree before metaprograms expand it, so piac and pia-lsp share them without LLVM and they point at the code the user wrote, not at generated code. piac --check, --verify and every --emit mode print them to stderr; pia-lsp publishes them as warnings from pia-lint and offers the fixes as quick fixes.

Lint Warns about range_requires a requires that bounds one parameter, or every element of a slice parameter, by constants range_ensures an ensures that bounds the result by constants redundant_bound a bound its type already states generic_candidate the same body as another function at other types metaprogram_candidate a body that differs from another only in its constants duplicate_function the same signature and body as another function derivable_eq a hand-written field-by-field equality on a record nonlinear_contract a product of two variables in a precondition's inequality, or a division by a variable in any contract deep_fuel @fuel(n) above 4 assume assume costly_goal after verification, a goal that cost 10% or more of the solver's resource limit

The bound lints are deliberately narrow. They fire only in @overflow(proof) functions, since wrapping at a range would wrap at the range; not on mutable, out or inout parameters; not in spec functions, lemmas or metaprograms; and not for a one-sided bound on a type wider than 16 bits, which would have to be written int{3..18446744073709551615}. The message notes when the range type is stored in a narrower machine integer, which changes the C signature, and when the parameter is used in arithmetic with nothing wider expected, where the fix is not marked preferred. A fix moves the bound into the type and removes the clause, or only the conjuncts it moved, keeping the rest of the clause as written.

nonlinear_contract leaves products in postconditions alone, since there they are usually the specification itself, as in a saturating multiply.

costly_goal needs each goal's cost, so piac now always records it and prints it in the report only with --solver-cost. The threshold is --costly-goal=<n>, by default a tenth of --solver-rlimit, and 0 turns it off. Its advice depends on the goal: lemmas and assert steps for postconditions and invariants, range types at the callee for preconditions, and range types or a helper function for overflow and bounds.

A function opts out of a lint with @allow(<name>) on its return annotation; IRGen accepts and ignores it. --no-lint=<name> turns one off for a run, and --no-lint turns all of them off.

docs.title: Statistics by origin
docs.text: --verify-stats adds type, type_smt, type_cost, contract, contract_smt and contract_cost. Type goals are raised by operations on typed values: overflow and narrowing into a range type, bounds, divisors, shifts, match exhaustiveness and out parameters. Contract goals are written: preconditions at calls, postconditions, loop invariants, measures, assertions and concept laws. Moving facts into types shows up as fewer contract goals sent to the solver, and the build-time benchmark can follow it.

docs.title: Decomposed reasoning
docs.text: The page also states how to keep each query small, since every goal is its own query (ADR 0032): functions are proof boundaries, so a loop body with its own contract is proved once; preconditions should stay linear, since every goal assumes them; assert splits a hard goal; --verify-only and --proof-cache keep iteration fast; and costly_goal names the goals worth splitting.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Constant preconditions in the docs became range types or relational contracts where that read better. Tests keep them, because they test contracts. Running the lints over docs/ found the remaining cases listed on the page: the stream demo's parallel fill/dem slices and its bound < 4294967295, and the VecDeque case study's one-sided 0 < old_cap.
  • Every piac run that compiles or verifies may print warnings. A test that checks stderr for the absence of warnings passes --no-lint, as tests/codegen/lower.pia does.
  • The lints are syntactic, so they can be wrong about meaning: they do not see type aliases, and they cannot tell whether a duplicated body uses operations a concept could name. They are warnings for that reason.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
These would make the types-first opinion cheaper to follow, and are tracked as issues:

  • Arithmetic on ranges at an exact range. (#151) An operation on range-typed operands with nothing wider expected could produce the exact interval of its result (x - 1 : int{0..63} for x : int{1..64}), which intervals already compute, and a literal could take its own value's range. Then a range type would never make code that was proved fail.
  • Intervals for preconditions. (#152) A callee's precondition that only bounds a parameter by constants could be discharged by the argument's range, as narrowing already is, without a solver query.
  • Ranges with an open side, (#153) such as u32{1..} or usize{3..}, so one-sided bounds on wide types can be types too.
  • More type-level facts: record where invariants and refinement types, which would let the lints move relational facts, such as lo <= hi on a record, into types as well.

docs.title: 38. Float kernels are proved against real-valued specifications by rounding-error bounds
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (2026-11-22, with Dean's answers to its questions below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0036 lets libraries reason in real arithmetic: a layer's Lipschitz bound is a real, a probability is a real, and the catalogue keeps its examples in integers, booleans and reals. Code computes in f32, f16 and bf16. When Dean accepted ADR 0036, he asked for a separate ADR on how a float kernel is proved against a real-valued theory.

What exists today:

  • Floats are strict IEEE 754 by default (ADR 0004), and the verifier can encode them in Z3's bit-precise floating-point theory (ADR 0011). That is exact, and it does not scale past a few operations.
  • ADR 0012 offers three licences for reassociation and FMA. One of them is an error tolerance written in ensures, under strict IEEE semantics, "proved by a rounding-error analysis pass". That pass was never designed.
  • Device placement (ADR 0015) can move a kernel to the GPU or the Neural Engine, whose float behaviour differs from the CPU's: subnormals may be flushed, and some operations are not correctly rounded.

Prior art: Higham's standard model of floating-point arithmetic and its γₙ bounds; Gappa and Frama-C/Why3, which prove such bounds with interval reasoning; FPTaylor, Daisy and Rosa, which compute bounds automatically; and Fluctuat's abstract interpretation of errors.

docs.title: Floats are related to reals by a rounding theory
docs.text:
Two spec builtins connect the types:

  • to_real (x : f32) : real is the value of a finite float (SMT fp.to_real), and finite x says x is neither infinite nor NaN. The same exist for f16, bf16 and f64.
  • eps t is the unit roundoff of float type t (2⁻²⁴ for f32, 2⁻¹¹ for f16, 2⁻⁸ for bf16), and tiny t is the absolute error of its subnormal range (half the smallest subnormal).

The library Pia.Float.Error is a theory in the sense of ADR 0036. It gives the standard model as an abstract round:

let theory Rounding = sig
  let spec round : (t : type) -> (x : real) -> real
  let axiom standard (t : type) (x : real)
    ensures abs (round t x - x) <= eps t * abs x + tiny t
end

Its model is the identity, so it is consistent and nothing is trusted. Its meaning comes from the compiler: in an error goal, the verifier encodes fadd a b at type t, with round-to-nearest, as round t (to_real a + to_real b), and likewise for -, *, / and sqrt. IEEE 754 guarantees that this holds for finite results. That encoding is part of the compiler's trusted base, as the meaning of + on u8 already is. An FMA is one round of a * b + c. Operations that are exact, such as max, abs, negation, comparison and multiplication by a power of two without overflow, are encoded without round. That is why ReLU costs no error.

docs.title: A tolerance contract
docs.text:
A kernel states its result against a real-valued spec function, with a bound:

let spec dot_r (xs : [f32]) (ys : [f32]) (n : usize) : real
  requires n <= len xs && n <= len ys
  decreases n
= if n = 0 then 0.0 else dot_r xs ys (n - 1) + to_real xs.[n - 1] * to_real ys.[n - 1]

let dot (xs : [f32]) (ys : [f32]) : f32
  requires len xs = len ys && len xs <= 4096
  requires forall i, i < len xs ==> abs xs.[i] <= 1.0e3 && abs ys.[i] <= 1.0e3
  ensures finite result
  ensures abs (to_real result - dot_r xs ys (len xs))
          <= gamma f32 (len xs) * dot_abs xs ys (len xs) + error_floor f32 (len xs)
= ...

gamma t n = n * eps t / (1 - n * eps t) is Higham's γₙ, and dot_abs is the same sum over absolute values. Both are spec functions in Pia.Float.Error. error_floor covers subnormals.

A goal of this kind is proved in three layers, cheapest first:

  1. Ranges and finiteness by interval analysis (ADR 0011's first stage, extended to floats): every intermediate is bounded, so finite result and the absence of overflow are proved without Z3 in the common case. An overflow is a failed goal, and its counterexample gives input magnitudes.
  2. Per-operation error for straight-line code: each operation gets a fresh δ with |δ| <= eps t (from standard), and the goal is a nonlinear real query that Z3's nlsat decides for small kernels. Interval bounds from the first layer are added as hypotheses, so the query has only a few products.
  3. Library lemmas for loops. A reduction is never unrolled. Pia.Float.Error proves, once and by induction (spec functions and lemmas with decreases, PR #133), the classical bounds for summation, dot products, matrix-vector products and Horner evaluation. A loop states the accumulated bound in its invariant and calls the step lemma. The query per goal stays the size of one iteration.

The bit-precise FP theory stays available for a goal that asks for it with @solver(fp_exact), for single operations and tests of the encoding itself.

docs.title: Reassociation keeps tolerance contracts valid
docs.text: The γₙ bounds for summation hold for every association order. So a kernel under @fp(reassoc) (ADR 0012), whose tiled or vectorised code sums in another order, keeps the same tolerance contract, and the proof uses the order-free lemma. This is how ADR 0012's licences and tolerance contracts compose: the licence lets codegen reorder, and the tolerance says by how much the result may then differ from the real value. FMA contraction only removes roundings, so it never invalidates a bound.

docs.title: Theories over reals, kernels over floats
docs.text:
A real-valued theory meets float code at the abstraction function (ADR 0036, "Connecting a theory to code"). For Lipschitz bounds, the float kernel is not exactly Lipschitz, because rounding errors do not shrink with the distance between inputs. What holds is a bound up to an error: if |f̂ x - f x| <= e for all x and f is L-Lipschitz, then |f̂ x - f̂ y| <= L |x - y| + 2e. The network theory therefore tracks a pair, lip and err, and composes both:

let axiom seq_err (f : layer) (g : layer)
  requires out_w f = in_w g
  ensures err (seq f g) <= lip g * err f + err g
let axiom residual_err (f : layer)
  requires in_w f = out_w f
  ensures err (residual f) <= err f + add_err (in_w f)

add_err is the error of the residual's own addition, from the per-operation rule. The summary model of ADR 0036 extends with an err field, and these axioms are proved in it as before. A dense kernel's tolerance contract supplies err for its layer, and ReLU's is 0.

docs.title: Mixed precision and devices
docs.text:
The rounding theory is indexed by type, so a kernel with bf16 weights and f32 accumulation is encoded exactly: a bf16 value converts to f32 without rounding, and then each product and each accumulation step is one round f32. Rounding a result down to bf16 adds one round bf16, and the γ bounds use the eps of the type each step rounds to.

Each placement target has a float model, part of the placement contract of ADR 0015. The CPU's (NEON on Apple Silicon) is strict IEEE with subnormals, since Pia never sets flush-to-zero. A GPU or Neural Engine model states its own eps, its absolute error for flushed subnormals, and the operations it does not round correctly, with their error in ulps. A kernel with a tolerance contract may only be placed on a device whose float model proves that contract, and the placement report says which devices were excluded and why. A device's float model is a trusted theory where its vendor does not document correct rounding, so it is listed like any other.

docs.title: Build time
docs.text: Error goals are new goals, so they go through ADR 0032's pool and proof cache like any other. The interval layer settles finiteness without solver queries in most kernels. Loops cost one iteration's query, because their bounds come from proved library lemmas. The standard library's float kernels join the proof benchmark, so a bound that becomes expensive shows up as a resource-count regression.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A float kernel can be proved to approximate a real-valued specification with an explicit bound, and real-valued theories (network bounds, probabilities, control envelopes) can be used to reason about float code through those bounds.
  • Tolerance contracts survive vectorisation and reassociation, so the fast code and the proved contract are the same code.
  • The compiler's encoding of float operations as round of the real operation becomes part of the trusted base. It is the IEEE 754 standard's own promise, and it is tested against the bit-precise encoding with @solver(fp_exact) on single operations.
  • Bounds are worst-case and can be pessimistic for long reductions. Tighter, probabilistic bounds would be a later theory, not a change to this one.
  • Devices that flush subnormals or do not round correctly need float models before kernels with tolerance contracts can run on them.
  • Implementation order, each step a PR with tests: (1) to_real, finite, eps, tiny, the Float concept with adapters for the builtin types, and float intervals in the interval stage; (2) the round encoding of operations in error goals, with per-operation δ and nlsat; (3) Pia.Float.Error with γₙ and the summation, dot product and matrix-vector lemmas; (4) order-free bounds under @fp(reassoc); (5) device float models in placement; (6) the ~= ... within form and derived bounds published in interfaces; (7) the approximate theory builder for Composable theories, with the network theory as a catalogue entry; (8) a block format (such as an MX format) as a Float type, as a worked example. Steps (1) to (3) need ADR 0036's steps 1 to 3 first.

docs.title: Answers to the review questions
docs.text: Dean accepted this ADR on 2026-11-22 and answered its three questions. These answers are part of the decision.

docs.title: 1. A dedicated tolerance form, for any float format that meets a concept
docs.text:
A tolerance is written with its own form, not with helpers:

ensures result ~= dot_r xs ys (len xs) within gamma f32 (len xs) * dot_abs xs ys (len xs)
  • Meaning. a ~= e within b means finite a && abs (to_real a - e) <= b, where a is a float-format value, e is a real and b is a real. ≈ is accepted as another spelling of ~=. ~ is otherwise only prefix bitwise not, and no expression starts with =, so lexing ~= as one token is unambiguous (grammar.md).
  • The bound is optional. Without within, result ~= e asks for the bound the verifier derives. The report shows the derived bound, and the contract that is published states it. That is the automatic error term of question 2.

The form is not tied to the builtin float types. It works for any type that meets the Float concept of Pia.Float.Error (ADR 0034):

let meta Float (t : type) : concept = sig
  let spec to_real : (x : t) -> real
  let spec finite : (x : t) -> bool
  let spec rel : real                       \ relative error of one rounding
  let spec abs_err : (scale : real) -> real \ absolute error at a given scale
  let spec round : (x : real) -> (scale : real) -> real
  let lemma standard (x : real) (scale : real)
    requires abs x <= scale
    ensures abs (round x scale - x) <= rel * abs x + abs_err scale
end
  • f32, f16, bf16 and f64 meet Float through adapters in the library. scale doesn't affect their error (abs_err is the subnormal term tiny t).
  • Block formats fit the same concept. Examples are device-specific formats with a shared exponent per block, such as microscaling (MX) formats, block floating point on a Neural Engine, or a vendor's packed GPU type. Each one is a Pia type: a record of the shared exponent and the element mantissas, with an adapter for Float on its element view. For a block format the error is absolute, relative to the block's largest magnitude, so abs_err scale carries it and scale is the block's maximum. The ≈ within form, the per-operation encoding and the γ lemmas are all written over the concept, so a kernel over a block type is proved the same way as one over f32.
  • Proving standard. An adapter proves it like any law, from a model of the format's encoding. When the format belongs to hardware whose rounding isn't documented, the adapter's standard comes from a trusted theory (ADR 0036). It is then imported with trusting and listed in --trust-report, as the device float models below are.

docs.title: 2. An automatic error term
docs.text:
• Kernels. A kernel whose contract says result ~= e without within gets its error bound derived by the verifier. The derivation uses the per-operation model, the interval bounds and the γ lemmas, and the derived bound is published in the kernel's interface. A caller's goals use that published bound, so error propagates through calls without being written at each one.
  • Theories. A theory used by float code through an abstraction function gets an error term without the author writing one. When a theory meets the prelude concept Composable (a sort, seq, and a Lipschitz bound lip with the usual composition axioms), the prelude theory builder approximate (ADR 0036, step 5) generates:
  • an err function;
  • the axioms err (seq f g) <= lip g * err f + err g and err (residual f) <= err f + err_add, plus one for each other combinator the theory declares in Composable form;
  • the extended model, in which every model gets an err field, so the new axioms are proved and nothing is trusted.

It is applied automatically wherever an abstraction function maps a Float type into the theory's sort. A theory that is not Composable gets no automatic term. Its author writes the error axioms, as the lip/err example above does by hand.

docs.title: 3. A placement that cannot prove a tolerance is a hard error
docs.text:
• Explicit placement. If a kernel with a tolerance contract is placed explicitly, with @place(gpu), @place(ane) or @place(auto, prefer = ...) naming a device, on a device whose float model cannot prove the contract, compilation fails. The error names the device, the contract and the goal that failed under that device's model.
  • @place(auto). The cost model prefers devices whose float model proves the contract, and the placement report lists every device it excluded with the reason. If automatic placement still resolves to a device that cannot meet the tolerance (for example because it is the only device that fits, or prefer selects it), that is the same hard error as an explicit placement.
  • No warning-only mode. A tolerance contract that holds on one device and not on another is never downgraded to a warning.

docs.title: 39. Modules are private by default: one module per file, interfaces list every export, imports name interfaces
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), with the answers recorded under "Review"

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked how a function is kept private in a module. ADR 0010 answers in principle: a module exports named interfaces, and an importer names each interface it uses, so a module depends on interface artifacts only. docs/design.md sketches the syntax (interface X = sig ... end, module M : X = struct ... end, import M.X), and the grammar already parses it. None of it is built. Today piac compiles one program from one or more files, and every top-level function gets a C entry point (codegen.md), so nothing is private.

Since ADR 0010, many decisions have added things an interface must carry or a module must own:

  • contracts, refinement types and module state as exported symbols (ADR 0006);
  • metaprograms and operators, found by module-qualified names and argument-dependent lookup (ADL) (ADR 0022);
  • the interface hash, the inline surface hash, witness symbols and certificates (ADR 0024), and layout hashes (ADR 0030);
  • @suspends, @blocking, @acquires, @protocol and sendable/shareable (ADR 0027);
  • error sets in result types (ADR 0028);
  • @init, initialised M and registries (ADR 0033);
  • concepts, adapters and overloads (ADR 0034), and type-level metaprograms (ADR 0035);
  • theories and import M trusting (ADR 0036);
  • the REPL's session environment (ADR 0031) and the language server (ADR 0021).

Build time is a tracked benchmark (ADR 0032). The module system is where most of it is won or lost: a change that cannot affect an importer must not make the importer rebuild.

Prior art. OCaml has one module per file, with an optional .mli that seals it. Anything not in the .mli is private, and open brings every name into scope. Standard ML and OCaml signatures can hide a type's representation (type t) or show it (type t = ...). Haskell export lists and Rust's pub mark exports at the definition. Rust adds pub(crate) for exports within a crate. Ada and Modula-3 split a specification from its body, and both are compiled separately. Go has one package per directory, exports by capital letter, and compiles against export data only. C++ modules (export module M;) have interface units whose compiled form (BMI) importers read. Dafny's export sets and reveals/provides say, per export, whether importers see a definition or only its signature. F* .fsti files seal a module and are checked against it. Bazel's Java rules build against interface jars (ijar), so a change to a method body does not rebuild dependents. That is the property Pia wants, with contracts in the interface.

docs.title: 1. A file is one module, named by a header
docs.text:
The first item of a file may be a module header:

module Pixels : PixelOps, PixelCodec

The header names the module and lists the interfaces it claims. The rest of the file is the module's body, so the body is not indented and needs no = struct ... end. Module names are dotted paths of capitalised segments, such as Pia.Sys.Posix or Image.Png. The name comes from the header, not from the file's path, and the build checks that no two modules share a name. Pia.* is reserved for the standard library.

Attributes on the module go after its name: module Pia.Sys.Posix @trusted : PosixCalls.

module M : I = struct ... end keeps its meaning as a nested module inside a file. A nested module is a namespace (M.f) sealed by I: the file's other code sees only what I lists. A nested module is private to its file, and cannot be exported in this version. It is useful for checking that an implementation meets an interface, and for keeping helpers apart. Adapters already use struct ... end (ADR 0034).

docs.title: 2. Everything is private unless an interface lists it
docs.text:
A top-level let in a module is private unless an interface the module claims lists its name. That covers functions, types, values, state, spec functions, lemmas, metaprograms, operators, concepts, adapters, theories and registries. A private item:

  • is still proved, like any other item;
  • gets internal linkage in LLVM and no C entry point, so it can be inlined, specialised and removed when unused;
  • is not hashed into any interface, so changing it, adding it or removing it never makes an importer re-prove, recompile or relink.

There is no pub, export or private keyword. The interface is the export list, which keeps one place that says what a module promises, and makes adding an export a visible change to an interface.

An interface is declared in the module that claims it, as today:

module Pixels : PixelOps, PixelCodec

interface PixelOps = sig
  let pixel : type                                  (* abstract: importers cannot see the fields *)
  let spec alpha : (p : pixel) -> u8                 (* opaque spec function: name and type only *)
  let opaque : pixel
  let blend : (a : pixel) -> (b : pixel) -> (t : u8) -> pixel
    ensures alpha result = max (alpha a) (alpha b)
end

interface PixelCodec = sig
  let encode : borrowed in [pixel] -> [u8]
  let decode : borrowed in [u8] -> result [pixel] decode_error
  let decode_error = type | Truncated | BadHeader    (* transparent: importers can match on it *)
end

let pixel = type { r : u8; g : u8; b : u8; a : u8 }
let opaque : pixel = { r = 0; g = 0; b = 0; a = 255 }
let spec alpha (p : pixel) : u8 = p.a
let mix (x : u8) (y : u8) (t : u8) : u8 = ...        (* private: in no interface *)
let blend (a : pixel) (b : pixel) (t : u8) : pixel = ...
...

An interface is an ordinary item and must also follow the no-shadowing rule. Its name is the last segment of an import path, so a module cannot have an interface and a nested module with the same name.

docs.title: 3. : hides, = shows
docs.text:
