An interface item written with : gives importers a name, a type and a contract. An item written with = also gives them the definition. This one rule covers every kind of item:

Item in a sig Importers see Changing the definition costs importers let t : type an abstract type, with its shape hash only (ADR 0030) nothing, unless the shape changes (relink) let t = type ... the representation: fields, variants, refinements re-prove, as it changes the interface hash let f : (x : a) -> b requires ... ensures ... a function's type and contract nothing let inline f : ... = body the body as well, for inlining recompile, through the inline surface hash let n : u32{1..8192} a fixed value's type and refinement; the value is folded at link time (ADR 0010) recompile, through the inline surface hash let n : u32 = 4096 the value itself, which proofs may use re-prove let spec s : ... an opaque spec function, known only through contracts and exported lemmas nothing let spec s : ... = body a transparent spec function, which proofs may unfold re-prove let lemma l ... the lemma's statement; its proof stays in the module nothing let meta m ..., let meta operator ... the metaprogram, which importers run re-prove, since its expansion is their code

So the representation of a value is hidden unless the author chooses to show it, and showing it is the choice that couples importers to it. Two kinds of change do not need the importer to be re-proved but do need it to be recompiled: a changed inline body and a changed foldable value. They are hashed separately into the inline surface hash (ADR 0024), so the build re-runs codegen but reuses proofs.

Generic functions follow the same split. An exported generic function is checked once against its constraints in its own module (the definition check of ADR 0034), and importers instantiate it. Its body goes into the inline surface, as instances need it for codegen. Its signature and constraints are in the interface hash.

Everything an exported contract mentions must itself be visible to importers. A requires that calls a private spec function, or an ensures that names a private type, is an error that names the item to export. This is what lets an interface compile on its own.

docs.title: 4. A module meets its interfaces by proof
docs.text:
For each item an interface lists, the module must define an item with that name and:

  • the same type, including parameter modifiers, refinements and the error set of a result. An implementation that raises fewer errors still declares the interface's set;
  • a contract at least as strong: the interface's requires implies the definition's, and the definition's ensures implies the interface's. This is the requirement check of ADR 0034, reused, so an interface can promise less than the body proves and keep the rest private. It is proved by the solver, and the result is cached like any goal;
  • compatible effects: @suspends and @blocking must match exactly, because they change the calling convention. The definition's @acquires levels must be a subset of the listed ones, and its inferred @protocol must refine the listed protocol (ADR 0027). Exported types list sendable and shareable when importers may rely on them, and the module must prove them;
  • for an abstract type, any type at all, with the interface's refinement, if it has one, proved as its invariant.

An item an interface lists that the module does not define is an error, and so is a module that claims an interface twice. Several interfaces may list the same item. An interface is hashed on its own, so each importer depends only on the interfaces it imports, even when they share items.

docs.title: 5. Imports name interfaces, and access is qualified
docs.text:
import Pixels.PixelOps                       (* Pixels.blend, Pixels.pixel *)
import Image.Png.Codec as Png                (* Png.decode *)
import Pia.Task.Tasks { scope, spawn, join } (* scope, spawn and join unqualified; the rest Pia.Task.* *)
import Pia.Nn.Spectral.Bounds trusting       (* required because the interface has trusted axioms *)
  • An import names one interface of one module, by its full path. Its items are then reachable as Module.name. The interface name is not part of the item's name, since an item belongs to the module and may be listed in several interfaces. Naming an item of a module that is in an interface this module does not import is an error that says which interface to import.
  • as gives the module a shorter local name. { a, b } also brings the listed names in unqualified. Both are checked against the no-shadowing rule (ADR 0022), so a clash is reported at the import.
  • There is no wildcard, like OCaml's open, and no import of a whole module. A library may add items to an interface as a compatible change (it refines its old baseline, ADR 0024). With a wildcard, a new item could clash with a name in an importer, and a compatible update would break its build.
  • trusting is the opt-in of ADR 0036: it is required when the imported interface, or an interface it depends on, has trusted axioms, and the error without it lists them.
  • An import is a fact the build checks. Each import must be provided by a declared dependency (strict dependencies), and an import that nothing uses is a lint warning (ADR 0037).
  • An interface can mention types from interfaces its module imports. Its hash then includes theirs, and an importer's build reads those artifacts too, to type check. The importer still cannot name their items without importing them.

docs.title: 6. Names reach across modules only through imports
docs.text:
ADR 0022 and ADR 0034 defined lookup for operators, derives, concept requirements and adapters in terms of "the type's module plus imported modules". With modules, that becomes:

  • ADL searches the interfaces this module imports from the type's own module, and the adapter interfaces it imports explicitly. A type reached without importing its module, for example the result type of another library's function, has no operators or concept functions in scope. The error says which interface to import. This keeps every name a module can use inside the interfaces it names, which is what makes the build graph explicit.
  • An operator or derive for a type is exported with the type: an interface that lists let meta operator ( + ) for vec<t, k> must also list vec, or import the interface that does.
  • Quotes produce module-qualified paths. A free name in a quote refers to its definition in the metaprogram's module (Pixels.mix, prelude.add). If that name is private, the expansion in an importer can still call it: the quoted path is resolved by the defining module, which links it as a hidden symbol that only expansions of its own exported metaprograms may reference. The [prelude] and [toplevel] marks of ADR 0022 go away.
  • Concept satisfaction is checked where it is used, against the functions and adapters visible there, as now. Its proof (requirement contracts implied) is cached by the interface hashes involved, so two importers that check Eq pixel share one proof.

docs.title: 7. Module state is a symbol, and importers cannot write it
docs.text:
Module state is a top-level let whose type is mutable, with an invariant, as in the REPL today (docs/repl.md, "State"):

module Counter : Counting

interface Counting = sig
  let count : fixed u32                    (* importers may read it, never write it *)
  invariant count <= 100                   (* importers may assume this between calls *)
  let bump : () -> unit
    ensures count = min 100 (old count + 1)
end

let count : mutable u32 invariant count <= 100 = 0
let bump () : unit = if count < 100 then count <- count + 1 else ()
  • State is private by default, like everything else. An interface may export it only as fixed, a read-only view. Writes go through exported functions, whose ensures (with old) say how the state changes. So the module alone keeps its invariant, and importers reason only through contracts (ADR 0006).
  • An interface may publish the state's invariant, or a weaker one. Every exported function must preserve the published invariant, and importers may assume it between calls. Private state can be described to importers through an exported opaque spec function, let spec level : () -> u32, so an interface can talk about state without exposing it.
  • A function that reads the module's state has the implicit precondition initialised Counter (ADR 0033). For exported functions it is part of the canonical interface, so piac --emit=interface prints it and importers' @inits are checked against it. @init itself is never listed in an interface, since nobody calls it, but its contract, error set and dependency set are hashed into the module's certificate, as ADR 0033 decided.
  • Registries are items like any other. let r : registry t where P is exported by listing it, and @register(M.r) needs an import of the interface that lists r.

docs.title: 8. Interfaces compile on their own
docs.text:
piac --emit=interface pixels.pia parses the file, runs metaprogram expansion to its fixed point, type checks the interfaces and the items they list, and writes one artifact per interface (Pixels.PixelOps.piai). It does not check bodies or run the verifier. An interface artifact holds the canonical serialisation of ADR 0024, and its SHA-256 is the interface hash. The inline surface is a second artifact with its own hash. Both must be byte-for-byte reproducible: no paths, no timestamps, and hygiene scope ids taken from the expansion site, as ADR 0022 required.

The Bazel rule pia_library builds one module. Importers depend only on its .piai artifacts, never on its object file or certificate, so:

  • a change to a private item, or to a body behind :, leaves the .piai artifacts byte-identical, and Bazel's action cache skips every importer;
  • every module that imports an interface can type check and verify as soon as that interface is extracted, which is fast, so module proofs run in parallel across the whole build, on top of the per-goal parallelism of ADR 0032;
  • the linker checks the certificates, and pia_binary names the root module, whose main is the program's entry point. main is never listed in an interface.

docs.title: 9. C entry points come from interfaces
docs.text: Only exported functions get external symbols. Their names are mangled from the module path (_pia$Pixels$blend, with overloads named as in ADR 0034). An interface marked @abi(c) gives its functions plain C names instead (blend), checked for clashes at link time, and must keep to types with a C calling convention (codegen.md). That is how a C harness, such as //tests/codegen:saturate_test, calls Pia code. The @abi(c) mark is in the interface hash.

docs.title: 10. A file without a header is a program with nothing exported
docs.text: A file with no module header is an anonymous program module. All of its items are private, and only main (if any) is an entry point. Every item is still proved, so piac --verify and the documentation examples, which only verify, behave as before. Tests that call Pia from C get a module header and an @abi(c) interface. This keeps the strongest guarantee as the default (ADR 0004): no file exports anything by accident. Several headerless files given to one piac command still form one program module, as now.

docs.title: 11. Internal interfaces
docs.text: An interface marked @within(Pia.Sys) can be imported only by modules whose names start with Pia.Sys. This is for interfaces that a library shares between its own modules but does not promise to users, such as Pia.Sys.Posix's raw calls, which only the rest of Pia.Sys should reach. It is an import rule, not a hiding rule: the interface is hashed, certified and checked like any other.

docs.title: 12. The REPL
docs.text:
• A REPL session is an anonymous module, as a headerless file is. Every cell's items are visible to later cells, and nothing is exported.
  • import M.I in a cell loads the interface artifact and the library that provides it through Pia.Dyn (ADR 0033), so a cell sees exactly what a compiled importer would.
  • pia repl --module pixels.pia opens a session inside a module: its private items are visible and can be redefined, which is how private helpers are explored and debugged. A redefinition must still meet every interface the module claims, which is the compatible-change rule of ADR 0031. A redefinition that would change an interface hash is refused with the importers it would affect, unless :redef is given --change-interface. The MCP server's execute takes the same commands.

docs.title: 13. The language server
docs.text:
• pia-lsp keeps an index of the workspace's interfaces, built with piac --emit=interface, which is front-end work and fast enough to run on every save. Imports, completion, hover and go-to-definition use the index, so they work across files without proofs.
  • Hover on an imported name shows the interface's contract, which is what the importer may rely on. Inside the module it also shows the definition's contract, when it is stronger.
  • Diagnostics: a use of a name that is private to another module, with the interface that would need to list it; a name in an interface the file does not import, with a code action that adds the import; an unused import. A code action that adds an item to an interface warns that it changes the interface hash, and how many workspace modules import the interface.
  • Proof diagnostics stay per file, but an edit that changes no interface artifact no longer invalidates other files' proofs.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
In steps, each a PR with tests, as for ADR 0034:

  1. Headers and privacy in one compilation. Parse the header, check interfaces as items, the matching rules of section 4, privacy (internal linkage, no C entry point), @abi(c), and headerless files as program modules. Migrate the tests that call Pia from C.
  2. Interface artifacts and separate compilation. --emit=interface, the canonical form and hashes, import M.I resolved through --iface-path, assume-guarantee verification against imported contracts, and the pia_library and pia_binary Bazel rules with strict dependencies.
  3. Names across modules. Qualified access, as and { ... }, cross-module ADL for operators, derives, concepts and adapters, exported metaprograms and qualified quotes.
  4. The inline surface. let inline, foldable values with link-time folding, and exported generic bodies.
  5. State, effects and initialisation. fixed state views, published invariants, implicit initialised M, and effect and protocol matching. This joins #101.
  6. Certificates and trust. Required interfaces and their hashes in the certificate, witness symbols, trusting and @within.
  7. REPL and language server. import in cells, pia repl --module, and the workspace interface index in pia-lsp.

Step 3 is landing in the order the standard library (ADR 0040) needs it: shown types first, then concepts and generic functions, spec functions in signatures, postconditions of out and inout functions, and then as, { ... } and cross-module ADL.

  • Shown types. An interface shows a type with =, including a generic one as it is defined: let option = let (t : type) => type | None | Some of t. An importer names it through its module, Pia.Core.Option.option u8, and gets the same definition, so the two modules agree on its layout. The constructors of an imported variant are in scope unqualified, as Some, and also as Pia.Core.Option.Some. Constructors are already one namespace in a program, so a clash between two imported variants, or with a local one, is an error at the type, as for any two constructors. Abstract types (let t : type) are not importable yet, since an importer needs their layout (ADR 0030).
  • Concepts and generic functions are exported with their definitions, which form the artifact's inline surface: after the interface, the .piai file holds the canonical text of each listed concept (let meta Ord : concept in the sig) and generic function (let min : (t : type where Ord t) -> ...). The interface entry of a generic function must have exactly the definition's parameters and result, and the definition may use only what the interface lists, which --emit=interface checks. An importer gets each as M.min or M.Ord, instantiates generic functions at its own types, and proves each instance, as every generic is proved today (#203). Code from M, an instance of M.min or a check of M.Ord, also finds M's functions by their own names, so Ord's requirement less is met for u8 by M.less. ADR 0043 will add the proof status of each generic and the hypotheses it assumed to this section of the artifact.
  • Spec functions are exported with their definitions too, since an importer reasons with the body: let spec total : (xs : [u8]) -> (n : usize) -> int in the sig puts the definition in the inline surface, and the importer names it M.total in its own contracts and spec code. The entry must repeat the definition's parameters and result. A spec function has no link symbol, since codegen erases it.
  • Functions that write their parameters may state postconditions in an interface, over the parameters after the call and, with old, before it, as swap's ensures xs.[i] = old (xs.[j]). A lemma cannot call such a function, so the module meets the entry with a function of its own that has the entry's contract and the parameters' modifiers, and whose body is the call; it is proved like any other.
  • as and { }: import M.I as X lets the file write X.f, X.t and X.C for M.f, M.t and M.C, and import M.I { f, t } lets it write f and t. The full path still works. A name brought in by either must not be one the file binds anywhere, an item, parameter or pattern variable, or one another import brought in; the error names the qualified path to use. They apply to the file's own code only: definitions imported with their bodies name things as their module does.
  • Values (step 4, in part): let n : u32 in a sig exports a value, which importers reach as M.n and link to, knowing only its type. let n : u32 = 4096 shows it: the interface repeats the definition exactly, and importers get the definition, which their proofs and code use. Module state (fixed) waits for step 5, and folding a hidden value at link time for a later part of step 4.
  • Concept instances are proved once (step 6, in part): a module proves every instance of the concepts its interfaces list that its exported functions meet at its own types or built-in ones, laws and requirement contracts included, whether or not it uses them. An importer whose use of such a concept resolves to those types and that module's functions alone does not prove them again: its lemmas are marked pia.certified with the module's name and the verifier skips them, as it skips imported functions and generics. The build guarantees the proof exists, since an importer links the module's object file, which piac writes only when every goal is proved. An instance at an importer's own type, or met by its own functions or adapters, is still proved by the importer.
  • Witness symbols (step 6, in part): an object defines a one-byte symbol pia$w$<module>$<interface>$<hash> for each interface its module provides, and references the one for each interface it imports, where the hash is the first 128 bits of the SHA-256 of the canonical .piai text, in base32 (abi.md). An importer linked against a module whose interface changed since it was proved, its inline surface included, fails to link with an undefined pia$w$... symbol. This is what makes skipping certified instances safe across separate builds. The certificate section and its link checker come later.
  • Certificates and the link check (step 6, in part): each object also carries a certificate in __TEXT,__pia_cert (.pia_cert on ELF) that names its module, the full hash of each interface it provides and of each it was proved against. pia-cert dump prints it, and pia-cert check refuses a set of objects where an import is not provided, or is provided with another hash, and says which object to prove again. pia_library runs the check over its closure as a validation action, so every Bazel build of a Pia module checks it. Format 1 has a text body (src/cert/Certificate.h). Trusted items, the ABI version and the compiler's identity come with the rest of abi.md.
  • Symbols come from interfaces (#204): a function exported under one name is linked and entered by that name even when private overloads share it. Only a name the interfaces list with several overloads carries parameter types in its symbols.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A function is private unless an interface lists it. Privacy costs nothing to write, and exporting is a deliberate change to one place.
  • Changing a private item, or a body behind :, never rebuilds an importer, which is the main lever on build time for large programs.
  • Interfaces can promise less than a module proves, so a module can strengthen its body's contracts freely without coupling importers to them.
  • Qualified names are longer to write than OCaml's open. { ... } and as cover the common cases, and the language server adds imports.
  • A type's operators and concept functions are only usable by a module that imports the type's interface. Some programs need one more import line.
  • Single-file programs keep working, but nothing in them is callable from C until they gain a header.
  • Nested modules cannot be exported yet. Re-exporting another module's items from an interface (a façade such as Pia.Io over Pia.Sys.Fs) is left for later, and so is choosing between implementations of one interface at link time (like OCaml functors or Backpack).

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Dean accepted this ADR on 2026-11-22 and answered its questions:

  1. A headerless file exports nothing (section 10). Accepted.
  2. Access is qualified unless an import lists names in { ... }, with no wildcard (section 5). Accepted.
  3. Importers can never write module state (section 7). Accepted: state changes go through interface functions, which is safer. Exporting mutable state needs a demonstrated case before it is considered again.
  4. Spellings @abi(c) and @within(...) (sections 9 and 11). Accepted.

docs.title: 40. The C++23 standard library, mapped onto Pia and proved
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for the C++23 standard library in Pia, now that Pia has generics, concepts, slices, result with ?, defer and Drop, @linear, borrows, with_arena and a proved generic vec over a bump allocator. ADR 0023 already decided that the library is written in Pia over a minimal core, and docs/stdlib.md lays it out in layers (Pia.Core, Pia.Sys, Pia.Mem, Pia.Io, Pia.Math, Pia.Par). What it does not say is how much of what a C++ programmer expects from std Pia provides, under which names, and in what order.

C++23 has about a hundred headers. Some translate directly (<bit>, <algorithm>, <charconv>). Some exist because of a C++ mechanism that Pia replaces (<exception>, <iterator>, <memory>'s std::allocator, <type_traits>). Some need things Pia does not have yet (floats, atomics, function values). And some are out of scope for reasons of principle (<locale>, wide characters, <any>).

A verified library also has to say more than C++'s does. The standard states preconditions in prose ("the behaviour is undefined if [first, last) is not sorted"), and results as "Effects:" and "Returns:" clauses. In Pia, each of those is a contract the compiler proves, so the library cannot be a transliteration: every function needs a specification precise enough to prove, which often needs a spec function the standard never names (sorted, count, permutation).

Prior art: Rust's core, alloc and std give the same capabilities as C++'s library under different idioms (slices for iterator pairs, Result for exceptions, traits for concepts). SPARK's formal containers and Ada's Ada.Containers show contracts written against a mathematical model. Dafny's and Verus's standard libraries (vstd) show which specifications are practical to prove. Zig's std shows a library where every allocating function takes an allocator.

docs.title: 1. Capability parity, not API parity
docs.text:
Pia provides what the C++23 library lets a program do, in Pia's idioms, not C++'s names and signatures. A C++ programmer finds each std entity through docs/cpp-std.md, a header-by-header map that says, for each header, which Pia module provides it, whether it is direct, replaced by a Pia idiom, deferred (and on what), or out of scope (and why). The map is updated by every library PR, so it is also the status page.

Each library function's doc comment names the C++ entity it corresponds to, as (** C++: std::lower_bound *), so the language server, search and the map agree.

Names follow Pia's style: snake case, single words where they are clear (find, count, fill, rotate), the C++ name where it is the established term (lower_bound, popcount, gcd, iota), and no std:: prefixes, _t suffixes or _if variants, whose forms are overloads instead (see section 6).

docs.title: 2. C++'s prose becomes proved contracts
docs.text:
• Every precondition is a requires. What is undefined behaviour in C++ is a proof goal at the call in Pia: an unsorted range passed to lower_bound, an index past the end, a pop on an empty heap, a shift by the width or more, midpoint of nothing, gcd overflowing. None of these has a run-time check, because none can happen in a proved program.
  • Every "Returns:", "Effects:" and "Postconditions:" clause is an ensures, written with spec functions in the module (sorted, count, permutation, is_heap, prefix). sort promises a sorted permutation of its input, lower_bound the first index whose element is not less than the key, and to_chars a string that from_chars reads back to the same value.
  • Where C++ leaves something unspecified, Pia picks one answer and states it: which of equal elements min_element returns, the order of a partition's halves, the contents of a slice after remove. Code may rely on what the contract says, and on nothing else.
  • Complexity clauses are documented, not proved. "At most log2(n) + 1 comparisons" goes in the doc comment. Pia has no cost proofs yet (see the gaps below), so the library is tested against them with benchmarks instead.
  • Laws a C++ concept states but cannot check are concept laws. Ord's strict weak order (irreflexive, transitive, and transitive incomparability), Eq's equivalence and Hash's agreement with Eq are lemmas proved for every instance (ADR 0034), so a sort over a type whose less is not a strict weak order is rejected where it is instantiated, rather than misbehaving at run time.

docs.title: 3. No exceptions: closed error sets
docs.text:
• A C++ function that throws becomes one that returns result t e, where e is a closed variant naming exactly the errors that can happen (ADR 0028). There is no std::exception hierarchy, no what() and no noexcept: a function with no error set cannot fail.
  • std::bad_alloc is OutOfMemory, returned by every allocating call and handled at its call site (ADR 0026). No container function allocates without saying so in its type.
  • C++'s pairs of checked and unchecked accessors collapse. v[i] and v.at(i) are both v.[i] with the bound proved. An accessor that returns option exists only where the caller cannot be expected to prove the bound, such as a lookup by key.
  • std::errc and std::error_code become the error variants of the module that raises them; Pia.Sys decodes errno into its own variants (ADR 0023).

docs.title: 4. Allocators are explicit, and every container is a pmr container
docs.text:
• Every allocating function takes a borrowed allocator that meets Allocator (ADR 0026). There is no std::allocator and no default global heap, so C++'s std::pmr is the only model, and <memory_resource>'s monotonic_buffer_resource, unsynchronized_pool_resource and synchronized_pool_resource are Pia.Mem's arena, pool and shared allocators.
  • <scoped_allocator> has nothing to do: a container's elements that allocate are given their allocator explicitly, and borrows (ADR 0026) prove that none outlives it.
  • There is no unique_ptr; there is one box (Dean, 2026-11-22). C++'s unique_ptr<T> is a nullable pointer plus a deleter, and its type says nothing about what it points to beyond T. Pia's box is an owning, non-null allocation from a stored allocator, and its parameter is either a type or a concept:
    • box t holds a t. Calls on it are direct, and proofs see the concrete value, as for any other t.
    • box c, for a concept c such as Shape or Function u8 bool (ADR 0044), holds a value of any type that meets c. Widening a box (box.widen) checks, statically, that its type meets c and that the instance's definitions satisfy the requirements' contracts and laws. The box carries the instance's table of requirement functions, and a call through it is an indirect call whose proof uses only the requirement's contract, as ADR 0043 proves a generic body over an abstract type. So everything in the box is proved to have the concept's shape, and no caller can tell which type it is. This replaces C++'s virtual base classes and std::function, and is the type-erased box that ADR 0044 reserves for Pia.Fn (box (Function a r) is Pia's move_only_function).
    • A box is never null: an optional box is option (box t), whose None is the null pointer in the layout. It has no deleter: dropping it drops the value (through the table, for a concept box) and returns the memory to the allocator it stores, so a custom deleter is a custom allocator. It is Drop, so it is freed at scope end, or @linear when the program must free it explicitly; moving it moves ownership and copying it does not exist.
    • make_unique is box.make alloc v, which can fail like any allocation. get, operator* and operator-> are borrows (borrowed(b)), release is box.release, which leaves the box empty until box.fill refills it, and reset is box.remove then box.fill.
    • The core part, a concept used as a type argument, and the rules for calls through a box (only requirements with one receiver) are ADR 0046.
  • shared_ptr and weak_ptr are Pia.Mem.Ref's ref and weak (ADR 0047): counted, with shared values changed only under leases proved exclusive, so strong cycles cannot be built; one thread first, and an atomic shared_ref with M12.

The allocators, vec and the containers built on them (issue #72) are owned by the Pia.Mem work (#59, #71, #86, #88). This ADR maps C++'s containers onto that work and adds the ones #72 does not list, but does not change Pia.Mem's design.

docs.title: 5. Iterators become slices and indices
docs.text:
• A pair of iterators [first, last) over contiguous storage is a slice [t], and a sub-range is xs.[a .. b]. An output iterator is an out slice whose length is proved to be enough, so copy, transform and set_union cannot write past the end. A position is a usize index, and "an iterator to the found element, or last" is an index in 0 .. len xs, with len xs meaning not found, so an index result composes with slicing as C++'s iterators do with ranges.
  • std::span is the slice type itself, std::array<T, N> is [T; N], and std::string_view is a str slice. None needs a library type.
  • Node-based containers (list, map, set) expose a cursor type of their own, an index into their node pool, proved valid by the container's invariant, instead of a general iterator concept. Iterator categories, sentinels, iterator_traits and <iterator>'s adaptors have no Pia counterpart.
  • Lazy views (<ranges>'s views::filter, transform, zip, chunk) wait for function values (see the gaps). The eager algorithms over slices come first.

docs.title: 6. Comparators and predicates come from concepts first
docs.text:
• Algorithms that compare use Eq and Ord instances found by argument-dependent lookup (ADR 0034), and hashing uses Hash. A different order is a different type: a record that wraps the value and has its own less, as Rust's Reverse does. This is the common case in C++ too, and it monomorphises and vectorises.
  • <compare>'s strong_ordering, weak_ordering and partial_ordering are variants in Pia.Core.Order, with compare (the three-way comparison) derived from less and same, and @derive(ord) as a library metaprogram (#61).
  • There are no _if variants (Dean, 2026-11-22). find_if, count_if, remove_if, replace_if, copy_if, partition_point and the rest are overloads of find, count, remove, replace, copy and so on, chosen by the argument's type (ADR 0034): find xs x takes a value and needs Eq t, and find xs p takes a predicate t -> bool. The same goes for an operation or a comparator: sort xs uses Ord t, and sort xs less takes a comparator, whose contract requires a strict weak order; accumulate xs init uses +, and accumulate xs init op takes the operation. all_of, any_of and none_of are all, any and none, which take only a predicate. When the elements are themselves functions, the value overload's Eq constraint fails and soft failure drops it (ADR 0035), so the two forms never clash.
  • A predicate's contract is part of the overload's. The algorithm's ensures names p x, so the predicate has to be a pure, total function whose result a spec can mention, and an effectful or partial predicate is rejected at the call. These overloads wait for function values and lambdas, designed separately (see the gaps).

docs.title: 7. Text is UTF-8 bytes
docs.text:
• str is [u8] refined to valid UTF-8, and string is a vec u8 with the same invariant (docs/stdlib.md, Pia.Io). char in C++'s sense is u8, and a code point is u32{0..0x10FFFF} without the surrogates.
  • There are no wide characters (wchar_t, <cwctype>, wstring), no char8_t/char16_t/char32_t string types and no locales (<locale>, <clocale>, <codecvt>). Classification is ASCII (<cctype>) in Pia.Core.Ascii; Unicode properties, normalisation and UTF-16 conversion for foreign APIs come later in Pia.Text, from tables generated by metaprograms.
  • std::format and std::print are Pia.Text.Format: format strings are checked when the program is compiled, as C++20's are, by a metaprogram that reads the literal and the argument types. std::formatter specialisations are instances of a Format concept.

docs.title: 8. Type traits and concepts are metaprograms
docs.text: <type_traits> and most of <concepts> exist because C++ templates cannot ask questions about types directly. In Pia, a metaprogram can (ADR 0035): is_integral t is a type match, make_unsigned is a type-level function, enable_if is a where clause, and std::same_as, std::integral and std::totally_ordered are concepts in Pia.Core.Order and Pia.Core.Int. Pia.Core.Traits collects the type-level metaprograms that turn out to be needed, rather than mirroring the header. <typeinfo>, <typeindex> and <any> have no counterpart: there is no run-time type information, and dynamic values are dyn (ADR 0003).

docs.title: 9. Tuples are a core type
docs.text:
Tuples are first-class types and values in the core, as arrays and records are, rather than a library type waiting for variadic generics (Dean, 2026-11-22). This needs a core change of its own, with its own ADR, before <tuple> is done; this section records what the library expects of it.

  • Values and types share one syntax. (a, b, c) is a tuple value and, since types are values, (u8, str, bool) is its type: a tuple of types is a tuple type. () is the empty tuple, the same value as unit. There is no one-element tuple: (x) is x in parentheses.
  • Access is positional. t.0, t.1 and so on, checked when compiled, so an index out of range is a type error, not a proof goal. Patterns destructure: match t with | (a, b) -> ... and let (a, b) = t in ...; a pattern is told apart from a function literal let (x) => ... by the =>, as grammar.md already plans.
  • A tuple is an anonymous record. It has the same layout, ownership and modifier rules as a record whose fields are named 0, 1, ...: layout optimisation (ADR 0030), struct-of-arrays buffers ([(u32, f32)] is one buffer per element), moved and @linear elements, borrows, and contracts that name t.0. Tuples of the same element types are the same type wherever they are written, which is what a named record is not.
  • Equality, order and hashing are structural. Eq, Ord and Hash instances for a tuple come from its elements' instances, element by element and lexicographically, with the laws proved once for the generic definition (ADR 0043). This is C++'s operator<=> on tuple.
  • Tuple types are the type lists for variadic code. A type parameter can stand for a tuple type, and a metaprogram walks it with a type match on () and on a head and tail, proved terminating by structural recursion as ADR 0035 requires. That is enough for apply, tuple_cat, tuple_size, tuple_element, std::get by type, and argument packs for format and make_unique, without a separate pack feature. variant<Ts...> stays a named variant for now: an anonymous sum type is a separate decision.
  • Foreign code sees a tuple as the C struct of its elements, in the order the layout chooses and advertises in the ABI, as for records.

std::pair is a two-element tuple, std::tie is a tuple pattern, and structured bindings are let (a, b) = ....

docs.title: 10. Maths is proved in Pia, never libm
docs.text: <cmath>, <numbers>, <complex>, floating-point <charconv> and the floating-point distributions of <random> are Pia.Math and wait for floats (M11), with error bounds in their contracts (ADR 0023, ADR 0038). Everything over integers comes first: <bit>, <numeric>, integer <charconv>, <chrono>'s integer durations and calendar, <ratio>, and <random>'s integer engines and uniform_int_distribution.

docs.title: 11. Module layout
docs.text:
The library is a tree of modules, one per file (ADR 0039), in lib/, named by path: lib/Pia/Core/Bit.pia holds module Pia.Core.Bit. Each module has a pia_library target in lib/Pia/<Layer>/BUILD.bazel, so it is proved on its own and its dependents build against its interface artifact.

Module C++23 headers Needs Pia.Core.Bit <bit>, <bitset> the bit builtins below Pia.Core.Int <numeric>'s gcd lcm midpoint, <utility>'s cmp_less in_range, <limits>, <climits>, <cstdint>, <cstdlib>'s abs div, C++26's saturating arithmetic available now Pia.Core.Order <compare>, <concepts>'s comparison concepts, <utility>'s swap exchange available now Pia.Core.Option, Pia.Core.Result <optional>, <expected> (<variant> is core sum types) available now; monadic operations wait for function values Pia.Core.Algo (Search, Modify, Sort, Heap, Set, Perm) <algorithm>, <numeric>'s iota accumulate reduce partial_sum inner_product adjacent_difference available now for the comparison-based forms Pia.Core.Ascii, Pia.Core.Utf8, Pia.Core.Charconv <cctype>, <cuchar>, <string_view>, <charconv> for integers available now Pia.Core.Hash std::hash available now Pia.Core.Fixed C++26's inplace_vector, a ring buffer value parameters in generic types Pia.Core.Rand <random>'s integer engines and integer distributions available now Pia.Core.Ratio, Pia.Time <ratio>, <chrono>, <ctime> integer durations and the civil calendar now; clocks need Pia.Sys.Clock; time zones need files Pia.Mem, Pia.Mem.* <memory>, <memory_resource>, <new>, <vector>, <deque>, <list>, <forward_list>, <map>, <set>, <unordered_map>, <unordered_set>, <flat_map>, <flat_set>, <queue>, <stack> the allocators (#59, #71) and #72 Pia.Text, Pia.Text.Format <string>, <format>, <print> Pia.Mem.Vec; print needs Pia.Io Pia.Io, Pia.Sys.Fs <iostream> and the stream headers, <cstdio>, <filesystem> Pia.Sys (#57) Pia.Rt <stacktrace>, <csignal>, <cassert>'s abort #58 Pia.Math <cmath>, <numbers>, <complex>, <cfenv>, <stdfloat> floats (M11) Pia.Sync, Pia.Task, Pia.Chan <atomic>, <thread>, <mutex>, <shared_mutex>, <condition_variable>, <semaphore>, <latch>, <barrier>, <future>, <stop_token>, <generator>, <execution> atomics and the concurrency runtime (M12, ADR 0027) Pia.Fn <functional> function values Pia.Text.Regex <regex> later: a linear-time automaton engine, so matching is proved to terminate

Out of scope, with what replaces each: <exception> and <stdexcept> (error variants), <typeinfo>, <typeindex> and <any> (metaprograms and dyn), <locale>, <clocale>, <codecvt> and <cwctype> (UTF-8 only), <valarray> (vec<T, k> and spread), <csetjmp> (nothing), <cstdarg> (Pia has no C variadics, and calling a variadic C function is not supported), <initializer_list> (array literals), <scoped_allocator> (explicit allocators), <iosfwd>, <streambuf> and <syncstream> (the reader and writer concepts), and <version> (the compiler version is a metaprogram builtin if it is ever needed).

docs.title: 12. Every component is proved and tested
docs.text:
• A library module is accepted only when it proves with no unproved goals and no --allow-unproved. assume, unsafe and @trusted appear only in Pia.Sys.Posix and Pia.Rt, so piac --trust-report on any program that uses only the library lists nothing from it outside those two.
  • Each module has a lit test in tests/std/ that checks its goal counts, and a test program that runs it on examples, including the edge cases the C++ standard calls out (empty ranges, one element, all equal, the extreme values of each integer type).
  • Proving the library is part of the build-time benchmark (ADR 0032): lib/ joins tools/bench/baseline.json, and a library PR that raises proof cost by more than the gate allows has to say why.

docs.title: 13. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase is a set of issues, one PR each, with a module, its tests, and its row of docs/cpp-std.md updated.

  1. Phase 0. This ADR, docs/cpp-std.md, and lib/ with its Bazel rules and the tests/std harness.
  2. Phase 1, Pia.Core without allocation, buildable today:
  3. the core bit builtins ADR 0023 lists and does not have yet (clz, ctz, popcount, rotl, rotr, bswap), then Pia.Core.Bit (<bit>);
  4. Pia.Core.Int (gcd, lcm, midpoint, cmp_less and friends, in_range, limits, saturating arithmetic);
  5. Pia.Core.Order (Eq, Ord with the strict weak order laws, ordering, compare, swap, exchange, lexicographic comparison);
  6. Pia.Core.Option and Pia.Core.Result (<optional>, <expected> without the monadic operations);
  7. Pia.Core.Algo.Search: find, count, contains, equal, mismatch, starts_with, ends_with, search, adjacent_find, min_element, max_element, minmax_element, lexicographical_compare, is_sorted, is_sorted_until;
  8. Pia.Core.Algo.Modify: fill, copy, copy_backward, swap_ranges, reverse, rotate, shift_left, shift_right, replace, remove, unique, and <numeric>'s iota, accumulate, reduce, partial_sum, adjacent_difference, inner_product, with overflow in their contracts;
  9. Pia.Core.Algo.Sort and Heap (binary search family, make_heap and friends, sort as heapsort first since it needs no recursion or buffer, partial_sort, nth_element, partition, merge into an out slice, is_permutation, next_permutation, prev_permutation), each sort proved to return a sorted permutation;
  10. Pia.Core.Algo.Set (includes, set_union, set_intersection, set_difference, set_symmetric_difference into out slices);
  11. Pia.Core.Ascii, Pia.Core.Utf8 and integer Pia.Core.Charconv, with to_chars/from_chars round trips proved;
  12. Pia.Core.Hash, Pia.Core.Rand (integer engines such as minstd_rand and mt19937, and an unbiased uniform_int), Pia.Core.Ratio and Pia.Time's durations and civil calendar.
  13. Phase 2, containers and strings over Pia.Mem, with #72: string, deque, flat_map, flat_set, priority_queue, stack, queue, unordered_map, unordered_set, map and set (B-trees whose nodes live in a pool), list and forward_list (pool-indexed nodes), box (for unique_ptr, virtual bases and move_only_function), and the algorithms that need a buffer (stable_sort, stable_partition, inplace_merge).
  14. Phase 3, the outside world, after Pia.Sys and Pia.Io (#57, #58): format, print, readers and writers for the stream headers, <filesystem>, <cstdio>, <chrono>'s clocks, <stacktrace>.
  15. Phase 4, floats (M11): Pia.Math, floating-point <charconv>, the floating-point distributions.
  16. Phase 5, concurrency (M12): Pia.Sync, Pia.Task, Pia.Chan, as ADR 0027 designs them.
  17. Phase 6, function values: the predicate, operation and comparator overloads of the phase 1 algorithms (C++'s _if forms), transform, monadic option and result, <functional>, and <ranges>'s views.
  18. Later: <regex>, <mdspan> (with value parameters in generic types), time zones, Unicode tables, shared_ptr.

docs.title: 14. Language gaps are listed, not worked around
docs.text:
Where the library needs something the language does not have, the library waits for it, and the gap is an issue of its own. Known now:

Gap Blocks Imported types and generic functions across interfaces (ADR 0039 step 3) every program importing a generic library module; until then a module's generics are proved by the definition check, and its tests are in the module's own test file Concepts as type arguments (box c: a type-erased box whose contents are proved to meet c; ADR 0046) box over a concept, Pia.Fn's dynamic function values, replacements for virtual dispatch Function values, closures and lambdas ("functions as values are not supported yet"; being designed with generic and typed lambdas) phase 6: predicate, operation and comparator overloads, views, <functional> Value parameters in generic types ([t; n] for a parameter n; designed in design.md) std::array algorithms generic over N, bitset<N>, inplace_vector<T, N>, mdspan extents Core tuple types, values and patterns (section 9; an ADR of their own) <tuple>, pair as a tuple, structured bindings, apply, argument packs for format and make_unique, multi-value returns in <algorithm> (minmax, mismatch) Anonymous sum types std::variant<Ts...> beyond named variants, and visit over one Recursive types (ADR 0047) ref and weak for shared_ptr and weak_ptr, recursive values such as the JSON DOM (ADR 0045); the node containers use pool indices instead, which is their design rather than a workaround Calls inside a callee's ensures are unconstrained at the caller composing generic algorithms whose contracts name each other's spec functions Floats (M11), atomics and the concurrency runtime (M12) phases 4 and 5 Cost proofs proving C++'s complexity guarantees Payloads of fixed-array type in constructors, partial moves, @derive(drop) some container element types

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A C++ programmer can find every std facility, or why it is missing, from one page, and the page stays current because every library PR updates it.
  • Pia's library promises more than C++'s: each function's contract is its specification, proved, and C++'s undefined behaviour becomes a compile-time obligation on the caller.
  • Some C++ idioms do not survive: iterator pairs, exceptions, default allocators, comparator objects in containers' types, locales and wide strings. Each has a stated replacement.
  • The phases are ordered by what the language can do today, so most of <algorithm>, <bit>, <numeric>, <charconv> and <compare> can land before function values or floats, and the gap table says which language work unblocks the most of the rest.
  • The library becomes the largest body of proved Pia code, so it is also the main test of the verifier's speed and of ADR 0037's idioms; slow or awkward proofs found here become verifier issues.

docs.title: 41. Allocator semantics are a theory, and allocators prove they refine it through spec-only state
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), with the answers recorded under "Review": there is no ghost keyword, since a spec-only type marks state that codegen erases (fewer keywords is better); and how an allocator keeps its promises is up to each implementation of the Allocator concept.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked whether allocator-specific semantics can be set up as a theory (ADR 0036).

What exists today (ADR 0026, issue #88):

  • Three allocators are proved Pia: a bump allocator (tests/verify/bump.pia), with_arena regions (#70), and a pool of slots with a free stack (tests/verify/pool.pia).
  • Each states its promises in terms of its own representation. The pool, for example, says "slot s is live" as p.pos.[s] = 65535, and says the free stack is distinct as forall j. p.pos.[p.free.[j]] = j.
  • Every user carries those quantified facts through every call. Proving pool.pia showed the cost: Z3 would not compose two quantified frame postconditions of put until they were restated as one.
  • The usual promises are the same for every allocator:
  • a block handed out was not live;
  • two live blocks do not overlap;
  • a block given back is dead;
  • a block goes back only to the allocator that handed it out (owns).

A theory can state those promises once, as facts about an abstract heap. docs/theories.md, "Allocators", is a working first step: a theory Alloc with a bitmask model proves fresh_apart and reuse from four axioms, and catches a use after give.

What is missing is the link to running code. A theory's sorts are spec-only (ADR 0036), so a pool cannot hold an Alloc.heap, and take cannot say how it changes one.

Prior art:

  • Dafny and Verus keep ghost fields and ghost variables that the compiler erases.
  • Verus's tracked permissions and Iris's resource algebras model ownership of memory as ghost resources.
  • VeriFast and the separation-logic tools describe an allocator by an abstract predicate that its implementation proves it refines.
  • seL4's allocator proofs relate an abstract heap to concrete free lists through a refinement relation.

docs.title: 1. Pia.Mem.Alloc is a theory with a proved model
docs.text:
The theory has these parts:

  • Sorts and functions: a sort heap, plus none, live, take, give, base and size.
  • Axioms: none of them quantify over a heap's contents.
  • take makes one block live, and give makes one block dead.
  • Distinct blocks are apart.
  • A size class (step 4) bounds size.
  • A model proves every axiom, as for every entry in docs/theories.md, so nothing is trusted.

docs.title: 2. Spec-only state: fields and parameters the verifier sees and codegen erases
docs.text:
• Declaring it: there is no keyword. A field or parameter whose type is spec-only (int, real or a theory's sort, ADR 0036) is spec-only state, as in (h : Alloc.heap) or { ...; heap : Alloc.heap }. A counter that only proofs need is an int. It is not meta: meta state lives only while metaprograms expand and has one value per compilation, but this state has a value per pool and per execution path, as p.top does.
  • Writing it: code may assign a spec expression to a spec-only place, as in p.heap <- Alloc.take p.heap s, and pass one as a spec-only argument.
  • The one-way rule follows from the type: code already cannot compute with spec-only values, so a spec-only place can only flow into other spec-only places and into contracts. Erasing it cannot change what a program computes.
  • Codegen drops spec-only fields and parameters. The C ABI and the layout (ADR 0030) do not include them.

docs.title: 3. Each allocator proves, privately, that it refines Alloc
docs.text:
How it does so is the implementation's own choice (Dean, 2026-11-22). The Allocator concept fixes only what users see; an implementation may keep its coupling invariant as module state, repeat it as requires/ensures, or use any other proof that meets the concept. The pool, for example, adds heap : Alloc.heap and proves a coupling invariant inside its module: forall s. Alloc.live p.heap s <==> p.pos.[s] = 65535.

Its exported contracts mention only the heap:

  • take ensures p.heap = Alloc.take (old p.heap) b.i and Alloc.live (old p.heap) b.i = false.
  • give requires Alloc.live p.heap b.i.

In Pia.Mem's default implementations the coupling invariant is module state (ADR 0006), so it is not in the interface (ADR 0039). Users reason with Alloc's axioms, with no quantifiers.

docs.title: 4. Owners are each implementation's choice too
docs.text: Reuse must not cross allocators (the owns fact of ADR 0026), and the concept requires give to say so, but not how. Pia.Mem's default implementations give each block a spec-only owner: a block is { i : u16; owner : Alloc.id }, and give requires b.owner = p.id. An implementation could instead have a theory of its own, generated by a metaprogram as machine is in docs/theories.md, if that suits its structure better.

docs.title: 5. Allocator is a concept, stated with Alloc the theory
docs.text: Allocators are a concept (Dean, 2026-11-22), and the Allocator concept of ADR 0034 states its requirements with Alloc's functions. So generic code such as Vec<t, a : Allocator> is proved once against the theory, not once per allocator.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. The theory and the bitmask model in docs/theories.md (done with this ADR).
  2. Spec-only parameters and fields in code: Sema, IRGen, the verifier, and codegen erasure, with errors when code computes with them.
  3. pool.pia refines Alloc through a spec-only heap, and reuse proves using only the theory.
  4. Owners, then size classes and general (the rest of #88).
  5. Allocator refers to Alloc, and Vec stores its allocator (Dean's choice of 2026-11-22). (Implemented: tests/verify/vec_allocator.pia, with the allocator's region a concept parameter, ADR 0042. A generic function cannot meet a requirement yet, so the example's bump is for u16.)

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Users of every allocator get the same small facts, and proofs get cheaper, because no user quantifies over an allocator's arrays.
  • Spec-only state is a language feature with uses beyond allocators: lock levels (docs/theories.md, "Lock levels") and units of measure already describe a "ghost argument" that code cannot pass today. It adds no keyword.
  • The one-way rule rests on the existing ban on computing with spec-only values. Getting it wrong would let erased state change behaviour, so it gets its own error tests.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Dean's answers (2026-11-22):

  1. ghost or @ghost? Neither. A spec-only type marks the state, and nothing else is needed: fewer keywords is better for the language.
  2. Is the coupling invariant module state? Each allocator implementation decides. Allocators are a concept, and Pia.Mem's default implementations do what they need to, which is module state.
  3. One theory with owner ids, or one per allocator? Each implementation decides, too. The defaults use owner ids.

docs.title: 42. Lifetimes are checked by liveness, marked where values cross boundaries, and escape analysis places memory
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted. Dean (2026-11-22) answered all three questions below yes: region parameters on types, spec-only generations, and escape analysis placing only compiler-owned memory. He also said borrows end at their last use (implemented, step 1), and values are released at their last use, as in Mojo, so that a tail call can reuse the frame (section 5).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-22): the language should have liveness checks for lifetime analysis, and grow explicit lifetime markers on values that cross boundaries. Escape analysis can then decide stack space reuse and generational arena allocation and reuse.

The rules today (ADR 0026, docs/irgen.md, "Bindings and mutation"):

  • Borrows are lexical. A borrow lasts to the end of the scope of the local that holds it, even after its last use. So a lender stays locked for longer than it needs to be. For example, an allocator cannot be reset after the last use of a buffer taken from it if that buffer's local is still in scope.
  • A lifetime is named by its lender. borrowed(m) on a result or an inout parameter says the value may hold a loan from parameter m. That is a lifetime marker already, but it exists only in function signatures. A record cannot hold a loan whose lender lives outside it. This is why Vec cannot yet store its allocator (ADR 0041, step 5).
  • Moves are checked by flow, and linear values by paths. These rules (the moved map and @linear) already track, per path, whether a value is still usable. That is a liveness question asked in a different form.
  • Memory placement is explicit and fixed. with_arena regions are stack memory made once per function entry. Locals, records and coroutine frames are placed by LLVM alone. Nothing tells LLVM which stack slots are dead, so two with_arenas in sequence use two regions of stack.

Prior art:

  • Rust's non-lexical lifetimes (NLL) and Polonius end a loan at its last use, computed by liveness over the control-flow graph. They also name lifetimes in signatures and in types ('a).
  • Cyclone, the ML Kit and Tofte–Talpin regions pass region parameters explicitly at boundaries and infer them inside bodies.
  • Go and HotSpot use escape analysis to place an allocation on the stack when it does not escape. LLVM's stack colouring reuses slots between llvm.lifetime.start and llvm.lifetime.end.
  • Generational arenas come from game engines and from Rust's generational-arena and slotmap crates. An arena is reset per frame or per request, and each handle carries a generation so that a stale handle can be told apart from a live one.

docs.title: 1. Liveness ends loans and checks uses
docs.text:
A loan ends at the last use of every value that holds it, not at the end of its scope. A liveness pass over each function's control flow decides this. It treats the following as uses:

  • a read, a call argument, a match, or a return;
  • a defer that touches the value, which runs at the scope's exit (ADR 0028), so the value lives until then (a value's own drop is not such a use: it runs at the value's last use, section 5);
  • every path out of a handler arm that can still reach the value.

The lexical checks in IRGen become liveness checks, with the same errors. Each error points at the later use that keeps the loan alive. For example:

error: 'm' is reset here while 'b' still borrows it
note: 'b' is used later, here

Moves and @linear values join the same pass. Using a value after it is moved, after its loan ends, or after its generation ends (section 4) is one kind of error: a use of a dead value. Contracts are exempt, as they are today, because they describe values rather than use them.

docs.title: 2. Lifetime markers appear only where values cross boundaries
docs.text:
Inside a function body, lifetimes are inferred and never written. A value that crosses a boundary carries an explicit marker, so each boundary can be checked on its own. That keeps modules separately verifiable (ADR 0039).

The boundaries are these:

Boundary Marker a function's result or inout/out parameter borrowed(m), naming the lender parameter (exists) a record or variant field a region parameter of the type: let vec = let (t : type) (r : region) => type { alloc : bump t r; buf : borrowed(r) mutable [t]; len : usize }, where the allocator and the buffer both borrow from r a task, spread worker or channel send borrowed(r) on what is sent; it must name a region that encloses the task (ADR 0027) a coroutine suspension point inferred, but checked against the frame's region an interface as in the function or type it lists

region is a builtin type name, like type, not a keyword. A region parameter is deduced from the arguments, as a type parameter is (ADR 0034), so users write vec u8 r or simply vec u8. It is spec-only state (ADR 0041): codegen erases it, and it costs nothing at run time.

docs.title: 3. Escape analysis places the memory the compiler owns
docs.text:
Escape analysis is modular. It reads only signatures and the markers of section 2, and never looks across function bodies. A value escapes its scope if one of these holds:

  • it is returned;
  • it is stored in a place that outlives the scope;
  • it is sent to a task;
  • it is passed where a marker lets the callee keep it.

The compiler uses this only for memory it owns: locals, records, with_arena regions and coroutine frames. Allocation through an allocator stays explicit (ADR 0026). The compiler never quietly moves an alloc call onto the stack, because the call's failure is part of what the program handles.

  • Stack reuse. Each stack slot gets llvm.lifetime.start and llvm.lifetime.end at the ends of its live range, so LLVM shares one slot between values that are never live together. That includes with_arena regions in sequence.
  • Frame size. A coroutine frame keeps only the values live across a suspension point, which makes the frame size the compiler proves smaller.
  • Advice. A lint (ADR 0037) reports an allocation from a long-lived allocator whose result never escapes a loop iteration or a scope. It suggests with_arena or a generational arena instead.

docs.title: 4. Generational arenas
docs.text:
A generational arena is a Pia.Mem allocator for memory whose lifetime is one generation: one loop iteration, one request, one frame or one task run.

  • Reset is O(1). next a ends a generation and starts the next one. It reuses the arena's pages without returning them, so a steady-state loop allocates nothing from the page heap.
  • Generations are spec-only state. Each loan carries its generation as a spec-only field. Liveness proves that no loan is used after next, so no generation check runs in proved code.
  • Run-time generations only where the verifier cannot see. A handle that leaves proved code, such as one given to C, kept in a REPL session (ADR 0031) or sent through an untyped channel, carries a real generation counter. It is checked on the way back in.
  • Escape analysis picks the generation. The lint in section 3 points at the innermost generation that encloses every use of an allocation. Alloc (ADR 0041) states generational arenas as a refinement, so next gives back every block live in the old generation.

docs.title: 5. Values are released at their last use, and tail calls reuse the frame
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-22) asked for Mojo's approach. Mojo destroys a value "as soon as possible", right after its last use, instead of at the end of its scope. Pia does the same.

  • A value with Drop is dropped right after its last use on each path, not at the end of its scope. The rule that decides a loan's end (section 1) also decides the drop's place.
  • A value that is never used is dropped where it is bound.
  • A value used on only one branch is dropped at its last use on that branch, and at the start of the other branch.
  • @linear values are unchanged: they must still be consumed explicitly, so they have no implicit drop to move.
  • defer is unchanged. A defer runs at the scope's exit, in reverse order, as ADR 0028 says, because it is code the programmer placed there. A value that a defer mentions lives until the defer runs.
  • Cleanup errors keep their rule. A drop that can fail is a defer? in all but name, so ADR 0028's rule applies: it must not shadow an error in flight. A drop that runs early, before the error, cannot shadow it.
  • Memory is released early too. A with_arena region whose arena is dead is freed at the arena's last use. The same goes for a buffer from general or a pool that has a Drop. Stack slots end there (section 3), so later values can reuse them.

Tail calls reuse the frame. A call in tail position, f x as the last thing a function does, is lowered to a guaranteed tail call (musttail). That happens when, after section 5's releases, nothing in the current frame is live across the call:

  • every local the call does not take has been dropped or moved by then;
  • no argument borrows from the frame: a borrowed argument must come from the caller's own parameters, not from a local or a with_arena region of the frame;
  • no defer of the frame is still pending, since a pending defer would run after the call.

Under those conditions a tail-recursive loop runs in constant stack. When a call in tail position is not eligible, it is an ordinary call. A lint (ADR 0037) then names the local, borrow or defer that keeps the frame alive, so that a recursion the programmer meant to run in constant stack does not silently grow it. @tail on a call makes eligibility an error instead of a lint.

Prior art: Mojo's ASAP destruction, and Scheme's and Zig's guaranteed tail calls (@call(.always_tail, ...)).

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. Liveness-based loan ends in place of the lexical borrow check, with moves and @linear in the same pass, and the new error notes. (Loan ends: implemented, tests/irgen/borrow_liveness.pia.)
  2. region parameters on records and variants, with borrowed(r) fields. With this, Vec can store its allocator (ADR 0041, step 5). (Records, functions and interfaces: implemented, tests/verify/vec_region.pia, tests/irgen/region_errors.pia and tests/modules/regions.pia; variants later.)
  3. Markers at task, channel and coroutine boundaries.
  4. Stack slot lifetimes in codegen, with a stack-size test of with_arenas in sequence.
  5. The generational arena in Pia.Mem, with its spec-only generations and its Alloc refinement.
  6. The escape lint, then run-time generations at FFI and REPL boundaries.
  7. Drops at last use (section 5), replacing scope-end drops.
  8. Guaranteed tail calls, the @tail attribute, and the frame lint.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Loans end where they are last used, so fewer correct programs are rejected. A lender is free again as soon as its borrowers are dead.
  • The only lifetime syntax is at boundaries: borrowed(m) (existing) and region parameters on types. Function bodies stay unannotated.
  • Stack use falls without new syntax, and coroutine frames shrink.
  • Memory and resources are released as early as possible, and tail-recursive functions run in constant stack.
  • A value's drop no longer runs at a fixed, visible place. Code that needs an effect at the scope's end writes a defer, as it does today.
  • Liveness errors are harder to explain than scope errors, because the cause can be a later use. So each error names that use.

docs.title: Questions for Dean (answered 2026-11-22)
docs.text:
1. Marker syntax. Name lifetimes by values (borrowed(m)) and by region parameters on types, rather than Rust-style 'a? It adds no keyword, and ' already means "primed name". Yes (Dean chose region parameters on types, and later wrote "Explicit with borrowed(m)"). So every marker is written, never inferred, and in one form: borrowed(m) names a value at a function boundary, and borrowed(r) names a region where a type must hold loans without naming a value, as a vector holding its allocator does. A function names a region only through a parameter whose type mentions it.
  2. Generations. Spec-only in proved code, with run-time counters only at FFI and REPL boundaries? Yes.
  3. Stack placement. Should escape analysis place only compiler-owned memory, and advise (through a lint) rather than rewrite alloc calls? This keeps allocation explicit and its failures handled. Yes.

docs.title: 43. Generic definitions are proved once, against their concepts
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22). Steps 1, 2 and 3 are implemented (verifier.md).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 0034 gave Pia concepts, constrained generic functions and a definition check. It left one thing for later: "Each instance is still proved on its own, so goals stay about concrete types. Proving a generic body once against the concepts' contracts would save build time (ADR 0032). It is sound once requirement contracts are proved at the use check, and it is left as a measured follow-up." The standard library (ADR 0040) is the measurement. Issue #203 records it.

docs.title: What happens today
docs.text:
Generics are monomorphised before verification:

  1. Definition check (IRGen::checkDefinition). Each generic body is generated once, with each type parameter standing for a stand-in type, a record named after the parameter with no fields. A call whose arguments have a stand-in type resolves only against the requirements its constraints promise. That is a name and use check, so the body can only call what its concepts promise. The generated function, and every instance it made, is then erased. Nothing about it reaches the verifier.
  2. Instances (IRGen::genericInstance). Each use with new type arguments queues an instance, lex_compare<u8>, generated after the function that first used it. An instance is an ordinary function at concrete types, with the requirement calls bound to the functions that met the concept at the use check.
  3. Laws are lemmas generated per type at the use check, such as Ord<u8>.irreflexive. Each is proved once per type that meets the concept. A requirement's contract, such as less's ensures result ==> less b a = false, is also a lemma per type (Ord<u8>.less.contract).
  4. The verifier sees only instances. Each is encoded at its own types: 68-bit (or wider) bit-vectors, SMT arrays from index to element for slices, and records replaced by their fields. The proof cache (ADR 0032) keys on the SHA-256 of each query, which mentions the types' widths and ranges. So two instances never share a cache entry.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• Re-proof at every instance. Splitting lib/Pia/Core/Order.pia's cost by the definition each goal belongs to:
  • The generic lexicographical_compare (a loop with an invariant over a recursive spec function) and its spec function lex_from were 96.6% of 73.1 million resource units: 60.3M and 10.4M, about 8.8M at each of 8 integer types.
  • Everything else was 2.4M: the concrete instances, the laws at 9 types, and the other generics.
  • The module now exports the lexicographic functions for u8 only, so it costs 9.75M. Each further type would cost about 8.8M again, for a proof that says nothing new.
  • No proof without an instance. This is accepted, with 0 proved, 0 failed:
let bad (t : type where Ord t) (a : t) (b : t) : bool
  ensures result = less b a
= less a b

With instances at u8 and u16 it is refuted twice. A library module whose generic nothing in it instantiates is never checked at all. So Pia.Core.Option makes a u8 use only so that its generics are proved. - Laws are not facts in generic bodies. A body cannot call irreflexive a: a law is a lemma per type, not something the body can name. Pia.Core.Order had to restate asymmetry as a contract on the less requirement (ensures result ==> less b a = false), which a body can use. - Generic functions cannot be exported. An interface cannot list (t : type where Ord t) -> ... (ADR 0039, step 3), partly because there is no proof of a generic to export. Each library module exports per-type instances, stamped out by a metaprogram, so every type an importer might need is proved and paid for in the library.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Dafny and Why3 verify a generic method once with each type parameter an uninterpreted sort, plus whatever the type's traits or clones provide. Verus does the same for Rust generics, with trait bounds as uninterpreted functions and spec trait methods. F* checks a polymorphic function once. None of them re-verifies at instances, because parametricity makes the instance proofs redundant. Coq and Lean do the same by construction. C++ templates are the opposite, checked only at instantiation, and Pia's instance proofs inherited that model.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A constrained generic function's body is proved once, at its definition, with each type parameter an uninterpreted sort and each concept function an uninterpreted function constrained by its requirement contract and the concept's laws. An instance is then proved by that proof, whenever its body is the generic body with the type parameters substituted. Bodies that use facts only a concrete type has fall back to the per-instance proof they get today.

docs.title: 1. The abstract encoding
docs.text:
The definition check already generates the body at stand-in types. The new step keeps that function, marks it pia.generic_definition, and verifies it:

  • Type parameters are sorts. A stand-in type t is (declare-sort t 0) in the query, not a record, so ScalarizeRecords leaves it alone. Its values are constants of that sort. A parameter, a let, a value returned from a requirement call: none of them has a width, a range or a bit pattern.
  • Buffers of t. [t] and [t; n] are SMT arrays from the index bit-vector to t, with their lengths as today. Indexing, slicing, views, old and the frame facts of inout buffers (verifier.md) are unchanged, since they never looked at the element.
  • Generic types. option t and result t e are SMT datatypes over the sorts, as variants are today over concrete payloads.
  • Concept functions are uninterpreted functions. Each requirement less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool of a constraint Ord t is (declare-fun Ord.less (t t) Bool), shared by every call in the body. A call in code and a call in a contract are the same application, so the body's less xs.[i] ys.[i] and the contract's agree. That is what a code call gives a pure function today, after the change in #202.
  • Requirement contracts are hypotheses. At each call, the requirement's requires is a goal and its ensures is assumed, as for any call. This is sound because the use check proves each requirement contract of each type that meets the concept (Ord<u8>.less.contract).
  • Laws are hypotheses. Each law of each constraint, irreflexive, less_transitive and so on, is a universally quantified axiom over the sort in every query of the body. They are guarded the way theory axioms are (ADR 0036): relevance by the functions a goal mentions, the fallback to every axiom of the theory before a goal fails, and tracking for the unsat core. This is also where laws become usable in generic bodies: a body or a spec function can rely on transitivity without restating it as a contract. Laws may also be callable as lemmas (irreflexive a), which instantiates one without the quantifier.
  • Generic callees. A call from one generic to another, lex_compare<t> from lex_compare_three_way<t>, uses the callee's contract at the sorts, as a call between concrete functions does.

The goals are the generic's own: overflow of usize arithmetic on indices, bounds, invariants, measures, postconditions. A goal about a value of type t can only come from what the body does with it, so it is about sorts and the concept functions alone.

docs.title: 2. What falls back to per-instance proof
docs.text:
The abstract encoding applies only to a body whose meaning does not depend on the type arguments beyond their concepts. The definition check already knows when it does not, because the same facts make it generate the body at stand-ins differently or not at all. A generic is parametric unless its body or signature:

  • does arithmetic, comparison or = on a value of a type parameter without a concept promising it (today an error at the definition check, so these never reach the verifier);
  • applies a type-level metaprogram to a type parameter in its signature, such as : widen t (ADR 0035). The definition check already sets opaqueStandIn_ and checks these bodies per instance;
  • matches on a type, uses size_of, type_kind or any metaprogram builtin that reads a type argument, or has a where predicate that is not a concept (ADR 0035);
  • depends on layout (a published object layout, ADR 0030), on an element's bit width (bits, bswap on t), or on a constant of type t;
  • is chosen between precondition overloads inside its body by facts that differ per instance. ADR 0034 already restricts a choice in a generic body to facts that hold in every instance. So this is the existing rule, and the abstract proof makes the same choice as every instance.

A non-parametric generic is proved per instance, as today, and the report says so (proved per instance: the signature applies 'widen' to 't'). A generic with no constraint, such as swap (t : type), is parametric: it has no concept functions, and nothing can be done with a t but move it.

docs.title: 3. Soundness
docs.text:
Two facts make an instance's proof follow from the generic proof:

  1. The instance meets the hypotheses. For each type that meets a concept, the use check already proves every requirement contract and every law as a lemma at that type. Those lemmas are proved, or the program fails, before any instance is used. So for t = u8 the uninterpreted Ord.less can be read as the u8 less, and every hypothesis of the generic proof holds of it.
  2. The body is parametric. Every operation the body applies to a value of type t is a requirement call, passing the value on, storing it in or loading it from a buffer, or comparing it by a concept function. The body cannot inspect the value's bits, size or type. So the instance's verification condition is the generic one with the sort read as the concrete type and each uninterpreted function read as the concrete function. This is the substitution lemma for a first-order theory: a formula valid in every model of the hypotheses is valid in the model the instance gives. The bounds and overflow goals on usize are the same formulas in both.

Section 2 is exactly what makes the second fact hold: it lists every way a body can see more of t than its concepts. The check is syntactic, made where the definition check generates the stand-in body. Anything it cannot classify falls back to per-instance proof, which is today's behaviour, so a mistake in the classifier costs build time, not soundness, as long as it only ever errs towards falling back.

Two cases need care:

  • Adapters (ADR 0034). An instance through an adapter, sort<t = u8, Ord = by_value>, binds the concept's functions to the adapter's. The adapter's contracts and laws are proved at the use check like any type's, so the generic proof still applies.
  • Termination. The generic proof proves decreases with the concept functions uninterpreted. A requirement function that does not terminate at some type would break fact 1, but requirement functions are ordinary functions whose own termination is proved where they are defined, or they are skipped goals there. The rule is that an instance whose type's requirement functions have skipped or unproved goals is proved per instance.

docs.title: 4. Instances, reports and the cache
docs.text:
• An instance of a parametric generic generates code as today, but its goals are not encoded. The report lists the generic's goals once, at the generic's lines, with the method [generic]. Each instance adds one line: proved: 'lex_compare<u8>' is an instance of a generic proof [generic].
  • --verify-stats gains generic= (goals proved at a definition) and instances= (instances discharged by one), so the bench shows the saving.
  • Proof cache. A generic goal's query mentions sorts and uninterpreted functions, not widths, so it is the same query in every program that uses the generic. It is cached under its hash as any goal is (ADR 0032). Instances need no cache entry. Editing a concept's contract or laws changes every generic query over it, which re-proves them, as it should.
  • Counterexamples. A failed generic goal reports a model over the sort, such as xs.[0] = t!val!0 with Ord.less(t!val!0, t!val!1) = true. That is an abstract counterexample: it shows which law or contract is missing. If the goal would hold at every instance in the program, the report also suggests the law that would close it. A generic that fails abstractly is not then re-proved per instance. Its definition is wrong for some model of its concepts, and the fix is a stronger constraint or law, not a narrower set of types.

docs.title: 5. Interfaces
