docs.text: An interface can then list a generic function with its constraints, let lex_compare : (t : type where Ord t) -> (xs : [t]) -> (ys : [t]) -> bool ensures ..., and its contract is checked against the definition once, by the generic proof (ADR 0039, step 3). Importers instantiate it without re-proving it, which is what lets Pia.Core.Order and its successors export one generic function instead of eight stamped instances. That also needs concepts in interfaces and exported generic bodies (the inline surface, ADR 0039 step 4). This ADR supplies the proof those steps assume.

docs.title: 6. Steps
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with its own tests and bench numbers.

  1. Abstract encoding, reported, with no effect on instances. Keep the definition-check function, encode stand-in types as sorts and requirement calls as uninterpreted functions with their contracts, and prove the generic's goals. Report them as [generic] alongside the instance goals, which are still proved. Tests: lex_compare over Ord t, swap over an unconstrained t, and the bad example above, which now fails with no instance. This step makes an uninstantiated generic checked at all.
  2. Instances discharged by the generic proof. For a parametric generic whose generic goals all proved, skip encoding its instances' goals and report the instance line. Bench: Pia.Core.Order with the lexicographic functions restored at 8 types should cost about what one instance does now.
  3. Laws as hypotheses, and as callable lemmas in generic bodies, with ADR 0036's relevance and fallback. Pia.Core.Order's asymmetry contract on less becomes a law again.
  4. Fallback rules (section 2), each with a test that a non-parametric generic is proved per instance and says why.
  5. Generic functions in interfaces, with ADR 0039 step 3.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A generic is proved once however many types use it, and an uninstantiated generic is proved at all. Library modules stop paying per type for the same proof, which is most of the cost of the generic algorithms ADR 0040 plans (Pia.Core.Algo.*).
  • Generic proofs are about uninterpreted sorts, so they never bit-blast a value of type t. For bodies like lex_compare, whose only operation on t is less, the abstract query should be no harder than the cheapest instance's. That is expected, not measured: step 1 measures it.
  • A generic that held only at the types a program happened to use, because some instance's concrete facts closed a goal, now fails at its definition with an abstract counterexample. That is the point, but it can turn a passing program into a failing one when step 1 lands. Step 1 only reports, so such generics show up before step 2 makes the generic proof the only one.
  • Failed generic goals show models over sorts, which are less familiar than integer counterexamples. The report names the uninterpreted functions after the concept (Ord.less) to keep them readable.
  • The per-instance path stays, for non-parametric bodies, so the verifier keeps both encodings.
  • Laws in every query of a generic body cost what theory axioms do, and get the same relevance filtering.

docs.title: Step 1 as built
docs.text:
Step 1 follows section 1 with these differences:

  • Stand-ins stay records. IRGen keeps the definition check's stand-in records rather than making the type parameters !pia.sort, which code cannot use. ScalarizeRecords sets the generic's proof aside, and the verifier reads a record with no fields in it as the sort generic.t. A sort is named after its type parameter, so every generic's t is the same sort, which is harmless because each proof is a query of its own.
  • Requirements are a theory. Each concept at the stand-ins is a theory, Ord<t>, whose functions are the requirements and whose axioms are their contracts. ADR 0036's relevance closure and fallback come with it. Its consistency check, which trusted theories get, is skipped, since every type that meets the concept proves the axioms. So is the second, tracked solve that reports which axioms a proof used.
  • More falls back. Generic types over a type parameter (option t, pair a b) and requirements with a precondition or a record result fall back to per-instance proof, rather than being encoded as datatypes over sorts. So Pia.Core.Order's compare, which returns an ordering, is proved only at its instances.
  • The report marks every proof goal [generic], and lists each fallback with its reason, outside the goal counts.

Measured on Pia.Core.Order, the generic proofs cost about what one instance does or less:

Generic Generic proof One instance lex_compare 5.69M 6.33M (u8) lex_from 1.17M 1.17M (u8) min, max 52 about 230 swap 744 about 83,000

The module costs 16.6M, up from 9.75M: the 6.86M of its generic proofs, while its instances are still proved, as step 1 intends. tests/verify/generic_proofs.pia proves the lexicographic compare once and again at u8, i32 and u64.

docs.title: Step 2 as built
docs.text:
• Order. Generic proofs are encoded and solved first. A generic whose proof's goals all held, and none was left out by --verify-only, discharges its instances, each reported as one [generic] line.
  • Which instances. An instance is discharged only when its calls correspond one for one with the proof's: a concept's function bound to a function that returns (no while without a measure, no recursion without one, to a depth of four calls), another generic's stand-in instance matched by that generic's instance at the instance's types, and every other call to the same function. Overload resolution can pick a more specific concrete function at an instance's types (Pia.Core.Order hit this), and then the instance is proved at its types.
  • Soundness notes. Calls into a discharged instance still prove its precondition at the call. The use check still proves each requirement contract and law at each type, so a type whose less breaks a contract is still rejected (tests/verify/generic_proofs.pia, at i8).
  • Equality. Step 1 encoded = on values of a type parameter as true: the stand-in record has no fields, and field-by-field equality of nothing holds. That made a generic proof of ensures result = b for a body a succeed, while the instance failed (tests/verify/generic_functions.pia, pick). Before instances were discharged that only mislabelled a report line, but step 2 would have made it unsound. = on a type parameter is now equality in its sort, a call of pia.eq<t> that the verifier encodes as SMT equality, and pick fails at its definition with a counterexample over the sort.

Pia.Core.Order exports lexicographical_compare for all 8 integer types again, at 8.49M for the module: 73.1M when every instance was re-proved, 9.75M with u8 only, 16.6M in step 1. Encoding takes 5.3 seconds of its 5.8-second run, and most of it is the per-instance proofs that remain. The three-way comparison still falls back, since it returns an ordering, so it stays exported for u8 only. tests/verify/generic_proofs.pia falls from 28.8M to 7.2M.

docs.title: Step 3 as built
docs.text:
Laws are axioms of the concept's theory in every generic proof whose constraints promise the concept, with a multi-pattern trigger of the concept calls in a law's requires (transitivity's less a b and less b c). A law the solver could not instantiate is left out, which only assumes less. Pia.Core.Algo.Search's min_element and max_element need transitivity and incomparability, and prove generically. Laws are not callable as lemmas yet, and an interface cannot list a lemma, so a generic exported with its body cannot call one.

Two changes came with it, found by Pia.Core.Algo.Search, the first library module whose generics are over another module's concepts: an importer does not prove an imported generic again (it cost each importer of Search about 42M), and an importer's instance finds a concept's functions in the concept's module.

docs.title: Feasibility
docs.text: No code spike was made. A spike needs the three changes of step 1: keeping the definition-check function, encoding the field-less stand-in record as a sort (today ScalarizeRecords removes it, since it has no fields), and giving requirement calls their contracts at verification (today the definition-check body calls declarations without them). Those are step 1 itself, more than a spike's hour. The measurements above bound the gain: re-proving lex_compare at 8 types cost 8 times one instance (70.7M against about 8.8M), and a once-proof replaces the 8 with 1.

docs.title: 44. Function values: typed and generic lambdas, a Function concept, and proofs through function arguments
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), with all three questions answered. Dean chose question 1 (2026-11-22): a function object is any type whose module defines apply.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia's design has always had function values. A nameless let is a function literal, let (x) => x * x, with no fun or lambda keyword, and function literals are curried (design.md). The parser reads them, and metaprograms run them in the interpreter: every operator in the prelude is one. Ordinary code cannot use them. IRGen has no lowering for Lambda outside with_arena, and the tour lists function values under "Designed but not built yet".

The C++23 standard library (ADR 0040) is blocked on them: predicates, comparators and operations for <algorithm> and <numeric>, <ranges> views, <functional>, and the monadic operations of option and result. Dean has set two requirements for that work (2026-11-22):

  • No _if variants. find, count, remove, replace, copy, sort and accumulate are each one overload set, with overloads that take a value and overloads that take a function (ADR 0040, section 6). So overload resolution (ADR 0034) must tell a value of type t from a function t -> bool cleanly.
  • A standard Function concept matches function objects, lambdas and plain functions alike, and the library's predicate overloads are constrained on it.

The library thread also needs:

  1. a callee's ensures to mention its predicate, as in find's ensures result < len xs ==> p xs.[result], which needs function arguments to be pure and total;
  2. a callee to require a law of its comparator, such as a strict weak order for sort;
  3. find xs (let (x) => x > 3) to compile to the same vectorised loop as a hand-written one.

Other constraints come from earlier decisions: fewer keywords is better; generic parameters are (t : type) with deduction (ADR 0034, ADR 0035); generic definitions are to be proved once (ADR 0043); there is no garbage collection (ADR 0026); and captured values must respect ownership and borrows (ADR 0042).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• C++ gives each lambda its own unnamed closure type with an operator(). Templates over the callable type monomorphise and inline, which is why std::find_if with a lambda vectorises. std::function is the separate, type-erased, allocating form. C++20 generic lambdas (auto parameters, or []<typename T>) are lambdas with a template operator().
  • Rust does the same with Fn, FnMut and FnOnce traits, impl Fn arguments and results, and Box<dyn Fn> for the dynamic form. Captures are inferred by use: by reference, by mutable reference, or by move.
  • Dafny and Why3 treat function values in specifications as total mathematical functions; Dafny's f.requires(x) and f.reads expose a function value's contract. Verus gives closures requires and ensures clauses that the caller can rely on through f.requires and f.ensures.
  • OCaml has closures as heap values, which Pia cannot copy without a garbage collector.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Function values are static by default, as in C++ and Rust: every lambda has its own type, a function parameter is a constrained type parameter, and each call with a lambda is a separate instance that codegen inlines. The proof follows ADR 0043: a higher-order function is proved once, with its function argument abstract and constrained by the contract of its parameter's type, and each argument is checked against that contract where it is passed.

docs.title: 1. Lambdas
docs.text:
A lambda is a nameless let, as today. It may carry types, modifiers, a result type and contracts, in the same places a named function does:

let square = let (x : i32) => x * x
let next = let (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 255 ensures result = x + 1 => x + 1
let between (lo : u8) (hi : u8) = let (x : u8) => lo <= x && x <= hi

The grammar gains the result type and the contracts:

lambda = "let" lparam { lparam } [ ":" annot ] { contract } "=>" seq ;

A lambda is curried like any function: let (a) (b) => a + b applied to one argument is a lambda of one parameter.

A lambda's body is its definition. Where a lambda is in scope, the verifier knows what it computes, as it does for pure scalar functions today (#202), so most lambdas need no contract. A written requires restricts where it may be called, and a written ensures is checked against the body like any postcondition.

docs.title: 2. Typed and generic lambdas
docs.text:
A lambda's parameters may be typed, untyped or explicitly generic.

  • Typed: let (x : u8) => x > 3 has type u8 -> bool.
  • Untyped, with an expected type: where the lambda is an argument, or bound by a let whose type is written, the parameter types come from the expected type. In find xs (let (x) => x > 3) with xs : [u8], x is a u8, deduced exactly as a generic argument is deduced from the expected type (ADR 0034).
  • Untyped, with no expected type: let gt3 = let (x) => x > 3 is a generic lambda, like a C++ auto lambda. Each untyped parameter is an implicit type parameter, and each use instantiates it. Its body is checked and proved per instance, as generic code was before ADR 0043, because there is no concept to prove it against. A lint (ADR 0037) suggests a type, or an explicit generic form, for a generic lambda that is exported or used at more than one type.
  • Explicitly generic: let (t : type where Ord t) (a : t) (b : t) => less a b has type parameters like a generic function, deduced at each application and constrained by concepts. A constrained generic lambda is proved once, against its concepts, by ADR 0043.

docs.title: 3. Function types
docs.text:
The arrow type that the grammar already has is the type of a function value. Its parameters may be named, and the whole arrow may carry contracts that talk about them and about result:

(p : t -> bool)
(f : (x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 255 ensures result > x)
(less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool)

arrow_type = arrow_dom "->" type { contract } ;

The contracts belong to the innermost arrow, so for a curried (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool they may name both a and b, and they apply once both are given. Modifiers on the parameters are written as for named functions: borrowed in [u8] -> usize.

A function type is a type like any other, with two exceptions. Function types never meet Eq, Ord or Hash, since Pia has no function equality. And a function type in a parameter's position is not one type but any type that meets Function (section 4).

docs.title: 4. The Function concept
docs.text:
Function is a standard concept, in the prelude, defined with ADR 0034's syntax:

let meta Function (f : type) (a : type) (r : type) : concept = sig
  let apply : (g : f) -> (x : a) -> r
end

A type f meets Function f a r when a value of it can be applied to an a to give an r. Three kinds of type meet it:

  • A lambda's type. Each lambda has its own anonymous type, a record of its captures (section 6), which meets Function with the lambda's own parameter and result types. Two lambdas with the same text are still two types.
  • A named function's type. A top-level function named as a value, find xs is_digit, has a singleton type with no fields, which meets Function with the function's signature. An overloaded name used as a value is resolved against the expected type, and is ambiguous without one.
  • A function object, a record or variant whose module defines apply for it. Application syntax calls it: for g : counter_below, g x is apply g x. This is how a library type such as a hash functor or a comparator with state is callable.

Curried functions meet Function one argument at a time: t -> t -> bool is a function to t -> bool, so a two-argument function object writes apply (g : f) (a : t) (b : t) : bool, which has the signature f -> t -> (t -> bool).

An arrow type in a parameter is sugar for a constrained type parameter. In

let find (t : type) (xs : [t]) (p : t -> bool) : usize

p : t -> bool means a fresh type parameter f with where Function f t bool, and p : f. Writing the constraint out is allowed and means the same thing. Each argument passed for p deduces f to its own type, so every call is an instance at that lambda or function. A result type written as an arrow, as in compose's, is the same: some type meeting Function, whose actual type the compiler knows, like Rust's impl Fn.

Overloading on a value or a function then needs nothing new. With

let find (t : type where Eq t) (xs : [t]) (v : t) : usize
let find (t : type) (xs : [t]) (p : t -> bool) : usize

find xs 3 is viable only for the first overload: deduction gives t = u8 from xs, and u8 does not meet Function u8 u8 bool. find xs (let (x) => x > 3) is viable only for the second, because a lambda's type is not u8. Searching a slice of functions for a function is never ambiguous either, since function types do not meet Eq. A user adapter that makes a scalar type meet Function would make such a call ambiguous, and ADR 0034 reports that ambiguity with both candidates.

docs.title: 5. Proofs through function arguments
docs.text:
Pure function values. A function value is pure when its parameters are all in (no inout or out) and its body neither writes module state nor calls anything that does. A pure function value whose body is proved to terminate (every let rec and loop in it has a measure) is a total mathematical function, and may be applied in contracts and spec functions. A non-pure function value may be passed and called in code, but not in a contract; the verifier reports that as an error at the contract.

In the callee, a function parameter is abstract. Each pure function parameter p is an uninterpreted SMT function, shared by every application in the body and in the contracts, as ADR 0043 makes concept functions. The arrow's contract is the only fact about it: at each call p x in code, p's requires is a goal, and its ensures is assumed of p x. A contract may mention p x freely, so

let find (t : type) (xs : [t]) (p : t -> bool) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  ensures result < len xs ==> p xs.[result]
  ensures forall (i : usize). i < result ==> p xs.[i] = false
= ...

is proved once, whatever p is.

At the call site, the argument is checked against the parameter's type, and the callee's contract is then usable with the argument substituted for p:

  1. Under the type's requires, the argument's requires holds: the callee may call it anywhere the type allows.
  2. Under the type's requires, the argument's result meets the type's ensures. For a lambda this is a proof of its body; for a named function, of its contract.
  3. The caller then assumes the callee's ensures, in which p xs.[i] is the argument applied to xs.[i]. A lambda in scope unfolds to its body, so find xs (let (x) => x > 3) gives the caller result < len xs ==> xs.[result] > 3 with no contract on the lambda.

Captured values (section 6) are part of the argument: the lambda in find xs (between lo hi) is checked, and unfolds, with lo and hi as they are at the call.

Laws of function arguments are preconditions over spec functions. The library defines them once, in Pia.Fn, as spec predicates over function values:

let spec strict_weak_order (t : type) (less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool) : bool =
  (forall (a : t). less a a = false) &&
  (forall (a : t) (b : t) (c : t). less a b && less b c ==> less a c) &&
  (forall (a : t) (b : t) (c : t).
     less a b = false && less b a = false &&
     less b c = false && less c b = false ==>
       less a c = false && less c a = false)

let sort (t : type) (xs : borrowed inout mutable [t]) (less : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool) : unit
  requires strict_weak_order less
  ensures sorted less xs && permutation xs (old xs)

The callee assumes the law, and each caller proves it for its argument. For sort xs (let (a) (b) => a > b) over u8, the lambda unfolds and the law is a bit-vector fact. For sort xs less where less met Ord t, it follows from Ord's laws. A law used as a precondition is proved where the argument is known, once per call site, and its goal is cached by ADR 0032 like any other.

docs.title: 6. Captures
docs.text:
Amended 2026-11-23: Dean asked for explicit captures, each one copied, borrowed or referenced. This replaces captures inferred from use, which steps 3 and 4 built.

A lambda lists what it captures, in brackets after let, before its parameters. Each capture says how it is captured, with the modifier words Pia already has, so no keyword is added:

let [lo, hi] (x : u8) => lo <= x && x <= hi           \ copied
let [borrowed keys] (k : u32) => contains keys k        \ borrowed
let [inout count] (x : u8) => count <- count + 1; x > 3 \ referenced

lambda   = "let" [ captures ] lparam { lparam } [ ":" annot ] { contract } "=>" seq ;
captures = "[" capture { "," capture } "]" ;
capture  = [ "borrowed" | "inout" ] IDENT ;

The three modes:

  • Copied, a bare name: the value is copied into the lambda when it is made. Only copyable values can be copied: scalars, fixed records and variants of them, never a buffer, a linear value or a drop value. Later changes to a mutable variable are not seen by the lambda, and the lambda cannot assign it.
  • Borrowed, borrowed x: a shared, read-only loan of x. The lambda's type holds a lent type, so it borrows from x exactly as a record holding borrowed(m) would (#70, ADR 0042): it cannot outlive x, and x cannot be moved or written while the lambda is live. The loan ends at the lambda's last use. Any value can be borrowed, scalars included.
  • Referenced, inout x: an exclusive, writable loan of a mutable variable. The lambda may read and assign x, and its writes are seen by the enclosing code after the lambda's last use. While the lambda is live, nothing else may read, write or move x, which is the exclusive form of the same loan rule. A lambda with a referenced capture has an effect, so it is not pure (section 5): it can be called in code but not in a contract, and a higher-order function may take it only for a parameter whose arrow is marked as effectful (below). This replaces the "writing through a capture is not allowed" rule of the first version.

A free variable of the body that is not in the list is an error that suggests the three forms: "'lim' is used but not captured: add it to the capture list as [lim] (copied), [borrowed lim] or [inout lim]". Listing a name twice, or listing one the body never uses, is also an error. A lambda with no captures has no list, so let (x : u8) => x > 3 is unchanged. Top-level functions, constructors and other module items are not captures, since they are not values of the enclosing scope.

Effectful arrows. A parameter that accepts lambdas with referenced captures writes inout before its arrow: (f : inout t -> unit). Inside the higher-order function such a parameter is called only in code, never in a contract, and its calls are ordered as written. A pure lambda may be passed for an effectful arrow, but not the reverse. This is what for_each with state needs; the effects follow-up in section 8 is reduced to effects through inout parameters of function types, which this covers for captures.

Moved captures stay step 7: moved x in the list, which makes the lambda own x and gives its type drop or linearity like a record holding it.

A lambda's type is still a record with one field per capture, of the captured value for a copy and a lent type for a loan. A lambda that captures nothing is a type with no fields, and costs nothing to pass.

docs.title: 7. Code generation
docs.text:
Each instance of a higher-order function at a lambda or named function is an ordinary function in which p x is a direct call to the lambda's body, with the lambda's captures as extra arguments. Codegen inlines small ones, as it does any small callee, so find xs (let (x) => x > 3) becomes the same loop, and the same vector code, as writing the comparison into find by hand. There is no function pointer and no heap allocation for a static function value, ever.

A lambda's type is private to the module that defines it. A module can export a function whose result is an arrow type, but the importer sees it as an opaque type meeting Function, and gets the instance through the interface (ADR 0039) as it gets other generic instances.

docs.title: 8. What this ADR does not decide
docs.text:
• Dynamic function values, a value whose function is chosen at run time from different lambdas, such as a table of handlers. That needs a type-erased value, a code pointer and an environment, and with no garbage collector it must take an explicit allocator. It is the library's box over a concept, box (Function a r), decided in ADR 0046, so there is no separate std::function type. An arrow type in box's position is sugar for Function at that arrow, contract included. A call through a box may appear in a contract only when the arrow is pure; otherwise it is code-only, with its facts from the arrow's contract (ADR 0046, section 5). An if that picks between two lambdas of the same type is not dynamic and needs no box.
  • Effects through function values beyond referenced captures (section 6): inout and out parameters inside function types.
  • Recursion through function values, such as a fixed-point combinator. A lambda cannot name itself; a recursive helper is a named let rec.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with lit tests in tests/verify and tests/codegen, and the tour's "Designed but not built yet" entry shrinks as it goes.

  1. Typed lambdas and named functions as arguments, with no captures. Arrow-typed parameters are instantiated per argument (find<lambda@file.pia:12:9>), the argument is checked against the arrow's contract, and the lambda unfolds at the caller. The verifier sees instances only, as generics did before ADR 0043.
  2. The Function concept and overloading on a function: arrow parameters become constrained type parameters, function objects with apply, application syntax for them, and the value-or-function overload sets the library needs.
  3. Captures by copy and by borrow, with the lambda's type as a record of its captures and ADR 0042's loan rules. Built inferred (PR #227); step 3b makes the list explicit and adds referenced captures and effectful arrows.
  4. Generic lambdas: untyped parameters from the expected type, implicit type parameters when there is none, and explicit (t : type) parameters.
  5. Laws of function arguments in Pia.Fn (strict_weak_order, equivalence, associative and friends), with the library's sort and accumulate using them.
  6. Proved once: function parameters as uninterpreted functions in ADR 0043's abstract encoding, so a higher-order function is proved at its definition and each instance is discharged by the argument's check.
  7. Partial application, lambdas as results, and moved captures: add 1, compose f g, and lambdas that own what they capture.

Steps 1 and 2 are what the standard library needs first, for find, count, all_of and the comparator overload of sort. Steps 3 and 4 follow, because predicates usually capture a bound and rarely spell out their types.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The library can write one overload set per algorithm, as Dean asked, and a predicate overload is constrained on Function like any other generic.
  • A call with a lambda costs what the loop costs. Monomorphisation does mean one instance per lambda, so code size grows with the number of distinct lambdas, as in C++ and Rust. Step 6 makes their proofs cost one check per argument, not a re-proof of the algorithm.
  • Contracts can be written about predicates and comparators directly (p xs.[result]), because function values are pure and total unless they reference a capture, which marks them effectful and keeps them out of contracts.
  • Laws such as strict weak ordering are ordinary preconditions. They are proved per call site, where a concrete lambda makes them decidable bit-vector facts, rather than being restated as contracts on every caller.
  • Captures are written out, so what a lambda copies, borrows or references is visible at the lambda, at the cost of a short list on every lambda that captures.
  • There is no dynamic function value in the core. Code that needs one waits for Pia.Fn's boxed type and passes it an allocator.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. Function objects. Should a function object be any type with an apply function in its module, called with ordinary application syntax (recommended), or should it need an explicit @derive(Function)-style declaration? Answered: any type with apply.
  2. Captures. Should captures stay inferred from use, with no capture list (recommended, since it adds no syntax), or should a lambda list what it captures, as C++ does? Answered 2026-11-23 by Dean: copy by default (a bare name), with borrowing (borrowed x) and mutable references (inout x) supported.
  3. Dynamic function values. Is a library box in Pia.Fn that takes an allocator (recommended) the right home for run-time-chosen functions, or should the core have a built-in dynamic function type? Settled by ADR 0046: box (Function a r).

docs.title: 45. JSON: derived streaming codecs, typed construction, and a DOM proved to conform to a type
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), with his answers to the four questions, which changed sections 2, 5, 6 and 8; see "Dean's answers" at the end.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked (2026-11-22) for a standard JSON serialiser and deserialiser in three parts:

  1. Metaprograms generate the efficient streaming code. Serialisation was a stated day-one use of metaprograms (ADR 0007, design.md): @derive(serialise, deserialise) was always the plan, and a derived reader "also emits the refinement checks, so a parsed value is proved to meet its type's invariants".
  2. Object creation that instantiates an instance of a type straight from JSON text, without building a tree first.
  3. A generic DOM that is provably structurally consistent with a type. Types are values in Pia, so "this document has the shape of t" can be a predicate over a type value and a document, and a document that satisfies it converts to t without a failure path.

Constraints from earlier decisions:

  • Errors are closed sets with ? and handlers (ADR 0028). There are no exceptions and no catch-all error type.
  • Every allocation goes through an explicit Pia.Mem allocator and can fail with OutOfMemory (ADR 0026, ADR 0041); vec stores its allocator (Dean, 2026-11-22). No garbage collection.
  • Text is UTF-8 only: str is [u8] refined to valid UTF-8 and string is a vec u8 with the same invariant (ADR 0040, section 7).
  • Tuples are a core type, and a tuple type is a type list for variadic code (ADR 0040, section 9).
  • The strongest guarantee is the default (ADR 0004). Fewer keywords is better.
  • Build time is a tracked benchmark (ADR 0032): derived proofs must stay small and per-type, and must not grow one query per program.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Rust serde + serde_json separate the data model (a visitor over a fixed set of kinds) from formats, and derive Serialize/Deserialize per type. Attributes rename fields, choose a variant tagging (external by default, internal, adjacent, untagged), deny unknown fields and supply defaults. serde_json::Value is the untyped tree, and from_value turns it into a type, failing at run time if the shapes disagree.
  • simdjson finds structural characters with SIMD in a first stage and writes a flat tape in a second: each container records where it ends, so skipping a subtree is one jump and the DOM is one allocation. Its On-Demand API parses lazily into the caller's types.
  • RapidJSON and Boost.JSON offer both a SAX-style push parser and a DOM; glaze and Boost.Describe use compile-time reflection to generate per-type readers with perfect-hash key matching.
  • Go encoding/json, aeson (Haskell, Generic deriving), ppx_yojson_conv (OCaml) and Zig std.json (parseFromSlice(T, ...), a type as an argument) all derive codecs from type structure.
  • JSON Schema and TypeScript type guards (x is T) state shape as a checkable predicate, but nothing proves the check matches the conversion that follows. F# type providers go the other way, from a sample document to a type.
  • RFC 8259 is the grammar. I-JSON (RFC 7493) is the interoperable subset: valid UTF-8, no lone surrogates, unique member names, numbers within IEEE double range.

What none of these give is a proof. serde's from_value and a hand-written type guard can disagree with each other and with the writer; a Pia library can prove that they agree.

docs.title: 1. One module family, one specification
docs.text:
The library is Pia.Text.Json, in lib/Pia/Text/Json/, one module per file (ADR 0039):

Module Provides Json.Spec the grammar of RFC 8259 as spec functions over bytes (valid s, value_at s i j), and the meaning of a number literal as an int or real Json.Lex a streaming tokenizer over a byte slice: proved to accept exactly the RFC 8259 token language, with every string token proved valid UTF-8 after unescaping Json.Write a writer of tokens into an output buffer or a vec u8, proved to produce Json.Spec.valid UTF-8 Json.Derive the @derive(json) metaprogram and the Json concept Json.Dom the untyped document (section 5) and its builder Json.Shape conforms, check and from_dom (section 6)

Everything is stated against Json.Spec, so the lexer, the writer, the derived codecs and the DOM are proved against one grammar rather than against each other.

docs.title: 2. Derived streaming codecs
docs.text:
@derive(json) on a type item generates a writer and a reader for it, as @derive(eq) generates eq_<name> today (meta.md):

let point = type { x : i32; y : i32 } @derive(json)

let shape = type
  | Circle of { r : u16 }
  | Rect of { w : u16; h : u16 }
  @derive(json)

For each type the derive emits:

  • write_json_<t> (w : borrowed inout mutable writer) (v : t) : result unit write_error, which streams tokens without building anything, and whose postcondition says the bytes it appended are Json.Spec.valid and denote v;
  • read_json_<t> (l : borrowed inout mutable lexer) ... : result t (json_errors t), which pulls tokens and builds the value as it goes, with no intermediate tree.

What makes them efficient is that they are generated per type, not interpreted:

  • Keys are matched by a decision tree the metaprogram builds at compile time from the field names: a switch on the key's length, then on the first byte where the remaining candidates differ, then one comparison against the whole name. An unknown key is found with no hashing and no allocation.
  • Fields are written in declaration order with their keys as constants, so a writer is a sequence of stores of literal bytes and integer formatting.
  • Integers are parsed directly into their range type, with the range check fused into the digit loop: a u8 field reads at most three digits.
  • Strings without escapes are borrowed from the input (section 4); only strings with escapes, or string fields, copy.
  • Nested types call each other's readers, which codegen inlines, so a record of records is one loop over the tokens.

Defaults follow ADR 0004, strictest first, with attributes to relax them (attributes, not keywords):

Situation Default Attribute Member name the field's name, and nothing else: a constructor's or type's name never appears in the output @json(name = "x") on the field, as serde's rename and Go's json:"x" tag Unknown member error Unknown @json(ignore_unknown) on the type Missing member error Missing, unless the field is an option @json(default = v) Duplicate member error Duplicate (I-JSON) none Variant untagged, told apart by structure: {"r": 3} is a Circle and {"w": 2, "h": 1} a Rect; the derive must prove that no document conforms to two constructors, or it is a compile error that suggests a tag @json(tag = "kind") on the type, an explicit tag member whose value names the constructor (its name, or @json(name = "c") on the constructor) Record field with where checked after the record is read; failure is Invalid none

Variants are disambiguated by structure or by an explicit tag, never by a name the type did not ask for.

  • By structure. For each pair of constructors, the derive proves that their shapes are disjoint: not (conforms A d i && conforms B d i) for every document (section 6). Most pairs are settled without the solver, because their payloads have different JSON kinds (a number and an object), or both are objects and each has a required member the other does not allow (unknown members are rejected, so that member decides). Anything else goes to the solver, as one small goal per pair. If a pair cannot be proved disjoint, such as two constructors with the same payload, or two constructors without payload, the derive fails and names the pair, and the fix is a tag. The streaming reader does not backtrack: it reads an object's members into slots for the union of the constructors' fields, and picks the constructor at the closing brace from the members it saw, which the disjointness proof says determine it. A member whose type differs between constructors keeps its raw slice of the input until the constructor is known, then parses it, which costs nothing because every token is already a slice of the input.
  • By tag. @json(tag = "kind") writes "kind": "Circle" as the first member of the payload object, and the reader accepts the tag anywhere among the members. A constructor without payload is then {"kind": "Empty"}. The tag member's name and values are written in the type's source, as Dean asked, so nothing about the encoding is implicit.

Each reader tracks which fields it has seen in a bit set and proves, at the closing brace, that every required field was set exactly once, so the record it returns is fully initialised by construction.

Error sets are exact per type. json_errors t is a type-level metaprogram (ADR 0035) that computes the closed set a reader of t can raise, as an error set union (#84): every reader can raise Syntax of pos, but Range only if t contains an integer narrower than the literal allows, Invalid only if it contains a where, OutOfMemory only if it contains a string or a vec, and Depth only for a recursive type (ADR 0047), because for any other type the nesting a reader accepts is bounded by the type's own depth. A handler for read point therefore lists four errors, not twelve, and the compiler checks the list is exact.

docs.title: 3. Typed construction: the type is an argument
docs.text:
A program asks for an instance of a type by passing the type, since types are values:

let load (text : str) : result point (json_errors point) =
  let p = Json.read point text? in
  Ok p

let load_all (a : borrowed inout mutable pool) (text : str)
  : result (vec point) (json_errors (vec point)) =
  Json.read (vec point) text a
  • Json.read (t : type) (s : str) ... is a generic function constrained on the concept Json t, which @derive(json) instantiates, and which the prelude provides for bool, the integer and range types, str, string, option t, vec t, fixed arrays [t; n] (the array's length is checked) and tuples. A JSON array of mixed kinds reads into a tuple type, (u8, str, bool), element by element: that is where variadic shapes come from, with no variadic machinery beyond tuple types.
  • The allocator parameter appears only when t needs one. That is decided by a type-level metaprogram, needs_alloc t, so Json.read point text takes none and cannot fail with OutOfMemory.
  • Json.read_into (t : type) (s : str) (dst : out t) builds the value in place, for large arrays and records the caller has already placed (an arena, a buffer of records). The out rules (ADR 0005) prove dst is fully written on success.
  • Json.write (v : t) (w : ...) and Json.to_string (v : t) a are the writing side.

The concept states the laws that make the two directions one codec (ADR 0034):

let meta Json (t : type) : concept = sig
  let write_json : borrowed inout mutable writer -> t -> result unit write_error
  let read_json  : borrowed inout mutable lexer -> result t (json_errors t)
  (** Writing then reading gives back the same value. *)
  let law round_trip (v : t) : read_json (lexer_of (encode v)) = Ok v
end

encode is the spec function that the writer's postcondition is stated with. A derived instance proves round_trip from its fields' instances, one lemma per field, so the proof is linear in the number of fields and never unfolds a nested type's codec (ADR 0043).

docs.title: 4. UTF-8 and strings
docs.text:
• Input is str, or [u8] that the lexer validates first. Outside string literals JSON is ASCII, so validation only runs inside strings, and every string token the lexer hands out is proved valid UTF-8.
  • \uXXXX escapes are decoded, surrogate pairs are joined, and a lone surrogate is a Syntax error (I-JSON). The writer escapes ", \ and the control characters, and writes everything else as UTF-8, so its output is valid UTF-8 and valid I-JSON.
  • A str field borrows from the input when the literal has no escapes: its result type is borrowed(s) (#70), so the value cannot outlive the text. A literal with escapes needs somewhere to put the unescaped bytes, so a str field reads through an arena the caller passes, and a string field copies into its own allocator.

docs.title: 5. The DOM is a recursive sum type over slices of the input
docs.text:
The untyped document is an ordinary recursive variant, declared with the explicit recursion of ADR 0047, and every leaf is a slice of the input text:

let rec json = type
  | Null
  | Bool of bool
  | Num of str               (* the literal, as it appears in the input *)
  | Str of str               (* the literal between the quotes, escapes intact *)
  | Arr of vec json
  | Obj of vec (str, json)   (* members in input order; keys as raw literals *)
  • Backed by the input. Parsing copies no text. A Num or Str is the exact range of the input it was read from, so a whole document is borrowed(s) from its text s (#70, ADR 0042) and cannot outlive it. Json.Dom.text (v : str) (out : out [u8]) unescapes a string literal on demand into a buffer the caller supplies, and Json.Dom.eq_key compares a raw key with a name without unescaping when the key has no escapes (the common case).
  • Recursion is explicit. let rec marks the type recursive, and the recursive occurrences sit inside vec, an indirection that owns its elements, as ADR 0047 requires. The only allocations are the vecs of arrays and objects. A document is usually parsed into an arena (ADR 0026), so it is freed by one release however many containers it holds, but any allocator works, since vec stores its own.
  • Its invariant is a spec function. Since json is a datatype, the verifier encodes it as a Z3 datatype, and Json.Dom.parse ensures valid_dom v, a spec function defined by structural recursion on v: every Num matches the number grammar, every Str is a well-formed literal (valid UTF-8, legal escapes, no lone surrogates), and no object has two equal keys. A program can also build a document by hand with the constructors, and valid_dom says what it must meet to be written out.
  • Numbers keep their literal text, with their value given by the spec function Json.Spec.number_value : str -> real. A typed conversion to an integer is exact; conversion to floats waits for floats (section 8).
  • "Generic" means one json type for every document and every target type. "Variadic" content (arrays of mixed kinds, objects with any members) needs nothing more: it is just constructors.
  • Depth. Json.Dom.parse takes a maximum depth as a range-typed argument, so its recursion is bounded and its stack use is proved, and Depth is in its error set.

docs.title: 6. A DOM proved to conform to a type
docs.text:
Since types are values, conformance is a function of a type and a document:

(* Spec: the subtree at node i has the shape of t. *)
let spec conforms (t : type) (v : json) : bool

It is defined by a type-level match on t, one arm per kind of type: [e] and vec e require v to be an Arr whose every element conforms to e; a record requires an object with exactly its required members, each conforming to its field's type, and its where to hold of the values they denote; a range type requires a Num whose number_value is an integer in the range; a tuple type requires an array of exactly that length whose elements conform position by position; option e allows Null; a variant requires that v conform to one of its constructors (to exactly one, by the disjointness proof of section 2), with its tag member if it has one. For a non-recursive t, recursion is on the type, which is a finite tree, so conforms is total by the structural rule of ADR 0035 and unfolds into a fixed formula. For a recursive t (ADR 0047), the recursive arm recurses on a sub-value of v as well, so it is total by structural recursion on the document, which is a finite datatype value.

Three functions use it, generated per type by @derive(json) and called through the concept:

let check (t : type) (v : borrowed json) : bool
  requires valid_dom v
  ensures result <==> conforms t v

let from_dom (t : type) (v : borrowed json) : or_oom t   (* t, or result t oom if t allocates *)
  requires valid_dom v && conforms t v

let to_dom (t : type) (x : t) (a : ...) : result json oom
  ensures (match result with | Ok v -> valid_dom v && conforms t v | Err _ -> true)
  • from_dom cannot fail on shape. Its precondition is the conformance, so the only error left is OutOfMemory, and only if t holds a string or a vec. Its result type is the type-level metaprogram or_oom t, which is result t oom for such a t and plain t otherwise, so for most types there is no error path to handle at all. A program proves conforms either by calling check and branching on it, or by having built the document with to_dom, or from any other fact that implies it:
let get_point (v : borrowed json) : option point
  requires valid_dom v
= if Json.check point v then Some (Json.from_dom point v) else None
  • The three paths agree, as a law of the concept: reading t from text gives Ok v exactly when parsing the text gives a document d that conforms to t and from_dom t d = v. So a program may stream, or parse once and convert several times, and get the same values and the same accepted inputs either way.
  • Branded documents come later. Once refinements on values work (status.md), conforming t will be a type, { v : json where valid_dom v && conforms t v }, so the proof travels with the value across function and module boundaries instead of as a requires on each function. Until then the precondition form is the same proof with more writing.

docs.title: 7. Streaming input, depth and speed
docs.text:
• The lexer is a state machine, stated with the prelude's machine theory (theories.md), and keeps no state outside its record. So it can stop at the end of one chunk and resume with the next, which is what streaming from a file or socket needs. The first version works over a complete slice; chunked input arrives with Pia.Io's reader concept, and a pull reader as a coroutine with ADR 0027.
  • Depth. Derived readers of non-recursive types need no depth limit (section 2). Readers of recursive types and Json.Dom.parse take a maximum depth as a range-typed argument, so their stack use is proved.
  • SIMD. The first lexer is scalar. A structural-character scanner in the style of simdjson's first stage comes with vec<T, k> (M10), proved against the same Json.Spec, so nothing above the lexer changes.

docs.title: 8. What this ADR does not decide
docs.text:
• Floating-point numbers wait for floats (M11), as Dean decided. Until then numbers read into integer and range types, exactly, and a DOM keeps every number as its literal. f32 and f64 fields then need a correctly rounded decimal conversion proved against real arithmetic (ADR 0038), which is its own piece of work.
  • JSON Schema import and export. A metaprogram could generate a schema from a type, or a type from a schema, but neither is needed here.
  • Other formats. The derive is JSON-specific. A serde-style format-independent data model can be factored out once a second format (CBOR, MessagePack, the PNG chunk readers of M13) exists to test it against.

docs.title: Gaps this depends on
docs.text:
These are listed, not worked around:

Gap What waits on it str and Pia.Core.Utf8 (C++23 library thread, phase 1) every string token, and the lexer's UTF-8 proof string and vec storing its allocator (Pia.Mem and Vec thread, #86, #72) string and vec t fields, the DOM's arrays and objects Metaprogram builtins attrs, variants, int_bounds and string bytes in metaprograms (stdlib.md, section 11) @json(...) attributes, variant codecs, fused range checks, key decision trees Generic types and concepts in interfaces (ADR 0039 step 3, in progress) importing Json from lib/Pia/Text/Json into other modules Core tuples (own ADR, per ADR 0040 section 9) tuple codecs and mixed-kind arrays Value refinements (where on values) branded conforming t documents (section 6) Lifetime markers on results (ADR 0042) zero-copy str fields, and a DOM borrowed from its input Recursive sum types (ADR 0047) the DOM (sections 5 and 6), and @derive(json) on user types that contain themselves Floats (M11) float fields (section 8) Pia.Io readers and writers chunked streaming from files and sockets vec<T, k> (M10) the SIMD scanner

The order below starts with what needs none of them.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. Json.Spec and Json.Lex over [u8]: tokens, positions, escapes and UTF-8 validation (with a minimal local UTF-8 spec if Pia.Core.Utf8 has not landed), proved memory safe, terminating and accepting exactly the token grammar.
  2. Json.Write into a caller's out [u8] with a proved capacity, then into vec u8; escaping and integer formatting proved against Json.Spec.
  3. The metaprogram builtins the derive needs (attrs, variants, int_bounds, string bytes).
  4. @derive(json) for records of integers, bools and fixed arrays: readers with key decision trees, seen-field sets, fused range checks and exact error sets; writers; Json.read t.
  5. Variants (structural disambiguation and tags), option, vec, str and string, then tuples once core tuples land.
  6. Json.Dom, once ADR 0047's recursive variants work: the json type, valid_dom, parse with a bounded depth, on-demand unescaping. Built (lib/Pia/Text/Json/Dom.pia) with these differences from section 5: a number or string is the span of its token, not a slice, since a recursive value does not yet hold borrowed slices of its input; null is JNull, since Null is the lexer's token kind; an array's vec and an object's are fixed-length, each counted before it is read and taken in one allocation from one of two bumps the caller lends, one of values and one of members; and valid_dom is @opaque (ADR 0063), revealed one constructor at a time, since unfolded in the parser's loops it cost a hundred times the goals. Unique keys and on-demand unescaping are not built yet.
  7. Json.Shape: conforms, check, from_dom and to_dom, per type, and recursive user types. Built for records of integers, range types and bools (lib/Pia/Text/Json/Shape.pia), as a companion derive, @derive(json, json_dom), so that @derive(json) alone needs no DOM: conforms_json_<t> (exactly one member per field, each in its field's range or a bool, no other member), check_json_<t>, which decides it, from_dom_json_<t>, with no failure path and each field its member's value, and to_dom_json_<t>, which writes the value with @derive(json)'s writer, parses it back and checks it, so its document is valid and conforms. An integer conforms when it has only digits after an optional minus, with no fraction or exponent, as for the streaming reader. Not yet: that to_dom's text always parses and conforms (a lemma relating the writer's digits, Spec.magnitude, to Shape's), option, array and nested record fields, variants and recursive user types.
  8. The laws: round_trip, and agreement between streaming and DOM paths, proved per derived type from per-field lemmas, with proof_bench watching their cost.
  9. A literate page, docs/json.pia.md, with every example doc-tested, and the C++ map updated (nlohmann::json and Boost.JSON have no std header, so it gets a row under "beyond the standard").
  10. Chunked streaming over Pia.Io, and the SIMD scanner with M10.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• JSON is the first full use of derives beyond eq, so it exercises the metaprogram builtins, error-set unions, type-level metaprograms, concepts with laws and allocators together. Gaps it hits are fixed in the core, not in the library.
  • A program that reads JSON into a type gets, from the type alone, a reader that cannot index out of bounds, cannot accept malformed or non-UTF-8 input, returns only fully initialised values that meet the type's refinements, and reports exactly the errors that type can produce.
  • Strict defaults (unknown and duplicate members rejected) mean some real-world documents need @json(ignore_unknown). That is the intended trade: the relaxation is visible in the type's source.
  • The DOM waits on recursive sum types, a core feature (ADR 0047). The streaming codecs do not, so they come first.
  • Untagged variants make some types need a tag where serde would silently use the constructor's name. That is the intended trade: the encoding is always what the type's source says.
  • Proof cost grows with the number of derived types and their fields, linearly by construction. Derived proofs go in the benchmark corpus from step 4.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-22)
docs.text:
1. DOM. Backed by the raw input as slices, and built with recursive types, not a tape. Dean wants algebraic sum types to support recursion explicitly, and, once there is a box type, a reference and a weak reference type that use a concept for recursive types. Section 5 now uses let rec; the core work is ADR 0047.
  2. Names. Only field names appear in the output, or the key a tag on the field gives, as in serde and Go. Variants are told apart by structure and type, or by a tag member that is also written explicitly. Section 2 now proves untagged variants disjoint and makes a tag the explicit alternative; there is no external tagging.
  3. Strictness. Yes: unknown and duplicate members are rejected by default.
  4. Numbers. Wait for floats: float fields arrive with M11, and there is no interim float representation beyond the DOM's literal text.

docs.title: 46. A box holds a type or any type meeting a concept, and what it holds is proved to have the concept's shape
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22), with his answers folded in: release and remove leave a box empty until it is filled again; a box over a concept forwards its interface directly, with no run-time checks; and a vec of boxes, above all vec (box c), comes first.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
C++ has three ways to own a value that lives elsewhere, and none of them says much about it:

  • unique_ptr<T> is a pointer that may be null, plus a deleter. Its type promises only that it points to a T, or to nothing.
  • A unique_ptr<Base> to a class with virtual functions holds any derived class. Whether the derived class keeps the base class's promises is a matter of documentation.
  • std::function<R(A)> and std::move_only_function hold any callable of the right signature, with a hidden allocation.

Dean asked (2026-11-22) why Pia would mirror unique_ptr, when a box type could take a concept as its parameter, so that anything put in it is proved statically to have the right shape. ADR 0040 section 4 took that answer: there is no unique_ptr, only one box. ADR 0044 section 8 left dynamic function values to "a type-erased box" in Pia.Fn, and that box is this one at the Function concept. This ADR decides the core part they both need: a concept used where a type is expected.

What the language has today:

  • Concepts (ADR 0034) are checked signatures with laws. A use check proves each type that meets a concept satisfies its requirements' contracts and laws.
  • Generic bodies are proved once over abstract SMT sorts, with concept functions uninterpreted and constrained by their contracts and laws (ADR 0043). That is the proof a call through an erased box needs.
  • dyn (ADR 0003) is a closed sum of tagged types, which a match takes apart. It cannot hold a type it does not list, and it has no requirement calls.
  • Allocators are explicit, and containers store theirs (ADR 0026, ADR 0041). Drop, @linear and borrows decide when a value is freed and who may see it.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Rust has Box<T> and Box<dyn Trait>. dyn Trait is unsized, so it lives only behind a pointer, which is a fat pointer to the value and a vtable. Only "object-safe" traits can be dyn: no generic methods, and no Self in argument or result position other than the receiver.
  • Swift has any P existentials with witness tables, and the same restriction on Self requirements until they are opened.
  • Haskell has existential types over a type class dictionary.
  • Dafny and Verus verify calls through traits from the trait method's specification, which is what ADR 0043 already does for generic bodies.

docs.title: 1. One box, never null
docs.text:
box is a library type in Pia.Mem.Box. A box t is an owning, non-null pointer to a t in memory taken from an allocator the box stores.

  • box.make alloc v moves v into a new allocation. It can fail, like every allocation, so its result is result (box t) alloc_error.
  • Reading and writing the contents are borrows: box.get b : borrowed(b) t, and box.get_mut for writes, which the borrow rules of #70 and ADR 0042 keep from outliving the box.
  • Emptying and refilling (Dean). A box has a spec-only state box.full b (ADR 0041's spec-only fields, erased by codegen), so there is no run-time flag:
    • box.release b : t (for box t) moves the value out and leaves b empty. box.remove b (for any box, including box c, whose value is unsized and cannot be returned) drops the value in place and leaves b empty.
    • An empty box keeps its allocation. box.fill b v requires not (box.full b) and a compatible value, and makes b full again: for box t, any t; for box c, a value of any type that meets c and whose size and alignment fit the allocation, which the box records from make (as a real field when its allocator's give needs the size, spec-only otherwise).
    • get, get_mut and every call through a box require box.full b, proved where they are used. An empty box is invalid until it is filled, and using it is a failed goal, not a run-time check.
    • box.free b requires not (box.full b) and returns the memory without dropping anything.
  • A box is Drop, and dropping requires it to be full: it drops the contents and then returns the memory to its allocator. A box that may be empty at scope end must be filled or freed first. A box of a @linear type is itself @linear.
  • There is no deleter. A different way to free is a different allocator.
  • There is no null box. A box that may be empty is option (box t), and the layout (ADR 0030) uses the null pointer as None, so it is still one pointer.
  • A box stores its allocator. A default allocator from module state (ADR 0041) has no fields, so with one, box t is a single pointer.

box t at a concrete t is an ordinary generic type. It needs nothing from this ADR beyond Pia.Mem storing allocators (ADR 0041, step 5). Every call on its contents is direct, and every proof sees the concrete value.

docs.title: 2. A concept in place of a type
docs.text:
A concept applied to all of its arguments but the first names a type: the type of a value of some type that meets the concept. Shape (from Shape (t : type) : concept) and Function u8 bool (from Function f a r, ADR 0044) are such types. They need no keyword, so the rule adds none.

  • They are unsized. Their size is not known when the program is compiled, so they may appear only as an argument of a type parameter marked @unsized. box's parameter is the only one in the library at first: let box (@unsized t : type) = .... Anywhere else, such as a let, a field, a slice element or a parameter, is a type error that suggests box.
  • Arrow types are sugar. box ((x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 255 ensures result > x) is a box of Function at that arrow type, contract included. That is Pia.Fn's dynamic function value: C++'s move_only_function, with its contract in the type.
  • Generic code at a concept. box Shape is a concrete type, and it meets Shape itself by forwarding (section 4), so code generic over (t : type where Shape t) is instantiated at box Shape like any type that meets Shape.

docs.title: 3. Widening is explicit and proves the shape
docs.text:
box.widen b turns a box t into a box c, as widen turns a value into a wider type elsewhere in Pia. Pia has no implicit conversions (ADR 0003), so the call is written out. Writing box.widen b where a box Shape is expected deduces c from the expected type. (The draft called this box.erase; it is renamed so it is not read as removing the contents, which is box.remove.)

  • The use check runs there. t must meet c, with instances found by argument-dependent lookup and adapters as ADR 0034 finds them. The requirements' contracts and the concept's laws are proved for t by the use check, as for any instance, once per type and not once per box.
  • The table. The erased box stores a pointer to the instance's table, which holds the requirement functions in the concept's declaration order, then drop, size and alignment. There is one table per pair of type and concept, emitted as a constant.
  • Restrictions on what can be erased. A @linear value cannot be erased unless the concept requires a consuming function, because the box would hide the obligation to release it. A value that borrows (borrowed(m)) cannot be erased, because the box could outlive its lender.

docs.title: 4. A box forwards its concept's interface, and only some requirements can be forwarded
docs.text:
A requirement can be called through a box c when its concept parameter appears exactly once among its parameters, as the receiver (in, inout or moved), and nowhere in its result. area : (s : t) -> f32 qualifies. lt : (a : t) -> (b : t) -> bool and clone : (s : t) -> t do not, because two erased values may hold different types, and an erased result has no size. This is Rust's object safety. Pia has no run-time type information to check that two boxes hold the same type, and adding it would be a separate decision.

A concept whose requirements are all excluded can still be widened to. Only drop can then be called through the box, and a program that tries anything else gets an error naming the requirement and the reason.

Forwarding, proved, with no run-time checks (Dean). When every requirement of c can be called through a box and every law of c mentions one value of the concept's type, the compiler gives box c an instance of c itself. Each requirement of that instance takes the box (as in, inout or moved, as the requirement takes its receiver), requires box.full b, and calls the boxed object's function through the table with the same arguments; nothing is checked at run time. The instance is checked like any other at the use check: its contracts are the requirement's own, which hold because the table's function was proved to meet them when the box was widened, and its laws hold for the same reason. So a box Shape exposes Shape's interface, proved to forward directly to the object. A concept with a binary requirement or a law over two values (Ord's transitivity) gives box c no instance, and its callable requirements are still usable on the box directly.

docs.title: 5. Proofs through a box
docs.text:
An erased box's contents are a value of an abstract sort, one sort per box value, so two boxes never share facts about their contents. A call area b through a box is proved the way ADR 0043 proves a call in a generic body:

  • the requirement is an uninterpreted function at that sort;
  • its requires is a goal at the call;
  • its ensures is assumed of the result;
  • the concept's laws hold for the sort, so a law over one receiver can be used.

The proof is sound because erasing ran the use check, which proved each requirement's contract for the actual type.

  • Mutation. A call with an inout receiver gives the box a fresh contents value afterwards, so facts from earlier calls are lost unless the requirement's ensures relates them with old.
  • Calls in contracts (agreed with the lambdas design, ADR 0044 section 5). A call through a box may appear in a contract or spec function only when the requirement is pure: only in parameters, no module-state writes, and a contract that does not say it may fail to terminate. Otherwise an erased call is code only, and its facts come only from the requirement's contract. For box (Function a r) that means applying the box in a contract is allowed only when the arrow type is pure. A box that calls something effectful never makes a contract depend on which function it holds.

docs.title: 6. Relation to dyn
docs.text: dyn stays a closed sum: its tags are listed, a match takes it apart, and the prover enumerates its cases. A box c is open: any module can widen a box of a new type into it, there is no match on what it holds, and no downcast. The two cover the two uses C++ gives variant and virtual base classes respectively.

docs.title: 7. Code generation and the ABI
docs.text:
• A box t is one pointer, and the allocator's fields when it has any. A box c adds the table pointer, so it is a fat pointer, as in Rust.
  • A call through a box is an indirect call through the table, unless the optimiser can see which table it holds, for example right after box.widen, in which case it is a direct call.
  • Tables are part of the published ABI (ADR 0030, ADR 0024):
  • a concept's table layout is its requirements in declaration order;
  • the concept's interface hash goes in the certificate;
  • a module whose table for a concept was built against a different version of that concept fails to load until it is relinked, as a changed object layout does.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Dean's priority is a vec of boxes, and most of all vec (box c), so steps 1 to 5 aim at one end-to-end test: a vec (box Shape) holding two different shapes, with a Shape function called on each element and proved.

  1. box t in Pia.Mem.Box, built with the Pia.Mem work ("Build Pia's core up to a proved Vec") once records can hold their allocator (ADR 0042's region parameters). This covers make, get, get_mut, release, remove, fill, free, the spec-only full state, Drop, and vec (box t). The one-pointer layout of option (box t) can follow with ADR 0030; a proved non-null invariant is enough at first. (Done in lib/Pia/Mem/Box.pia: make, get, set, release, remove, fill, free and a generic drop that requires a full box and drops the value with it; tests/std/mem*.pia, with mem_drop_errors.pia for a box left empty or freed full. get_mut is set for now. Still to come: vec (box t) in the library, which is proved as a prototype in tests/verify/vec_boxes.pia, and a box over an allocator that frees one by one.)
  2. Concepts as unsized types. Parsing a partially applied concept in type position, @unsized parameters, the error everywhere else, and arrow types as Function.
  3. box.widen. The use check at widening, tables as constants, the @linear and borrow restrictions.
  4. Calls through a box and forwarding. The receiver rule, the generated forwarding instance, the verifier's one sort per box, contracts and laws as hypotheses, havoc after inout, and purity in contracts.
  5. Code generation, within a module. box C lowers to a tagged union of the types the module widens to C (its closed world). A call through a box is a switch on the tag into each type's requirement, and a direct call where the tag is known. With step 1 this gives the vec (box Shape) test. A box may not cross a Pia module boundary yet: two modules would disagree on the union.
  6. The ABI. Fat pointers to a function-pointer table, one per pair of type and concept, with forwarding thunks and indirect calls: the cross-module layout, with ADR 0030's published layouts, the table layout in the published interface, and the loader's check.
  7. Pia.Fn's dynamic function values as box at arrow types, and the library's handler tables.

docs.title: Steps 2 to 4 as built
docs.text:
Steps 2 to 4 are built for the verifier (src/irgen/Boxes.cpp), and step 5 for code generation within a module.

  • The type. A type function whose first parameter is @unsized, let box = let (@unsized t : type) (r : region) => type { slot : borrowed(r) mutable [t]; state : int }, takes a concept there. box Shape r is then its own type, box_Shape: the tagged union of the types this module widens to Shape (step 5), found by a first pass of IRGen, so the second makes type | Box_Shape_square of square | Box_Shape_rect of rect. In tests/codegen/box_concept.pia that is 4 bytes, a tag and the largest field set, square's side or rect's w and h, laid out as one buffer per field. A concept anywhere else a type is expected is an error that suggests box (tests/irgen/box_concept_type_errors.pia).
  • The verifier's view. Each requirement callable through a box is an uninterpreted function of the box in a generated theory erased_Shape, area_of. The union's switch is code; the verifier is told only that its result is area_of b (an assumption the use check at widen justifies), so a proof through a box sees the contract and not which types the module widens. The requirement's contract is an axiom about it, and so is each law of the concept over one value. The axioms hold because widen runs the use check. One sort serves every box, which is sound because only single-receiver requirements are callable, and one address is one object.
  • widen b turns a full box t (b.state = 1, as for box t) into a box Shape. It is generic over t where Shape t, so the use check runs at each instance. It refuses a @linear t and a t that borrows (tests/irgen/box_concept_errors.pia).
  • Calls through a box. area b, with b : box Shape, is a generated function: its precondition is the requirement's, and it ensures result = erased_Shape.area_of b.slot. Those functions are box Shape's instance of Shape, so box Shape meets Shape, and a generic over Shape instantiates at it and is discharged by its generic proof. A requirement with two values of the concept's type, or one returning that type, gets a stub whose call is an error naming the reason. For now a box forwards only a receiver it lends.
  • Gaps.
  • widen gives the box a fresh object, so facts about the boxed value do not carry over. A later step links them: a requirement's result on the box equals its result on the value.
  • Function-pointer tables and the cross-module layout are step 6; until then an interface may show a box only to C (@abi(c)), and a box over an imported concept is refused.
  • A requirement's precondition that names another requirement is not carried into the switch's call.
  • remove and fill for box c are not built, so a box c is always full, which lets the forwarding instance meet the concept without a full precondition.
  • Only a concept of one parameter can be boxed.
  • A program that boxes two concepts gets two widen overloads that differ only in their result.
  • tests/verify/box_concept.pia holds a square and a rectangle in one slice of box Shape, proves the sum of their areas from Shape's contract, calls a generic over Shape at box Shape, and fails a requirement's precondition through a box. tests/codegen/box_concept.pia compiles it, and box_concept_test.c runs it and checks the sum, 19. tests/codegen/box_direct.pia checks that a call through a box straight after widen has no test of the tag, and that one through a box from a slice does.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• C++'s unique_ptr, virtual base classes, std::function and move_only_function become one type with one set of rules. Whatever a box holds is proved, statically, to meet the concept it is boxed as, laws included, which C++ cannot check for a derived class.
  • A box over a concept has the same proof cost as a generic body: requirement contracts and laws, proved once per type at the use check. No proof re-runs per box.
  • Binary requirements such as lt, and requirements returning the concept's type, cannot be called through a box. Code that needs them uses generics, or a concept written for the erased use.
  • Pia gains its first unsized type. The @unsized marker keeps unsized types out of every position that needs a size.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-22)
docs.text:
1. Emptying. Taking the contents out is release (or remove), and it leaves the box invalid until it is filled with another compatible value (section 1). Widening stays an explicit call, renamed from erase to widen (section 3).
  2. Forwarding. Whatever is placed in a box must be proved to expose the concept's interface and forward directly to the object, with no run-time checks (section 4). So there is no run-time type check for binary requirements, which stay uncallable through a box.
  3. Where the work goes. Yes: box t is built with the Pia.Mem work, and vec must hold box t values. A vec (box c) is the most valuable result, so the implementation order aims at it.

docs.title: Amendment, 2026-11-26: a box c knows its object's size and drop
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-26): "box<Concept> c should have a special implementation where the size of the element placed in the tag is known, and a reference to the drop function for the item is also known. This would be like a unique_ptr<T> with an allocator that knows how to dispatch to the delete implementation of T, but instead of a vtable we have an explicit ref to the type's drop implementation."

So a box c is not a tagged union of values, as step 5 built it. It owns its object the way a box t does, through a slot, and carries what an owner needs to end it without knowing what it holds:

  • The object's place. The slot that make allocated for the box t, kept by widen: the object is not copied into the box.
  • Its size and alignment, in bytes, of the type widen was given. A container that moves or frees the object, such as an allocator that frees one by one or a vec (box c) that copies its slots when it grows, uses them without a switch.
  • A reference to that type's drop: the instance of drop for the boxed type (drop<square>), or a function that does nothing for a type with no drop. Dropping a box c calls it on the object, then gives the slot back to its allocator if the allocator frees one by one.
  • A reference to each of the concept's requirements for the boxed type, so a requirement's call through the box is an indirect call, as Rust's dyn Trait does through its vtable. The size, alignment, drop and requirement references live in one static table per type and concept, shared by every box of that type, and the box holds a reference to the table (Dean, 2026-11-27); ADR 0071, section 6, says how tables are made, consolidated and checked, and section 6a how the REPL redefines them. This replaces step 5's tag and switch; a call is still direct where the compiler can see what the box holds.

What the verifier sees does not change: the contents are still an abstract value, and a requirement's result on the box is still the erased requirement's. Dropping a box c requires it full, as dropping a box t does, and remove and free for box c follow, so a box c can be emptied (closing the gap that a box c is always full).

The size and drop also serve ADR 0048's inline slots: a buffer of inline box c slots stores each element's table reference next to it, so moving, dropping and calling elements needs no switch.

Implementation, replacing step 5's representation:

  1. Function references in code generation: a function's address as a value, and an indirect call through it, lowered to LLVM.
  2. box c's layout: the slot and a reference to the type's table (size, alignment, drop and one reference per requirement), made by widen from a box t; requirement calls go through the table.
  3. drop, remove and free for box c, with drop called through the reference; tests that a box Shape of a type with a drop runs that drop, from Pia and from C.
  4. Inline box c slots (ADR 0048, section 5) with the size and drop kept per element.

Step 6's cross-module ABI is then the box's layout above: an importer calls a requirement or the drop through the box's table, whose layout is published with the concept (ADR 0030).

docs.title: Note, 2026-11-27: a box over a concept as an error payload
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-27), on the roadmap's C++ interop: "There should be a way to box an error (or have the error constructor host a concept box that then subsumes the C++ exception interface)", needed before 0.1.0.

Nothing new is decided here: this records that the rules above already give it. A constructor's payload may be any sized type, and box c is sized (it is the box, not what it holds), so an error set may have a case that carries one:

let io_error = type | Closed | Cxx of box Exception
  • The set stays closed (ADR 0028). Its cases are a fixed list, so a handler still covers exactly the errors that can reach it. Only the payload of Cxx is open: any type that meets Exception can be boxed into it, from any module once boxes go through tables.
  • Raising is Err (Cxx (widen b)) from a full box t, and widen runs the use check for t (section 3), so each type's requirement contracts and one-value laws are proved once, where it is boxed.
  • Handling binds the box, | Cxx e -> code e, and calls through it are proved as in section 5: from Exception's contracts and laws, never from which type was boxed.
  • C++ exceptions (0.5, with the C++ FFI) are then a library concept exception with what and the nested exception as single-receiver requirements, and a generated shim at each bound C++ call that catches, boxes what it caught into the error set's Cxx case, and returns it as an Err. It is std::exception_ptr with the interface checked. There is no downcast (section 6): a handler that must tell C++ types apart asks through a requirement of the concept.

As built: tests/verify/box_error_payload.pia proves an error set whose Cxx case holds a boxed not_found or overflow, passed on by ? and handled through the box, and tests/codegen/box_error_payload.pia runs it from C. Within a module this uses step 5's tagged union. A payload boxed in one module and handled in another needs the amendment's tables, ADR 0071's section 6, which come next. A payload whose type has a drop is not dropped through the box until the amendment's step 3.

docs.title: Amendment, 2026-11-27: a box c is one cache line, with small objects inline
docs.text:
