Dean (2026-11-27), so that a box c can be made in one module and used in another, which the boxed error payloads of the note above need before 0.1.0: the box holds a reference to a descriptor generated for the boxed type and hidden from the language, "the aligned storage laid out at the end of the box ... proved and computed to have the maximum bytes that fit in a cache line, and for anything bigger we have a pointer to a block that's been allocated at construction time of the object. Every box should have a lease on the allocator and the allocator must outlive the box provably. This is the small object optimisation."

The problem it solves. A buffer of records compiles to one buffer per field (codegen), and a box's slot is a buffer of one record, so a boxed rect is two pointers, one per field. A descriptor shared by every box of a type cannot say where one box's fields are, and a box holding one pointer per field has a size that depends on what it holds. Step 5's tagged union got around this by copying the fields into the box, which works only while one module knows every type it holds.

The layout. A box c is one cache line of the target (Target.cache_line, ADR 0049: 64 bytes on x86_64 Linux, 128 on Apple silicon), aligned to it:

  • a reference to the boxed type's descriptor;
  • the lease: a borrow of the allocator the box was made from, so the borrow rules (ADR 0042) prove the allocator outlives the box. An allocator with no fields leases in no bytes;
  • the rest, the inline storage. A type whose size and alignment fit is stored there, in its C layout (ADR 0030's c: fields in declaration order, each at its natural alignment), with offsets codegen deduces from the type. A larger type is stored in one block of that layout, allocated through the lease when the box is made, and the inline storage holds the block's address.

Whether a type is inline is decided by its size, so the descriptor knows it and the box has no run-time flag. size_of t <= capacity is a fact codegen computes per target, as size_of is today (ADR 0035). Nothing is written on the type, and every type can be boxed: buffers of records elsewhere stay one buffer per field, which is what vectorises.

The descriptor is ADR 0071's table (section 6), one link-once constant per type and concept, pia$t$<type>$<concept>, unreachable from Pia: the type's size and alignment, whether it is inline, a thunk that drops the object at an address (and, out of line, gives the block back through the lease), and one thunk per requirement callable through a box, taking the object's address in the receiver's place. A call through a box loads the thunk and calls it, one indirection, as Rust's dyn does and without C++'s hop from the object to its vtable pointer. Where the compiler can see which descriptor a box holds, as right after it is made, the call is direct. To the verifier a call through a box is a proxy carrying the requirement's contract (the pia.proxy pattern of ADR 0071), so proofs through a box do not change.

Making and moving.

  • box.make alloc v : result (box c) oom makes a box c from a value of any type that meets c, running the use check as widen does (section 3). It can fail only for a type too large for the inline storage, and for one that fits it ensures Ok, so callers prove that case needs no handler. widen from a full box t stays, for code that already holds one.
  • Moving a box copies its cache line, which is sound because a Pia value never points into itself (ADR 0042).
  • Dropping a box calls the descriptor's drop, then ends the lease.

Across modules. The descriptor's layout is the concept's: its requirements in declaration order after the fixed entries, published with the concept (ADR 0030). So an interface may show a box c, a module may box values of a concept it imports, and step 5's refusals go. A box c is part of each target's ABI as one cache line; to C it is an opaque, aligned block of that size, and C code calls into it only through Pia.

This replaces step 5's tagged union, and ADR 0048 section 5's inline slots sized to the widest widened type: a buffer of box c is a buffer of cache lines.

Implementation:

  1. The layout within a module: box c as a cache line with the descriptor reference, the lease and the inline storage; make and widen storing inline or out of line; calls and drops through the descriptor; direct calls where it is known. tests/codegen/box_concept.pia and box_error_payload.pia move to it, with C harnesses that treat the box as an opaque block.
  2. Across modules: an interface shows a box c, and a test boxes an error payload in one module and handles it in another.
  3. Buffers of boxes: vec (box c) over cache-line elements.

docs.title: 47. Recursive sum types are explicit, recurse through an owning indirection, and share through strong and weak references
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-22): let rec and Indirect as proposed; shared mutation through leases (section 5a) instead of immutability alone. See "Dean's answers" at the end.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia has records, variants, generic types, and, with ADR 0046, a non-null box that owns a value from an allocator it stores. It has no recursive types: a type that mentions itself is "not supported yet" (status.md). Several pieces of work wait on them:

  • The JSON DOM (ADR 0045). Dean decided (2026-11-22) that the DOM is a recursive sum type whose leaves are slices of the input, not a flat tape.
  • Proof by reflection (ADR 0036, verifier.md) needs a datatype of formulas.
  • Trees and lists in the library: shared_ptr and weak_ptr, deferred in ADR 0040 section 4 until there were atomics and "a proof that cycles cannot leak, which needs recursive types".

Dean's requirements (2026-11-22): algebraic sum types support recursion explicitly, and once there is a box type, there is a reference and a weak reference type that use a concept for recursive types. Earlier decisions constrain the design: no garbage collection, ever (ADR 0026); every allocation can fail and is handled at its call site; no implicit conversions (ADR 0003); fewer keywords; Drop, @linear and borrows decide when memory is freed; and proofs must stay cheap (ADR 0032).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• OCaml, Haskell and F# make every type definition recursive implicitly, and allocate constructors on a garbage-collected heap. OCaml marks recursion for values with let rec and for types with type nonrec (the opposite default).
  • Rust rejects a type of infinite size ("recursive type has infinite size, insert some indirection") and accepts recursion through Box, Vec, Rc and Arc. Rc<T>/Weak<T> share with counts; cycles of Rc leak, and avoiding them is left to the programmer. Rc::get_mut gives a mutable reference only when the count is one.
  • Swift has indirect enum (a keyword) and ARC with weak and unowned.
  • Z3 and SMT-LIB have algebraic datatypes (declare-datatypes), including mutually recursive ones, with constructors, testers and accessors. Dafny and F* encode inductive datatypes this way and prove termination by a well-founded "rank" on datatype values.
  • Koka and Lean 4 use reference counting with reuse ("Perceus", "counting immutable beans"): shared values are immutable, mutation in place happens when the count is one, and cycles cannot be built from immutable values.

docs.title: 1. Recursion is explicit: let rec on a type
docs.text:
A type that refers to itself is declared with let rec, the form functions already use, so there is no new keyword:

let rec tree = type
  | Leaf
  | Node of { left : box tree; key : u32; right : box tree }

let rec json = type
  | Null | Bool of bool | Num of str | Str of str
  | Arr of vec json
  | Obj of vec (str, json)
  • Without rec, a type that names itself is an error that suggests let rec. A let rec type that does not name itself is a lint (needless_rec).
  • Mutual recursion is a group of let rec types that refer to each other. Every type in the cycle must be marked, so a reader can see which types are recursive from their declarations.
  • Generic recursive types take type parameters as usual: let rec list = let (t : type) => type | Nil | Cons of (t, box (list t)). The recursive occurrence must use the same arguments in the same order (regular recursion), which is what Z3's datatypes and codegen's layouts need. Nested, non-regular recursion (box (list (t, t))) is an error.

docs.title: 2. Every recursive occurrence goes through an owning indirection
docs.text:
A recursive occurrence must sit inside a type that holds its argument behind a pointer, so every type keeps a size known when the program is compiled:

  • Indirections are recognised by a concept. The prelude declares Indirect, a concept on one-argument type constructors whose layout does not depend on their argument: box, vec, ref and weak (section 5) meet it, and so does a library type that holds its argument only behind pointers and states the concept. An occurrence anywhere else, such as a field of type tree or a fixed array [tree; 2], is an error that suggests box. This is the "concept for recursive types" Dean asked for.
  • Ownership is unchanged. box and vec own their contents uniquely, so a tree is a tree of unique owners and is dropped exactly once, as any other value is. Moves, borrows and @linear work as for non-recursive types.
  • A box over a concept (box c, ADR 0046) may also be an indirection, for open recursion such as an expression tree whose nodes are any type meeting Expr. Each such box has its own abstract sort, so the verifier knows only the concept's contracts about what it holds, and structural reasoning (section 3) does not see through it.
  • Every recursive type must be inhabited. At least one constructor, or a path through option or an empty vec, must build a value without already having one. Since box is never null, let rec l = type | Cons of (u8, box l) has no values and is an error.

docs.title: 3. Proofs: recursive variants are datatypes
docs.text:
• Encoding. The verifier encodes a recursive variant as an SMT-LIB datatype, mutually recursive types as one declare-datatypes group, and generic ones per instance as today. box t and vec t are encoded by their contents (a box t is its t, a vec t its sequence), because they own their contents uniquely, so the proof sees a recursive value as a value, not as a heap.
  • Structural recursion terminates without a measure. A recursive function or spec function whose recursive calls are on components of its argument (names a match binds below the top, an element of a vec) is accepted as terminating, as Dafny does, using Z3's datatype rank. Other recursion needs decreases, which may now use the spec builtin depth v or size v of a recursive value.
  • Spec functions unfold under fuel. A recursive spec function over a recursive type, such as ADR 0045's valid_dom or conforms, unfolds @fuel(n) levels (ADR 0036), and lemmas proved by structural induction (a tactic like induction, meta.md) cover the rest. Goals over recursive values stay as small as their unfolding.
  • Proof by reflection becomes possible: a datatype of formulas, a total decide, and a soundness lemma proved once (ADR 0036, step 6).

docs.title: 4. Code generation: layout and a drop that cannot overflow the stack
docs.text:
• A recursive variant is laid out like any variant (ADR 0030): a tag and the largest payload, where a recursive occurrence is a pointer (box), a pointer and a length (vec), or a counted pointer (ref). option (box t) is one pointer with null as None.
  • Drop runs in constant stack. The generated drop of a recursive type must not recurse once per level, since a list a million long would overflow the stack. It frees iteratively: it loops along one recursive child, and threads the other children onto a worklist built inside the memory of the nodes it is freeing (each freed node's own pointer slot links the list), so it needs neither recursion nor an allocation. The verifier proves the generated drop terminates and frees each node once, from section 3's encoding. ADR 0072 replaces the worklist with pointer reversal, fixes the order of drops, and extends the rule to box c, ref chains and hand-written drops.
  • Construction and pattern matching are as for other variants. Building a Node allocates its boxes explicitly (box.make a v?), so every allocation in a recursive structure is visible and handled at its call site.

docs.title: 5. Shared references: ref and weak
docs.text:
Pia.Mem.Ref provides shared ownership, next to Pia.Mem.Box:

  • ref t is a counted box: one allocation holds a strong count, a weak count, the allocator and the value. ref.make a v can fail with the allocator's error. ref.share r makes another reference and increments the count; it is a function call, never an implicit copy. Dropping the last strong reference drops the value, and dropping the last reference of either kind frees the memory.
  • Shared values change only under a lease. ref.get r is a borrowed(r) read. ref.get_mut r requires ref.unique r (the strong count is one and no weak reference can upgrade), which the caller proves or checks with ref.try_unique, as Rust's Rc::get_mut and Koka's reuse do. A value that is shared is changed only through a lease (section 5a), and there is no other interior mutability.
  • So strong cycles cannot exist. Without leases, a value can only be changed through a unique reference, and while it is borrowed for writing, the borrow rules (#70) stop the program from sharing it, so no reference to a value can be stored inside it, directly or through other values. The case to check is ref.get_mut r followed by storing ref.share r into r's own contents: get_mut lends r for writing, so r cannot be shared, or used at all, until that loan ends, and the store is rejected. Every value graph built from refs is acyclic by construction, and every value is freed when its last reference goes. This is the proof ADR 0040 asked for: it follows from the rules, so no program has to prove it. It is stated as a lemma of Pia.Mem.Ref's model, proved once, and the verifier keeps the counts as spec-only state (ADR 0041). Leases keep the property with one extra rule (section 5a).
  • weak t is a reference that does not keep the value alive: weak.of r, and weak.upgrade w : option (ref t). Back pointers, such as a tree node's parent, are weak. A cycle that goes through a weak reference is fine, since it never keeps anything alive.
  • Over a concept. ref c and weak c share any type meeting the concept c, as box c owns one (ADR 0046): the table pointer lives in the counted allocation, and the same single-receiver rule applies. Since a shared value is immutable, ref.get on a ref c allows only the requirements that read their receiver (in). A requirement that writes it needs ref.get_mut, and so a unique reference.
  • Encoding. Since shared values are immutable, the verifier encodes ref t by its value, like box t, plus a spec-only identity that ref.ptr_eq compares. A weak t is an identity and an option t that upgrade may return.
  • One thread first. ref and weak are not sendable (ADR 0027): their counts are not atomic. A shared_ref with atomic counts comes with atomics in M12, with the same rules, and with leases that are proved not to overlap across threads (section 5a).

docs.title: 5a. Leases: mutation of shared values, proved exclusive across threads
docs.text:
Dean asked (2026-11-22) for a lease method that gives a mutable reference to a shared value, with a proof, within a theory, that leases held by different threads never overlap.

  • The operation. ref.lease r gives a lease t: a @linear value that lends the shared value for writing, lease.get_mut l : borrowed(l) out mutable t, until the lease is released by lease.end l or by its drop. Many references may exist while one of them holds a lease; what is exclusive is the lease, not the reference. ref.read r gives a read lease, which many holders may share, so a reader never sees a value in the middle of a write.
  • The theory. Pia.Mem.Lease states the discipline as a theory (ADR 0036), with a model, so it is proved consistent rather than trusted. Its sorts are the shared allocations and the lease holders (tasks, ADR 0027); holds_write h a and holds_read h a are its spec functions. Its axioms: a write lease on a excludes every other lease on a, read or write, by any holder; read leases exclude only write leases; ending a lease removes exactly that lease; and the value an acquire sees is the value the last release left, which is a happens-before edge (theories.md) from that release to this acquire. Race freedom then follows from ADR 0027's permission rule, with a lease as the permission that justifies each access to the leased value.
  • Proving leases do not overlap. Each acquire is a proof goal: the task must not already hold a lease on a (re-entering would deadlock or alias), and either the program proves no other holder can hold one (a value only this task's references reach, or a protocol the model checker proves), or the acquire waits. Within one thread, for ref, this is usually settled from the borrow rules, since a lease lends r and a second ref.lease on any reference to the same allocation must be proved to be a different allocation (not (ref.ptr_eq r r2)) or rejected. Across threads, for shared_ref, lease suspends until the allocation is free and try_lease returns option (lease t); their implementation is an atomic state word, and the model checker proves it meets the theory's axioms, as ADR 0027 does for the other primitives.
  • Deadlock. A waiting lease is an acquire of a lock, so it takes a lock level (@level(n) on the shared type, or the theory's Levels from theories.md), and a task may only lease above every level it holds. Lease-order deadlock is then a type error, as lock-order deadlock is.
  • Leases and cycles. A lease could otherwise build a strong cycle: store, through a lease on a, a reference that reaches a. So storing a strong reference through a lease is a proof goal, not (reaches x a), over the spec-only reference graph that the Ref model keeps. For most types it is discharged by the types alone: if t cannot contain a ref to a type that contains t, nothing stored into a t can reach it, and the goal is not even generated. Weak references can always be stored, since they keep nothing alive. With that rule, the acyclicity lemma of section 5 still holds, and so does leak freedom.
  • Encoding. While no lease is held, the verifier still sees a ref t as its value. A lease makes the value at that allocation a fresh spec-only state from the acquire to the release, related to what the previous release left by the theory's axioms, so code that reads a shared value across a lease it does not hold learns nothing it should not.

docs.title: 6. Metaprograms over recursive types
docs.text:
• Inside a type-level metaprogram, a recursive occurrence appears as the type's name, as json appears inside json. is_rec t is true for a let rec type, and rec_group t lists its mutually recursive group.
  • The totality rule of ADR 0035 treats a recursive occurrence as a leaf: a metaprogram that recursed into it would unfold the type forever, so the checker rejects such a call. A derive that needs to handle recursion, such as @derive(json) or @derive(eq), generates a recursive function (let rec eq_tree ...) that calls itself where the type recurses, and that function terminates by structural recursion (section 3).

docs.title: 7. What this ADR does not decide
docs.text:
• Garbage collection and cycle collection: never (ADR 0026). Cyclic graphs use weak references, or indices into a pool, which ADR 0040 already uses for node containers.
  • Interior mutability other than leases (unchecked cells inside shared values). Leases are the one way to change a shared value.
  • Lazy or infinite (codata) types.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. let rec types in the parser and Sema: the explicit-recursion rule, regular recursion, guardedness through Indirect types, the inhabitation check, needless_rec.
  2. Verifier: recursive variants as SMT-LIB datatypes, box and vec by their contents, structural termination, depth and size. It lands in two parts. First the dialect: a recursive variant is the leaf type !pia.rec<"name">, its constructors are in a module-level pia.datatype, and pia.rec_make, pia.rec_tag and pia.rec_payload build and take apart its values, which ScalarizeRecords leaves whole; until the encoding exists, a goal over a recursive value is unproved, a compile error by default (irgen.md). Then the encoding: datatypes whose buffers are handles to their arrays (Z3 does not decide datatypes over arrays well), depth and size known through ground facts that a component's is smaller, and structural recursion as decreases depth on the first recursive parameter (verifier.md).
  3. Codegen: layouts with pointer occurrences, construction, matching, and the constant-stack drop, proved. Needs box t (ADR 0046 step 1, built in Pia.Mem after the ADR 0042 region parameter decision). Built without the drop: a recursive value is a struct of its tag and payload fields, a box's slot its memref descriptor, and let rec types may be shown in interfaces. Every allocator so far is a region's, so dropping a value frees nothing and no drop runs; the iterative drop comes with the first allocator that frees one block at a time (codegen.md).
  4. Metaprograms: is_rec, rec_group, the totality rule, and @derive(eq) on recursive types.
  5. ref and weak in Pia.Mem.Ref, with the uniqueness rule and the acyclicity lemma; docs/cpp-std.md maps shared_ptr and weak_ptr to them. Then single-threaded leases with the Lease theory and its model, and the reachability goal for stores through a lease.
  6. ref c and weak c over concepts, after ADR 0046's concept boxes.
  7. shared_ref with atomics (M12), with waiting and try_lease leases, lease levels, and the model-checked atomic state word.

The JSON DOM (ADR 0045 step 6) needs steps 1 to 3. Proof by reflection needs steps 1 and 2.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Recursive types are visible in their declarations, and their memory is visible in their constructors: every node is an explicit, fallible allocation, freed exactly once.
  • Recursive structures are proved as values. Shared ones are too, because sharing is immutable.
  • Leak freedom of shared references is a property of the library's rules, not of each program. Mutation of a shared value goes through a lease, which costs a proof at each acquire (often free, from the types and borrows) and, across threads, an atomic state word. Programs that need a densely mutable graph can still use a pool with indices.
  • Z3 datatypes make goals over recursive values heavier than goals over flat records. Fuel and structural lemmas keep each goal to a bounded unfolding, and recursive types join the proof benchmark from step 2.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-22)
docs.text:
1. Spelling. Yes: let rec on types.
  2. Guards. Yes: recursion through any type meeting Indirect.
  3. Shared mutation. A lease method that gives a mutable reference, with a proof, within a theory, that leases held by different threads do not overlap. Section 5a.

docs.title: 48. Buffers may hold slices: owned slices are written through, shared ones only read
Context
docs.text:
A buffer cannot hold a value that holds a slice today: [box u16] is "not supported yet: its elements hold a slice". That blocks Dean's priority for box (ADR 0046): a vec (box t), and most of all a vec (box c). It also blocks a vector of strings, the JSON DOM's arrays of nodes whose leaves are slices of the input (ADR 0045, ADR 0047), and any buffer of records with a slice field.

The verifier models every buffer as an SMT array of its own. A slice taken from a buffer is a view of it, an offset and a length into the same array, and a buffer a call returns, such as an allocation, is a fresh array. That is sound because each slice knows which array it views. A slice stored in a buffer element loses that: two elements may hold views of the same memory. A write through one must then show through the other, and the encoding cannot tell when.

Rust's answer is that a mutable reference is unique. Pia already has the same fact in two places. An owning value (@linear, or a type with a Drop, such as box) is never copied, so the slot it owns is reached only through it. And a shared slice, such as a JSON leaf viewing its input, is only read.

docs.title: 1. A buffer of slices is an array of arrays
docs.text: A buffer whose elements hold a slice is stored, as buffers of records are, one buffer per field (buffers of records). A slice field becomes a buffer of slices. The verifier encodes a buffer of slices of t as two arrays: the contents, from an index to an array of t, and the lengths, from an index to a length. xs.[i] gives element i's slice, len xs.[i] its length, and xs.[i].[j] reads its contents. A write xs.[i].[j] <- v updates element i's array and no other.

docs.title: 2. Only owned slices are written through
docs.text:
That encoding is sound only when no two elements share memory. So a write through a slice held in a buffer is allowed only when an owning value holds it: the element type, or the record on the path to the slice, is @linear or has a Drop. A box is one. Ownership is what proves the elements apart, so the user writes no apartness invariant, and the solver needs no quantifier for it.

A slice held in a buffer through anything else is read-only there: reading is sound whatever it aliases. Writing through one is an error that says the element does not own its slice, and suggests a box or a @linear record.

A slice taken out of an owning element, let s = xs.[i].slot, is a loan from the buffer (#70, ADR 0042). While it is live, the buffer cannot be written, so the element cannot be replaced under it.

docs.title: 3. Regions carry over
docs.text: An element's slices borrow from what its type says: [box u16 r] borrows from the region r, as each box does (ADR 0042, step 2). A loan in a buffer lasts as long as the buffer's own borrows.

docs.title: 4. Code generation
docs.text: Each element slice is a pointer and a length. The buffer of slices becomes two buffers, one of pointers and one of lengths, so it stays struct-of-arrays like every buffer of records. A C entry point takes both, as it takes one pointer per field today.

docs.title: 5. Inline boxes: vec (box t) is a specialisation of vec
docs.text:
A buffer of owning boxes need not point anywhere: each element's slot can be the element itself (Dean, 2026-11-23). A buffer whose element type is a box t of a sized t is compiled as one aligned buffer of t, with each box's slot the one-element slice at its own index, and its spec-only state erased. There is then no pointer, length or allocation per box, and moving boxes between buffers, as growing a vector does, copies their contents.

The proofs do not change. The verifier still sees each element as owning a slice of length one, and a box taken out of the buffer borrows its slot in place, lent from the buffer as in section 2. Inline storage changes only where the slot lives.

A box over a concept, box c, holds values of different sizes. Stored inline, each slot must fit the largest value it will hold. The compiler knows which those are: every widen into a box c names its type, so the types that reach a given buffer of box c are known statically from the specialisations the program makes (Dean, 2026-11-23). The slot size and alignment are the largest of that set, and the user writes no bound. The set is part of the buffer's layout, which the ABI advertises (ADR 0030): a module that widens a new type into it changes the layout, and dynamic loading against the old one fails and requires a relink. A box c outside a buffer of inline boxes is the fat pointer of ADR 0046.

docs.title: 6. Moving an owned element out
docs.text:
An owning element read as a value, nb.[i] <- old_buf.[i] or push v xs.[i], moves out of its buffer, as growing a vector does. The element left behind must not still own the box's slot, or two boxes would share it while the verifier models them apart. So each element of a buffer of owning elements has a held state (Dean, 2026-11-23), and the held state is its slices' lengths: a move leaves every slice of the element behind empty. A box is held when its slot has length one, which ok already says, so contracts need no new spec state and no new word. Reading or writing through an element moved out is then out of bounds, and a second move gets a box with an empty slot, which owns nothing and fails ok.

The element left behind keeps its contents: the moved value still reads them. Codegen keeps the emptying store, so the element's length is 0 at run time too, as the proof has it, and a program that reads it sees what was proved.

A read through the element, xs.[i].slot.[0], len xs.[i].slot, or an argument of a borrowed parameter, borrows it and moves nothing, as a field read of a linear local does. Moving out needs a buffer the function may write. Moving an element out of a borrowed buffer is an error, since the caller would still hold the box.

Storing a whole owning element, xs.[i] <- b, needs the element written over to be empty, so that no box is lost by writing over it: the verifier proves that every slice of the old element has length zero. A buffer that is out, as a parameter or as the buffer a function lends, holds nothing yet, so all its elements are empty. A vector says the same of its spare capacity: good v states that the elements past v.len have empty slots.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. Sema accepts buffers whose elements hold slices; IRGen stores them as buffers of slices, with the ownership rule for writes and the loan rule for slices taken out.
  2. The verifier's array-of-arrays encoding, with reads, len, writes through owned elements, and element replacement. (Steps 1 and 2 implemented: tests/verify/slice_buffers.pia. Spec-only fields in buffer elements, which box's state needs, are proved and erased by codegen: tests/verify/spec_buffers.pia. Element lengths in callee and spec-function contracts are encoded too.)
  3. Codegen: pointer and length buffers, and C entry points; buffers of box t inline as buffers of t (section 5). (Pointer and length buffers and C entry points implemented: tests/codegen/slice_buffers_run.pia runs from C, and tests/codegen/vec_boxes_core.pia checks a vector of boxes' lowering. Running a vector of boxes from C waits on regions in interfaces; inline boxes are not done yet.)
  4. vec (box t) proved end to end, with push of boxes and set on an element (ADR 0046's priority test, at a concrete type). (Implemented over a fixed buffer: tests/verify/vec_boxes.pia, vec (box u16). Growing, which moves the boxes into a larger buffer, is proved too, and so is that a box is stored only where no box is (section 6).)

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• vec (box t), vectors of strings and buffers of records with slice fields work, with no apartness invariants to write.
  • A buffer of shared, writable slices, such as several views of one array kept in a vector, cannot be written through. Such code keeps indices into one buffer instead, which is also what a proof of it would need.
  • Aliasing between an owned slot and a slice that is not in a buffer is ruled out by the borrow rules already: the owner lends it.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. Writes only through owned slices? The alternative, a region heap with explicit apart invariants, would allow writes through shared slices but needs quantified invariants that make proofs slower. Answered 2026-11-27 by Dean: yes, writes only through owned slices.
  2. Is Drop enough to count as owning, or must the type be @linear? box has a Drop; a @linear record cannot be dropped implicitly. Both stop copies, which is what the proof needs. Answered 2026-11-27 by Dean: Drop is enough.
  3. Inline box c slots: should a buffer of boxes over a concept carry a slot size, vec (box c) n, or should such boxes always stay out of line? Answered (Dean, 2026-11-23): neither. The slot fits the set of types the program statically widens into it, found from its specialisations (section 5).

docs.title: 49. Linux x86_64 is a second target, tested in Linux CI, and each target is a model of a built-in Pia.Target theory
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-22

Status: Accepted (2026-11-23, with Dean's answers to its three questions, recorded under "Answers" below and folded into the decision).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every Pia build target is restricted to Apple silicon. Codegen defaults to arm64-apple-macosx14.0.0 with -mcpu=apple-m1 (src/codegen/Codegen.h), and nine BUILD files mark everything that runs piac as target_compatible_with = [macos, arm64]. So every proof, build and test runs on Dean's iMac or on the macOS CI runner, which is slow when cold (about 2.5 hours) and is the only place proof work happens.

Dean asked for three things: run the proof work in the cloud, add Linux x86_64 as a real target, and encode the differences between platforms, such as the arm64 and x86_64 memory models, as theories the solver knows about.

Most of the compiler is target-independent already. The parser, sema, IRGen and the verifier never look at the target, and LLVM is configured with both the AArch64 and X86 back ends (MODULE.bazel). What depends on the target today:

  • Codegen. The triple, the CPU, the data layout, and the C calling convention. Pia's C ABI (docs/codegen.md) passes records through an out-pointer and extends integers narrower than 32 bits at the call, which both Apple arm64 and the x86_64 System V ABI expect.
  • Facts the proofs assume but never state. Pointers are 64 bits, so usize is u64. Bytes are little-endian. Pia.Mem.alloc returns 16-byte-aligned blocks. A page is 16 KiB. A cache line is 128 bytes, which is what false-sharing padding is sized by. None of these hold on every target, and two of them (pages and cache lines) differ between the two targets here.
  • The hardware memory model. arm64 is weakly ordered: loads and stores may be reordered with each other unless a barrier or an acquire/release instruction orders them. x86_64 is TSO: the only reordering is a later load passing an earlier store to a different address. ADR 0027 defines Pia's memory orders at the language level (sequentially consistent, release/acquire, and relaxed where its value orders nothing), and docs/theories.md gives them as a theory.
  • The operating system. System calls, errno values, open flags and mmap constants differ between Darwin and Linux. Pia.Sys goes through libc on both, because Darwin's system-call numbers are not a stable ABI.
  • Layouts. ADR 0030 publishes the optimised layout of each type in the ABI. Layouts depend on pointer width, alignment and endianness.

Several hardware differences matter less to Pia than to C, because the proofs already exclude the behaviour that differs. Integer division by zero and INT_MIN / -1 trap on x86_64 and do not on arm64, shifts by the width or more are masked differently, and signed overflow wraps on both. Pia proves every division nonzero, every shift in range and every overflow handled, so a proved program never reaches any of them.

docs.title: 1. Proofs and the compiler run on Linux, and CI runs there too
docs.text:
The constraint applies only to what runs compiled Pia code: a cc_test, sh_test or cc_binary that links a Pia object. Proving a file, compiling it to an object, IRGen and the lit tests run on any host, so their target_compatible_with is removed, and each Pia object is compiled for the platform Bazel is building for (section 2).

CI gets a second job, bazel test (Linux x86_64), on ubuntu-24.04, which builds and tests //... with the same disk-cache scheme as the macOS job. It also runs the proof benchmark (ADR 0032). A separate Linux baseline was planned, in case Z3 built on Linux spent a different rlimit on the same query, but the first Linux run matched the iMac's baseline on several files exactly and cost no more than 1.5% above it on any, so both jobs gate on tools/bench/baseline.json. The macOS job stays, because arm64 macOS is still the product target and the only place Apple-specific code runs.

For day-to-day work, slow proofs move to Linux: a cloud session can prove, compile and test the x86_64 build on its own, and the iMac is needed only for what must run on arm64 macOS.

docs.title: 2. x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu is a codegen target
docs.text:
piac has two targets, named by their LLVM triples:

Target Triple Default CPU Object Apple silicon (product) arm64-apple-macosx14.0.0 apple-m1 Mach-O Linux x86_64 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu x86-64-v3 ELF

x86-64-v3 is AVX2, FMA and BMI2, which every x86_64 server sold since about 2015 has, and which gives the vectoriser 256-bit vectors. It is the minimum, not just the default: piac refuses an x86_64 --cpu that lacks any v3 feature, so older machines are not supported.

piac's default target is the host it runs on, chosen when piac is built, and --target overrides it. Bazel never relies on the default: pia_object and pia_library pass --target and --cpu from the platform being built for, through a select, so cross-compiling is a platform flag, and the object always matches the code it is linked with.

The C ABI is unchanged. Both targets extend integers narrower than 32 bits at the call and return records through an out-pointer, so the same lowering serves both. The code that adds those attributes says so for both ABIs, and the C harness tests in //tests/codegen and //examples run on both.

Pia.Sys and Pia.Mem get a Linux side wherever they name an OS constant: MAP_ANON is 0x1000 on Darwin and 0x20 on Linux, and the errno values in each error set are mapped per OS. These constants come from the target's model (section 3), never from literals in the library.

docs.title: 3. Each target is a model of a built-in theory, Pia.Target
docs.text:
Pia.Target is a theory in the sense of ADR 0036, built into the compiler rather than written in a library. Its signature names every fact about the machine a proof may use:

let theory Target = sig
  let spec ptr_bits : usize
  let spec little_endian : bool
  let spec max_align : usize          \ alignment Pia.Mem.alloc guarantees
  let spec page_size : usize
  let spec cache_line : usize         \ destructive interference size
  let spec vector_bits : usize        \ widest vector the CPU executes natively

  let axiom ptr_pow2 ensures is_pow2 ptr_bits && ptr_bits >= 32
  let axiom little ensures little_endian
  let axiom align_16 ensures max_align = 16
  let axiom page_pow2 ensures is_pow2 page_size && page_size >= 4096
  let axiom line_pow2 ensures is_pow2 cache_line && cache_line >= 64
  let axiom vector_min ensures vector_bits >= 128
end

The axioms are what both targets have in common, and they are all a target-generic program may assume. A program proved against them holds on both targets, and on any later target whose model meets them. Each axiom must be true of every build of the architectures Pia targets, not just of the two triples it has today, so a later triple on the same architecture can never break a target-generic proof:

  • Little-endian is an axiom. x86_64 is little-endian in every mode, on Intel and AMD alike: AMD64 and Intel 64 are one architecture, and nothing in it is byte-order configurable. arm64 can run big-endian (the aarch64_be triples), but Apple's platforms never do, and a big-endian arm64 target would be a new architecture variant for Pia, with this axiom reconsidered then.
  • 64-bit pointers are not an axiom. Pointer width is a property of the ABI, not of x86_64. The same 64-bit CPU runs 32-bit code with 32-bit pointers in compatibility mode (the i386 ABI under a 64-bit OS), and Linux's x32 ABI (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnux32) runs in 64-bit mode with 32-bit pointers. So ptr_bits is a value of each model, 64 for both of Pia's triples, and the theory only says it is a power of two of at least 32. usize is then as wide as the model says, and target-generic code that needs 64-bit pointers marks itself @target(m) for the models with 64-bit pointers, or branches on if Target.is m, which folds to one branch per target. Even on 64-bit ABIs, only 48 bits of a virtual address are in use with 4-level paging and 57 with 5-level paging (LA57), which is one more reason ADR 0030 never tags a pointer's high bits.

Every axiom a module's proof used is listed in its certificate (ADR 0024).

Each target is a model of the theory, with each spec given its value:

Spec arm64-apple-macosx x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu ptr_bits 64 64 little_endian true true max_align 16 16 page_size 16384 4096 cache_line 128 64 vector_bits 128 (NEON) 256 (AVX2 at x86-64-v3)

piac proves that each model meets the axioms, as for any model (ADR 0036), so the theory is consistent by construction.

Code that needs a target's own value says so with @target:

let huge_page_count (bytes : usize) : usize @target(x86_64_linux)
  requires bytes <= 1000000
  ensures result * Target.page_size >= bytes
= (bytes + 4095) / 4096

Like @overflow, the attribute follows the return type. Inside @target(m), the solver sees model m's definitions as well as the axioms, and the item is compiled only for that target. An exported @target item appears only in that target's interface, and its importers must be @target of the same model, or reach it from the then of an if Target.is m, which piac folds at compile time, so the other target's branch is never compiled. This is an ordinary if, not a new keyword. The certificate lists each module's @target items.

Constants such as cache_line are values, not just facts: Pia.Sync pads a contended atomic to Target.cache_line, so it is 128 bytes on Apple silicon and 64 on x86_64, and the layout (ADR 0030) published for each target says which.

docs.title: 4. The hardware memory model is part of the target, and the language model stays the same on both
docs.text:
Pia programs are proved against the language memory model of ADR 0027, on every target. That is what makes a target-generic proof about atomics hold on both machines.

Each target's model also includes its hardware memory model, as a theory of the same shape as Order in docs/theories.md: po, rf and the hardware's preserved program order, ppo. On x86_64 (TSO), ppo relates every pair of accesses except an earlier store and a later load. On arm64, ppo relates an access to a later one only through an address, data or control dependency, a barrier, or an acquire or release instruction.

The hardware models are used in two ways:

  1. The lowering is proved. For each memory order and each target, codegen picks instructions: on arm64, ldar/stlr for acquire and release, and dmb ish where a fence is needed; on x86_64, plain mov for acquire loads and release stores, and xchg (or mov and mfence) for sequentially consistent stores. A lemma per target proves that the hardware order of the chosen instructions gives every happens-before edge the language model promises. These are compiler lemmas, proved when the compiler is built, and a mistake in the instruction table is a failed lemma rather than a miscompiled program.
  2. Code may rely on TSO, but only inside @target(x86_64_linux), only for atomics, and only as far as it is proved at compile time. Under TSO every atomic store is a release and every atomic load an acquire at no cost, but only if the compiler does not reorder them either: LLVM may move a monotonic access past another. So on x86_64 Pia lowers relaxed atomics to LLVM release stores and acquire loads. They compile to the same mov instructions, and they forbid only the compiler's own reorderings. The target model then adds two axioms, every atomic store releases and every atomic load acquires, which are true of the code Pia emits. They are not trusted: after LLVM's optimisation, piac checks every atomic access in each @target(x86_64_linux) item that relied on them, and each must still be an acquire or release (or stronger) access in the final IR, with no fence or ordering removed. A check that fails is a compile error, like a failed goal, so the axioms are proved of each program rather than assumed. With them, the message-passing idiom with a relaxed flag (publish_relaxed in docs/theories.md) proves on x86_64 and fails everywhere else, which is exactly the hardware's behaviour.

Plain, non-atomic accesses are never ordered by either model. A data race on them is a race on both targets, and stays a compile error (ADR 0027).

docs.title: 5. Build order
docs.text:
1. Linux builds and proves (section 1): constraints relaxed, Linux CI job, Linux proof baseline. No language change.
  2. The x86_64 target (section 2): piac default target from the host, --target from the Bazel platform, C harness tests on Linux.
  3. Pia.Target and the hardware memory models (sections 3 and 4), after Dean has reviewed this ADR.

docs.title: Answers (Dean, 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
1. TSO-reliant code: yes, and it must be proved at compile time. Section 4.2 now checks, for each program, that the emitted atomics really are acquire and release after optimisation, on top of the per-target lowering lemmas.
  2. The x86_64 CPU: x86-64-v3, and no older. It is the minimum, and piac refuses a CPU without its features (section 2).
  3. Axioms for pointer width and byte order: only if true of every x86_64 build. Little-endian is, on Intel and AMD alike, since they implement one architecture. 64-bit pointers are not: compatibility mode and the x32 ABI both run 32-bit pointers on a 64-bit CPU, so the width is per ABI, not per vendor or architecture. Section 3 keeps little as an axiom and makes ptr_bits a model value.

The questions, as they were asked:

  1. TSO-reliant code (section 4.2). Allowing @target(x86_64_linux) code to rely on TSO for relaxed atomics costs nothing at run time, but it makes such code non-portable by design. The alternative is to prove every program only against the language model and use the hardware models only for the lowering lemmas. The recommendation is to allow it: it is opt-in, it is visible in the certificate, and a port to arm64 then fails to prove rather than failing at run time.
  2. The default x86_64 CPU. x86-64-v3 (AVX2) or x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2 only)? The recommendation is v3, since Pia is aimed at SIMD pipelines and every current cloud and desktop x86_64 machine has it.
  3. Should ptr_64 and little be axioms? They make target-generic code simpler today. Leaving them out would make code that depends on them say @target, or prove a when Target.ptr_bits = 64 branch, so a 32-bit or big-endian port would be free of hidden assumptions from the start. The recommendation is to keep them as axioms, listed in the certificate, until a target without them is planned.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Proof work, the whole x86_64 build and its tests run in a cloud session and in Linux CI. The iMac is needed only for arm64 runs.
  • usize is as wide as the target model says. Today it is 64 bits on both targets, and piac refuses a model whose pointers are another width until usize can follow it.
  • Every proof that used a machine fact now names it, through the Pia.Target axioms or a model under @target, and the certificate lists it.
  • Two targets means two published layouts per type and two interfaces where @target items differ.
  • On x86_64, relaxed atomics lose some compiler reorderings, which costs nothing in the instructions emitted.
  • The lowering lemmas need the hardware memory models written as theories, which is new work, and the model checker's RC11 mode (ADR 0027) is still needed for relaxed on arm64.
  • CI cost doubles: a second cold build of LLVM, MLIR and Z3, cached as on macOS.

docs.title: 50. Asynchronous work is senders and receivers whose completion rules are proved, over io_uring on Linux and a kqueue completion adapter on macOS
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (2026-11-23, with Dean's answers to its five questions, recorded under "Answers" below and folded into the decision)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for Sender and Receiver abstractions in the style of Eric Niebler's work on C++ std::execution (P2300, with Lewis Baker, Kirk Shoop, Michał Dominiak, Lucian Radu Teodorescu and others, in C++26). They should hide the operating system's I/O interface, and Pia should make them stronger. The proof point is io_uring on Linux and its nearest equivalent on macOS, behind one interface.

The design so far (ADR 0027, docs/concurrency.md, issue #79) has Pia.Io wrap kqueue as a readiness loop that parks tasks. It mentions "epoll or io_uring on a later Linux port". Nothing in it is built yet. That leaves room to choose the abstraction before the first line of I/O code.

docs.title: What P2300 is
docs.text:
• A sender describes work and does nothing until it is started. A receiver is where the result goes. It has three completion channels: set_value, set_error and set_stopped.
  • connect(sender, receiver) gives an operation state, and start(op) runs it. The operation must then call exactly one of the receiver's channels, exactly once.
  • A sender advertises its completion signatures: the value types, error types and whether it can stop. Generic algorithms (then, let_value, when_all, upon_error, continues_on, sync_wait) compute their own signatures from their inputs.
  • A scheduler is a factory of senders (schedule) that complete on its execution context. Cancellation goes through a stop token that the receiver's environment supplies.

The model fits completion-based I/O directly: an io_uring submission is an operation state, and its completion queue entry is the receiver call.

docs.title: Where P2300 relies on the programmer
docs.text:
The C++ design states several rules that the compiler cannot check:

  1. Exactly once. A receiver must get exactly one completion. Calling two, calling one twice or calling none is undefined behaviour or a hang. Only the documentation states this rule.
  2. Operation states never move. After start, the operation state must stay where it is until it completes, because the kernel or another thread holds its address. Moving or destroying it early is undefined behaviour.
  3. Buffers outlive the operation, including through cancellation. When a stop is requested, io_uring still writes into the buffer until the cancelled operation's own completion arrives. Releasing the buffer when the stop is requested, rather than when that completion arrives, is a use-after-free in the kernel's hands. Rust's async runtimes face the same problem: a future that owns an in-flight io_uring buffer can be dropped mid-flight.
  4. Stop races. A stop request can race the completion it is cancelling. Stop callbacks must be deregistered without racing a callback that is still running. Getting this right is notoriously subtle in stdexec and libunifex.
  5. Detached work. ensure_started and start_detached let work outlive its caller. Both were removed before C++26 (P3187) in favour of async scopes (P3149).
  6. Error types are open. set_error can carry any type, so a caller cannot know it has handled every error.

Pia already has the tools to turn each of these rules into a type rule or a proof goal. @linear types must be consumed exactly once on every path (stdlib.md). moved parameters transfer ownership. Closed error sets come with exhaustive handlers (ADR 0028). Structured scopes allow no detached tasks (ADR 0027). Lifetimes and regions are checked by liveness (ADR 0042). Generics are proved once against their concepts (ADR 0043). Contracts carry through function arguments (ADR 0044). The model checker handles what types cannot express (ADR 0027, section 4).

docs.title: What the operating systems offer
docs.text:
Linux macOS Completion-based io_uring: shared submission and completion rings, one completion queue entry per submission (except multishot), a 64-bit user_data token, sockets and regular files, IORING_OP_ASYNC_CANCEL, IORING_OP_TIMEOUT Dispatch I/O (dispatch_io_*): callbacks as Objective-C blocks on libdispatch's own thread pool, with dispatch_data_t buffers. POSIX AIO with SIGEV_KEVENT: files only, with small default limits set by sysctl Readiness-based epoll: registers the open file description, not the descriptor kqueue: EVFILT_READ, EVFILT_WRITE, EVFILT_TIMER, EVFILT_USER; it removes a registration when the descriptor is closed Availability io_uring can be missing or refused: ENOSYS on old kernels, EPERM when kernel.io_uring_disabled is set (Linux 6.6 and later), or a container's seccomp profile always

macOS has no equivalent of io_uring. The candidates are kqueue with a completion adapter written in Pia, or Dispatch I/O.

docs.title: 1. Four concepts in Pia.Exec
docs.text:
Pia.Exec is Pia's <execution> (ADR 0040). It defines Receiver, Sender, Operation and Scheduler as concepts (ADR 0034). Each P2300 rule that C++ only documents becomes a type rule or a law:

(* Designed syntax. `v` is what the work produces, `e` its closed error set,
   which includes `Stopped` when the work can be cancelled. *)
let meta Receiver (r : type) (v : type) (e : type) : concept = sig
  @linear r                                       (* consumed exactly once *)
  let value   : (self : moved r) -> (x : moved v) -> unit
  let error   : (self : moved r) -> (x : moved e) -> unit
  let env     : (self : borrowed r) -> env        (* stop token, scheduler, allocator *)
end

let meta Operation (o : type) : concept = sig
  @linear o
  let start : (self : moved o) -> unit
end

let meta Sender (s : type) : concept = sig
  let connect : (r : type where Receiver r (value_of s) (error_of s))
             -> (self : moved s) -> (rcv : moved r) -> op_of s r
  law Operation (op_of s r)
end
  • Exactly once is a type rule. A receiver is @linear, and each of its two channels takes it moved. An operation that holds a receiver must consume it on every path, by calling exactly one channel. A path that calls two channels is a use-after-move, and one that calls none fails the @linear check. Both are compile errors in the operation's own module. The rule holds for every receiver, including the ones the algorithms build.
  • Completion signatures are type-level metaprograms. value_of s, error_of s and op_of s r are type-level metaprograms over the sender's type (ADR 0035), which plays the role of P2300's completion_signatures_of_t. error_of s is a closed error set, so the union in when_all a b is error_of a | error_of b (ADR 0028), and a match on it must be exhaustive.
  • Values carry their facts. A value type is an ordinary Pia type, so its facts live in the type (ADR 0037). A read completes with { n : usize; buf : moved [u8] } where n <= len buf, and the bytes it wrote are written buf 0 n. A receiver is proved under those facts. then s f completes with f's result and f's ensures, proved once for every s and f (ADR 0043 and ADR 0044).
  • Operation states move freely. Pia never gives the kernel the address of a Pia value, other than buffers, whose memory does not move when their slice value moves. A backend that needs a stable token, such as io_uring's user_data, uses an index into its own table of in-flight slots (section 3). C++'s immovable operation states need no counterpart.
  • Cancellation is an error. P2300 has a third channel, set_stopped. In Pia a sender that can be cancelled has Stopped in its error set, so a stop arrives on the error channel like any other outcome that is not a value (Dean, 2026-11-23). It is a closed-set member, so a handler must cover it, recover can remove it (section 6), and error_of s says whether s can be stopped at all. Algorithms that treat a stop specially, such as when_all cancelling its siblings when one fails, match on Stopped explicitly.
  • No detached work. Pia.Exec has no ensure_started and no start_detached. Work that must run alongside other work is spawned into a scope (ADR 0027), which also serves as P3149's async_scope: spawn s sender. A scope cannot end until each operation it holds has completed, because each one is @linear.

The first algorithms are just, just_error, then, upon_error, let_value, when_all, continues_on, starts_on and sync_wait. bulk waits for the spread work. split waits until sharing an operation's result, which needs ref from ADR 0047, comes up in practice.

docs.title: 2. I/O senders own their buffers, and cancellation is proved
docs.text:
Pia.Io offers I/O as senders: read_some, write_some, accept, connect, recv, send, after (a timer) and close. A buffer is passed moved into the sender, and every completion gives it back: value returns it with the byte count, and error returns it with the error, unchanged when the error is Stopped.

  • Nobody touches a buffer while the kernel owns it. Between start and the completion, the buffer belongs to the backend's in-flight slot. No Pia code can read or write it, so there is no race with the kernel. This is ADR 0027's race rule with the kernel treated as one more task.
  • A buffer returns only when the kernel's completion arrives. A stop request does not complete the operation. It asks the backend to cancel (IORING_OP_ASYNC_CANCEL, or deregistration on a readiness backend), and the receiver is called only when the target operation's own completion arrives. The buffer lives in the slot, and only the completion handler can take it back out, so a handler that returns it early does not type-check. That closes hole 3.
  • Stopped means nothing happened. When an operation was cancelled after it transferred data, such as a read that completed in the same instant, its receiver gets value, never Err Stopped, so no data is lost. This is a law of every I/O sender. A readiness backend proves it. On io_uring it is the trusted meaning of -ECANCELED from io_uring_enter(2).
  • At most one read and one write in flight per stream. A connected stream splits into a @linear read half and a @linear write half. A pending read consumes the read half, and the completion gives it back. So the type system rules out two concurrent reads on one socket, and a readiness backend needs at most one registration per direction.
  • Borrowed buffers come later. A buffer could instead be borrowed, with a region that encloses the operation (ADR 0042). That is sound, because a @linear operation cannot be dropped before it completes. It is left for later because moving the buffer and getting it back is simpler to prove and to explain.

Inside a @suspends function, wait s connects the coroutine's frame as the receiver, as co_await does in C++. value resumes the coroutine with Ok, and error with Err, which includes Err Stopped for a cancelled operation. So the read loop in docs/concurrency.md is unchanged. read is now a sender, and wait is how a coroutine consumes one. Senders also work without coroutines, through then chains and sync_wait. That matters because the coroutines (#77) are not built yet.

docs.title: 3. Backends: io_uring on Linux, and one proved completion adapter over kqueue and epoll
docs.text:
Pia.Exec concepts  (Sender, Receiver, Operation, Scheduler)
                               │
                     Pia.Io senders and io_context
             ┌─────────────────┴───────────────────┐
     Pia.Io.Uring                        Pia.Io.Ready r   (completion over readiness,
     @target(x86_64_linux)               proved once for every r : Readiness)
     native completion                   ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                                  Pia.Io.Kqueue          Pia.Io.Epoll
                                  @target(arm64_macos)   @target(x86_64_linux)

Linux uses io_uring. Pia.Io.Uring maps a sender's start to one submission queue entry. Its user_data is a slot index and a generation, and each completion queue entry calls the receiver held in that slot. glibc has no io_uring wrappers, and most of liburing is static inline code that cannot be called through FFI. So the module calls io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter and io_uring_register through syscall, and it sees the mapped rings through unsafe view (stdlib.md). Ring heads and tails are read with acquire loads and written with release stores. The split between trust and proof:

  • Trusted, with each item citing io_uring(7) or io_uring_enter(2): the kernel writes only completion entries between the head and the tail it publishes, it returns each user_data it was given exactly once (outside multishot), and -ECANCELED means the operation did not run.
  • Proved: ring indexing by mask, which is affine and suits Presburger (ADR 0020). A submission happens only when the ring has room. Every slot index taken from a completion is in bounds and in flight. Each slot is delivered once. The number of operations in flight never exceeds the table's capacity, so completion-queue overflow cannot happen. IORING_FEAT_NODROP is required anyway, as a belt to the braces.

macOS uses kqueue with a completion adapter written in Pia. Pia.Io.Ready r turns any readiness interface into completions. On start it tries the system call nonblocking. If the call returns EAGAIN, it registers one-shot interest (EV_ONESHOT or EPOLLONESHOT) in that descriptor's direction and parks the operation in its slot. When the event fires, it retries the call, and either completes or rearms. The adapter is generic over a Readiness concept (register, rearm, deregister, wait events timeout, wake), so it is proved once (ADR 0043). Pia.Io.Kqueue and Pia.Io.Epoll are its two models, each @target of its own platform (ADR 0049). Each model differs only in what it trusts:

  • Cross-thread wakeups use EVFILT_USER on kqueue and an eventfd on epoll.
  • Timers are a proved heap in Pia (Pia.Core.Algo.Heap) that drives the wait's timeout. That costs no system call per timer, and it is the same code on both platforms. io_uring uses IORING_OP_TIMEOUT.
  • epoll registers the open file description, so a descriptor that is closed while registered can leave a stale registration behind if it was duped. A registration is therefore @linear, and close takes the registration first, which makes EPOLL_CTL_DEL before close a type rule. kqueue removes a registration on close, and the same rule costs it nothing.
  • Regular files are always "ready" to a readiness API, yet their reads can still block on the disk. So the adapter sends file operations to the blocking pool (offload, docs/concurrency.md), as libuv and Tokio do. io_uring runs them natively.

Dispatch I/O is rejected for now. Its callbacks are Objective-C blocks, which would need the blocks ABI in FFI. It runs on libdispatch's own thread pool, whose interleavings Pia cannot see, so race and deadlock proofs would stop at its boundary. It owns its buffers as dispatch_data_t, so the moved-and-returned ownership of section 2 does not apply. Its file I/O is a thread pool anyway, and that pool competes with Pia.Task's workers for the same cores. It could come back later as a separate scheduler, for interoperating with Apple frameworks.

The backend is chosen at run time on Linux. io_context.create tries io_uring_setup. If that fails with ENOSYS or EPERM, it falls back to Ready Epoll. The context is a variant of the two backends, so a submission costs one match. Both backends satisfy the same sender laws, so a program's proofs do not depend on which one runs. On macOS there is only Ready Kqueue, chosen at compile time through when Target.is arm64_macos. Linux CI runs the I/O tests twice, once with each backend (with PIA_IO=epoll to force the fallback), and macOS CI runs them once.

No allocation per operation. The in-flight table is allocated once, when the context is created, from the allocator it is given, and that allocation can fail like any other (ADR 0026). After that, start never allocates. A full table is back-pressure: the schedule sender waits for a free slot. A context is @linear, and close requires its table to be empty, so it cannot be closed with work in flight.

docs.title: 4. The stop race goes to the model checker
docs.text: Each in-flight slot is a small state machine: free, submitted, cancel requested, completed, free. A stop request from another thread races the completion handler. The goal is that every slot delivers exactly one completion, and that a stop callback is never running after its slot is freed. That is a protocol goal for the model checker (ADR 0027, section 4, issue #81), proved once for the slot table and the stop-token implementation, and not per program. Until the model checker exists, Pia.Io accepts stop requests only from its own run-loop thread, where the race cannot happen. A cross-thread stop is an unproved goal that --allow-unproved=race: must accept.

docs.title: 5. Files, pipes and sockets share one set of senders
docs.text:
Nothing in sections 1 to 4 is specific to sockets. Pia.Io's senders cover every kind of descriptor:

  • Streams and files alike. read_some and write_some work on any descriptor: a file, a pipe, a socket or a terminal. Files also get positional read_at and write_at (pread and pwrite), whose footprints are byte ranges, so tasks that write disjoint ranges of one file are proved race-free by FPL (docs/concurrency.md). The flagship demo's parallel tile writes need exactly that.
  • File operations are senders too. open (openat), close, fsync, stat, rename and unlink are senders. read_all and write_all are senders composed from the others, proved to transfer exactly the buffer's length or to fail.
  • The backend chooses how, per descriptor kind. open returns a file, and accept, connect and pipe return a stream, so the choice is static. io_uring runs all of them natively (IORING_OP_READ, WRITE, OPENAT, STATX, FSYNC and CLOSE). The readiness adapter runs streams through kqueue or epoll and sends file operations to the blocking pool, since readiness says nothing useful about regular files. It is the same sender with the same laws either way, so the caller cannot tell the difference.
  • Cancelling a file operation on the blocking pool completes it with Err Stopped only if it had not started. A pread that is already running cannot be interrupted, so it completes with its value, and the law that Stopped means nothing happened still holds.
  • Blocking I/O is the same layer. The reader and writer concepts of Pia.Io (docs/stdlib.md, docs/cpp-std.md) are implemented over these senders, and the blocking forms are sync_wait of them. There is one I/O layer, not a blocking one beside an asynchronous one.

docs.title: 6. Pipelines: |>, with every error case proved handled
docs.text:
A sender adapter takes the sender as its last argument, then f s, and the prelude operator |> passes its left side as the last argument of its right side: s |> then f is then f s. It is defined by a metaprogram, as every operator is (ADR 0008). P2300 spells this |, but in Pia | already separates match arms and variants, and |> is OCaml's and F#'s spelling for the same idea. A pipeline is then dataflow between senders, written in the order it runs:

(* Designed syntax. *)
let load_config (path : cstr) (buf : moved [u8]) =
  open path o_rdonly                                   (* errors: OpenError *)
  |> let_value (let (f) => read_all f buf)             (* ... | IoError *)
  |> then parse_config                                 (* ... | ParseError *)
  |> recover (let (e) =>
       match e with
       | ParseError _ -> just default_config
       | NoEntry -> just default_config)
(* value_of: config.  error_of: (OpenError | IoError) without NoEntry *)
  • Errors flow through the types. Each stage's error set is the union of its inputs' error sets (ADR 0028). recover and upon_error take a handler whose match is checked against that set, and the cases it handles are removed from the set: the stage's error_of is the remainder, computed by a type-level without on closed error sets. An arm for an error that cannot reach it is an error, as an unreachable arm always is.
  • A pipeline must end with nothing left unhandled. A pipeline ends in sync_wait, which returns a result that the caller must match; in wait, whose Err arms or handle block must cover the set; or in spawn into a scope, whose handler must cover it. There is no way to start a sender and drop its errors, so an unhandled error is a compile error, never a run-time unwind.
  • Values carry their facts forward. then f is proved under the facts of the previous stage's value type (section 1), so parse_config may assume that read_all filled its buffer, and the pipeline's own value has parse_config's ensures.
  • Resources come back on every path. A buffer moved into a stage comes back in that stage's value or in its error, so a handler that recovers from IoError gets the buffer back to reuse or free, and the @linear rules check that it does.
  • Fan-out and fan-in are when_all a b c (variadic, ADR 0051), with split later. A channel from ADR 0027 bridges in both directions: recv ch and send ch x are senders. A pipeline of senders is acyclic by construction, because values only flow forward, so only channels can close a cycle, and ADR 0027's channel topology check covers those.

Why this is stronger than exceptions. An exception can be of any type, thrown from any call, and it is invisible in signatures: C++ has only noexcept or nothing. Through asynchronous boundaries it travels as a type-erased exception_ptr, and no compiler checks that a handler exists for what can reach it. Here, every pipeline's error set is in its type and is closed, every handler is checked exhaustive against it, what a handler removes is gone from the type, the end of every pipeline must have handled the rest, and cleanup is by linearity, with resources returned along the error path too.

docs.title: 7. A pipeline is a dataflow graph, and devices are schedulers
docs.text:
Senders are lazy and their types say what they are, so a pipeline is a value describing a dataflow graph before anything runs: then is an edge, when_all is a join, and split is a fork. Each node runs on a scheduler. That makes CPU and GPU compute one more pair of schedulers, as NVIDIA's stdexec does for CUDA:

(* Designed syntax. *)
let step (gpu : borrowed metal) (cpu : borrowed pool) (tile : moved [f32]) =
  just tile
  |> continues_on gpu
  |> then sediment_kernel                 (* runs as a Metal compute pass *)
  |> continues_on cpu
  |> then summarise                       (* runs on a CPU worker *)
  |> upon_error report_device_error
  • A device is a Scheduler. Pia.Exec.Metal schedules work as command buffers on a Metal queue, and its completion handler is the receiver call. Pia.Task's workers are the CPU scheduler, and the Neural Engine can come later the same way. continues_on d moves the rest of the pipeline to d.
  • Data moves with ownership. A buffer is moved into a GPU stage and comes back in its value or its error, exactly as with I/O (section 2). So the CPU cannot touch a buffer while the GPU writes it, which is ADR 0027's rule for device queues, now expressed as a sender. On Apple silicon's unified memory, moving costs no copy. A device with its own memory makes continues_on insert the transfer, and the transfer is a sender too.
  • Placement chooses the schedulers. A pipeline whose stages say @place(auto) instead of a fixed continues_on is placed by the cost model of ADR 0015, which sees the whole graph because it is a type. The model can keep neighbouring stages on one device to avoid transfers, and fuse a chain of thens into one kernel. Placement must never change the proved result. So a stage's float tolerance has to be proved on the device it is placed on (ADR 0038), and a device that cannot prove it is excluded or is an error, as ADR 0038 already decided.
  • Device errors are ordinary errors. A command buffer that fails, or a device that is lost, completes with an error from a closed set (DeviceLost | OutOfMemory | Timeout), so the pipeline must handle it like any other (section 6).
  • The graph is checked as a whole. It is acyclic by construction, except through channels, so ADR 0027's topology check covers its deadlock goal. Its race freedom is the ownership rule above, and its error handling is section 6's rule.

This is the generic form of the flagship demo's CPU and GPU pipeline (ADR 0016). Its tile loop becomes a graph of senders, placed by the cost model, instead of hand-written queue code.

docs.title: 8. What this changes
docs.text:
• ADR 0027 and issue #79. Pia.Io offers senders instead of a parking API, and the kqueue loop becomes one backend of several. Pia.Task's scheduler is a Scheduler, and spawn s x accepts a sender as well as a closure. The @blocking and offload rules are unchanged.
  • The earlier poller plan (a readiness poller as the public I/O interface) becomes Pia.Io.Ready's internal Readiness concept.
  • C++ mapping. docs/cpp-std.md gains <execution> mapped to Pia.Exec.
  • Blocking Pia.Io (stdlib.md, section 8) becomes sync_wait over the same senders (section 5).

docs.title: Prerequisites, in order
docs.text:
1. FFI (#55): variadic foreign calls, as ADR 0051 section 6 designs them (syscall, open and fcntl are variadic, and Apple arm64 passes variadic arguments on the stack), C structs passed as byte buffers (sockaddr, kevent, epoll_event, io_uring_sqe), and errno (__error on macOS, __errno_location on glibc).
  2. @target items and when Target.is (ADR 0049, step 3c, PR #292).
  3. Pia.Sys.Posix, Pia.Sys.Fs and Pia.Sys.Net (#57), blocking and per target: constants, sockaddr (macOS has a sin_len byte, Linux does not), the packed epoll_event on x86_64, and SO_NOSIGPIPE versus MSG_NOSIGNAL.
  4. Pia.Mem as a module (#59), for buffers and the in-flight table.
  5. Tuples and variadic generics (ADR 0051), for when_all over any number of senders. Function values stored in data (ADR 0044, a later step), because an operation state holds its receiver and then's function, and acquire and release atomics on foreign memory, for the io_uring rings.
  6. Pia.Exec: the concepts and algorithms, with an inline scheduler and sync_wait, the |> operator, and recover with the type-level without on error sets. It is pure Pia with no system calls, so it can be proved and tested first.
  7. Pia.Io.Ready, Pia.Io.Kqueue and Pia.Io.Epoll, the run loop and the timer heap, with a proved echo server as the demo, tested on both CI jobs.
  8. Pia.Io.Uring, and the Linux run-time choice between the two backends.
  9. Pia.Exec.Metal, a GPU scheduler, once Metal placement lands (ADR 0015), and placement of @place(auto) stages over a sender graph.
  10. Cross-thread stop, when the model checker lands (#81). wait on senders, when coroutines land (#77).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every P2300 rule listed under "Where P2300 relies on the programmer" is checked. Exactly-once completion and the absence of detached work are type rules. Buffer ownership during I/O and through cancellation are type rules too. Closed error sets come with exhaustive handlers. The stop race is a model-checker goal.
  • Files, pipes and sockets go through one set of senders, and blocking I/O is sync_wait of them.
  • A pipeline is a dataflow graph whose nodes run on schedulers, so CPU and GPU compute use the same interface as I/O, with ownership moving buffers between them.
  • Pipelines written with |> are checked to handle every error that can reach their end, which exceptions cannot offer.
  • One interface hides three backends. Only the system-call contracts differ between them, and they are listed per target in the trust report.
  • On macOS, completion is emulated, so an operation can cost one extra system call compared with io_uring, and file I/O runs on the blocking pool. Pia does not claim equal performance across the two platforms, only the same semantics.
  • The I/O stack is larger than a bare poller. Its lower layers are still needed (Pia.Sys), and the poller survives as Readiness inside the adapter.
  • wait gets a precise meaning: it connects a coroutine frame to a sender.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Dean's answers (2026-11-23):

  1. Stopped is a member of the error set, not a third channel. Receivers have value and error only (section 1).
  2. Linux probes io_uring and falls back to epoll at run time, and CI tests both backends (section 3).
  3. On macOS, regular files go to the blocking pool first. POSIX AIO with SIGEV_KEVENT can come later as an optimisation behind the same senders (sections 3 and 5).
  4. Multishot completions wait for their own ADR, on sequence senders in the style of P2849. Version 1 loops over single-shot senders.
  5. The module is Pia.Exec, after std::execution.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes P2300 std::execution, stdexec, libunifex senders, receivers, operation states, completion channels, schedulers, environments, stop tokens P3149 async_scope, P3187 scoped spawning instead of detached work tokio-uring, glommio, monoio buffers moved into the operation and returned with the completion libuv, Tokio completion over readiness, and file I/O on a blocking pool Austral, ATS linear types consuming a resource exactly once, as a type rule

docs.title: 51. Variadic functions and types take a pack that is called like any argument list, walked by metaprograms and proved once; foreign bindings are generated from tables
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (2026-11-23, after two revisions with Dean's answers, recorded under "Answers" below and folded into the decision)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-23): "we need the equivalent of variadic functions that are provably safe. We should have language features for generic variadic functions and types, like C++ gives us, but with more straightforward syntax through metaprograms."

Three things need variadics now:

  • C functions. open, fcntl, ioctl and syscall are C variadic functions. ADR 0050 needs syscall for io_uring, and Pia.Sys.Fs needs open with a mode. Apple arm64 passes variadic arguments on the stack, while named arguments go in registers, so declaring open with a fixed third parameter gives the wrong ABI. x86_64 System V also needs %al set to the number of vector registers a variadic call uses. Pia's FFI today takes only fixed integer, bool and buffer parameters (genForeign).
  • Generic code over any number of types. when_all (a, b, c) in ADR 0050 completes with the values of all its senders and the union of their error sets. format takes any number of arguments of types that meet Format. apply, tuple_cat, std::get by type and argument forwarding for constructors are the same shape.
  • Types over any number of types. An operation state for when_all holds one child per sender, and std::variant<Ts...> is a sum over a list of types.

C++ answers with parameter packs: typename... Ts, pack expansions f(xs)... in a dozen syntactic positions, fold expressions (... + xs), sizeof..., and recursion through partial specialisation or if constexpr. They are powerful, but the syntax is irregular. Pack indexing only arrived in C++26, and an error inside an expansion surfaces at instantiation. C varargs (va_list) are unchecked: the callee trusts the caller's count and types, which is the root of format-string bugs.

ADR 0040, section 9, already decided that tuples are a core type and that tuple types are the type lists for variadic code, "without a separate pack feature", and said core tuples need their own ADR. This is that ADR. It also covers the parts section 9 left open: how generic code walks a tuple and is proved, variadic types, and foreign varargs.

docs.title: 1. Core tuples
docs.text:
This section builds what ADR 0040 section 9 specifies, unchanged:
