  • (a, b, c) is a tuple value, and (u8, str, bool) is its type, since types are values. () is unit. There is no one-element tuple.
  • t.0, t.1: positional access, checked at compile time.
  • A tuple is an anonymous record with fields 0, 1, ... It has the same layout, ownership, moved, @linear, borrow and contract rules as a record, and struct-of-arrays buffers. Two tuple types with the same element types are the same type.
  • Eq, Ord and Hash are structural, proved once (ADR 0043).

docs.title: 2. A variadic function is called like any other function
docs.text:
The last parameter of a function may be a pack, written ..., with its type a deduced type parameter:

(* Designed syntax. *)
let print (ts : type where All Format ts) (w : borrowed inout writer) (xs : ...ts) : unit = ...

print w x name 42u8              (* ts = (u32, str, u8), deduced *)
print w                          (* ts = (), an empty pack *)
  • The call site is ordinary application. A pack takes every argument that follows the fixed ones in that application. An application ends where it always ends: at a closing parenthesis, an operator, ;, then, in and so on. So print w x name 42u8 is one call with three pack arguments, and print w (f x) y is one call with two. Nothing about the call says the function is variadic.
  • Inside the body, the pack is a tuple. xs has the tuple type ts. Its elements are xs.0, xs.1 and so on, or xs.[u8] by type, which is the one element of type u8 and a type error when there is not exactly one (C++'s std::get<T>; types are values, so a type is an index like any other). The pack can be passed on whole, so ADR 0040's tuple decision still holds: a pack is a tuple, and only the parameter is marked.
  • Passing a tuple as a pack is ...t at the call: print w ...pair. This is how one variadic function forwards its pack to another, as C++'s f(xs...) does.
  • Partial application goes through the expected type. When a variadic call is in a place that expects a function, such as an argument whose parameter type is u32 -> unit, the call is partial, and the expected function's parameters close the pack. So map (print w) xs passes print w as a function of one argument, with ts deduced as (t) from map's parameter, and for_each (print w prefix) xs fixes the first element too. When nothing expects a function, the call is complete, and print w prints nothing. Binding that unit result to a name is warned about by the variadic_unit_binding lint (ADR 0037), because it is probably a partial application that was meant. This is the same deduction from the expected type that generic results already use (docs/irgen.md).
  • Variadic function values. bind_front print w keeps the pack open: it is a function object whose apply is itself variadic, so a later call can pass any number of arguments. Pia.Fn has the usual combinators over packs: bind_front, bind_back, compose, flip, apply (a function and a tuple, as std::apply) and unpack (a function of a tuple, turned into a variadic one). The Function concept (ADR 0044) takes a pack of argument types, Function f (...args) r, so higher-order functions can accept variadic function values and be proved once over them.
  • All c ts is a prelude concept over pack types: every element type meets c. Concepts are already values that type-level metaprograms take (ADR 0046).

docs.title: 3. Packs are walked by metaprograms, not by recursion
docs.text:
Code never recurses over a pack. Two kinds of metaprogram do the walking instead.

Type-level metaprograms over a list of types. The builtin elements ts gives a pack type's element types as a metaprogram list, and tuple_of xs builds a pack type from a list. Everything else is the list functions metaprograms already have, map, fold and length (docs/meta.md):

let meta size (ts : type) : usize = length (elements ts)

(* when_all's value and error types (ADR 0050). *)
let meta values_of (ss : type) : type = tuple_of (map value_of (elements ss))
let meta errors_of (ss : type) : type = fold (let (a) (e) => a | e) never (map error_of (elements ss))

These are total by the rule tactics already follow (docs/meta.md): the only recursion is map and fold over the components of a parameter.

A loop over a pack, unrolled by expansion. In code, a for over a pack runs its body once for each element, and the expansion stamps out one copy of the body per element, as Zig's inline for does. x has each element's own type in its copy:

let print (ts : type where All Format ts) (w : borrowed inout writer) (xs : ...ts) : unit
  ensures written_count w = old (written_count w) + size ts
= for i, x in xs
    invariant written_count w = old (written_count w) + i
  do format w x done

The library's Pia.Core.Pack is written the same way: map, fold, apply, cat, get by type and zip. C++'s fold expressions become fold, sizeof... becomes size, and pack indexing becomes xs.i with a constant i, or xs.[t] by type.

docs.title: 4. Proved once, though compiled per element
docs.text:
The loop above is proved once, as an ordinary loop. Its body is proved for an abstract position i and an abstract element type element i ts, which is an abstract sort constrained only by Format, because All Format ts says that much of every element (ADR 0043). The invariant is the induction over positions, exactly as for for i in 0 .. n. Each unrolled copy is then discharged by that one proof, as an instance of a generic is.

So a variadic function is proved and checked once, at its definition, for every pack, and errors are reported there rather than at an instantiation (ADR 0034's definition check). That closes C++'s gap, where a pack expansion fails only when instantiated. Codegen still compiles straight-line code: print w a b c becomes three calls of format, with no loop and no run-time dispatch.

docs.title: 5. Variadic types
docs.text:
A generic type's last type parameter may be a pack too, and an instance is written like any other generic application, when_all_sender a b c. Its fields use type-level metaprograms over the pack:

(* when_all's operation state: one child operation per sender (ADR 0050). *)
let when_all_op (r : type) (ss : ...type where All Sender ss) = type {
  children : tuple_of (map (let (s) => op_of s (child_receiver r)) (elements ss));
  results  : tuple_of (map (let (s) => option (value_of s)) (elements ss));
  rcv      : r;
}

A sum over a pack is one_of ts, C++'s std::variant<Ts...>: a value that holds exactly one element of the pack, and knows which. It is a core anonymous sum, with no constructor names, because types are values and the type of the active element is enough to tell the alternatives apart:

let reading = one_of u32 str (option u8)

let describe (w : borrowed inout writer) (r : reading) : unit =
  match r with
  | (n : u32) -> format w n
  | (s : str) -> format w s
  | (o : option u8) -> format_opt w o

let r : reading = 42u32                      (* injected: the expected type is a one_of *)

(* Generic over the alternatives: one arm, proved once for an abstract element. *)
let show (ts : type where All Format ts) (w : borrowed inout writer) (v : one_of ...ts) : unit =
  match v with
  | x -> format w x
  • match on the active element's type is how a one_of is read. Arms are type patterns, and the match must cover every element type, or end in an arm that binds the rest generically. That one generic arm is visit, with no library function needed.
  • Element types must be distinct (answer 5), which one_of checks with a type-level distinct ts, so a type always names exactly one alternative. A variant whose alternatives share a type, such as two u32s that mean different things, is a named variant (type | Celsius of u32 | Kelvin of u32), which says what each one means.
  • v.[u32] is the element when it is a u32, with the precondition holds v u32, a spec function that a match arm or an if holds v u32 establishes. index v is the position of the active type in the pack.
  • Layout is a tag and the largest element, as for named variants, and Eq, Ord and Hash come from the elements, as for tuples.

docs.title: 6. Foreign bindings: variadic C calls, and declarations generated from tables
docs.text:
A C variadic function is declared once, with a pack. A pack in a foreign declaration is restricted to C-promoted types, and each call passes whatever its arguments are, with the ABI emitted for that call:

(* open(2): the mode is read only when O_CREAT or O_TMPFILE is set. *)
let open (ts : type where All CPromoted ts) (path : cstr) (flags : i32) (mode : ...ts) : i32
  requires (flags & o_creat <> 0) = (size ts = 1)
  requires size ts = 1 ==> element 0 ts = u32
  ensures result >= -1
= extern "open"

open path o_rdonly                         (* 2 arguments *)
open path (o_creat | o_wronly) 420u32      (* 3 arguments; 420 is 0644 *)
  • Calls use the variadic ABI. Codegen emits each call as a variadic LLVM call with the argument types of that call, so Apple arm64 puts the pack on the stack and x86_64 sets %al.
  • CPromoted holds for i32, u32, i64, u64, isize, usize, buffers (passed as pointers) and, once floats land, f64. A narrower integer or a bool fails the constraint with a message that says to widen it, because C would promote it and the callee would read an int. A record fails it, because C cannot pass a struct through ... portably.
  • The contract decides what a call may pass. What the C function reads depends on its other arguments, as open reads a mode only with O_CREAT. So the declaration's requires relates the pack's size and element types (size ts, element i ts) and values (mode.0) to the other arguments, and every call proves it. This is the "provably safe" part: the va_arg reads that C trusts become goals.
  • cstr is a [u8] refined to end in a NUL byte, which Pia.Sys builds and proves. It is not a new core type.
  • Pia functions are never C-variadic. Pia's own variadic functions take packs, which are tuples, and nothing in Pia makes or reads a va_list. Exporting a variadic function to C is not supported.
  • Format strings stay in Pia. printf and its family are not declared. Pia.Text.Format uses section 2, with requires placeholders fmt = size ts, which the verifier folds when fmt is a literal. So a format string with the wrong number of arguments is a failed goal, not a crash.

Declarations are generated from the platform's headers, with contracts beside them. POSIX alone needs a few hundred declarations, most of them per target, so Pia.Sys.Posix writes none of them by hand. Writing them as tables by hand would drift from the platforms, so they are generated:

  • A generator reads the headers. tools/bindings runs the pinned clang on a list of headers for one target (<fcntl.h>, <sys/socket.h>, <linux/io_uring.h> and so on), with -ast-dump=json, and writes lib/Pia/Sys/Gen/<target>.pia: every function's C signature, including whether it is variadic, every constant (O_CREAT, EAGAIN, SYS_io_uring_enter), and every struct's size, alignment and field offsets (sockaddr_in, kevent, epoll_event, io_uring_sqe). Nothing in it is written by hand.
  • The generated files are checked in, and CI keeps them honest. A build cross-compiling for a target needs that target's bindings without its SDK, so the files are in the repository. Each CI job regenerates the file for its own platform from the real headers and fails if it differs from the checked-in one. Drift is a red build on the platform that drifted.
  • Contracts are a hand-written overlay. Headers carry types, not promises, so a contract table beside the generated file says what each manual page guarantees. It has one row per symbol: the manual page, the contract clauses, the Pia modifiers of each parameter (out mutable [u8] for read's buffer, cstr for a path), the condition that decides a variadic pack (open reads mode only with O_CREAT), and attributes such as @blocking. The posix metaprogram joins each overlay row with its generated signature and stamps out the declaration, as bit_family stamps out Pia.Core.Bit (lib/Pia/Core/Bit.pia). An overlay row that names a symbol the header lacks, or whose parameters do not match the generated signature, is a compile error. A symbol with no overlay row is declared without a contract, so it can be called only as unsafe (stdlib.md).
  • The overlay is shared, and the generated files are per target. @target picks the generated file (ADR 0049). The overlay's rows hold for both platforms, unless a row is marked for one target. A system call on Linux is a row whose symbol is syscall and whose number comes from the generated SYS_ constant, so no number is written by hand. macOS has no system-call rows, because the library goes through libSystem there.
  • The trust report lists overlay rows. Every generated declaration is a trusted foreign contract. The report names its overlay row and manual page, and the header and target it was generated from, so an audit reads the overlay.

docs.title: Implementation steps
docs.text:
1. Foreign bindings first (section 6), since ADR 0050's I/O stack and Pia.Sys (#55, #57) need them: tools/bindings and the generated files for both targets, the CI regeneration check, the contract overlay and the posix metaprogram, and variadic calls. Until packs exist (step 3), an overlay row with a pack is stamped out as one fixed declaration per arity (open and open_mode), with the variadic ABI. That restriction is internal to the bindings and goes away in step 4.
  2. Core tuples (section 1): syntax, sema as anonymous records, IRGen, codegen and the verifier through the record paths, patterns, t.0, t.[type], and the structural instances.
  3. Pack parameters and calls (section 2): ...ts parameters, deduction, the argument-collection rule, partial application from the expected type, ...t spreading, and All and CPromoted.
  4. Walking packs (sections 3 and 4): elements and tuple_of, for over a pack with its expansion, the proof against an abstract element, and unrolled codegen. Foreign packs replace the per-arity declarations.
  5. Pia.Core.Pack and Pia.Fn's combinators: map, fold, apply, cat, get and zip; bind_front, bind_back, compose, flip and unpack, with Function over packs; and Pia.Text.Format on top.
  6. Variadic types (section 5): pack type parameters, then one_of with type-pattern match.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A variadic call looks like any other call, partial application included, and a variadic definition looks like an ordinary loop. The only new syntax is ... on the pack parameter and on a spread argument.
  • There is no recursion over packs, in types or in code. Type-level work is list metaprogramming, and code-level work is a loop that expansion unrolls.
  • Variadic code is proved and checked once, at its definition. Each call still compiles to straight-line code.
  • one_of is a core anonymous sum read by matching on types, so std::variant needs no constructor names, no visit function and no index-based access.
  • Calls to C varargs are typed by their arguments, checked against C's promotion rules, and constrained by contracts, with the ABI right on both targets.
  • Foreign signatures, constants and layouts cannot drift from the platforms, because CI regenerates them from each platform's headers. Only the contracts are written by hand, and the trust report audits them.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Dean's answers to the first revision's questions (2026-11-23):

  1. Partial application of variadic functions is wanted, with higher-order functions and combinators. Section 2 does this through the expected type, with bind_front and friends for function values that keep the pack open.
  2. ... rather than ... .. is already the range operator, and open-sided ranges are planned (u32{1..}, #153). A prefix ..n range would then read the same as a spread ..n in f ..n. ... costs one token, cannot clash with any range, and is what C++ and JavaScript readers expect for packs and spreads.
  3. Index by type, and match on the alternatives. xs.[u8] indexes a pack by type, since types are values. one_of is read by a match on the active element's type (section 5), not through positional constructors.
  4. Generate the bindings from the headers to avoid drift, with contracts in a hand-written overlay (section 6).

Dean's answers to the second revision's questions (2026-11-23):

  1. one_of requires distinct element types, so a type names exactly one alternative. Two alternatives that share a type are a named variant.
  2. let g = print w with no expected type is a complete call. A lint, variadic_unit_binding, warns when the unit result of a variadic call is bound to a name, since that is probably a partial application that was meant.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes C++11 parameter packs, C++17 fold expressions, C++26 pack indexing the capabilities: variadic functions and types, folds, size and indexing C++ std::tuple, std::apply, std::variant tuples as the pack value, apply, sums over a type list C++'s std::bind_front, Haskell's uncurry combinators over argument lists Zig's inline for over tuples and comptime type lists a loop over a pack unrolled per element, and types computed by ordinary compile-time code Rust's libc crate and bindgen per-target bindings generated from headers, and why types from headers are not contracts Go's zerrors_* and zsysnum_* tables, generated per platform constants and system-call numbers as per-target data, checked against the platform GCC's format attribute argument checking for format strings, here as a proved requires

docs.title: 52. Atomics are a core cell type with checked orders and stated overflow, modelled by RC11 with a litmus battery before tasks exist, and lowered per target by a table proved against each hardware model
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-23), with his answers folded in: relaxed becomes acquire and release only inside @target(x86_64_linux) items; atomic arithmetic always states its overflow handling, and the lowering uses what each target does; and the memory model is modelled now, with a battery of litmus tests, so that tasks have it ready when they land.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia has no atomics. ADR 0027 designs them as atomic<T> in Pia.Sync, with every operation taking a memory order, seq_cst, acquire, release and acq_rel checked from the start, and relaxed unproved until the model checker has an RC11 mode, except where the value read orders nothing. stdlib.md lists the operations as core builtins for milestone M12. Neither says how the verifier sees an atomic, how the orders are checked, or what each target emits.

Three pieces of accepted or proposed work are waiting on them:

  • ADR 0049, section 4. Dean accepted that @target(x86_64_linux) code may rely on TSO, provided it is proved at compile time: after optimisation, every atomic access in such an item must still be an acquire or release access. Step 3d of that ADR cannot be built without atomics to check. The same section asks for per-target lemmas proving that the instructions chosen for each order give every happens-before edge the language model promises.
  • ADR 0047, shared_ref. Its counts and its lease word are atomic.
  • ADR 0050, io_uring. Ring heads and tails live in memory shared with the kernel, read with acquire loads and written with release stores.

ADR 0027's primitives (mutex, chan, once, the work-stealing deque) are written over atomics too, but they also need tasks and the model checker, which this ADR does not build.

C and C++ get three things wrong that Pia can do better. A memory order that is wrong for the operation (a release load, a compare_exchange failure order of release) is undefined behaviour in C and quietly strengthened by compilers. An atomic object that is not lock-free silently becomes a lock in libatomic. And memory_order may be a run-time value, which compilers treat as seq_cst.

docs.title: 1. atomic t is a core cell type
docs.text:
atomic t holds one value of t, which is an integer type (u8 to u64, i8 to i64, usize, isize) or bool, or a refinement of one (section 3). There are no atomic records, floats or 128-bit cells in this ADR.

  • Always lock-free. Every allowed t is 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, and both targets do every operation on those widths in one instruction or one ldxr/stxr loop. piac never emits a call to libatomic. A future cell type that would need one is a compile error, not a hidden lock.
  • Layout. Size and alignment are those of t, so an atomic u32 is 4 bytes at 4-byte alignment. A cell that tasks contend for can be padded with Pia.Sync.padded, aligned and sized to Target.cache_line (128 bytes on Apple silicon, 64 on x86_64), which makes its published layout per target (ADR 0030, ADR 0049 section 3).
  • A place, not a value. An atomic cell is reached by borrowing it. Copying one is not atomic, so atomic t is not copyable. Moving one is allowed, because a moved value has a single owner and no other task can be touching it.
  • Concepts. atomic t is sendable and shareable (ADR 0027), and it is the only built-in type with interior mutability that is shareable. Two tasks may borrow one cell at once, even both mutable, because no access to it is a data race (ADR 0027's rule 5).
  • Creation. atomic_new v makes a cell holding v. It is a plain store, since nothing else can see the cell yet.

docs.title: 2. Operations are builtins, and their orders are checked
docs.text:
The operations are core builtins, as stdlib.md already lists, with the order first:

Builtin Meaning Orders allowed atomic_load o c read relaxed, acquire, seq_cst atomic_store o c v write relaxed, release, seq_cst atomic_swap o c v write v, return the old value all five atomic_cas ok fail c expected desired if the value is expected, write desired; return the old value either way ok: all five. fail: relaxed, acquire or seq_cst, and no stronger than ok atomic_add o c v, atomic_sub (each with its overflow mode, below), atomic_and, atomic_or, atomic_xor, atomic_min, atomic_max read, modify, write; return the old value all five fence o order the surrounding atomics acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst

atomic_cas returns the old value, and it succeeded exactly when that equals expected, so it needs no tuple. It is the strong form: it never fails spuriously. A weak form is left until a loop needs the difference, which on arm64 with LSE (every Apple silicon CPU) it does not, since cas is one instruction.

The five orders are the constants relaxed, acquire, release, acq_rel and seq_cst of the core type order. They are names in the prelude, like true, not keywords. An order must be a compile-time constant. An order the table does not allow is a compile error that says which orders the operation takes, so the cases C leaves undefined cannot be written.

Overflow. atomic_add and atomic_sub never take an overflow mode from anywhere else: each one states its own, as @wrap (atomic_add o c v) or the other three forms (design.md), and one without a mode is a compile error, even inside an @overflow(...) function. Nothing is assumed about what the hardware does on overflow. The four modes keep their ordinary meanings, and each target lowers them by what its instructions do:

Mode Meaning arm64 x86_64 wrap modular ldadd lock xadd trap the program traps when the result does not fit; the cell already holds the wrapped value, and other tasks may read it before the program stops, so trap is for counters whose overflow is a bug ldadd, then the overflow is computed from the old value it returns (old > max - v) lock xadd or lock add, then jo or jc on the flags the instruction set saturate the result is clamped, and no wrapped value is ever stored a compare-and-swap loop a compare-and-swap loop proof the result must be proved to fit for every value the cell's type allows ldadd lock xadd

The target model says which of these a target has: x86_64_linux sets rmw_flags = true, because a lock-prefixed add sets the overflow and carry flags, and arm64_macos sets it to false, because LSE's ldadd sets none. The verifier sees the same meaning on both targets, so no proof depends on the value. Codegen reads it, and the lowering lemmas of section 5 prove each entry. proof mode is rarely provable on a cell of a plain integer type, since another task may have left any value there. It is meant for refined cells (section 3), where the refinement bounds the old value.

docs.title: 3. The verifier treats every access as if any task wrote just before it
docs.text:
Within one function, the verifier models a cell as a value that another task may change between any two accesses. So:

  • atomic_load returns a fresh value of t, about which the verifier knows only its type.
  • atomic_swap, atomic_cas and the read-modify-writes return a fresh old value. After atomic_cas, the verifier knows that it succeeded exactly when the old value equals expected, and nothing about the cell afterwards.
  • atomic_store has no result.

This is sound under every interleaving, because it assumes nothing about other tasks, and it is cheap: no event structure, no new sorts, and no quantifiers. It is also the most a single function can know. Anything that relates the values seen by two tasks (a counter that only grows, a flag that publishes data) is a claim about the whole program, and it belongs to ADR 0027's model checker and to the Order theory (docs/theories.md). Code that wants exact values in one task should use a plain mutable.

Refined cells. When t is a refinement, every value stored is a goal: atomic_store, atomic_swap and the desired of atomic_cas must be proved to meet the refinement, and every value read may be assumed to meet it. The refinement is then an invariant of the cell that holds across all tasks, proved one store at a time, just as a lock invariant is the refinement of a mutex's data (ADR 0027). The bitwise read-modify-writes are not allowed on a refined cell, since their result is never known. atomic_add and atomic_sub are allowed only in proof mode, with a goal that for every value the refinement allows, the result fits and meets the refinement. Pia.Sync.atomic_update o c f is the replacement: a compare-and-swap loop in the library that calls f on the old value and stores its result, and f's result must meet the refinement:

let slots = type { n : u32 | n <= 64 }

let take (c : borrowed atomic slots) : bool
= let old = atomic_update acq_rel c (let (n) => if n > 0 then n - 1 else n) in
  old > 0

Across tasks, the verifier needs a memory model, and section 4 gives one now.

docs.title: 4. The language memory model is a theory now, with a battery of litmus tests
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-23): model it now, so that when tasks land there is a battery of tests ready for them.

The theory. Pia.Memory is a built-in theory of executions, extending the Order theory in docs/theories.md to the whole of RC11 (Lahav, Vafeiadis, Kang, Hur and Dreyer, 2017), the repaired C11 model:

  • Events: atomic loads, stores, read-modify-writes and fences, each with its order, and plain loads and stores, each with its location and value.
  • Relations: program order po; reads-from rf; the modification order mo, a total order of the stores to each location; rmw, linking the read and write halves of a read-modify-write; synchronises-with sw, built from release sequences and fences as RC11 defines it; happens-before hb = (po ∪ sw)+; and the seq_cst order psc.
  • Axioms: coherence (hb ; eco? irreflexive, where eco is rf, mo and from-reads closed), atomicity of read-modify-writes, psc acyclic, and no thin-air values (po ∪ rf acyclic). That last axiom is what lets RC11 give relaxed a meaning without out-of-thin-air results.
  • Races: two accesses to one location race when at least one is plain, at least one writes, and neither happens before the other. That is ADR 0027's definition, and a race is a compile error.

With RC11 in place, relaxed is modelled from the start, not left unproved: ADR 0027's model checker reasons about every order under the same axioms, and the "value orders nothing" rule is no longer needed.

Litmus tests. A litmus test is a small concurrent program, with a few threads and a few locations, and the outcomes it may or may not have. Tasks are not built yet, so the tests are written with a litmus metaprogram in the prelude, beside machine (docs/theories.md). Each thread is a block of atomic and plain accesses to named cells, and the result says whether an outcome is allowed or forbidden, or that the test has a race:

litmus "MP+rel+acq"
  cells (data : u32) (flag : atomic u32)
  thread (data <- 1; atomic_store release flag 1)
  thread (let r1 = atomic_load acquire flag in let r2 = data in ())
  forbidden (r1 = 1 && r2 = 0)

litmus "MP+rlx"
  cells (data : u32) (flag : atomic u32)
  thread (data <- 1; atomic_store relaxed flag 1)
  thread (let r1 = atomic_load acquire flag in let r2 = data in ())
  race

The metaprogram expands a test into the test's events and a goal over Pia.Memory. A forbidden outcome is proved when no consistent execution has it. An allowed outcome is proved by a witness execution, which the solver finds and piac prints. A race is proved by an execution with two racing accesses. The tests are finite, so each one is a small, decidable query: relations become Boolean matrices over the test's events, and acyclicity becomes a ranking of them.

The battery is tests/memory/, one file per family, with each expected result taken from the published tables for RC11 and checked against herd7 (diy and herd, the tool most memory-model papers use) where they give one:

  • the classic shapes: MP, SB, LB, S, R, 2+2W, WRC, ISA2, IRIW, CoRR, CoRW, CoWR and CoWW, each under every combination of orders the operations allow, with fences in place of orders as well;
  • read-modify-write atomicity, release sequences, and seq_cst fences;
  • thin-air shapes (LB with dependencies), which RC11 forbids;
  • races: plain accesses published by relaxed, by release and acquire, and by fences.

When tasks land, each test also becomes a program of spawned tasks, with the same outcomes as contracts on join. The model checker must agree with the battery, the deterministic replay mode can run each witness schedule, and on hardware a stress run of each test must never show a forbidden outcome. So tasks arrive with their memory model already proved against a few hundred tests, and with the tests ready to run as programs.

docs.title: 5. Each target lowers the orders by a table that is proved against its hardware model
docs.text:
piac emits LLVM load atomic, store atomic, atomicrmw, cmpxchg and fence with the matching LLVM ordering, and LLVM's backends pick the instructions. Those choices are the standard mappings from C11 to each architecture:

Order arm64 (Apple silicon: LSE and RCpc) x86_64 relaxed load / store ldr / str mov / mov acquire load ldapr mov release store stlr mov seq_cst load / store ldar / stlr mov / xchg read-modify-write, cas ldadd, swp, cas and so on, with a, l or al lock xadd, xchg, lock cmpxchg; a loop of lock cmpxchg for and, or, xor, min, max when the old value is used fence acquire, release, acq_rel dmb ishld for acquire, dmb ish otherwise nothing (compiler barrier only) fence seq_cst dmb ish lock or of zero to the stack, which LLVM prefers to mfence as a full barrier

Since Pia trusts LLVM for instruction selection, the table is checked in two halves:

  1. The table is what LLVM emits. A codegen test per target compiles one function per (operation, order) pair and checks the instructions with FileCheck. A change in the pinned LLVM that picks other instructions fails that test.
  2. The table is proved against the hardware model. Each target model in Pia.Target gains its hardware memory model, as ADR 0049 section 4 says: x86-TSO (Owens, Sarkar and Sewell) for x86_64, and the Armv8 axiomatic model (Pulte, Flur, Deacon and others, the one Arm publishes in its herd cat file) for arm64, written as theories of the same shape as Order. A compiler lemma per target states that the instructions the table chooses give every happens-before edge the language model promises. The lemmas are the battery of section 4 run a second time, against each hardware model: for every test, each outcome the hardware allows for the compiled instructions must be an outcome Pia.Memory allows for the source. The battery's file for each family runs against all three models. That includes the overflow lowerings of section 2: a trap on x86_64 reads the flags of the same lock instruction, so the check cannot see another task's update. The general theorem, that these mappings are correct for every program, is the published result of Lahav, Vafeiadis and others for RC11 and of Podkopaev, Lahav and Vafeiadis for Armv8, and Pia cites it rather than reproving it. The lemmas are what catch a wrong entry in Pia's table.

The lemmas live in src/irgen/Target.pia beside the models, so the build proves them, as it already proves the models' axioms (tests/verify/target_theory.pia).

docs.title: 6. On x86_64, code may rely on TSO, and each program proves it did not lose it
docs.text:
This builds ADR 0049 section 4.2 as Dean accepted it, limited, by his answer to this ADR, to the items that may rely on TSO.

  • Which code. The model x86_64_linux gains two axioms, store_releases (every atomic store releases) and load_acquires (every atomic load acquires). Like every model fact, they are visible only inside @target(x86_64_linux) items. Target-generic code sees only the Pia.Target theory, so it never relies on them.
  • The lowering. Inside @target(x86_64_linux) items, relaxed loads are emitted as LLVM acquire and relaxed stores as release. On x86_64 they are the same mov instructions, so the only cost is that LLVM may no longer reorder them, which is what the axioms need. Relaxed read-modify-writes are already lock-prefixed full barriers on x86_64, so they are emitted as acq_rel. Outside @target(x86_64_linux), relaxed stays LLVM monotonic on both targets, since no proof there can depend on more.
  • The check. Each atomic access emitted for a @target(x86_64_linux) item carries !pia.tso metadata naming its source location. After LLVM's optimisation pipeline, and before instruction selection, piac checks two things. First, every instruction with !pia.tso is still acquire, release, acq_rel or seq_cst. Second, every source location tagged before optimisation still has at least one tagged instruction afterwards, so an access the optimiser deleted or merged away is noticed. Inlining and unrolling may copy an access, which is fine, since every copy is checked. A failure is a compile error at the source location, saying that the optimiser weakened or removed an access the proof relied on. A goal that the axioms did not prove would have been proved without them, so the check can be stricter than necessary, never weaker.

With this, publish_relaxed from docs/theories.md, the message-passing idiom with a relaxed flag, proves inside @target(x86_64_linux) and fails everywhere else, which is the hardware's behaviour. The battery has both versions of publish_relaxed: as a source test under Pia.Memory, where the outcome is allowed, and under x86_64_linux's axioms, where it is forbidden.

docs.title: 7. Atomics on foreign memory are unsafe views
docs.text: io_uring's rings and other memory shared with the kernel or another process are not Pia cells. An unsafe view of such memory (stdlib.md) can be viewed as atomic cells with unsafe Pia.Sync.atomic_at v offset : borrowed atomic u32 (and the other widths), with a goal that offset is in bounds and aligned to the cell's size. What the other side does is outside Pia's proof, so each such view is a trust item with the citation the module gives, such as io_uring(7) for the ring heads and tails (ADR 0050 section 3).

docs.title: 8. Build order
docs.text:
1. Cells and operations. atomic t, atomic_new, the builtins, the order checks and the overflow modes (section 2), the verifier's view (section 3), refined cells and atomic_update, and lowering with LLVM's orderings. Tests: proved uses in tests/verify/atomics.pia, order and overflow errors in tests/irgen, and the instruction tables for both targets in tests/codegen.
  2. Pia.Memory and the litmus battery (section 4): the theory with a model proving it consistent, the litmus metaprogram, and tests/memory/.
  3. The hardware models and lowering lemmas (section 5): x86-TSO and Armv8 in src/irgen/Target.pia, and the battery run against each.
  4. The x86_64 TSO lowering and check (section 6), which is ADR 0049 step 3d.
  5. Foreign atomic views (section 7), when Pia.Io.Uring needs them, and padded with the per-target layout.
  6. Tasks (ADR 0027, issue #75 onwards) then connect: spawned code produces Pia.Memory events, the model checker and race prover use the theory, and the battery runs as programs.

docs.title: Notes from step 1 (2026-11-23)
docs.text:
Building step 1 changed four details, none of which changes the design:

  • Refined cells are range types. Sema does not resolve a scalar refinement such as { n : u32 | n <= 64 } yet, so a refined cell is written with a range type, atomic int{0..64}, which is the same invariant. Its storage is the range's, a byte here, not a u32.
  • atomic_update retries a bounded number of times. A compare-and-swap loop that can lose every race cannot be proved to end, and a while without a measure is not proved. The version in tests/verify/atomics.pia takes a number of tries and returns the old value it last saw. Pia.Sync will need the same, or a measure that tasks can supply.
  • fence seq_cst on x86_64 is lock or, which is what LLVM emits; the table above is corrected, since the codegen test checks what LLVM emits.
  • trap reads the old value on both targets for now. rmw_flags is in the target models, but no lowering reads the flags yet, so on x86_64 the overflow is recomputed from the old value, as on arm64.

docs.title: Notes from step 2 (2026-11-23)
docs.text:
• Litmus tests are data. A metaprogram cannot take code apart yet, so litmus takes its threads as lists of events, [ write "data" 1; store "release" "flag" 1 ], with orders as strings, and its outcome as is and final conditions; "race" is the third verdict. An allowed outcome fails with its witness as the counterexample, since the verifier reports a satisfiable query that way.
  • Derived relations are lower bounds, in the theory and in each test. Every RC11 axiom only forbids, so the least relations that meet the bounds decide every verdict, including races, and no relation needs to be computed as a closure.
  • The battery is a first family of tests, 43 of them, not yet every combination of orders, and the expected results are RC11's published ones, not yet checked against herd7. cas, which writes only when it succeeds, is not in the litmus vocabulary yet.

docs.title: Answers (Dean, 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
1. relaxed as acquire and release on x86_64: yes, only inside @target(x86_64_linux) items (section 6). Elsewhere it stays LLVM monotonic.
  2. Overflow of atomic_add and atomic_sub: "Do not assume, but use the target theory based on what we know the platform does... the simplest thing is to always require the overflow handling/expectations." Each operation states its mode, and the target model records what the hardware gives (rmw_flags), which the lowering uses (section 2).
  3. Happens-before from atomics: "No, let's model it now so that when we implement tasks (ASAP) we have a battery of tests we can use." Pia.Memory and the litmus battery are step 2 (section 4).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• ADR 0049 step 3d can be built: the TSO check has atomics to check, and the lowering lemmas have a table to prove.
  • ADR 0047's shared_ref and ADR 0050's io_uring rings have the cells and orders they name.
  • A wrong memory order, a hidden lock, a run-time order and an atomic add without stated overflow handling cannot be written.
  • The verifier's view of an atomic within one function is weak on purpose: a function proves nothing about values other tasks write. Cross-task facts go through Pia.Memory, which exists before tasks do, with a battery of litmus tests that tasks, the model checker and both targets must pass.
  • relaxed is modelled by RC11 from the start, which replaces ADR 0027's plan to leave it unproved.
  • Refined cells give cross-task invariants with one goal per store, without the model checker.
  • Pia trusts LLVM's instruction selection for atomics, but a change in what it emits fails a test, and the table it emits is proved against each hardware model.
  • Writing RC11, x86-TSO and the Armv8 model as theories is new work. The battery runs three times, once per model, and its cost is tracked by the proof bench (ADR 0032).

docs.title: 53. Protocols and deadlock are checked in Z3, as transition systems proved by constrained Horn clauses; explicit search stays for atomics, and TLA+ is an export format
Context
docs.text:
ADR 0027 plans a model checker for what the type system cannot express: the library's primitives, channel protocols, deadlock, and user code built from atomics (docs/concurrency.md, sections 4 and 5). It is to be an exhaustive explicit-state search with dynamic partial-order reduction (DPOR), as in Nidhugg, GenMC and Loom, where a search that hits its limit is unproved. ADR 0050 adds a goal for it, the in-flight slot table's stop race, and ADR 0052 adds RC11 with a battery of litmus tests. Nothing of the checker is built.

Dean asked (2026-11-23) whether the checker could use TLA+ as a library, or whether this could just be a theory that Z3 handles.

  • TLA+ as a library. TLC, the explicit-state checker, and Apalache, the symbolic one, both run on the JVM, and neither is a library to link. Using them would put a Java runtime and a second specification language inside piac's proof path. Their results would also be outside what the certificate (ADR 0024) and --trust-report record about a goal.
  • Z3 already decides most of it. A protocol is a transition system: states, an initial condition, and a transition relation. Deadlock freedom, exactly-once delivery and mutual exclusion are safety properties, each saying that no reachable state is bad. Z3's Spacer engine proves safety of transition systems without a bound, by solving constrained Horn clauses (CHC). It finds an inductive invariant, or a counterexample trace if one exists, which is what IC3 and PDR do for hardware. That is the approach Apalache takes for TLA+, except here it runs in the process.
  • The front end exists. The prelude's machine metaprogram (docs/theories.md, ADR 0036) already turns a table of transitions into a theory with a model. ADR 0027's protocol inference produces automata of the same kind for each channel end.

docs.title: 1. Safety goals are CHC queries discharged by Spacer
docs.text:
A protocol goal becomes a transition system, and its safety property becomes three kinds of Horn clauses over an invariant predicate Inv. The initial states satisfy Inv. A transition from an Inv state reaches an Inv state. No Inv state is bad. Z3 solves the clauses with Spacer:

  • Proved when Spacer returns an invariant. The invariant is kept as the goal's witness, so the proof cache (ADR 0032) and the certificate store it, and checking it again later is three ordinary SMT queries, not a new search.
  • Failed when Spacer returns a derivation. That is a trace of transitions from an initial state to a bad one. piac prints it as a schedule with source locations, as ADR 0027 already plans for counterexamples, and Pia.Task.run_deterministic replays it.
  • Unproved when Spacer runs out of budget, which is a compile error like any unproved goal, accepted only by --allow-unproved. Bounded unrolling (BMC) is used only to find a counterexample sooner. A bounded "no counterexample" is never a proof, as ADR 0027 requires.

The verifier reaches Z3 directly through its C++ API already (src/verify/Strategy.cpp), so the CHC queries go through z3::fixedpoint, or through HORN logic, beside the smt dialect's per-goal queries rather than through it.

docs.title: 2. What becomes a transition system
docs.text:
• Channel protocols and deadlock (ADR 0027, section 5, stages 2 and 3). The state is each task's protocol automaton state together with each channel's occupancy, and data is abstracted to what the protocols read. The bad states are those where a set of tasks is blocked forever on one another. The topology check and the pattern lemmas still come first. Spacer takes what they leave, in place of the explicit search.
  • Parametric claims. A worker pool of n tasks is a transition system over a counter of tasks in each state, which is a counter abstraction. Spacer then proves it for every n at once, where an explicit search needs a cutoff lemma.
  • Library protocols. These include the in-flight slot table and stop tokens (ADR 0050, section 4), once, the barrier, and the channel's own implementation above its atomics. Each is a machine, or an inferred automaton, with its invariant proved once when the library builds.
  • Generated state machines in user code, such as a connection's states. These stay theories as today, and Spacer adds the reachability questions a machine theory alone cannot answer: "can Draining be reached without shutdown?"

docs.title: 3. Explicit DPOR stays for fine-grained atomics
docs.text: Code over atomics under RC11 (ADR 0052) has interleavings at every load and store, and a symbolic encoding of that grows with every pair of events. DPOR over the event graph, as GenMC does, is the known good approach. So the explicit checker remains, with a narrower job: the primitives built directly on atomics (the work-stealing deque, the mutex's fast path, the channel's ring) and user code that uses atomics. Its litmus battery is ADR 0052's. Everything above the atomic layer, where a protocol's steps are whole operations, goes to Spacer.

docs.title: 4. Liveness is reduced to safety
docs.text:
"Every operation eventually completes" and "a waiting task is eventually woken" are liveness properties, which need fairness. Two reductions cover the cases Pia needs:

  • Ranking functions. A protocol whose progress has a measure, such as the operations left in the slot table or the items left in a bounded channel, proves liveness as a safety property: the measure decreases on every fair step. That is how decreases already works for loops.
  • Liveness to safety. For the rest, the standard construction of Biere, Artho and Schuppan turns "no fair infinite run avoids the goal" into a reachability query over a doubled state, which Spacer then decides.

A liveness goal that neither discharges is unproved. ADR 0027's channel deadlock goal is a safety property, so it needs neither.

docs.title: 5. TLA+ is an export, not a dependency
docs.text: piac --emit=tla writes a goal's transition system as a TLA+ module: its variables, Init, Next, the invariant to check and, when proved, Spacer's invariant as a candidate inductive invariant. It lets someone cross-check a protocol with TLC or Apalache, or read it as a specification. Nothing in the build depends on it, and its results are not proofs to piac.

docs.title: Implementation steps
docs.text:
1. CHC goals in the verifier: a goal kind for transition systems, queried through z3::fixedpoint with Spacer. Invariants are stored in the proof cache and re-checked as three SMT queries. Traces are printed as schedules.
  2. machine reachability: theories built by machine get reachability and invariant goals. This is the first user-visible use, and it needs no tasks.
  3. ADR 0050's slot table and stop tokens, as the first library protocol proved this way.
  4. Channel deadlock, stages 2 and 3 (#112, #113), on protocol automata, with counter abstraction for parametric topologies.
  5. Liveness by ranking functions, then by liveness to safety.
  6. --emit=tla.
  7. Explicit DPOR for atomics (#81, #83), against ADR 0052's battery.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Most of the model checker becomes a goal kind in the existing verifier, using the solver and proof cache Pia already has, instead of a separate search engine. Its proofs are invariants that can be re-checked cheaply and recorded in certificates.
  • Parametric protocols, such as a pool of n workers, are proved for every n without hand-written cutoff lemmas.
  • Spacer can fail to converge on some protocols, and those goals are unproved. The explicit checker is still needed for atomics, so Pia keeps two engines, each with a narrower job than ADR 0027 planned for one.
  • TLA+ users can read and check Pia's protocols with their own tools, and Pia does not depend on them.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. Should the explicit DPOR checker be built at all? The recommendation is yes, but last, and only for code directly over atomics. The alternative is to encode RC11 executions as CHC too, which avoids a second engine at the cost of queries that may not scale. Answered 2026-11-27 by Dean: yes, built last, only for code directly over atomics.
  2. What is Spacer's budget per goal? The recommendation is the verifier's usual per-goal rlimit (ADR 0032), scaled by a per-goal @solver setting for large protocols. The alternative is a separate, larger default for CHC goals. Answered 2026-11-27 by Dean: the usual per-goal rlimit, scaled by @solver.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes Z3's Spacer (Komuravelli, Gurfinkel and Chaki), IC3 and PDR (Bradley, Een) safety of transition systems by CHC, with inductive invariants as certificates Apalache symbolic checking of TLA+ in an SMT solver TLA+ and TLC the specification format that --emit=tla writes Counter abstraction (Pnueli, Xu and Zuck) parametric protocols as counts of tasks in each state Biere, Artho and Schuppan, liveness to safety liveness goals as reachability queries GenMC, Nidhugg, Loom explicit DPOR for code over atomics

docs.title: 54. GIF and inflate are proved total on every input, decode to a written specification, and GIF round-trips exactly
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-23), with his answers to both questions, recorded at the end.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked (2026-11-23) for proved image codecs, "so we don't have the rendering related bugs that other shaders and renderers have encountered". ADR 0016 already puts image I/O on the path of the flagship demo. M13 (#14) is the image I/O milestone, and stdlib.md lists Image.Gif, with "GIF LZW", as one of the library's stress tests.

Dean also decided three things on 2026-11-23:

  • The codecs run in parallel with the GPU work. They are pure Pia over byte buffers. This was decided in the survey of the path to the GPU demo.
  • GIF comes first, then inflate. Inflate (RFC 1951) is here because PNG and the Copernicus GeoTIFF elevation tiles both need it later.
  • JPEG is deferred entirely. It is complicated, and it may be patent encumbered. Issue #313 holds it, with the design that the first draft of this ADR worked out.

Image and compression decoders are among the most attacked code there is, because their input arrives from anywhere and is decoded before anyone looks at it. The bugs fall into a few classes, and the verifier can already state a goal that rules out each one:

Bug class Example What rules it out here A length field trusted before it is checked zlib CVE-2022-37434: a large gzip header extra field overflowed inflateGetHeader's buffer every length is a range type, and every copy is proved to lie inside both its source and its destination A table built from a code the input describes libwebp CVE-2023-4863: Huffman tables were written past their allocation before the code was validated (case study) a Huffman code is proved complete, or rejected, before any table is written, and each table index is proved in bounds A back-reference before the start of the output inflate's "distance too far back", which reads memory before the output buffer every distance is proved <= bytes written so far before the copy An index used before the table holds it LZW decoders that accept a code above the next free entry, or let the dictionary grow past 4096 each code is proved <= next before it is looked up, and next <= 4096 is an invariant A palette index outside the palette giflib's gif2rgb (CVE-2016-3977, through the background colour index) every index written is proved < palette size, or the decoder pads the colour map to 256 entries Pixels never written a frame or a truncated code stream that leaves part of the canvas as old heap contents the decoder proves that every pixel of the output is written: from the frame, from disposal, or from the background Frames outside the canvas a GIF frame rectangle that does not fit inside the logical screen a frame is proved to lie inside the screen, or is clipped to it, by the type of its rectangle Decompression bombs a 65535 x 65535 header with a few bytes of data, or a deflate stream that expands a thousandfold the caller gives a budget, and width * height * channels <= budget is checked, and the output length bounded, before any output is written

The renderer bugs Dean mentions are one step further on, in code that consumes the pixels: a shader that samples past an edge, or one that assumes values a decoder did not deliver. The codecs cannot fix that code, but they can hand it facts. A decoded image carries its dimensions and sample ranges in its type. A kernel in the dataflow graph of ADR 0050 that reads it starts from those facts instead of hoping for them.

What the compiler can do today shapes the plan:

  • Integers only. Neither codec needs floats, which are not compiled yet (M11).
  • Products of header values. width * height * channels meets verifier issue #45 (multiplication). It goes through lemmas in the style of index_2d_lt from stdlib.md, with each dimension capped at 65535 as GIF's 16-bit fields already cap it.
  • No Pia.Mem module yet. Allocators, box and vec are prototyped as tests (CODEMAP.md, section 3), so the codecs should not need to allocate.
  • The pattern exists. Pia.Core.Utf8 proves both round trips of a codec, and Pia.Text.Json proves a tokenizer against a grammar written as spec functions (ADR 0045). The codecs take the same shape: a Spec module that says what the bytes mean, and code proved equal to it, function by function.

docs.title: 1. What "proved correct" means
docs.text:
Each codec function has up to four levels of guarantee. The first two hold for every function, and the last two hold where the format allows them.

  1. Total and safe on every input. For any byte slice, decoding returns Ok, or an Err from a closed set. There is no out-of-bounds access, no overflow and no uninitialised read, and a termination measure (the input bits left to read) proves that decoding ends. This is the strongest-guarantee default of ADR 0004. Nothing is @trusted.
  2. Bounded. The output's size is checked against the caller's budget before decoding. The decoder needs no memory beyond the output and fixed-size tables: 4096 entries for the LZW dictionary, and a few hundred for inflate's Huffman tables plus its 32 KiB window, which is the output itself.
  3. Conforming decode. Decoding returns Ok exactly when the input is in the format's grammar, which is written as spec functions, and the output is the one the specification defines. For GIF that means the GIF89a block grammar and the LZW semantics. For inflate it means RFC 1951's blocks, codes and back-references, and RFC 1950's framing with Adler-32.
  4. An exact round trip. For GIF, decoding what was encoded gives back the frames, palettes and timing exactly, and this is proved. Inflate is decode only in this ADR, so its round trip comes with deflate (section 2).

docs.title: 2. Scope
docs.text: Codec In scope Out of scope GIF decode GIF87a and GIF89a; global and local colour tables; LZW code sizes 2 to 12; interlacing; transparency and disposal from the Graphic Control Extension; every frame of an animation, with its delay; the NETSCAPE2.0 application extension's loop count; other extensions, skipped by their length nothing: every valid GIF decodes GIF encode indexed images with a palette of up to 256 colours, interlaced or not, with a dictionary reset when it fills; animations with one global palette shared by every frame (a local palette only where a frame asks for one), a delay, disposal method and transparent index per frame, a loop count (the NETSCAPE2.0 extension), and frames that cover only the changed rectangle of the screen colour quantisation from RGB, which is a separate function (section 5) Inflate every RFC 1951 stream (stored, fixed Huffman and dynamic Huffman blocks) into a caller's buffer whose length bounds the output; zlib (RFC 1950) framing, checked with its Adler-32 deflate (compression), which comes with PNG encode in a later ADR; gzip framing until something needs it JPEG none all of it, deferred to #313

docs.title: 3. Modules
docs.text:
The codecs live under Pia.Image and Pia.Compress, one module per file (ADR 0039). Each format has a Spec that the rest is proved against, as Json.Spec is for JSON.

Module Provides Image.Raster raster c: width, height and c channels of u8 over a borrowed slice, with len = width * height * c in its type; and rect, a rectangle inside a raster Image.Bits bit readers and writers over a byte slice, LSB first (GIF and deflate), each proved against a spec function of "the bit at position k" Image.Gif.Spec the block grammar, and the meaning of a code stream: lzw_decode as a spec function over a dictionary of strings Image.Gif.Lzw the decoder over prefix and suffix tables, and the encoder over a hash of (prefix, byte), each proved equal to the spec Image.Gif.Decode, Image.Gif.Encode the container: the screen descriptor, colour tables, image descriptors, extensions, interlace order and frames Image.Gif.Quantise RGB to a palette of at most 256 colours (section 5) Compress.Huffman canonical Huffman codes built from code lengths, with the completeness check, and fast lookup. Later formats reuse it. Compress.Inflate.Spec, Compress.Inflate RFC 1951 as spec functions (block types, the length and distance codes, the code-length code), and a decoder proved equal to it Compress.Zlib RFC 1950 framing, with Adler-32 from Pia.Core

None of these needs an allocator or the OS, so they belong with Pia.Core in what stdlib.md says can later run in a GPU kernel.

docs.title: 4. Decoding is in two steps and does not allocate
docs.text:
let info : (s : [u8]) -> result gif_info GifError
let decode_frame : (s : [u8]) -> (i : gif_info) -> (k : usize)
                 -> (out : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) -> result frame GifError
  requires k < frames i && len out = width i * height i * 4

info reads the headers and returns the dimensions and the frame count, proved to agree with Spec. The caller checks them against its own budget, allocates the output with whatever allocator it holds, and calls decode_frame to fill it. Inflate takes an output slice, and returns the number of bytes written or OutputFull with the input offset, so a caller can grow its buffer and resume. Wrappers that take an allocator and a budget, and return an owned image or byte vector, come once Pia.Mem is a module.

Errors are a closed set per format (ADR 0028), such as Truncated, BadSignature, BadBlock, BadHuffmanCode, BadCode, DistanceTooFar, BadChecksum and TooLarge. Each error carries the byte offset at which the spec stops accepting the input, and that offset is proved, as Json.Lex proves its own.

docs.title: 5. The GIF encoder takes indexed input, and quantisation is separate
docs.text: The GIF encoder takes an index raster and a palette, so its round trip is exact. Image.Gif.Quantise maps RGB to a palette, median cut first. It is proved to produce indices below the palette size, and it makes no claim about visual quality.

docs.title: 6. Tests beside the proofs
docs.text:
Proofs cover the Pia code. Three kinds of test cover the claims the proofs do not reach, and would catch a wrong spec:

  • Differential tests. Every file in a corpus decodes to the same output as giflib for GIF, and as zlib for inflate. The corpus holds giflib's test images, zlib's test streams and the streams demo's own output. The tests run on the iMac and in Linux CI.
  • Fuzzing. libFuzzer, through --sanitize=fuzzer once that exists (ADR 0025), checks that the compiled code matches the proved code. It does not check the proofs themselves.
  • Case studies. zlib CVE-2022-37434 and giflib CVE-2016-3977 join docs/cases, written from primary sources. Each shows the unsound decoder failing piac --verify, and the library's version proving.

docs.title: 7. Build order
docs.text:
Each step is one issue and one pull request, prototyped in the REPL first:

  1. Image.Bits and Image.Raster. Any verifier fix that #45 needs is a pull request of its own.
  2. GIF LZW decode against Gif.Spec, then the container decode. After this step, every GIF decodes.
  3. GIF LZW encode and the round-trip theorem, then the container encode, animations included. After this step, the streams demo can write its output as a GIF. Dean's next demo renders terrain evolving under rainfall models as an animated GIF (2026-11-23, ADR 0055), so the encoder writes each frame as the rectangle that changed since the last one, and the round trip is proved over the composited frames that a viewer shows.
  4. Image.Gif.Quantise.
  5. Compress.Huffman, then inflate against Inflate.Spec, then zlib framing.
  6. The case studies.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. Should decoders allocate? I recommend two-step decoding into a caller's buffer (section 4). That way the codecs work before Pia.Mem exists, and they run anywhere Pia.Core runs. The alternative is to take an allocator now, which means waiting for Pia.Mem.
  2. Is colour quantisation (RGB to a 256-colour palette) part of this work? I recommend yes, proved safe but not proved good, because the streams demo renders in RGB. The alternative leaves GIF encoding to callers that already have indexed images.

docs.title: 8. An image theory where the proofs need one
docs.text: Image code proves the same facts over and over: that y * w + x < w * h given x < w and y < h, that a rectangle inside a raster keeps its rows and columns inside it, that an interlaced pass visits each row once, and that compositing a frame writes each pixel of its rectangle. Where lemmas in each module stop being enough, the facts go into a library theory, Image.Theory (ADR 0036), with a model that proves it consistent, so nothing is trusted. Its sorts and spec functions cover rasters, rectangles, pixel indices and row orders, and its axioms carry triggers so they only fire on image goals. The first candidates are the 2D index facts behind #45 and the interlace permutation. The theory is added when a step needs it, not ahead of time, and each axiom names the step that first needed it.

docs.title: Answers (Dean, 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
1. Decoders write into a caller's buffer (section 4): "Yes, that's good design anyway."
  2. Colour quantisation is part of this work (section 5): yes, proved safe.
  3. Dean added that image processing is special enough to warrant a theory of its own if the proofs need one, so section 8 records that.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• GIF and inflate join Json and Utf8 as codecs proved against a written spec. The pattern (a spec module, code proved equal to it, and a round trip where the format is lossless) becomes the house style for formats.
  • PNG and GeoTIFF need only their own containers on top of Compress.Inflate.
  • The streams demo's GIF output no longer needs a C harness.
  • Pixels from these decoders carry proved dimensions and ranges into the code that renders them.
  • The proofs add to build time (ADR 0032). The LZW and inflate decoders go into the proof benchmark corpus when they land.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes CompuServe GIF89a specification the block grammar, the LZW variant, the interlace order and the extensions RFC 1950 and RFC 1951 the zlib and deflate formats, written as Inflate.Spec giflib and zlib the reference decoders for the differential tests Wuffs (Google) memory-safe, bounds-checked GIF and deflate decoders that do not allocate. They show that two-step decoding into a caller's buffer works at production speed. Pia adds functional specs and round trips. EverParse (Project Everest) parsers proved against a format grammar, with the grammar as the specification

docs.title: 55. Sediment transport is integer mass moved downhill in height order, with conservation proved exactly
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0016 makes sediment transport, with a proved conservation law, the second half of the flagship demo. docs/design.md states the law "within the chosen float tolerance", which ties the stage to floats (M11, #12) and to ADR 0038's rounding bounds. Neither is built.

Dean decided (2026-11-23, on the survey of the path to the GPU demo) to build sediment transport now, in fixed point, without waiting for floats.

The delineation in streams.pia.md already gives this stage what it needs: a filled surface fill, a direction down for every cell that points strictly downhill or at itself (an outlet), the slope drop of each route in the 10:7 weights, and the flow accumulation acc.

docs.title: 1. Mass is an integer, so conservation is an equation
docs.text:
Sediment is counted in whole units of mass, u32 per cell, in two buffers: bed, the erodible sediment resting in each cell, and load, the sediment carried in the water leaving it. One more u64 counts out, the mass that has left the map through outlets.

The law is that the total never changes:

sum bed + sum load + out = old (sum bed + sum load + out)

This is exact. There is no tolerance and no rounding term, which is a stronger theorem than the float version in design.md. That version can come back after M11 as a refinement: a float model whose result is within a proved distance of this one.

Because the total is fixed, it also bounds every partial sum. A precondition that the initial total fits in u32 proves that no cell's bed or load and no running sum can overflow, with no saturation.

docs.title: 2. The model: capacity, erosion and deposition per cell
docs.text:
Each cell has a transport capacity, how much the water leaving it can carry. It is a monotone function of the flow and the slope, computed in integers from acc and the route's drop:

capacity c = min cap_max (scale (acc.[c]) (drop c))

scale is chosen to keep the proof linear: shifts and additions, or a widening u64 product whose bound intervals settle without Z3, never a product of two variables inside a quantified goal (#45). The conservation proof does not depend on the formula at all, only on its result being a u32, so the formula can be tuned later without touching the proof.

A cell receives inflow, the loads of the cells that drain into it. Then:

  • if inflow < capacity, the water erodes e = min (capacity - inflow) bed.[c]: the bed loses e and the load is inflow + e.
  • otherwise it deposits d = inflow - capacity: the bed gains d and the load is capacity.

Each branch moves mass between bed and load and creates none, which is the whole of the per-cell proof.

docs.title: 3. Cells are processed from high to low, so one pass is one time step
docs.text:
down points strictly downhill, so ordering the cells by decreasing fill is a topological order of the flow graph: every cell comes after all the cells that drain into it. A step walks the cells in that order and pushes each cell's load into inflow.[down.[c]], or into out at an outlet. Sediment then travels the whole way to the outlet in one step, as water does in the accumulation.

The order is a buffer of cell indices, sorted once per map with Pia.Core.Algo.Sort and passed in with its contract (a permutation of 0..n, decreasing in fill). The same order serves the topological flow accumulation that replaces walk for large maps (item 1 of the survey), so the two share it.

docs.title: 4. The proof is a sum and a point-update lemma
docs.text:
sum is a spec function over a slice, with one lemma proved by induction: writing v at index i changes the sum by v - a.[i]. Every transfer in a step is a pair of such writes, one down and one up by the same amount, so the loop invariant is the conservation equation itself, and each iteration preserves it by two uses of the lemma. Nothing is nonlinear and no quantifier holds a product, which keeps the goals out of #96's slow cases.

The other theorems of the stage:

  • No overflow, from the fixed total (section 1).
  • Every transfer goes downhill or out: mass moves only from a cell to down.[c], which is lower, or to out.
  • Erosion is bounded by the bed: no cell's bed goes below zero, by construction of e.

docs.title: 5. The terrain stays fixed at first
docs.text:
In this first version, fill, down and capacity do not change between steps. Sediment moves over a fixed landscape, which is enough to colour the streams by load, as the demo's render step needs. Letting erosion and deposition change the heights (landscape evolution) means recomputing the fill and the directions every few steps. It is a later step, and the conservation law carries over unchanged, since it does not mention heights.

Dean decided (2026-11-23) that the fixed terrain is for building and proving the transport model only. The goal after it is terrain evolution under rainfall models, rendered as an animated GIF:

  • Rainfall models replace the uniform one unit of water per cell in acc with a rainfall field per time step (uniform, a storm moving across the map, or seasonal), so each step's flow is accumulated rainfall, not area.
  • Evolution: each step's erosion lowers fill and deposition raises it, in integer height units, and the fill and the directions are recomputed every few steps. The conservation law still holds across a recomputation, because it counts mass, not heights.
  • Animated GIF: one frame per few steps, through the proved GIF encoder of ADR 0054 (multiple frames with a delay, and a palette shared across frames so colours stay stable between frames).

docs.title: 6. The GPU form comes later and is proved against this one
docs.text:
Processing cells in height order is sequential. The GPU form (survey, items 3 to 7) is a "pull" step: every cell reads its eight neighbours and adds the loads of those that drain into it. Each cell writes only itself, so the step is race-free. Its conservation proof needs one more lemma, that summing every cell's inflow counts every pushed load once (a reindexing of the sum over down). Moving mass one cell per step, that form needs as many steps as the longest flow path to carry sediment to the outlet. So it is a second implementation proved to conserve the same total, not a replacement for the sequential one.

Dean decided (2026-11-23) the order: sequential first, then concurrent on the CPU, then GPU offload last. The CPU step needs no new lemma: cells in different basins never exchange mass, so each basin (the cells sharing an outlet label from the accumulation) is an independent sequential problem in height order, and basins run in parallel with spread (M12), each owning its disjoint set of cells. The total is the sum of the basins' totals, each conserved. The pull step above is the GPU form, after that.

docs.title: 7. Render
docs.text: render colours stream cells by load, through an integer colour map: a ramp over log2 load from Pia.Core.Bit's count of leading zeros. No exp or log is needed, so Pia.Math is not on this path either.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. sum and the point-update lemma, prototyped in the REPL, then in tests/verify.
  2. The per-cell erode-or-deposit function and its conservation contract.
  3. The height order: a proved sort of cell indices by fill, and the topological accumulation that uses it.
  4. transport, one step over the whole map, with the conservation equation as its postcondition; steps n repeats it.
  5. In docs/streams.pia.md: the new stage, render by load, and the theorems listed under "What is proved".
  6. Rainfall fields in place of uniform water, then heights changed by erosion and deposition, with fill and directions recomputed every few steps.
  7. The animated GIF, once ADR 0054's encoder writes multiple frames.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The flagship demo's conservation law is proved now, exactly, and does not wait for M11.
  • design.md's "within the chosen float tolerance" becomes "exactly, in integer mass units", and the float form becomes a later refinement.
  • The topological order is shared by sediment transport and the scalable accumulation, so building one advances the other.
  • The physics is simplified: one sediment class, fixed terrain, a capacity rule rather than a calibrated erosion law. It is a demonstration of a proved conservation law, not a geomorphology model.

docs.title: Questions for Dean (answered 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
1. ~~Fixed terrain first (section 5)?~~ Answered: fixed for building the model only, then terrain evolution under rainfall models, rendered as an animated GIF.
  2. ~~Sequential first, pull step later?~~ Answered: sequential first, then concurrent on the CPU (basins in parallel), then GPU offload last.

docs.title: 56. Tests are generated by metaprograms from contracts, types and theories; a case the verifier can decide is proved, and only the rest is run
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-23), with his answers to the three questions, recorded at the end.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked (2026-11-23) for a unit testing framework that is "a little more special than the usual": test case generators, written as metaprograms, driven by a theory of what the unit under test should support, with cases derived from the contracts of its interface and from combinatorial generation over the static properties of the modules under test. He asked whether that is feasible with Pia's metaprogramming, and for a sketch.

It is feasible, and most of the parts exist. This ADR says what testing is for in a language whose programs are already proved, where the cases come from, what decides whether a case passed, and the metaprogram builtins that are missing.

docs.title: What testing adds when the code is proved
docs.text:
A proof says the code meets its contracts on every input, assuming everything the proof rests on. Tests are for what the proof rests on, and for what the contracts do not say:

Gap Example What a generated test does Trusted boundaries an extern whose ensures is trusted; an assume in a @trusted file; a theory imported trusting (ADR 0036); a goal accepted with --allow-unproved runs the code across the boundary on generated inputs and checks the trusted facts at run time Foreign code C and C++ called through FFI, and the generated POSIX bindings (ADR 0051) the same, plus differential runs against the C++ it replaces The compiler a wrong lowering in IRGen or codegen, which the proof cannot see (ADR 0023) runs the compiled code on cases whose answers the verifier already knows; under a sanitizer, a report in proved code is a compiler bug (ADR 0025) Behaviour the contract leaves out complexity clauses, which ADR 0040 documents and does not prove; time, memory, throughput benchmarks and scaling runs with budgets A specification that says the wrong thing a contract that is proved but too weak (ensures result <= len xs on a search that always returns 0) examples that pin the intent: an expected output the contract allows but does not imply is reported as "not implied by the contract", which says the contract is too weak Change over time a contract weakened in a refactor, a slower proof, a different result on the other target (ADR 0049) a regression corpus kept with the module, run on both targets Floats tolerances proved against real-valued specifications (ADR 0038), and devices that cannot prove one runs against a reference at higher precision

The standard library already does this by hand. Each module in tests/std has a goal-count test, an _edges.pia file of facts an importer can prove from the interface alone, and a _run.pia program whose exit status is the number of the first wrong answer, with the edge cases of the C++ standard written out (ADR 0040, section 12). ADR 0054 plans differential tests against giflib and zlib and fuzzing for the codecs. All of these are written by hand today, and they are what this ADR generates.

docs.title: What exists
docs.text:
• Metaprograms can read the program. listing () returns every item, and on a function item hypotheses, conclusion and params give its requires, its ensures and its parameter names. children, op and kind walk any syntax, including a parameter's type, and make_call builds calls (docs/meta.md). Tactics (ADR 0036, step 6) are built on exactly this, so contract-driven generation needs no new kind of metaprogram.
  • Expansion runs to a fixed point (ADR 0007), and what a metaprogram produces is type checked and proved like hand-written code. So a generated test is ordinary Pia, and can be read with --dump-expanded.
  • Types carry the static properties. Integers are ranges (int{lo..hi}, u8), arrays have lengths, records have fields, variants and error sets are closed (ADR 0028), and the type-level builtins (type_kind, field_types, element, size_of) read them.
  • Theories say what a unit should support. A let theory declares sorts, operations and axioms, and a model proves the axioms (ADR 0036). Concepts carry laws (ADR 0034). The prelude's machine builds a theory from a table of transitions.
  • Interfaces carry contracts across modules. A .piai holds every exported signature with its contracts (ADR 0039), so a black-box test of a module needs only its interface.
  • The verifier finds counterexamples, and models are tried first for them (verifier.md). A counterexample is a test case.
  • The REPL proves and runs cells (ADR 0031), and a session file replayed through pia repl is already a test. pia mcp exposes the same to agents.

docs.title: 1. Prove what can be proved, and run the rest
docs.text:
A generated case is an input together with an oracle, a fact that must hold of the output. Every case is first offered to the verifier as a goal, with the inputs as constants:

  • Proved. The case holds for the source program. It is reported as proved, and by default not run. It costs one cached query, and it guards against regressions for as long as it stays in the corpus: if a later change makes it fail, the build fails with the counterexample.
  • Not decidable statically. The answer depends on something outside the proof: an extern, a trusted axiom, the compiled code itself, a float on a device, a timing. The case is compiled into the test binary and run.
  • Refuted. The verifier shows the case fails. That is a bug found at compile time, reported like any failed goal, before anything runs.

This is what makes the framework different from QuickCheck or a unit test runner: the generator produces many cases, and most of them never execute, because a fully proved unit decides them all. What is left to run is exactly the part the proof cannot vouch for. Proved cases stay available to test the compiler (Dean, 2026-11-23). --run-proved runs every case anyway, and the compiler's own test suite, the sanitizer jobs and both targets' CI run with it, so the cases generated for the standard library also check IRGen and codegen.

docs.title: 2. Where cases come from
docs.text:
