Each source is a metaprogram in a new prelude module, Pia.Test.Gen, written in Pia. A user can write more, since they are ordinary metaprograms.

Generator Reads Produces edges each parameter's type: a range int{lo..hi} or an integer type, an array's length, a record's fields, a variant's constructors boundary values per parameter: lo, lo + 1, hi - 1, hi, zero where it is in range, and the constants that the requires compare a parameter with, on both sides (from i < len xs, the cases len xs - 1 and len xs) combine the per-parameter domains their product, filtered by the requires; above a budget, a pairwise covering array instead of the full product paths the function's branches and match arms, through the verifier one witness per feasible path: Z3 is asked for a model of the requires together with the path condition. An infeasible path is reported as dead code errors the closed error set of a result t e for each constructor of e, an input that returns it, found by the solver; or a proof that none does, reported as an error constructor that is never produced. The same for each arm of a handle block laws a theory's axioms, or a concept's laws property tests: each axiom instantiated over generated values of its sorts, for a model that is trusted or foreign and so is not proved walks a machine theory, or module state with an invariant (ADR 0006) sequences of operations that cover every transition, and every pair of transitions up to a depth, with the invariant checked after each step against a reference implementation, usually C++ through FFI differential cases: the same inputs to both, outputs compared corpus the module's checked-in case file the regression cases: every counterexample the verifier ever reported for the module, every failing run, and hand-picked examples

edges, combine and corpus read only syntax and types, so they are ordinary expansion-time metaprograms. paths and errors need the solver, so they run in a test stage after verification (section 5).

docs.title: 3. What decides a case
docs.text:
• Postconditions. The ensures of the unit is the default oracle. In a test build, the compiler checks each ensures of a unit under test at run time, together with the ensures of every extern it calls. This is the contracts mode of --sanitize from ADR 0025, restricted to the units a test names. The generator does not have to rewrite contracts into code itself.
  • Laws and axioms, for laws and walks.
  • A reference, for against: equal outputs, or outputs within a stated tolerance for floats (the ~= form of ADR 0038).
  • Round trips, as a law between two functions: decode (encode x) = x.
  • Expectations the author writes, for intent the contract does not state.
  • Budgets, for performance (section 6).

docs.title: 4. The surface
docs.text:
Tests can be written in two places, and both work the same way (Dean, 2026-11-23):

  • In the module, in test mode, as Rust does. A top-level generator call, or a hand-written test, carries @test. It is expanded, proved and compiled only by piac --test (and the REPL's :test), and an ordinary build drops it before expansion, so it adds nothing to the module's interface, its proofs or its object code. It sees the module's private functions.
  • In a separate test module that imports the interface under test, as tests/std/*_edges.pia does, so it sees only what the module exports. This is the black-box form, and the standard library uses it.

Cases are top-level calls of generator metaprograms, with no new keyword. A sketch, in proposed syntax, of a separate test module:

import Pia.Core.Clamp.Clamp as C
import Pia.Test.Gen { cases, edges, paths, errors, laws, against, corpus }

\ Boundary values from the types and the requires, combined, filtered by the
\ precondition, checked against the ensures. Proved cases are reported, not run.
cases C.clamp [edges; paths]

\ For a function returning `result t e`: one case per error constructor.
cases Json.Lex.next [edges; errors]

\ Pia.Algo.sort against libc++'s std::sort, through a generated binding.
cases Algo.sort [edges; against Cpp.std_sort; corpus "tests/std/cases/sort.piac"]

\ A foreign type claims Ord: its laws are tested, since its model is trusted.
laws Ord Posix.timespec

In the module itself, the same call is marked for test mode:

let clamp (v : u8) (lo : u8) (hi : u8) : u8
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
= if v < lo then lo else if v > hi then hi else v

@test cases clamp [edges; paths]

In the REPL, :test C.clamp runs the same generators on a definition in the environment, and pia mcp gives agents the same command. piac --test builds and runs a test file, and a pia_test Bazel rule in tools/piac/pia.bzl does the same in the build.

docs.title: 5. Stages
docs.text:
1. Expansion. Generators that read only syntax and types run with every other metaprogram, and produce the case items.
  2. Verification. Each case is a goal (section 1). The verifier's results decide which cases are compiled.
  3. Witness generation. paths and errors ask Z3 for models. Whether the answers are kept is the user's choice (Dean, 2026-11-23): piac --test --cases=DIR writes them to a case file per module and reads them back on later builds, and without it they are found again on each build. A case file makes a build deterministic, keeps a change of solver from changing the tests silently, and shows in review what was added. This repository checks its case files in, so that what was generated can be inspected and debugged. Either way, what was generated can always be seen: piac --test --dump-cases prints every case with its source (which generator, which parameter's boundary, which path or error constructor) and how it was decided, and :source in the REPL shows a generator call's expansion.
  4. Run. The undecided cases are compiled into one binary per test file, which reports each case. Under --sanitize=address,undefined it doubles as the sanitizer run.

A metaprogram that calls the solver is not total in the sense of ADR 0035: it depends on a solver's answers. So it may not be called from a type, a where predicate, a theory builder or a tactic, only from a test file.

docs.title: 6. Beyond functional cases
docs.text:
• Performance. bench f [sizes 1000; 10000; 100000] within ns 50 per n runs f on generated inputs of each size and checks a budget, and a complexity claim in a doc comment ("at most log2 n + 1 comparisons") is checked by fitting the measured counts. Budgets live in the same baseline file style as the proof benchmark (ADR 0032, tools/bench/baseline.json).
  • Fuzzing. The case file is the seed corpus for libFuzzer once --sanitize=fuzzer exists, and the generators' domains describe the input's structure, so a fuzz harness is generated rather than written.
  • Both targets. The run stage runs on arm64 macOS and x86_64 Linux (ADR 0049), so a case that passes on one and fails on the other shows a target difference the theory did not model.

docs.title: 7. The report
docs.text: The report follows the other reports of the project: wall-clock time for generation, proof and run; for each unit, the number of cases from each generator, and how many were proved, ran and passed, ran and failed, or were skipped by the precondition; the costliest case goals; every trusted fact a run checked; and the error constructors and paths that no input reaches. A failing case is printed as a call with its arguments, which can be pasted into the REPL.

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text:
The generator below was prototyped in pia repl on 2026-11-23 (macOS arm64, a build of main near #321), using only the metaprogram builtins that exist today. It reads clamp's parameters, parameter types, requires and ensures from listing (), forms the product of the boundary values, and generates one function, clamp_cases, that returns 0 when every case passes and otherwise the number of the first case that fails. A case whose requires is false is skipped. The oracle is the ensures, with the call substituted for result.

let clamp (v : u8) (lo : u8) (hi : u8) : u8
  requires lo <= hi
  ensures lo <= result && result <= hi
  ensures (lo <= v && v <= hi) ==> result = v
= if v < lo then lo else if v > hi then hi else v

\ List helpers the interpreter lacks, written with fold. A pair is a function of a bool.
let meta nth (xs : list) (i : int) : syntax =
  (fold (let (acc) (x) =>
          let k = acc true in
          (let (b) => if b then k + 1 else if k = i then x else acc false))
        (let (b) => if b then 0 else fail "nth: index out of range") xs) false
let meta drop1 (xs : list) : list =
  (fold (let (acc) (x) =>
          let seen = acc true in
          let got = acc false in
          (let (b) => if b then true else if seen then concat got [x] else got))
        (let (b) => if b then false else []) xs) false
let meta indices (xs : list) : list = fold (let (a) (x) => concat a [length a]) [] xs
let meta reverse (xs : list) : list = fold (let (a) (x) => concat [x] a) [] xs
let meta product (doms : list) : list =
  let none = [] in
  fold (let (acc) (d) =>
         fold (let (sofar) (tuple) => concat sofar (map (let (x) => concat tuple [x]) d)) [] acc)
       [none] doms

let meta find (n : string) : syntax =
  let it = fold (let (acc) (i) => if kind i = "LetItem" && name i = n then i else acc)
                `( 0 ) (listing ()) in
  if kind it = "LetItem" then it else fail (concat "no item named " n)

\ Substitution of `result`, rebuilding operators as calls of their builtins.
let meta builtin_of (o : string) : string =
  if o = "&&" then "and" else if o = "||" then "or" else if o = "==>" then "implies"
  else if o = "<==>" then "iff" else if o = "=" then "eq" else if o = "<>" then "ne"
  else if o = "<" then "lt" else if o = ">" then "gt" else if o = "<=" then "le"
  else if o = ">=" then "ge" else if o = "+" then "add" else if o = "-" then "sub"
  else if o = "*" then "mul" else if o = "/" then "div" else if o = "%" then "rem"
  else fail (concat "subst_result: no builtin for operator " o)
let meta subst_result (e : syntax) (r : syntax) : syntax =
  if kind e = "Name" && op e = "result" then r
  else if kind e = "Apply" then
    make_call (op e) (map (let (c) => subst_result c r) (drop1 (children e)))
  else if kind e = "Binary" then
    make_call (builtin_of (op e)) (map (let (c) => subst_result c r) (children e))
  else e
let meta conj (xs : list) : syntax = fold (let (a) (h) => `( $a && $h )) `( true ) xs
let meta param_type (p : syntax) : syntax = nth (children (nth (children p) 0)) 1

\ The generator: the contract of `n`, the implementation `impl`, a domain per parameter.
let meta cases_for (n : string) (impl : string) (doms : list) : item =
  let it = find n in
  let ps = params it in
  let tys = map param_type (children (nth (children it) 0)) in
  let idx = indices ps in
  let pre = conj (hypotheses it) in
  let call = make_call impl ps in
  let post = subst_result (conclusion it) call in
  let check = `( if $pre then $post else true ) in
  let one = (let (tuple) =>
    fold (let (body) (i) =>
           let p = nth ps i in
           let t = nth tys i in
           let v = nth tuple i in
           `( let $p : $t = $v in $body ))
         check (reverse idx)) in
  let rows = product doms in
  let fname = concat impl "_cases" in
  let case_name = (let (k) => concat (concat impl "_case_") (k + 1)) in
  let chain = fold (let (rest) (k) =>
                     let cn = case_name k in
                     let num = k + 1 in
                     `( if $cn then $rest else $num ))
                   `( 0 ) (reverse (indices rows)) in
  let run = fold (let (body) (k) =>
                   let cn = case_name k in
                   let c = one (nth rows k) in
                   `( let $cn : bool = $c in $body ))
                 chain (reverse (indices rows)) in
  `( let $fname () : u32 = $run )
let meta cases (n : string) (doms : list) : item = cases_for n n doms

cases "clamp" [[0; 255]; [0; 255]; [0; 255]]

What the REPL reported:

Run Result cases "clamp" over [0; 255] for each parameter (8 cases) clamp_cases : u32 = 0, 24 goals proved (the precondition of clamp at each call in the substituted postcondition); 271 ms in the solver, 10.5 s verifying, 13.4 s for the cell over [0; 1; 255] (27 cases) 0, in about 2 minutes 12 seconds over [0; 1; 254; 255] (64 cases) not finished after 9 minutes, and stopped cases_for "clamp" "clamp_bad", where clamp_bad is if v < lo then lo else v with no ensures clamp_bad_cases : u32 = 5: case 5, v = 255, lo = 0, hi = 0, breaks result <= hi the same run function with ensures result = 0 for clamp, proved (25 goals) from clamp's contract alone; for clamp_bad, refuted at definition, so nothing is committed

The last row is section 1 in miniature: for a proved unit, the generated cases are decided by the verifier and add nothing at run time, and for an unproved one they are refuted before anything runs. The bad implementation had to be a separate function tested against clamp's contract (cases_for spec impl), because a proved unit cannot be given a bug: --allow-unproved accepts an unproved goal, not a refuted one.

docs.title: What is missing
docs.text:
The prototype works, and it shows what a real generator needs that the metaprogram language does not have:

  • More than one item from a metaprogram. A metaprogram returns one item, and a quote cannot splice a variable number of items. So every case went into one function, where one function per case would let the verifier and the report treat each case separately, and in parallel.
  • Speed. 8 cases took 13 seconds, 27 about 2 minutes, and 64 did not finish in 9 minutes. The solver took 271 ms of the 13 seconds: the cost is in the verifier around it, and the REPL appears to verify the environment again on every cell. Generated tests multiply goals, so this is the first thing to fix, and it is a verifier issue more than a testing one.
  • Signature reflection. params gives names only. The prototype reaches each type by position (Params, then Param, then its annotation's second child). Generators need param_types f, return_type f, for a type the bounds of its range (range_of t, giving lo and hi), and the constructors of a variant or an error set (constructors t, with payload types).
  • List operations. The interpreter's lists have map, fold, length and concat. The prototype writes nth, drop1, indices, reverse and product with fold, quadratically. They belong in the interpreter or in a prelude module of list metaprograms. [[]] does not parse, and fold's initial value is evaluated eagerly, so a fail there fires even when it is not needed.
  • Substitution. subst e name value replaces a name in syntax. The prototype substitutes the call for result by walking the syntax, and has to handle two forms of the same operator, because hypotheses returns operators already expanded to calls (le a b) while conclusion joins clauses with an unexpanded &&. Both should return the same form. Substituting the call also calls the function once per result, where a binding would call it once.
  • Contracts as code mean something different. A contract is evaluated over unbounded integers, but a case that copies it into code runs it at the operands' types. ensures result + 1 = d on dec (d : int{-2..2}) : int{-3..1} proves as a contract, and fails as a case (found in step 1, tests/meta/generators.pia): 1 + 1 overflows int{-3..1}. So an oracle copied from a contract must be checked in the contract's own semantics, as a goal over int or by the run-time ensures check below, not as ordinary code. Step 2 writes each case as a lemma, which is a contract and so is read over int.
  • A contract that no result can meet must fail, not pass (Dean, 2026-11-27). The overflow above is in the generator's copy, and the contract is right. The opposite is a wrong contract: ensures result = a + b on plus_c (a : u8) (b : u8) : u8 = extern "plus_c" cannot hold at a = b = 255, since no u8 is 510. Nothing proves an extern, so piac reported nothing for it, and the step 1 generator's cases over it all proved, because each assumed the contract and a contradiction proves anything. Generated tests exist to catch exactly this, so step 2 checks the specification first: for each case, some value of the result type meets the ensures. When none does, the goal fails as a specification failure that names the case and its inputs. The cases are never widened or evaluated so that they pass.
  • Interfaces. listing () lists the current program. A black-box test needs exports I, the items of an imported interface with their contracts, read from the .piai.
  • Solver access, for stage 3: witness f path and reach f constructor, which return a model or none, cached in the case file.
  • A run-time check of an ensures, in codegen, which is the contracts sanitizer of ADR 0025 limited to the units under test. With it, a generator produces inputs only and needs no substitution for the oracle.
  • Seeing what was generated. Every goal of a generated case is located at the generator's call, so a failure cannot name its case, and the REPL has no --dump-expanded. A generated item should carry the location of the case that made it, and :source should show the expansion.
  • Smaller things. A parameterless let f () : u32 is a value, computed when it is defined, so the cases ran at definition (which is useful, but should be a choice). out and row are reserved and cannot name a lambda's parameter, with the unhelpful error "expected a pattern". listing makes a generator impure, so it can never be a tactic or a theory builder, which is consistent with section 5.

docs.title: Implementation steps
docs.text:
Each step is one PR with its tests, and each replaces some hand-written test in tests/std.

  1. What the prototype needed: several items from one metaprogram, list operations, param_types, return_type, range_of, constructors and subst, one form for expanded contracts, and generated items located at their case, in src/meta/Interpreter.cpp, Expand.cpp and a prelude module, with tests in tests/meta. The verifier cost per cell in the REPL is a separate issue, #334. Done, except for locating generated items at their case: several items from one metaprogram (a list), nth, zip, range, reverse, filter, product, param_types, return_type, range_of, constructors, subst, and conclusion joined in the form its clauses are in (meta.md, tests/meta/generators.pia).
  2. Pia.Test.Gen with edges and combine, generating cases whose oracle is written out by subst, and the proved, refuted and run triage of section 1. The first user is one tests/std module whose _run.pia becomes generated. Done in part: lib/Pia/Test/Gen.pia has edges, combine (a pairwise covering array above a budget) and cases, which writes a specification check and an oracle lemma per case, named by @case (see the bullet on specification failures above, meta.md, tests/std/test_gen.pia). Proved and refuted cases are decided by the verifier; an extern's oracle, which only a run decides, waits for step 3, as does generating a tests/std module's _run.pia.
  3. Test mode: @test items dropped from ordinary builds, run-time ensures checks in test builds, piac --test, --run-proved, --dump-cases and the pia_test rule.
  4. Case files (--cases=DIR) and the regression corpus, with every verifier counterexample offered to the corpus.
  5. paths and errors through the solver, cached in the case file.
  6. laws and walks, for concept laws, trusted theories and machines.
  7. against, differential tests against C++ through generated bindings, starting with the tests/std modules that map C++23 components.
  8. :test in the REPL and the MCP server.
  9. bench, then fuzz harnesses once --sanitize=fuzzer exists.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Tests of proved code are cheap: most cases cost a cached query and never run, and the run binary holds only what the proof cannot vouch for.
  • Every trusted fact gets a test without anyone writing one: an extern's contract, a trusted theory's axioms and a foreign type's concept laws are all checked on generated inputs.
  • An error constructor that is never produced, and a path that is never taken, become findings, which a proof alone does not report.
  • The regression corpus grows by itself from counterexamples, and lives next to the module in review.
  • Metaprograms gain a stage that may call the solver. Keeping it to test files, and caching its answers in the case file, keeps ordinary expansion total and builds deterministic.
  • Generated cases can grow combinatorially. combine has a budget and falls back to pairwise coverage, and the report says when it did.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. Surface. Top-level generator calls in a separate test module that imports the interface, or an attribute on the definition itself, which also reaches private functions?
  2. Proved cases. Report a proved case and not run it by default, with --run-proved for CI and sanitizer jobs, or always run every case?
  3. Solver-found cases. Write them to a case file checked in beside the module, or find them again on each build?

docs.title: Answers (Dean, 2026-11-23)
docs.text:
1. "It should be doable in either. I see value in having test cases in the module themselves, like what Rust does, in test mode." Section 4 now has both: @test items in the module, built only in test mode, and separate test modules over the interface.
  2. Yes, proved cases are not run by default, "but they should be available for the compiler testing cases." Section 1: --run-proved is what the compiler's own tests, the sanitizer jobs and CI use.
  3. "That should be up to the user. For us, I think it's worth seeing what it generates so that we can inspect and debug it." Section 5: --cases=DIR is the user's choice, this repository checks its case files in, and --dump-cases always shows what was generated.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• QuickCheck and Hypothesis: property tests with generators and shrinking. Here the properties are the contracts, and most cases are proved rather than run.
  • Pex and IntelliTest, KLEE, and concolic testing generally: inputs found by a solver, one per path. Here the solver is the verifier's own, and it already has the path conditions.
  • Dafny's test generation (dafny generate-tests) and SPARK's combination of proof and test (DO-178C credit for proof): cases from verified specifications, with tests kept for what is not proved.
  • Category partition and pairwise covering arrays (Ostrand and Balcer; NIST ACTS): boundary values and combinations from the input domains.
  • Csmith and translation validation: differential testing of a compiler against a reference.

docs.title: 57. Pia.Sys.Posix is one generated module per target behind one hand-written interface, and the generator joins the contract overlay
Context
docs.text:
ADR 0051, section 6, generates Pia's POSIX declarations from each target's headers and puts the contracts in a hand-written overlay. A posix metaprogram was to join each overlay row with its generated signature. Steps 1 and 2 are built:

  • @variadic(n) foreign calls (PR #308);
  • tools/bindings/gen.py, which writes lib/Pia/Sys/Gen/<target>.pia, and a CI job that regenerates it on each platform (PR #322).

The generated files are per target, and every item in them is @target(m). Building step 3 shows three gaps in the plan:

  • A metaprogram cannot do the join. listing () sees only the items of the module it runs in (meta.md), and a module is one file (ADR 0039, section 1). An overlay that is shared between targets cannot sit in the same file as two per-target generated files.
  • Target-generic code cannot call @target items. Only @target code of the same model can call them, or the then branch of an if Target.is m (ADR 0049). Pia.Sys.Fs and Pia.Io are written once for both targets. Wrapping every call in a per-target dispatch would double the library.
  • Constants would leak into proofs. ADR 0049 says that OS constants come from the target's model, so a target-generic proof sees only what holds on every target. A literal let o_creat : i32 = 64 in scope would let a proof rely on Linux's value.

docs.title: 1. One module, one interface, one file per target
docs.text:
Each target's generated file is the module Pia.Sys.Posix for that target. The build picks the file by target, as select already picks per-target flags (tools/piac/targets.bzl). The module meets one interface, Posix, which is written by hand in lib/Pia/Sys/Posix.pia:

interface Posix = sig
  (** read(2): reads at most n bytes, and writes no more than it returns. *)
  let read : (fd : i32) -> (buf : out mutable [u8]) -> (n : usize) -> isize
    requires n <= len buf
    ensures result >= -1 && result <= n
  let o_creat : i32
  let eagain : i32
end
  • The interface is the overlay. Each let in it is one row of the overlay. A row holds the Pia modifiers of each parameter, the contract with its manual page, and any @blocking or variadic condition. Importers see only the interface, as for any module (ADR 0039).
  • Constants are opaque. let o_creat : i32 in the interface has no value, so importers' proofs cannot depend on 64 or 512. Inside the module the value is known, and codegen links the constant per target. This is ADR 0049's rule (constants come from the target's model), reached through the module system instead of a new theory.
  • Target-only names are @target rows. Examples are epoll_wait, eventfd, kevent and so_nosigpipe. Per ADR 0049, section 3, they appear only in their own target's interface. Pia.Io's io_uring and kqueue models reach them from @target code, which ADR 0050 already plans.

docs.title: 2. The generator joins the overlay, and fails on any mismatch
docs.text:
tools/bindings/gen.py reads lib/Pia/Sys/Posix.pia together with the headers. For every row of the interface, it writes the contracted declaration into the generated module:

let read (fd : i32) (buf : out mutable [u8]) (n : usize) : isize
  requires n <= len buf
  ensures result >= -1 && result <= n
= extern "read"

It fails if any row does not fit the header:

  • the row names a symbol or constant the target's header lacks;
  • a parameter's Pia type is not the C type's width and signedness;
  • a parameter marked mutable or out is a const pointer in C;
  • the row is not variadic where C's function is, or the other way around.

Each of these is something a metaprogram could not see, because it knows only Pia types. The join runs when the file is generated, and the drift check runs it again on each platform in CI. So a header change that breaks a row is a red build on that platform. piac also proves that the module meets Posix, since the module and its interface are compiled as any other (ADR 0039, section 4).

docs.title: 3. Symbols without a row stay out of the interface
docs.text: The generated module still declares every symbol listed in posix.toml, without a contract, so the generator can check it. A symbol with no row in the interface is private to the module. So unsafe calls to uncontracted POSIX functions are not possible outside Pia.Sys.Posix. To use a symbol, give it a row. This is stricter than ADR 0051, which allowed unsafe calls to any generated declaration, and it keeps the trusted surface to the rows that have been read against a manual page.

docs.title: 4. The posix metaprogram is not built
docs.text: The join is done by the generator, so the metaprogram planned in ADR 0051, section 6, is dropped. bit_family and other stamping metaprograms are unaffected.

docs.title: 5. Amendment (2026-11-24): errno through @deref
docs.text:
Pia.Sys.Fs decodes errno into its error variants (ADR 0023). glibc reaches the thread's errno through int *__errno_location(void), and Darwin through int *__error(void). Pia has no foreign pointers, so neither can be declared yet.

A foreign declaration marked @deref names a C function that returns a pointer to a value of its Pia result type. The call reads that value, and the pointer never reaches Pia:

let errno () : i32 @deref
  ensures true
= extern "__errno_location"
  • The row. The interface gains let errno : i32 @deref with ensures true, because errno can hold any value. The rule that errno is meaningful only after a call that returned -1 belongs to Pia.Sys.Fs, which reads it only then.
  • The symbol is per target. posix.toml gains [<target>.aliases] tables: errno = "__errno_location" on Linux and errno = "__error" on macOS. The generator writes @deref on the row's extern. It fails unless the C function takes no parameters and returns a pointer to an integer of the row's width and signedness.
  • Codegen. The C function is declared as returning ptr, and the call is followed by a load of the result type. A @deref function returns an integer for now, like any foreign function.
  • Trust. @deref trusts that the pointer is valid and aligned when the call returns. That is what both manual pages promise. The trust report lists it with the row.

docs.title: Implementation steps
docs.text:
1. lib/Pia/Sys/Posix.pia with the Posix interface, first for the rows Pia.Sys.Fs needs (open, close, read, write, pread, pwrite, lseek, fsync, fstat, unlink, the O_ and SEEK_ constants and the errno values).
  2. gen.py reads the interface, checks each row against the header, and writes module Pia.Sys.Posix : Posix with the contracted declarations. Its @target attributes go, since the build picks the file.
  3. A pia_library per target, selected by platform, and a test that each file meets the interface on its own target (tests/std).
  4. @deref and the errno row (section 5).
  5. Then Pia.Sys.Fs (#57) on top, written once for both targets.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pia.Sys.Fs, Pia.Io and the rest of the library are target-generic, and call Posix.read without dispatch.
  • Proofs above Pia.Sys.Posix cannot depend on a platform's constant values, which ADR 0049 requires.
  • The trusted surface is the interface file, one row per symbol, each citing its manual page. The trust report lists the rows.
  • The header checks are done in Python, at generation, rather than in a metaprogram. They are stronger, since they see C's const and its exact types, but they run only when the file is regenerated, which CI does on every pull request.

docs.title: Dean's answer
docs.text: 1. Where should the overlay be joined? In the generator (2026-11-24), as section 2 says.

docs.title: 58. Spec buffers: spec-only arrays that code writes, contracts read and codegen erases
Context
docs.text:
ADR 0054 promises that the GIF and inflate decoders match a written specification over the whole stream, and that GIF round-trips exactly. Step 2a proved the GIF LZW decoder (#338) total and safe. It also proved that each code writes exactly its dictionary entry's string. It could not state the whole-stream claim: that the output equals what a reference LZW reading of the stream gives (#339). That claim needs the reference's state as a value, and its state evolves code by code. The dictionary after each code, and the sequence of indices so far, are both arrays.

What exists today:

  • Spec-only scalars. int, real and the sorts of library theories can be held in spec-only parameters, locals and fields, and code can update them (t.heap <- Alloc.take t.heap b, ADR 0041).
  • Spec-only fields of buffer elements. These come from ADR 0048 and tests/verify/spec_buffers.pia. A buffer of { slot : [u16]; state : int } keeps state as a buffer of its own, which the verifier sees and codegen erases.
  • What is missing. A buffer whose elements are wholly spec-only, such as [int], is an error, because its length is in code (verifier.md, "Spec-only int and real"). There is no spec-only array whose length is spec-only too. Spec functions cannot return arrays.

The same gap will block three later proofs: the GIF encoder's round trip (ADR 0054 step 3), inflate's conformance against Inflate.Spec (step 5), where the sliding window and dynamic Huffman tables evolve over the stream, and any proof that relates a streaming algorithm to its batch specification.

docs.title: 1. spec marks a spec-only local, parameter or field of any type, buffers included
docs.text:
let decode (s : [u8]) (dst : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) : result usize lzw_error
  ensures (match result with
           | Ok n -> forall (i in 0 .. n). dst.[i] = ref_out.[i]
           | Err _ -> true)
= let spec ref_out : mutable [u8; 65536] = zeros in
  let spec ref_dict : mutable [u16; 4096] = zeros in
  ...
  • A spec binding is spec-only, whatever its type. That covers fixed arrays ([t; n]), whose length is a constant, and record fields marked spec.
  • Code may write a spec binding: ref_out.[o] <- b and ref_dict.[k] <- p. Contracts, loop invariants, asserts and lemma calls may read it.
  • Nothing that code computes may read a spec binding. Sema checks this by the same rule as spec-only int: a spec value can flow only into spec places and into contracts.
  • Codegen erases every spec binding and every write to one, as it already erases spec-only state.
  • A spec parameter lets a caller and a callee share spec state across a call. A spec result is out of scope for now.

docs.title: 2. The whole-stream specs are reference implementations kept in spec state
docs.text:
A whole-stream spec is the reference algorithm, written plainly and run in spec state beside the fast decoder. The theorem is that the two agree at every step. For LZW, the reference keeps its dictionary as explicit strings, in spec buffers of offsets and lengths, and its output as a spec buffer. The decoder's loop invariant says its tables expand to the same strings, and that its output so far equals the reference's.

For the round trip, the encoder keeps the input indices as spec state. The decoder's theorem, applied to the encoder's output, gives the round trip as forall i. out.[i] = in.[i].

docs.title: 3. Encoding
docs.text: A spec buffer is an SMT array, exactly like a real buffer, with no codegen. Writes and reads use the verifier's existing array encoding, so this is mostly a front-end change: the keyword, the flow check and erasure. Spec writes do not count as effects for purity or concurrency: a spec buffer is per-thread spec state.

docs.title: 4. Build order
docs.text:
1. spec on locals of fixed-array type, with the flow check, erasure and tests in tests/verify/spec_locals.pia.
  2. Spec parameters.
  3. Spec record fields. This generalises ADR 0048's spec-only fields.
  4. Use it in Gif.Lzw for the whole-stream spec, then in the GIF round trip.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-24)
docs.text:
1. Keyword: spec. "I don't like the ghost spelling. Let's use spec instead to be consistent." spec already marks spec functions, so this adds no keyword: let spec ref_out : mutable [u8; 65536] = zeros. A spec binding is spec-only whatever its type.
  2. Fixed-size first. Dean did not answer this one separately, so the proposed default stands until he says otherwise. spec buffers start as fixed arrays [t; n], which cover LZW (4096 entries, bounded output) and inflate's 32 KiB window. Unbounded spec sequences need a seq sort and can come later as a library theory over Z3 sequences.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• ADR 0054's conformance and round-trip claims become provable, not only tested.
  • One more spec-only form joins int, real and theory sorts. The rule stays one rule: spec-only values flow only into spec-only places.
  • Spec state adds solver terms. A large spec buffer adds quantified invariants, so the proof-cost benchmark watches the codec modules that use it.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes Dafny ghost var, Why3 ghost, SPARK Ghost aspect spec-only state that code updates and the compiler erases VeriFast and Viper ghost fields spec state attached to data structures Senjak and Hofmann, "An implementation of Deflate in Coq" (2016) a verified streaming codec whose specification is a relation over the whole stream

docs.title: 59. Digits group with ' or _; min t and max t are an integer type's bounds, folded to literals
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-23

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-23). Dean asked for both parts, chose the spelling min u8 / max u8, and asked that the bounds follow the target.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean noticed (2026-11-23) bare bound constants across the library: 4294967295, 9223372036854775808, 65535. They are hard to read and easy to get wrong by one digit, and nothing ties 65535 to u16. lib/Pia/Core/Int.pia alone spells out every bound of u16 to u64 and i16 to i64, several times each, in its saturating contracts. He asked for two things:

  1. digit separators in number literals, such as 100,000 or 100'000;
  2. named constants for type bounds, so that code stops using bare numbers. He prefers them as functions of the type, min u8 = 0, rather than a table of names, and wants them to follow the target.

Two facts constrain the design. Pia has no shadowing at all (ADR 0022), and min and max are already taken: Pia.Core.Order exports min a b and max a b at every width, and Pia.Core.Charconv has a local called max. And a let constant is an unknown value inside a contract (the pia-language skill's pitfalls), so let u16_max : u32 = 65535 would not help the very contracts that need it most.

docs.title: 1. Digits group with ' or _
docs.text:
100'000, 0xFFFF'FFFF, 0b1010'0101, 4'294'967'295u64 and 1'000.25 are literals. A ' must sit between two digits of the literal's base, as in C++14, so 100' and 1'_0 are errors. _, which the lexer already accepted, keeps its looser rule, so no code changes. Separators mean nothing to the value: every reader of a literal's text (Sema, IRGen, the metaprogram interpreter, the lints) skips both, through one helper, syntax::isDigitSeparator.

, cannot group digits. It separates tuple elements and arguments, so f (1,000) would be ambiguous. Dean typed a typographic ’ (U+2019), which a phone substitutes for '; Pia's source is ASCII outside strings and comments, so only ' is accepted.

' was free after a digit: inside a name it is a prime (x'), and a name never starts with a digit.

docs.title: 2. min t and max t
docs.text:
min t and max t are the least and greatest values of the integer type t: min u8 = 0, max u16 = 65535, min i64 = -9223372036854775808, max byte for let byte = u8, and the bounds of a range type named by a let.

  • They overload min and max by argument. A call of min or max with one argument that names an integer type is a bound. Every other call, such as Order.max a b, resolves as before. Neither name is reserved, so Pia.Core.Order keeps its functions and Charconv's local max stays; where a local max is in scope, max u8 is that local applied to u8, which is an error, as shadowing would have been.
  • They fold to literals. IRGen replaces max u16 with the literal 65535 before overload resolution, so it takes its context's type like any literal, and works in contracts, where a let constant would be unknown. ensures a * b > max u16 ==> result = max u16 reads as the number did and proves the same way, with no cost.
  • They follow the target. Each bound comes from the type as Sema resolves it, so max usize and min isize are the bounds of the target's usize (ADR 0049). Both of Pia's models have 64-bit pointers today, and piac refuses a model with other pointers until usize follows the model's ptr_bits; when it does, max usize follows with it, and code that wrote max usize instead of 18446744073709551615 is already right.
  • Metaprograms. Dean's min u8 = 0 is the reading of a type-level function. In ordinary code the fold is done by IRGen, since an ordinary expression has no metaprogram calls. Inside a metaprogram, range_of t (ADR 0056) already gives [lo; hi].

Not yet: max t for a generic body's type parameter t. A generic body is checked once, against a stand-in type (ADR 0043), whose bounds are not known. This is the numeric_limits gap that Pia.Core.Int documents. It needs a concept that promises bounds, and is left for a later ADR.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Named constants in a module, Limits.u32_max: a name per type and bound, and a let constant is unknown in contracts unless it becomes a spec function. Rejected.
  • Members of the type, u32.max: reads well, but . after a type name is new syntax, and types as values have no fields today.
  • Other names, lowest/highest or min_of/max_of: no overloading, but Dean chose min/max.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The library's bare bounds become min t and max t, starting with Pia.Core.Int, Order, Bit and Image.
  • docs/grammar.md documents the separators, docs/irgen.md the bounds, and the pia-language skill both. The VS Code grammar and the reference lexer in grammar/pia_lexer.py accept '.
  • Tests: tests/grammar (valid and invalid separators, shared by both lexers), tests/verify/digit_separators.pia and tests/verify/type_bounds.pia.

docs.title: 60. spread v0: iterations own the cells they write, proved one iteration at a time; MLIR's async runtime runs them
Context
docs.text:
M12 (#13) starts with spread, the parallel loop of ADR 0014. Today spread parses, and the pia_par dialect has a spread op over a tiled grid, but IRGen rejects it, there is no runtime, and nothing proves that its iterations do not race. The first program that needs it is sediment transport over basins (ADR 0055, section 6): cells in different basins never exchange mass, so each basin can run its steps on its own core.

docs/concurrency.md says how races are ruled out in general: every pair of possibly concurrent accesses is justified by ownership, shared reading, proved disjointness, a lock, atomicity or ordering, and disjointness goes to FPL (ADR 0020) for affine indices and to Z3 otherwise. Two things are left open for a first version:

  1. How disjointness is proved when the indices are not affine. A basin's cells are not a tile or a range: they are the cells c with owner.[c] = b, for an owner array computed at run time. FPL cannot express that, and FPL is not built yet. Asking Z3 whether two iterations i <> j can write the same cell means encoding the body twice, with everything it computes, which the verifier does not do and which would be slow.
  2. What runs the iterations. ADR 0027 puts the scheduler in Pia (Pia.Task, work-stealing over Pia.Sys.Thread), and spread moves onto it in step 4 of the plan. None of that exists yet, and #13 asks for a C++ runtime on CPU threads in the meantime.

docs.title: 1. An iteration owns the cells it writes
docs.text:
Each buffer that a spread body writes has an ownership predicate that says which of its cells iteration i owns. A body may write a cell, and may read a cell of a buffer it writes, only if it owns that cell. Buffers that no iteration writes may be read anywhere (shared reading).

  • By default, iteration i owns cell i. spread i in 0 .. len out do out.[i] <- f xs.[i] done needs nothing more. This is the identity owner, and covers the maps and stencils that write their own cell.
  • @owns(buf, owner) on the spread names an owner array: iteration b owns buf.[c] exactly when owner.[c] = b. The owner array must be read-only in the loop. Sediment over basins is spread b in 0 .. nb @owns(bed, label) @owns(load, label) ... do, with label the basin of every cell.

Each access becomes one goal about one iteration: e = i for a write buf.[e] under the identity owner, owner.[e] = i under an owner array. These are ordinary goals of the body, proved like an index bound, with the loop variable an arbitrary value in the range. They imply that no two iterations touch the same cell, because an owner array is a function: if iterations i and j both owned cell e, then owner.[e] = i and owner.[e] = j, so i = j. No goal compares two iterations, and the body is encoded once. When FPL lands, an affine index that is not the identity (out.[2*i], a tile) is proved disjoint there instead, and this rule stays for data-dependent owners.

The predicate is a property of the loop, so the race check is local and its cost is linear in the number of accesses. It also tells the reader of the code who writes what.

Other rules of the first version, all checked by the type checker:

  • The body may not assign a variable declared outside it. A reduction is all_reduce or an atomic, later.
  • A buffer the body writes may only be written by buf.[e] <- v in the body itself. Passing it to a call is an error until calls have footprints (modifies contracts), except as a view buf.[a .. b] whose every cell the iteration owns, which is one goal per call: forall (c in a .. b). owner.[c] = i.
  • What is known after the loop is what a spread's ensures p says, proved for an arbitrary iteration at the end of its body, and assumed as forall (i in lo .. hi). p after the loop. p may read a written buffer only at cells the iteration owns, which is one goal per read, as in the body, so another iteration cannot invalidate it.

docs.title: 2. The runtime is MLIR's async runtime, as a trusted v0
docs.text:
IRGen lowers spread i in lo .. hi to scf.parallel, and codegen runs MLIR's async-parallel-for, which outlines the body, splits the range into blocks and runs them on the MLIR async runtime (mlirAsyncRuntime*, over LLVM's thread pool, one thread per core), with a join at the end of the loop. The runtime is a static C++ library from the LLVM tree we already build, linked into programs that use spread. It is listed in the trust report, as the pthreads wrappers of ADR 0027 will be.

This is temporary in the way ADR 0027 already plans: when Pia.Task exists, spread lowers to it instead, and the trust item goes. The language-level rule of section 1 does not change.

docs.title: 3. Spec functions say what they read (amendment, 2026-11-24)
docs.text:
A spread's ensures is proved after every cell that another iteration owns has been given an unknown value (section 1). A sum over the cells an iteration owns, which is what a conservation law per basin needs, is a spec function, and the solver cannot see that its value is unchanged when only cells it does not read changed: that is an induction. So such an ensures could not be proved.

A spec function over a buffer may say which cells it reads:

let spec rsum (xs : [u32]) (lo : usize) (hi : usize) : u64
  requires lo <= hi && hi <= len xs
  reads xs.[lo .. hi]
  decreases hi - lo
= if lo = hi then 0 else rsum xs lo (hi - 1) + xs.[hi - 1]
  • The footprint is reads xs.[a .. b], a range of a buffer parameter, or reads xs where p, the cells c of xs with p (for example owner.[c] = b). A spec function with no reads reads all of every buffer it takes, as today.
  • The frame lemma is a goal. piac proves, once, for the spec function: for two arrays that agree on the footprint, it gives the same result. It is proved by induction on the function's own decreases, with the function unfolded once on each side, so it needs no lemma from the user; if it fails, the reads clause is wrong and the error says so.
  • The verifier uses the frame. Wherever a buffer's contents change, by a write, a call, a loop or a spread's forgetting of other iterations' cells, a call of a framed spec function on the new contents equals the same call on the old contents when every changed cell is outside its footprint. The verifier states this as a fact for the calls it meets, the way it unfolds a spec function's definition once, so a goal never needs a frame lemma by hand.

With frames, a basin's conservation law rsum bed lo hi + rsum load lo hi + ... = old (...), over the range of the basin's cells in a basin-major layout, is stable under the other basins' writes, and a spread over basins proves it per basin. The sum over all basins is then a telescoping lemma over the ranges.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Two iterations encoded at once, asking Z3 for i <> j writing the same cell: general, but it encodes the body twice, with every value it computes, and a model mixes two iterations' states. Rejected for v0; FPL takes the affine cases, and owner arrays take the rest.
  • A runtime of our own over pthreads: about 150 lines of C, a fixed pool and a chunked range, but codegen would have to outline the body and pack its captures itself, which async-parallel-for already does and tests.
  • OpenMP (scf-to-openmp): needs libomp, which macOS does not ship.
  • Grand Central Dispatch (dispatch_apply): simple on macOS, but not on the Linux targets Pia also builds for.
  • Writing Pia.Task first: the right end state (ADR 0027), but it needs coroutines, scope and spawn, which are several steps away. Sediment over basins should not wait for them.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• spread over an index range compiles and runs on all cores in the first version, and its race freedom is proved, with a goal per access that names the cell and the iteration in its counterexample.
  • Sediment transport can run basin by basin in parallel, with the basin labels of drainage as the owner array.
  • Programs that use spread link the MLIR async runtime and say so in their trust report, until Pia.Task replaces it.
  • Calls that write a shared buffer wait for footprints. spread over tiles (the pia_par grid op) and the collectives are still to come.
  • With reads frames (section 3), a spec function's value is known to survive writes outside what it reads. This helps sequential code too: the frame lemmas written by hand today, such as the sediment sum's frame, become facts the verifier states itself.

docs.title: Questions for Dean
docs.text:
1. The ownership rule (section 1): one predicate per written buffer, the identity by default and @owns(buf, owner) for an owner array. Is @owns the spelling you want, or would you rather write it in the header, as in spread b in 0 .. nb owning label do? Answered 2026-11-27 by Dean: @owns(buf, owner).
  2. ~~The runtime (section 2): MLIR's async runtime as a trusted v0, replaced by Pia.Task later, or a small pthreads runtime of our own now?~~ Answered 2026-11-24: MLIR's async runtime, trusted.
  3. ~~Frames (section 3): reads clauses on spec functions, with a generated frame lemma, or (the weaker choice) per-iteration totals computed at run time, so that the global conservation law becomes a run-time check rather than a proof?~~ Answered 2026-11-24: reads frames on spec functions.

docs.title: 61. Lean proves the facts Z3 cannot: lemmas and theory models are proved in Lean against statements piac generates, recorded in certificates by statement hash, and checked outside the edit loop; cost bounds are proved by Z3, and their asymptotics in Lean
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, with Dean's answers below; the Z3 half of cost proofs moved to ADR 0062, which goes first)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked whether Lean could take part in the proof pipeline, for claims such as complexity bounds and general theorems that Z3 handles poorly.

Pia proves code with intervals and Z3 (ADR 0011). Z3 is a decision procedure with quantifier heuristics. It is very good at the goals code raises: bounds, overflow, frames, loop invariants, the instances of a theory's axioms. It is poor at three kinds of claim, and Pia already meets all three:

  1. Induction beyond one step. Z3 does no induction. Pia's answer is a recursive lemma with decreases, one step per unfolding (verifier.md). That works for a sum or a count. It does not work for a proof that needs a strengthened induction hypothesis, a lemma about a closed form, or several nested inductions, such as the suffix reversal of next_permutation, which costs 482M on one invariant and is parked (cpp-std.md).
  2. Mathematics. Real analysis, linear algebra and asymptotics are outside what Z3 decides. ADR 0036 names the spectral norm bound as its example of a fact that is true but has to be trusted, because Z3 will not prove it over a faithful model of matrices. ADR 0038 needs rounding-error bounds and, later, Taylor remainders. Today each such fact becomes a trusted axiom.
  3. Complexity. Pia has no cost proofs. ADR 0040 documents C++'s complexity clauses and does not prove them, and ADR 0056 checks them by fitting benchmarks. "At most log2 n + 1 comparisons" is a claim about every n, and O(n log n) is a limit statement, which no SMT solver handles.

Lean 4 with Mathlib handles all three. It has induction of every kind, a large library of analysis, algebra and asymptotics (Asymptotics.IsBigO, and a formalised Akra–Bazzi theorem in Mathlib.Computability.AkraBazzi), and a small kernel that checks every proof. It is also slow to set up (a toolchain and gigabytes of Mathlib), and its proofs are written by people or agents, not found automatically. So the question is where it fits without making the edit loop slower, without widening the trusted base silently, and without a second semantics of Pia to keep in step.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: System What it does What Pia takes Lean-SMT (Mohamed, Mascarenhas, Barbosa, Tinelli et al., 2025) An smt tactic: Lean goal to SMT-LIB, cvc5 solves it, and cvc5's proof is rebuilt in Lean and checked by the kernel. About 200 of cvc5's proof rules are reconstructed. The mapping from SMT-LIB sorts to Lean types (bit-vectors to BitVec n, Int to ℤ, Real to ℝ, uninterpreted functions to variables) is worked out and tested. It is the same mapping, run in the other direction, that piac needs. Lean-auto (Qian et al.) Translates Lean goals into first-order logic for SMT solvers and ATPs, and calls them as hammers. Agents writing Lean proofs of Pia's statements can use it, and Lean-SMT, as automation, so most easy goals need no hand proof. Loom and Velvet (Verse lab, 2025–26) A Dafny-style verifier embedded in Lean: VCs go to grind, then to an SMT solver through Lean-auto, and the rest are proved by hand in Lean. The same split between automatic and interactive proof, but inside Lean. Pia keeps Z3 as the main prover and uses Lean only where Z3 fails, so its edit loop does not depend on Lean. Aeneas (Ho, Protzenko) Translates safe Rust into pure Lean functions, using the borrow checker to make the translation functional, and proofs of the code are in Lean. A warning about scope. Translating code means a second semantics of the language, which must agree with codegen. Pia translates only spec-level statements, which already have a pure, total meaning. Dafny, F*, Why3 Automatic provers with escape hatches: Why3 sends a goal to Coq or Isabelle when SMT fails, and the goal is printed in the target's logic. Why3's model, with one change. Why3 exports raw goals, which change on every edit. Pia exports lemmas, whose statements are stable. Isabelle's Sledgehammer ATPs and SMT find proofs, and Isabelle reconstructs them. The reverse direction (SMT inside the proof assistant). Pia does not need it to use Lean, but it is the route to re-checkable certificates (below). CompCert, CakeML The compiler itself is proved in a proof assistant. Out of scope. Pia's compiler and VC generator stay trusted, as they are today, and nothing here changes that. RAML (Hoffmann), time credits (Charguéraud and Pottier), Liquid Haskell's resource analysis (Handley, Vazou, Hutton), calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin, Harper) Cost as a resource in the logic: a counter or credits consumed by each step, bounded in the specification. RAML infers polynomial bounds by linear programming. Cost as a ghost counter in contracts, proved by Z3 like any other contract. The asymptotic claims about the bound are proved in Lean.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Lean is a second prover for facts at the level of specifications: lemmas, models of theories, and closed forms and asymptotics of cost bounds. It never sees code, and it never runs while a program is verified. Four parts.

docs.title: 1. A lemma can be proved in Lean
docs.text:
A lemma (or a theory's lemma) can name a Lean theorem instead of a body:

let lemma reverse_suffix (xs : [u8]) (k : usize) : unit
  requires k < len xs && descending xs (k + 1) (len xs)
  ensures ascending (reversed xs (k + 1) (len xs)) 0 (len xs - k - 1)
= by lean Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation.reverse_suffix

piac --emit-lean M writes one Lean file per module, M/Statements.lean, with every spec function the lemmas mention, translated to Lean definitions, and every by lean lemma's statement as a def ... : Prop. The author, or an agent, writes the proof in a separate file:

import Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation.Statements

theorem Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation.reverse_suffix :
    Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation.Statements.reverse_suffix := by
  intro xs k hk hdesc
  ...

Lean checks that the theorem's type is the generated statement, so the author cannot prove a different statement by mistake. In Pia the lemma is then an ordinary lemma: its callers prove its precondition and assume its postcondition, and Z3 never sees its proof.

Lemmas, not raw goals, are the unit, because their statements are stable. A goal's SMT query changes with every edit to the function around it, with slicing and with the relevance closure, so a Lean proof of a raw query would go stale on every edit. A lemma's statement changes only when its author changes it. For exploration, piac --emit-lean --goal file.pia:line still prints one failed goal as a Lean statement, with its hypotheses, to help an author decide what lemma to write.

The translation. Only spec-level terms are translated, and they are already pure and total. Each construct maps to Lean as its SMT encoding does (verifier.md), so the Lean statement means what Z3 would have been asked:

Pia Lean bool Prop in statements, Bool in values int, real ℤ, ℝ (Mathlib) u8 ... u64, usize, i8 ... i64 BitVec n, with Pia's operations, which are guarded against overflow where Pia's are slices [t] and spec buffers a length and a function from indices, the SMT array encoding records, sums, let rec sums structure, inductive spec functions with decreases m Lean definitions with termination_by m and the same measure a theory's sorts and abstract functions fields of a Lean structure, with the axioms as fields too (below)

The places where the two logics differ are where translation bugs hide, so each is a rule with a test. SMT's x / 0 is an unspecified value and Lean's is 0, so division and mod are translated as guarded uninterpreted functions unless a nonzero divisor is in scope. Pia's partial spec functions (with requires) become Lean functions with the precondition as an argument. Every translated construct has a round-trip test: a lemma proved in Pia by Z3 is emitted, proved in Lean by decide, omega or grind, and a lemma that is false in Pia must be unprovable in Lean (its negation is proved).

docs.title: 2. A theory can be modelled in Lean
docs.text:
An ADR 0036 theory is either modelled (consistent, proved by a model in Pia) or trusted. A model in Lean is a third way to give one:

-- Generated from `let theory Lip = sig ... end`
structure Pia.Nn.Lip (layer : Type) where
  in_w : layer → ℕ
  lip : layer → ℝ
  seq : layer → layer → layer
  ...
  lip_nonneg : ∀ f, 0 ≤ lip f
  seq_lip : ∀ f g, out_w f = in_w g → lip (seq f g) ≤ lip f * lip g
  ...

-- Written by the library: the true Lipschitz constant of linear maps
noncomputable def Pia.Nn.Spectral.model : Pia.Nn.Lip LinearLayer := { ... }

let model spectral : Lip = by lean Pia.Nn.Spectral.model names it. The model proves the theory consistent, as a Pia model does, so the theory is modelled, not trusted, and importers do not write trusting. A Lean model can do what a Pia model cannot: it can give the functions their real meaning (the operator norm of a matrix over ℝ, not a summary record), so the theory's axioms are true of what the names say, not only consistent. That turns ADR 0036's example trusted axiom, "the spectral norm is at most the Frobenius norm", into a proved fact.

A theory lemma proved in Lean is proved from the structure's axiom fields only, for every instance, so it holds in every model and does not depend on which model the importer found.

docs.title: 3. Cost bounds are proved by Z3; their closed forms and asymptotics in Lean
docs.text:
Most complexity clauses are exact bounds, not asymptotics, and Z3 can prove exact bounds if cost is part of the contract. So cost comes in two layers.

Cost in contracts, proved by Z3. A function bounds what it spends on a named counter with a costs c <= e clause, proved by Z3 like any other contract, with the spec-only value spent c bounded by loop invariants. That design is its own decision, ADR 0062, and it needs no Lean. This section is only about what Lean adds to it.

Closed forms and asymptotics in Lean. Some bounds are recurrences: a divide-and-conquer function's costs is a recursive spec function t n = 2 * t (n / 2) + n, which Z3 can check step by step but cannot solve. Two kinds of lemma about such a t are proved in Lean by part 1 of this ADR:

  • a closed form, t n <= 2 * n * log2 n + n, which callers then use in their own cost clauses, so Z3 never sees the recurrence;
  • an asymptotic claim, written with the spec-only form t in O(fun n => n * log2 n), translated to Mathlib's IsBigO atTop. Mathlib's Akra–Bazzi theorem covers most divide-and-conquer recurrences. An asymptotic claim is documentation that is proved: no Pia goal can use it, since contracts are about concrete runs, but the interface publishes it, and the C++ library's complexity clauses become proved facts instead of comments.

Amortised bounds (a vec push, union–find) use a potential as a spec function over the data structure's model, as in Charguéraud and Pottier's work: costs calls <= 1 + potential (old v) - potential v. Z3 proves the per-operation bound (ADR 0062), and Lean proves any closed form of the potential that needs induction.

docs.title: 4. Certificates and trust
docs.text:
A Lean-proved fact is neither proved by Z3 nor trusted in ADR 0036's sense. It is a third status, lean, recorded per item in its module's certificate (ADR 0024):

lean Pia.Core.Algo.Permutation.reverse_suffix
  statement <SHA-256 of the canonical Pia statement>
  lean-statement <SHA-256 of the generated Lean statement>
  toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.x.y
  mathlib <commit>
  axioms propext Classical.choice Quot.sound
  • The statement hash is over the lemma's canonical form, the same serialisation the interface hash uses, so a changed statement invalidates the proof, and a proof cannot be attached to another statement.
  • The axioms are what Lean's #print axioms reports for the theorem. The standard three (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) are allowed. sorryAx is an error. Lean.ofReduceBool (from native_decide, which trusts Lean's compiler) is allowed only in a @trusted module and is listed as a trusted item, under the same rules as assume.
  • --trust-report lists Lean facts in their own section, with --why naming the goals that used each one, exactly as it does for trusted axioms. What they rest on is stated plainly: Lean's kernel, Mathlib's definitions, and piac's translation of the statement. The translation is the new trusted component, and it is small: it covers spec terms only.
  • The loader never runs Lean, as it never runs Z3. pia-cert audit can re-check a Lean fact by regenerating the statement and replaying the proof with Lean, or with an independent kernel such as lean4checker.

Importing a module whose certificate lists Lean facts needs no trusting, because nothing in it is unproved.

docs.title: Where Lean runs, and what it costs
docs.text:
Lean never runs inside piac --verify, the REPL or the language server. piac reads a receipt for each by lean item: a small file with the statement hash, the Lean statement hash, the toolchain, the Mathlib commit and the axioms, as in the certificate. A receipt whose statement hash does not match the current statement is a failed goal, "the Lean proof of reverse_suffix is for another statement; run bazel build //lib:lean_proofs", and the goal is reported like any unproved goal. So an edit costs nothing more than reading a receipt, and an edit that changes a Lean-proved statement fails fast and says why.

Receipts are produced by a Bazel rule, pia_lean_proof, which runs piac --emit-lean, then lake build over the proof files, then #print axioms, and writes the receipt. The rule is in a separate target, like the proof benchmark, so ordinary builds and tests use the receipts from the Bazel cache and only a change to a Lean file or a Lean-proved statement runs Lean. Receipts are build outputs, never checked in, so a receipt always comes from a real Lean run.

The costs, to be measured in step 1 and tracked by the build-time benchmark (ADR 0032):

  • The toolchain is one download of a few hundred megabytes per Lean version, fetched by Bazel from Lean's release assets as a pinned, hashed archive.
  • Mathlib is the large part: several gigabytes of compiled .olean files. Building it from source takes hours, so Bazel fetches the prebuilt cache for the pinned commit. Proof files import only the Mathlib modules they need, which keeps each lake build to seconds or minutes after the cache is warm. Proofs that need no Mathlib (most induction lemmas over lists and bit-vectors, which Lean's core library and omega, grind and bv_decide handle) use a target without it.
  • Pinning. Lean and Mathlib change often, and an upgrade can break proofs. The toolchain and Mathlib commit are pinned in MODULE.bazel, upgraded deliberately in their own PR, and every receipt names them.

Lean proofs are checked in the Linux CI job of ADR 0049 and on the iMac. They are independent of the target, so they are checked once, not per target.

docs.title: What Lean is not used for
docs.text:
• Not for code. Lean never sees a function body, so there is no second semantics of Pia's code to keep in step with codegen, as there would be with an Aeneas-style translation.
  • Not instead of Z3. A goal goes to Lean only through a lemma that its author chose to prove there. The default remains "every goal proved automatically, or a compile error".
  • Not, yet, as the checker of Z3's proofs. Lean-SMT shows that SMT proofs can be rebuilt in Lean, which would let certificates carry proofs that a consumer re-checks without trusting Z3 (the proof objects docs/abi.md reserves room for). Its reconstruction covers cvc5, not Z3, and a fraction of the rules. It is a later decision.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Facts that are trusted today, such as ADR 0036's spectral norm bound, can become proved, and the theory can mean what its names say, not only be consistent.
  • Lemmas that Z3 cannot prove by one-step induction, such as the parked next_permutation, have a way forward that does not need more fuel or new solver strategies.
  • With ADR 0062's exact bounds, Pia gains closed forms and asymptotic claims proved in Lean, so the C++ library's complexity clauses become proved.
  • The trusted base gains one component, piac's translation of spec statements into Lean, which is listed in --trust-report. It is small and tested in both directions, but a mistake in it can make a Lean proof prove the wrong statement.
  • The build gains Lean and Mathlib, several gigabytes, but only in the targets that check Lean proofs, so the edit loop and the default test suite are unchanged.
  • Lean proofs are written, not found. Agents can write them, with Lean-auto, Lean-SMT and grind doing most of the work, but every Lean-proved lemma is something a person or an agent has to maintain across Lean and Mathlib upgrades.
  • New syntax: by lean Name as a lemma's or model's body, and the spec form f in O(g). lean is a keyword only after by.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with tests.

  1. Toolchain and a receipt. Lean as a Bazel module (pinned toolchain, no Mathlib), piac --emit-lean for spec functions over int, bool and records, by lean on lemmas, pia_lean_proof and receipts, and the round-trip tests. Measure the download size, the cold and warm build times and the disk used.
  2. Certificates and trust report. The lean status in certificates, axioms from #print axioms, --trust-report and --why, pia-cert audit replay.
  3. The rest of the translation. Machine integers as BitVec, slices and spec buffers, sums and let rec sums, real with Mathlib, --emit-lean --goal.
  4. Lean models of theories, and the spectral norm as the first trusted axiom made proved.
  5. Closed forms and O(...), with Akra–Bazzi, starting with merge sort and heap sort's bounds. This needs ADR 0062's costs clauses.

Cost in contracts (ADR 0062) needs no Lean and goes first. Step 1 includes a pia-lean skill: how to read the generated statements, and which tactics to try first.

Step 1 as built (2026-11-27). Four choices differ from or add to the text above:

  • The flag is piac --emit=lean, like the other emit modes, and receipts come in with --lean-receipt=<file>.
  • A receipt has one hash, the SHA-256 of the Lean text of the statement and of every definition it uses. It covers the Pia statement too, since the translation is a function of it. The separate Pia statement hash comes with certificates in step 2.
  • A spec function with a requires is, outside it, an opaque Lean constant f'outside applied to the arguments. Pia says nothing about the function there, and Lean can prove nothing about an opaque constant, so no Lean fact depends on how the translation made the function total.
  • Lean is an http_archive of the release for each host, v4.36.0, about 600 MB compressed per platform, and runs only in pia_lean_proof actions, locally rather than on the remote executors. The cold and warm build times are in the PR that built it.

Step 2 as built (2026-11-27). Certificates and the trust report:

  • The certificate has a proved lean <lemma> <hash> <theorem> <toolchain> <axioms> line per proved lemma, in format 3 with the spelling ADR 0073 gives per-item Lean lines, so that format holds both ADRs' lines. There is no Mathlib field until Mathlib is in the build.
  • One hash, still: the Lean closure hash covers the Pia statement and everything it uses, since the translation is a function of them, so a second Pia hash would add nothing a reader could check that this one does not.
  • native_decide fails the goal, [native_decide], outside a @trusted file. Its axioms are Lean.ofReduceBool and Lean.trustCompiler in older Lean, and in 4.36 one per use, T._native.native_decide.ax_1_1. Inside a @trusted file it is a trusted native_decide item in the certificate and the trust report.
  • --trust-report lists each proved Lean lemma after the trusted items, with its theorem, toolchain, axioms and hash, and with --why the goals that use it, then how many proved goals use one.
  • The translation now types every literal as Int. A term of literals alone was a Nat, where 0 - 1 = 0 holds, so Lean could prove a statement that is false in Pia.
  • pia-cert audit replay waits for pia-cert audit itself (docs/abi.md, step 8). Meanwhile a receipt comes only from a pia_lean_proof run, and its hash ties it to the statement.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
Dean answered when he accepted it (2026-11-24):

  1. Cost goes first, in its own ADR. Cost bounds proved by Z3 are ADR 0062, and they are built before Lean, since they need none of it.
  2. Lean facts need no opt-in. They are proved, so importers write no trusting. --trust-report lists them in their own section, with what they rest on (Lean's kernel, Mathlib and piac's translation), and --why names the goals that used each.
  3. Mathlib is in scope from the start. It is already on the iMac. Step 1 still keeps a target without Mathlib for proofs that need only Lean's core, so they stay fast, and it measures the disk Mathlib takes.
  4. Lean is installed on the iMac for step 1, and the Linux CI job fetches the same pinned toolchain.

docs.title: 62. Cost bounds are contracts: costs c <= e bounds what a function spends on a named counter, tracked by a spec-only spent c and proved by Z3
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, with Dean's answers below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia proves what a function computes, but not how much work it does. ADR 0040 documents C++'s complexity clauses ("at most log2(n) + 1 comparisons") and does not prove them. ADR 0056 checks them by fitting benchmark counts, which tests a few sizes, not every size. ADR 0061 puts asymptotic claims (O(n log n)) and closed forms of recurrences in Lean, but they need an exact bound to be about, and that bound has to be proved of the code.

Dean decided, when he accepted ADR 0061, that cost proofs by Z3 come first, in their own ADR, since they need no Lean.

Most complexity clauses are exact upper bounds on a count: comparisons, swaps, loop iterations, calls. A count is an integer that the code increases. If the verifier tracks it like any other value, then a bound on it is an ordinary postcondition, and Z3 proves it with the loop invariants and lemmas Pia already has. This is the approach of time credits (Charguéraud and Pottier, in Coq with CFML), of Liquid Haskell's resource analysis (Handley, Vazou and Hutton, "Liquidate your assets"), and of calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper). RAML (Hoffmann) infers polynomial bounds automatically by linear programming. Pia starts with stated bounds, which are checked, and leaves inference for later.

docs.title: 1. costs c <= e bounds what a function spends on one counter
docs.text:
A function may state its cost after its other contracts, and every cost clause names what it counts:

let find (xs : [u32]) (v : u32) : usize
  ensures result <= len xs
  costs iterations <= len xs
= ...

costs c <= e means that every run of the function, from any state meeting its requires, spends at most e on the counter c. e is a spec expression of type int (unbounded, so a bound never overflows) over the parameters and their old values. A function may have several cost clauses, one per counter, such as costs less <= n and costs swap <= n for a sort. Each is proved on its own.

Only upper bounds are in scope, because they are what callers need: a caller that knows each callee's bound can add them up. Lower bounds and exact counts are out of scope. costs is a keyword only in contract position, like requires and ensures.

docs.title: 2. Counters
docs.text:
There is no default cost model. A bound always says what it is in units of, so two bounds are never compared in different units by accident (Dean, 2026-11-24). A counter is one of:

  • A function, a function parameter, or a concept requirement such as Ord's less: each call to it counts one. This is how C++ states its clauses, in comparisons, swaps or assignments.
  • iterations: each iteration of a loop in the function counts one.
  • calls: each call to a function that is not a spec function or lemma counts one.

iterations and calls are names only after costs and spent, not keywords, so they do not take names away from code.

What a callee contributes. A call adds the callee's own bound for the same counter, with its arguments substituted, so cost composes. The callee contributes nothing if the counter cannot be reached from it: for a function counter f, the callee is not f, does not take f as an argument and has no concept that provides it, which the type checker decides from its signature. For iterations and calls, every callee can reach the counter, so it must have a bound for it. A callee with no loops and no recursion has one without writing it: the compiler works out the constant from its body. Any other callee without a bound for the counter is an error that names it: "sort has no bound on less, so the cost of top_k on less cannot be proved; add costs less <= ... to sort."

A counter counts events, not time. A count says nothing about caches or vector width, so performance budgets stay benchmarks (ADR 0056). What a cost bound proves is the shape that a benchmark measures: how the work grows with the input.

docs.title: 3. spent c counts what has been spent so far
docs.text:
Inside a function with a cost clause on c, the spec-only value spent c is what the function has spent on c so far. It is 0 on entry. Each counted event adds one, and each call adds the callee's bound. At each return, spent c <= e is a goal, with e evaluated at the parameters' entry values.

spent c is a loop-carried value like any other, so loops bound it with an invariant, and the loop machinery that exists today (verifier.md) does the rest. Binary search, counting calls to less:

let lower_bound (xs : [t]) (v : t) : usize
  requires sorted xs
  costs less <= Pia.Math.Log.bits (len xs)
= let lo : mutable usize = 0 in
  let hi : mutable usize = len xs in
  while lo < hi
    invariant lo <= hi && hi <= len xs
    invariant spent less + Pia.Math.Log.bits (hi - lo) <= Pia.Math.Log.bits (len xs)
  do
    let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 in
    if less xs.[mid] v then lo <- mid + 1 else hi <- mid
  done;
  lo

bits m is the number of binary digits of m, which is floor (log2 m) + 1 for m >= 1: exactly C++'s "at most log2(n) + 1 comparisons". Each iteration costs one less and leaves a range of at most (hi - lo) / 2, and bits drops by one when its argument is halved. That fact is a lemma of Pia.Math.Log, so the invariant's goal is linear.

(Step 1, 2026-11-24: the count is encoded as a usize that saturates at 2^64 - 1, not an int, because Z3 relates an int to machine integers through bv2int and timed out on the simplest loop invariants; see verifier.md.)

spent c can appear in loop invariants, asserts and lemma calls. It cannot appear in code, in requires or in ensures, and codegen erases it like any spec value. Encoded, it is a spec int local per counter, which IRGen threads through loops, branches and error handlers like a mutable local (ADR 0028's ? returns are returns, so each has the goal).

docs.title: 4. Recursion
docs.text:
A recursive function with costs must have decreases. At a recursive call, the call's bound is the function's own costs at the call's arguments, as its ensures is assumed there. That is sound by induction on the measure, which is why the measure is required. Its cost is then a recurrence, which is often best written as a recursive spec function:

let spec merge_cost (n : int) : int
  requires n >= 0
  decreases n
= if n <= 1 then 0 else merge_cost (n / 2) + merge_cost (n - n / 2) + n

let merge_sort (xs : inout [t]) (scratch : out [t]) : unit
  requires len scratch = len xs
  ensures sorted xs && permutation xs (old xs)
  costs less <= merge_cost (len xs)
  decreases len xs
= ...

Z3 proves that the code follows the recurrence, one call at a time. It cannot solve the recurrence. A closed form such as merge_cost n <= n * bits n needs induction beyond one step, and an asymptotic claim such as merge_cost in O(fun n => n * log2 n) is a limit. Both are lemmas for Lean, by ADR 0061. Until then, a closed form that a recursive lemma can prove in Pia is proved there, and callers use it.

docs.title: 5. Amortised bounds
docs.text: An operation that is cheap on average, such as vec's push or a union–find union, states its bound with a potential: a spec function of the structure's model (docs/stdlib.md, ghost models), such as costs calls <= 1 + phi (old v) - phi v. It is an ordinary costs expression, using old, so nothing new is needed to prove it. A sequence of k pushes then costs at most k + phi (first) - phi (last), which is linear, because the potential is never negative (a lemma about phi). This is the banker's method of time credits, written as a contract.

docs.title: 6. Pia.Math.Log
docs.text:
A small spec-only module of the functions cost bounds use, with their laws as lemmas proved in Pia:

  • bits (m : int) : int, the number of binary digits of m >= 0, with bits 0 = 0, bits (m / 2) = bits m - 1 for m >= 1, and monotonicity;
