  • log2 (m : int) : int, bits m - 1 for m >= 1, the floor of the binary logarithm;
  • clog2 (m : int) : int, the ceiling, for bounds such as a heap's height.

They are recursive spec functions, so their laws are proved by induction lemmas, and goals use the lemmas rather than unfolding the definitions.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces and certificates
docs.text: A costs clause is part of its function's contract, so it is in the interface and in the interface hash (ADR 0024). Importers rely on it as on ensures. A new version of a library refines the old one if its bound is no larger under the old requires, which is one more goal in the refinement check. Removing a costs clause breaks the interface. No item is trusted: a cost bound is proved like any other contract, so certificates record nothing new.

docs.title: 8. Build time
docs.text: A function without a cost clause has no spent and no cost goals, so existing code costs nothing more to prove. A function with a cost clause gets one more loop-carried int per counter and one more goal per return and per invariant. These goals are linear when the bound is linear or written with bits and its lemmas. Bounds such as n * bits n are nonlinear. They are proved through lemmas that do the multiplication once, or with @solver(nlsat), and they join the benchmark corpus (ADR 0032), so a costly bound shows up as a regression.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The C++ library's complexity clauses become proved contracts: binary search, heap operations, sorts and partitioning first (docs/cpp-std.md), and their doc comments stop restating them.
  • Callers can bound their own cost from their callees' published bounds, so cost composes across modules like correctness does.
  • Recurrences are proved to be followed, not solved. Solving them, and asymptotic claims, need ADR 0061's Lean lemmas, or induction lemmas in Pia where those are enough.
  • A step is not time. Bounds say how work grows, and benchmarks still say how fast it is.
  • Pia goes on being an upper-bound system. Lower bounds, worst-case inputs and parallel span (for spread, ADR 0060) are left for later.
  • New syntax: the costs c <= e clause and the spec-only spent c. costs is a keyword only in contract position, and iterations and calls are names only after costs and spent.
  • Every exported Pia.Core function with a loop or recursion states a bound, which a lint checks (below).

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with tests in tests/verify/costs.pia.

  1. costs c <= e and spent c for iterations and calls: loops, calls, inferred bounds for functions with no loops or recursion, the error for a callee without a bound, and spent c in invariants and asserts.
  2. Recursion and function counters, including function parameters and concept requirements, and Pia.Math.Log with its lemmas.
  3. Interfaces: cost clauses in .piai, the interface hash and the refinement goal; then the first proved clauses in Pia.Core.Algo (lower_bound, upper_bound, push_heap, pop_heap), with docs/cpp-std.md updated.
  4. Amortised bounds with a potential, starting with vec's push.
  5. Reporting: --verify-stats and the REPL report cost goals separately, so their proof cost is visible.
  6. The lint unbounded_cost (ADR 0037): an exported function of a Pia.Core module with a loop or recursion and no cost clause is a warning. It is on for lib/Pia/Core from the start, and the warnings it finds there are fixed module by module.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
Dean answered when he accepted it (2026-11-24):

  1. Every bound names what it counts. There is no default cost model, so costs always names its counter (iterations, calls, or a function such as less), and spent takes the counter too. This replaced the proposed default of steps and the @counts(f) attribute.
  2. A lint asks for bounds on the library. unbounded_cost warns on an exported Pia.Core function with a loop or recursion and no cost clause (step 6).

docs.title: 63. Opaque spec functions: a spec function marked @opaque keeps its definition out of every goal until a proof reveals it
Context
docs.text:
ADR 0058 made whole-stream specifications writable: a reference LZW decoder, or Huffman's canonical code, held in spec state beside the real decoder. Two proofs built on it have stalled in the same way:

  • GIF LZW against its whole-stream spec (#339, branch claude/lzw-whole-stream) proves 229 of 234 goals. The 5 that fail are the step lemmas emit_kwk and link_new, and two loop invariants after an iteration. A 300 s solver timeout does not help. Changing one lemma's body moved the count from 5 to 17, so the proof is brittle, not merely slow.
  • Huffman's decode against the canonical code (inflate step 2, branch claude/huffman-proved) proves 213 of 220. Putting kraft l n <= 32768 in decode's precondition made even its old u32 overflow goals time out. They proved again once the call was removed.

The cause is the same in both. verifier.md ("Spec functions") encodes a call f a as F a with the fact pre(a) ==> F a = body(a), and adds that fact wherever the call appears. A spec over a whole stream or table, such as lzw_ok, kraft or tab_from, has a large body that calls other spec functions. Once it is in a loop's context, every goal in the loop carries the unfolded body and its quantifier instances, including goals that never needed it. The workarounds so far fight this with lemmas whose contracts hide the body. That works, but only after many rounds, and it breaks again when an unrelated body changes.

Dafny, F* and Verus solved this the same way: a function can be opaque. Its definition is a fact only where a proof asks for it.

docs.title: 1. @opaque on a spec function
docs.text:
let spec lzw_ok (s : [u8]) (x : [u8]) (k : usize) : bool @opaque
  requires ...
= ...
  • At a call to an opaque f, the solver gets F a, its range and pre(a) ==> post(a, F a) (f's ensures), but not F a = body(a).
  • f's own goals are unchanged: its body is still checked, and its ensures are proved from its body.
  • An imported opaque spec function stays opaque in the importer. The interface carries the attribute.

docs.title: 2. with f reveals the definition, reusing the existing with and in
docs.text:
There is no new keyword. with already appears in match ... with and in { r with ... }.

As a clause after a function's or lemma's contracts, with f reveals f in that whole body. This is the common case:

let lemma emit_kwk (s : [u8]) ... : unit
  requires lzw_ok s x k
  ensures ...
  with lzw_ok
= ...

As an expression, with f in e reveals f only in e, for a narrower scope inside a body:

(with lzw_ok, lzw_from in step_facts s x q);
  • Either form may name several functions, separated by commas. Codegen erases the clause and the expression's wrapper, leaving e.
  • Inside the scope, calls to f get the definition fact as if f were not opaque, with the usual @fuel depth. Outside it, they do not.
  • The intended pattern is to reveal in small step lemmas, never in the loop of the code itself. The loop then sees lzw_ok s x k only as an atom, together with the lemmas' contracts.
  • match e with still parses as before: a with that follows match's scrutinee belongs to the match, so the expression form starts only where an expression can start.

docs.title: 3. Nothing changes for spec functions that are not marked
docs.text: Default unfolding stays as it is, so every existing proof keeps its meaning and cost.

docs.title: 4. Build order
docs.text:
1. @opaque and with f, with a test tests/verify/opaque.pia. The test covers a goal that fails without with and proves with it, the clause form and the with f in e form, and an imported opaque function.
  2. Retry LZW (#339) with lzw_ok and the trace functions opaque, revealed only in the step lemmas.
  3. Retry Huffman step 2 with kraft, tab_from and room opaque.
  4. Record the per-file goal counts and costs before and after, as the ADR 0032 benchmark does.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-24)
docs.text:
1. No new keyword. Dean asked: "Can we use a normal with or let ... in instead of having a new keyword?" Section 2 uses with: a with f clause for a whole body, and with f in e for one expression. let ... in binds a name, and a reveal binds nothing, so it would need a placeholder such as let _ = f in. Dean confirmed it: "with looks like the right call."
  2. Opt-in. "Opaque as an opt-in sounds better." A spec function is opaque only when it is marked @opaque.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Whole-stream proofs can keep the spec as an atom in loops. A lemma's cost depends on the definitions it reveals, not on everything in scope.
  • Proofs become less brittle: changing an opaque function's body affects only the lemmas that reveal it.
  • One more attribute and no new keyword. A proof that forgets to reveal a definition fails with an unproved goal, so the error report should hint "f is opaque here; with f may prove it".

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes Dafny {:opaque} and reveal f() opaque definitions, revealed per proof F* [@@"opaque_to_smt"] and reveal_opaque keeping big definitions out of the SMT context Verus #[verifier::opaque] and reveal(f) the same, for Rust verification over Z3

docs.title: 64. type always makes a new type: let length = type u32 is distinct from u32, converts only by applying a type to a value, and inherits only what it derives
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-27, with the answer below). Dean asked for strong type aliases (2026-11-24), and chose the spelling in section 1, type always makes a new type, over a separate distinct word (2026-11-24). Steps 1 to 3 are built (#414, #425, #441), and step 4 with @derive(hash) and @derive(json) on distinct types.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Reading the tour, Dean asked for strong type aliases: after let length = type u32, a length is a type of its own, never mixed up with a u32 or with another type over u32, and every conversion is an explicit function call. He suggested a metaprogram could make the conversion functions.

Today let byte = type u8 is another name for u8 (irgen.md): types are structural, so u64 and usize are one type and int{0..255} is u8. Records and variants are the exception. They are named, so two records with the same fields are different types. The language has no way to give a scalar, a range or an existing record a name that the type checker keeps apart, so a function area (w : u32) (h : u32) cannot stop a caller swapping its arguments, and a u32 of pixels can be added to a u32 of bytes.

The questions to settle are how it is spelled, whether the underlying type's bounds and contracts carry over, which operators and concepts the new type gets, how it meets types as values, concepts, error sets, @derive(json) and the ABI, and what it costs at run time and in proofs.

docs.title: 1. type makes a new type; a let of a type names one
docs.text:
let length = type u32              (* a new type, distinct from u32 *)
let percent = type int{0..100}     (* a new type over a range *)
let byte = u8                      (* another name for u8, as before *)

type already makes a new type when it is followed by a record or a variant. This ADR makes that the whole rule: type e is a new type whose values are the values of e, whatever e is. Since types are values (ADR 0002), naming an existing type needs no keyword at all: let byte = u8 binds the type u8 to a second name, as let y = x binds a value. That is how a transparent alias is spelled from now on.

No keyword is added. The existing aliases spelled with type (about ten of them in tests, docs/theories.md and ADR 0051's example, such as let blk = type int{0..63}) become let blk = int{0..63} in the same change that flips the meaning, so their programs do not change. max byte and min byte keep working for an alias (ADR 0059).

On the right of let, a type expression with no type is an alias: a type name, a range int{lo..hi} (written with no space before {, by the adjacency rule of ADR 0019), an applied generic such as option u8, or a type-level metaprogram's call (ADR 0035). Sema tells it apart from a value binding because it names a type.

docs.title: 2. It is built by a prelude metaprogram
docs.text:
The expander rewrites let n = type e, where e is not a record or variant literal, into a call of the prelude metaprogram distinct, which returns:

let length = type { raw#length : u32 } @distinct
let length#make (x : u32) : length ensures length#raw result = x = { raw#length = x }
let length#raw (x : length) : u32 ensures result = x.raw#length = x.raw#length
  • A one-field record. Records are already nominal through Sema, IRGen, generics, interfaces and certificates, so a distinct type reuses all of it. The field's and the functions' names carry a #, which no source name can, so no program can write l.raw; the only ways in and out are the conversions below.
  • A type is called to convert (Dean, 2026-11-24). Types are values, and applying one to a value converts it: length 5 makes a length, IRGen's call of length#make, and u32 l takes one apart, a call of length#raw. Both are explicit, both read the same in code and in contracts, and no new names are made. Applying the underlying type unwraps exactly one layer: for let width = type length, length w gives the length and u32 (length w) the number. The result of u32 l widens implicitly like any u32, so u64 l is u32 l widened; applying a narrower type, u8 l, is the narrowing goal it would be for the u32. Applying a type to a value that is neither of the type's underlying type nor of a distinct type over it is an error. A module may leave the conversions out of its interface (section 6), and a type is not a function value yet: map length xs is an error that suggests map (let (x) => length x) xs.
  • Names. Named functions, to_length and from_length after the library's to_chars, were the first proposal. Dean chose calling the type (2026-11-24), which adds no names and reads the same both ways.
  • @distinct marks the record so that the rest of the compiler can tell a distinct type from a hand-written one-field record: diagnostics print length (distinct u32), derives write the underlying value (section 4), and the metaprogram builtin underlying t returns e for a distinct type and unit for any other.

distinct is ordinary Pia in src/syntax/Prelude.cpp, like derive_eq and machine, and a program can call it itself.

docs.title: 3. Bounds and contracts carry over; conversions are explicit both ways
docs.text:
• Bounds. The field has the underlying type, so a percent holds 0 to 100 and the prover knows it about every percent, for free, as for the range itself. percent x has the narrowing goal x fits int{0..100} at its argument, as any call does, and int{0..100} p (or u8 p, widened) returns an int{0..100}, which widens implicitly to anything larger.
  • Contracts. length#raw is a pure function of scalars, so in a contract u32 l means its body (tests/verify/pure_calls.pia), and requires u32 w * u32 h <= max u32 reads and proves as the scalar version did.
  • No implicit conversion, in either direction. let l : length = 5 is an error that suggests length 5, a u32 where a length is expected is an error that suggests length x, and a length where a u32 is expected suggests u32 l. Two distinct types over one type never convert into each other except through the underlying type, width (u32 l).
  • min and max. max length is an error that suggests length (max u32): the bounds are values of the underlying type, and folding them to a bare literal would be the implicit conversion this ADR rules out. @derive(bounds) (section 4) gives min_length and max_length as values of length.

docs.title: 4. Nothing is inherited; operators come from derives
docs.text:
A distinct type starts with no operators, no equality in code, and meets no concept. This is the point of it: a length that could be added to itself could also be multiplied by itself, and length times length is an area. Each family is opted into with a derive, which writes ordinary overloads on the record:

Derive Gives Meaning eq =, <> the existing derive_eq: compares the underlying values ord <, <=, >, >= compares the underlying values, each with a postcondition that says so add +, - between two values of the type results of the type; overflow is a goal as for the underlying type (ADR 0004) scale *, /, % by the underlying type, on the right length * u32 : length, never length * length bounds min_n, max_n the underlying type's bounds, as values of the type hash an instance of Pia.Core.Hash the underlying value's hash; needs eq json write_json_n, read_json_n and the Json instance the underlying value, not an object: a length is the JSON number 5, read with the underlying type's range check 
let length = type u32 @derive(eq, ord, add, scale)

A derive's postconditions are written in terms of the underlying values, u32 a, so callers prove facts about a + b the way they would about the underlying numbers. Concepts follow from the functions: a concept whose signature ord meets is met by any distinct type that derives it, and an adapter (ADR 0009) covers anything else. A program can write any operator itself, such as let mul (a : length) (b : length) : area, which is how units are built (theories.md, "Units").

@derive(add) on a distinct type over a type with no add, such as a record, is an error at the derive, which names the missing function.

docs.title: 5. Types as values, generics, error sets
docs.text:
• Types as values. length is a type value like any record: option length, [length; 8], vec length and a generic's (t : type) all take it. A generic over (t : type where Ord t) accepts length when it derives ord.
  • Over records and variants. let celsius = type reading is a distinct type over the record reading. It does not copy reading's fields or constructors (constructors are one namespace, and copies would clash); it wraps one reading, reached as reading c.
  • Error sets. An error set's members are variants (ADR 0028), so a distinct type is not one, even over a variant. A handler matches the variant itself. Making a distinct type over a variant usable as an error set member is left until someone needs it.
  • Distinct of distinct. let width = type length wraps a length: width l takes a length, not a u32.

docs.title: 6. Interfaces, certificates and abstract types
docs.text:
• Interfaces. An interface shows a distinct type as it is defined, let length = type u32, and exports the functions it chooses. The .piai carries the @distinct record, so importers agree on its layout, and the interface hash covers the type's name and its underlying type: changing u32 to u64 changes the hash and the importers' witnesses (ADR 0024).
  • Abstract types. An interface that lists let length : type and exports one conversion but not the other, or a checked constructor in place of length x, keeps the type's values under the module's control. This is what makes a distinct type with an invariant possible (a sorted slice, a nonzero divisor). Abstract types are not importable yet (ADR 0039); this ADR does not change that, and invariant-carrying distinct types are a later ADR.

docs.title: 7. Zero cost
docs.text:
• Proofs. transforms::scalarizeRecords replaces each record with its fields before the verifier runs (irgen.md), so a proof about a length is the proof about a u32, with the same goals and cost. Conversions are calls of pure scalar functions, which the verifier unfolds.
  • Code. After scalarization a length is a u32: a buffer of length is one buffer of u32, and the conversions inline away.
  • The C ABI. A record parameter is already passed as its fields. A record result is written through an out-pointer today (codegen.md); this ADR makes a record of one scalar field return that scalar instead. That is what C does for a struct { uint32_t v; } on arm64 and on x86_64 System V, so the entry point is the same as for the underlying type, and also what a C caller expects for a one-field struct.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• A distinct word, keeping type u32 as an alias (let length = distinct u32). Additive, with nothing to migrate, but it adds a word for something type already means for records and variants, and leaves two spellings of "name a type" (type u8 and u8). Dean chose type instead (2026-11-24).
  • A core nominal type in Sema and the dialect (!pia.distinct<"length", ui32>). Every pass that compares types would learn a new case, and the verifier and codegen would need to strip it, for the same result the record gives already.
  • One-constructor variants (type | Length of u32). Nominal today, but a variant carries a tag, matching is the only way out, and a derive would have to treat one-constructor variants specially.
  • Inheriting everything the underlying type has. Rejected: it re-admits length * length : length, which is the class of bug the feature exists to stop. Haskell's GeneralizedNewtypeDeriving and Rust's newtype pattern both make derivation explicit for this reason.
  • Implicit conversion from literals. let l : length = 5 would be pleasant, but it is a conversion the reader cannot see, and it makes length x optional in exactly the places (constants, defaults) where units are most often wrong.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Implementation, one PR each:

  1. Aliases spelled let byte = u8. Sema accepts a let whose right side is a type expression as an alias, type <scalar> keeps meaning an alias for now, and every existing type-spelled alias in the repository moves to the new spelling. Tests: tests/verify/type_aliases.pia, tests/irgen/alias_errors.pia.
  2. type e is distinct. The prelude's distinct, the @distinct attribute, the underlying builtin, calls of a type as conversions, the diagnostics that suggest them, and one-scalar-field records returned as the scalar in the C ABI. Tests: tests/verify/distinct_types.pia, tests/irgen/distinct_errors.pia, tests/codegen/distinct_abi.pia, tests/meta/distinct.pia.
  3. Derives. ord, add, scale and bounds in the prelude, and eq checked on distinct types. Tests: tests/verify/distinct_derives.pia.
  4. json and hash. derive_json and Pia.Core.Hash write and hash the underlying value: derive_hash is exported by Pia.Core.Hash's interface, and json_record hands a distinct type to json_distinct. Tests: tests/std/hash_derive.pia, tests/std/hash_derive_errors.pia, tests/std/json_derive_distinct.pia and json_distinct_run_test.

Docs: the tour's Records section and docs/irgen.md (types), docs/meta.md (distinct, underlying, the new derives), docs/grammar.md (aliases), and the pia-language skill. ADR 0059's let byte = type u8 example becomes let byte = u8.

Answered questions:

  1. Whether @derive(add) should also give +| and -| (saturating) when the underlying type has them. Dean (2026-11-27): no. Saturating operators get their own derive target, such as @derive(saturating_add), so @derive(add) gives only + and -. saturating_add is not built yet.

docs.title: 65. Pia code extends the compiler's lowering: @lower gives a function an MLIR form and a type an MLIR type, the Pia definition stays the specification, and each lowering is proved to refine it or is listed as trusted
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, with Dean's answers below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for a way to extend the compiler from Pia itself: to say that certain Pia types lower to MLIR types and certain functions lower to MLIR ops, with tensors, memrefs and linalg as the key cases. The motivation is matmul and SIMD kernels that are represented and optimised as linalg on memref, and run on GPUs by going down through MLIR to SPIR-V. That is the path Dean chose for the GPU demo on 2026-11-23: SPIR-V, then SPIRV-Cross to MSL for Metal now, other vendors later.

Today the lowering is closed. Codegen.cpp maps each pia type and op to arith, scf, memref and func by a fixed table (docs/codegen.md): [T; n] is memref<n x T>, a slice is a strided memref<?xT>, and nothing produces linalg, tensor, vector or gpu, although ADR 0018 always meant code to lower through them. Every new kind of op needs C++ in IRGen and Codegen. What Pia does have:

  • Metaprograms that run to a fixed point (ADR 0007), build items from quotes, compute strings, and are proved total when their output becomes a proof hypothesis (ADR 0035).
  • Theories (ADR 0036): a library extends the solver with sorts, functions and axioms, made safe by a model or listed as trusted. This ADR is the same move for the code generator, and borrows its answer: whatever a library adds is either proved, or named in the trust report.
  • Foreign functions (= extern "sym", docs/codegen.md): the body is elsewhere and the contract is trusted; with no contract, every call is unsafe. Their contracts are trusted items in the certificate (ADR 0024).
  • Placement and dataflow (ADR 0015, ADR 0050 section 7): @place(gpu) and GPU schedulers in a sender graph, which must never change the proved result. spread (ADR 0060) reaches codegen as an scf.for, run by MLIR's async runtime.
  • Lean (ADR 0061) for facts Z3 cannot prove, recorded by statement hash.

The soundness question is the whole design. A lowering replaces the code the verifier proved with code it did not see. If matmul is proved over its Pia body and then compiled as linalg.matmul, the proof is about a program that never runs, unless something shows that the op does what the body does.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Mojo exposes MLIR directly: __mlir_type[...], __mlir_op.<name> and __mlir_attr inside ordinary functions, and its standard library builds Int, SIMD and its tensor types on them. It is the most direct model for the surface, and has no proofs: what the op does is what MLIR does.
  • Rust intrinsics (#[rustc_intrinsic]) are functions the backend implements. Since 2024 an intrinsic may have a fallback body, used by backends that do not override it; -Z force-intrinsic-fallback runs the fallback everywhere for testing, and #[miri::intrinsic_fallback_is_spec] marks a fallback that is the specification, a requirement the docs call strong. That is the shape Pia wants, with the claim proved instead of asserted.
  • Lean's @[extern] and @[implemented_by] keep a Lean definition as the logical meaning and compile calls to other code. The kernel reasons about the definition; nothing checks the implementation, and a mismatched implemented_by is a known way to make compiled Lean disagree with proved Lean.
  • Zig comptime computes types and code at compile time with no separate macro language, and exposes the backend's vectors and intrinsics as builtins (@Vector, @reduce). It shows how far ordinary compile-time code can go before a new form is needed.
  • Julia reaches MLIR through MLIR.jl's bindings, and Reactant.jl traces Julia functions into StableHLO and compiles them with XLA: the lowering is a library, not the compiler.
  • Halide, and MLIR's transform dialect after it, split the algorithm (what is computed) from the schedule (tiling, vectorisation, mapping to threads). The schedule is a script the author writes, and it cannot change the result, by construction of the transforms.
  • mlir-tv (Bang et al., CAV 2022) translation-validates MLIR transformations, linalg and tensor included, by encoding both sides in SMT and proving refinement with Z3, with an abstraction of float arithmetic refined on failure. Inspired by Alive2, it found mismatches between MLIR's documented semantics and its implementation. It shows that linalg on tensors and memrefs has an SMT encoding that scales to real kernels.

docs.title: 1. One attribute, @lower, on a function or a type
docs.text:
No new keyword. @lower(e) on a let gives the item an MLIR form, where e is a string of MLIR, or a call to a metaprogram that returns one. $name in the string splices a parameter of the function, the result, or a type, as MLIR values and types.

(** C[i, j] := sum over p of A[i, p] * B[p, j], row-major. *)
let matmul (m : usize) (n : usize) (k : usize)
    (a : [i8]) (b : [i8]) (c : out mutable [i32])
  requires len a = m * k && len b = k * n && len c = m * n
  ensures forall (i in 0..m). forall (j in 0..n).
    c.[i * n + j] = Linalg.dot a b k n i j k
  @lower("linalg.matmul ins($a, $b) outs($c)")
= for i in 0..m do ... done
  • The Pia body stays, and it is the specification. The verifier proves the body against the contract, as for any function, and every caller proves from the contract. The body is also the fallback: the REPL's JIT runs it, a target without the lowering's dialects compiles it, and --lower=off compiles it everywhere, for differential tests (ADR 0056 can run both forms on generated inputs). This is Rust's fallback body, with the "fallback is the spec" claim proved (section 3) instead of asserted.
  • The MLIR is checked when it is expanded. piac splices the operands and parses the string with MLIR's own parser against the dialects the build registers, so a misspelt op or a type mismatch is an error at the attribute, with MLIR's diagnostic, and not a crash in codegen. A metaprogram that computes the string runs at expansion like any other, so a lowering can depend on the shape, the element type or the target (@lower(matmul_for $t)).
  • Operands are the function's parameters, by name and modifier. An out or inout buffer may be written by the MLIR form, and an in buffer may not: a structural check on the op's memory effects (for linalg, its outs). A buffer lowers as it already does, a memref.
  • @lower on a type names the MLIR type its values have and how the Pia fields map onto it. The Pia definition is again the meaning:
let matrix = let (t : type) => type {
  data : [t]; rows : usize; cols : usize
} where len data = rows * cols
  @lower("memref<?x?x$t>", data, [rows; cols])

Codegen builds the descriptor from data's pointer with sizes [rows; cols] and row-major strides, and the verifier proves that the where keeps the descriptor in bounds. Version 1 allows ranked memref and tensor of identity (row-major) layout over one buffer field; strided and affine layouts come with FPL (ADR 0020). A value type such as [t; n] held as a tensor lowers through one-shot bufferisation, and Pia's ownership facts (a moved value has no other reader, a borrowed one is not written) are what tell bufferisation it may write in place, the way ADR 0013 passes proved facts to the vectoriser.

Alternatives considered: = extern mlir "linalg.matmul" reuses a keyword, but extern means "no body, trusted contract", and the point here is to keep the body and prove the op against it. A quoted MLIR builder in metaprograms (mlir`( ... ), with ops as values) is more structured than strings, but needs a second quote language, and MLIR's own textual form is already the most stable interface MLIR has. Mojo's inline __mlir_op in expressions is the most flexible, and it would let MLIR ops appear anywhere in a body, where the verifier cannot see them.

docs.title: 2. @schedule says how, as a transform-dialect script
docs.text:
The algorithm is the lowered op. How it is tiled, vectorised and mapped onto threads is a schedule: a transform-dialect script that piac runs after lowering, written in @schedule(e) with the same string-or-metaprogram rule:

@schedule("
  %mm = transform.structured.match ops{[\"linalg.matmul\"]} in %root
  %tiled, %forall = transform.structured.tile_using_forall %mm tile_sizes [32, 32]
  transform.structured.vectorize %tiled")

A schedule can only call upstream transforms, which preserve meaning by construction, so it is trusted the way LLVM's -O2 is trusted: as part of the compiler. It is still listed (section 4), because upstream transforms have had bugs (mlir-tv found some), and on integer kernels piac can check a schedule by translation validation (section 3, step 8). A transform that reassociates a reduction (split_reduction, vectorising a reduction, a GPU tree reduction) is an error on a float kernel under strict IEEE (ADR 0012), and allowed under @fp(reassoc) or a tolerance contract (ADR 0038). This is the rule that placement never changes the proved result, applied to schedules.

docs.title: 3. Who proves the MLIR form matches the Pia definition
docs.text:
Each lowering is in one of three states, chosen by what the op is, not by the author:

  1. Proved (the default). When piac knows the meaning of every op in the MLIR form, it proves the refinement goal: under the function's requires, the MLIR form's meaning implies its ensures, and it writes nothing but its out and inout operands. The goal is an ordinary obligation, reported, sliced and cached like any other. The ops piac gives a meaning to, in version 1: arith and index on integers, memref and tensor shape and element ops, scf, and linalg.generic, which covers every named linalg op, since piac first generalises a named op with MLIR's own generalizeNamedOp. A linalg.generic is a perfect loop nest over its iteration domain, in order, so its meaning is: for every point of the parallel dimensions, the output cell is a fold of the scalar body over the reduction dimensions. piac writes that as Pia spec functions (a forall over the parallel dimensions, and a recursive spec fold with a decreases measure over each reduction dimension, built from the indexing maps and the scalar region), and the refinement goal is proved from them. If the function's ensures is written with the matching library spec (section 5), the goal closes by unfolding the same definition; otherwise it needs a lemma, as any recursive spec does.
  2. Trusted. An op piac has no meaning for (gpu.*, spirv.*, nvvm.*, arm_sme.*, any vendor intrinsic) can be the target of a lowering only in a @trusted module, and then the refinement goal is accepted, not proved: the lowering is a trusted item, exactly like an extern contract, and the body is still proved against the contract. Differential tests of the body against the lowering (--lower=off, section 1) are the check that remains.
  3. Proved in Lean. A refinement goal Z3 cannot close, such as a fold equal to its specification only by a ring identity, can be proved in Lean against the generated statement, by ADR 0061's rules, and recorded with the lean status and the statement's hash.

The meaning piac gives an op is the only new trusted component in state 1: it is piac's reading of MLIR's semantics. It is kept small and testable: each op's meaning is checked against MLIR's own reference lowering (convert-linalg-to-loops, then scf and memref, which piac already encodes) on generated kernels, in a test suite like the litmus battery of ADR 0052.

Floats wait on M11. With floats, a linalg reduction has a fixed order, so strict IEEE refinement is exact, but every useful schedule reorders it, so float kernels will in practice carry a tolerance contract (c ~= spec within e, ADR 0038) proved against a real-valued specification, with the reduction's error term derived by ADR 0038's automatic bound. Integer kernels need none of this, and include the quantised i8 × i8 → i32 matmul that ML inference runs on GPUs, so they come first.

docs.title: 4. Trust report and certificates
docs.text:
Two new kinds of trusted item join the four of docs/abi.md (extern contract, @assume, --allow-unproved goal, unsafe call):

  • lowering: a function or type whose MLIR form is trusted (section 3, state 2), recorded with the item, the ops it uses, and the SHA-256 of its spliced MLIR text.
  • schedule: a transform script, recorded with the functions it applies to, the transforms it calls, and its hash.

A proved lowering is not a trusted item, and a Lean-proved one has the lean status. piac --trust-report lists both new kinds, and --why names the callers whose proofs went through a trusted lowering's contract. The lowering is not in the interface hash: like a body, it is the module's own business, so changing a kernel's tile sizes does not invalidate importers' proofs. It is in the certificate, so pia-cert trust-report on a shipped binary says which kernels ran as GPU code nobody proved.

docs.title: 5. linalg ops get Pia contracts from MLIR itself
docs.text:
Pia.Linalg declares each linalg named op as a Pia function: a Pia body, a contract written with spec functions that mirror the op's definition (dot, conv_2d_nhwc_hwcf, pooling_nhwc_max), and @lower to the op. These declarations are generated, not written by hand, as the POSIX bindings are (ADR 0057): a small tool links MLIR, builds each named op on symbolic shapes, generalises it, and writes the spec functions from the indexing maps and the scalar region. Each declaration's refinement goal is then proved by section 3, so a generator bug fails a proof instead of shipping a wrong contract. Named ops whose definitions moved from OpDSL to ODS (linalg.matmul with its indexing_maps, the elementwise ops) are handled the same way, since the tool reads the generalised op and not the YAML.

User code calls Linalg.matmul and proves from its contract, as from any library. A kernel author who wants their own op writes a Pia function with @lower to a linalg.generic and gets the same proof.

docs.title: 6. How it reaches the GPU through SPIR-V
docs.text:
The driving example is a tiled integer matmul on the GPU:

  1. The function is proved over its Pia body.
  2. @lower replaces the body with linalg.matmul on memrefs, and the refinement goal is proved.
  3. @schedule tiles it with tile_using_forall and maps the scf.forall onto GPU blocks and threads (transform.gpu.map_forall_to_blocks, map_nested_forall_to_threads). The tiles' disjoint writes are what tile_using_forall constructs; once the schedule's output is lifted back to pia_par, ADR 0060's ownership goal (each tile owns the cells of its slice) proves it, instead of trusting it.
  4. gpu-kernel-outlining, the memref storage-class mapping, and convert-gpu-to-spirv produce a spirv.module, serialised to SPIR-V, then SPIRV-Cross writes MSL for Metal.
  5. The host side, gpu.launch_func, calls a small trusted Metal shim through extern contracts, which is the GPU ADR's subject, along with @place(gpu) over these kernels and Pia.Exec.Metal (ADR 0050, step 9).

The same function with no @place(gpu) lowers through the same linalg and a CPU schedule (tile, vectorise, arm_neon or AVX2), which is the SIMD half of Dean's motivation and needs no GPU work at all.

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text:
A 4x4 integer matmul (u8 × u8 → u32, row-major), with dot written as the spec that linalg's generalised matmul would give the verifier, a client corner that proves one cell from the contract alone, and an all-parallel elementwise add were run on the iMac with piac --verify --verify-stats --jobs=4 (piac at 436306d).

  • The fixed-shape case proves: 51 of 51 goals in 17.5 s (48 by Z3, 3 by intervals, cost 102M). The costliest goals are corner's last step relating dot … 4 to the written-out sum (cost 53.9M, 10.5 s), the inner loop's invariant (20.7M, 10.6 s), corner's postcondition (14.9M, 2.1 s), and the + in the constant-stride index i * 4 + j (7.1M, 4.4 s), which intervals should own. The elementwise add is trivial: 7 goals, cost 37K, under 10 ms each.
  • A generated reduction spec gets @fuel(1). With @fuel(4) the same file took 522 s and failed two goals, because Z3 unfolded dot under the nested quantifiers. Each loop step needs exactly one unfolding, so the generated spec and the loop invariants it implies are written for fuel 1.
  • Clients need an unrolling lemma for static extents. Relating dot … 4 to a closed form takes five unfoldings, which corner got from a chain of five asserts. The generator emits that lemma (dot_unroll4) for each static reduction extent instead.
  • Names collide with core builtins. add, sub, mul, div and max are core builtins, and Pia has no shadowing (ADR 0022), so Pia.Linalg cannot use those op names. The generator names elementwise ops ewise_<op>, as linalg's own elementwise op does by kind.
  • Symbolic shapes do not prove as written. With m, n and k as parameters and slices of length m * k, every nonlinear index goal (i * k + p < len a, the overflow of i * k) timed out at 30 s: 16 of 33 proved, cost 3.7G. So the generator proves each indexing map's bounds once, as a lemma per map (i < m && p < k ==> i * k + p < m * k, proved with range-typed dimensions, or in Lean by ADR 0061), and states the op's contract over an accessor that uses it, rather than leaving the products to every goal.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is one PR, and each is useful on its own.

  1. Link linalg, tensor, bufferization and transform into piac, and lower a function marked @lower with a trusted lowering (state 2) only, on CPU: linalg to loops, then the existing path. The lowering trusted item, in the trust report and the certificate. --lower=off.
  2. The splice-and-parse check at expansion, metaprograms that compute lowerings, and the operand-effect check.
  3. Proved lowerings for integer linalg.generic and named ops through generalizeNamedOp: the meaning as spec functions at fuel 1, a bounds lemma per indexing map and an unrolling lemma per static extent (see the prototype), the refinement goal, and the reference-lowering test suite for piac's encodings.
  4. Pia.Linalg, generated, starting with matmul, batch_matmul, add, fill, conv_2d_nhwc_hwcf and the poolings.
  5. @schedule on CPU: tile and vectorise, the reassociation check, the schedule trusted item. Benchmarked against the Pia body's own codegen.
  6. @lower on types: ranked memref and tensor over one buffer field, one-shot bufferisation fed by ownership facts.
  7. GPU: the GPU ADR first (SPIR-V, SPIRV-Cross, the Metal shim, @place(gpu)), then the schedule's scf.forall mapped to threads, proved disjoint by ADR 0060's rule.
  8. Translation validation of schedules on integer kernels: the refinement goal re-proved after the schedule, so a schedule stops being trusted.
  9. Floats, after M11: tolerance contracts for linalg reductions under ADR 0038.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Library code, not compiler C++, decides how kernels lower, and the compiler gains linalg, tensor, transform and, later, gpu and spirv without a new keyword.
  • A lowering cannot quietly change what was proved: it is proved to refine the Pia definition, proved in Lean, or listed as trusted in every report and certificate that depends on it.
  • Every lowered function keeps a body that the REPL runs and that differential tests compare against, so the REPL never needs the GPU pipeline.
  • piac's reading of MLIR's semantics becomes part of the trusted base for proved lowerings. It is limited to integer arith, index, scf, memref, tensor and linalg.generic, and tested against MLIR's own reference lowering.
  • piac links more of MLIR, which costs build time, a tracked benchmark (ADR 0032); step 1 measures it.
  • MLIR's textual syntax becomes part of Pia libraries' source, so an LLVM upgrade that changes an op's syntax breaks the lowerings that use it, at expansion time with MLIR's diagnostic. The generated Pia.Linalg is regenerated on each upgrade, as the POSIX bindings are on each SDK.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
Dean answered all three on 2026-11-24, each with the recommended option:

  1. The surface: one attribute, @lower, carrying MLIR text with $ splices, or a metaprogram that returns it, on an ordinary let (section 1). There is no MLIR quote language, and no MLIR ops inline in expressions.
  2. The body: every lowered function keeps a Pia body, as its specification and its fallback. There are no lowerings with only a contract, not even in @trusted modules. A foreign function without a body stays an extern.
  3. Schedules: @schedule holds transform-dialect scripts, trusted as compiler passes and listed in the trust report until step 8 validates them (section 2). A friendlier Pia vocabulary, if one is wanted later, is metaprograms that write these scripts.

docs.title: Notes from step 1
docs.text:
Step 1 (trusted lowerings on the CPU) is implemented as decided, with these details settled in the code (codegen.md):

  • Placement. @lower(...) goes where every other function attribute goes, after the return type and before requires, as @opaque and @variadic do, not after ensures as the sketch in section 1 shows.
  • The wrapper. MLIR's parser takes the text as the body of func.func @pia_lowering with the function's core signature, with return added for a function that returns nothing; a function that returns an integer or a bool writes its own return. The body is moved into the real function, every op located at the attribute.
  • Splices and results. A spliced parameter is an integer, a bool or a buffer of them, since a record is several values once records are scalarized; a lowered function returns unit, an integer or a bool, since an array result becomes a buffer the caller makes after IRGen.
  • Named ops on memrefs. linalg.matmul and the other named ops verify on memrefs, so step 1 needs no tensors: memref.expand_shape views a [i8; 16] as memref<4x4xi8>, and convert-linalg-to-loops, expand-strided-metadata and lower-affine take the result to the existing passes. tensor and bufferization are linked and registered but nothing bufferises yet (step 6). transform is linked and registered for step 5.
  • The certificate. Format 2 adds a trusted <kind> <name> <hash> <ops> line, written only by an object that has a lowering, so every other object stays format 1 and older readers still read it. The other trusted kinds of docs/abi.md are not recorded in certificates yet.

docs.title: Notes from step 2
docs.text:
Step 2 (computed lowerings and the checks at expansion) is implemented with these details (codegen.md):

  • Computed text. @lower(gen args) runs the let meta gen during expansion, after the tactics of @by and before operators expand, and its string replaces the call, so IRGen and codegen see a written lowering. The function's parameters are passed as names, as a tactic's are; a metaprogram has no type values during expansion, so element types and shapes are passed as strings and integers (@lower(square_matmul 4 a b c "i8" "i32")) until lowerings can be computed where types are values.
  • Where the check runs. The core types a splice needs exist only after lowerToCore, so "at expansion" is, concretely, right after IRGen, on a copy of the module: checkLowerings runs eraseContracts, lowerToCore and the splice-and-parse on it before any goal is proved, in --emit=mlir, --verify, codegen and the REPL. A module lowerToCore cannot compile yet is skipped there, so --verify keeps working on programs codegen does not support.
  • The operand-effect check reads MLIR's MemoryEffectOpInterface, following memref's view ops back to the parameter. Writing or freeing an input buffer is an error, and so is passing one to an op that declares no effects and has no regions that would. An scf.for that carries an input buffer as an iteration argument is not followed yet.

docs.title: 66. Nonlinear goals are tried first with Z3's int-blasting solver, and other solvers are kept out of the pipeline for now
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-25

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-25, with the answers below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The verifier encodes Pia's integers as signed bit-vectors, wide enough that no term wraps: 68 bits, or 132 bits when a product needs it (encodingWidth in src/verify/Verifier.cpp). Z3 bit-blasts those queries. Bit-blasting is exact, and fast for sums, comparisons and bitwise operations. A 68- or 132-bit multiplier or divider, though, becomes a large circuit, and Z3's SAT search on it is what times out on goals such as a <= b ==> a * c <= b * c. Several pieces of work have run into this:

  • #45, the raster index. (y * w + x) * c + k < w * h * c times out. Pia.Image.Raster works around it with a lemma mul_mono, proved by induction under @solver(tactic = "(using-params smt :bv.solver 2)"), which is Z3's int-blasting solver chosen by hand. The GIF encoder uses the same annotation on put_blocks, frames_bound and blocks_fit.
  • #306, the to_chars round trip. One step of v = q * b^k + dval(...) times out at 60 s.
  • Pia.Core.Rand is parked on a u64 division goal, and Pia.Core.Int's gcd has a weak contract because divisibility is nonlinear.
  • divisionLemma in the verifier states the facts of division beside each / and %, because Z3 cannot bit-blast (a / b) * b + a % b = a at 32 bits within its timeout.

Dean asked (2026-11-24) whether Z3 extensions or other solvers already handle nonlinear goals better. ADR 0061 covers general laws that need induction, in Lean. This ADR covers concrete goals: products and quotients of bounded integers, which are decidable and should be proved automatically.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
Two sets of goals were benchmarked in the cloud (4 x86_64 cores, 30 s per query, one solver per query, 4 at a time).

Hand-written goals. These are 15 of the hard goals above, written in the verifier's encoding: signed bit-vectors at Pia's width, each type's range asserted, and the claim negated. 13 are true and 2 have counterexamples. Each was written four ways: at Pia's width (68 or 132), at the narrowest exact width, as integers (QF_NIA), and as reals (QF_NRA, for goals without division). Z3 is 4.15.1 (piac pins 4.15.2).

Solver, on Pia's bit-vectors True goals proved Counterexamples found Slowest Z3 as piac calls it today (bit-blasting) 2 of 13 2 of 2 timeouts Z3, smt tactic with smt.bv.solver=2 (int-blasting) 13 of 13 2 of 2 1.1 s cvc5 1.4.2, --solve-bv-as-int=sum (int-blasting) 13 of 13 2 of 2 1.2 s cvc5 1.4.2, default (bit-blasting) 2 of 13 2 of 2 timeouts Bitwuzla 0.11 3 of 13 2 of 2 timeouts Yices 2.6.5 2 of 13 2 of 2 timeouts

On the same goals written as integers, Z3's default nonlinear integer arithmetic proves all 13 (slowest 1.5 s), Yices's MCSat proves 11 and gives up on 2 (slowest 0.03 s), and cvc5 proves all 13. The narrowest exact width does not help the bit-blasters: a 66-bit multiplier is as hard as a 68-bit one. The real relaxation, which Z3 decides with nlsat, is fast, but it fails on every goal with a strict < between integers (x < w admits x = w - 0.5), so it adds nothing to integer int-blasting.

Real queries. piac --dump-smt on lib/Pia/Core/Int.pia gives 473 SMT queries (on the iMac, main at 436306d).

Solver Proved Total time Slowest Z3, bit-blasting (the full query) 473 144.8 s 13.7 s Z3, int-blasting on every query 473 34.6 s 20.0 s Z3, int-blasting on the 267 nonlinear queries, bit-blasting the rest 473 15.8 s 1.0 s cvc5, int-blasting on every query 473 38.5 s 0.4 s

The slowest int-blasted query is linear, a chain of bvashr that is cheap to bit-blast and costly to state as integers, so int-blasting is for nonlinear goals only. On the nonlinear queries Z3 bit-blasting took 135.8 s and Z3 int-blasting 6.8 s. In piac's own resource count, routing the nonlinear goals to int-blasting would take the file from 22.6M to 15.1M. piac's count is lower than the plain bit-blasting run above, because piac first tries each division with multiplication and division uninterpreted (abstractArithmetic). The costliest goal, Int.pia:369, falls from 5.3M to 12k.

The Z3 version matters too. Z3 5.4.1 bit-blasts the same 473 queries in 46.9 s, three times faster than 4.15.1, but its int-blasting is slower on the linear ones (170.2 s on every query). Routed as above, 5.4.1 takes 18.0 s. Upgrading Z3 is a separate step, measured by the benchmark on its own.

No solver disagreed with another on any query: none proved a goal that another refuted.

docs.title: The options
docs.text:
1. Encode bit-vectors as integers in the Encoder (QF_NIA). This is exact while no term wraps, which encodingWidth already guarantees for arithmetic. But Pia's goals mix arithmetic with bvand, shifts, rotations and popcounts, which have no cheap integer form. It is a rewrite of the Encoder, and the counterexample printer, for what Z3's int-blasting already does inside the solver.
  2. Z3's int-blasting (smt.bv.solver=2). Z3 translates the bit-vector query to integers inside the solver, with bitwise operations axiomatised lazily. It needs no new dependency, it is deterministic (the same rlimit count on every run), and it is selectable per solver from the C++ API: z3::tactic(ctx, "smt").mk_solver() with the parameter smt.bv.solver = 2. No global parameter is needed, so other goals' solvers are untouched. The smt tactic is needed, because the default solver for a bit-vector query runs the bit-blasting tactic before the SMT core sees it.
  3. nlsat over a real relaxation. It is complete for real arithmetic, but it is weaker than integers wherever integrality matters, as above.
  4. A portfolio with cvc5 and Yices2. cvc5's int-blasting matched Z3's on every goal and was steadier on the real queries (slowest 0.4 s). But cvc5 is a second solver to build with Bazel, with GMP (LGPL) under it, and a second SMT-LIB dialect to keep in step with the smt dialect's export. Yices2 is GPLv3, so it cannot be linked into piac without making piac GPL. It could only run as a separate process that the user installs. Bitwuzla (MIT) is a bit-blaster, and it fails on the same goals as Z3's.
  5. A user propagator for interval multiplication. It is not needed while int-blasting decides the same goals, and a propagator is code inside the trusted base.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A quantifier-free nonlinear goal is tried first with Z3's int-blasting solver. A goal is nonlinear when its query has a bvmul of two terms neither of which is a constant expression, or a bvsdiv or bvsrem by a term that is not one (multipliesVariables, which tracks constant let-bindings so linear products such as (max u32 + 1) * n stay on the bit-blaster). After the abstract attempt (division and multiplication uninterpreted), solve gives such a quantifier-free goal to (then ackermannize_bv smt) with smt.bv.solver = 2, in a context of its own, with a budget of 5M rlimit (kIntBlastRlimit), or the goal's rlimit if that is smaller. The translation is exact both ways, so unsat is a proof. On sat or unknown, the bit-blaster decides the goal as before, and gives the counterexample. Ackermann's reduction (ackermannize_bv) runs first so ground applications of uninterpreted functions, such as opaque spec functions (ADR 0063) and the verifier's own pia_N symbols, do not stall int-blasting: a <= b && f a = a * c ==> f a <= b * c times out at 30 s without it, and proves in 0.07 s after the reduction. On Int.pia's 473 queries the reduction also takes the total from 34.3 s to 27.9 s, with every nonlinear query proving within 90k rlimit (and tests/verify/int_blast.pia's hardest within 585k).
  2. What stays as it is. A goal with a @solver strategy of its own, with theory axioms, with assumptions, or with quantifiers (forall, exists, lambda) keeps today's path. Quantified goals leave int-blasting incomplete and stall on quantified definitions (a single goal can spend minutes hitting a high rlimit). Linear goals keep the bit-blaster.
  3. Reported. A goal proved this way is reported as [smt], as before, and --verify-stats counts these goals as intblast=. --no-int-blast turns the attempt off, for comparison and as an escape hatch. The proof cache is keyed by the query, so its entries are unchanged.
  4. No second solver for now. cvc5 is the fallback to revisit if Z3's int-blasting stops being enough: it is BSD-licensed and was as good on every goal measured, but it means building GMP. Yices2 is not bundled, because of its licence. Bitwuzla and the real relaxation are not used.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Z3 upgraded to 5.4.1. CI on Z3 4.15.2 hit ast.cpp:388 assertion violations and segmentation faults non-deterministically on array-bearing quantifier-free nonlinear queries (Charconv, Gif.Encode, Gif.Quantise, gif_quantise_run) due to use-after-free and soundness bugs in Z3 4.15.2's bv2int_translator / theory_intblast / asserted_formulas (fixed upstream in Z3 PRs #10109, #10485, #10546, #10596, #10707, #10714, #11066, #11098, #11166 and #11417). Pinning Z3 5.4.1 brings all of those fixes (including bvsmod int-blasting). Making piac catch solver crashes cleanly remains tracked under #371.
  • The @solver(tactic = "(using-params smt :bv.solver 2)") annotations in Pia.Image.Raster, Gif.LzwEncode and Gif.Encode become unnecessary, and so may lemmas such as mul_mono that exist only to get around #45. Removing them is a follow-up, done one module at a time with the benchmark.
  • Parked work can be retried: the to_chars round trip (#306), Pia.Core.Rand, gcd's divisibility contract, and the exact sums of Pia.Core.Algo.Numeric.
  • A nonlinear goal that int-blasting cannot prove pays for both attempts. The 5M budget bounds the extra cost, and the benchmark (tools/bench/proof_bench.py) shows whether it ever matters. The baseline is regenerated in the PR that turns the attempt on.
  • The measurements and the scripts that produced them are in the PR. The hard nonlinear goals are a lit test, tests/verify/int_blast.pia.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-25)
docs.text:
1. Int-blasting is on by default. --no-int-blast stays, for comparison.
  2. cvc5 is deferred. It is not built now, and is revisited only if Z3's int-blasting stops being enough.
  3. Nothing GPL, ever. Pia does not bundle, link, call or script any GPL-licensed tool, so Yices2 is out entirely, in the pipeline and in the benchmark scripts.

docs.title: Opaque spec functions and revealed definitions (2026-11-25)
docs.text:
Dean asked how this meets opaque spec functions (ADR 0063). Measured with hand-written goals at Pia's 68-bit width (Z3 4.15.1, 30 s limit):

Goal Bit-blasting Int-blasting After Ackermann's reduction f opaque, the goal nonlinear around f a timeout timeout 0.07 s f revealed with with f: its definition forall x. f x = x * x timeout unknown (6 s) not applicable: quantified f revealed at the arguments used, f a = a * a and f b = b * b timeout — 0.03 s

So an opaque function costs int-blasting nothing once it is reduced to a constant, which is what the decision above does. A reveal that arrives as a quantified definition leaves int-blasting incomplete: Z3 answers unknown, and the goal falls through to the bit-blaster, which times out too. cvc5's int-blasting proved all three, and is the alternative if that matters before step 2.

Step 2, when a reveal meets a product. A with f reveal in a nonlinear goal should give the definition at the ground applications the goal contains, the way fuel unfolds a recursive spec function, instead of as a forall. Then the query is quantifier-free, and the reduction and int-blasting apply. This belongs with ADR 0063's encoding of reveals, and it is measured on the LZW and Huffman goals once they use @opaque.

docs.title: 67. Release 0.1.0 is a small Llama-architecture LLM ported from PyTorch to Pia, proved where a proof means something, running inference on an M3 Mac on CPU SIMD and on the GPU through linalg
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, with Dean's answers to its questions below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for 0.1.0 to ship when Pia has floats and the linalg work, shown by a large language model ported from PyTorch to Pia: start with a small model, prove what can be proved, and have an inference stack that runs on his M3 Mac.

Where the pieces stand today (main at 738b5ec):

  • Floats do not exist yet. 0.5 is a spec-only real; a suffixed literal such as 0.5f32 is refused in genRealConst (src/irgen/IRGen.cpp), and there is no f32 type in Sema, IRGen, the verifier or codegen. ADR 0038 (Accepted) designs how float kernels are proved against real specifications, and none of its eight steps is built. ADR 0012's licences and milestone M11 (#12) are open.
  • Reals exist in specs. real and unbounded int reach Z3 (ADR 0036, step 1), so spec functions over reals, which ADR 0038's error goals need, already work.
  • linalg is designed, not linked. ADR 0065 (Proposed) gives @lower and @schedule, proved lowerings for integer linalg.generic, and the GPU route (tile, map to blocks and threads, convert-gpu-to-spirv, SPIRV-Cross to MSL, a trusted Metal shim). Its 4x4 integer matmul prototype proved 51 of 51 goals in 17.5 s. piac links none of linalg, tensor, gpu or spirv yet.
  • Nonlinear index goals such as i * dim + j < len w are what a transformer's indexing is made of. ADR 0066 (Accepted, in review as PR #421) turns on Z3 int-blasting for them, which proved 13 of 13 such goals in about a second each where bit-blasting timed out.
  • Libraries that help: the JSON library (ADR 0045) reads a safetensors header, Pia.Mem allocators and vec (ADR 0041, 0046) hold weights and the KV cache, Pia.Sys.Posix reads files, and contract-driven tests (ADR 0056) run kernels against references.
  • libm is never trusted (stdlib rule, 2026-11-21). exp, sin and cos must be written and proved in Pia. sqrt is an IEEE 754 operation, correctly rounded by the hardware (fsqrt on arm64), so it is in ADR 0038's round encoding like + and needs no library.
  • Nothing GPL may be used, bundled or depended on, including the model, its tokenizer and any tool in the release path (Dean's standing rule).

docs.title: 1. The model: Karpathy's TinyStories Llama checkpoints, stories260K first, then stories15M
docs.text:
The demo ports the PyTorch Transformer of llama2.c (model.py), a Llama 2 architecture trained on the TinyStories dataset, and runs the checkpoints Karpathy published in karpathy/tinyllamas:

Checkpoint Shape Weights (f32) Tokenizer Licence stories260K dim 64, 5 layers, 8 heads, 4 KV heads (grouped-query attention), context 512 about 1 MB tok512, a 512-token SentencePiece BPE that Karpathy trained MIT (code and weights) stories15M dim 288, 6 layers, 6 heads, context 256 about 60 MB Llama 2's 32,000-token SentencePiece vocabulary MIT for code and weights; the vocabulary file came from Meta's Llama 2 release

Why this family:

  • It is a real modern LLM, small enough to prove. Token embedding, RMSNorm, rotary position embeddings (RoPE), grouped-query attention with a KV cache, SwiGLU feed-forward, residuals, a tied output projection, then sampling. This is the architecture of Llama, Mistral and Qwen, so the kernels are the ones a larger port needs, and every shape is a small constant.
  • It is PyTorch at the source. model.py is the PyTorch module the checkpoints were trained with, so "ported from PyTorch" is literal: each method of Transformer, Attention, FeedForward and RMSNorm becomes a Pia function with the PyTorch line it ports beside it.
  • It has a reference implementation to test against. run.c in the same repository runs the same checkpoints in f32, so token-for-token agreement under greedy decoding is a test, not a claim.
  • The licence is clean. MIT, with no GPL anywhere. stories260K and tok512 are entirely Karpathy's own work; stories15M's vocabulary is Meta's, which is not GPL but is not MIT either, so the release ships stories260K in its tests and fetches stories15M only for the larger demo (open question 1).

Rejected: GPT-2 124M (MIT), which needs LayerNorm, GELU's tanh, learned positions and a 50,257-token byte-level BPE, at 500 MB of f32, with no proof that the extra kernels teach anything Llama's do not; and roneneldan/TinyStories-1M and its siblings, whose model cards state no licence.

f32 throughout for 0.1.0. bf16 or block-format weights (ADR 0038, step 8) are a later example.

docs.title: 2. Weights load from safetensors, checked once at load
docs.text:
A one-off script, tools/llm/export.py (PyTorch, BSD; not in the trusted base and not in the build), converts a llama2.c checkpoint to safetensors with the config in the header's __metadata__. The Pia side, Pia.Format.Safetensors, is pure Pia over bytes read through Pia.Sys.Posix:

  • an 8-byte little-endian header length, a JSON header parsed by the JSON library into a typed record per tensor (dtype, shape, byte offsets), and the data region;
  • proved total on every input: every offset pair is in bounds and ordered, every shape's element count times the dtype size equals its byte range, and a malformed file is an error value, never a crash (the same standard as ADR 0054's codecs);
  • Pia.Llm.Llama.load then checks each tensor's name and shape against the config, and that every weight is finite with |w| <= bound, computing bound from the file. Those checks are what the type of the loaded weights records, so the forward pass starts from proved facts about its inputs, not from trust in the file.

docs.title: 3. What is proved, and what is not
docs.text:
Each property names the layer that proves it. "Every input" means every token sequence and every weight file that passes the load checks.

Property Proved how Status of the claim Shapes. Every matmul, slice and cache access agrees with the config Types and requires: the config is a record of constants, and each kernel takes slices whose lengths are stated in terms of it Proved Bounds. No out-of-bounds read or write, including the KV cache at position pos < seq_len and GQA's head mapping h / (n_heads / n_kv_heads) Index goals, int-blasted (ADR 0066), with one bounds lemma per indexing map (ADR 0065's prototype finding) Proved No NaN, no infinity, no overflow anywhere in a forward pass Float intervals (ADR 0038, layer 1) from the load-time weight bound: RMSNorm's output is bounded by sqrt dim * max |g|; softmax subtracts the row maximum, so every exp argument is <= 0 and every probability is in [0, 1]; the residual stream's bound grows by a computed amount per layer; logits are finite Proved, for the loaded weights' bound Termination and memory. Generation stops after steps <= seq_len tokens; every allocation is fallible and handled Ordinary measures and ADR 0026 Proved Kernels equal their specification. The SIMD, tiled and GPU kernels compute what the scalar Pia kernel says, up to a stated tolerance ADR 0065's refinement goal for each @lower; under @fp(reassoc) the tolerance is the order-free γₙ bound (ADR 0038, section on reassociation) Proved on CPU; on the GPU, proved against the device float model, which is trusted (section 4) Per-kernel float error. Each of matvec, rmsnorm, softmax, silu, rope and exp is within a bound of its real-valued specification ADR 0038 layers 2 and 3: per-operation δ with nlsat for straight-line code, Higham's γₙ lemmas for reductions, ~= with derived bounds published in interfaces Proved exp, sin, cos against the real functions Range reduction proved in Z3; the polynomial's distance from the real function proved in Lean with Mathlib (ADR 0061), because Z3 has no exp Proved, with Lean lemmas listed by hash End-to-end error of the logits against the real-valued model Composed from the per-kernel bounds by ADR 0038's lip/err pair Derived and reported, not claimed useful: through 5 layers of attention a worst-case bound is likely far looser than the observed error, so the release reports both Agreement with PyTorch Differential test against run.c and model.py: identical greedy tokens for a fixed prompt set, and the maximum absolute logit difference Tested, not proved: reductions sum in a different order, so bit-equality is not the goal Tokenizer. Encoding terminates, every emitted id is < vocab_size, and decoding an encoding gives back the input bytes BPE merges as a loop with a decreasing measure; byte fallback makes the round trip total Proved Sampling. The sampled id is < vocab_size; temperature and top-p keep the distribution's support; the PRNG is the integer xorshift run.c uses Contracts on sample; the PRNG is integer code Proved; the randomness of the PRNG is not Model quality: that the stories are coherent, that the weights mean anything Nothing Not provable. The demo says so on its first page

docs.title: 4. Execution on the M3, in three stages
docs.text:
The same Pia functions are the specification at every stage. A later stage replaces a body's code, never its contract.

  1. Scalar CPU. The plain Pia port, compiled by today's codegen (with f32 added) and run by the REPL's JIT. This is the stage that first matches run.c token for token. stories260K runs interactively at this stage.
  2. CPU SIMD. matvec, rmsnorm, softmax and the attention dot products vectorised for NEON: first by LLVM's vectoriser under @fp(reassoc) (ADR 0012), then with ADR 0065's @schedule (tile and vectorise, step 5) where the vectoriser does not. Benchmarked in tokens per second against run.c built with -O3 -ffast-math.
  3. GPU. The matmuls (the Q, K, V, O, gate, up, down and classifier projections) lower with @lower to linalg.matvec/linalg.matmul on memref, are scheduled with tile_using_forall and mapped to threads, go through convert-gpu-to-spirv, and SPIRV-Cross writes MSL, which a trusted Metal shim compiles and launches (ADR 0065, section 6). The device's float model (ADR 0038, "Mixed precision and devices") is a trusted theory: it states, for each operation, the precision the Metal Shading Language specification gives with fast math off (compiled with fast math off), and treats subnormals as possibly flushed, so the tolerance contracts account for both. Softmax, RMSNorm and sampling stay on the CPU for 0.1.0. For stories260K the GPU will be slower than the CPU, since each matmul is tiny; the GPU stage is measured on stories15M, where it can win.

Prompt processing runs the same per-token path as generation in 0.1.0 (batched prefill with linalg.matmul is a later step).

docs.title: 5. Dependency PRs
docs.text:
Sizes: S is about a day of work and one PR, M two to three days, L a week or more, possibly split. Owners are the threads already working in the area.

Floats (M11, ADR 0012, ADR 0038)

# PR Size Status F1 f32 and f64 types: suffixed literals, arithmetic, comparisons, conversions to and from integers, to_bits/from_bits, strict IEEE codegen (no flush-to-zero) L not started F2 The verifier's float encoding, step 1 of ADR 0038: to_real, finite, eps, tiny, the Float concept with builtin adapters, float intervals in the interval stage; bit-precise FP behind @solver(fp_exact) L not started F3 Step 2: the round encoding with per-operation δ, nlsat for straight-line error goals M not started F4 Step 3: Pia.Float.Error with γₙ, and the summation, dot product and matrix-vector lemmas M not started F5 Step 4 plus ADR 0012's licence: @fp(reassoc) and contract in codegen, order-free bounds M not started F6 Step 6: a ~= e within b, derived bounds published in interfaces M not started F7 Step 5: device float models in placement, with the Apple GPU's model S not started; needed only for stage 3

Maths without libm (Pia.Math)

# PR Size Status X1 sqrt as a builtin IEEE operation, and rsqrt as 1 / sqrt with its error S needs F1, F3 X2 exp for f32: reduction by ln 2, a degree-6 polynomial, scaling through the exponent bits; finite on x <= 88.7, error bound against a real exp theory whose model and polynomial lemma are proved in Lean M needs F1-F4 and ADR 0061's runner X3 sin and cos for f32 on the range RoPE uses (|x| <= seq_len), the same way M needs X2's machinery

Kernels (Pia.Nn) and the model (Pia.Llm)

# PR Size Status K1 matvec with its γₙ tolerance and bounds lemmas S needs F4 K2 rmsnorm, softmax (max-subtracted, probabilities in [0, 1], sum within tolerance of 1), silu/SwiGLU, residual add M needs X1, X2 K3 rope and grouped-query attention over a KV cache M needs X3, K1, K2 M1 Pia.Format.Safetensors, proved total, and tools/llm/export.py M integer-only, can start now M2 Tokenizer: tok512 vocabulary loader, BPE encode, decode, the round trip M integer-only, can start now M3 Sampling: argmax, temperature, top-p, xorshift S needs F1 for the probabilities M4 Pia.Llm.Llama: config, weights, load checks, forward, generate; examples/llm/stories.pia as a command; the differential test against run.c L needs K1-K3, M1-M3

Execution

# PR Size Status E1 CPU SIMD: @fp(reassoc) kernels vectorised to NEON, tokens-per-second benchmark against run.c M needs F5, M4 E2 ADR 0065 steps 1-4 with float linalg.generic meanings (arith.addf/mulf under the round encoding), Pia.Linalg.matvec and matmul L ADR 0065 thread; needs F3 for the float meaning E3 ADR 0065 step 5: @schedule on CPU M ADR 0065 thread E4 The GPU ADR, then ADR 0065 step 7: SPIR-V, SPIRV-Cross, the Metal shim, @place(gpu) for the projections L GPU demo thread and ADR 0065 thread E5 The literate walkthrough, docs/llm.pia.md: the port beside model.py, the proof report, the trust report, the benchmark M last

The critical path is F1, F2, F3, F4, X2, K2, K3, M4, then E1 and E4 in parallel. M1 and M2 run alongside floats from day one; E2 and E3 run alongside the kernels.

docs.title: 6. The 0.1.0 release checklist
docs.text:
0.1.0 is tagged when all of these hold:

  • [ ] stories260K generates a story on Dean's M3 with the stories command built from examples/llm/stories.pia, matching run.c's greedy tokens for the fixed prompt set, on the scalar, SIMD and GPU paths.
  • [ ] stories15M runs on the GPU path, with its tokens per second reported against run.c.
  • [ ] Every goal in lib/Pia/Math, lib/Pia/Nn, lib/Pia/Llm and lib/Pia/Format is proved, with no --allow flags; the report gives goals per file, wall-clock time, the costliest goals, and the split between Z3, intervals and Lean.
  • [ ] piac --trust-report for the demo lists exactly: the IEEE round encoding, the Apple GPU float model, the Metal shim's extern contracts, the GPU lowering and schedule items, and nothing else.
  • [ ] The proof benchmark (ADR 0032) includes the float kernels, and the gate passes on CI.
  • [ ] M11 (#12) is closed; ADR 0065 is Accepted and its steps 1 to 5 and 7 are merged.
  • [ ] docs/llm.pia.md is on the site and doc-tested, and the status page and the skill pack list floats, Pia.Math, Pia.Nn and Pia.Llm.
  • [ ] Licences audited: no GPL in the build, the release or the fetched model; stories15M's vocabulary licence stated where it is fetched.
  • [ ] piac --version prints 0.1.0; release notes say what 0.1.0 proves and what it does not (section 3's last rows); macOS arm64 binaries attached to the GitHub release.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• 0.1.0 is gated on floats, which are the largest missing piece: F1 to F4 are about three weeks of PRs before the first float kernel proves. The integer parts of the model (safetensors, tokenizer) start now, so they are ready when the kernels are.
  • The demo turns ADR 0038 and ADR 0065 from designs into code with a user, and the kernels it needs (matvec, softmax, rmsnorm, exp) are the start of a reusable Pia.Nn.
  • The claims are bounded and stated: safety, shapes, finiteness and per-kernel error are proved; agreement with PyTorch is tested; quality is not addressed. The end-to-end bound is reported even when it is loose, because hiding it would overclaim.
  • The trusted base grows by the GPU's float model and the Metal shim, both named in the trust report, as ADR 0038 and ADR 0065 already require.
  • Lean becomes part of the release path for exp, sin and cos, so ADR 0061's runner must work on the iMac and in CI by then.

docs.title: Answers to the review questions
docs.text:
Dean accepted this ADR on 2026-11-24 and answered both questions. These answers are part of the decision.

  1. The headline is stories260K, with stories15M on the GPU. Every test, proof report and CI run uses stories260K. stories15M is fetched, not committed, for the GPU benchmark, and the place that fetches it states its vocabulary's licence.
  2. The GPU path gates 0.1.0, for the matmuls. The projections run on Metal through @lower, linalg, SPIR-V and SPIRV-Cross before the tag. ADR 0065 step 7 and the GPU ADR are on the critical path; softmax, RMSNorm and sampling stay on the CPU.

docs.title: 68. GPU compute: a proved spread placed on the GPU, lowered through SPIR-V and SPIRV-Cross to Metal, launched by a small trusted shim
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-25

Status: Accepted (2026-11-25, with Dean's answers below). Section 9 and step 4b, a placed sequence, are an amendment Accepted on 2026-11-27, with Dean's answer below.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0015 lets code be placed on the GPU with @place(gpu) and requires that placement never change the proved result. Nothing implements it yet: the compiler has no GPU code, and pia_par has no lowering to a device. Three things now need it:

  • The flagship demo (ADR 0016, ADR 0055 section 6). D8 directions, rendering and the pull form of the sediment step all write one cell per iteration. On a real SRTM tile (13.0M cells, PR #422) the CPU pipeline takes 3.7 s.
  • Lowerings written in Pia (ADR 0065 section 6). That ADR takes a linalg kernel down to a spirv.module and defers the host side, the Metal shim and @place(gpu) to "the GPU ADR". This is that ADR.
  • Release 0.1.0 (ADR 0067, Proposed). Its milestone is a proved small Llama model on the M3, which needs f32 matrix-vector products on the GPU, with weights kept on the GPU across tokens.

Dean decided on 2026-11-23 (on the survey) that the GPU path is SPIR-V, so that AMD, Intel and NVIDIA can come later through Vulkan, with SPIRV-Cross translating it to MSL for Metal now.

What is already in place:

  • spread v0 (ADR 0060) proves that each iteration writes only the cells it owns, one iteration at a time. This is exactly the fact a GPU kernel needs: each thread is an iteration, and no two threads write the same cell.
  • ADR 0038 defines tolerance contracts over a rounding theory. Each device has a float model that states its eps, its tiny (the absolute error term) and the operations it does not round correctly. A kernel may be placed only on a device whose model proves its contract.
  • Apple Silicon has unified memory. A MTLBuffer in shared storage mode is the same physical memory to the CPU and the GPU, so placing work on the GPU copies nothing.

docs.title: 1. A kernel is a spread placed on the GPU
docs.text:
@place(gpu) on a spread makes each iteration a GPU thread. The loop is proved exactly as on the CPU: by the body, the ownership goals of ADR 0060 and the loop's ensures. Nothing about the proof depends on the placement. The rules of spread v0 carry over unchanged: no assignment to outer variables, writes only through owned cells, and calls only with footprints.

A GPU body has extra rules, checked by the type checker:

  • No calls that cannot run on the device. Allowed are other functions the compiler can inline, or that are themselves GPU-placeable: no allocation, no foreign calls, no I/O, no recursion.
  • Element types the device supports. These are integers of 8 to 64 bits and, after M11, f32. Storage of 8- and 16-bit elements uses SPIR-V's StorageBuffer8BitAccess and 16BitAccess.
  • Every buffer the body touches is a device buffer (section 4), or a slice the shim can wrap without a copy.

A function marked @place(gpu) is a function whose body is one such spread plus scalar set-up, so let directions (dem) (out) @place(gpu) = spread i in 0 .. len out do ... done reads as one kernel.

Placement does not change an integer result. The body that runs on the GPU is the body that was proved. Integer operations have one meaning in Pia: wrap, saturate and checked are explicit, and division by zero and shifts out of range are already proved absent. Codegen lowers each operation to the same SPIR-V arithmetic on every device. So for integer kernels, ADR 0015's rule holds by construction, and the differential tests (section 6) check the toolchain rather than the proof.

docs.title: 2. The lowering: scf.parallel to gpu to SPIR-V to MSL
docs.text:
IRGen already lowers spread to scf.parallel (ADR 0060). For a GPU-placed loop, codegen then runs upstream MLIR passes only:
