  1. gpu-map-parallel-loops and convert-parallel-loops-to-gpu make a gpu.launch with one thread per iteration, in blocks of a fixed size (256 by default; a @schedule from ADR 0065 can choose it).
  2. gpu-kernel-outlining moves the body into a gpu.module, and gpu.launch_func stays on the host.
  3. The storage-class mapping and convert-gpu-to-spirv (with arith, memref and scf to SPIR-V) produce a spirv.module. It is serialised to a SPIR-V binary with the target environment Vulkan 1.1 plus the capabilities above.
  4. SPIRV-Cross translates the binary to MSL, with the Metal version and argument-buffer options fixed by the target model.
  5. The Metal compiler (xcrun metal, then metallib) builds a .metallib, which is embedded in the object file as a section. At load, the shim finds kernels by name.

The host side of gpu.launch_func lowers to calls into the shim (section 3), not to MLIR's GPU runtime wrappers. Those wrappers exist for CUDA, ROCm and Vulkan, but not for Metal.

ADR 0065's linalg kernels join the same pipeline at step 1. Their @schedule maps scf.forall to blocks and threads, and steps 2 to 5 are shared.

docs.title: 3. The host shim is small, written in Objective-C, and trusted
docs.text:
src/runtime/metal/ is one Objective-C file over Metal, compiled with ARC, plus a C header. It exposes about eight functions, each declared in Pia as an extern with a contract:

  • device_open returns a device or Gpu_unavailable.
  • buffer_new makes a shared-storage buffer of n bytes, or returns Gpu_out_of_memory. buffer_view gives the CPU a slice over it, with no copy. buffer_free releases it.
  • kernel_get looks a kernel up in the embedded library by name, with a pipeline cache.
  • dispatch takes a kernel, its buffers, scalar arguments and a grid size. It encodes one compute pass, commits it, and waits for completion. It returns Ok, Gpu_fault (a command buffer error) or Gpu_timeout.

v0 is synchronous, so when dispatch returns, the GPU's writes are visible to the CPU and no buffer is in use by the device. That keeps ownership trivial: the host cannot touch a buffer while a kernel writes it, because the host is blocked. Asynchronous launches come with Pia.Exec.Metal (ADR 0050 step 9), where a buffer is moved into the GPU stage and returned in its value. That is the same rule, expressed as a sender.

The shim, SPIRV-Cross, the Metal compiler and the upstream MLIR GPU and SPIR-V conversions are trusted items, listed in the trust report and the certificate (ADR 0024). They are trusted the way the MLIR async runtime is in ADR 0060, and for the same reason: they are external toolchain pieces with wide use. Section 6 says how they are tested.

docs.title: 4. Device buffers are linear resources that stay on the GPU
docs.text:
Pia.Gpu.buffer t is a @linear resource (ADR 0026) that holds len elements of t in a shared-storage MTLBuffer. Making one is fallible, like every allocation. drop frees it. It lives as long as its owner, so weights loaded once stay resident across many launches. This is the LLM's requirement: load once, then one matrix-vector product per token.

On the CPU, view b is a slice of t over the same memory. It is borrowed, so it cannot outlive the buffer, and the type checker forbids holding it across a dispatch that writes b. A kernel takes buffers, not slices. Slices of a buffer (b.[lo .. hi]) are passed as a buffer and an offset.

On a device with its own memory (later, Vulkan), the same type holds device memory, and view becomes an explicit, fallible transfer. The Pia code does not change.

docs.title: 5. Errors: placement may fail, and the caller decides
docs.text: A @place(gpu) function's error set gains Gpu.error (Gpu_unavailable | Gpu_out_of_memory | Gpu_fault | Gpu_timeout), handled with ? as any other error (ADR 0028). An explicit placement never silently runs on the CPU. @place(auto, prefer = gpu) may fall back to the CPU, because both run the same proved body. For integers the result is the same. For floats the fallback is allowed only when the CPU's float model also proves the contract, which the strict IEEE CPU model always does when the GPU's does.

docs.title: 6. Testing what is trusted
docs.text:
• Differential tests. Every @place(gpu) test runs the kernel on the CPU too. Integers must match bit for bit. Floats must lie within the proved tolerance of each other and of a f64 reference.
  • A litmus battery for the float model (section 7), run on each Apple GPU we support. It checks the rounding of +, -, * and fma against a correctly rounded reference, subnormal inputs and outputs, and whether a * b + c was contracted, for every rounding-sensitive pattern. It runs as for atomics (ADR 0052).
  • GPU tests run on the iMac only, tagged requires-gpu. Linux CI has no Metal, so it builds the SPIR-V and the MSL (SPIRV-Cross runs anywhere) and checks them with spirv-val, but does not run them. A Vulkan runner can come with a Linux GPU.

docs.title: 7. The Apple GPU float model
docs.text:
Each placement target has a float model under ADR 0038. Pia.Device.Apple_gpu is a theory with one model per GPU family (M1 to M4 first). For f32 it states:

  • Rounding. +, -, * and fma round to nearest even when fast math is off, so eps f32 = 2⁻²⁴. Pia compiles MSL with fast math off (-fno-fast-math), and the MSL specification's accuracy table lists these operations as correctly rounded. The litmus battery confirms it for each family. Division and sqrt are not correctly rounded on all families, so the model gives their error in ulps from the battery, or leaves them out, which makes a kernel that uses them unplaceable until it is measured.
  • Subnormals may be flushed. The model takes tiny = 2⁻¹²⁶ (the smallest normal) as the absolute error term of every operation, instead of the CPU's half-subnormal. That is sound whether or not a family flushes. If the battery shows that a family keeps subnormals, its model can use the CPU's value.
  • Contraction is stated, not assumed away. SPIR-V marks an operation that must not be contracted with NoContraction. Pia marks every float operation NoContraction unless ADR 0012 licenses contraction for that expression, so the GPU computes what was proved. Whether SPIRV-Cross carries the decoration into MSL is checked in step 6. If it does not, contraction is turned off for the whole kernel with the Metal compiler's options. If the battery finds a family that contracts anyway, its model says "may contract", which is still sound for ADR 0038's bounds because a contraction only removes a rounding.
  • Reduction order is free. Threadgroup reductions reorder sums, so a GPU reduction is proved with ADR 0038's order-free bound, γₙ for a sum of length n. That bound does not depend on the tree, so the proof holds for any schedule.

f16 and bf16 are later. The model is a trusted theory, since Apple documents correct rounding only in prose, and it is listed in the trust report.

docs.title: 8. Threadgroup memory, barriers and SIMD-group matrices
docs.text:
A spread v0 iteration shares nothing with other iterations, so it cannot use threadgroup memory. A tiled reduction or matmul needs a tile in threadgroup memory, a barrier, and threads that read each other's writes after it. These come through ADR 0065's @schedule (tile_using_forall with promotion to workgroup memory, upstream gpu.barrier), trusted at first and translation-validated later (ADR 0065 step 8), not through new spread syntax. A language-level form, a group of iterations with a scratch buffer they share between barriers, is left for a later ADR, once a kernel needs it that a schedule cannot express.

Apple's SIMD-group matrix operations (simdgroup_matrix) are vendor ops with no SPIR-V equivalent that SPIRV-Cross maps. If used, they are a trusted @lower to MSL (ADR 0065, state 3) behind a Pia contract. They are optional.

docs.title: 9. A sequence of placed spreads is one command buffer (amendment, Accepted 2026-11-27)
docs.text:
Step 4 put each wave of the sediment pull step on the GPU, one wave per placed spread, with the commit pass on the CPU between waves. It is correct, but slow. On the tile N46E008, 3,924 waves a step take 33 to 57 s, against 0.5 s on the CPU. Each wave is one pia_gpu_run: it wraps about nine tile-sized buffers, which maps their pages into the GPU's address space, then commits one command buffer and waits. That costs 8 to 15 ms a wave, while the kernel takes only microseconds. A step that waits for the GPU between waves cannot beat the CPU, whatever the shim caches. Dean chose (2026-11-27) to remove the waits: a whole step becomes one command buffer.

@place(gpu) on a sequential for makes a placed sequence. Its body may hold spreads, ghost code (lemma calls and assertions), and scalar lets. The spreads need no @place of their own: each becomes a kernel, and each iteration of the for encodes their dispatches, in order, into one command buffer. The host wraps every buffer once, commits once and waits once. For the pull step:

let ok = for k in 0 .. waves @place(gpu)
  invariant ...
do
  let lo = starts.[k] in
  let hi = starts.[k + 1] in
  spread q in lo .. hi do ... done;                  (* the wave *)
  spread q in lo .. hi @owns(bed, pos) @owns(flux, pos) @owns(seen, pos)
  do ... done                                       (* its commit *)
done

The rules, each checked by piac:

  • The host runs the scalar code while it encodes. A scalar let in the body may read only buffers that no kernel of the sequence writes, such as starts above. So each dispatch's bounds are known when it is encoded, and no value has to come back from the GPU. Reading back a value the GPU computes, such as indirect dispatch, is left for later.
  • Dispatches run in order, each after the one before has finished. Metal's default serial compute encoder gives this, so the sequence means what the for means on the CPU: every spread sees all writes of the spreads before it. A sequence that needs no ordering between two dispatches can say so later, with a concurrent encoder.
  • The proof does not change. The for is proved as written, with its invariants, and its spreads are proved as in section 1. Placement adds no goal.
  • Errors are as in section 5. The sequence evaluates to result unit gpu_error. On Ok, the for's postcondition holds. On Err, every buffer the sequence writes may be partly written, and nothing about it is promised.
  • After a spread, the cells no iteration of its range owns keep their values. An iteration writes only cells it owns, so this holds on the CPU and on the GPU, whatever the run's status. Today the verifier forgets every cell of a written buffer after a spread, so a wave's commit could not say that the cells of other waves are unchanged. The verifier gains this frame fact for every spread, placed or not.
  • A spread in a sequence may own cells through an owner array (@owns(buf, owner), ADR 0060), not only by identity. On the device an owner is only a proof fact: the kernel writes where the body says. This lifts step 3's rule against @owns on the GPU, for spreads in a sequence and on their own. The pull step needs it: the commit writes cell order.[q] from slot q, and pos is its owner array, since pos.[order.[q]] = q.

The shim gets three new entries: pia_gpu_seq_begin makes the command buffer and its encoder, pia_gpu_seq_dispatch encodes one dispatch (a kernel, its buffers, its bounds and its scalars), and pia_gpu_seq_end commits the command buffer and waits for it once. Codegen calls pia_gpu_seq_begin before the for and pia_gpu_seq_end after it, and each spread in the body becomes a pia_gpu_seq_dispatch, so the dispatches are encoded as the for runs and nothing runs on the GPU until the end. The shim wraps the pages of each buffer once a sequence, and sets each dispatch's scalars with setBytes, which copies them into the command buffer as they are encoded. A table of every dispatch, made first and passed in one call, would hold about 8,000 entries a step on the host stack; encoding as the for runs needs none.

The pull step's other work moves out of the loop. The wave boundaries, which wave_end finds one at a time, are found before the step by a proved scan into starts. The mass sent off the map, which copy_back added up wave by wave, is osum order down flux n of the final loads, summed on the CPU after the step. Both are linear and cheap next to the step. The commit of a wave, a spread with owner array pos, needs a lemma that commits a whole wave at once, commit_wave. It is proved from the same facts copy_cell uses: the cells of a wave have the same height, so none drains into another, and committing one cell leaves the others' inflows as they were.

The expected cost of a step is the kernels plus the encoding, about 8,000 dispatches. At a few microseconds each that is tens of milliseconds, against 0.5 s on the CPU. The measurement on the tile decides it.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is one PR and useful on its own. Steps 1 to 4 are integer-only.

  1. Toolchain. Link the gpu and spirv dialects and conversions into piac. Add SPIRV-Cross and SPIRV-Tools as Bazel modules (from the Bazel Central Registry where they are, otherwise pinned like Z3). Add a macOS-only rule that runs xcrun metal and metallib and embeds the library. Test: a hand-written gpu.module that adds two buffers goes all the way to a .metallib, and spirv-val passes.
  2. The shim and Pia.Gpu.buffer. src/runtime/metal/, the extern contracts, the trust items, and buffer with view and drop. Test: a C harness dispatches step 1's kernel on the iMac.
  3. @place(gpu) on a spread with identity ownership, with the device rules of section 1 and the error set of section 5. First kernels: D8 directions and render from the streams demo, with differential tests against the CPU on the SRTM fixture and the full tile. Done (2026-11-27). src/gpu/Place.cpp outlines, lowers and embeds each placed spread at compile time (taking in issue #435), and the shim's pia_gpu_run runs it. placed.pia.md has both kernels. On the 3601 × 3601 tile N46E008, both match the CPU on every cell. With a warm device on the iMac, directions take 35 to 52 ms on the GPU against 41 ms on the CPU, and render 66 to 83 ms against 37 to 50 ms. The first run adds about 70 ms to open the device and load the library. Each run copies every buffer into a new MTLBuffer and back, and the copies dominate, so the next step is to wrap page-aligned host memory without a copy (newBufferWithBytesNoCopy) or to keep Pia.Gpu.buffers resident. Copies removed (2026-11-27). On Apple silicon pia_gpu_run wraps each buffer that starts on a page boundary with newBufferWithBytesNoCopy, and copies only the scalars and any other buffer, counting both. That is safe because the run is synchronous (section 3). macOS's malloc already puts tile-sized buffers on a page. Pia allocates no heap buffers of its own: they come from the caller, or are local arrays on the stack. On the full tile, directions now take 6 to 16 ms on the GPU against 41 ms on the CPU, and render 9 to 12 ms against 25 to 30 ms, warm; the first run of directions takes 50 to 60 ms.
  4. The sediment pull step on the GPU, once its equality proof against the sequential step is merged (ADR 0055 section 6). The demo page then shows CPU and GPU timings on real tiles. Built (#463, 2026-11-27). The page docs/pull_gpu.pia.md places each wave and imports the commit pass and its proof through pull.pia.md's PullWaves interface. It matches the CPU on every cell of the tile, at 33 to 57 s a step against 0.5 s on the CPU, one GPU run per wave (section 9). 4b. A placed sequence (section 9): @place(gpu) on a for, @owns on the device, the shim's sequence entries, and the pull step as one command buffer a step, with its CPU and GPU timings on the tile. Built (#471, 2026-11-28). On N46E008 the pull step takes about 236 ms on the GPU against 530 ms on the CPU, 31,392 dispatches in four steps, matching the CPU on every cell (pull_gpu.pia.md). Pre-warmed (2026-11-28). A kernel's first run used to pay for opening the device, loading its library and building its pipeline: 37 to 54 ms for directions on the tile, against 5 ms warm. Now each object with placed kernels has a load-time constructor, pia$gpu$warm, that hands every kernel to the shim's pia_gpu_warm. A background queue then builds them while the program starts, and a run that comes first waits for the one it needs instead of building it again. Setting PIA_GPU_WARM=0 turns this off, so a cold first run can still be timed. On N46E008, over three runs each way, the first run of directions drops from 42 to 57 ms to 13 to 19 ms. The first run of render (18 to 40 ms) and the first pull step (246 to 274 ms, against 235 ms warm) are the same either way, so what they pay for first is not the pipeline. The likely cause, not yet measured, is the GPU's first touch of newly wrapped buffers. Pre-warming adds no goal and changes no result. It needs no syntax either: a program that places a kernel will run it.
  5. ADR 0065 schedules on the GPU: tile_using_forall mapped to blocks and threads, workgroup promotion, an integer matmul.
  6. Floats, after M11: the Apple GPU float model and its litmus battery, NoContraction, and an f32 matrix-vector product with a tolerance contract (γₙ, n up to 768) for the 0.1.0 LLM.
  7. Pia.Exec.Metal: asynchronous launches as senders (ADR 0050 step 9), and placement of @place(auto) stages by the cost model.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The flagship demo and the 0.1.0 LLM get the GPU through one path, and that path is SPIR-V, so Vulkan devices need only a second shim.
  • Integer kernels are proved once, and placing them on the GPU adds no proof obligation. The new trust is the toolchain (MLIR GPU and SPIR-V conversions, SPIRV-Cross, the Metal compiler) and a small shim. All of it is listed, and all of it is checked by differential tests.
  • Float kernels on the GPU are proved against a stated device model, with subnormal flushing and contraction accounted for, so no kernel relies on Metal behaviour that wasn't written down.
  • Building GPU code needs Xcode's Metal toolchain on macOS. Linux builds the SPIR-V and MSL but cannot run them.
  • Pia.Gpu.buffer is a new resource type, and the type checker gains device rules for GPU-placed bodies.

docs.title: Answers to the review questions
docs.text:
Dean answered on 2026-11-25. Each answer is the proposed option:

  1. ~~Explicit placement and failure?~~ @place(gpu) adds Gpu.error to the function's error set. An explicit placement never runs silently on the CPU. Only @place(auto, prefer = gpu) may fall back.
  2. ~~Where is MSL compiled?~~ At build time, by xcrun metal and metallib, into a .metallib embedded in the object file. No compiler runs or is trusted at run time, and GPU builds need Xcode's Metal toolchain.
  3. ~~The shim's language?~~ Objective-C with ARC. It is one small file compiled by clang, with no extra dependency.

docs.title: Answer to the review question for section 9
docs.text:
Dean answered on 2026-11-27:

  1. ~~How is a placed sequence written?~~ @place(gpu) on a sequential for, so its spreads need no @place of their own, and no new keyword is added. The alternative was a new block form, such as gpu do ... done, around spreads that each keep @place(gpu).

docs.title: 69. Pure and impure functions: computed purity, @pure assertions, and @impure interface boundaries
Context
docs.text:
Issue #375 showed that when an ordinary function returning a record — such as Pia.Time.civil_from_days — is named more than once in a contract, the verifier encoded each mention as an unrelated fresh value. The interface conformance check substitutes result with a call at every mention, so ensures days_from_civil result.year result.month result.day = z became three separate calls whose fields were never tied together.

Inside a single module, the verifier can walk a function's body and call graph to decide whether it is deterministic. Across a module boundary, it cannot. Today a .piai interface (ADR 0039) carries no purity information:

  • Pia.Sys.Posix.open, close, lseek and errno take no out or inout parameters, yet wrap extern C syscalls with observable side effects (file descriptors, global errno, OS state).
  • Pia.Time.civil_from_days is genuinely pure, yet an importer sees the same kind of signature as Posix.open.
  • Existing contractOnly in src/verify/Verifier.cpp encodes every single-scalar imported function as one uninterpreted function, which is unsound for impure scalar FFI wrappers such as Posix.close or Posix.errno when called more than once.

At the same time, programmers have no way to assert that a function is pure and have the compiler reject an accidental side effect, nor to see from an interface whether an exported function has hidden effects.

docs.title: 1. Three levels of purity, computed by the compiler
docs.text:
Every function in Pia has a purity level computed by the compiler from its signature, its body and its transitive call graph:

  1. Strongly pure (total, no effects). Takes no out, inout, mutable, atomic or dyn parameters; performs no hidden effects (section 2); and is proved to terminate (every while loop and recursive cycle has a decreases measure, matching ADR 0043 and ADR 0044). Local mutation (let mutable locals, non-escaping local buffers from with_arena, and calling weakly-pure functions on local buffers) and returning fixed arrays [T; N] are allowed: repeated calls on equal arguments always return equal values and change no observable state outside the call.
  2. Weakly pure (parameter mutation only, total). Takes one or more out, inout or mutable parameters, performs no hidden effects, and is proved to terminate. Examples include Algo.Sort.sort and Vec.push. Its effects are completely visible in its parameter modifiers, so it needs no @impure attribute and may be called on local buffers inside a strongly-pure function. It cannot be called directly in contracts.
  3. Impure (@impure). Performs or transitively calls any hidden, concurrent, or potentially non-terminating effect:
  4. any foreign = extern "..." declaration (always impure; see section 3),
  5. any unsafe call or unsafe view,
  6. any pointer-address operation (AddressOp / AtAddressOp),
  7. any atomic operation or atomic parameter (ADR 0052),
  8. any while loop or recursion without a proved decreases measure,
  9. any call to an impure function (including imported @impure functions).

Calls to let spec functions and let lemma proofs never make a function impure.

docs.title: 2. @pure and @impure attributes
docs.text:
(* Private functions infer purity automatically; no attribute is needed. *)
let civil_from_days (z : int{-365962028..364523337}) : ymd = ...

(* Optional @pure asserts strong purity + totality; violation is an error. *)
let civil_from_days (z : int{-365962028..364523337}) : ymd @pure = ...

(* Exported impure functions must declare @impure in their interface. *)
interface Posix = sig
  let open : (path : [u8]) -> (flags : i32) -> i32 @impure @variadic(2)
    requires len path >= 1 && path.[len path - 1] = 0
    ensures result >= -1
  let close : (fd : i32) -> i32 @impure
    ensures result >= -1 && result <= 0
end
  • Private functions: purity and impurity are computed automatically, so private helpers and atomic primitives (such as tests/verify/atomics.pia) need no annotation.
  • @pure: an explicit, compiler-checked assertion of strong purity and totality. Placing @pure on a function that takes out/inout/mutable or atomic parameters, performs a hidden effect, calls an impure function, or lacks proved termination is a compile-time error.
  • @impure: explicitly declares hidden, concurrent or non-terminating effects.
  • Lint (ADR 0037): a lint (impure_interface) recommends adding @impure on definitions and interface rows whose computed purity is impure when they are part of a module's interface, so the annotation stays visible at the definition as well as the interface.

docs.title: 3. Foreign (= extern "...") functions are always @impure
docs.text: Every = extern "..." declaration is unconditionally @impure. Marking a foreign declaration @pure is a compile-time error, even inside a @trusted module: pure functions are proved in Pia (or modelled as a library theory, ADR 0036), never trusted through C FFI. Purity therefore adds zero unverified trust surface to --trust-report.

docs.title: 4. Interfaces, .piai export and conformance
docs.text:
Matches ADR 0004 ("the strongest guarantee is always the default; every weakening is visible in the source and, where it affects callers, in the interface"):

  • Unmarked interface rows default to non-impure (strongly pure when there are no out/inout/mutable parameters; weakly pure when there are). An implementation whose computed purity is impure fails interface conformance unless the interface row carries @impure.
  • Subtyping: a strongly-pure (or weakly-pure) implementation satisfies an @impure interface row (stronger meets weaker, matching weaker requires and stronger ensures). An impure implementation cannot satisfy an unmarked or @pure interface row.
  • Always exported in .piai: the compiler always writes the computed purity property into .piai interface artifacts and includes it in the interface hash (ADR 0024). Importers always know statically whether an imported function is strongly pure, weakly pure or @impure.

docs.title: 5. Contracts and verifier encoding
docs.text:
• No impure calls in contracts: calling an @impure function (or a weakly-pure mutating function) inside requires, ensures, invariant, assert, let spec or let lemma is a compile-time error — generalising ADR 0044 section 6's ban on effectful lambdas in contracts.
  • Interface conformance for @impure functions: an @impure function may still carry requires and ensures about its own result and parameters (such as Posix.open's ensures result >= -1). Its conformance check uses queueContractCall (calling the function once as the body and checking ensures on result) rather than substituting calls into ensures.
  • Verifier uninterpreted-function encoding (#375): strongly-pure functions — both module-local and imported — are encoded lazily as one uninterpreted SMT function per scalarized result field whenever called more than once or demanded in a contract or quantifier, so repeated calls (such as civil_from_days z in Calendar.civil_from_days.contract) agree. @impure imported functions (such as Posix.close, Posix.lseek and Posix.errno) are never encoded as uninterpreted functions, closing the contractOnly soundness gap.

docs.title: 6. Higher-order functions and purity polymorphism
docs.text:
Higher-order functions such as map, fold and find are generic over their callback's Function instance (ADR 0044) and monomorphised per callback:

  • Purity polymorphism: an arrow parameter (f : a -> b) accepts either a pure or an @impure callback unless annotated @pure (or called in the higher-order function's contracts, which requires f to be strongly pure). Each monomorphised instance computes its purity from its body and the concrete callback f: map xs f is pure when f is pure and @impure when f is @impure.
  • Generic proofs (ADR 0043): a generic proved once whose contracts apply f requires f to be strongly pure and total; one whose contracts do not apply f holds for impure callbacks too.

docs.title: 7. Code generation
docs.text: Once purity is checked by the compiler, LLVM lowering can attach memory(none) / willreturn attributes to strongly-pure functions where sound. Codegen remains unchanged in the initial steps.

docs.title: Dean's answers (2026-11-25)
docs.text:
1. Default polarity: pure by default (when no out/inout/mutable or atomic parameters), with @impure for hidden effects and optional @pure as an explicit checked assertion.
  2. Purity boundary: externally pure and total — local mutation (let mutable, local buffers / with_arena) and fixed-array [T; N] returns are allowed, and purity requires proved termination (decreases on while and recursion).
  3. Foreign (extern) functions: always @impure; no @pure on C FFI, even in @trusted modules. Pure code is written in Pia or modelled as a theory.
  4. Parameter mutation vs hidden effects: D-style weak vs strong purity. Functions whose only effect is mutating out/inout/mutable parameters (like sort) need no @impure and may be called on local buffers inside pure functions; @impure marks hidden effects, and @pure asserts neither mutable parameters nor @impure.
  5. Computed purity, .piai export and lint: purity/impurity is computed automatically by the compiler (including for atomics) and always exported in .piai interfaces; unmarked interface rows default to pure (hard conformance error if the implementation is impure), and a lint recommends writing @impure on exported impure functions.
  6. Higher-order functions: include purity polymorphism (e.g. map inherits the purity of its callback).
  7. Rollout: fold this ADR into the same PR as the #375 verifier fix, then build the compiler checks in follow-up steps.

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
1. Verifier encoding for repeated pure calls (#375, this PR): lazy uninterpreted-function encoding per scalarized result field for module-local pure functions, with tests/verify/pure_contract_calls.pia.
  2. Computed purity, @pure/@impure attributes, and contract checks: compute strong/weak/impure purity (including termination) in IRGen/Verifier, accept @pure and @impure in genAttributes, reject @pure on extern and impure calls in contracts/specs/lemmas, and route @impure interface conformance checks through queueContractCall.
  3. Interfaces, .piai, Pia.Sys.Posix, and contractOnly fix: export computed purity in .piai and include it in the interface hash; enforce unmarked interface rows as non-impure; annotate lib/Pia/Sys/Posix.pia (and tools/bindings/gen.py) with @impure; restrict imported uninterpreted-function encoding in Verifier.cpp to strongly-pure imports.
  4. Lint and skills: add the impure_interface lint in src/syntax/Lint.cpp (with tests/lint/), and document @pure and @impure in docs/design.md, docs/idioms.md, and skills/pia-language/SKILL.md.
  5. Purity polymorphism: propagate callback purity through monomorphised higher-order functions and ADR 0043/0044 checks, with tests in tests/verify/.
  6. Codegen (optional follow-up): emit LLVM memory(none) / willreturn attributes for proved strongly-pure functions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Purity becomes a compiler-computed, interface-visible property rather than a verifier-internal heuristic.
  • Imported strongly-pure functions returning records (such as Pia.Time.civil_from_days) work in contracts across module boundaries, while impure FFI wrappers (Pia.Sys.Posix) cannot be falsely equated by the solver.
  • Private functions and weakly-pure mutating algorithms (Algo.Sort, Vec, codecs) require no new annotations; only exported functions with hidden, concurrent, or non-terminating effects carry @impure in their interfaces.
  • No unverified trust surface is added: = extern "..." is always @impure.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Source What Pia takes D pure Weak vs strong purity: local mutation and calling mutating helpers on local state inside strongly-pure functions F* Tot / Pure vs ML / Dv Pure and total by default, with explicit effectful boundaries Dafny function vs method Only pure total functions appear in contracts and act as SMT functions Koka / Flix effect systems Purity polymorphism for higher-order functions

docs.title: 70. Raw binary embedding: @embed for compile-time fixed byte blobs, hermetic roots, opaque verification and direct LLVM emission
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-26

Status: Accepted (2026-11-26, from Dean's answers on the design questions)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Step 1 of the GPU toolchain (ADR 0068, PR #430) builds a compiled Metal library (.metallib) and embeds it into a binary by piping the file through xxd -i into a generated C source file wrapped in a cc_library (tools/gpu/metal.bzl), which C code then reads through extern const unsigned char <symbol>[] and <symbol>_len (tests/gpu/embed_test.c).

In review of PR #430, Dean asked that embedding a compiled .metallib (or any binary asset) become a first-class Pia feature so a pure Pia binary with a main entry point can bind and embed binary blobs directly without a cc_library or xxd wrapper:

  • GPU kernels (ADR 0068): a Pia program with @place(gpu) or a Metal shim needs the compiled .metallib embedded in the object file and passed as a read-only byte slice to the shim at launch.
  • 0.1.0 LLM & codecs (ADR 0067): small model checkpoints (stories260K), tokenizer vocabularies (tok512), lookup tables and test fixtures benefit from the same mechanism.
  • Today's ConstArrayOp does not scale to binary blobs. src/codegen/Codegen.cpp lowers literal arrays by materializing an MLIR IntegerAttr per element and emitting a memref.global. That is suitable for small tables, not for kilobyte- or megabyte-sized .metallib or weight files, and it cannot read external files. Meanwhile, src/codegen/Codegen.cpp already emits raw binary data directly as an LLVM ConstantDataArray global (with optional custom section and alignment) for proof certificates (pia$cert, ADR 0024).

docs.title: 1. Surface syntax: @embed(file = ..., ...)
docs.text:
A top-level let binding embeds a raw binary file via the @embed(...) attribute on its return type, with no = body:

let add_metallib : [u8] @embed(file = "add.metallib")

Because fixed is Pia's default immutability qualifier, an embedded binding is always fixed (read-only); combining @embed with mutable is a type error.

Supported named arguments inside @embed(...):

Argument Required Meaning file = "<path>" Yes Relative path to the binary file, resolved hermetically (section 2). symbol = "<name>" No Optional C/linker symbol name for the emitted byte array (section 4). When omitted, the compiler assigns a private mangled name. section = "<name>" No Optional target object section (e.g. "__DATA,__pia_metal" on Mach-O or ".rodata.pia_metal" on ELF). Defaults to the target's read-only data section. align = <power-of-two> No Optional byte alignment (positive power of two, default 8).

At run time, the binding has type [u8] (a fixed read-only slice backed by static storage with lifetime 'static) whose length equals the file's exact byte size N. A pure Pia main can pass it directly to Pia functions or extern shims (such as Metal's device_load_library), or inspect its bytes and length normally:

let add_metallib : [u8] @embed(file = "add.metallib", symbol = "pia_test_add_metallib")

let main () : i32 =
  if len add_metallib >= 4 &&
     add_metallib.[0] = 0x4d && add_metallib.[1] = 0x54 &&
     add_metallib.[2] = 0x4c && add_metallib.[3] = 0x42
  then 0 else 1

docs.title: 2. Hermetic file resolution (CLI and Bazel)
docs.text:
piac never reads arbitrary paths from the ambient filesystem. Every @embed(file = "...") path is resolved strictly against explicitly declared roots or mappings:

  • Relative paths only. Absolute paths (starting with / or a drive prefix) and parent traversals (..) are compile-time errors.
  • CLI flags (mirroring --iface-path in tools/piac/pia.bzl):
  • --embed-path=<dir> (repeatable): search roots checked in flag order for <dir>/<file>.
  • --embed=<logical>=<physical> (repeatable): explicit logical-to-physical mapping, taking precedence over --embed-path (useful when Bazel generates files under bazel-bin/... with target-dependent paths).
  • Resolving a file not found under any declared mapping or root is a hard error naming the missing path and the searched roots.
  • Bazel integration (tools/piac/pia.bzl): pia_library, pia_object and pia_binary gain an embeds attribute (label_list(allow_files = True) or label_keyed_string_dict) that declares every embedded file as an explicit action input to PiaCompile (and to PiaInterface only when needed; see section 5) and forwards --embed / --embed-path to piac.
  • REPL / MCP (pia): respects the same --embed-path / --embed flags; with none passed, @embed is refused rather than opening host files.

docs.title: 3. Compile-time metafunction access vs. opaque verification
docs.text:
Embedded blobs have two distinct compile-time roles, kept strictly separate so verification stays O(1) regardless of blob size:

  • In let meta (metafunctions): compile-time fixed byte array. The metaprogram interpreter (src/meta/Interpreter.cpp) sees an @embed binding as a compile-time fixed byte array of exact length N whose elements are readable by metafunctions (length and byte indexing). A metaprogram can validate magic bytes (e.g. "MTLB" for a .metallib), parse a small header or manifest, or extract kernel names at compile time and fail compilation on a malformed blob — without ever sending those bytes to Z3.
  • In regular code and the Z3 verifier: opaque blob with exact length N. To Sema, IRGen and the verifier, an @embed binding is an opaque fixed [u8] slice with one known fact: len blob = N (a constant usize equal to the file's byte count) and every element has type u8 (0 <= blob.[i] <= 255). No per-byte axioms are emitted into SMT queries. Embedding a 1 MB .metallib or model file adds zero per-byte solver cost; any property of the bytes needed by runtime code is either checked by a metafunction at compile time or validated by proved Pia code at run time (as in Pia.Format.Safetensors, ADR 0067).
  • Spec functions: because the bytes are opaque outside metafunctions, len blob is exact in contracts (len blob = N), while blob.[i] is an uninterpreted u8 value (deterministic: repeated reads blob.[i] at equal i return equal values).

docs.title: 4. Codegen and symbol binding
docs.text:
Codegen bypasses per-element MLIR attribute expansion and emits the raw bytes directly in LLVM IR:

  • MLIR representation: a module-level binary asset table (or DenseResourceElementsAttr / pia.embed_data attribute referencing raw bytes held outside the MLIR IR printer's per-element array format) and a pia.embed op returning the [u8] slice descriptor {ptr, len} with static length N.
  • LLVM IR emission (src/codegen/Codegen.cpp): lowers each embedded blob directly to a read-only llvm::GlobalVariable initialized with llvm::ConstantDataArray::get(ctx, llvm::ArrayRef<uint8_t>(...)):
  • isConstant = true (matches Pia's fixed semantics; placed in .rodata / __TEXT,__const by default, or the requested section).
  • alignment = align (default 8).
  • Linkage & symbol binding:
    • Private @embed without symbol: PrivateLinkage (internal to the object file, zero dynamic symbol table pollution, respects issue #120).
    • Explicit symbol = "<name>" or exported in an interface: ExternalLinkage with the specified symbol name (or canonical module-mangled name if exported without symbol). When symbol = "<name>" is set, codegen also emits <name> pointing at the raw byte array and <name>_len (uint64_t) if C ABI interop is requested, or callers bind directly through the Pia slice {ptr, len} (C ABI pia_slice_u8).
    • When section is specified, the global is added to llvm.used so dead-stripping does not drop unreferenced section entries if an external loader scans the section.
  • Replaces tools/gpu/metal.bzl's cc_library hack: metal_library produces the .metallib file alone; a Pia target embeds it via embeds = [":add_metallib"] and @embed(file = "add.metallib"), eliminating xxd -i, generated _embed.c, and cc_library.

docs.title: 5. Interfaces and SHA-256 certificate hashing
docs.text:
• Private @embed bindings (not listed in interface I = sig ... end) do not appear in .piai and do not affect the module's interface hash. Rebuilding a private .metallib does not re-verify or rebuild importers, and piac --emit=interface does not need to read private embedded files.
  • Explicitly exported @embed bindings may be listed in an interface as a read-only byte slice: 
    interface Kernels = sig
  let add_metallib : [u8] @embed
end
    When piac --emit=interface emits the .piai for an explicitly exported @embed binding, it records both its exact length and its SHA-256 content hash (lowercase 64-char hex, computed with llvm::SHA256 as in src/cert/Certificate.cpp): 
    let add_metallib : [u8] @embed(len = 4096, sha256 = "e3b0c442...")
    Because __pia_cert (ADR 0024) hashes the canonical .piai text with SHA-256, pia-cert check automatically enforces at link time that every importer was verified and compiled against the exact byte length and content hash of the exported embedded blob, catching stale objects with zero extra certificate format changes.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is one PR:

  1. Syntax, hermetic resolution & opaque verifier encoding: parse @embed(file = ..., symbol = ..., section = ..., align = ...) on top-level let bindings; add --embed-path and --embed flags to piac and pia; resolve files hermetically in Sema; encode @embed in IRGen and the verifier as a fixed [u8] slice with exact constant len = N and opaque u8 elements.
  2. Direct LLVM codegen & Bazel embeds: add pia.embed lowering directly to llvm::ConstantDataArray in src/codegen/Codegen.cpp (with symbol, section, align); add embeds to pia_library, pia_object and pia_binary in tools/piac/pia.bzl.
  3. Exported interface .piai & SHA-256 hashing: support let name : [u8] @embed in interface ... = sig ... end, emit len and sha256 into .piai (only when explicitly exported), and verify pia-cert check rejects a mismatched embedded blob at link time.
  4. Metafunction compile-time byte access: expose @embed bindings to let meta as compile-time fixed byte arrays (len and indexing), with a test validating "MTLB" magic in a metafunction at compile time.
  5. Migrate tools/gpu/metal.bzl and tests/gpu/: drop the xxd -i / _embed.c / cc_library rule from tools/gpu/metal.bzl and replace tests/gpu/embed_test.c with a pure Pia pia_binary embedding the .metallib via @embed.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pure Pia binaries (main with no C glue) can embed .metallib archives, model weights, vocabularies and static fixtures directly, with full bounds verification on len and zero Z3 blowup.
  • Metafunctions can inspect and validate embedded binary headers at compile time without pushing raw bytes into SMT queries.
  • Private embedded blobs keep incremental builds fast (importers never see them), while explicitly exported embedded blobs are content-addressed by SHA-256 through the existing .piai and __pia_cert link check.
  • tools/gpu/metal.bzl no longer depends on xxd or cc_library to embed compiled Metal libraries.

docs.title: 71. Function references: a function is a value that travels by reference
Context
docs.text:
ADR 0044 made every function value static: a lambda or a named function passed to a higher-order function is a direct call in that function's instance, and "there is no function pointer and no heap allocation for a static function value, ever". A value whose function is chosen at run time was left to the library's box over Function (ADR 0046).

The case that needs this is a box over a concept, box c (Dean, 2026-11-27): what Rust's dyn Trait is for traits. A Box<dyn Shape> in Rust is a pointer to the object and a pointer to a table holding the object's drop, its size and alignment, and one function pointer per method. A box Shape must do the same job, ending and calling an object whose type its user does not know, and it can only do it with function references:

  • Its drop. The amendment to ADR 0046 of 2026-11-26 gives a box c a direct reference to the boxed type's drop, "like a unique_ptr<T> ... but instead of a vtable we have an explicit ref to the type's drop implementation" (Dean).
  • Its requirements. A call of a concept's requirement through a box must reach the boxed type's implementation. Step 5 of ADR 0046 does it with a switch on a tag, which works only inside the module that knows every widened type. A reference to each requirement's implementation works anywhere, including in a module that imports the box and never saw the types.

The same references then serve tables and callbacks: a table of handlers, a state machine's transitions, a C library that takes a callback (qsort, pthread_create), or C code that calls back into Pia. For a function that captures nothing, a box and an allocator are more than those need.

Dean decided on 2026-11-27 that function references are visible to programs, and that they need no address operator: "we can treat a function as a value that travels by reference (cannot be cloned or duplicated)". The function itself is never copied, and a reference to it can be (Dean, 2026-11-27).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• C has function pointers and an implicit decay from a function's name to its address. Nothing stops a call through a pointer of the wrong type.
  • C++ has the same decay, std::function for owning closures, and std::function_ref (C++26) for a borrowed callable: a code pointer and a pointer to the callable's state.
  • Rust has fn(A) -> R, distinct from the Fn traits, to which named functions and capture-free closures coerce. It is never null; Option<fn(...)> is the nullable form. dyn Trait is a fat pointer, the data and a vtable of drop, size, alignment and one fn pointer per method, shared by every value of one type and trait.

docs.title: 1. A function is a value that travels by reference
docs.text:
A function's name is a value of its arrow type (ADR 0044, section 3). Wherever that value is stored or passed by reference, what travels is a reference to the function, never a copy of its code. There is no address operator and no separate reference type:

let succ (x : u8) : u8 requires x < 255 ensures result = x + 1 = (x + 1)

let h : (x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 255 = succ
let keys = type { on_key : (k : u8) -> unit; on_quit : unit -> unit }
let table : [(x : u8) -> u8 requires x < 100; 3] = [succ; twice; succ]
  • The function has static lifetime, so a reference to it is a shared borrow that never ends. It may be stored in a let, a record field, a variant, a buffer or module state, returned, and sent to another task.
  • A reference can be copied, as any shared borrow can, so one function may sit in many places. The function itself cannot be cloned or duplicated.
  • A reference is a proxy for its function (Dean, 2026-11-27): wherever it is used, it behaves as the function's name would, so it is called, passed on and stored the same way. It is fixed by default, like every binding: h names succ for as long as h lives, and a call through it, where the compiler can see which function it was bound to, is a direct call. A place written mutable, such as let h : mutable (u8 -> u8) = succ or a mutable table slot, can be rebound to another function of the same arrow with h <- twice; a call through it is indirect unless the compiler can see the last binding.
  • Semantically it is ADR 0047's ref t to the function (Dean, 2026-11-27): a shared, immutable value that every copy of the reference reaches. Because a function lives for the whole program, there is no count to keep and nothing to free, so it is laid out as a bare address and needs no word of its own.
  • A reference is never null. option (u8 -> u8) is the nullable one, laid out as one address with zero as None.
  • Function types still never meet Eq, Ord or Hash (ADR 0044): two references cannot be compared.

What can be referenced: a top-level function, an instance of a generic one (sort<u32>; an uninstantiated generic has no single body), and a lambda that captures nothing. A lambda that captures is section 4.

docs.title: 2. Parameters: inlined, or by reference
docs.text:
ADR 0044's parameters keep their meaning, and borrowed chooses the other one:

  • (f : u8 -> u8) is any type meeting Function (ADR 0044, section 4). Each argument gets its own instance, and the call inlines. This stays the default, because it is the fast one.
  • (f : borrowed (u8 -> u8)) takes a reference. The function has one instance for every argument, and calls through the reference.

A stored arrow type, in a let, a field, a buffer or a result, is always a reference, since a stored value has one layout.

docs.title: 3. Meeting the arrow, and calling through it
docs.text:
Making a reference, by storing a function or passing it borrowed, checks the function against the arrow. Its requires must follow from the arrow's and its ensures must give the arrow's, the same check ADR 0044 makes when a named function is passed for an arrow parameter, proved once where the reference is made. When the arrow's contract differs from the function's, the reference is to a wrapper with the arrow's contract, as in ADR 0044's step 1. Modifiers must match exactly, since they are the calling convention.

A call through a reference, h x, knows only the arrow:

  • Its goals are the arrow's requires, at the call.
  • Its facts are the arrow's ensures, about result and any out or inout parameters, and nothing else.
  • When the arrow is pure (ADR 0069), a call is an uninterpreted function of the reference and the arguments, so two calls through one reference on equal arguments are equal, and the call may appear in a contract. A call through an arrow that is not pure is code-only, as ADR 0044 and ADR 0046 already rule for boxes. A function referenced at a pure arrow must be pure.

docs.title: 4. Borrowed closures
docs.text:
A lambda that captures is a record of its captures (ADR 0044, section 6). A reference to it is two words, its code and a pointer to that record, as C++'s function_ref is. It is an ordinary loan (ADR 0042): it lasts no longer than the closure it borrows, so it can be passed borrowed and stored in a local, but not returned past the closure or stored where the closure does not reach. A closure that must outlive its maker, chosen at run time, is still a box (Function a r) with an allocator (ADR 0046).

A reference to a function that captures nothing has no environment, and is one word.

docs.title: 5. Code generation and the ABI
docs.text:
• A reference is the function's address: func.constant, then llvm.mlir.addressof. A call is func.call_indirect, then an indirect llvm.call. In a record or a buffer a reference is stored as a pointer, as ADR 0048's buffers of slices store addresses.
  • A reference to a function with a C-compatible signature is a C function pointer at the C boundary (ADR 0039's @abi(c)). So an extern may take one, and C's qsort can take a Pia comparator. The arrow's contract is what the extern declares the callback to be, trusted like every extern contract and listed in the trust report.
  • A reference that crosses into Pia from C, as a parameter of an exported function or the result of an extern, is trusted to meet its arrow, and the trust report lists it. A reference made in Pia is proved where it is made.
  • An interface may export a function that takes, stores or returns references. The arrow is part of the signature, so an importer checks its calls against it.

docs.title: 6. Boxes over concepts
docs.text:
This is what the references are for first, and what makes a box c work as Rust's dyn Trait does.

One static table per type and concept. For each type t that is widened into box c, the compiler makes one table, a constant in read-only data, shared by every box c that holds a t (Dean, 2026-11-27: references in every box would be wasteful). It holds:

  • t's size and alignment, in bytes (the ADR 0046 amendment);
  • a reference to t's drop, through a thunk that takes the slot and drops the object in it, or one that does nothing for a type with no drop;
  • a reference to t's implementation of each of c's requirements, through a thunk that takes the slot in the receiver's place and forwards to t's function.

A box c is then two words, the slot and a reference to its table, whatever c requires. area b on a box Shape loads area from the table and calls it; dropping the box calls the table's drop, then gives the slot back to its allocator. Where the compiler can see what a box holds, such as straight after widen, the call is direct, as it is today.

Unreachable from Pia (Dean, 2026-11-27). A table has no name a program can write, no type a program can spell, and no value a program can hold: it is not a field of box c, and nothing reads, copies, compares or stores it. Only code the compiler makes uses it, for a call through a box, a drop, and the size and alignment an allocator or a vec (box c) needs, which box c's own functions return. So a program cannot call a requirement of a type it never widened, swap a box's table, or keep a reference into one past the box. Metaprograms cannot see tables either, including Pia.Live's in the REPL, which lists the session's definitions but not the tables derived from them.

Consolidated across modules. A table is named by its type and concept, pia$t$<type>$<concept>, and emitted as a link-once constant in each module that widens a t into box c, so the linker keeps one copy however many modules make such boxes. Its layout is the concept's requirements in declaration order after the three fixed entries, published with the concept (ADR 0030), so a module that imports c can call and drop a box made elsewhere, and ADR 0046's step 6 needs nothing more.

Checked once. Each entry is checked where the table is made, against the requirement's arrow with the receiver erased: exactly what ADR 0046's section 4 asks, that what is placed in a box exposes the concept's interface. The verifier's view of a box does not change. A call through it has the requirement's contract and nothing else, and the table itself never appears in a goal.

docs.title: 6a. Tables in the REPL
docs.text:
A table ties a type, a concept and the functions that implement it, so the REPL's redefinition rules (ADR 0031) must cover all three. A table is a derived definition the session keeps for itself, out of reach of cells and metaprograms (section 6), depending on the type, the concept and each implementing function, so every :redef of one of them reaches it.

  • An implementation changes, and refines. The table's entry is a thunk that calls through the function's REPL slot, as every call between REPL definitions already does, so a new body proved against the old contract is swapped into the slot and the table does not change. Live boxes carry on.
  • An implementation stops meeting the concept. The table's check fails like any dependent's proof, and the redefinition is refused, naming the concept and the type.
  • The type's layout changes. Boxes alive in a task hold objects of the old layout, and only the old table's size, drop and implementations are right for them. The old table stays, with the old type's code, as Erlang keeps two versions of a module, and boxes made after the change get the new type's table. Each version is proved against its own type, so neither table is ever used for the other's objects. The old table and its code are freed when no task can still reach a box made with it; until then the session lists it.
  • The concept changes. Adding, removing or reordering a requirement changes every table's layout, so it is refused while any box c is alive in a running task or in REPL state, as ADR 0031 refuses a layout change with live values and no migration. With none alive, every table for c is rebuilt and every type widened into it is checked against the new concept. A change only to a requirement's contract follows ADR 0031's cases: if every implementation still meets it and callers' proofs still hold, it commits; otherwise the callers and tables are verified again and swapped together at a quiescent point.

docs.title: 7. What this ADR does not decide
docs.text:
• Comparison of references, such as testing which handler a table holds. A program that needs it keeps a tag beside the reference.
  • Owning closures chosen at run time: those are boxes (ADR 0046).
  • References across dynamic libraries beyond what a symbol's address gives, which waits for ADR 0024's loader work.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with lit tests in tests/verify, tests/irgen and tests/codegen, with pia-language's syntax table and pia-porting's feature map updated as it lands.

  1. References and their proofs. Arrow types in a let, a field and a buffer, borrowed arrow parameters, the check against the arrow where a reference is made, calls through the arrow's contract, pure arrows as uninterpreted functions, and errors for a generic without arguments, a capturing lambda stored past its captures, and mismatched modifiers.
  2. Code generation. Addresses and indirect calls, references in records, variants and buffers, option of an arrow as a nullable pointer, and a run test that picks handlers from a table.
  3. The C boundary. References as parameters of externs and @abi(c) exports, with a test of qsort over a Pia comparator and of C calling back into Pia, and the trust report's entries.
  4. Borrowed closures: two-word references to capturing lambdas, with ADR 0042's loan checks.
  5. Boxes over concepts through tables (the ADR 0046 amendment, steps 2 and 3): one link-once table per type and concept, widen storing a reference to it, calls and drops through it, and a box made in one module used in another.
  6. Tables in the REPL: tables as derived definitions, slot thunks, old tables kept for live boxes of an old layout, and the refusal of a concept change while boxes are alive.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Tables of handlers and C callbacks need no allocator, no box and no new syntax. A call through one costs one indirect call.
  • A function's name means the same thing everywhere, and borrowed is the only word that picks a reference over an instance, so no keyword or operator is added.
  • What a reference can do is exactly what its arrow says, so a caller proves what it would about any function with that arrow, and the referenced function is checked once, where the reference is made.
  • ADR 0044's promise still holds for functions passed without borrowed: they never become pointers.
  • A reference from C is trusted, the same trust an extern already carries, and the trust report shows it.

docs.title: 72. A drop never grows the stack: every drop is one walk, proved against the recursive drop, with a fixed stack bound per type
Context
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-27): "I want to think about the recursive drop case where we can get stack overflows. Independent of whether or not there's recursion actually happening, for deep enough drop calls we need to be mindful of the stack usage. We should figure out whether we need to do some sort of mark-sweep instead of the naive calls to drop recursively."

And, after a first cut that bounded drop depth by a lint: "If we are guarding for stack overflow, we need to make drop never be the cause of it. I'd like us to use a proof to maintain that a drop never causes a stack overflow with a theory, and make sure the implementation is correct. ... Local reasoning in a function's scope cannot be a proxy for global reasoning during runtime. So let's avoid that trap. What I do want to know is whether there's ever a case when we need to do this stack-based drop, or whether we can always rely on the mark and sweep approach."

A naive drop calls the drop of each field, which calls the drop of each of its fields, one stack frame per level of nesting. How deep that goes depends on the value:

  • A value of a type that is not recursive nests as deeply as its type does. A box (box (box u8)) is three levels, whatever is in it.
  • A value of a recursive type (ADR 0047) nests as deeply as it was built: a list a million long is a million levels.
  • A box c (ADR 0046) hides its type. If a type that meets c holds a box c, as a node of a heterogeneous list does, box c is recursive through the concept, though no let rec says so.
  • A ref t drops its value when its last strong reference goes (ADR 0047, section 5), so a chain of last references is a recursive drop too.

ADR 0047's section 4 says the generated drop of a recursive type runs in constant stack, by a loop and a worklist kept in the memory of the nodes being freed. This ADR answers Dean's question, that no drop ever needs to recurse, and says what is proved and how.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Rust drops recursively, so dropping a long Box-linked list overflows the stack; the fix is a hand-written Drop that loops with take(), and a tree needs an explicit stack. C++'s unique_ptr chains have the same problem.
  • Garbage collectors mark with an explicit stack or by Deutsch–Schorr–Waite pointer reversal (1967), which walks a graph in constant extra space by turning each pointer it follows around to point back where it came from, and restoring it on the way out. Its correctness is a classic of verification: Bornat (2000) proved it in Jape, Mehta and Nipkow (2003) in Isabelle/HOL, and Hubert and Marché (2005) in Why/Caduceus.
  • Swift and Koka release counted references iteratively where the compiler can see the chain.

docs.title: 1. What is claimed, and what is not
docs.text:
The claim is about drop alone, so it is local and decidable: for every type t there is a number of bytes S(t), fixed when t is compiled, such that dropping any value of t uses at most S(t) bytes of stack beyond the frame of the code that drops it, whatever the value holds. Dropping a list of ten nodes and one of ten million uses the same stack.

Nothing is claimed about the whole program's stack. Whether a program overflows depends on how deep its calls go at run time, which no check in one function's scope can bound, and this ADR does not try. What it guarantees is that a drop is never the cause: a program that has S(t) bytes left where it drops a t cannot overflow in that drop, and S(t) is small and known. A whole-program stack bound, if one is wanted later, would be a cost bound on a stack counter (ADR 0062), proved by the program's own contracts, and is outside this ADR.

docs.title: 2. Every drop is a walk; no drop recurses
docs.text:
There is never a case that needs a recursive drop. Every drop, of every type, is one walk: a loop over a fixed-size state that visits the value's parts in order, drops each part's own fields, and frees each slot. Each way a value can hold another is covered:

  • An owned child out of line, through box, the last ref, or a box c: the walk descends by pointer reversal. It turns the child's pointer in the parent around to point to the parent's parent, keeps which child it took in the pointer's low bits, and restores nothing on the way up, since the parent is being freed. A slot that holds a pointer is aligned to at least eight bytes on both targets (ADR 0049), so three low bits are always free; a node with more out-of-line children than they can count keeps its cursor in the pointer slot of a child it has already dropped, which exists once the cursor is past the first child, whose number the low bits can hold.
  • A buffer of owned children, vec t or a slice of boxes (ADR 0048): the cursor is the buffer's own length, counted down as its elements are dropped, so it needs no extra room.
  • A child inline, a record field or a fixed array of records: its place is a fixed offset in its parent, so the walk's state for it is a position in the type, not in the value. The type's own nesting is fixed, so this state has a fixed size, and in practice it compiles to the same straight-line code a nested drop would.
  • A variant: its tag says which payload to walk.
  • A hand-written drop: a step of the walk (section 4).
  • A box c: its table's drop entry (ADR 0071, section 6) is a step of the walk, which hands back the boxes of c it finds instead of dropping them (section 5).

A type with no recursive indirection compiles to straight-line code, as today, because every position its walk can reach is known; reversal appears only at an indirection that can lead back to the same type. So the uniform walk costs nothing where the naive drop was already fine, and it is the only drop, so there is no second implementation to keep in step.

docs.title: 3. Order
docs.text: The walk drops children in declaration order, depth first, and a node's own fields after its children, as the recursive drop would. A value whose fields close files or release locks does so in the same order however deep it is, and slots are freed after everything in them is dropped. Section 6 proves this order.

docs.title: 4. Hand-written drops
docs.text:
A type may have its own drop (#85). Its body is ordinary Pia, run as one step of the walk:

  • It sees the node's fields other than the owned children the walk descends into, which the compiler drops after it.
  • Its call graph may not cycle. A call that can reach itself from a drop, directly or through other functions, is an error, drop_recursion. This is a check of which functions call which, not of whether a loop terminates, so it asks nothing undecidable: loops are fine, and they cost no stack. Every value the body drops is dropped by its own walk.
  • With no cycle, the body's stack is the largest sum of frames along a path in its call graph, which codegen reads from LLVM's frame sizes. That is part of S(t).
  • A drop that is an extern (ADR 0057's bindings, a C destructor) runs C code whose stack Pia cannot see. It must state its bound, @stack(256), which is trusted and listed in the trust report, like every extern contract.

docs.title: 5. Through box c and ref
docs.text:
• box c. When a type that meets c can hold a box c, its table's drop entry drops the object's fields that are not boxes of c, and returns each box c it finds to the walk, which descends into it by reversal. The table stays out of reach of Pia (ADR 0071), so this protocol is the compiler's own.
  • ref t. Releasing a reference that is not the last only decrements its count. Releasing the last one is a descent into the value, so a chain of last references unwinds in the same walk.

docs.title: 6. The theory and the proof
docs.text:
The claim is a theorem in a library theory, Pia.Drop (ADR 0036), proved as follows:

  • The meaning. The theory's spec drops t v is the recursive drop, written as the obvious recursive spec function over a value's shape: the sequence of hand-written drop steps it runs and slots it frees, in order. It is never compiled; it is what the walk must equal.
  • The walk, once. The generic walk is a transition system over a value's shape: a current node, a cursor, and the reversed path. Its invariant is the one the Schorr–Waite proofs use: the reversed path, read back, is exactly the continuation the recursion would hold on its stack. Its measure is the number of parts not yet visited. From these, the walk terminates, runs exactly drops t v, frees each slot once, and keeps a state of fixed size. This is proved once, in Lean, for every shape the type grammar allows (Dean, 2026-11-27).
  • Through ADR 0061, with no Lean written by hand (Dean, 2026-11-27). Everything the proof is about is written in Pia, in lib/Pia/Drop.pia: the shape type, drops t v, the walk's step function, its invariant and its measure, all as spec functions, and the theorem as a lemma, let lemma walk_runs_drops ... = by lean Pia.Drop.walk_runs_drops. piac --emit-lean Pia.Drop generates the Lean definitions and the statement (ADR 0061), so the Lean side never restates what the walk is, and a change to the Pia definitions changes the statement and fails its receipt until it is proved again. Only the proof script is Lean, in the proof file ADR 0061 provides for it, and pia_lean_proof checks it and writes the receipt, whose statement hash goes into the compiler's certificate.
  • Each type. For each type, the compiler emits its walk's step function as Pia, against the type's layout, and Z3 proves that it refines the generic step for that shape: the same next state for every state. These are small, quantifier-free goals, one per kind of position in the type.
  • The bound. S(t) is the walk's frame plus the largest stack of any step it calls (section 4). The walk has no call cycle and no dynamically sized frame, which codegen checks after LLVM has fixed the frames, and refuses to emit otherwise. The machine fact it rests on, that a call graph with no cycle and fixed frames uses at most its largest path's frames, is an axiom of the Pia.Target theory, true of both targets' calling conventions.

What the verifier sees of a drop in an ordinary program does not change: it is still the type's drop contract, and each node is still dropped exactly once.

docs.title: 7. What programs see
docs.text:
• --verify-stats reports S(t) for every type a module drops, and the largest in each function.
  • The lint deep_drop remains for one case only, a hand-written drop whose own body's stack is more than an eighth of the target's task stack (task_stack_bytes in Pia.Target: 512 KiB on arm64 macOS, 8 MiB on x86_64 Linux). It names the call path. No other drop can be large.
  • Nothing about drop depends on how large a value is, so there is no depth limit and no flag for one.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is a PR with tests in tests/codegen run from C, and the skills updated as features land.

  1. The theory. lib/Pia/Drop.pia with the shape type, drops t v, the generic walk, its invariant and measure, and the by lean lemma of section 6; the proof script, checked by pia_lean_proof, and the receipt in the certificate. Needs ADR 0061's step 1 (--emit-lean, by lean, receipts), which is not built yet, so that comes first.
  2. The walk for every shape. Lists, trees, buffers, inline fields and variants; the per-type refinement goals; S(t) in --verify-stats; codegen's check that drops have no cycle and fixed frames. Tests: a list of a million nodes and a left-leaning tree of a million nodes dropped on a thread with a 64 KiB stack, with the order of their drops checked, under the sanitizers (ADR 0025).
  3. Hand-written drops as steps, drop_recursion, @stack on extern drops, and the deep_drop lint.
  4. box c and ref, after ADR 0071's tables: a heterogeneous list of box Shape a million long, and a chain of last references.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No drop can overflow the stack because a value is large, and no drop allocates, so dropping never fails.
  • There is one drop implementation, proved once against the recursive meaning and refined per type, rather than a fast recursive drop and a safe iterative one.
  • Drops run in the order a programmer reads from the recursive definition.
  • A hand-written drop of a recursive type sees less than it would in Rust or C++: its owned children are the compiler's to drop, and it may not recurse.
  • Pointer reversal writes into the value being dropped. That is safe because it is owned uniquely and about to be freed, and ADR 0042's loan rules already forbid dropping a value another task borrows.
  • The claim stops at drop. A program can still overflow its stack by calling too deep, which is a property of the program's own calls, as it is in every language.

docs.title: 73. Certificates record who proved a module and with what, advisories revoke trust in faulty provers, and every breaking change ships a migration
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-26

Status: Accepted (2026-11-26, from Dean's answers on the design questions)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A Pia certificate (ADR 0024, src/cert/Certificate.h) says which interfaces an object provides, which it was proved against, and (format 2) its own trusted items. It does not say which compiler proved it. A certificate stands for "piac proved every goal", so it is only as sound as the piac, Z3 and Lean that did the proving. If we find a soundness bug in piac (a goal never emitted, an encoding that drops a hypothesis, an interval rule that proves too much) or in a solver, every object that bug may have touched carries a certificate that is no longer worth what it says, and today nothing can tell those objects apart from good ones.

docs/abi.md already plans for parts of this. Its certificate header has a Pia ABI version and a target, its image record has a "compiler identity", the Layer 2 check may require "the compiler identity is in an allowed set", and "Proof and build identity" lists the compiler version, a hash of the piac binary and the Z3 version. None of it is built: format 2 has no header fields beyond magic, format and length, and piac has no version (MODULE.bazel says 0.0.0, and there is no piac --version). ADR 0061 gives every Lean-proved item a receipt naming the Lean toolchain, the Mathlib commit and the axioms, which the certificate should carry too.

Dean asked (2026-11-26) for four things: encode the compiler version that proved a module and its interfaces, encode ABI compatibility, have a way to mark modules whose proofs may be faulty because of a bug in an earlier compiler so that they are not trusted, and an automated way to migrate code from one Pia version to the next: every new or deprecated feature comes with transformation rules, so the compiler either rewrites old code mechanically or rejects it with a suggestion a person or an agent can follow.

The last ask is the other half of the first three. A revoked module is fixed by rebuilding it with a newer piac, and that only works if the newer piac still accepts the module's source, or says exactly how to change it. Pia changes every week until 0.1.0 (ADRs 0064, 0069, 0071 and #453 all change what valid source looks like), and today a change in syntax or meaning just breaks old code with whatever error the new parser happens to give.

Prior art:

  • Rust records the compiler version in every .rlib and refuses to link crates built by another rustc. That is ABI compatibility, not soundness: it has no way to say "1.52.0 had a miscompile, distrust what it built" (the 1.52.1 incremental-compilation bug was handled by a point release and an advisory blog post).
  • RustSec, Go's vulnerability database and OSV publish advisories as data: an id, the affected package, version ranges introduced and fixed, and optionally the affected symbols, so govulncheck reports only programs that reach the faulty function. Tools ship a copy and can be given a newer one.
  • Certificate revocation (CRLs, Apple's notarization revocation) marks a signed thing untrusted after the fact without changing the thing.

  • Proof assistants (Lean, Coq) record the kernel and library versions in .olean/.vo files and refuse mismatched ones, and Lean's #print axioms lists what a proof rests on. Narrowing distrust to "proofs that used feature X" is what an axiom list makes possible.

  • Migrations. Rust editions with cargo fix --edition (each lint that guards an edition change carries a machine-applicable suggestion), Go's go fix and gofmt -r, clang-tidy and Clang fix-its, Swift's migrator, Python's 2to3 and OpenRewrite's recipes all rewrite old source to new. The ones that work best attach the rewrite to the diagnostic that reports the old form, so the same rule serves the compiler, the editor and the batch tool, and they mark which suggestions are safe to apply blindly and which need a human.

The Pia-specific point is that a soundness bug rarely touches every proof. Most bugs live in one rule: a lint's rewrite, int-blasting, the Presburger path, interval analysis, the float rounding model, a lemma cache. If the certificate records which proof engines a module's goals actually used, an advisory can name an engine and a version range, and only the modules that used that engine in that range lose trust.

docs.title: 1. The certificate records the prover
docs.text:
Certificate format 3 adds lines to the text body, after module:

module Image.Pixels
abi 1 arm64-apple-macos
prover piac 0.1.0+512.9f3c2e1a7b04
solver z3 4.15.4
engines intervals,z3,int-blast,presburger
lean leanprover/lean4:v4.25.0 mathlib 3c1b2d0e 2
provides Image.Pixels.Ops <hash>
requires Image.Pixels.Ops <hash>
trusted lowering matmul <hash> linalg.matmul
  • prover is piac's identity: the release version and, for builds between releases, the number of commits on main since the root and the short commit (0.1.0+512.9f3c2e1a7b04). The commit count makes builds on main totally ordered, so an advisory can name a range. Bazel stamping (--config=release, src/version/workspace_status.sh) puts it into the piac that CI publishes. Every other build, including CI's own build and test run, records piac dev, which no advisory range covers and which a deployment policy can refuse (pia-cert check --require-released).
  • solver names each SMT solver that decided a goal, with its version. Today that is only Z3. The options that change what a proof means (none do today; strategies and rlimits only change whether a proof is found) would be listed here if any ever did.
  • engines is the set of proof engines that discharged at least one of the module's goals, from a fixed list in the verifier: intervals (interval analysis), z3 (default solver), int-blast (ADR 0066), presburger (ADR 0020), nlsat and float-model (ADR 0038), uf-div (division as uninterpreted functions, verifier.md), theory:<name> per library theory (ADR 0036), lemma-cache (certified instances skipped by importers, ADR 0043), generic (an instance proved by its generic's proof over sorts, ADR 0043), proof-cache (a goal answered by --proof-cache), lean and refinement (ABI baselines). An engine is added to the list in the same PR that adds the engine. The verifier already knows which path proved each goal (--verify-stats counts them), so this is a set union, not new analysis.
  • lean appears once per Lean toolchain and Mathlib commit used, with the number of receipts. Each Lean-proved item is also a line proved lean <item> <receipt hash>, so an advisory against one Lean proof can be precise.
  • abi is the Pia ABI version (docs/abi.md), a single integer in src/cert/Certificate.h, and the target triple. It starts at 1. It covers the calling convention, the canonical .piai serialisation the interface hashes are taken over, and the certificate format's meaning. The link check refuses two objects with different ABI versions or targets, with the message "built by a piac with Pia ABI 1; this one has ABI 2: rebuild it". The ABI version is also the first thing hashed into every interface hash, as ADR 0024 already says, so a bump changes every witness symbol and dyld refuses a mismatch without the runtime check.

The prover is not hashed into the interface hash or into any witness. Upgrading piac must not, by itself, break every importer: a new compiler with the same ABI version proves the same interface to the same hash. The prover is policy and audit data, which is what ADR 0024 and abi.md already say for "compiler identity".

piac keeps writing the lowest format that holds what it writes (format 1 without trusted items, format 2 with them), until format 3 is written by every piac: from then on every object has an abi and a prover line, so a format 1 or 2 certificate is itself evidence of a build from before this ADR, and pia-cert check treats it as piac unknown (see 3).

piac --version prints the same identity, the solver versions and the ABI version.

docs.title: 2. Advisories say which proofs are faulty
docs.text:
An advisory is a small file, PIA-2026-0001.toml, in security/advisories/ in this repository:

id = "PIA-2026-0001"
summary = "Interval analysis proved u32 subtraction cannot wrap when the bounds came from a loop invariant"
piac = { introduced = "0.0.0+380", fixed = "0.1.0+514" }
engines = ["intervals"]          # optional: only modules whose certificates name one of these
solver = {}                      # or { z3 = { introduced = "4.15.0", fixed = "4.15.2" } }
lean = []                        # or receipt hashes of individual Lean proofs
