severity = "unsound"             # unsound: a proved goal may be false; incomplete: never revokes
fixed_by = "https://github.com/deanberris/pia-lang/pull/530"

A certificate matches an advisory when its prover is in the advisory's piac range (or its solver in the solver range, or one of its Lean receipts is listed), and, if the advisory names engines, the certificate's engines contains one of them. An advisory with no engines matches every certificate in its range: that is the right answer when we do not know which rule was at fault.

Advisories are data, not code, and are reviewed like any PR. Publishing one is the response to a soundness bug, together with the fix and a regression test in tests/verify/ that the faulty piac proved and the fixed one refuses. The advisories are also published on the documentation site.

docs.title: 3. Checks refuse matching modules
docs.text:
• pia-cert check (and so every pia_library and pia_binary validation action, and piac link) reads the advisories and refuses an object whose certificate matches one, naming the advisory, the module, the engine and the fix: "Image.Pixels was proved by piac 0.0.0+402, which PIA-2026-0001 says may prove false goals with interval analysis, and its proofs used interval analysis: rebuild it with piac 0.1.0+514 or later". It also refuses a missing or older-format certificate's piac unknown once format 3 is the only format piac writes, unless the deployment allows it.
  • Importers. A module proved against an interface whose provider is revoked is not itself unsound (its proof is assume-guarantee), but the program is. The check reports every revoked object, and, transitively, which programs and libraries contain or load one.
  • Accepting a revocation. pia-cert check --accept-advisory=PIA-2026-0001:Image.Pixels lets that one module through. An accepted advisory becomes a trusted item of the image, listed by --trust-report like an @assume, so trusting a known-faulty proof is visible and never silent. This follows ADR 0004: the strongest guarantee is the default, and weakening it is explicit and narrow.
  • Rebuilding. Proofs are deterministic under an rlimit (ADR 0032), so the fix for a revoked module is to rebuild it with a fixed piac. In Bazel that happens anyway when piac changes. pia-cert check --why lists the modules to rebuild, and an advisory against a library someone else ships says which version to ask for.
  • The proof cache. A proof cache entry is keyed by the Z3 version, the rlimit and the query, not by piac, and a piac bug produces a wrong query, not a wrong answer about a query: the cached fact "this query is unsat" is still true. So piac advisories never purge the cache. A solver advisory does: piac refuses cache entries made by a revoked solver version, which the key already contains.
  • Launch and Pia.Dl.open. The runtime's certificate check (abi.md, Layer 2, not built yet) will check the ABI version and the advisories compiled into the runtime that was linked. A loader cannot fetch newer advisories, so this catches only what was known when the program was built. pia-cert audit on a built program, with the current advisories, is how a deployment finds out later.

docs.title: 4. Where advisories come from
docs.text: The advisories in security/advisories/ are compiled into pia-cert, piac and the runtime at build time, so every tool knows every advisory older than itself. pia-cert check --advisories=<dir> adds a newer set, so an old toolchain can be checked against today's list. pia-cert advisories lists them.

docs.title: 5. Every breaking change ships a migration
docs.text:
A breaking change is any change after which some source that piac accepted is rejected or means something else: a renamed keyword, a new syntax, a removed feature, a changed default, a stdlib interface that drops a baseline. A PR that makes one adds a migration rule for it, in the same PR, in src/migrate/rules/. A rule has:

  • an id and the piac version that introduces it (the prover identity of section 1, so 0.1.0+530);
  • a matcher over the parsed (not yet expanded) syntax tree, which finds the old form;
  • either a rewrite to the new form, or a suggestion: a message saying what to change and why, with the new form spelled out where it can be, for when no mechanical rewrite is safe (a meaning that depends on intent, such as which of two new keywords an old one should become);
  • a test: before.pia, after.pia (or the expected suggestion), proved by the test runner like every tests/verify file.

Rules run in two places.

  • In piac, every build. For one release after the change, piac still parses the old form and reports it as a deprecated warning with the rewrite attached as a fix-it. After that, the old form is an error, but the rule keeps running on the error path, so the error says what to write instead, forever. A rule never silently accepts old source: a warning or an error always names the rule. The language server shows the same fix-it as a code action, and the REPL and pia mcp return it in the cell's diagnostics, so an agent sees the exact edit.
  • In piac migrate. piac migrate [--from=<version>] [--check] <files> applies, in version order, every rule introduced after --from (default: the oldest), rewriting files in place, then proves the result. Rewrites must be idempotent and must leave the file's comments and layout as they were outside the rewritten span. Suggestions that have no rewrite are printed as a list of file:line: [rule] what to do, the same shape as lints, so a person or an agent works through them. --check changes nothing and fails when any rule would fire, which is how CI keeps lib/, tests/, examples/ and the docs migrated.

A rewrite is checked by proof, not trusted. After piac migrate, the new source must prove, and where the old and new forms both elaborate (during the deprecation release) the rule's test also checks that both produce the same pia_contract obligations and the same interface hash. A rewrite that changes an interface hash is a breaking change to the module's ABI as well, and piac migrate says so.

Enforced in CI. tools/migrate/check.py fails a PR that changes the grammar (src/syntax), a keyword table, a lint's default level or a stdlib interface baseline without adding or updating a rule, unless the PR's description says no-migration: <why> (for example, a change that only accepts more programs). Like tools/skills/check.py, it makes the missing piece impossible to forget, not impossible to skip with a reason.

Skills. The pia-porting and pia-language skills point agents at piac migrate and the fix-its, and a new or deprecated feature's skill change (CLAUDE.md's skill-pack rule) names its migration rule.

Connection to advisories. An advisory's fix is "rebuild with a fixed piac". When that piac is newer than the source, pia-cert check --why says to run piac migrate --from=<the old prover's version> first, which it knows from the certificate's prover line. That is why certificates record the version even for modules nothing revokes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every Pia object says who proved it, with what solvers and engines, and for which ABI, and pia-cert dump shows it.
  • A soundness bug becomes an advisory, a fix and a regression test. Builds that contain a module the bug may have touched stop at the next check, and only those: a bug in interval analysis does not revoke modules that never used it.
  • Trusting a revoked proof is possible, but it is a listed trusted item, never a default.
  • Upgrading piac does not break importers. Bumping the ABI version breaks all of them, by design, and is rare.
  • Only the published piac is stamped. A stamped piac changes with every commit, so stamping every build would rerun every test that runs piac on every pull request, even one that changes only docs or lib/. CI builds and tests with piac dev, then relinks piac once with --config=release to publish it, and checks the stamp on pull requests by building only the stamped header.
  • The engines line depends on which engine proved each goal, which is reproducible under an rlimit. If a later change makes engine choice depend on timing, the certificate would not be reproducible, so engines must stay deterministic.
  • Advisories rest on the trust model ADR 0024 already states: they make honest-but-buggy builds safe to combine, and they do nothing against a malicious producer, who can write any prover line. Code signing and, later, re-checkable proof objects are the answer there.
  • Every breaking change costs a rule and a test in the same PR, and in exchange old code is never stranded: it migrates in one command, or fails with the exact edit to make. Deprecated forms cost one release of parser support each.
  • Because rules key on piac versions, the version identity of section 1 is a dependency of migration, not only of trust.
  • An advisory can only be as narrow as the engine list. A bug in goal generation (a goal never emitted) is not in any engine, so its advisory names no engines and revokes every module in the range. A later refinement could record which goal kinds a module raised, if advisories turn out to be too broad.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
1. Identity. piac --version, Bazel stamping in CI and release builds, and the prover, solver and abi lines in a format 3 certificate. The link check refuses mismatched ABI versions and targets. pia-cert dump prints the new lines. Skills: piac-build (the new lines, --version).
  2. Engines and Lean. The verifier records which engine proved each goal and writes the engines line and the Lean receipt lines.
  3. Advisories. The TOML format, security/advisories/, compiled into pia-cert; pia-cert check refuses matches, --accept-advisory, --advisories=<dir>, --require-released, pia-cert advisories; accepted advisories in --trust-report. A test advisory against a fake engine, with objects that match and do not. Skills: piac-build and piac-verify (the flags), and a page on the site.
  4. Proof cache. Refuse cache entries from a solver version an advisory revokes.
  5. Migration framework. src/migrate, rules over the syntax tree with rewrites and suggestions, deprecated warnings with fix-its in piac, the LSP code action and REPL/MCP diagnostics, piac migrate with --from and --check, and a first rule for the next breaking change that lands. Skills: piac-build (the command), pia-idioms (the deprecated warning).
  6. The CI rule. tools/migrate/check.py in CI, and piac migrate --check over the repository.
  7. Runtime. The launch check, when the runtime's certificate check from abi.md Layer 2 lands.

docs.title: Decisions on the design questions
docs.text:
Dean answered each question on 2026-11-26, in every case with the proposal:

  1. Granularity. An advisory names a version range, narrowed by the proof engines a module's certificate lists. An advisory with no engines revokes every module in its range.
  2. Response. The check refuses a module that matches an advisory, unless that module is accepted by name with --accept-advisory=ID:Module, which makes it a trusted item.
  3. Build identity. Builds between releases are the release version plus the commit count on main and the short commit (0.1.0+512.9f3c2e1a7b04). Unstamped builds are dev.
  4. Distribution. Advisories are checked in under security/advisories/ and compiled into piac, pia-cert and the runtime. --advisories=<dir> adds a newer set. Nothing is fetched over the network.
  5. Deprecation. A deprecated form keeps compiling for one release with a deprecated warning and a fix-it, then becomes an error that still names the fix.
  6. Source version. Source does not declare a Pia version. Rules detect old forms from the source, and piac migrate --from takes a version from the user or from a certificate's prover line.

docs.title: 74. Library types: a type written in Pia gets an MLIR type, ops and proofs from its library, and Pia.Tensor over MLIR tensor is the proof point
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-27

Status: Accepted (2026-11-27, with Dean's answers below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for a tensor library that uses MLIR tensors under the hood while keeping contracts in Pia that are proved at compile time, and for it to be "the proof point for a way to extend Pia without having to add more primitive types in the language".

Today every type the compiler understands is a primitive in C++: integers, floats (ADR 0067 F1, PR #440), bool, fixed arrays, slices, records and variants. Each one has a row in Codegen.cpp's type table, an encoding in the verifier, and its own printing, layout and FFI rules. A tensor done the same way would be another row in each of those tables, and so would every type after it: complex numbers, fixed-point, SIMD vectors, big integers, quantised weights. That is the path this ADR avoids.

ADR 0065 already gives most of the mechanism, for functions. @lower gives a function an MLIR form, the Pia body stays the specification and the fallback, and the lowering is proved to refine it or is listed as trusted. Steps 1 and 2 are merged (PRs #423 and #459): a trusted @lower on a function, metaprograms that compute the MLIR text, a parse check before proving, and the operand-effect check. ADR 0065 also sketched @lower on a type (section 1, step 6), and left it at one paragraph. This ADR turns that paragraph into a design, and puts Pia.Tensor on top of it.

What exists, and what a prototype with today's piac showed (2026-11-27, the latest prerelease):

  • Types can take types and regions, not values. let mat = let (t : type) (r : region) => type {...} works; let mat = let (t : type) (m : usize) (n : usize) => type {...} is rejected ("only a generic type can take type arguments"). So a shape cannot be part of a type yet.
  • A field can carry a where about itself, not about its siblings. rows : usize where rows <= 65536 proves, and callers keep the fact. data : [t] where len data = rows * cols is "unknown name 'rows'", and a record-level } where ... is "refinements ('where') are not supported yet". ADR 0006 designed refinement types; they are not built.
  • With the shape as fields, every function must restate the invariant. A mat of rows, cols and data with a spec ok a = len a.data = a.rows * a.cols proves get and fill (17 goals, 0.34 s) once each requires ok a. A matmul cell against a dot spec with symbolic rows and cols needs one bounds lemma per indexing map (as ADR 0065's prototype found), and its nonlinear index goals are where the time goes (see Prototype below).
  • With constant shapes the same proof is cheap. ADR 0065's 4 x 4 i8 matmul over [i8; 16] proved 51 of 51 goals in 17.5 s, because every extent is a literal and the index products fold.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• MLIR's tensor dialect and destination-passing style. A tensor is an immutable value. linalg ops on tensors take an outs operand, the destination, and return a new tensor of its shape; one-shot bufferisation then turns each op into an in-place write when the destination has no other reader, and inserts a copy when it does. tensor.empty makes a destination with no contents. This is the semantics the library takes, because it is already the one MLIR optimises.
  • Futhark, Dex and Idris put sizes in types: [n][m]f32 in Futhark, n=>m=>Float in Dex, Vect n a in Idris. A shape mismatch is a type error, and the compiler knows every extent that is a constant. Futhark also has the uniqueness types that make in-place updates of arrays safe, as Pia's moved does.
  • Mojo builds its Tensor and SIMD types in the standard library on __mlir_type, with no proofs.
  • Rust's const generics ([T; N], struct Matrix<const R: usize, const C: usize>) are the mainstream form of a value as a type parameter, restricted to integers and other simple constants.
  • mlir-tv (CAV 2022) gives tensor and linalg on tensors an SMT encoding as arrays from indices to elements, which is simpler than the memref encoding because there is no aliasing.

docs.title: 1. A library type is a Pia type, its MLIR type, its ops, and its proofs, all in the library
docs.text:
A library type is a type whose meaning and whose machine form are both written in Pia, in a library, with no row for it in the compiler's tables. It has four parts:

  1. A Pia definition: a record (or variant) of existing types, with its invariant. This is the type's meaning, what the verifier reasons about and what the REPL's JIT and --lower=off run.
  2. An MLIR type, given by @lower on the type (ADR 0065, section 1): which MLIR type a value has, and how the Pia fields map onto it.
  3. Ops: Pia functions with contracts, each with a Pia body (the specification and the fallback, ADR 0065's rule that a body is always kept) and a @lower that gives its MLIR form.
  4. Proofs: each op's @lower is proved to refine its Pia body (ADR 0065's refinement goal, step 3), or is listed as trusted. Clients prove from the contracts only, and never see MLIR.

The compiler learns nothing about tensors. What it gains, once, are four general mechanisms that any library type uses:

Mechanism What it is Status @lower on types The MLIR type of a value, and how fields map onto it ADR 0065 step 6, designed here (section 3) Value-returning lowerings A lowering whose result is a value ($result), not only writes to out buffers New here (section 4) Type invariants A where on a whole record, over its fields, kept by every value of the type ADR 0006, not built; needed here (section 2) Value parameters on types A type that takes a usize or a [usize; r], so a shape is part of the type New here, an open question (section 2)

Each of those is a language or compiler feature, but none is a type: complex numbers, fixed-point, quantised blocks and SIMD vectors all use the same four and need nothing else. The test of this ADR is that after Pia.Tensor lands, a second library type (Pia.Complex, or vec<T, k> from ADR 0013 rebuilt as a library type over MLIR's vector) needs no compiler change at all.

docs.title: 2. tensor t s: shape in the type, extents as values
docs.text:
let tensor = let (t : type) (s : shape) (r : region) => type {
  data : borrowed(r) mutable [t]
} where len data = size s
  @lower("tensor<$s x $t>", data)
  • s : shape is a value parameter: an array of extents, [4; 4], where each extent is a literal, a constant, or ? for one fixed at run time. A type with all-literal extents lowers to a static MLIR type (tensor<4x4xi8>), and every index product in its proofs folds, which is what made ADR 0065's static matmul cheap. A ? extent is carried as a field the library adds, and lowers to tensor<?x4xi8>.
  • The invariant len data = size s is a type invariant (ADR 0006): it holds of every value, is assumed on every parameter and proved at every construction, so no op restates it. Without type invariants, every op requires ok a, which the prototype shows works but which every client then has to prove again.
  • Rank is the length of the shape, so tensor i8 [64] is a vector, tensor i8 [4; 4] a matrix, and there is one type, not a family. A shape mismatch is a type error at the call site, not a goal.
  • Elements are any type the core has: integers now, f32 and f64 once floats have their meanings (ADR 0067 F2 and F3). A tensor of a library type (complex, quantised) needs the element type's own @lower to name a scalar MLIR type.

docs.title: 3. @lower on types
docs.text: @lower(mlir_type, buffer_field, extents...) on a type names the MLIR type its values have, the field that holds the elements, and the fields that give the ? extents. Version 1 allows ranked tensor and memref with the identity (row-major) layout over one buffer field, as ADR 0065 said; strided views come with FPL (ADR 0020). Codegen builds a value of the type from the buffer's pointer and the extents with bufferization.to_tensor (or a memref descriptor), and a value of the type passed to Pia code that is not lowered goes back through bufferization.to_memref. A function whose parameters and result are all tensors never makes that round trip.

docs.title: 4. Ops are values in destination-passing style, and nothing allocates behind the program's back
docs.text:
Pia's memory rule is that nothing allocates implicitly and every allocation is fallible (ADR 0026). MLIR tensors look like values that are made fresh by every op. Destination-passing style reconciles the two:

let matmul (a : tensor i8 [m; k] r) (b : tensor i8 [k; n] r)
           (c : moved tensor i32 [m; n] r) : tensor i32 [m; n] r
  ensures forall (i in 0 .. m) (j in 0 .. n). at result [i; j] = dot a b i j k
  @lower("%r = linalg.matmul ins($a, $b : $a.type, $b.type) outs($c : $c.type) -> $c.type")
= ...
  • Every op takes its destination, moved, and returns it. The destination is the only storage the result uses. Pia.Tensor.empty alloc s is the only function that allocates, and it returns an error on failure like every other allocation (ADR 0026); drop frees.
  • moved is what makes bufferisation in place, the way ADR 0065 section 1 said ownership facts would. A moved destination has no other reader, so one-shot bufferisation writes it in place. After bufferisation piac checks that it inserted no memref.alloc and no copy, and it is an error if it did: a hidden allocation is a bug in the library or in piac, never something a program silently pays for.
  • $result is a lowering's result value, new in this ADR: ADR 0065's lowerings so far only write out operands. A lowering on tensors returns the op's result, and the operand-effect check (step 2) becomes: the result's buffer is the destination's.
  • Inputs are read, never written, which on tensors is true by construction, since a tensor value cannot be written.

docs.title: 5. Contracts are about elements, through one spec accessor
docs.text:
Each op's contract is stated with the library's spec accessor at t [i; j], never with data and index arithmetic, so clients never see the layout and never prove an index product. The accessor's bounds lemma (one per indexing map, ADR 0065's prototype finding) is proved once in the library. Reductions use the same spec folds as Pia.Linalg (ADR 0065, section 5): matmul is specified by dot, and the library's ops are generated from MLIR's own op definitions where Pia.Linalg already is, so Pia.Tensor.matmul and Pia.Linalg.matmul share one meaning and one proof.

The meaning of the MLIR form on tensors (for the refinement goal of ADR 0065 step 3) is the memref meaning without memory: a tensor is an SMT array from an index tuple to an element, tensor.extract and tensor.insert are select and store, extract_slice and insert_slice are index maps, and linalg.generic on tensors is the same fold as on memrefs, writing a new array instead of a buffer. One-shot bufferisation is an upstream pass, trusted the way -O2 is, and listed in the trust report.

docs.title: 6. What Pia.Tensor has in version 1
docs.text: empty, fill, at (spec) and get, set (an insert that returns the tensor), map and zip_with over a lambda (linalg.generic with a scalar body from the lambda), reduce, transpose, reshape (tensor.reshape, expand_shape, collapse_shape), slice and insert_slice, matvec, matmul and batch_matmul, and dot. These are exactly what the llama2.c port needs (ADR 0067: the projections are matvec, attention is dot, slice and matvec, the KV cache is insert_slice), so the LLM's kernels become the library's first client.

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text:
Run with the latest prerelease piac in the cloud (2026-11-27). Shapes as fields, since types cannot take values yet:

  • mat t r = {rows; cols; data} with rows, cols bounded by field wheres, and the invariant as a spec ok: get and fill prove, 17 goals in 0.34 s.
  • A matmul cell (i8 elements, i32 sum) against a recursive dot spec over symbolic rows and cols: 46 of 50 goals proved in 10 min 7 s of wall-clock time (20 min 46 s of CPU at 4 jobs). The 4 that timed out are the two index-bounds goals inside dot and the two loop invariants after an iteration, all nonlinear in the symbolic cols. That compares with 51 of 51 goals in 17.5 s for the same cell at a literal 4 x 4 shape (ADR 0065's prototype). Shapes that are literals in types are the difference between a library whose proofs are cheap and one whose every client fights nonlinear goals.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
Each step is one PR and useful on its own.

  1. Type invariants: a where on a record over its fields (ADR 0006), assumed on parameters, proved at construction and after each field write. Useful to every record, not only tensors.
  2. Value parameters on types: a type that takes usize and [usize; r] arguments, with literal and ? extents, and generic functions over them ((m : usize) deduced from an argument's type, as type arguments are). Also gives [t; n] generic functions.
  3. @lower on types (ADR 0065 step 6): ranked tensor and memref, identity layout, one buffer field; value-returning lowerings with $result; one-shot bufferisation with the no-allocation check.
  4. Pia.Tensor with trusted lowerings on CPU: the version 1 ops, each with its Pia body and contract, tested against --lower=off.
  5. Proved lowerings on tensors: the tensor meaning of section 5 added to ADR 0065 step 3, so Pia.Tensor's lowerings stop being trusted.
  6. Floats: f32 tensors once ADR 0038's meanings are in (ADR 0067 F2, F3), and the LLM's matvec on Pia.Tensor.
  7. The second library type, with no compiler change, as the test of the mechanism.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New numeric types become library code: a type, its MLIR form, its ops and their proofs, reviewed like any library, with no new primitive and no new row in Codegen or the verifier.
  • Two general language features (type invariants and value parameters on types) come first, and they are worth having on their own; the tensor library waits for them.
  • piac's trusted base grows by its reading of tensor semantics and by one-shot bufferisation, both listed in the trust report; the no-allocation check keeps bufferisation from adding hidden costs.
  • Pia.Tensor and Pia.Linalg share meanings, so there is one proof of matmul, not two.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Shapes in types, or shapes as values? This ADR puts the shape in the type (section 2). The alternative is shapes as fields with contracts, which works today but makes every client prove shape agreement and index bounds, and costs more to prove (Prototype).
  2. Destination-passing, or ops that allocate? This ADR has every op take a moved destination (section 4). The alternative is ops that take an allocator and return a result or an error, which reads more like NumPy and puts an allocation and an error path on every op.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
• Shapes in the type (question 1), Dean, 2026-11-27: tensor t s takes its shape as a value parameter, as section 2 says, so value parameters on types (step 2) come before Pia.Tensor.

  • Destination-passing (question 2), Dean, 2026-11-27: every op takes a moved destination and returns it, as section 4 says. Only Pia.Tensor.empty allocates.

  • How a function names a value parameter, Dean, 2026-11-27: implicitly. A name in a value parameter's place that no parameter declares, n in (b : block t n), is deduced from the argument like a type parameter, and in the body and contracts it is the argument's value. This replaces step 2's (m : usize) and needs no new syntax. The matmul signature in section 4 is already written this way.

docs.title: Amendment, 2026-11-27: ops lower through pia_lib.call (ADR 0078)
docs.text:
ADR 0078 changes how section 4's ops reach MLIR. A Pia.Tensor op no longer puts linalg.matmul in place of the call at IRGen. It lowers to pia_lib.call @Pia.Tensor.matmul, whose meaning is the Pia body, and the @lower form becomes a substitution rule. A late pass, pia-lib-lower, either substitutes the rule's linalg op or expands the body. Section 4 reads with these changes:

  • The destination is an operand of pia_lib.call, the way it is of linalg's outs. Substitution runs before one-shot bufferisation, so bufferisation still sees only upstream ops, and the no-allocation check is unchanged. ADR 0065's linalg pipeline, and @schedule, run after the substitution, so a substituted op is still tiled and vectorised.
  • Expansion sends a tensor operand back through bufferization.to_memref into the body's buffer field, writing the destination's buffer. The no-allocation check covers that path too, so expanding an op cannot copy behind the program's back.
  • $result is ADR 0078's value-returning rule. ADR 0078 builds the scalar case first, for Pia.Math.sqrt (#487), and step 3 here extends it to tensors.
  • Each rule's obligation is ADR 0065's refinement goal, which section 5 extends to tensors. It is proved once, when the op is verified, whether or not a build applies the rule. A rule nobody has proved yet is trusted and listed in the trust report, the same as step 4's lowerings.

Steps 3 to 5 build on this: step 3 adds @lower on types and the tensor case of $result, step 4's trusted lowerings are ADR 0078 rules, and step 5 proves them.

Steps 1 and 2 are built: record invariants (PR #472), and value parameters on types and on functions (PRs #499 and #515). Shapes, (s : shape) with [4; 4] or [m; k], complete step 2 with literal extents; a ? extent needs a field to carry it, so it comes with step 3.

Step 3 is built in two parts. Step 3a is @lower on types with memref only. A record names its MLIR type and the field that holds its elements, @lower("memref<$s x $t>", data), where $s and $n splice value parameters and $t the elements' type parameter. A function lowering that splices a value of the type gets a view of its buffer. An array is viewed with expand_shape. A slice is cast to the length its type's invariant proves, and the body proves that length, so its view keeps a dynamic offset (strided<[4, 1], offset: ?>). An inout value whose elements are a slice is written through its loan and returned as it came in. Every extent is static, and there are no extent fields yet. Step 3b adds tensor, $result on tensors and one-shot bufferisation with the no-allocation check.

docs.title: 75. Codegen is benchmarked against C, C++, Rust and Zig on public problems, same algorithm first, counted in instructions on Linux and timed on Apple Silicon
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-27

Status: Accepted (2026-11-27, with Dean's answers below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Dean asked for public benchmarks of C, C++, Rust and Zig on common problems, so that Pia's generated code can be replicated against, or measured against, their best implementations: "a good representation of how well the code gen competes".

Pia already tracks two costs as benchmarks: proof cost (ADR 0032, tools/bench/proof_bench.py, three Linux shards that gate every PR) and build time. Nothing measures the code piac emits. The codegen tests (tests/codegen) check that compiled Pia gives the same answers as C, not how fast it is.

docs.title: The public suites, and what their licences allow
docs.text:
Suite Problems Languages Licence What we may do plb2 (attractivechaos, 2024) nqueen, matmul, sudoku, bedcov 25, including C, Rust, Zig (nqueen, matmul only), Swift, Nim, D CC0 1.0 vendor freely Computer Language Benchmarks Game (CLBG) n-body, spectral-norm, mandelbrot, fannkuch-redux, fasta, k-nucleotide, reverse-complement, binary-trees, pidigits, regex-redux C, C++, Rust and about 25 others; no Zig Revised BSD (3-clause); the names "The Computer Language Benchmarks Game" and "The Benchmarks Game" may not endorse a derived product vendor with the notice kept; never say "Benchmarks Game" in a claim about Pia Programming Language Benchmarks (hanabi1224) the CLBG problems plus nsieve, edigits, merkletrees, lru, json-serde, coro-prime-sieve adds Zig, Odin, V, Nim and others to CLBG's set; runs in GitHub Actions MIT vendor with the notice; the source of most Zig versions kostya/benchmarks Brainfuck (bench.b, mandel.b), base64, JSON, matmul, primes, havlak C, C++, Rust, Zig, D, Go and more MIT vendor with the notice niklas-heer/speed-comparison one problem (Leibniz π) many MIT too small to be worth it

None of the suites is GPL, so the licence rule (never use, bundle or depend on GPL code) is met by every reference program as written. Two programs need care anyway: CLBG's fastest pidigits programs link GMP, which is LGPL/GPL, and regex-redux links PCRE2 or a language's regex library, which measures the library, not the compiler. Neither is in the shortlist.

The suites answer different questions. plb2 is the closest to Dean's: every language runs the same algorithm, written by one author, with no library calls in the hot loop, so the difference is the compiler. CLBG is the opposite: each language's fastest known program, often hand-vectorised with intrinsics and multithreaded, so it measures how far an expert can push a language. hanabi1224 sits between them and is the only suite with Zig for most CLBG problems.

docs.title: What Pia can express today
docs.text:
Checked against docs/status.md on main (2026-11-27) and the latest prerelease of piac:

  • Built: bounded integers with proved overflow, bit operators, fixed arrays and slices, records, variants, loops with invariants, recursion with decreases, saturating and wrapping arithmetic, f32/f64 with + - * / and strict IEEE codegen (no FMA contraction), C calls both ways, spread on the CPU (ADR 0060), @lower to linalg (ADR 0065).
  • Not built yet: conversions between floats and integers (PR #452, open), a square root (no sqrt yet; it will be a proved Pia.Math function with @lower, #487, and libm is never trusted), vec<T, k> (M10), recursive types in codegen, a hash map, Pia.Sys.Fs (PR #444, open).

piac compiles at CodeGenOptLevel::Default and runs MLIR's optimising transformer at -O<n>; for x86_64 it requires x86-64-v3 (ADR 0049), so references must be built for the same CPU to be comparable.

docs.title: Prototype: plb2 nqueen
docs.text:
nqueen ported to Pia with the prebuilt piac (latest, 2026-11-27) and run in a cloud container (Intel Xeon at 2.1 GHz, 4 cores, clang 18.1.3, rustc 1.97.0, Zig 0.14.1), n = 15, all built for x86-64-v3 at -O3 / opt-level=3 / ReleaseFast:

let rec place (n : int{1..31}) (k : u32) (l : u32) (c : u32) (r : u32) : u64
  requires k < n
  decreases n - k
= let m : mutable u64 = 0 in
  let used : u32 = (l | c | r) in
  let nn : u32 = n in
  for i in 0 .. nn do
    let z : u32 = 1u32 << i in
    if used & z = 0 then
      (if k + 1 = n then m <- m +| 1
       else m <- m +| place n (k + 1) (((l | z) & 0x7FFF'FFFF) << 1) (c | z) ((r | z) >> 1))
    else ()
  done;
  m

All 19 goals proved in 0.12 s (14 by intervals, 5 by Z3).

Program Wall time, 5 runs (s) Instructions at n = 12 (cachegrind) plb2 C (explicit stack) 3.35 – 3.57 62.07 M plb2 Rust (explicit stack) 3.58 – 3.68 plb2 Zig (explicit stack, n a constant) 3.76 – 3.98 C, the Pia program's recursion transcribed 3.76 – 3.91 93.72 M Pia 3.90 – 4.05 93.80 M

Three findings:

  1. Against the same algorithm in C, Pia's code is within 0.1% in instructions (93.80 M against 93.72 M) and about 3% in wall time, which is inside this container's noise. The assembly of place is the loop clang emits, with bt for the test and shlx for the shift.
  2. Against plb2's C, Pia is about 14% slower, and the cause is the algorithm, not codegen. plb2 backtracks with an explicit stack in a for (k = 0; k >= 0;) loop. That loop's termination needs a lexicographic measure over the stack, which Pia cannot state as one decreases today, so the port recurses instead. This is the most useful kind of result the benchmark can give: it names a language gap (a lexicographic or well-founded decreases), not a codegen one.
  3. Proof shapes the code, a little. C lets bits fall off the top of l << 1; Pia proves << does not overflow, so the port masks first (one and a call), and the count uses +| because the number of solutions has no bound the verifier can see. Neither shows up in the instruction count. Each such change is recorded with the port.

Wall times in the cloud vary by 5% between runs; instruction counts do not vary at all. That decides the metric (section 4).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Principle (Dean, 2026-11-27): every gap a benchmark finds is fixed on principle, for every Pia program. The benchmarks show where Pia's codegen falls short. A fix goes into the compiler, a pass or the library, and it makes every program with that shape faster. Nothing is tuned to a benchmark: no flag, rule, pattern or library function that exists for one benchmark program, and no change that matches a benchmark's code. A fix that helps a benchmark but no other program is not a fix.

docs.title: 1. Two lanes: same algorithm (the headline) and best known (the stretch)
docs.text:
• Same algorithm. The Pia port and every reference run one algorithm, as plb2 requires. This is the codegen comparison Dean asked for, and the number we publish first. When a proof forces the Pia port away from the reference's shape (as nqueen's recursion did), the benchmark also carries a C control: the Pia program transcribed back into C, so that "codegen" and "algorithm" separate.
  • Best known. The fastest single-threaded and multithreaded C, C++, Rust and Zig programs from CLBG and hanabi1224, against the best Pia program we can write, with spread for parallelism. It is reported, never headlined, because it measures intrinsics and experts as much as compilers.

docs.title: 2. The shortlist, by what Pia needs
docs.text:
Wave 1: buildable now (integers, buffers, recursion, floats without conversions):

Problem Source References (same algorithm) Best known Exercises nqueen plb2 C, Rust, Zig (plb2) same bit operators, recursion sudoku (kudoku) plb2 C, Rust (plb2); C++ port of the C same small fixed arrays, branches fannkuch-redux CLBG, hanabi1224 single-threaded C and Rust (CLBG); C++ 1-im.cpp, Rust 1.rs, Zig 1.zig (hanabi1224) the fastest multithreaded C, C++ and Rust (CLBG), Rust 1-m.rs, Zig 2-m.zig (hanabi1224) permutations in fixed arrays, spread matmul, 1500 × 1500 f64 plb2 C, Rust, Zig (plb2) the same through @lower to linalg float loops, vectorisation, @lower nsieve hanabi1224 C 1.c, C++ 1.cpp, Rust 1.rs, Zig 1.zig (hanabi1224) same a byte buffer, strided loops Brainfuck (bench.b, mandel.b) kostya C, C++, Rust, Zig (kostya) same an interpreter loop, variants, a jump table base64 encode and decode kostya C test-nolib.c (kostya), with a C control (bench/codegen/base64) kostya's Rust and Zig (library codecs), and C with aklomp's SIMD codec (BSD 2-clause), reported only byte tables, slices

matmul's input is filled by the C driver, so only the multiply is Pia (bench/codegen/matmul).

Wave 2: after a feature lands:

Problem Waits on mandelbrot, spectral-norm float to integer conversions (PR #452) n-body a proved sqrt in Pia.Math, lowered to math.sqrt with @lower (#487) bedcov allocation and sort from the standard library on a 1 M-element array (Pia.Mem, sort) fasta, reverse-complement Pia.Sys.Fs (PR #444) for output, or a C driver that writes the buffer mandelbrot, spectral-norm, fannkuch-redux with spread wave 1, then the best-known lane

Out of scope: binary-trees and merkletrees (recursive types are not compiled, and they measure allocators), pidigits (GMP), regex-redux (a regex library), k-nucleotide and lru (a hash map, the standard library's not the compiler's), JSON (a library comparison; Pia.Text.Json can join later as a library benchmark).

C++ has its own entry only where CLBG's best C++ differs from its C (fannkuch-redux, Brainfuck); elsewhere a C++ build of the C program measures the same compiler and says nothing new.

docs.title: 3. Layout and Bazel targets
docs.text:
• bench/codegen/<problem>/ holds the Pia port (<problem>.pia), its C driver (main.c, which parses arguments and prints the result, so every program has the same argv and output), the C control when there is one, and a README.md with the source, the input size, and every change the proof forced.
  • third_party/benchmarks/{plb2,clbg,hanabi1224,kostya}/ holds the reference programs, unmodified except for a header that names the origin, each directory with the suite's LICENSE (the BSD and MIT notices must be kept). A reference that must change (Zig 0.11 syntax, a constant n turned into an argument so the compiler cannot specialise on it) gets a patch file beside it, not an edit.
  • Bazel builds everything with one CPU target: C and C++ with the repository's clang toolchain; Rust with rules_rust; Zig with rules_zig. Both are Apache 2.0 or MIT and come from the Bazel Central Registry. Flags are fixed per lane and listed in one file, bench/codegen/flags.bzl: -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 or -mcpu=apple-m1, -ffp-contract=off for C and C++ (Pia does not contract FMAs unless licensed, and clang does by default), Rust opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=…, Zig ReleaseFast -mcpu=…; no LTO and no PGO, since piac has neither.
  • //bench/codegen:<problem>_test runs every build of a problem on a small input and checks that they print the same answer. These run in bazel test //..., so a wrong Pia program fails CI like any other test.
  • tools/bench/codegen_bench.py --bazel-bin=… runs every program on its benchmark input and writes one JSON file: per program, the instruction count, the wall times, and the ratios to C.

docs.title: 4. What is measured, where, and what gates
docs.text:
• Instructions on Linux CI (cachegrind, --cache-sim=no): deterministic, so they can be compared across commits like Z3's rlimit in the proof benchmark. Inputs are scaled down so that each program runs in under a second under cachegrind. They are reported against a baseline, bench/codegen/baseline.json.
  • Wall time on Apple Silicon: the median of 10 runs after one warm-up, in the nightly macOS job, with the machine's chip in the report. This is the number to publish for the 0.1.0 target (Dean's M3).
  • Wall time on Linux: reported, never compared across runs, because shared runners vary.
  • No gate (CLAUDE.md: only the proof shards gate besides build and tests). The report lands in the job summary and as an artifact. Gating on a Pia/C instruction ratio is an open question below.

docs.title: 5. Reports
docs.text: Each run's report follows the project's report format: per problem, the input, Pia's instructions and wall time, each reference's, the ratio to the same-algorithm C, the proof cost and goal count of the Pia port, and for each port the list of changes the proof forced. The summary line is the geometric mean of Pia/C over wave 1. Any claim made from it names the suite (plb2, CLBG, hanabi1224, kostya) as the source of the problems and reference programs, and never uses CLBG's names to endorse Pia.

docs.title: 6. Steps
docs.text:
1. This ADR.
  2. bench/codegen/nqueen and the harness: Bazel targets for C, Rust and Zig through rules_rust and rules_zig, the output test, codegen_bench.py, and a codegen benchmark (Linux) report job in CI.
  3. The rest of wave 1, one problem a PR, each with its proof stats and first numbers.
  4. The nightly macOS wall-time run, and the Linux instruction gate once wave 1 is complete.
  5. Wave 2 as its features land, and the multithreaded best-known programs against spread; the hand-vectorised ones after M10.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Each port is also a test of the language on code it did not grow up with. Gaps found this way (nqueen's lexicographic decreases) become issues, and the README of each port lists what the proof cost in code shape.
  • CI gains a toolchain for Rust and one for Zig, both from the registry; the first cold build downloads them once. Neither enters piac or its release.
  • Vendored programs carry BSD and MIT notices, which third_party/benchmarks keeps beside them. Nothing in it is linked into Pia.
  • A Pia/C ratio becomes a number Pia is judged by. The same-algorithm lane keeps that number about codegen; the best-known lane keeps us honest about what experts get from intrinsics, until vec<T, k> (M10) gives Pia its own.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Should a codegen regression gate PRs, on the instruction count against the baseline, as the proof benchmark does? Proposed: report only until wave 1 is complete, then gate at +5% instructions on Linux.
  2. Where should Apple Silicon wall times come from: the nightly macOS CI job (an M1 VM, shared), or occasional runs on the iMac (Dean's M3, the 0.1.0 target)? Proposed: CI nightly for tracking, the iMac only for a published comparison, by hand and with Dean's say-so.
  3. Should the best-known lane be built at all before vec<T, k>? Proposed: yes for the multithreaded programs with spread, no for the hand-vectorised ones until M10.

docs.title: Answers to the open questions
docs.text:
Accepted by Dean on 2026-11-27 ("0075 LGTM").

Dean, 2026-11-27:

  1. Gating: report only until wave 1 is complete, then gate PRs at +5% instructions on Linux against bench/codegen/baseline.json.
  2. Apple Silicon timings: the nightly macOS CI job tracks them. The iMac (Dean's M3) runs only a published comparison, by hand and with Dean's say-so.
  3. Best-known lane before vec<T, k>: build the multithreaded programs now, against spread. Leave the hand-vectorised references out until M10.

docs.title: Gaps to the fastest programs
docs.text:
Dean asked (2026-11-27) for issues covering what Pia needs to match the fastest published programs. They are tracked in #485:

  • #486: lexicographic and well-founded decreases (nqueen's explicit stack; 1.51 times plb2 C's instructions today).
  • #487: sqrt as a proved Pia.Math function with @lower to math.sqrt, not a builtin (n-body).
  • #488: ADR 0012's reassociation and FMA licences (vectorised float reductions).
  • #489: compiled recursive types with arenas (binary-trees, merkletrees).
  • #490: -O3 as LLVM's Aggressive level, and LTO with C callers.
  • #491: exact ranges for loop variables over a range-typed bound.
  • #492: the best-known lane with spread.
  • Already open: #11 (vec<T, k>), #62 (Pia.Math), #72 (containers).

docs.title: 76. Transparent exports: an importer proves against an exported function's body, as a caller in its own module does
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-27

Status: Proposed

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Indigo (actuals.com) put a claim to Dean (2026-11-27). Building modules separately against exported contracts may cost callers two things: proofs that let the optimiser remove branches, and proofs of the callers' own contracts. Some of those losses could even be soundness problems. Dean asked for the property to be proved in Lean against the current implementation, and for the compiler to be changed if it falls short. The change he named was grafting in shipped Pia bodies, the standard library's first, so that "all the contracts and branches are visible to the prover".

The claim mixes two properties, and they come out differently:

  • Soundness. Nothing proved against a contract is false for an implementation that meets it.
  • Precision. What a caller cannot prove because the contract says less than the body does.

docs.title: What the call rule is today
docs.text:
stepCall in src/verify/Verifier.cpp (docs/verifier.md, "Calls") takes a call on its callee's contract. The precondition is a goal at the arguments, the result is fresh, and the postcondition is assumed about it. There are three exceptions:

  • Pure functions of scalars in the same module (definesValue, "Pure functions of scalars"). One with no loop, buffer, abort or recursion is unfolded at every call: pre(a) ==> F a = body(a).
  • Spec functions, generics and metaprograms. These are exported with their definitions (inlinedSig in src/syntax/Interfaces.cpp), and importers unfold the spec functions.
  • Imported ordinary functions. These are only their contracts: "An imported function of scalars is, to the verifier, an uninterpreted function that meets its interface contract".

So a module boundary changes what proves. A call that the body settles in its own module fails across the boundary. This happens on today's latest piac:

module Clamp : C
interface C = sig
  let clamp_to : (x : u8) -> (hi : u8) -> u8
    ensures result <= hi
end
let clamp_to (x : u8) (hi : u8) : u8
  ensures result <= hi
= if x > hi then hi else x
let three_here (k : u8) : u8 ensures result = 3 = clamp_to 3 10    (* proved *)

module Use : U
import Clamp.C
let three (k : u8) : u8 ensures result = 3 = Clamp.clamp_to 3 10   (* failed, k = 0 *)
let dead (x : u8) : u8 ensures result = x
= if Clamp.clamp_to x 255 <> x then 0 else x                       (* failed, x = 127 *)

dead is the optimisation half of the claim. Its then branch is dead, but nothing outside Clamp can know that. Codegen sees the same boundary. Contracts are erased (docs/codegen.md, step 1), and an imported function is a declaration in the importer's object, so LLVM cannot inline it or fold the branch either. Within a module, private functions have internal linkage and LLVM inlines them.

docs.title: What Lean proves about the rule
docs.text:
tests/lean/CallRule.lean (checked by //tests/lean:call_rule_test) models the rule over a small language: each function has one integer parameter and result, bodies are trees of calls, and an erased call stands for a lemma call or a call in a contract. It proves, with Lean's own axioms only:

Theorem Says partial_sound For code that runs, the rule is sound with no termination argument at all: every run that returns meets its contract, mutual recursion included ghost_unsound For calls that never run, it is not sound without termination: two lemmas that call each other prove False, and a caller that returns 3 is proved to return 7 verifier_sound, verifier_partial, lex_descends With the goals the verifier now raises, it is sound, erased calls included. Calls between the call graph's cycles go down the DAG, and calls within a cycle make a measure go down modular A caller's proof holds for every implementation of its callees that is verified against their contracts, which is what separate compilation and the certificate check rely on refine_preserves A weaker precondition and a stronger postcondition (ADR 0024's evolution rule) keep every caller's proof precision_gap Some property of the real program cannot be proved from a contract weaker than its body strongest_complete Using each callee's exact behaviour as its contract (inlining it) proves everything that holds strongest_not_modular A proof made by inlining does not survive a change to the callee's body that keeps its contract

ghost_unsound was a real bug in the verifier, not just a property of the model. Termination was checked for direct recursion only, so this program proved and compiled, and returned 3:

let lemma a (x : int) : unit ensures false = b x
let lemma b (x : int) : unit ensures false = a x
let seven (x : u8) : u8 ensures result = 7 = a 0; 3

PR #496 fixes it: each call within a cycle of the call graph is now a termination goal (tests/verify/mutual_recursion.pia). That is the Descends relation the Lean proof assumes, so the theorems describe the verifier as it now is.

So the answer to the claim:

  1. Soundness. With PR #496, modular verification is sound. Proving against contracts loses no soundness, and modular says why separate builds are safe. The unsoundness was in termination, not in modularity.
  2. Precision. Precision really is lost, but only at module boundaries, and only for functions whose bodies the verifier would otherwise unfold. Inlining wins it back (strongest_complete), and the price is that the body becomes part of what callers depend on (strongest_not_modular).

docs.title: 1. An exported function the verifier can unfold is exported with its body
docs.text:
An exported ordinary function that definesValue accepts is transparent: a pure function of scalars, or a spec-only projection such as held. Its definition goes into the interface's inline surface, as a spec function's or a generic's already does. An importer encodes a call to it exactly as a caller in its own module does: pre(a) ==> F a = body(a), with the callee's own goals proved once, in its module, as for imported spec functions (ADR 0039). That makes a module boundary proof-neutral for these functions: three and dead above prove.

This needs no new keyword. The rule for what unfolds is the one the verifier already applies within a module, so moving a function into another module never changes what proves.

Functions with loops, buffers, abort, recursion, atomics or foreign calls stay contract-only. For them, the body's strongest fact is its loop invariants and its ensures, which the contract already is.

docs.title: 2. @opaque on an ordinary function keeps it contract-only
docs.text: @opaque already means "the definition is not a fact here" for spec functions (ADR 0063). On an exported ordinary function it keeps the body out of the interface and out of importers' goals, and with f reveals it in a proof inside the module. A library whose body must change without rebuilding its importers marks the function @opaque.

docs.title: 3. A transparent body is part of the interface hash
docs.text: The interface hash is the SHA-256 of the .piai text (interfaceHash in src/cert/Certificate.cpp), which already holds the inline surface. So a changed transparent body is a changed interface. Importers re-verify and relink, and the witness symbols make the linker and dyld refuse a mismatch. That is strongest_not_modular turned into a rule: a proof made with a body depends on that body. docs/abi.md already describes a separate inline surface hash, so that a change to a body breaks only the importers that used it. Building that split is a later step (step 5), and nothing here depends on it.

docs.title: 4. Codegen gets the body too (Dean, 2026-11-27)
docs.text: An importer compiles each transparent function it calls as an LLVM available_externally definition. LLVM may inline it and fold the branches it decides, and the symbol still comes from the defining module's object, so no code is duplicated in the link. This is the optimisation half of the claim, and it is sound for the same reason the proof is: the hash ties the importer to the body it inlined.

docs.title: 5. An LTO mode links modules into one optimisation unit (Dean, 2026-11-27)
docs.text:
Transparent bodies reach importers only for loop-free functions of scalars. A link-time mode covers everything else: piac --lto emits LLVM bitcode rather than machine code, and pia_binary(lto = True) links a program's Pia objects, and C objects compiled with -flto, through LLVM's LTO (ThinLTO by default, full LTO as an option). LLVM can then inline across modules, fold branches and run its peephole passes over the whole program, loops and buffers included. This is #490 in the codegen benchmark plan (#485), "LTO across Pia objects and their C callers", so the two land as one change.

LTO changes no proof. Each module is still proved against its imports' contracts and its certificate still names the interface hashes it used, so modular covers whatever LLVM links. LLVM only uses what the IR says, and since contracts are erased first, it cannot assume anything a proof did not establish. What LTO gives up is the separate shipping of objects: a module whose code was inlined into another under LTO is part of that binary, so a shared library is never built this way, and the witness symbols are still emitted so the certificate check runs at link time as it does now.

docs.title: 6. A whole-program mode, for builds that do not mind its cost (Dean, 2026-11-27)
docs.text:
Dean's worry is that LTO may not be enough: it optimises after proving, from IR with the contracts erased. So the question is what a single compilation unit, the whole program compiled and proved together, would add beyond sections 1 to 5.

  • For proofs, nothing. Within one module, the verifier already takes every call to a function with a loop, buffer or recursion on its contract, and unfolds only what section 1 exports. A loop's strongest postcondition is not computable in general, so the verifier would use its invariant even if it had the body. So putting every module into one unit proves exactly what transparent exports prove. strongest_complete is the limit: a proof can use a body only where the body is a definition. The check of this is step 1's test, which proves three and dead across modules as they prove in one.
  • For optimisation, two things LTO cannot do. LLVM sees the whole program under full LTO, but only as LLVM IR. A single unit also lets MLIR's passes work across modules (linalg fusion across a library boundary, Pia-level folding before lowering), and it lets codegen use what was proved. A proved ensures at a call can become an llvm.assume, so a branch a callee's contract decides is folded even where the body is not available. That fact comes from a proof, so it holds, and only this mode carries the proofs and the code to one place.

So the mode is opt-in, piac --whole-program with pia_binary(whole_program = True). Each module is still proved on its own against its imports, with its proof cache and certificate unchanged. Then their verified MLIR is linked into one module, the proved postconditions at calls are emitted as assumptions, and the result is optimised and lowered once.

Separate (default) + LTO (section 5) Whole program (section 6) What proves contracts, plus transparent bodies the same the same Cross-module inlining transparent bodies only everything LLVM chooses everything, and at MLIR level Branches folded from proved facts no no yes, through llvm.assume Proof time per module, cached the same the same (proofs are per module) Build time per module, parallel plus one link-time optimisation (ThinLTO stays parallel) plus one optimisation of the whole program, serial, which grows with the program What a change rebuilds the module, and importers of a changed interface plus the link the whole program's optimisation and codegen Distribution objects and shared libraries, certificates per object static binaries only static binaries only, one object and certificate set

An assumption that is too strong is undefined behaviour in LLVM, so the mode emits only ensures that were proved (not trusted ones, @assume, or --allow-unproved goals), and a test checks each emitted assumption against the report.

docs.title: 7. Steps
docs.text:
1. Export transparent definitions in .piai and unfold them at importers. Prove tests/modules/transparent.pia (the Clamp example), and record the change in the Linux proof-cost shards.
  2. @opaque on ordinary functions, with f across them, and the docs (verifier.md "Calls", tour, features).
  3. available_externally bodies in codegen, with a test that dead's branch is gone from the importer's assembly.
  4. A lint, opaque_export, for an exported function that is not transparent and whose ensures does not determine its result, pointing at the precision it gives up.
  5. The inline surface hash split from the interface hash (docs/abi.md), recorded per importer in its certificate.
  6. piac --lto (bitcode objects) and pia_binary(lto = True) through LLVM ThinLTO, with C objects built -flto, measured on the codegen benchmark (#485, #490).
  7. piac --whole-program: link verified MLIR modules, emit proved ensures as llvm.assume at calls, and compare with ThinLTO on the codegen benchmark.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Soundness is unchanged. An importer assumes about the body only what the body's module proved: its precondition-guarded definition, which strongest_complete shows is exact. The certificate check keeps the body the importer used equal to the one it links, since the body is hashed.
  • Proof cost. A goal that mentions a call to a transparent function carries its body, and the bodies of the transparent functions it calls, the same cost in-module callers already pay. These are loop-free bodies of scalars, so the terms are small, but transitive unfolding can add up: Pia.Core.Ascii's classifiers call between, so is_alnum unfolds three betweens. The Linux proof bench gates every PR, so step 1 reports the change per file, and @opaque is there for any function that turns out costly.
  • Rebuild invalidation. Changing a transparent body re-verifies its importers. The proof cache keys each goal on its query, so only the goals whose query contained the body are solved again, and the rest are cache hits. Changing an @opaque body, or any function with a loop, still re-verifies nothing outside its module.
  • ABI (ADR 0030, 0073). A transparent body is inline surface, like a C++ inline function or a generic: a shared library that changes one breaks its importers' certificates until they rebuild, and pia-cert check says which interface changed. Layout hashes are unaffected. ADR 0073's migration rules apply to changed interfaces as they do now.
  • What stays modular. Loops, recursion, buffers and anything @opaque are still proved once against their contracts, and modular still covers those calls, so separate builds and the proof cache keep working where they matter most.
  • Not covered here. Calls through function references (ADR 0071) are calls the verifier cannot see the callee of. They stay contract-only, and they need their own termination rule before a lemma can be called through one.

docs.title: 77. A definition that states no contract takes the contract of the interface that lists it
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-27

Status: Accepted (Dean, 2026-11-27)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
An interface lists each function a module exports with its type and contract (ADR 0039). The module meets it by proof: the interface's requires must imply the definition's, and the definition's ensures must imply the interface's. That rule lets an interface promise less than the body proves. But it also means that, for the usual case where the two are the same, the module writes every contract twice, in the same file:

module Counting : Counter

interface Counter = sig
  let count_to : (n : u32) -> u32
    requires n < 1000
    ensures result = n
end

let count_to (n : u32) : u32
  requires n < 1000      (* the same contract, again *)
  ensures result = n
= ...

Dean (2026-11-27): "we need a way for an implementation to not repeat the interface declaration's contracts in a module. It seems ugly to have to repeat the contracts in the same file."

Leaving the definition's contract out does not work today. A definition with no contract has requires true and promises nothing, and on today's latest piac:

  • The interface check passes only when the body unfolds. The check is a lemma that calls the function, so it sees the body only if definesValue unfolds it: a pure function of scalars with no loop, buffer, abort or recursion (docs/verifier.md, "Pure functions of scalars"). A count_to with a while loop fails it (counterexample: m = 992), because a call to a loop is taken on its contract, and the contract is empty.
  • Callers in the module never see the interface's contract. A call inside the module is taken on the definition's contract, so let five (k : u32) : u32 ensures result = 5 = count_to 5 fails (counterexample: k = 0), even though importers would prove it from the interface.
  • The body is never proved under the interface's precondition. A body that needs n < 1000 to avoid an overflow cannot use it.

Prior art. Ada lets a body omit the aspects its specification states: the Pre and Post of a subprogram declared in a package spec apply to its body, and SPARK proves the body against them. Eiffel's redefinitions inherit their ancestors' contracts and may only weaken require (require else) or strengthen ensure (ensure then). Dafny refines a module's abstract methods by repeating only the body, with the specification taken from the refined module. C++ contracts (P2900) are stated on the first declaration and may be omitted on a redeclaration, which then has the same contract.

docs.title: 1. A definition that states no contract takes its interface's
docs.text:
When a function that an interface of its file lists is defined with no requires, ensures, costs or reads clause, it takes that interface's clauses, as if they had been written on the definition:

module Counting : Counter

interface Counter = sig
  let count_to : (n : u32) -> u32
    requires n < 1000
    ensures result = n
end

let count_to (m : u32) : u32
=
  let i : mutable u32 = 0 in
  while i < m
    invariant i <= m
    decreases m - i
  do
    i <- i + 1
  done;
  i

let five (k : u32) : u32
  ensures result = 5
= count_to 5

Everything that reads a definition's contract then reads the interface's. The body is proved against it, a caller in the module takes the function on it (five proves), and the interface check is met trivially, since the two contracts are the same. Nothing changes for importers: they always used the interface's contract.

The interface names the parameters its own way. The copy is renamed to the definition's names (the interface's n is count_to's m above), so the definition is free to name them as it likes. If one of the interface's quantifier binders has the name of one of the definition's parameters, the renaming would capture it, and the compiler asks for one of the two to be renamed. Hygiene (ADR 0022) already forbids that shadowing in written code.

docs.title: 2. All or nothing (Dean, 2026-11-27)
docs.text:
A definition that states any of those clauses states its whole contract, and inherits nothing. Its contract is checked against the interface's as it is today (ADR 0039), so it may still be stronger than what the interface promises, and tests/verify/modules.pia is unchanged in meaning.

The alternative, inheriting clause by clause (a definition with an ensures and no requires takes the interface's requires), saves a line in some files, but a reader can no longer tell a definition's contract from the definition alone: adding an ensures to a definition would silently change its precondition. With all or nothing, a definition's contract is either all on the definition or all on the interface.

A decreases measure is not part of the contract. It is about the body, not about what callers get, so a definition with only a measure still inherits.

docs.title: 3. What inherits
docs.text:
• Ordinary functions and lemmas listed with : in an interface the module claims, in the same file (a module claims only interfaces declared in its own file, ADR 0039).
  • Not spec functions, generics or metaprograms. These are exported with their definitions, and the definition's contract is the one importers get (sameSignature), so the interface entry is a copy of the definition's and there is nothing to inherit.
  • Overloads. An interface entry is matched to the definition of the same name and arity, and, when the name is defined more than once, to the overload whose parameter types are written the same.
  • Several interfaces. When two interfaces the module claims list the function with the same contract, it takes that contract. When their contracts differ, there is no one contract to take, and the compiler asks for the definition to state one that meets both, which the existing check then proves.

docs.title: 4. Where goals point
docs.text: The inherited clauses keep their source locations, so a goal they raise points at the interface's line: a body that breaks the inherited ensures fails at the ensures in the interface. That is where the contract is written, and where it must be fixed or the body changed.

docs.title: 5. Where it is done
docs.text:
inheritInterfaceContracts in src/syntax/Interfaces.cpp copies the clauses into the definitions, after metaprograms expand and before anything reads a contract. irgen::generate runs it, so piac, pia repl, pia mcp and pia-lsp all see the same program, and piac runs it before the Lean statements are made (ADR 0061), so an inherited lemma's statement is the interface's. Running it twice changes nothing, since a definition that has inherited a contract states one.

The interface artifact (.piai) is the interface as written, so it and the interface hash are unchanged.

docs.title: 6. Steps
docs.text:
1. The rule, tests/verify/inherited_contracts.pia, and the docs and skills that teach modules. Done (PR #500).
  2. A lint, repeated_contract, for a definition whose contract is exactly its interface's, parameter names aside, with the fix of deleting it (tests/lint/repeated_contract.pia). Foreign functions keep theirs, since the bindings generator writes the contract on every row. The repository moved to the short form in the same change (Dean, 2026-11-27): 527 clauses on about 210 definitions in 67 files, the standard library, tests/codegen, tests/modules, the demos and the literate pages. Done.
  3. pia-lsp hover shows an inherited contract on the definition, renamed to its parameters and marked with the interface it came from (tests/lsp). Done.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A contract is written once. A module whose definitions match their interfaces writes each contract in one place, where importers read it. The interface stays the module's documentation.
  • Soundness is unchanged. The definition is proved against exactly the contract it would have had if the clauses were written on it, so every existing argument (ADR 0039's check, modular in tests/lean/CallRule.lean) applies as it does to written contracts.
  • A changed meaning for an uncontracted definition. A listed definition with no contract used to have requires true inside the module. Now it has the interface's precondition, so a caller in the module that called it outside that precondition gets a failed goal. Only two files in the repository define a listed function with no contract: tests/verify/modules.pia, whose double now states the weaker contract the test is about, and tests/grammar/valid/module_header.pia, which is only parsed.
  • Proof cost. A definition that inherits a contract proves it, which costs what writing the contract costs. Its interface check becomes trivial.
  • Reading a definition. A definition with no contract no longer means "promises nothing" if an interface lists it. The interface is in the same file, and step 3 shows the inherited contract on hover.

docs.title: 78. Library functions lower to pia_lib.call, a Pia-owned op whose meaning is its Pia body, and a late pass either expands it into the body or substitutes an upstream op through a rule proved against the body
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-27

Status: Proposed

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pia's codegen benchmarks (ADR 0075) need sqrt for n-body (#487). Dean's rules, from the thread and #487 (2026-11-27):

  • No builtins. A compiler extension is a Pia function with a special lowering, unless that's impossible. Builtins are kept to what @lower cannot express, and never added to cheat for performance. Pia still needs provable low-level maths.
  • A Pia-owned dialect as the lowering target: "a Pia dialect in MLIR that we can lower to, that we control the implementation of. So that way we can choose to lower to the Pia and still be able to detect that the implementation is correct, whether or not we do the substitution at lowering time."

ADR 0065's @lower puts the upstream op (linalg.matmul, or math.sqrt for sqrt) in place of the call when the function is compiled. That decides the substitution early, at IRGen, and the only record of the Pia function left in the IR is its symbol. ADR 0074 section 4 plans value-returning lowerings ($result) for tensors on the same mechanism.

sqrt shows what that leaves out. A pure Pia sqrt that is proved correctly rounded is an integer algorithm over to_bits and from_bits (#452): about 53 steps of a digit-by-digit square root, a few hundred cycles. The hardware's fsqrt takes 10 to 15. The pure body is the definition and the proof, and the hardware op is the speed. Both should be in the build, with a check that they agree.

docs.title: 1. One generic op, pia_lib.call, names the Pia function
docs.text:
A new dialect, pia_lib, has one op:

%r = pia_lib.call @Pia.Math.sqrt(%x) : (f64) -> f64

It names the Pia function whose body is its meaning. There is no op per function, so a library adds no C++ and no ODS, which is the point of ADR 0074. The function's body stays in the module as a private func.func, so the op can always be expanded.

IRGen emits pia_lib.call, not func.call, for a call to a function with a substitution rule (section 2). The op is Pure when the function is pure (ADR 0069), so CSE and hoisting treat it like any pure op, and Elementwise when the function is marked so, so the vectoriser can widen it (M10, #11) before the late pass.

Operand and result types are whatever the function's types lower to. That includes a library type's MLIR type (ADR 0074 section 3, such as tensor<?x?xf32>), not only scalars and memrefs. A tensor op carries its moved destination as an operand, the way linalg's outs does.

docs.title: 2. A substitution rule is @lower, read as a rule rather than an immediate rewrite
docs.text:
The surface does not change: @lower(...) on the function, with ADR 0065's MLIR text and $ splices. What changes is when it applies. The lowering is now a rewrite rule from pia_lib.call @f to the upstream form, applied late.

A rule may return a value with $result. It is pulled forward here from ADR 0074 step 3, for scalars, and extended to tensors there. The operand-effect check gains one rule: $result is the op's only output.

(** IEEE 754 square root: the real square root, rounded once to nearest even. *)
let sqrt (x : f64) : f64
  @lower("$result = math.sqrt $x : f64")
= (* to_bits, a digit-by-digit integer square root of the scaled
     significand, round to nearest even, from_bits; NaN, -0, +0, +inf
     and negatives first *)

docs.title: 3. A late pass expands or substitutes
docs.text:
pia-lib-lower runs after the vectoriser, before one-shot bufferisation, and before the lowering to LLVM. For each pia_lib.call it does one of two things:

  • Substitute: apply the function's rule when --lower=on (the default) and the target supports the rule's dialects.
  • Expand: otherwise call or inline the body. A tensor operand goes back through bufferization.to_memref into the body's buffer field.

Substitution runs before bufferisation, so bufferisation only sees upstream ops. "After the vectoriser" is for scalar rules. A tensor rule substitutes linalg.matmul, linalg.generic and the like, which still need linalg's own tiling and vectorisation. So the linalg pipeline, with ADR 0065's @schedule, runs after pia-lib-lower and before one-shot bufferisation, and a substituted op is never left unvectorised. ADR 0074's no-allocation check runs on both paths. On the expand path, the operands go through to_memref into a body that writes to the destination's buffer, so an expansion cannot quietly copy either. --lower=off means "always expand", which keeps ADR 0065's differential tests.

docs.title: 4. Each rule's correctness is proved once, whether or not it is applied
docs.text:
A rule's obligation is ADR 0065's refinement goal (step 3), the same one ADR 0074 section 5 extends to tensors. Under the function's requires, the meaning of the rule's MLIR form satisfies the function's ensures, and writes nothing else. There is no second kind of goal.

For a scalar op, "meaning" is the op's SMT semantics: - math.sqrt on f64 is fp.sqrt RNE in Z3's floating-point theory; - arith ops are what piac already gives them.

When the ensures is "equals the body", which is what sqrt's contract will say once ADR 0038's encoding lands, the goal is exactly "the upstream op computes the Pia implementation".

A rule has one of ADR 0065's states: - Proved by Z3; - Proved in Lean (ADR 0061); - Trusted: listed in the trust report and the certificate as a lowering item, as today, until it is proved.

The goal is checked when the function is verified, not at each call, so the result holds wherever the rule is applied and wherever it is not.

docs.title: 5. Scope: every maths function, and anything that would otherwise be a builtin
docs.text:
Dean, 2026-11-27: "this idea scales to pretty much every math function that we want to optimize for the Pia standard library. Likewise, for anything that needs to look like some sort of built-in, we can do the MLIR side expansion on our terms instead of reaching into specifics in other dialects."

  • All of Pia.Math (#62) takes this shape: exp, log, pow, sin, cos, atan2, fma, rsqrt, hypot. Each one is a Pia function whose body is the proved implementation, called through pia_lib.call. Most need no rule at all. A body built from range reduction and a polynomial is already the fast path, and the vectoriser widens it through Elementwise. A rule is added only where the target has a better form.
  • Anything that would otherwise be a builtin takes this shape too: bit counts, byte swaps, saturating and widening multiplies, checksums such as CRC32, atomics' fences, memory copies. The expansion is ours: by default the body, which is pure Pia. The decision of what a pia_lib.call becomes stays in Pia's code, not in another dialect's conventions.
  • A rule may also target the llvm dialect, for assembly-style implementations. This covers LLVM intrinsics (llvm.intr.*, such as llvm.intr.sqrt, llvm.intr.fma, llvm.intr.ctpop) and llvm.inline_asm with a fixed instruction sequence per target, such as fsqrt d0, d0 on arm64, a NEON or AVX2 sequence for a kernel, or crc32cx. The rule names its target (@lower(target = arm64, ...), one rule per target), and the pass picks the rule for the target being built, else the body. Its obligation is the same refinement goal. An intrinsic piac gives a meaning to is proved like any other op. Inline assembly has no meaning piac can read, so its rule is trusted. It is listed in the trust report with the target and the instruction text's hash, and the differential test against the body (--lower=off) runs on that target in CI.

docs.title: 6. sqrt first
docs.text:
1. pia_lib and pia_lib.call, emitted for functions with a rule, and the expand path of pia-lib-lower. Nothing is substituted yet, so behaviour is ADR 0065's --lower=off.
  2. Scalar $result, and the substitute path.
  3. Pia.Math.sqrt on f32 and f64: the body proved correctly rounded with integer facts, @lower to math.sqrt, and the rule trusted at first. A test runs both forms against C's sqrt on special values and a sweep of bit patterns.
  4. The rule's refinement goal with fp.sqrt, for f32 first.
  5. n-body in bench/codegen (ADR 0075).

ADR 0065's existing function lowerings (linalg.matmul in tests/codegen/lower_linalg.pia) move onto pia_lib.call in step 1. They keep their states and their tests.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pia.Math and every would-be builtin become Pia functions with optional rules, so the compiler's C++ grows by one dialect and one pass, not by one op per function.
  • The IR keeps the Pia function as an op until late. Passes see sqrt as one pure, elementwise value rather than a call or an upstream op, and the substitution choice can depend on the target or on --lower.
  • Correctness of an implementation no longer depends on whether it was substituted. Each rule is proved, Lean-proved or listed as trusted, once.
  • pia_lib is a fourth dialect beside pia, pia_contract and pia_par (ADR 0018). It has one op.
  • ADR 0074 section 4 becomes "a tensor op lowers to pia_lib.call, and its substitution rule targets linalg". The tensors thread will amend ADR 0074 to point here.
  • Bit-blasting fp.sqrt on 64 bits against an integer algorithm may be too slow for Z3. f32 is small enough to try first; f64 may need a lemma split or Lean, and stays trusted until then.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
