1. ~~Is one generic op naming the function right, or should libraries be able to declare named ops (pia_lib.sqrt)?~~ Decided (Dean, 2026-11-27): one generic op. Named ops would bring back ODS per library.
  2. ~~For f32, is running both forms on all 2³² inputs at build time an accepted proof of a rule?~~ Decided (Dean, 2026-11-27): no. A rule is proved by Z3 or Lean, or it is trusted. There is no exhaustive state, though a run over every input may still serve as a differential test.
  3. ~~Should a rule that has not been proved be applied by default?~~ Answered by a principle instead (Dean, 2026-11-27): the compiler changes on principle to make every Pia program faster, not only the benchmarks (ADR 0075). So a rule belongs to the library function, not to a program. It applies to every call of that function on its target, in every program, or to none. It is never chosen per program, per benchmark or by flag. A rule is added only when it makes the function faster for every caller on that target. It is proved by Z3 or Lean, or listed as trusted in the trust report until it is. Trusted is a temporary state, kept for pragmatism (Dean, 2026-11-27). The goal is to have no unproved rules, reached one rule at a time as a hygiene task. Each trusted rule has an issue that tracks its proof, and the trust report's count of trusted lowerings should only go down.

docs.title: 79. Pia IR: a versioned op schema Pia controls, in lock-step with piac, with deprecations and migrations
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-28

Status: Proposed. Amended by ADR 0080 (Proposed, 2026-11-28): the schema becomes lib/Pia/Ir/ir.proto and the encoding becomes protobuf's wire format in a canonical form, with strict must-understand fields; versions, migrations and the proof table stay.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0076 needs per-module artifacts that a later step reads back. The whole-program mode (section 6) links each module's verified program before optimising. Transparent exports ship bodies to importers, and abi.md already plans an optional proof bundle in __PIA_PROOF,__bundle as "pia_contract MLIR bytecode".

MLIR bytecode would be the easy choice, and Dean ruled it out (2026-11-28): "I'm not sure I want to be tied to an (unstable, not guaranteed) MLIR bytecode. Let's explore specifying one that we control." The concern is real:

  • MLIR's bytecode format has a version number, and readers accept older versions, but only within an LLVM release's policy. The builtin dialect and the upstream dialects Pia lowers through (arith, scf, memref, func, math, linalg, tensor) promise no stability: an op's operands, attributes or properties change between LLVM revisions. Their C++ APIs move just as fast. arith::ExtFOp's builder was deprecated under us, which broke main's -Werror build (#495).
  • Pia pins one LLVM revision per piac build and bumps it often. An artifact written by one piac would be readable only by a piac at the same LLVM revision.
  • A certificate or hash over MLIR bytecode would change when LLVM changes the encoding, even though the program has not changed.

Dean then set the direction (2026-11-28): "We can write a versioned schema which can encode whatever MLIR op we support/use in the compiler and have that schema be enforced in lock-step with the compiler/language version. We have an opportunity here to define a deprecation path and a migration policy for the bytecode too like we're planning on doing with the source code." ADR 0073, section 5, is that policy for source. This ADR is the same policy for the IR.

docs.title: 1. The schema: every op piac writes, named and numbered by Pia
docs.text:
Pia IR is defined by one checked-in schema, written in Pia: lib/Pia/Ir/Schema.pia, a table of records, one per op and one per type (section 7 says why it is Pia and not TableGen). It lists every op that can appear in a verified module, which is the input of codegen and of ADR 0076's whole-program mode:

  • Pia's own dialects: pia, pia_contract, pia_par.
  • Every upstream op piac emits or keeps: the arith, scf, memref, func, math, linalg, tensor and async ops that IRGen, the transforms and the @lower checks produce.

For each op, the schema gives:

  • A stable numeric id, never reused.
  • The schema version that introduced it, and the one that deprecated it, if any.
  • Its fields: operands, results, regions and attributes, each with a Pia-defined type such as u64, i1, string, type, value, region, an enum by name or a list. Upstream properties are flattened into named fields.
  • Its meaning: a line saying what it computes, written in the schema, not inherited from upstream documentation.

Types are in the schema too (!pia.int<lo, hi>, slices, records, sorts, and the upstream i1, iN, index, f32, f64, memref and tensor shapes), each with its own id.

So Pia IR is a description of the ops Pia uses, at the meaning Pia gives them. The mapping from each schema op to the current MLIR op is generated code in piac, src/ir/Map.cpp, produced from the schema by tools/ir/gen, which reads it through piac --emit=interface's typed tree, the same way tools/bindings/gen.py generates Pia.Sys.Posix. When an LLVM bump renames a builder, adds a property or splits an op, only the mapping changes. The schema, the encoding and every artifact stay the same.

docs.title: 2. Lock-step with piac and the language
docs.text:
The schema version is a single integer, kIrVersion in src/ir/Schema.h. It is recorded in every certificate (format 4) next to the ABI version, and it is hashed into the module hash.

  • A piac writes only the current schema version.
  • A piac reads the current version and the versions still inside the deprecation window (section 4).
  • CI enforces the lock-step. tools/ir/check.py fails a PR that makes piac emit an op, type or field the schema does not list, which a round-trip test over every tests/verify module catches. It also fails a PR that changes the schema without bumping kIrVersion and adding a migration, unless the PR says no-ir-migration: <why>, for example for an op that is only added. This is the same shape as ADR 0073's tools/migrate/check.py.
  • An LLVM bump that changes an upstream op's meaning, not only its API, is a schema change like any other: a new version and a migration.

docs.title: 3. The encoding
docs.text:
The encoding is deterministic, so equal modules give equal bytes and a hash over the bytes is a hash over the program:

  • A header: magic PIAIR, the schema version and the ABI version.
  • A string table and a type table, each in first-use order.
  • Ops in pre-order, each written as its id, then its fields in schema order. Integers are LEB128 and values are numbered in definition order.
  • Locations go in a separate table, so a module's hash does not change when only its comments or layout move. The table is kept, so that diagnostics after a read still point at the source.
  • zstd for shipping, not for hashing.

piac --emit=ir writes it, piac --dump-ir prints it as text for review and diffs, and piac --from-ir reads it.

docs.title: 4. Deprecation and migration
docs.text:
These follow ADR 0073 section 5, with the same window:

  • Deprecating an op or a field marks it in the schema with the version that deprecated it and the migration that replaces it. Readers accept it for one schema version, with a deprecated warning naming the migration. After that window it is an error that still names the migration, forever.
  • A migration lives in src/ir/migrate/: a rewrite from version N to version N+1 on the decoded tree, before mapping to MLIR. Typical ones rename an op, split a field, change an attribute's encoding, or expand an op into others. piac migrate --ir <file> upgrades an artifact in place, and readers apply migrations on the fly inside the window.
  • Migrations keep proofs only when they keep meaning. Each migration is marked preserving or changing:
  • A preserving migration has a test: the obligations of the old and new forms are the same goals, by query hash. A certificate then carries over, recording migrated <old module hash> <migration id>.
  • A changing migration invalidates the module's proofs. The artifact must be proved again from source, and pia-cert check says so.

docs.title: 5. A proof table beside the IR
docs.text: Each artifact carries a proof table: for each obligation, its stable id (the function, then the goal's index in walk order), its status, its method and the SHA-256 of its query. A reader that maps the IR back walks the same goals and takes each status from the table without solving. A goal missing from the table, or one whose query hash differs, is an error, never a silent re-proof. The table replaces the "MLIR bytecode" of abi.md's proof bundle. The table's hash and the module hash go into the certificate, so pia-cert check can tell that an artifact, its table and an object came from one program.

docs.title: 6. What stays text
docs.text:
• .piai interfaces stay canonical Pia source. They are what people and agents read, and the interface hash is already over that text.
  • @lower bodies stay the MLIR text the program wrote (ADR 0065). They are trusted items whose hash the certificate already records, and their ops need not be in the schema.
  • LTO (ADR 0076, section 5) stays LLVM bitcode, because it is written and read within one build and never shipped.

docs.title: 7. Portable, and readable by Pia itself
docs.text:
Dean (2026-11-28): "What I don't want is to be locked to MLIR's format, but I want a portable format as well. One ulterior motivation here might be if we can eventually self-host Pia so that the compiler can handle the bytecode produced to replicate what the MLIR infrastructure gives us but in Pia. That's probably a 1.0 feature."

So Pia IR is defined independently of any one implementation, piac's C++ included:

  • The spec is a document, not code. docs/ir.md defines the encoding byte by byte: the header, LEB128, the tables, op and field order, and how each field type is written. The schema gives the op list. A conforming reader can be written from those two alone, in any language.
  • The schema is Pia, not TableGen. TableGen is LLVM's. A schema in lib/Pia/Ir/Schema.pia is data a Pia program can read, so a self-hosted compiler loads the same table that generates piac's C++ mapping today. The schema is a module with an interface, so changing it is an interface change, and the hash and the migration check see it.
  • Portable bytes. Integers are LEB128, floats are IEEE 754 bit patterns written little-endian, strings are UTF-8 with a length, and nothing depends on the host's word size, endianness or alignment. Target-specific facts, such as the size of usize or a @place(gpu) op, are fields with the target named, never assumptions of the encoding. A module proved for one target is readable on any host.
  • No MLIR in the definition. The mapping to MLIR is one consumer. A self-hosted Pia that implements its own passes over Pia IR is another, and the schema's stated meaning of each op, not MLIR's, is what both must agree with.
  • Self-hosting path (1.0, not before). Pia.Ir, an encoder and decoder written in Pia, proved to round-trip, as the GIF and inflate codecs are proved against their specs (ADR 0054). Then passes written in Pia over the decoded tree, each proved against the schema's meanings. ADR 0065's @lower and ADR 0074's library types are already moving compiler extensions into Pia, and this gives them a stable IR to work on. Nothing before 1.0 depends on it; the C++ mapping remains the implementation until a Pia one proves equal on the round-trip suite.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
Pia IR schema (chosen) Canonical expanded Pia text MLIR bytecode Stable across LLVM bumps Yes: only the generated mapping changes Yes: it is the language No Versioned by kIrVersion, in lock-step with piac, with migrations the language version and ADR 0073 MLIR's bytecode version Reading back Decode and map: no sema or IRGen Parse, sema and IRGen again Decode Keeps IR-level results Yes: transforms, lowering checks, proof attributes No, they are redone Yes Cost to build The schema, the generated mapping, the encoder and a migration per change A canonical printer for every node kind None

Canonical text was this ADR's first proposal. It loses to the schema because it throws away work the reader must redo (sema, IRGen and the transforms) and cannot carry IR that has no source form, such as the output of ScalarizeRecords or a verified @lower replacement. The schema keeps that, and stays ours.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An LLVM bump changes the mapping code and nothing shipped. A schema change is visible, versioned and migrated, like a language change.
  • Every op piac emits must be in the schema, so a new upstream op costs a schema entry with its meaning. That is a deliberate friction: it is the list of upstream semantics Pia depends on, written down.
  • One release of deprecated ops is the reader's cost, the same as one release of deprecated syntax in ADR 0073.
  • Hashes are over Pia's encoding, so a certificate means the same thing under every piac with the same schema and ABI versions.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. lib/Pia/Ir/Schema.pia and the byte-level spec in docs/ir.md for the pia, pia_contract and pia_par dialects and the upstream ops a tests/verify module uses, the generated mapping, --emit=ir, --from-ir and --dump-ir. The test round-trips every file in tests/verify and checks that the reports are identical.
  2. tools/ir/check.py in CI: no emitted op outside the schema, and no schema change without a version bump and a migration.
  3. The proof table, and --verify --proof-table=<file>.
  4. Certificate format 4: ir <version>, the module hash and the proof table hash, checked by pia-cert check.
  5. The migration framework in src/ir/migrate, piac migrate --ir, and the first migration when the first schema change lands.
  6. ADR 0076's whole-program mode and transparent bodies read Pia IR.
  7. (1.0) Pia.Ir: an encoder and decoder in Pia, proved to round-trip against docs/ir.md, then passes over it in Pia.

docs.title: 80. Protocol Buffers in Pia: a metaprogram that turns .proto into proved types and codecs, and Pia IR as a protobuf schema
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-28

Status: Proposed

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0079 defines Pia IR: a versioned op schema in Pia, a generated mapping to MLIR, and an encoding of Pia's own made of LEB128 integers, numbered fields and length-prefixed strings. Dean then asked (2026-11-28): "How hard would it be for us to just use protobufs for the IR? Let's jump the queue and implement a protobuf metaprogram that generates the types, operations, interfaces, so that we can just encode it in a forward compatible way?"

Three facts make this a small step:

  • ADR 0079's encoding is already most of the protobuf wire format. A protobuf varint is LEB128, a field is a number with a wire type, and strings and nested messages carry their length. Using protobuf costs little, and gains a schema language anyone can read, readers in every language through protoc, and evolution rules that are well understood.
  • The 0.2.0 roadmap needs the same metaprogram. Its gRPC plugin generates Pia from .proto: message types, a Protocol Buffers theory, a model per message, and proved codecs, with services as interfaces. Building it now for the IR means building it once.
  • Pia already derives proved codecs from types. derive_json (ADR 0045, meta.md) reads a type with metaprogram builtins and writes a reader and a writer that prove. A protobuf generator has the same shape, but its input is a .proto file instead of a Pia type.

Protobuf also leaves four things open that a proved IR needs:

  1. Its forward compatibility is syntactic. A reader skips a field it does not know, which is right for metadata and wrong for an op: skipping an op changes the program.
  2. Its bytes are not canonical. The protobuf spec does not fix a serialisation: field order, packed or unpacked repeated fields, default values written or left out, and unknown fields all vary between writers. ADR 0079 hashes modules over their bytes.
  3. Nesting is bounded. Common parsers stop at about 100 nested messages, and regions nest ops inside ops without a bound.
  4. The runtime is large. The protobuf C++ library is BSD-licensed, so it is allowed (no GPL), but it is a big dependency for piac to carry.

docs.title: 1. Pia.Proto: the wire format, proved
docs.text:
Pia.Proto.Wire implements the wire format, as Pia.Text.Json does JSON:

  • Varints (up to 10 bytes for 64 bits), zigzag for sint32 and sint64, little-endian fixed32 and fixed64, and IEEE 754 bit patterns for float and double.
  • Tags (field << 3 | wire_type), and length-delimited fields for string, bytes, nested messages and packed repeated fields.
  • Skipping one field of each wire type, which is what unknown-field handling needs.

Each reader is proved never to read past its input, to reject an overlong or overflowing varint, and to round-trip with its writer (read (write v) = v). A string is checked for UTF-8 as it is read, so it arrives as Pia's str (ADR 0040, section 7).

docs.title: 2. The .proto metaprogram
docs.text:
Pia.Proto.Gen exports a metaprogram that takes a proto3 file and returns items:

import Pia.Proto.Gen.Gen as P
P.generate (read_text "ir/ir.proto")
  • Types. A message becomes a record. A field becomes a record field of the matching Pia type (int32 becomes i32, uint64 becomes u64, bool, string and bytes as above). A repeated field becomes a vec with the allocator ADR 0026 requires, an optional field becomes an option, a oneof becomes a variant, an enum becomes a variant with its numbers kept as a range type for unknown values, and nested messages become records named Outer_Inner.
  • Codecs. For each message: write_<m>, which writes it, with room stated in its precondition as derive_json's writers do, and read_<m>, which reads it into a fully initialised value, with errors in a closed set (Truncated_<m>, WireType_<m>, Utf8_<m>, Range_<m>, Missing_<m> for a required field, see section 4). It dispatches on field numbers with a decision tree built at compile time.
  • Services. A service becomes a Pia interface (ADR 0039), one function per RPC, from request to result of response. 0.2.0's gRPC transport implements it.
  • Options as attributes. Protobuf options the generator understands (deprecated, and the Pia options of section 4) become attributes on the generated items. Others are kept as attributes and ignored.

The metaprogram is ordinary Pia that runs in the interpreter. Its .proto parser uses the builtins metaprograms already have (bytes, string compare, lists). It needs one more builtin: read_text path, which returns a file's contents as a string at expansion time. The file is resolved hermetically, with the same roots and flags as @embed (ADR 0070, section 2), and its hash goes into the module's interface hash, so a changed .proto rebuilds its importers. It is a metaprogram builtin with no run-time form, not a language builtin.

docs.title: 3. A theory of Protocol Buffers, and a model per message
docs.text:
Pia.Proto.Theory states the encoding as a spec: a message is a finite map from field numbers to lists of values, encoding is a function of that map, and decoding follows protobuf's rules. The last value wins for a singular field, repeated values are concatenated, packed and unpacked forms both decode, and unknown fields are skipped or kept. The generated code is proved against it:

  • decode (encode m) = m for every generated message.
  • decode accepts every encoding of m that the protobuf spec allows (any field order, packed or unpacked, defaults written or left out), not only the canonical one.
  • canonical m (section 5) is a function of m's value alone.

These are the lemmas 0.2.0's gRPC work needs as well, so they are written once here.

docs.title: 4. Forward compatibility that keeps meaning
docs.text:
Protobuf's skip-unknown rule is kept for fields that cannot change meaning, and made an error for those that can:

  • Must-understand by default. In a schema marked option (pia.strict) = true;, as Pia IR is, a reader that meets an unknown field number or an unknown oneof case is an error that names the number, the message and the schema version that introduced it, if the reader knows it. An unknown op is always this error.
  • Advisory fields. A field marked [(pia.advisory) = true] (locations, debug names, optimisation hints, extra proof-table data) is skipped when unknown, and preserved when the message is re-written.
  • Required fields. [(pia.required) = true] makes a missing field Missing_<m>, which protobuf 3 cannot express on its own.

Outside strict schemas, as for gRPC messages, the generator follows plain proto3 rules.

docs.title: 5. A canonical form for hashing
docs.text: A Pia writer always writes the canonical form: fields in ascending number order, repeated scalars packed, default values of fields without presence left out, no unknown fields, and map entries (if a schema uses map) sorted by key. Hashes, certificates and the module hash of ADR 0079 are over canonical bytes. A reader accepts any valid encoding, and before it checks a hash it re-encodes canonically and hashes that. Section 3 proves the canonical form is a function of the value, so equal programs hash equal however their bytes were written.

docs.title: 6. Pia IR as a protobuf schema (amends ADR 0079)
docs.text:
• Section 1 (the schema). The IR schema is lib/Pia/Ir/ir.proto, in strict mode. An op is a message, and its stable numeric id is its field number in the Op oneof, never reused (protobuf's reserved enforces that). A type is a message in a Type oneof in the same way. Each op's meaning is a doc comment on its message. Pia.Proto.Gen reads the file to make Pia's types for it, and tools/ir/gen reads it to make piac's C++ codec and the MLIR mapping, so there is one schema. This replaces lib/Pia/Ir/Schema.pia, pending Dean's choice of source of truth.
  • Section 3 (the encoding). The encoding is protobuf's wire format in the canonical form of section 5. A module is a Module message: a header (magic PIAIR in field 1, the schema version, the ABI version), a string table, a type table, an op table, and a separate location table, which is an advisory field. Regions do not nest messages: a region lists the indices of its blocks, and a block the indices of its ops in the op table, so the message depth stays constant however deep the program nests. Values are numbered in definition order, as before. zstd is still for shipping, not for hashing.
  • Section 7 (portable). docs/ir.md still specifies the format, now as ir.proto plus the canonical-form rules and the table layout. Any language with a protobuf library can read Pia IR. The self-hosting path is unchanged, and gets shorter: Pia.Ir's encoder and decoder are the ones this metaprogram generates, proved by section 3.
  • piac carries no protobuf runtime. tools/ir/gen writes a small wire reader and writer in C++ from ir.proto, the same way it writes the mapping. protoc and its C++ library are used only in tests: CI decodes piac's output with protoc-generated code and compares the canonical bytes both ways.
  • Unchanged. kIrVersion, deprecation for one schema version, migrations marked preserving or changing, the proof table and tools/ir/check.py all stay as ADR 0079 decides. Protobuf's compatibility rules are the floor (never reuse a field number, never change a field's type); kIrVersion and a migration are still required for any change in meaning.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Protobuf schema and wire format (chosen) ADR 0079's own encoding FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto Readers outside Pia Every language, through protoc Only ones written from docs/ir.md Many, through their compilers Forward compatibility Skip-unknown for advisory fields, strict for the rest (section 4) Version and migrations only Built in, but no must-understand fields Canonical bytes A canonical form we define and prove (section 5) Deterministic by construction Not canonical (vtables, padding) Reuse for 0.2.0 gRPC The same metaprogram and theory None None: gRPC uses protobuf Cost Wire module, metaprogram, theory, read_text The encoder and decoder only A new format with no 0.2.0 reuse

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pia IR becomes readable with off-the-shelf tools, and the .proto metaprogram that 0.2.0 needs is built now, against a demanding first user.
  • The ops Pia depends on are still written down one by one with their meanings, now as protobuf messages.
  • Strict mode means an old piac refuses a newer module instead of misreading it, as ADR 0079 intends; protobuf's laxer rules apply only where they are safe.
  • read_text makes a metaprogram's output depend on a file, and the interface hash records it.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Pia.Proto.Wire, proved: varints, zigzag, fixed-width numbers, tags, length-delimited fields and skipping, prototyped in the REPL first, with tests/std/proto_wire.pia.
  2. read_text in the metaprogram interpreter, hermetic like @embed, with its hash in the interface hash.
  3. Pia.Proto.Gen for messages of scalars, string, bytes, nested messages, enums and repeated: types, writers and readers that prove, and a C round trip against protoc-generated code.
  4. oneof, optional, map, and the Pia options of section 4.
  5. Pia.Proto.Theory and the lemmas of section 3; the canonical form of section 5.
  6. lib/Pia/Ir/ir.proto for the ops of ADR 0079 step 1, tools/ir/gen writing the C++ codec, and the protoc cross-check in CI.
  7. Services as interfaces, for 0.2.0's gRPC transport.

docs.title: Famous bugs, proved away
docs.text:
Some of the most expensive bugs in software history were not subtle. A length was trusted, an index ran one past the end, a sum overflowed, a conversion lost its top bits. Code review, testing and fuzzing missed each of them for months or years, because they only show up on inputs nobody tried.

Each page in this section takes one such bug, recreates its essence in Pia, and shows piac --verify refusing to compile it, with the counterexample the solver found: an input that triggers the bug. Then it shows the fix, proved. Every example on these pages is run by the test suite, so the failures and proofs you read are the compiler's real output.

The point is not that these programs were written carelessly. It is that a compiler which proves bounds, overflow and contracts before it generates code turns each of these from a production incident into a compile error.

docs.title: The cases
docs.text:
Bug Year What went wrong Pia catches it with Heartbleed (OpenSSL, CVE-2014-0160) 2014 a length field from the network was trusted, and memcpy read past the record slice bounds done Binary search midpoint (Java, C) 2006 (low + high) / 2 overflows on large arrays overflow goals done Cloudbleed (Cloudflare) 2017 an HTML parser's end-of-buffer test used ==, and a pointer stepped past the end bounds and loop invariants done CrowdStrike Channel File 291 2024 a template defined 21 input fields, the sensor supplied 20, and the 21st was read out of bounds bounds and preconditions done Rust str::repeat (CVE-2018-1000810) 2018 a wrapping multiplication sized a buffer that unsafe code then overran overflow goals and postconditions done Rust VecDeque (CVE-2018-1000657) 2017 reserve compared against the wrong "capacity", and unsafe code moved elements past the end preconditions done libwebp Huffman tables (CVE-2023-4863) 2023 tables sized for valid codes were filled before the code was checked bounds and loop invariants done Bun readFile on Windows (Zig) 2026 a byte count past 2 GB was truncated to a C int, and the negative result was cast to usize narrowing goals and postconditions done zlib gzip extra field (CVE-2022-37434) 2022 a copy into the caller's buffer was clamped by extra_max - len, which wrapped once the buffer was full overflow goals and postconditions done giflib background colour (CVE-2016-3977) 2016 the background colour's index from the file was looked up in a colour table it did not fit bounds and preconditions done Ariane 5 flight 501 1996 a 64-bit float converted to a 16-bit integer overflowed narrowing goals needs floats (M11) Therac-25 1985 to 1987 a race between operator input and the treatment setup race proofs needs concurrency (M12)

The Rust and Zig cases matter because those languages are memory-safe by default. Their bugs live where the guarantees stop: in unsafe blocks, and in checks that release builds turn off. Pia has no unchecked mode for arithmetic or indexing; every goal is proved or the program does not compile (ADR 0004).

Each page cites its primary sources: the advisory, the fix and the code before it.

docs.title: Binary search
docs.text:
Binary search is the first algorithm many programmers learn to prove correct. In June 2006 Joshua Bloch, who wrote java.util.Arrays, published "Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken": the binary search he wrote for the JDK had a bug, and so did the one in Jon Bentley's Programming Pearls. It had sat in the JDK, in his words, "lying in wait for nine years or so" before it broke someone's program.

The bug is one line, and it is not in the logic of the search. It is in the arithmetic.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/binary-search.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed search, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
Here is the JDK's search as Bloch's post shows it, lightly reformatted:

public static int binarySearch(int[] a, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = a.length - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = (low + high) / 2;
        int midVal = a[mid];

        if (midVal < key)
            low = mid + 1;
        else if (midVal > key)
            high = mid - 1;
        else
            return mid; // key found
    }
    return -(low + 1);  // key not found.
}

int mid = (low + high) / 2; "fails if the sum of low and high is greater than the maximum positive int value (2^31 - 1)." The sum wraps around to a negative number, mid is negative, and a[mid] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. In C, where signed overflow is undefined behaviour, anything can happen. It takes an array of 2^30 elements or more, "roughly a billion", which few test suites ever build.

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
Pia has no early return, so the loop records what it found and stops by closing the range. Otherwise this is the JDK's code, with i32 for Java's int. A Java array has at most 2^31 - 1 elements, which the precondition says:

let search (xs : [i32]) (key : i32) : i32
  requires len xs <= 2147483647
=
  let n : i32 = len xs in
  let low : mutable i32 = 0 in
  let high : mutable i32 = n - 1 in
  let found : mutable i32 = -1 in
  while low <= high
    invariant 0 <= low && low <= n && -1 <= high && high < n
    decreases high - low + 1
  do
    let mid : i32 = (low + high) / 2 in
    let v = xs.[mid] in
    if v < key then low <- mid + 1
    else if v > key then high <- mid - 1
    else (found <- mid; low <- high + 1)
  done;
  if found >= 0 then found else -(low + 1)

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify search.pia
...
search.pia:12:26: failed: '+' does not overflow i32
  counterexample: len xs = 2147483647, key = 0, result = 2147483648
...
search.pia:18:39: failed: '+' does not overflow i32
  counterexample: len xs = 2147483647, key = 264, result = 2147483648
...
13 proved, 2 failed, 0 skipped

The first failure is Bloch's bug: on the largest array, low + high reaches 2^31, one more than an i32 holds.

The second is one the post does not mention. When the key is larger than every element, the search ends with low = len xs, and the "not found" result -(low + 1) overflows too, on an array of exactly 2^31 - 1 elements. In Java the result wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, which is still negative but encodes the wrong insertion point. Whether a JVM will allocate an array that large at all varies, which is how a bug like this stays hidden. The verifier does not need to know; it only needs the contract to allow it.

docs.title: Unsigned is no escape
docs.text:
The usual C fix is to use size_t, an unsigned type as wide as a pointer. That moves the edge, but the edge is still there:

let search (xs : [i32]) (key : i32) : usize =
  let low : mutable usize = 0 in
  let high : mutable usize = len xs in
  let found : mutable usize = len xs in
  while low < high
    invariant low <= high && high <= len xs
    decreases high - low
  do
    let mid : usize = (low + high) / 2 in
    let v = xs.[mid] in
    if v < key then low <- mid + 1
    else if v > key then high <- mid
    else (found <- mid; low <- high)
  done;
  found

$ piac --verify search_usize.pia
...
search_usize.pia:9:28: failed: '+' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len xs = 18446744073709543424, key = 0, result = 32286305728651853941
...
7 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

No real machine has a buffer of 2^64 elements, but the type allows one, and Pia proves what the types and contracts say, not what seems likely. A precondition such as requires len xs <= 9223372036854775807 would prove it; so does computing the midpoint without the sum.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
Bloch's fix is int mid = low + ((high - low) / 2);. Since low <= high, high - low cannot overflow, and adding half of it to low stays at or below high. The "not found" result becomes -low - 1, which cannot overflow because low is never negative.

With the arithmetic fixed, the search can also be held to its full specification. The precondition says the slice is sorted. The postconditions say what the result means: a non-negative result is an index holding the key, and a negative one means the key is nowhere in the slice. The two invariants that make the second one true say that everything left of low is smaller than the key and everything right of high is larger.

let search (xs : [i32]) (key : i32) : i32
  requires len xs <= 2147483647
  requires forall (i in 0..len xs). forall (j in i..len xs). xs.[i] <= xs.[j]
  ensures result >= 0 ==> result < len xs && xs.[result] = key
  ensures result < 0 ==> forall (k in 0..len xs). xs.[k] <> key
=
  let n : i32 = len xs in
  let low : mutable i32 = 0 in
  let high : mutable i32 = n - 1 in
  let found : mutable i32 = -1 in
  while low <= high
    invariant 0 <= low && low <= n && -1 <= high && high < n
    invariant found = -1 || (0 <= found && found < n && xs.[found] = key)
    invariant found = -1 ==> forall (k in 0..low). xs.[k] < key
    invariant found = -1 ==> forall (k in high + 1..n). xs.[k] > key
    decreases high - low + 1
  do
    let mid : i32 = low + (high - low) / 2 in
    let v = xs.[mid] in
    if v < key then low <- mid + 1
    else if v > key then high <- mid - 1
    else (found <- mid; low <- high + 1)
  done;
  if found >= 0 then found else -low - 1

Every goal on this page is proved, including that the loop ends:

$ piac --verify binary-search.pia.md
...
binary-search.pia.md:177:5: proved: the measure decreases [smt]
...
binary-search.pia.md:165:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
binary-search.pia.md:166:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
24 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

In a 2008 update, Bloch corrected his own C fix, which was not guaranteed to work under C99's rules for signed overflow, and wrote: "Now that we've made this change, we know that the program is correct;)". With Pia, the compiler is the one who knows.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Joshua Bloch, "Extra, Extra - Read All About It: Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken", Google Research blog, 2 June
  • The JDK code, the buggy line, the 2^30-element threshold and the fixes are quoted from it.
  • Jon Bentley, Programming Pearls, chapter 5 (Addison-Wesley, 1986; second edition 2000), which the post names as the source of the same bug.

docs.title: Bun's readFile on Windows
docs.text:
Zig is a safe language in some build modes and not in others. Its language reference lists four: Debug and ReleaseSafe have "Safety checks enabled", and ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall have "Safety checks disabled". One of the checks is on @intCast, which "Converts an integer to another integer while keeping the same numerical value". A value that does not fit is, in the reference's words, "safety-protected Undefined Behavior": a panic where safety is on, and nothing at all where it is off.

Bun, the JavaScript runtime, is written in Zig. Its issue #23849 is titled "Incorrect integer type used in readFile on Windows". Reading a file bigger than 2 GB in one call crashed Bun with the panic "integer does not fit in destination type", in preadv in src/sys_uv.zig. The safety check caught it. In a build mode without the check, the same cast would have handed a garbage byte count to the code that reads the buffer.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/bun-readfile.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
On Windows, Bun reads files through libuv. uv_fs_read returns a C int, and as the fix's description explains, for a synchronous call that int is (int)req->result, where req->result is the full ssize_t byte count. Past INT_MAX bytes the conversion wraps, and the count comes back negative. Bun then converted it to a usize:

const bytes_read: usize = @intCast(rc.int());

Two narrowings sit in that line's history. The first is C's, from ssize_t to int, which no build mode checks. The second is Zig's, from a negative int to an unsigned usize, which Bun's build did check, so the program stopped instead of carrying on with a wrong count. The fix, "windows: fix readFile panic on files >2GB", by Dylan Conway, merged on 15 April 2026, stops using the truncated return value and reads the untruncated one instead:

const bytes_read: usize = @intCast(req.result.int());

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
Pia has no truncating cast hidden in an assignment. A conversion to a narrower type is a goal, like every index and every sum: it must be proved to fit. So here is libuv's conversion, written as plainly as C wrote it:

let uv_fs_read (req_result : isize) : i32 = req_result

$ piac --verify uv.pia
uv.pia:1:45: failed: the value fits in i32
  counterexample: req_result = 1946436263233978368, value = 1946436263233978368
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

That is the first narrowing, the one C never checks, refused with a count that does not fit. The second is Bun's, the @intCast of whatever int came back to a usize:

let bytes_read (rc : i32) : usize = rc

$ piac --verify cast.pia
cast.pia:1:37: failed: the value fits in usize
  counterexample: rc = -2147483648, value = -2147483648
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The counterexample is the crash: a negative int, which no usize can hold. This is Zig's @intCast check, done once, at compile time, for every input. There is no build mode in Pia that turns it off (ADR 0004): a narrowing either proves or the program does not compile.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the fixed program. Like Bun's fix, it reads the untruncated count, so there is no int in the way. An error is a negative count, and a successful read returns the count as a usize, which proves because the branch has just checked it is not negative:

let read_result = type { failed : bool; bytes : usize }

let preadv (req_result : isize) : read_result
  ensures result.failed = (req_result < 0)
=
  if req_result < 0 then { failed = true; bytes = 0 }
  else { failed = false; bytes = req_result }

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify bun-readfile.pia.md
bun-readfile.pia.md:106:34: proved: the value fits in usize [smt]
bun-readfile.pia.md:103:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
2 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

docs.title: What this says about safe build modes
docs.text: Zig gives the programmer a choice, per build and even per block with @setRuntimeSafety, between checking a cast and trusting it. Bun's check turned a wrong count into a crash, which is the best a run-time check can do. It still shipped, and it still crashed for users with large files. A proof moves the same check to the compiler, where it runs for every input before the program exists, and there is nothing to turn off.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The Zig 0.13.0 language reference: Build Mode, @intCast and Cast Truncates Data.
  • Bun issue #23849, "Incorrect integer type used in readFile on Windows".
  • Bun PR #29327, "windows: fix readFile panic on files >2GB", by Dylan Conway, merged 15 April 2026: the explanation of the int return, the crash report and its panic message, and the diff.

docs.title: Cloudbleed
docs.text:
On 18 February 2017, Tavis Ormandy of Google's Project Zero contacted Cloudflare: some of its edge servers were returning chunks of uninitialized memory inside ordinary web pages. Other sites' cookies, authentication tokens and private messages were turning up in responses, and in search engines' caches. Cloudflare's incident report traced it to the HTML parser behind three features (email obfuscation, Server-side Excludes and Automatic HTTPS Rewrites). At its peak, around 1 in every 3,300,000 HTTP requests through Cloudflare could leak memory, and the earliest date memory could have leaked was 2016-09-22.

The root cause, in the report's words: "reaching the end of a buffer was checked using the equality operator and a pointer was able to step past the end of the buffer."

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/cloudbleed.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed scanner, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
The parser was generated by Ragel, which turns a grammar into a state machine in C. The generated code walks a pointer p through the buffer and stops when it reaches the end pointer pe:

/* generated code */
if ( ++p == pe )
    goto _test_eof;

That test is correct as long as p only ever moves one byte at a time. Cloudflare's grammar had an error action, for an attribute left unfinished at the end of a buffer (an HTML page ending in <script type=, say), that jumped to another state without first stepping p back. So p was already at pe when the next state ran ++p. Now p was one past the end, p == pe was never true again, and the parser kept reading whatever memory came next. As the report says: "Had the check been done using >= instead of == jumping over the buffer end would have been caught."

The bug was not in Ragel, the report says, but in Cloudflare's use of it. A C compiler had no way to know that p and pe point into the same buffer, let alone that p must never pass pe.

docs.title: The same shape in Pia
docs.text:
Pia has no pointers into buffers, but an index does the same job. This scanner is not Cloudflare's parser; it is the shape of the bug. It counts the attributes in some HTML, and when it sees an = it steps over the character after it too, the opening quote of the value. The loop stops when p equals the end, as the generated C did. The invariant says what the C code silently assumed, that p never passes the end:

let count_attrs (html : [u8]) : usize =
  let p : mutable usize = 0 in
  let n : mutable usize = 0 in
  while p <> len html
    invariant p <= len html && n <= p
    decreases len html - p
  do
    if html.[p] = 61 then (n <- n + 1; p <- p + 2)
    else p <- p + 1
  done;
  n

61 is =. piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify scan.pia
...
scan.pia:8:47: failed: '+' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len html = 18446744073709551615, result = 18446744073709551616
...
scan.pia:5:5: failed: the loop invariant holds after each iteration
  counterexample: len html = 18446462598732840960
...
5 proved, 2 failed, 0 skipped

The invariant failure is Cloudbleed. Counterexamples do not show the contents of a slice yet, only its length, but the case the solver found is the one that triggered the leak: p at the last byte, and that byte an =, an attribute cut off at the end of the buffer. The step takes p to one past the end, and the loop, testing only for equality, never stops. (The first failure is the same step from the other side: on a buffer of 2^64 - 1 bytes, p + 2 does not even fit in a usize.)

docs.title: Without the invariant
docs.text:
Leaving the invariant out does not help. Then the verifier knows nothing about p inside the loop, and the read itself is the goal that fails:

let count_attrs (html : [u8]) : usize =
  let p : mutable usize = 0 in
  let n : mutable usize = 0 in
  while p <> len html
    decreases len html - p
  do
    if html.[p] = 61 then (n <- n +| 1; p <- p +| 2)
    else p <- p +| 1
  done;
  n

$ piac --verify scan_no_invariant.pia
scan_no_invariant.pia:7:8: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len html = 12583104, index = 18446744073696968511, length = 12583104
...
1 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

Either way, the program does not compile. In C, both compiled.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The fix the report names is to test with >= instead of ==: in Pia, loop while p < len html. Here that is only half the fix:

let count_attrs (html : [u8]) : usize =
  let p : mutable usize = 0 in
  let n : mutable usize = 0 in
  while p < len html
    invariant p <= len html + 1 && n <= p && n <= len html
    decreases len html + 1 - p
  do
    if html.[p] = 61 then (n <- n + 1; p <- p + 2)
    else p <- p + 1
  done;
  n

$ piac --verify scan_lt.pia
...
scan_lt.pia:8:47: failed: '+' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len html = 18446744073709551615, result = 18446744073709551616
...
scan_lt.pia:5:5: proved: the loop invariant holds after each iteration [smt]
...
6 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The loop now stops, and every read is proved in bounds, but the step past the end is still there: on the largest possible buffer, p + 2 overflows. A C program would wrap the pointer around and carry on. The other half of the fix is not to step over a byte that is not there. The scanner skips the quote only when the buffer has one, so p never passes the end, and the loop test and the invariant say so. The postcondition is a small theorem about the result: there are never more attributes than bytes.

let count_attrs (html : [u8]) : usize
  ensures result <= len html
=
  let p : mutable usize = 0 in
  let n : mutable usize = 0 in
  while p < len html
    invariant p <= len html && n <= p
    decreases len html - p
  do
    if html.[p] = 61 && p + 1 < len html then (n <- n + 1; p <- p + 2)
    else p <- p + 1
  done;
  n

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify cloudbleed.pia.md
...
cloudbleed.pia.md:173:5: proved: the loop invariant holds after each iteration [smt]
...
cloudbleed.pia.md:168:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
9 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

The deeper fix is the one Pia makes the default. In the C code, the fact that p stays inside the buffer lived in the programmer's head. In Pia it is a goal at every read, so a grammar action that breaks it is a compile error at the line that breaks it, with the input that breaks it.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Cloudflare, "Incident report on memory leak caused by Cloudflare parser bug", 23 February 2017. The generated C, the root cause, the >= remark, the triggering features, the timeline and the figures above are from it.
  • The report credits Tavis Ormandy of Google's Project Zero with finding and reporting the bug.

docs.title: CrowdStrike Channel File 291
docs.text:
At 04:09 UTC on Friday 19 July 2024, CrowdStrike pushed a routine content update to its Falcon sensor, the endpoint security agent that runs inside the Windows kernel. Windows hosts that received it crashed, and crashed again on reboot. CrowdStrike reverted the update at 05:27 UTC, but the machines that had it stayed down until someone fixed each one, often by hand. Microsoft estimated that the update "affected 8.5 million Windows devices". Airlines, hospitals, banks and broadcasters went offline.

CrowdStrike's root cause analysis traces it to a count: a template that defined 21 input fields, fed by code that supplied 20.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/crowdstrike.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
The sensor's detection logic is partly data. Rapid Response Content, delivered in channel files, holds Template Instances: lists of matching criteria, one per input field, that the sensor's Content Interpreter checks against live system activity. Each instance belongs to a Template Type compiled into the sensor, which says how many fields there are.

In February 2024, sensor 7.11 added a Template Type for Windows interprocess communication (IPC), whose instances arrive in Channel File 291. From the RCA:

The new IPC Template Type defined 21 input parameter fields, but the integration code that invoked the Content Interpreter with Channel File 291's Template Instances supplied only 20 input values to match against.

For five months nothing went wrong, because every instance used a wildcard for the 21st field, and a wildcard matches without reading its input. The tests did too: "a regex wildcard matching criterion in the 21st field for all Template Instances". The Content Validator, which checks new content before it ships, "based its assessment on the expectation that the IPC Template Type would be provided with 21 inputs." Then, on 19 July, one new instance "introduced a non-wildcard matching criterion for the 21st input parameter", and:

The Content Interpreter expected only 20 values. Therefore, the attempt to access the 21st value produced an out-of-bounds memory read beyond the end of the input data array and resulted in a system crash.

In a kernel driver, an out-of-bounds read is a blue screen.

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
Here is the interpreter's core, reduced to integers. An instance is two slices of the same length, one entry per field: wild.[i] says whether field i is a wildcard, and want.[i] is the value it must equal otherwise. inputs holds the values the sensor supplies. The loop checks every field, and reads an input only for a field that is not a wildcard, just as the real interpreter did:

let matches (wild : [bool]) (want : [u32]) (inputs : [u32]) : bool
  requires len want = len wild
=
  let ok : mutable bool = true in
  for i in 0..len wild do
    if wild.[i] then () else if inputs.[i] <> want.[i] then ok <- false else ()
  done;
  ok

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify interpreter.pia
interpreter.pia:6:8: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
interpreter.pia:6:33: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len wild = 9223372036854775936, len want = 9223372036854775936, len inputs = 0, index = 9223372036854775934, length = 0
interpreter.pia:6:47: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
2 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The read of inputs.[i] fails, and the counterexample has fewer inputs than fields (here none at all). The reads of wild and want prove, because the precondition ties their lengths together. This is the point testing could not reach: the read happens only when the criterion is not a wildcard, and every test used a wildcard there. The verifier does not sample criteria; it proves the read is safe for all of them, or shows one where it is not.

docs.title: The count belongs in the contract
docs.text:
The RCA's first finding is that "the number of fields in the IPC Template Type was not validated at sensor compile time". In Pia, the place to say how many inputs the interpreter needs is its precondition. Now the interpreter proves, and the obligation moves to every caller. Here is the integration code for the IPC template, with the template's 21 fields and the sensor's 20 inputs written into the types:

let matches (wild : [bool]) (want : [u32]) (inputs : [u32]) : bool
  requires len want = len wild && len inputs = len wild
=
  let ok : mutable bool = true in
  for i in 0..len wild do
    if wild.[i] then () else if inputs.[i] <> want.[i] then ok <- false else ()
  done;
  ok

let check_ipc (wild : [bool; 21]) (want : [u32; 21]) (inputs : [u32; 20]) : bool =
  matches wild want inputs

$ piac --verify integration.pia
...
integration.pia:11:3: failed: the precondition of 'matches' holds
6 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

There is no counterexample, because none is needed: the lengths are fixed by the types, so the precondition fails whatever the inputs are. That is the bug, as a compile error in the sensor's own build, before any content was ever written for it. No channel file, wildcard or not, could then have reached the read.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the fixed program. The interpreter states its requirement, and its postcondition says what a match means: every field that is not a wildcard equals its input.

let matches (wild : [bool]) (want : [u32]) (inputs : [u32]) : bool
  requires len want = len wild && len inputs = len wild
  ensures result ==> forall (k in 0..len wild). wild.[k] || inputs.[k] = want.[k]
=
  let ok : mutable bool = true in
  for i in 0..len wild
    invariant ok ==> forall (k in 0..i). wild.[k] || inputs.[k] = want.[k]
  do
    if wild.[i] then () else if inputs.[i] <> want.[i] then ok <- false else ()
  done;
  ok

The integration code supplies all 21 inputs, which is CrowdStrike's own fix: "The sensor code defining the IPC Template Type was updated to provide the correct number of inputs (21)."

let check_ipc (wild : [bool; 21]) (want : [u32; 21]) (inputs : [u32; 21]) : bool =
  matches wild want inputs

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify crowdstrike.pia.md
...
crowdstrike.pia.md:139:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
...
crowdstrike.pia.md:156:3: proved: the precondition of 'matches' holds [smt]
10 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

CrowdStrike's other fix was a runtime bounds check in the interpreter, added on 25 July. In Pia that check is unnecessary, so the compiled code has none: the proof that every read is in bounds is the check, and it ran once, at compile time.

docs.title: What Pia needs for the rest
docs.text: The real interpreter matches strings against regular expressions, and the template's field count comes from a definitions file rather than the type of an array. Pia's verifier handles neither yet. The count can still be checked at compile time once modules export interfaces with contracts (M8): the Template Type would be an exported symbol whose field count is a constant, and the sensor would be proved against it.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• CrowdStrike, "External Technical Root Cause Analysis — Channel File 291", 6 August 2024. The quotations, the findings and the fixes above are from it.
  • CrowdStrike, "Preliminary Post Incident Review", 24 July 2024, for the update and revert times: "On Friday, July 19, 2024 at 04:09 UTC" and "reverted on Friday, July 19, 2024 at 05:27 UTC."
  • Microsoft, "Helping our customers through the CrowdStrike outage", 20 July 2024: "We currently estimate that CrowdStrike's update affected 8.5 million Windows devices, or less than one percent of all Windows machines."

docs.title: giflib's background colour
docs.text:
In April 2016, giflib fixed CVE-2016-3977, a heap buffer overflow in gif2rgb, the utility that converts GIF images to RGB. The CVE record says a crafted GIF crashes it "via the background color index". Henri Salo found it with the afl fuzzer and reported it as giflib bug #87.

A GIF names its background colour by an index into its colour table, and nothing makes the index fit the table.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/giflib-background.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text: The logical screen descriptor at the start of every GIF holds the background colour's index in one byte, so it can be 0 to 255. The global colour table holds 2 to 256 colours, as the same descriptor says. As Red Hat's analysis of the report (bug 1325771) describes, gif2rgb fills the first row of its screen buffer with SBackGroundColor, and DumpScreen2RGB later looks every pixel up as ColorMap->Colors[GifRow[j]] with no check against the table's ColorCount. The reproducer's table has two colours and a background index of 255, so the lookup reads far past the end of the table. The fix checks the index before the dump: if SBackGroundColor is negative or at least ColorMap->ColorCount, it prints "Background color out of range for colormap" and exits.

docs.title: The same shape in Pia
docs.text:
This is not giflib's code; it is the shape of the bug: an RGB colour table and an index read from the file.

let background_red (colors : [u8]) (bg : u8) : u8 =
  let i : usize = bg in
  colors.[3 * i]

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify colours.pia
colours.pia:3:13: proved: '*' does not overflow usize [intervals]
colours.pia:3:3: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len colors = 1, bg = 239, index = 717, length = 1
1 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The counterexample is the bug: a table shorter than the colour the file names.

docs.title: The fix, proved, two ways
docs.text:
giflib's fix rejects a file whose index does not fit its table. In Pia the check is what lets the index through:

let background_red (colors : [u8]) (bg : u8) : result u8 usize
= let i : usize = bg in
  if 3 * i + 2 < len colors then Ok colors.[3 * i] else Err i

Pia's own GIF decoder, Pia.Image.Gif.Decode (ADR 0054, step 2), takes the other way: it copies every colour table into a 256-entry map padded with black, so every index a byte can hold has a colour, and states that in the type of what it indexes. Then there is nothing left to check:

let padded_red (colors : [u8]) (bg : u8) : u8
  requires len colors = 768
= let i : usize = bg in
  colors.[3 * i]

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify giflib-background.pia.md
...
giflib-background.pia.md:77:3: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
6 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

The decoder proves the same of every pixel: each index its LZW decoder writes is below 2^8, and the map it looks them up in is 768 bytes, so no frame of any input can read past its colour table. Its run test decodes every one-byte corruption of three GIFs without a crash.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The CVE record, CVE-2016-3977, published 21 April 2016: giflib 5.1.2's util/gif2rgb.c.
  • giflib bug #87, "Heap buffer overflow in 5.1.2 gif2rgb.c:531", by Henri Salo, March 2016.
  • giflib commit ea8dbc5786862a3e16a5acfa3d24e2c2f608cd88, "Fix SF bug #87 Heap buffer overflow in 5.1.2 (gif2rgb)", by Eric S. Raymond, 2 April 2016: the range check on the background colour.
  • Red Hat bug 1325771: the analysis of the out-of-bounds read through ColorMap->Colors.

docs.title: Heartbleed
docs.text:
In April 2014, OpenSSL disclosed a bug that let anyone who could open a TLS connection read up to 64 KB of a server's memory per request, over and over: private keys, session cookies, passwords, whatever happened to sit next to the request in the heap. It was CVE-2014-0160, and it became known as Heartbleed. The cause was one missing comparison.

This page recreates the bug in Pia, shows piac refusing to compile it, and then proves the fix. It is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/heartbleed.pia.md: the pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
TLS has a heartbeat extension (RFC 6520): one side sends a request carrying some bytes, and the other side echoes the same bytes back, to show the connection is alive. A heartbeat message is a type byte, a 16-bit payload_length, the payload, and at least 16 bytes of random padding:

+------+----------------+----------------------+------------------+
| type | payload_length | payload              | padding (>= 16)  |
| 1 B  | 2 B, big-endian| payload_length bytes |                  |
+------+----------------+----------------------+------------------+

The sender writes payload_length itself, so the receiver must check it against the size of the record that actually arrived. OpenSSL 1.0.1 to 1.0.1f did not. Here is the start of tls1_process_heartbeat in ssl/t1_lib.c, as it was before the fix (source):

unsigned char *p = &s->s3->rrec.data[0], *pl;
unsigned short hbtype;
unsigned int payload;
unsigned int padding = 16; /* Use minimum padding */

/* Read type and payload length first */
hbtype = *p++;
n2s(p, payload);
pl = p;

and the response it built:

buffer = OPENSSL_malloc(1 + 2 + payload + padding);
bp = buffer;

/* Enter response type, length and copy payload */
*bp++ = TLS1_HB_RESPONSE;
s2n(payload, bp);
memcpy(bp, pl, payload);

n2s reads the two length bytes. memcpy then copies payload bytes starting at the payload, whatever the record's real length was. A request that says "65535 bytes" but carries one byte gets back that byte and the 65534 bytes of heap after it. Nothing in C connects pl to the length of the buffer it points into, so no compiler could object.

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
A Pia slice carries its length, and every index and every subslice is a goal the compiler must prove in bounds. Here is the heartbeat handler written the way OpenSSL wrote it. req is the received record and resp the response buffer, which the caller makes big enough for any payload. copy copies one slice into another of the same length:

let copy (dst : out mutable [u8]) (src : [u8]) : unit
  requires len src = len dst
  ensures forall (k in 0..len dst). dst.[k] = src.[k]
=
  for i in 0..len dst
    invariant forall (k in 0..i). dst.[k] = src.[k]
  do dst.[i] <- src.[i] done

let heartbeat (req : [u8]) (resp : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len resp >= 3 + 65535
=
  let payload : usize = ((req.[1] << 8) | req.[2]) in
  resp.[0] <- 2;
  resp.[1] <- req.[1];
  resp.[2] <- req.[2];
  copy (resp.[3 .. 3 + payload]) (req.[3 .. 3 + payload]);
  3 + payload

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify heartbleed.pia
...
heartbleed.pia:12:27: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len req = 0, len resp = 98304, index = 1, length = 0
...
heartbleed.pia:12:43: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len req = 2, len resp = 98304, index = 2, length = 2
...
heartbleed.pia:16:35: failed: the slice is within bounds
  counterexample: len req = 4, len resp = 131039, start = 3, end = 5, length = 4
...
18 proved, 3 failed, 0 skipped

The third failure is Heartbleed. The counterexample is an attack: a 4-byte record, one byte of payload, whose length field says 2, so the slice req.[3 .. 5] would run past the end of req. Make the length field say 65535 and it is the real exploit. The first two failures are a second bug the C code shares: a record shorter than three bytes has no length field to read, and n2s reads past it too.

docs.title: Half a fix
docs.text:
The obvious patch checks the length field against the record:

let copy (dst : out mutable [u8]) (src : [u8]) : unit
  requires len src = len dst
  ensures forall (k in 0..len dst). dst.[k] = src.[k]
=
  for i in 0..len dst
    invariant forall (k in 0..i). dst.[k] = src.[k]
  do dst.[i] <- src.[i] done

let heartbeat (req : [u8]) (resp : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len resp >= 3 + 65535
=
  let payload : usize = ((req.[1] << 8) | req.[2]) in
  if 3 + payload + 16 > len req then 0
  else (
    resp.[0] <- 2;
    resp.[1] <- req.[1];
    resp.[2] <- req.[2];
    copy (resp.[3 .. 3 + payload]) (req.[3 .. 3 + payload]);
    3 + payload)

The copy is proved now, but reading the length still is not:

$ piac --verify half_fixed.pia
...
half_fixed.pia:12:27: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len req = 0, len resp = 98304, index = 1, length = 0
...
half_fixed.pia:12:43: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len req = 2, len resp = 98304, index = 2, length = 2
...
half_fixed.pia:18:37: proved: the slice is within bounds [smt]
...
21 proved, 2 failed, 0 skipped

OpenSSL's real fix (commit 96db902, by Adam Langley and Bodo Möller) has both checks, the first one before the length is read:

/* Read type and payload length first */
if (1 + 2 + 16 > s->s3->rrec.length)
    return 0; /* silently discard */
hbtype = *p++;
n2s(p, payload);
if (1 + 2 + payload + 16 > s->s3->rrec.length)
    return 0; /* silently discard per RFC 6520 sec. 4 */
pl = p;

In C, nothing told the authors the first check was needed; they had to see it. In Pia, leaving it out is a compile error with a counterexample.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the fixed program: the handler, with both of OpenSSL's checks, and the request type checked as tls1_process_heartbeat does. It returns the length of the response it wrote, before padding, or 0 when RFC 6520 says to discard the message: "If the payload_length of a received HeartbeatMessage is too large, the received HeartbeatMessage MUST be discarded silently." The postcondition is the property Heartbleed broke, stated and proved: a response is never longer than the request it answers, and every payload byte in it came from that request. The copy is written out as a loop, so its invariant carries that second fact straight to the postcondition.

let heartbeat (req : [u8]) (resp : out mutable [u8]) : usize
  requires len resp >= 3 + 65535
  ensures result = 0 || result + 16 <= len req
  ensures forall (k in 3..result). resp.[k] = req.[k]
=
  if 3 + 16 > len req then 0
  else (
    let payload : usize = ((req.[1] << 8) | req.[2]) in
    if 3 + payload + 16 > len req then 0
    else if req.[0] <> 1 then 0
    else (
      resp.[0] <- 2;
      resp.[1] <- req.[1];
      resp.[2] <- req.[2];
      for i in 3..3 + payload
        invariant forall (k in 3..i). resp.[k] = req.[k]
      do resp.[i] <- req.[i] done;
      3 + payload))

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify heartbleed.pia.md
...
heartbleed.pia.md:196:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
heartbleed.pia.md:197:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
22 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Because the bounds are proved, the compiled code has no bounds checks in it: the safety costs nothing at run time. And the proof is in the interface. A caller of heartbeat knows from its postcondition, without reading its body, that it cannot leak memory beyond the request.

docs.title: What Pia needs for the rest
docs.text: The real handler allocates its response buffer, writes 16 random bytes of padding and hands the message to the record layer. Pia has no allocator or I/O yet, so the caller passes resp and adds the padding. With the memory module (ADR 0026), the allocation would be one more call whose failure the caller must handle.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:

Affected: 1.0.1 to 1.0.1f and 1.0.2-beta1; fixed in 1.0.1g.
