docs.title: libwebp's Huffman tables
docs.text:
In September 2023, Chrome shipped an urgent fix for CVE-2023-4863, a heap buffer overflow in libwebp, the library that decodes WebP images in Chrome, Firefox, Android, and countless apps that embed it. As Ben Hawkes recounts in "The WebP 0day", the bug was reported by Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture team, and Chrome's release notes said: "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2023-4863 exists in the wild." A crafted image could write past the end of a heap buffer during decoding, before any of it was displayed.

The code was not careless. Its table sizes came from a careful worst-case analysis. The analysis just assumed the input was valid, and the code checked that only after it had written.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/libwebp.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
Lossless WebP compresses pixels with Huffman codes, which the image itself describes. The decoder turns each code into lookup tables: a root table, plus second-level tables for the longer codes, all built into one allocation. In src/dec/vp8l_dec.c that allocation had a fixed size per image, taken from a table whose comment explains where its numbers came from:

// All values computed for 8-bit first level lookup with Mark Adler's tool:
// https://github.com/madler/zlib/blob/v1.2.5/examples/enough.c
#define FIXED_TABLE_SIZE (630 * 3 + 410)
static const uint16_t kTableSize[12] = {
  FIXED_TABLE_SIZE + 654,

enough.c computes the largest tables any complete Huffman code can need. BuildHuffmanTable in src/utils/huffman_utils.c then fills the second-level tables, moving table forward by each table's size as it goes:

if ((key & mask) != low) {
  table += table_size;
  table_bits = NextTableBitSize(count, len, root_bits);
  table_size = 1 << table_bits;
  total_size += table_size;
  ...
}
...
ReplicateValue(&table[key >> root_bits], step, table_size, code);

and only after every table is written does it check that the code was complete:

// Check if tree is full.
if (num_nodes != 2 * offset[MAX_ALLOWED_CODE_LENGTH] - 1) {
  return 0;
}

An incomplete code can need more second-level table space than any complete one, so the worst case enough.c computed did not cover it. By the time the check rejected the code, the writes had already gone past the end of the allocation; Hawkes' proof of concept writes "as far as 400 bytes past the end". The fix, "Fix OOB write in BuildHuffmanTable", reorders the work: "First, BuildHuffmanTable is called to check if the data is valid. If it is and the table is not big enough, more memory is allocated."

docs.title: The same shape in Pia
docs.text:
This is not libwebp's decoder; it is the shape of the bug. The input determines a list of second-level table sizes. The builder writes each table after the previous one, in a buffer whose size was fixed in advance, and checks at the end whether the code was valid. The invariant says what the buffer's size was chosen to guarantee: the tables fit.

let build (table : out mutable [u16]) (sizes : [u16]) (complete : bool) : usize =
  let pos : mutable usize = 0 in
  for t in 0..len sizes
    invariant pos <= len table
  do
    let size : usize = sizes.[t] in
    for k in 0..size do table.[pos + k] <- 1 done;
    pos <- pos + size
  done;
  if complete then pos else 0

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify tables.pia
...
tables.pia:7:25: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len table = 1, len sizes = 1, complete = false, index = 1, length = 1
...
tables.pia:4:5: failed: the loop invariant holds after each iteration
  counterexample: len table = 65538, len sizes = 1, complete = false
2 proved, 4 failed, 0 skipped

The smallest counterexample is the whole bug: a one-entry buffer and an input asking for a table bigger than that, so the first write past the end happens at index 1. (The other two failures are the running offset overflowing on absurdly large inputs.) Nothing in the builder connects the sizes the input asks for to the space that was allocated. The worst-case analysis made that connection, for valid inputs, outside the program, where no compiler could check it, and the validity check came too late to matter.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the fixed builder. Before writing each table it checks that the table fits in the space left, and once one does not, it writes nothing more and reports the input as invalid. That is the same guarantee libwebp's fix gets from its first, size-only pass: no write happens until the space for it is known. The postcondition says the result never claims more space than the buffer has.

let build (table : out mutable [u16]) (sizes : [u16]) : usize
  ensures result <= len table
=
  let pos : mutable usize = 0 in
  let ok : mutable bool = true in
  for t in 0..len sizes
    invariant pos <= len table
  do
    let size : usize = sizes.[t] in
    if ok && size <= len table - pos then (
      for k in 0..size do table.[pos + k] <- 1 done;
      pos <- pos + size)
    else ok <- false
  done;
  if ok then pos else 0

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify libwebp.pia.md
...
libwebp.pia.md:135:5: proved: the loop invariant holds after each iteration [smt]
libwebp.pia.md:130:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
8 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

In Pia, a precomputed worst case can still be used, but only as a contract the code proves: if kTableSize were a precondition, the builder would have to show its writes stay inside it for every input it accepts, valid or not.

docs.title: What Pia needs for the rest
docs.text: The real builder derives the table sizes from the code lengths, with shifts and counts over a 16-entry histogram, and grows the allocation when a valid code needs more room. Proving the size bound for the real derivation is a good stress test for the verifier, and growing the allocation needs the memory module (ADR 0026). Pia's own image codecs, which will have to get exactly this right, are milestone M13.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• libwebp commit 902bc9190331343b2017211debcec8d2ab87e17a, "Fix OOB write in BuildHuffmanTable.", by Vincent Rabaud, 7 September 2023.
  • The code before the fix: src/utils/huffman_utils.c and src/dec/vp8l_dec.c at its parent commit.
  • Ben Hawkes, "The WebP 0day", 21 September 2023: the analysis, the report by Apple's SEAR team, the quotation from Chrome's release notes and the 400-byte overflow.
  • Chrome's stable channel update of 11 September 2023.

docs.title: Rust's str::repeat
docs.text:
Rust is memory-safe by default, and that default is what makes this case worth studying. On 21 September 2018 the Rust team announced "a security vulnerability affecting the standard library's str::repeat function. When passed a large number this function has an integer overflow which can lead to an out of bounds write." It became CVE-2018-1000810. The full announcement calls it "an instance of CWE-680: Integer Overflow to Buffer Overflow", says it entered the standard library in a pull request merged on 6 March 2018, first shipped in Rust 1.26.0, and was fixed in 1.29.1. It credits Scott McMurray with finding it.

The overflow was in safe code. The out-of-bounds write was in an unsafe block a few lines further down, which trusted what the safe code had computed.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/rust-str-repeat.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
str::repeat calls [u8]::repeat, which in Rust 1.29.0 (src/liballoc/slice.rs) begins:

pub fn repeat(&self, n: usize) -> Vec<T> where T: Copy {
    if n == 0 {
        return Vec::new();
    }
    ...
    // Using `Vec` to access `set_len()`.
    let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(self.len() * n);

and then fills the buffer by doubling it, with raw copies:

            unsafe {
                ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(
                    buf.as_ptr(),
                    (buf.as_mut_ptr() as *mut T).add(buf.len()),
                    buf.len(),
                );
                // `buf` has capacity of `self.len() * n`.
                let buf_len = buf.len();
                buf.set_len(buf_len * 2);
            }

The comment is the whole story: "buf has capacity of self.len() * n." The unsafe block depends on it, and it is false when self.len() * n overflows. In a release build, Rust's integer arithmetic wraps on overflow by default, so the capacity silently comes out small, and the copies write past the end of the allocation. The program the borrow checker accepted could write anywhere.

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
The capacity calculation, written as plainly as Rust wrote it:

let capacity (size : usize) (n : usize) : usize = size * n

$ piac --verify capacity.pia
capacity.pia:1:56: failed: '*' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: size = 10879383879352893286, n = 17176544054727634905, result = 186870216491998611994851295411633747830
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

By default every Pia multiplication is a goal: it must be proved to fit. This one does not, and the counterexample is the attack.

docs.title: Wrapping does not make it safe
docs.text:
Rust's release builds give overflow a meaning, wrapping, so the multiplication is "defined". Pia can say the same with @overflow(wrap), and then the multiplication has nothing left to prove. But the comment in the Rust source is a claim about the result, so write it down as one:

let capacity (size : usize) (n : usize) : usize @overflow(wrap)
  ensures result = size * n
= size * n

$ piac --verify capacity_wrap.pia
capacity_wrap.pia:2:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample: size = 18418166063394745921, n = 12079500963941582858
0 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

Arithmetic in a contract is exact, so size * n in the postcondition is the true product, and the wrapped result is not equal to it. The comment the unsafe code relied on becomes a goal, and the goal fails. Defined behaviour is not correct behaviour.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
Rust's fix, in 1.29.1, was one line:

let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(self.len().checked_mul(n).expect("capacity overflow"));

checked_mul reports the overflow instead of hiding it, and expect panics on it. The same idea in Pia returns whether the product fits along with the product, and the postconditions say exactly when it fits and what it is. A caller cannot get a capacity without the proof that it is the true one.

The check itself is a saturating multiplication: in an @overflow(saturate) function, a product too big for a usize comes out as the largest usize. So a result below that is the true product, and the largest value itself is treated as overflow, which costs nothing, since Rust never allocates more than isize::MAX bytes anyway.

let capacity = type { ok : bool; bytes : usize }

let checked_capacity (size : usize) (n : usize) : capacity @overflow(saturate)
  ensures result.ok = (size * n < 18446744073709551615)
  ensures result.ok ==> result.bytes = size * n
=
  let bytes : usize = size * n in
  { ok = bytes < 18446744073709551615; bytes = bytes }

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify rust-str-repeat.pia.md
rust-str-repeat.pia.md:133:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
rust-str-repeat.pia.md:134:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
2 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

The postconditions are exact, even in a saturating function: size * n in a contract is the true product, so the first one says ok is set exactly when the product fits. That is the property the Rust code needed and stated only in a comment.

While this page was being written, the verifier itself had this bug: it applied a function's overflow mode to the arithmetic in its contracts, so the wrapping capacity above was wrongly proved. The fix landed with this page, and a test in tests/verify/spec_exact.pia keeps it fixed.

docs.title: What this says about unsafe
docs.text:
Rust's guarantee stops at unsafe, and the code inside an unsafe block is only as sound as the facts it assumes. Here the fact was in a comment. Pia has no unsafe for arithmetic or indexing: a fact the code relies on is a contract, every contract is proved, and a fact that could be false is a compile error (ADR 0004).

Pia's version of the rest of repeat, which allocates the buffer and fills it, needs the memory module (ADR 0026), where every allocation can fail and the caller must handle it.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The Rust Core Team, "Security advisory for the standard library", 21 September 2018.
  • The full announcement, "Security advisory for the Rust standard library, 2018-09-21", on the rustlang-security-announcements list: the affected versions (1.26.0 to 1.29.0), the fix in 1.29.1, the CWE classification, and the credit to Scott McMurray. A later reply on the same thread gives the CVE number.
  • The code: src/liballoc/slice.rs at 1.29.0 and at 1.29.1.
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-2cg9-g249-7mf2 for CVE-2018-1000810.

docs.title: Rust's VecDeque::reserve
docs.text:
On 24 September 2017 a Rust user reported "seg fault pushing on either side of a VecDeque", in safe code, on Rust 1.19 and 1.20. Steven Fackler reduced it to four lines the same day:

let mut deque = VecDeque::with_capacity(32);
deque.push_front(0);
deque.reserve(31);
deque.push_back(0);

Valgrind reported an "Invalid write of size 4", "0 bytes after a block of size 256 alloc'd". The standard library's double-ended queue was writing past the end of its own buffer. The bug, later CVE-2018-1000657, had been there since Rust 1.3.0, and the advisory lists 1.22.0 as the first fixed release.

The fix was one comparison.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/rust-vecdeque.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
A VecDeque is a ring buffer: a buffer of cap slots, a power of two, with the elements running from tail round to head, possibly wrapping past the end. When the buffer grows, the elements that wrapped must be moved so they are contiguous again. That is handle_cap_increase, an unsafe function in src/liballoc/vec_deque.rs. Its middle case moves the wrapped part to just after the old end:

} else if self.head < old_cap - self.tail {
    // B
    self.copy_nonoverlapping(old_cap, 0, self.head);
    self.head += old_cap;
    debug_assert!(self.head > self.tail);
}

That is only safe if the buffer really did grow, to at least twice its old size. reserve decides whether it did. In Rust 1.20.0:

pub fn reserve(&mut self, additional: usize) {
    let old_cap = self.cap();
    let used_cap = self.len() + 1;
    let new_cap = used_cap.checked_add(additional)
        .and_then(|needed_cap| needed_cap.checked_next_power_of_two())
        .expect("capacity overflow");

    if new_cap > self.capacity() {
        self.buf.reserve_exact(used_cap, new_cap - used_cap);
        unsafe {
            self.handle_cap_increase(old_cap);
        }
    }
}

self.capacity() is not the buffer's size: it is self.cap() - 1, the number of elements the user can store, since a ring buffer keeps one slot free. So when new_cap equals old_cap, the test new_cap > self.capacity() is still true, nothing is allocated, and handle_cap_increase runs on a buffer that did not grow. In the four-line example the buffer has 64 slots, reserve(31) asks for 64, and case B moves head to 64, one past the end, where the next push_back writes. The fix, "Fix capacity comparison in reserve", changed one line:

if new_cap > old_cap {

The PR's description: "You can otherwise end up in a situation where you don't actually resize but still call into handle_cap_increase which then corrupts head/tail."

docs.title: The same code in Pia
docs.text:
Here is handle_cap_increase in Pia. The ring's ends are a record, and buf is the buffer after the allocator has run, so len buf is the new capacity. The precondition says only what the Rust code's types say: the old capacity fits in the buffer, and both ends are inside it.

let ring = type { head : usize; tail : usize }

let handle_cap_increase (buf : inout mutable [u32]) (old_cap : usize) (r : ring) : ring
  requires 0 < old_cap && old_cap <= len buf
  requires r.tail < old_cap && r.head < old_cap
  ensures result.head < len buf && result.tail < len buf
=
  if r.tail <= r.head then r
  else if r.head < old_cap - r.tail then (
    for i in 0..r.head do buf.[old_cap + i] <- buf.[i] done;
    { head = r.head + old_cap; tail = r.tail })
  else (
    let new_tail : usize = len buf - (old_cap - r.tail) in
    for j in 0..old_cap - r.tail do buf.[new_tail + j] <- buf.[r.tail + j] done;
    { head = r.head; tail = new_tail })

The postcondition is Rust's own debug_assert!(self.head < self.cap()), which debug builds checked at run time. piac checks it, and the copy, for every input:

$ piac --verify grow.pia
...
grow.pia:10:40: failed: '+' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len buf = 18221564092244557822, old_cap = 17996384110746009596, r.head = 1441151880758558720, r.tail = 14627691589472878591, result = 19437535991504568314
grow.pia:10:48: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
grow.pia:10:27: failed: the index is within bounds
  counterexample: len buf = 16233511021939330180, old_cap = 15098680658861804673, r.head = 3530892493789154496, r.tail = 4541436590208057858, index = 17879290520661494913, length = 16233511021939330180
grow.pia:11:21: failed: '+' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len buf = 18446726485818605566, old_cap = 18446726481523507198, r.head = 4611650834055299072, r.tail = 4611668426241343489, result = 23058377315578806270
...
grow.pia:6:3: failed: the postcondition holds
  counterexample: len buf = 12677269138058477485, old_cap = 11124079053479378995, r.head = 1757134085014192249, r.tail = 9315894506577822301
9 proved, 4 failed, 0 skipped

The index failure and the postcondition failure are both buffers that did not grow enough: len buf only a little above old_cap, so case B moves head past the end and the copy writes there. (The two overflow failures are the same mistake on enormous buffers, where r.head + old_cap does not even fit in a usize.) In Rust that assumption lived in the word unsafe. In Pia it has to be written down, or the function does not compile.

docs.title: The assumption, stated
docs.text:
So say what handle_cap_increase needs: the buffer at least doubled. Then it proves, and the obligation moves to its caller, reserve. Here is reserve with Rust 1.20's comparison. The allocator either leaves the buffer alone or grows it to a power of two at least twice as big, which the second precondition says:

let ring = type { head : usize; tail : usize }

let handle_cap_increase (buf : inout mutable [u32]) (old_cap : usize) (r : ring) : ring
  requires 0 < old_cap && old_cap + old_cap <= len buf
  requires r.tail < old_cap && r.head < old_cap
  ensures result.head < len buf && result.tail < len buf
=
  if r.tail <= r.head then r
  else if r.head < old_cap - r.tail then (
    for i in 0..r.head do buf.[old_cap + i] <- buf.[i] done;
    { head = r.head + old_cap; tail = r.tail })
  else (
    let new_tail : usize = len buf - (old_cap - r.tail) in
    for j in 0..old_cap - r.tail do buf.[new_tail + j] <- buf.[r.tail + j] done;
    { head = r.head; tail = new_tail })

let reserve (buf : inout mutable [u32]) (old_cap : usize) (r : ring) : ring
  requires 0 < old_cap && r.tail < old_cap && r.head < old_cap
  requires len buf = old_cap || old_cap + old_cap <= len buf
=
  let capacity : usize = old_cap - 1 in
  if len buf > capacity then handle_cap_increase buf old_cap r else r

$ piac --verify reserve.pia
...
reserve.pia:22:30: failed: the precondition of 'handle_cap_increase' holds
  counterexample: len buf = 16583426343899006287, old_cap = 16583426343899006287, r.head = 433509266868928512, r.tail = 0
reserve.pia:22:30: proved: the precondition of 'handle_cap_increase' holds [smt]
15 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The verifier finds the bug report's case: the buffer did not grow, the comparison against capacity still passed, and the unsafe move would have run. A call reports one goal per precondition of the callee, in order, so the failure is the first one, the doubling; the second holds.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The rest of this page is the fixed program. handle_cap_increase states the growth it needs:

let ring = type { head : usize; tail : usize }

let handle_cap_increase (buf : inout mutable [u32]) (old_cap : usize) (r : ring) : ring
  requires 0 < old_cap && old_cap + old_cap <= len buf
  requires r.tail < old_cap && r.head < old_cap
  ensures result.head < len buf && result.tail < len buf
=
  if r.tail <= r.head then r
  else if r.head < old_cap - r.tail then (
    for i in 0..r.head do buf.[old_cap + i] <- buf.[i] done;
    { head = r.head + old_cap; tail = r.tail })
  else (
    let new_tail : usize = len buf - (old_cap - r.tail) in
    for j in 0..old_cap - r.tail do buf.[new_tail + j] <- buf.[r.tail + j] done;
    { head = r.head; tail = new_tail })

and reserve compares against the old capacity, as Rust's fix does:

let reserve (buf : inout mutable [u32]) (old_cap : usize) (r : ring) : ring
  requires 0 < old_cap && r.tail < old_cap && r.head < old_cap
  requires len buf = old_cap || old_cap + old_cap <= len buf
  ensures result.head < len buf && result.tail < len buf
=
  if len buf > old_cap then handle_cap_increase buf old_cap r else r

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify rust-vecdeque.pia.md
...
rust-vecdeque.pia.md:199:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
...
rust-vecdeque.pia.md:217:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]
16 proved, 0 failed, 0 skipped

Two numbers named "capacity", one of them off by one from the other, is an ordinary way to write a bug. What made it a memory-safety bug was that the function trusting the number was unsafe, so nothing checked what it trusted. In Pia, what a function trusts is its precondition, and every caller proves it.

  • rust-lang/rust#44802, "Fix capacity comparison in reserve", by Steven Fackler, merged 27 September 2017.

docs.title: zlib's gzip extra field
docs.text:
In August 2022, zlib fixed CVE-2022-37434, a heap buffer overflow in inflate(). The CVE record describes a heap-based buffer over-read or overflow in inflate.c, triggered by a large gzip header extra field. Only programs that ask for the gzip header with inflateGetHeader() are affected, but zlib is in nearly everything, so the advisories ran from Debian and Fedora to Apple and Siemens, and the record links a curl issue it tags as an exploit.

The bug is one subtraction whose operands were assumed to be in order.

This page is a literate Pia file, docs/cases/zlib-gzip-extra.pia.md. The pia blocks are the fixed program, which the test suite proves, and the other code blocks are the broken versions, each checked to fail exactly as shown.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
A gzip header can carry an extra field of up to 65535 bytes, announced by a 16-bit length. A program that wants it gives zlib a buffer, extra, of extra_max bytes, and zlib copies as much of the field as fits. The field can arrive over several calls to inflate(), so the copy runs in pieces: state->length counts the bytes still to come, and the piece goes at offset len = extra_len - state->length. Before the fix, the code in inflate.c was:

if (state->head != Z_NULL &&
    state->head->extra != Z_NULL) {
    len = state->head->extra_len - state->length;
    zmemcpy(state->head->extra + len, next,
            len + copy > state->head->extra_max ?
            state->head->extra_max - len : copy);
}

The length clamps the copy to the space left, extra_max - len. That is right while len is inside the buffer. Once the field's earlier pieces have filled it, len is past extra_max, the subtraction wraps around to a huge unsigned number, and zmemcpy writes it at extra + len, past the end of the buffer. The fix, "Fix a bug when getting a gzip header extra field with inflate()", adds the missing clause to the if: len < state->head->extra_max.

docs.title: The same shape in Pia
docs.text:
This is not zlib's code; it is the shape of the bug. have is how much of the field came before this piece, a 16-bit count like zlib's, and chunk is the piece. The copy is clamped as zlib clamped it.

let copy_extra (extra : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) (have : u16) (chunk : [u8]) : unit
  requires len chunk <= 65535
= let n : usize = if have + len chunk > len extra then len extra - have else len chunk in
  for k in 0..n do extra.[have + k] <- chunk.[k] done

piac will not compile it:

$ piac --verify extra.pia
extra.pia:3:27: proved: '+' does not overflow usize [smt]
extra.pia:3:66: failed: '-' does not overflow usize
  counterexample: len extra = 0, have = 61438, len chunk = 4101, result = -61438
extra.pia:4:32: proved: '+' does not overflow usize [smt]
extra.pia:4:40: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
extra.pia:4:20: proved: the index is within bounds [smt]
4 proved, 1 failed, 0 skipped

The counterexample is CVE-2022-37434: a buffer smaller than the part of the field already seen, so len extra - have is negative. In C that is a huge unsigned; in Pia it is a goal that does not hold, so the program never compiles. The copy's own bounds were proved: once n is the space left, every write is inside extra. The only gap is the clamp itself.

docs.title: The fix, proved
docs.text:
The fixed version is zlib's: copy only while the buffer has room, and return how far into it the field now reaches. The postcondition says that never passes its end.

let copy_extra (extra : borrowed inout mutable [u8]) (have : usize) (chunk : [u8]) : usize
  ensures result <= len extra
= if have < len extra then (
    let n : usize = if len chunk > len extra - have then len extra - have else len chunk in
    for k in 0..n do extra.[have + k] <- chunk.[k] done;
    have + n)
  else len extra

Every goal on this page is proved:

$ piac --verify zlib-gzip-extra.pia.md
...
zlib-gzip-extra.pia.md:89:3: proved: the postcondition holds [smt]

docs.title: Pia's own inflate
docs.text: Pia's decoder for deflate and zlib, Pia.Compress.Inflate and Pia.Compress.Zlib (ADR 0054, step 5), does not read gzip headers yet, but it copies in the same way: a stored block's LEN bytes, and every back-reference. Each copy is checked against the input left and the output left before it starts, and the verifier proves every byte of it is in bounds, for every input. A back-reference's distance is proved at most the bytes written so far. When gzip framing comes, its extra field will be one more copy that has to prove the same thing.
